Beyond Eyes is not a game, and it is;
it's not a graphic novel, and it is;
it's not a walking simulator it is, a very slow walk. I hope that has saved you some time, but if you are looking for a game that will change you, please join me. By their very nature video games change your world, sometimes they train you in keyboard mashing or in bad physics , always involving explosives. Beyond Eyes is a "game" that belongs in a genre of the kind of games that change your outlook. I call these contemplative games. The story starts with Rae, a young girl, around 8 or 9 by my guess, and blind.
Created by Tiger and Squid, Beyond Eyes took over 2 years of solo work until being adopted by Team17 (of Worms fame.) Published on Xbox , PC and Playstation4 in August 2015 the game is intended to create empathy, and to experiment with the act of exploring one's environment.  It's the exploring of a blind person executed in beautifully rendered watercolours, clean pastels on a muted back cloth of white which lends itself to the empathy experience that any game making it into this genre must have. You play as Rae, but soon I felt I was not playing as the young girl, but rather playing the part of the one thing glaringly missing, the parent. A parent who should be protecting what was once a promising and outgoing child but now damaged and terribly alone in the world.
[h1Empathy builds[/h1]
The sense of being alone is very strong in the game and it is personified in the appearance of a stray ginger cat whom Rae names Nani. Some people have drawn lots of conclusions from Nani's name or behaviour or meaning, but to me she is just a gentle but aloof cat. Nani appears in Raes' life just at the point when she is suddenly alone, and attempts to draw your character out of their shell by doing what cats do. The cat doubles as a kind of symbol, but Nani introduces you to the idea that a blind persons world is built using sound and smells. Which is why Nani smells like and behaves like a stray ginger cat. Wandering off and luring you through the garden gate into the exploring part of this game. The exploring mechanics introduces and uses an element that creator Sherida Halatoe capitalizes upon to emphasise the sensation of blindness. Your world as a blind person (and Raes' broken social life) is very small, and as you explore you must rebuild these 2 and at the same time overcome obstacles. You will get lost as you explore and search for Nani, and even temporarily stuck because you have to feel your way about because Raes' vision is built using sound. Sound which misleads her sometimes, resulting in some surprises and fun and leading to frustrations too. The game is played at a slow walking pace, I mean blind people can run, but the way the world fades slowly back to white after she passes, and the slow exploring speed really make you feel blind and trapped. You cannot move fast enough to rebuild the fading surroundings, and at one point it rains which literally washes away the beautiful watercolour rendered world. I started to feel a sense of urgency at this point and got totally hooked.
But even before this all, the game fell down for me. Just a few minutes into the game that will keep you busy for about 2 hours (more if you explore fully) I decided to see if closing my eyes would work. The sound-scape is really good, with chapters or stages are introduced with some brilliant piano work to compliment the mood. But the sound has holes, little things like a fountain that does not sound like a fountain if you approach it from the wrong side. Different walking surfaces are accurately rendered in the sound-scape with grass crunching giving way to the hard sound of stone and a crunch of gravel. But then the woodpecker at the bottom of the yard sounds out the same toc toc toc with no natural variations. Subtle environmental sound hardness changes and depth or echoes is another thing I expected to hear too, but to be fair I've not experienced in all but high budget games anyway. But these are made up for by the huge variety of sounds, smells and locations you must explore and the fact that Rae does not find a gun or a sword. Which would have come in handy in some of the threatening situations she finds herself in. Which is why I liked this game. I hope I've not given anything away, and helped you to decide if it's your kind of game. Creator Sherida Halatoe has added a few other elements to the game and story, but I'll leave you to find them.

Pros:
- The idea is really good. I was looking forward for it.
- The graphics are ok for me; probally they should have made the possibility for higher graphic settings.
- Also the  fire is cool. Unfortunately you can't really burn down the enemy villages; you can put them on fire but this    doesn't change a lot. Even in missions where you need to burn down things these things will respawn.
- Stroy has good basic approaches, but there could have been done much more.
- Language is interesting. But again, there would have been MUCH more potential.
- enviroment looks nice and interesting
Cons:
The game is much too easy: The beast taming is incredible easy, you can get a cave lion in the first few hours of the game, even on hardest difficulty. And if you have one you will have no trouble at all anymore, because then you have in short time ALL beasts. You can run through the country with your cat following you scaring and killing everyone you meet while collecting everything you see on the minimap, so that your village is fully upgraded after 10 hours of game play.
It has nothing to do with survival:
- no starvation etc
- healing too easy; beast revival too (even if the beast is killed in battle you can run to it, give it 3 meat and it will have full health again)
- your population can only grow (even if you see your people dying by a enemy attack. Population is only reduced by teamkills)
- too much population on close room (bascially every 10m a enemy patrol etc)
- beast taming is a joke: throw a few flesh infront of an cave bear who attacked you 2 seconds ago and be best friends with the cave bear 4 seconds later. You can even kill your animals or put them on fire; they won't hurt you at all if you tamed them once.
- you can use a owl to scout but its the only owl in the whole world
- combat is awful (melee is nothing more than a click orgy; archery is ok though). Beasts will kill everything. You kill a wolf with 1 strike? The enemy warriors of a naturally stronger tribe are murdered 3vs1 by a normal wolf. And I don't even need to say what happens if you have a saberthoot cat...
- Poisonous snakes are a joke. You got bitten by such snake? Eat 3 meats and feel fresh like bevor. Or better: You can find the snake with your x-ray before and give it a headshot with your bow).
- No weather (no storm, winter etc) which makes the life in stone age hard

Grey Goo is a simply excellent modern Real Time Strategy.
Perhaps the simplest way to describe this game is "Not-Starcraft". Whilst your units have many unique and interesting abilities, they are all passive, and so you won't be needing any hotkey mastery to use them. That's not to say managing your army is easy; keeping tabs on some of the more unique factions such as the beautifully fresh Goo can be exhilirating. But overall, this is a simpler RTS, a throwback to a simpler time.
The story mode is a lot better than I was expecting, with some lovely CG cutscenes backed up by 10/10 music by Frank Klepacki. This game is worth it for the soundtrack alone, with different themes for each of the 4 factions. Each faction has a different feel, in gameplay, design, and music, which makes them all feel exciting to play.
Cannot reccomend this highly enough to any RTS fan.

This game is easily the greatest RTS game I've ever played, and I'm extrememly unlikely to forget it.  I have absolutely adored this game since I first tried a test build at PAX South, and the final version is a masterpiece for those that can appreciate it.  The campaign is brutally challenging and fairly engaging, but the real meat and potatoes of the game is in the multiplayer, which is just fantastic.
The game operates at a speed somehwere between command and conquer and starcraft 2, little slower than starcraft, but not by much.  Because of this, unit positioning is of extreme importance.  The bulk of the game rests in microing armies of slow-moving artillery pieces, to barrage your opponent's armies, and countering for their unit-splitting measures, line of sight, and elevation.  It's really intrieguing stuff that you're sure to enjoy if you were into command and conquer in the past, but couldn't get into the imbalanced and chaotic multiplayer of the older titles.  It's CnC through the lens of starcraft, borrowing mechanics from other games all the while.
If you're at all interested, it gets featured in bundles, and goes on sale frequently.  I cannot reccomend this game more highly at all.  I fell in love with this game, and I hope you will as well.

Grim Dawn is a top-down Action Role Playing Game. I would have said Isometric if the camera wasn't adjustable though. With many similar gameplay elements to THQ's Titan Quest, the game has its own distinct art style and unique flair with plenty of modern day ARPG improvements. As I mentioned, this game is a great spiritual successor to Titan Quest and although it's a little slower paced than...say...Diablo 3, I'd say the rewards and overall character progression feels much more satisfying. At the time of this review I'd still say this game and Path of Exile are the two best ARPGs out there right now and I've played them all except an obscure few. Difficulty progression is along the lines of Diablo 2. Where you start at normal difficulty, complete it and redo the whole story again in the next difficulty tier and so until a 3rd, final playthrough. You can also enable a veteran difficulty option that makes your current playthrough even tougher.
Let's get the bad out of the way first. The multiplayer can break your character if you're not careful, unless they've fixed this since this happened to me and my friend. If the host is further along in the game than the friend you invite, it will break your friends' quests and replace them with yours, making it possible to skip everything they haven't done yet and miss important NPCs and quest items with no way to return things to normal other than starting over. But as long as you stick together with fresh toons on the same quests throughout your playthrough, you'll be fine.
The story is okay, it feels like it drags on at times but it is well told and thought out. With dozens and dozens (hundreds?) of NPCs to interact with as well as a few plot altering choices along the way, Grim Dawn manages to stay fresh up until the very end. Compound that with an amazing variety of multi-class options and skill selection mixed with all types of weapons and armor to supplement your playstyle, it's a joy to play. And hey, if you screw up your skill placement there's always an NPC that can fix that....for a price. There's also an added feature called Devotion, whose points are earned from shrines scattered throughout the game and can be used to further solidify your position as a walking weapon of mass destruction.
Speaking of NPCs there are blacksmiths that will craft items from blueprints, faction based shops that will sell you items based on how friendly you are to the different factions in the area. A respec NPC, a few different types of item merchants and even a bounty system. There are tons of sidequests to be found along the path and given by NPCs.
The music, sound effects and ambient noises mix well with the game's "grim" atmosphere. Everything fits together nicely. If you're interested I suggest looking up the Grim Dawn OST on youtube at the very least.
More content is still being added, which is great. There will be an Illusionist NPC that lets you transmogrify equipment to look like other equipment you've found, much like Diablo 3's Mystic. An expansion on the way and there's already some extra dungeons and events like the Crucible that have been added over time too. Even for the full price I still think this game is worth it. I recommend it, highly. One of my all-time favorite ARPGs.

I watched all the Game of Thrones series and have to say that I am very impressed with some of the complexities of the show.  With the first few episodes, I thought that I might have been introduced into a porno.

If you watched the series of GOT, then you should already know that "winning" isn't commonplace.  The decisions you make in the game don't really alter the effects much.  For example... if you chose to walk down path a instead of path b, you go through a similar path with a slight variance of something, but will eventually get back to the main story.  There is two decisions that will stick for a bit longer, but will eventually fade and make no impact anyway later on....  Other decisions will have an immediate, but permanent end to them. So, after I caught up with everything for GOT, my review doesn't much change.  I still think this game is a great "show."  The "game" moments are easy to get through so I can't really call it a game.
If you are not sure whether this is a game or not, stop thinking and call it a show.  That is pretty much what it is.  Yes you can make decisions, but they have little to no impact on the story.  Think of them as side quests or less than that.
I recommend this.  Think of it this way though when you buy it.  "It is a show within another show that has many similarities and guest appearances."

Are you fan of Telltale games? You won't be disappointed. Are you fan of "Game of Thrones"? You won't be disappointed. Are you fan of both? What are you even waiting for?!
I've played the first episode quite some time ago, just to check if the game will have anything to do with the TV series and how faithful to the show atmosphere it will be. I like Telltale games, though usually they do disappoint me - I will write a little more about that below - so when I started playing, I really wasn't sure what to think about all this. We play as members of Forrester family. The events from the game are linked to those from the show, though it's just a background for our protagonists and completely different story. And even though I wasn't convince to the game at first, after playing the first episode I was left with only one thought - this truly is "Game of Thrones". Not just by the title, but because of atmosphere and the way the story is unfolding. I decided to wait until all six episodes will be out and this proven to be the right decision.
Does this game have flaws? Of course. Classic Telltale flaw sadly - "important" decisions, that turn out to be absolutely meaningless. Also, there were few moments when options were not really clear - so I choose something with one intention in mind and then it turns out that the character say something in completely different tone and manner, which may be a bit annoying. Still, I think Telltale is trying to answer for criticism and give us a little bit more ending variations.
Nevertheless, it's the game worth experiencing.

Very good game. Beautiful, dense open world, great sense of progression, absolutely wonderful fluid parkour movement, a unique spin on the "day/night" cycle all featuring much more refined versions of the promising yet flawed looting and crafting systems from Dead Island.
Story is meh, mainly because there is very little in the way of passive storytelling or character/world building. Cutscenes are, thankfully, kept brief; a lot of dialogue occurs while you are actively playing the game. Actually, even though I say "thankfully" when regarding the lack of long cutscenes in the game, they are the only way the story ever truly moves forward, so those looking for a rich plot filled with nuance need to go play another game.
Honestly I couldn't tell you the slightest gist of the story off of the top of my head and had to wiki it just to tell you that you are some special-agent type guy who gets dropped into the plague-infested quarantined city of Harran to recover a stolen file for your employer, the GRE. Personally, I was far too busy gutting zombies with an electrified machete with a flametorch attached to the end while darting across shanty-town rooftops to care about the lackluster story.
For the uninitiated - imagine Fallout 3's or Skyrim's loot system, where everything is physically placed in the game world (although a lot of it is in chests or crates), but take out literally all of the "junk" loot and leave behind only the essentials such as crafting components like duct tape and nails, lockpicks, weapons and mods, health-recovering items such as food and bandages, and money.
Crafting weapons and customizing them is a fun and integral part of the game. Weapons break fairly quickly when unmodified, so you are always on the lookout for the next big upgrade or mod or crafting them from the components you find to keep you going until the later parts of the game.
Perhaps the most interesting of all features is the dynamic day/night cycle. During the day, Harran is the post-apocalyptic zombie sinkhole we've all seen before. Crashed or abandoned cars litter the streets, smoke and fire loom on the horizon, and yes, the dead walk - pretty slowly. At night Dying Light is a different beast altogether (hmm it's almost like the title of the game is trying to tell you something. . .).
Thanks to a beautifully realised lighting system, the night is disarmingly dark and foreboding. Howls echo through the night air. In and of itself the darkness is pretty terrifying, but it gets worse once you realize the shambling undead of the day have all turned into way-too-fast-to-be-okay mega-zombies with red eyes that would love nothing more than to partake in a bit of your innards by moonlight. Oh yeah, and these larger, more grotesque guys with like tendril-y mouths come out and sprint after you until you reach a safe house and are generally just asses about things. So in short, if day time is like Trump's presidential campaign 6 months ago, night time is pretty much like America a month into his first term.

I originally picked up this game after binging on all five current seasons of the Game of Thrones TV series in the span of a week, so it was something of a withdrawal purchase. But I'm a fan of other Telltale games so it seemed like an easy decision when I found this game on sale.
If I could describe the game in one word it would be: disappointing. Telltale was just out of their element here. Unlike many of their other titles, which generally steer clear of the source material's main plot, the GoT game meshes directly with the events of the HBO show. This is where the game really fails because a) so many of the tie-ins, be they character interactions or events, feel forced and unnatural, and b) it takes away a lot of the decision making drama, because you know that you can't actually accomplish anything that would interfere more than tangentially with any of the characters for the show.
Not to mention, the original characters and storylines just aren't that great. The Forresters feel like a discount Stark family, and most of the major plot points are predictable and/or wink-and-nudge references to the show. The whole experience feels more like bad fanfiction than a Telltale game.

This is a steampunk themed competitive tower defence PvP game, which is quite an intriguing genre.
You build towers on a map composed from hexagon tiles, to defend from enemy armies. Nothing special here, typical set of towers available.
You send your own armies to attack enemy in order to get battle points which allow you to unlock new units and upgrade old ones. There's more freedom here, and if you know what you're doing, this is a great place to showcase your tactical skills, especially at late stages of the game when some interesting units are available.
There's also a little resources gathering aspect to the game.
Biggest trick is to efficiently balance your defence, offence, upgrades and resources. If you screw up anywhere, you're done.
There's one huge problem with this game, which is why this is a negative review. It has pretty much no tutorial available, no single-player campaign to gradually develop your skills, UI is un-intuitive, controls are messed up, etc. All you have are bots, weakest of which will probably defeat you up to five times untill you grasp basics of the game, and after that you only have try-and-fail approach to figure out why some more sophisticated things work and some don't.
And then, playing multiplayer, game becomes over-competetive pretty fast, so unless it's inline whith your character, you will not be able to really casually enjoy the game ...
It's a pity, if devs would've spent a little more time to implement decent in-game tutorial and usable UI and controlls, game would be much more playable.

Rating 8.5/10
Overview: Real Time Strategy
The Good:
+4 very different factions, 3 for single player and an extra faction for multiplayer. Each faction presents its own unique units, structures, build order, perks.
+ Lots of graphical options
+The AI is very competent, with different difficulty options to adjust the behavior.
+The game strikes a great balance between macro and micro management. For those looking to get into a RTS game this
is a good place to start. Unlike other RTS games of this nature the focus is more about building the right type of units as opposed to managing your economy/units. If you ever played StarCraft or Warcraft you may find this game a bit easier as you don’t have to micro manage too much.
+Single player campaign has a variety of different mission with some unique ideas. Not every mission is about destroying the enemy bases.
+Skirmish mode allows you play against AI’s in a variety of different maps.
The Average:
The story and characters is where the game is a lacking. Despite the great CGI scenes, the characters are not really interesting and the story doesn’t provide any new ideas. Despite this, the story does maintain a cohesion throughout the game.
The Bad:
- Takes a long time to save and load
- Grey Goo…really…. that’s the best name you came up with for a game? Nobody in the company said this sound terrible?
- Multiplayer is dead which is really sad because this is a really great RTS game.
Conclusion:
Probably the closest thing to StarCraft you are going to see on Steam. It has a ton of interesting ideas, combines different RTS elements in one package and feels very polished. RTS genre fans should be playing this game.

This is such an amazing game, it's beyond words to explain how beautiful and jaw-dropping it is.
Half-Life 2 changed the scene for first person shooters, action games, and video games in general with its release in 2004. It was so ahead of its time that you might think it was a game from 2010 or 2011. Half-Life 2's graphics, engine, gameplay, so fresh, so new, so revolutionary.
A great campaign, so well-crafted. You have a personal feeling to the characters and the massive length of the game is long enough to keep you amazed at the game, but not long enough to keep you bored.
The Source engine truely shows what an amazing engine it is to today's standards, and the best game its true power is shown in is Half-Life 2. From the interactive characters and buttons, the awesome graphics and fluid gameplay, the Source engine's biggest capabilities are not shown off in Team Fortress 2, Left 4 Dead, or Counter-Strike, but in Half-Life 2.
Half-Life 2 changed the standards for games today. Its graphics would be acceptable today and so would the gameplay. Half-Life 2 as a game is better than most AAA games that release on the market nowadays.
Should you buy Half-Life 2? YES, YOU SHOULD. It is a cheap game with not-very demanding requirements of a graphics card, dynamic gameplay and interactions, great voice acting and characters, and jaw-dropping cinematic moments. So yes, BUY THIS GAME. YOU BETTER GET THAT STEAM WALLET READY FOR THAT NEXT SALE, BECAUSE THIS WILL BE THE FIRST THING YOU BUY. IT WILL.

The matchmaking system works great and there is never a problem finding people to play with. Dull characters, infuriating arbitrary events, and a cliff hanger ending are a few of the reasons why you should skip Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series.
As you can tell by the above statement, I don't think highly of this game.  In fact, I think it's one of the worst Telltale point and click adventure games.  I know that is harsh, so let me explain.
To start off, a majority of the characters in this game are dull and generic. This is mainly caused by two factors.  First, throughout the game you are usually switching between 3 to 4 player characters in any given episode. This overly board focus results in a lack of depth and detail for the main and supporting cast. You'll learn people's names and role in the game, but beyond that, there isn't much to any of them.  Personally, I never found myself emotional connecting with any of the characters, since they all felt underdeveloped.  The second factor is that named characters from the television show are constantly showing up in the game.  Which sounds cool in theory, except for the fact that it follows it source matter to the letter. Nothing you do with any of the named characters matters, since what happens to them and what they are planning to do has already occurred on the TV show. So whenever they show up in the game you know that you're about to either have something horrible happen to your characters that you can't do anything about, or you're about to hear one of them give you a lecture on something. Dull and generic characters are bad for any game, but in an story driven game such as this one, they ruin it.
The next problem with this game are its arbitrary events, as mention above, this game follows the TV show and uses the events and themes from it. This results in large portions of your choices being undermined by pre-existing story lines or the writers' desire to make it more like the TV show. Am not trying to imply that your choices would otherwise matter if there wasn't source material, since nearly all Telltale games are design so that only a handful of your choices affect anything at all.  More of that the story that you are trying to tell yourself through the choices you make for the characters, is constantly falling apart because the game want to tell you a different story.  With most other Telltale games, it feels like you are guiding the main character(s) and making them into what you want them to be.  However, with this one, I often felt like I was being told a story about characters which results in the feeling that I didn't have control over them or the game at all.  This lack of control and the feeling that events were constantly happening to me, and not a result from me, made me not care about a majority of the cast. And when I say I didn't care about them, I mean that I didn't see them as characters I wanted to spend any time with. After a few episode I started to intentional choose harmful options and failing quick time events, in order to see what would happen.  I felt that I had such little control over what was happening, that I actively started to rebel against the game's design, and well... that is a horrible mark against a game, when a player decide that trying to break a game is more fun than playing it.
Lastly, this game has a cliff hanger ending. I know developers of well... everything like books, tv, or video games in this case, want to serialize their products in order to make more money, but to have a cliff hanger ending in a episodic game feel like a sin. It's one thing to leave the door open for more adventures, but it's a whole different beast to leave the main story unresolved.  And that is what this game does. You have two overarching quests in this game, and by the end, you are further from one than you were at the start, and the other one results in a lot of questions and few unsatisfactory answer.
Overall, this game is bad. I would say that if you're into Game of Thrones (the tv series) than you might like this, but you would have to be really, into it. For everyone else, looking for a good point and click adventure game, I strongly recommend you skip this title.

Excellent city builder with intrinsic flaws. I love this game, it is a very good city builder sim.
A lot of building types compliment and/or require other buildings, so there is a realistic synergy to how to plan and build a city. For instance you can mine ores and simply sell it. Or you could build factories to refine it and make items out of them and sell those. Most commercial building types have complimentary building types.
It's a very layered game, but easy enough to get into, for novice or experienced city sim player alike.
Downside is that your city will only last for a certain amount of years, but even with that there's usually ample time to develop and play one, and it has a lot of scenario's to play through as well as the ability to create your own scenario's. You can go as long as you want after a scenario ends but eventually cities become very unwieldy.
Overall, a very enjoyable city building sim that touches all the bases; resource management, population, political, commerce and trade, natural disasters. It's the whole package, just served up in nice big scenario's to play through. with lots of inexpensive DLC's introducing new building types and scenario's to experiment with. And if you don't like any of those, create your own scenario with your own set of unique goals.

A simple but deep fighting game. There are only a few attacks and they take only single button presses to use, unlike the complex extended combos of more traditional fighters. However, manipulating ball physics, setting up bunt and jump combos, the need for impeccable timing and special moves to switch it up make for a satisfying game with a high skill ceiling.
It also packs an amazing soundtrack, but you will probably get bored of it pretty quick and start substituting your own music because there aren't many tracks and the constant repeats can get dull. Similarly the characters are well voiced but there are only a few lines for each. The visual style is retro, colorful and compelling, and very Jet Set Radio.
I got it cheap as part of a humble bundle, but I wouldn't have been cheesed if I had paid full price for this game. A little light on content (there are only 6 characters and the player vs ai challenge mode is skimpy), but the game is fun enough to pull through regardless.

To clarify what is happening here, is that the person is buying items from the cash shop with real world money, to melt them down to allow him to easily reach the end game last tier of gear with little no risk involved. [/edit]
The biggest point of contention I have for this game. Is the cash shop, I hold the opinion that this game is p2w and you MUST pay more than the base price (which is low) to be able to play on the same level as other people who choose to pay. While some will say that it’s okay you only need to invest £20 maybe £40 into the cash shop to ensure that you can grind efficiently. While this is true someone who can and will put hundreds of pounds into the game WILL ALWAYS have an advantage over you.
Whether that is more storage faeries than you can imagine to basically allow them to stay and grind on something for as long as they want, artisan memories to allow them cheaper and faster repair costs allowing them to upgrade their gear faster than a normal player and the BIGGEST slap in the face that there is cosmetic items give you real in game bonuses, I can't even fathom what they were thinking when they did this but it is a complete joke, Along with pets being completely and utterly needed if you want to be able to farm mobs AT ALL without blowing your brains out makes this game one of but not the worst offenders of P2W currently on the market.
And of course the hidden cost of £20 a month to pay for value packs. But wait you can buy them on the marketplace right? Time to rant about that now!!!
The marketplace (auction house/player to player trading) is an ineffectual and awkward beast that only causes players misery and hatred of the game. I can tell you it has already almost made me quit the game when I first wanted to get something from the marketplace, it is such a bad system of trading people will go out of their way to avoid it and to craft and enhance everything they need.
How it works. There is no free trade or player set prices, the prices are set by the developers, Kakao Games you cannot go outside of the set max and min prices, the marketplace also takes a 30% cut as a money sink to handle inflation, which is understandable. So when you want to sell something even if you are the only person to ever have that item and it is so rare it hasn't even been seen before? You can only set the price of this rare object of desire by kakao's price.
Now if you want to BUY something from the marketplace, god help you if it is a high demand item. Though if it is not the only problem you need to worry about is if someone registers another of the item on the marketplace for a cheaper price then you need to wait an arbitrary amount of time before you can buy the cheapest item.
Now if its a high demand item? You have the same chance at being run over or winning the actual lottery. You select bid and then through some sort of magical process of RNG a winner is decided who wins the item, the winner must then click on the bidding result of the item and receive it. There is no other way to get a high demand item. If the winner of said lottery doesn't click it on time then it will go to the buy phase where it is simply who can click the buy button the fastest which favours the people closer to the server and with a better connection.
This is the weakest part of the game, I can deal with the p2w but this might break me. Though that was more of a rant than reviewing the game, I have become zen at the fact of overcoming this frustrating system and now ENJOY the fact I can watch my fishing boat being won by another player for the 3rd week in a row constantly refreshing and spam clicking for it.
There is none. Node wars is the only thing you are working towards gear wise, and that ends up being a laggy zerg from my understanding with individual player skill being an afterthought, as long as you can survive for more than 10 seconds against the wizard/witch meta you can help attack a tower for 5 minutes until either side zergs the hardest.
But enough of that, that's for the next part.
Your endgame, reaching level 61 finally after weeks of grinding mobs and nothing else to help you get to that sweet level. You are rewarded with... wealth grinding? zerg pvp? friendly duels to perfect your cc combo oneshot? I understand that this isn't a typical MMO and dungeons and raids aren't something the developers want to introduce, I've seen some argument that adding dungeons or raids turns the game into a gear treadmil of farming, but then what are world bosses but them in zerg format?
You are rewarded with nothing for attaining a high level and gearscore and the treadmil of Pri to Tri then attempt TET and going back to pri is just something to prolong the "gear treadmil". There is simply no reason to grind it out when you are going to be doing the same things that you do at level 61 than what you were doing at 56. Grinding Sausans because they cannot figure out how to balance grind spots.
The PVP aspect of the game is probably the strongest part, but it falls so flat on its face. Everything at the end game that includes PVP is a complete zerg. Personal skill matters so little, the only thing that guilds look for is having a high enough gear score to survive the current wizard/witch meta we're in or if you're a witch or wizard. This is both for Red Battleground (Which is completely unneeded and dumb imo) and Node Wars. While the Battle Arena functions more of a FFA place for friends and guildies to practice rather than anything competative.
Small scale PVP arenas are coming in the next major update patch Kamasylvia Part 1, hopefully this solves the large scale PVP problem.

A short, beautiful experience, might actually suit Parents and small children as an alternative to story books?

I usually don't write reviews after only playing for a half hour. I tend to wait until I've either finished the game or played a large enough portion before getting bored with it to come to a valid conclusion.
What I've seen of Lethal League so far indicates that it's a supremely addictive game. Simple mechanics are coupled with a very high skill ceiling and lots of challenge, which over the course of each match escalates to ludicrous heights. Each character has a very different set of abilities beyond simply tossing the ball around and the combination of a variety of characters make on-the-fly strategizing against them very entertaining. Overall I'd give Lethal League a big recommendation on that front.
However, the connection issues are what absolutely kill this game for me at the moment. Every other match doesn't load properly and I've had plenty of disconnects even with players in my own region. Mind you that I have a 15MB/s (that's Megabyte, not Megabit) connection where my PC is connected via Ethernet cable and not Wi-Fi, so my connection is about as solid as you can get, and yet it still fails around 50% of the time. I won't cry about connection times since I realize that they're mostly down to the amount of active players, but once a connection is established, it's amazing how bad the game manages to function. Not to mention that when the game does actually hang up and never starts the next match, you can't simply get out again by pressing Escape or any other keys. You have to terminate the application with Alt+F4 every single time this happens, and it can get very annoying.
I was fortunate enough to have bought the game with the recent Humble Monthly, so it cost me around $1.2, or 90% less than what's asked for here on Steam, which is why I'll keep the game and give it a mild pass in order to see if the issues get resolved in the future. But for the record, had I paid full price, I'd have refunded this broken mess immediately. Which is unfortunate, a game with solid mechanics and the potential for hours of fun is shot in the kneecaps by terrible connection issues.
If the issues get resolved, I will edit this review to reflect any future changes made here.

This is an amazing game. One of the best new RTS games to come out since the Dawn of War series. Incredibly well made; the production values are top-notch. The voice acting, the graphics, the models, and the sound are all incredibly well done. The writing is very solid - telling a familiar sci-fi cautionary tale with an excellent twist.
The gameplay is smooth and well thought out. The only complaint I can recall is that the mini-map isn't as full-featured as I expect from a modern RTS. You can't seem to (or at least, I never could) click on the mimi-map to instantly move your camera to that location. But these misses were minor, few, and far between.
By far my favorite part of the game was the titular faction. The Grey Goo is the most innovative RTS concept I've ever seen. I dare say that they perform the "Zerg motif" better than the Zerg do - and before you declare me a blasphemer, let me explain. Part of the Zerg flavor was always that they arrive at a planet. murder a bunch of living things, and then use that biomass to increase their own numbers. Sort of like a sci-fi version of a necromancer: your fallen enemies increase your strength.
And that was awesome. But that flavor rarely found its way into the mechanics, really. Sure, you could infest a Terran HQ to produce an infested marine. But that was it. For the vast majority of the time, you harvested crystals and vespene, just like everyone else. And you spawned units out of buildings (albeit gooey buildings) just like everyone else. Not a lot of the "murdering for biomass" flavor in there.
But the Grey Goo take that concept to its logical conclusion in the mechanics. You have only one production "building" - the mother goo. It can roam around looking for suitable mass to absorb, but it is also a dangerous unit in its own right. It can traverse any terrain, and it can occupy the same space as enemy units and buildings, damaging them and healing itself while it does so. And its health is the only resource the goo needs. It spends goo (its health) to spawn specialized constructions. Mechanisms made from goo that perform specialized tasks (like murdering things from far away). Then, once the murdering is done, the enemy becomes goo and heals the mother goo. It's a perfect implementation of the "murdering for mass" flavor that the Zerg made us fall in love with.
But the Grey Goo is just one part of this game that makes it so excellent.
All in all, a highly recommended game.

At last a game based on the eastern front, which is a nice change to all of those set on the western front. Until recently when I watched an excellent, Russian made documentary series called 'Soviet Storm' on YouTube, I didn't know hardly anything about this theatre of war, apart from the key elements of the conflict. The Soviets lost over 25 million soldiers and civilians in this conflict - more than all the Allies put together!!
The brutality and cruelty of this conflict, which Hitler himself called "a war of annihilation," was unsurpassed. The atrocities commited by both sides, initially by the Germans, but in their bloodlust for revenge, also perpetrated by the Soviets, it highlighted perfectly the cruelty mankind is capable of inflicting on itself.
Does this game capture the cruelty and brutality of the conflict? No. It attempts to at certain parts with cut scenes, but these are very cliched and amateurish. An early example is the depiction of Soviet leader Stalin's order to open fire on their own men if caught retreating. Although done badly, it does highlight the reality that Stalin, just like Hitler, was perfectly prepared to use his own men as mere 'cannon fodder' when he thought it necessary. It also shows how early on in the conflict when supplies were low, many soviet soldiers were sent to the front without any kind of weapon and another cutscene shows soldiers asking for a weapon before being told to "go find one," usually from a fallen comrade.
So although I think the game doesn't capture the cruelty of that particular theatre of war, it's still a well made RTS, which Relic ,the developer, excels in. It offers more of the same kind of gameplay seen in it's predecessor, 'Company Of Heroes' and it's expansions.
There are a few negatives about this title that unfortunately, now seems to be becoming the norm - unnecessary and expensive DLC. I mean £2.38 for a pack of skins (of which there are many different kinds to buy)! And that's in the Steam Xmas Sale otherwise it would be £4.77! For Skins! Plus there's loads more to pay extra for, like different commanders, doctrines, etc, etc. To me, this just treats customers with contempt and they wonder why people pirate the game!
Anyway, despite all these negatives, I do actually like the game. It's a well honed RTS done by one of the masters of the RTS genre, Relic Entertainment. If you liked the previous Company Of Heroes, then you will definitely enjoy this one too.
Personally, I'm not going to waste my money on DLC like different skins for tanks for example. I'll stick with what I consider to be relevant and substantial DLC like the Stalingrad campaign (while it's at sale price anyway).
So although with reservations, I do recommend this to any RTS fan.

Tower Wars pits you against an AI as you are trying to conquer each other's HQ, on a hex battlefield, where you have to build defense towers to stop the enemy units, while improve the mines to get more resources to fund your factories, upgrade your units, and eventually produce enough units to conquer the enemy HQ.
The game uses a whimsical / comical / steampunk look for its units, which hides a serious RTS underneath.
There is a serious tower defense game (where you have to build towers to "manage" the enemy horde by making them walk through your field of fire. And yes, you can improve the towers too. It's a regular tower defense game.
There is resource management in that you have to control the mines to ensure you have proper flow of resources to fuel your tower building as well as unit making and unit improvement research. You mainly do this by making sure the mines are controlled by towers, and improved to ensure they have good throughput.
Then you need to research units, each of which have a different use against certain types of enemy towers. Some are fast but low armor, some are juggernauts that move slowly, some heal, some shield, etc. And add them, in the right order, to yoru build queue, and hopefully, push the enemy back enough to take out his HQ.
There are many different maps and different AI to keep you busy. If you can take the art style, this game can be interesting.

Tropico 4 is a sim game where you control an island in the carribean. As the supreme ruler, you have power over everything. But don't take this to mean you can do whatever you want. You have to manage relations with the various factions on the island. If you treat them badly, they will make your life difficult. Some may even join the rebels and contend militarily for power. You must do this while keeping funds up and trying to pad your offshore bank account as much as possible.
The game has a robust campaign that's relatively fun to play through. Sandbox is ok, I mainly use it for fooling around and trying self-imposed goals. There are a massive amount of user created challenges. Those are where the true fun comes in. But these things can become boring after time.
It has some DLC. The best bang for your buck would come from Modern Times. Modern Times adds a ton of buildings and edicts. It also has it's own campaigns. The other DLCs are ok, but they don't really warrant the $5 price point. They add traits for your president, a special building, a mission, and some vanity items. Get them on sale.
In all, I would reccommend this for anyone who enjoys sim games and some that don't. It is much easier to get into than some of the others (I'm looking at you Cities XL)
Edit: The soundtrack is also fabulous. Very nice island themed music

This is by far the greatest of what I would put into the Blockbuster category of video games alongside Metro Last Light, Mass Effect, and Fallout New Vegas. When people say, "Did you ever play Dying Light?" you do not just answer,"Yes". You look right through that man's skull and you say, "Harran? Yeah, I've been there."
The opening scene (the game being more akin to a film than a video game) places you directly into a world wide crisis of zombial proportions, there is an overwhelming sense of dread and importance. You are there for a reason bigger than yourself. As a member of the Global Relief Effort, it's your job to get in there and track down the man that will later become your nemesis. While hiding your identity from the very people you must fight to protect, you fall in love with a cagefighter as the graying ethics of the organization you are sworn to are crushed underneith your instinctual allegiance to humanity and the American bravado that paints it all in red white and blue; eagle screech, F-15 fly-by, the New England Patriots! If your panties aren't wet already then I'll just have to keep going til they are because I promised you that much the last time we spoke on the phone and I hung up on you too soon.
There is a day/night cycle that will make you dread the dying of the light. When the sun goes down the monsters come out. I promise you will get so absorbed into this game for at least the first couple weeks that it will ruin your relationships with other human beings. Remember to drink plenty of fluids and get enough rest. You need to pace yourself because even though your body is screaming for the bed your mind will always be in Harran with 'Kiss Me Now Sex Face' Jade and 'Whisper to Me Again in that Voice of Yours' Brecken. "Let me out there! I gotta get that last drop before Rais' crew! There are people starving here in the tower!" that's you. That's what you'll be saying if you get this game. 10/10, would bang again.
There is in here struck the most perfect of balances between direction and open world. While you may go off a pillaging there will always be that nagging sense of dread helped on by the end of the world ambience and an erie atmosphere of a once lively city now gone dead. The storyline will keep you going on the main road, the side missions will keep you wandering down alleyways and into the gutters of eastern mediterranean slums. When people ask you for help, there is an instant sense of empathy for people who outwardly look and act just like human beings. That may sound obvious but very few games get this right which brings me to my next point. The voice acting is probably the best I have ever seen. You will realize just how far ahead the voice acting in this game is when you try playing any other game afterwards. You'll never be the same.

The marketplace (auction house/player to player trading) is an ineffectual and awkward beast that only causes players misery and hatred of the game. I can tell you it has already almost made me quit the game when I first wanted to get something from the marketplace, it is such a bad system of trading people will go out of their way to avoid it and to craft and enhance everything they need.
How it works. There is no free trade or player set prices, the prices are set by the developers, Kakao Games you cannot go outside of the set max and min prices, the marketplace also takes a 30% cut as a money sink to handle inflation, which is understandable. So when you want to sell something even if you are the only person to ever have that item and it is so rare it hasn't even been seen before? You can only set the price of this rare object of desire by kakao's price.
Now if you want to BUY something from the marketplace, god help you if it is a high demand item. Though if it is not the only problem you need to worry about is if someone registers another of the item on the marketplace for a cheaper price then you need to wait an arbitrary amount of time before you can buy the cheapest item.
Now if its a high demand item? You have the same chance at being run over or winning the actual lottery. You select bid and then through some sort of magical process of RNG a winner is decided who wins the item, the winner must then click on the bidding result of the item and receive it. There is no other way to get a high demand item. If the winner of said lottery doesn't click it on time then it will go to the buy phase where it is simply who can click the buy button the fastest which favours the people closer to the server and with a better connection.
This is the weakest part of the game, I can deal with the p2w but this might break me. Though that was more of a rant than reviewing the game, I have become zen at the fact of overcoming this frustrating system and now ENJOY the fact I can watch my fishing boat being won by another player for the 3rd week in a row constantly refreshing and spam clicking for it.

This was a charming little tale about a blind girl on an adventure to find her only friend, an orange tabby. Along the way, she ends up meeting an actual human girl, and they become friends.
...and that is pretty much all there is to this tale besides the message to move on and live your life despite sad and/or tragic events that change the path you are on.
The graphics themselves were beautiful watercolor art which opened up as you encounter and experience things.
The controls were simple. You basically just walk around interacting with a few items along the way.
There are 10 achievements, which I personally wont bother trying to complete. Why? Because you slow walk everywhere, and I just dont have the patience to ever play this game again. It was a nice experience, and I get that you walk slowly because you are blind, but that also doesn't make for an amazing experience repeated to try and find everything.
Overall, I liked the game, but I also found it to be a tad boring as well. Still, the game basically weighed in at about two hours, so just at the point where I was starting to get tired of it, I reached the end. Perfect length for this game.
As much as there are some negatives regarding pacing though, I thought the journey itself was worth taking. I'd give it 7 butterflies floating around a path of enlightenment out of 10 possible.

Beyond Eyes is a third person, story rich adventure game developed by Tiger and Squid. This game tells a story of a blind girl that befriends a ginger cat in her garden, but one day the cat leaves and does not return. When her friend does not return she sets out on a journey to find the cat discovering the world around her on the way.
What I liked about the game was the emotional story that captured me from the start right to the finish. The music complemented the emotion in the game and added a lot to the whole experience while not being too intrusive. The painting-like art style really worked well with the discovery mechanic, they both complemented each other greatly. I also loved that the game awarded you with achievements and small cut-scenes for exploring, it really gives you that extra push to go and explore.
Some things wherent so great tho and made the expirance of the game some what worse. The walking speed for example was allright while exploring new areas, but as walking through areas allready explored the speed seemed way to slow and was quite painfull. While the music was great there was a noticible lack of it while exploring, I would have like to seen the music being used a bit more.
Over all this game is great! I think it potrays being blind very well and the story is well thought out and presented. The whole thing comes together with the exploration mechanics. I reccomend picking up the game on a sale as it is quite short and the price of £9.99 is quite steep.(Finished with all achivements in 2.5 hours)

This is not an actual review of the game as I haven't played enough of it; I just want to report my experience regarding the game's performance.
I installed the game on 3 computers. My main rig, AMD FX-8350, 16Gb RAM, SSD, GTX 980, running the game on ultra settings, 1440p; my media PC, AMD FX-6300, 8Gb RAM, HDD, GTX 770, high settings, 1080p; and my laptop, i7-4710HQ, 16Gb RAM, HDD, GTX 860M, medium-high settings, 1080p.
I didn't get any error messages nor crashes on any of my systems. Performance is overall playable: got 50-60 FPS on my main and media PCs, and 40-50 on my laptop. The framerate does drop to 30 sometimes for no apparent reason, but it's occasional and thankfully doesn't last more than 3-4 seconds.
Is the game well-optimized? Nope. Far Cry 4 runs at a better framerate, has better-looking graphics and doesn't hiccup as much as this one. But Primal's performance, while not great, is not horrible. All things considered, it's very playable.
So, should you buy this game? Well,  I only gave a positive recommendation because it worked for me and I personally don't mind the performance issues all that much.  It's a bit of a roll of the dice when it comes to getting the errors, but either I got very lucky (game worked on 3 very different systems) or chances are most people won't get them. Now, if you're not in a hurry you can always wait a month or two until everything is smoothed out (I'd wait until the Summer Sale in that case). But if you REALLY want to play it now, give it a try, my guess is you probably won't struggle a lot with it. And if you do, thankfully you can always ask for a refund.

FTL is an interesting mix of hands-on spaceship management sim (such as Star Command), and event-chain, decision-based roguelike (such as the classic Oregon Trail). The first thing you'll notice when you jump into FTL is the main theme: a quirky bit-trip lullaby that is guaranteed to make you nostaligic every time you boot the game from hereon out. The next thing you pick up on? FTL is nails. The first two battles you face, you'll go 'oh wow that was easy,' and then BOOM you make one wrong decision BOOM you respond wrongly, and then BOOM... you're dead. It will make you pull your hair out with rageand hatred, then jump back in like a deprivation-suffering crack addict.
If that doesn't sound like your cup of tea, it's probably your cup of coffee- you WILL love this game. It's impossible not to.

The last Petroglyph RTS I played was Empire at War... or I should say, I STILL play it. It's an incredible game, and so I was glad to be able to try out their latest offering in the genre.
Grey Goo is graphically impressive and intensive, and has some interesting features including 3 (4 with DLCs) very distinct factions. They have very independent play styles and technologies, e.g. the Goo are very offensively geared and need to secure a ton of resource points to build their army whereas the Beta are strongly defensively oriented with fortifiable walls. Humans and Beta can operate with relatively few resource points and protect them a lot better, plus have air units. However, literally every single Goo unit can be used in combat, including their 'bases' which are mobile.
The graphics and sound (especially music) are very well done, though on older systems expect a bit of lag and long load times even on low quality.
Aside from the 3 factions, you have a pretty typical RTS setup. There is one resource- catalyst- which is harvested from vents in the ground. There is research and upgrades. All sides have cheap infantry units, tanks, anti-air, and a 'super' unit that is ridiculously expensive, slow to build, and devastatingly powerful. The general rock-paper-scissors concept does apply. The main draw of Gray Goo is a pretty well-done campaign and the very different way the factions play. They are distinctive enough and interesting enough that it's fun trying them all out and getting good with them.

Grey Goo is a blander, kind of budget Starcraft. It has innovative base building and unit mechanics between it's three (initial) very diverse factions and much of the polish, too, with great CGI cinematics and a a raft of relatively 'hard' (i.e. plausible) sci-fi pretensions. But gameplay just lacks excitement somehow.
It has novelty, but in the context of obvious derivative echos: the aliens are junky, lower tech (like the Terrans), with South African sounding accents and are more sympathetic that the human faction, with a colder, clinical aesthetic, touting smoothly curved hovering units (echoing the Protos). Their structures need unbroken adjacent conduit connection to the core base building to operate, which is interestingly different.
The titular Goo would be the obvious Zerg swarm stand in. They're unique in having no base structures to build, all splitting off bigger mother blobs that harvest resources directly.
But as a core concept they're emblematic of the game's lack of pizazz. Fundamentally problematic to work with artistically: typically, the 'grey goo' concept involves out-of-control nano-bots that consume all matter around them, reducing entire planets to a mush of their replicas. Nightmarish and unstoppable.
But of course, to fit the RTS genre there needs to be units of some kind to click on and control. So the game goes half way and has undulating grey pancake things and specialised bug-eyed offspring for most offense unit that look kind of arbitrary and ridiculous. It all feels a little too naff, that they can't munch on trees and scenery, or even enemy units all the much, since the game has to be somewhat balanced and playable.
The story ark was ok, but predictable and uninspiring for me as a hard sci-fi aficionado. They make use of a fair bit of real world terminology (e.g. Von Neumann probes, etc), as well as genre tropes, which is cool to get it out there, but kind of trite.
I can't comment on multi-player, which I didn't really try, with no friends owning the game to play with and little enthusiasm after the single player.
By the time I'd completed the main campaign and Emergence DLC I was just glad I'd made it to the end! I struggled a lot with the final missions, not really in a fun way. Although they were presumably meant to crescendo, I had to check out multiple YouTube videos, use save games prodigiously and really take a lot of time sitting around to make sure my Goo forces were built up to max strength before attacking, etc.
Overall, if you're an RTS fan then you could do worst than grabbing this while it's on sale. Far more artistic value than Ashes of the Singularity, for example, and slightly better money's worth, with an extra DLC mission and forth faction added on for free earlier this year. So, check it out, why not. :-)

Speaking of annoying, forget the "Oros is a dangerous place where you aren't on top of the food chain"-thing, frequent animal attacks become a huge thorn in your side after a while.
All in all, I think that this game is nice (if a bit overpriced). It is a fresh idea, which I like, from the Proto-Indo-European language, to the Beast taming, to exploring the huge map. Just like the titular saga Game of Thrones follows the lives of several different characters tied to House Forrester in their efforts to save themselves and their lands after the events that have affected House Stark.
If you have played other graphics adventures by Telltale then you know what to expect in terms of gameplay and, as far as story and narrative go, the game is yet another pretty good entry despite a few blemishes.
-manages to capture the essence of the Game of Thrones saga with its web of lies, betrayals, violence and death
-excellent soundtrack
-great voice acting, you also get the actors from the tv series voicing their characters
-good story featuring quite a few sudden twists, a good amount of mysteries and an overall strong momentum to keep you engaged
-a good array of characters (both from the saga and newly created), they all have a nice amount of depth and it's easy to get attached thus caring for their fate
-while it features the usual quicktime events you find in Telltale games the combat is more satisfying due to the level of violence and gore involved
-nice length, it'll take you at least 12 hours to finish it
-as usual in Telltale games your choices generally create nuances in the narrative rather than a whole new path, I personally don't mind much as I'm more interested in the narrative itself and the story I end up with rather than what'd have been but I understand how others may feel it to be a poor system
-the ending chapter is a mixed bag, on one hand it does provide a good and emotional closure to several story arcs but it also lets some plot points unresolved or at least unclear and could be regarded a bit too much as on the cliffhanger-ish side
-if you're not a fan of the saga you might miss a bit of backstory as the game begins without bothering to explain who's who, who the other houses are etc...there's a small codex dedicated to the Forrester but the game assumes you already know much about the world of Westeros
-the art style chosen for the game is so-so as there's a weird effect that makes certain textures appear quite "fuzzy", said effect also tends to bleed on the sides of objects and characters making them appear fuzzy or jagged: reading up online it'd resemble an oil painting but, while it works well on certain vistas, it's simply too distracting or weird most of the time
-a few clipping problems can sometimes be noticed on character models
-still a few bugs here and there, I had one ctd while loading a save and, most of the time, had to force quit the process after exiting the game as it'd keep running in the background
I quite enjoyed my time with the game as its story is quite good for all the story arcs you'll be facing, the characters tied to said stories are also equally good and'd feel right at home even in the original novels. The world of Westeros has been represented well both in its look and its spirit: the game takes you in various places so you'll be seeeing quite a bit of land from the deep south to the dangerous territories past the wall.
Gameplay-wise it's a pretty standard Telltale game with usually four choices in dialogues, a few very important dual choices and some fights here and there: as mentioned above I found the fights to be a bit better than usual since they look more realistic and involve the right amount of violence to be on par with the saga.
As for its blemishes, well, the new art style looks weird for the most part and I honestly found it distracting, it looks even worse in screenshots or when the fuzzy oil effects bleed on borders or character faces: thankfully it's a bit better when things move and there's a few vistas used to introduce chapters that are truly nice. The last chapter is also a bit weak in some aspects, as mentioned above.
All things considered Game of Thrones is a good game and, while it's not Telltale's best adventure ever, it's a good and lengthy journey that fans of the saga will easily enjoy and a full thumbs up from me.

This is by far the greatest of what I would put into the Blockbuster category of video games alongside Metro Last Light, Mass Effect, and Fallout New Vegas. When people say, "Did you ever play Dying Light?" you do not just answer,"Yes". You look right through that man's skull and you say, "Harran? Yeah, I've been there."
The opening scene (the game being more akin to a film than a video game) places you directly into a world wide crisis of zombial proportions, there is an overwhelming sense of dread and importance. You are there for a reason bigger than yourself. As a member of the Global Relief Effort, it's your job to get in there and track down the man that will later become your nemesis. While hiding your identity from the very people you must fight to protect, you fall in love with a cagefighter as the graying ethics of the organization you are sworn to are crushed underneith your instinctual allegiance to humanity and the American bravado that paints it all in red white and blue; eagle screech, F-15 fly-by, the New England Patriots! If your panties aren't wet already then I'll just have to keep going til they are because I promised you that much the last time we spoke on the phone and I hung up on you too soon.
There is a day/night cycle that will make you dread the dying of the light. When the sun goes down the monsters come out. I haven't been this scared of something this terrifying since I was a little girl. While you may go off a pillaging there will always be that nagging sense of dread helped on by the end of the world ambience and an erie atmosphere of a once lively city now gone dead. The storyline will keep you going on the main road, the side missions will keep you wandering down alleyways and into the gutters of eastern mediterranean slums. When people ask you for help, there is an instant sense of empathy for people who outwardly look and act just like human beings. That may sound obvious but very few games get this right which brings me to my next point. The voice acting is probably the best I have ever seen. You will realize just how far ahead the voice acting in this game is when you try playing any other game afterwards. You'll never be the same.

RTS is not my favorite genre of game but I must say that Grey Goo is one of the most-liked and most-played games I own. I am of the opinion that a good story is what ultimately makes or breaks a game for me, and this one is a superb sci-fi that seems believable enough in its depiction of science and the advance of technology to maintain my suspension of disbelief throughout the game. Adding to that was the quality of the cinematic graphics, which were so life-like for the human characters in particular that at first I thought they'd been filmed with live actors.
As for the gameplay itself I appreciate how they designed each faction to cater to a particular tactical bent, and yet also be sufficiently adaptable for tactical styles to be overlapped in each faction. One feature in particular that I appreciate, that has been absent in other RTS games I have played, is the ability to select all of one type of selected unit at a time, so that you don't have to micro-manage your units, like I've had to do in games like Command and Conquer. It requires a lot of processing power though to render all of gameplay in great detail, more than my computer can provide without lagging, but even on its lowest settings it is still very detailed and beautiful, and runs at a decent speed.
My only real complaint at this time is that the fourth and final faction, the Shroud, does not seem to have been sufficiently developed for balanced gameplay, such that, for the main antagonists of the story, they are not difficult to beat in skirmishes, but I assume further fine tuning is to come.
Overall, I find it to be a very respectable RTS with an engaging backstory that I eagerly await the conclusion of.

And the title for my most surprisingly fun game of the year goes to... Block N Load!!
I saw that this game was now free to play on steam after many months of ridicule towards both the game itself and it's unappealing £15 price tag and so, given my laptops inability to render any graphics more advanced than that of minecraft, I decided to give it a go. And boy was I wrong to mock it. This game takes the fun strategic multiplayer of csgo, gives it a dash of TF2 and smothers it in a minecraft art style and building system, creating a rather odd frankenstein's monster which actually plays surprisingly well.
The main gamemode in Block N Load is a 'defend the objective' mission in which you must build defences around one or more cubes to prevent the enemy team doing melee damage to it, and attacking the enemies cube until either objective loses all of it's health and explodes. Simple enough. But through playing the game, I discovered it's extremely strategic and team based undertones which sets Block N Load apart from other generic shooters. For example, the multiple classes of characters, that can be unlocked through either in game cash or real money, offer a unique play style for either attacking the enemy or defending your own cube. They all feature different items and blocks to place to both remain balanced and also fill in their specific role.
You may have noticed that I mentioned the purchase of characters through real money. Although I, along with many people on the internet, hate microtransactions this game manages to implement them in a way that doesn't really give people who pay a large advantage. They do this by making the heroes relatively easy to unlock by earning cash through playing the game and also having skins for the heroes that can be purchased that offer NO ingame advantages.
the graphics for this game, with some special blocks and the heroes as an exception, are very similar to that of minecraft making for an interesting looking game that actually performs well on any PC. I personally use a HP pavillion G6 2000 series laptop and the game constantly runs at 30fps on low settings, not impressive for many but it is an achievement for my little piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥

Quite disappointed. Only about 3 choices actually matter in the entire game.
We have a franchise built on plotting, scheming, people making more or less honorable decisions and seeing their actions with the movies/books. So you'd expect things to carry on here too. At least at a basic level, right? Wrong. The game has a fantastic way of ignoring many of your decisions or finding some totally unrealistic way for your enemies to bypass them. Take in mind that some characters, like Ramsey Snow, also have plot immunity, so they can't die, so their influence in the setting is something you can't change at all or even alter.
Thus, you have moments when your enemies enter your fortress against higher forces, you have someone surviving at the end (even two people actually) just to continue the story for one an who knows how for the other when he had been pinned down. We never find out what the North Grove actually does by the way, just getting this out of the way since this is a major point from the very first chapter in the first episode.
The game also does a lousy job at remembering some decisions. Did you let a crow brother live even if you hate him? Well bad luck, he still died and you're still to blame! Did you tell your sister to take care of herself? Well no, the recap of the last episode remembers you telling her to watch out for traitors.
But what I disliked most was the ending. It's not a true ending, it's more of a "see you next season". Remember The Walking Dead? Lee died and it was his story, it ended, the next season was about Clementine and how she grew up. Remember The Wolf Among Us? Well, our dear wolf had a case to solve, he solved it. They all had good moments and bad ones, but the story felt at least mostly ended.
What was the deal here? Well, seeing what happens with the Forresters and finding about the power at the North Grove. Since the story was left in a tree for many of the Forresters and you didn't find anything about the North Grove besides the fact that there were people there (oh, gee, what a surprise), I found this to be♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not to mention that I don't think there's any true good moment in here. There's disaster after disaster, whenever you think something is going good, surprise, your enemies get super plot powers and everyone on your side is incompetent!
The game has great visuals, at least I really liked some landscapes and some characters are truly believable in how they act. Pity the other side usually gets superpowers and does miracles since then the whole story goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥
I do not recoment this game, this is not the standard Telltale has given us before, it's worse. If you like Game of Thrones, get it at a discount.

I think it's finally time I share my opinion about this game with the world, since I just reached the 300 mark and the game is on a big sale.
People can hate all they want on my PERSONAL OPINION, but here we go.
I'm going to start off by saying "Dying Light" is my favorite game of all time. It takes my favorite elements of ANY game (Zombies, Parkour, Open-World) and combines them into an original piece of art.
So, the base game by itself offers two huge maps, which you can easily traverse with this game's delightful parkour system (I say screw Assassin's Creed, THIS is freedom). The story will be taking you through every street of "The Slums" and "The Old Town", and the side-quests will be taking you into people's personal lives. Doing each of these things, along with smashing Zombies to bits, will reward you with points towards unlocking new Skills which MAKE THE GAME MORE FUN! Along with that, you will be rewarded with unique weapons and sometimes even things like ziplines connecting parts of the city making the travelling, again, more fun. People overlook this part of the game, thus avoiding more than half the fun of it, stick to the main storyline, and then get disappointed by the ending. Oh, and about the ending, you will be using your Parkour and Zombie-fighting Skills all the way until the very end of the last mission, and then instead of doing all sorts of cool combinations with the game they created, the Devs decided to fill it with talking and Quick-Time Events.
And oh, the Devs. After seeing how they react to the Community's feedback on this game, I started loving Techland. They encourage the Community to send them messages saying what they liked about the game, how it could be improved and take it all into consideration. Their customer support for this game is amazing, with sometimes even giving away their PERSONAL E-mail address just to help people with problems they have in the game.
They ensured the game is equally supported on all platforms, while most of the community is on PS4, a bit less on Xbox One, and the least on PC (the numbers are probably changing very often, last time I checked, actually quite a while ago, it was like this.), they included the Developer Tools for this game on PC, allowing the community to make maps that have every enjoyable aspect from the actual game. However, they STILL kept it balanced, with porting the best community maps to consoles.
And that was it for "Dying Light". But wait, we're here to talk about "Dying Light: The Following - Enhanced Edition". This package is completely worth the price even without a sale, including the game and the Season Pass, as well as improved graphics and optimization. Going back to the topic of the great support this game has, even the physical copy owners, like me, today have access to the "Enhancements" for free, and have the chance to upgrade to only the Season Pass. However, if you're looking to buy the game, you'll get all you need in DL: TF -EE.
The contents of the Season Pass are:
- MASSIVE The Following DLC (which I have covered in a seperate review, it's still worth knowing it offers a map bigger than both from the base game combined and introduces driving)
- INTENSE The Bozak Horde DLC, making your heart pump insanely fast while you race with time in an attempt to win the "Bozak Bow", a great stealth weapon
- Ultimate Survor Bundle, I consider it more like bonus content for the Season Pass, offering 3 Outfits and 4 kick♥♥♥♥♥weapon Blueprints
- Cuisine & Cargo, along with USB I consider it just 2 bonus Quarantine Zones that give you a chance to get some epic loot.
You do not, however, get the most recent 4 personalization bundles, each one offering an Outfit, weapon Blueprint(s) and a Buggy Paintjob in this package. I was not happy about this at first, but I realized people should just consider it as an opportunity to support the Devs even more.
Oh, but with the base game comes another great feature, the "Be The Zombie" mode. Starting off as a pre-order bonus, making it's way to a DLC, and then becoming a part of the game itself, BTZ lets you play as a super-powerful Night Hunter, on a quest to kill all humans. From the Survivor's point of view, the Night Hunter's invasions are a terrifying experience. You won't know what I'm talking about until you try it, but trust me, the feeling of a deadly creature watching you from the dark and coming for you, while the only way to defend yourself is a UV Flashlight and flares that burn out way too fast, both of them being an easy target for your enemy's disgusting spit is scary AF.
So, this review's targets are the people who are looking for a good game in the crowded-with-unfinished-unsupported-abandoned-by-developers-junk Zombie genre as it is today.
This game's Demo says that the full game offers 50 hours of gameplay, while it has offered me 6 times the amount!
For all of you considering buying this game, it is very well optimized, supported, finished, smooth and worth every penny.
