Other than that I would like to include another person's review, Drunk Bear Man, because it sums up how I feel about the game as well:
"6/10
It's a unique kind of mix-up to the Tower Defense genre, where you have to defend using towers like always... AND send out units to act as enemies FOR the opposing team, who has to defend themselves by building their OWN towers. If it would have been a perfect game, it would have gotten a 10 for a really cool mix-up of the genre. But sadly, it's far from perfect. This game has a VERY steep learning curve, and when it was first released it had virtually no singleplayer until they updated it, but guess what? The first bot for singleplayer is hard if you don't know what the hell to do, and the description for it says otherwise! Also, there isn't that much variation and only 10 bots to fight against, meaning this game is predominantly multiplayer, which I honeslty don't like for the TD genre. "

Once upon a time somebody decided to combine a visual novel with a cliche JRPG. And so Hyperdimension Neptunia was born.
This game takes place in a world where the console wars are made real and each console is represented by a scantily clad anime Goddess because of course they are. The story follows a colourful(and all-female) cast of characters as they fight to save the world of Gamindustri(seriously?) from the forces of darkness. The setting is constantly used to poke fun at videogame and anime cliches, and the characters break through the fourth wall so many times they might as well install a revolving door. You can also expect quite a bit of fan service. The questionable attire of the Goddesses is just the tip of a kinky iceberg
On the gameplay side of things this is nothing special. You'll read through VN style story segments and then fight your way through dungeons full of treasures and palette swapped monsters. The flashy, over the top animations make combat fun but don't expect a design revolution here. It's your average JRPG on the gameplay front.
So this game is basically the videogame equivalent of fast food. Not the most classy thing on the menu but still pretty damn good.

Half-Life 2 is, simply put, the best single-player shooter ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Half-Life 2 compared to other single player shooters. What Valve has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there is an excellent shooter here. Half-Life 2 doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of first-person shooters to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure here.
Before I really get into the review, you should know the background of how this game was reviewed. Valve did not want to send out copies of their game (for fairly obvious reasons) before it was released to the public. In order to play the game, I, and several of my colleagues throughout the industry, took a trip up to Seattle to visit Valve in order to have some private time with the title. I was given a little room to myself where I could close the door, turn off the lights, click my little red slippers, and pretend that I was sitting at home. It worked for the most part, largely because I was so engrossed with the game that when I came out of my trance I often had to take a moment to get my bearings. Obviously, Valve was happy to bring me into a controlled environment for ideal playing conditions.
What's particularly impressive about the game running so well is that it does so without compromising any part of gameplay or design. Environments are complex, colorful, and highly detailed; AI is certainly impressive in that NPCs work as teams, flank, react to sound and movement, and then engage with lifelike aggression. But like I said, we're going to have to wait and see what the game runs like on a more standard system after it's released. Therefore, you can look for an additional supplement to this review about how the game runs on lower-end systems after i've had the chance to check.
So I Would Give This Game A 9.7/10

As someone that hasn't been able to play through a Far Cry game since 2 came out, I must say that so far this game has redeemed the series. I am hesitant to compare the game on that note however, considering the fact that it generates a world that feels entirely different than previous games.
Wildlife feels dangerous until you're better equipped. Night-time is accompanied by an increased traffic of carnivorous animals that of course only furthers itself as you travel away from your Village. Every enemy will become increasingly agressive as you progress further into the world. At first a pack of wolves hunting game might seem trivial, with you crouched in the bushes ready to strike. Though as soon as a cave lion, a group of yak, and a mammoth walk into the picture... you're met with a sudden sense that things could get very bad. They usually do.
I can almost guarantee your first encounter with a Sabretooth will leave you wanting one of your very own, so long as it doesn't eat you first.
There is slightly more gathering than you might expect, though the game includes a "Rewards Stash." Your stash will increasingly flow with free "loot" items (wood, stone, hide, etc.) as you upgrade your main tribesman's huts. This causes gathering to become an optional thing further into the game, so long as you take the time to upgrade said huts.
The skill tree is broken down into 8 branches, with each having skills that unlock as you find your fellow Wenja and complete their quests. Upgrading the weapons that each person also gives allows you to craft plenty of dangerous items, giving you plenty of combinations to take down whatever beast, or man is rushing toward you.
Like previous games, this one doesn't immediately tell you what to do once you're through the initial introductions. There are enemy tribes that you will encounter that follow a main story arc. Side-quests begin popping up across the map, and give you the opportunity to earn easy Skill Points, as well as giving you a distraction and well needed practice throwing spears into wolves' faces. Caves allow you a much more stealthy exploration of the game, though often end up with you face to face with the game's stealthier creatures as well. Beast Master Hunts that allow you to kill, or tame the most dangerous animals in Oros. There's plenty to collect and explore!
What truly struck me right away with this game is the simple fact that, well... it's pretty. Very, very pretty. If you're able to run this game at higher settings in 1080p and above, you will not be disappointed.
If you're unsure about the game, wait! This game will be on sale in no time, and is plenty worth your time when you can get it for $30-40!

Beyond Eyes set out to accomplish a lofty goal, create a game that would give the player a taste of what it would be like to go blind.  Not only did it accomplish this goal via very creative game concepts, but it tells a simple and endearing yarn of a blind child in search of her feline friend that really made me feel for the main character, Rae.
From a technical standpoint the gameplay is simply walking and exploring, but as you can imagine walking and exploring without sight would be anything but simple.  Beyond Eyes world is beautifully colored and rendered, think watercolor painting, but most of it is shrouded in white except for your near vicinity.  As you move thru the landscape your world literally pops into existence out of the white, often with annoying reality like a fence right where you are trying to walk.  Sound is a key part of the experience too, not only in the stellar game audio but in distant visual bubble that becomes a beacon in the unknown for Rae to navigate towards.  Smell is also represented visually by wind waves, but be warned, both smell and sound can be misleading.
Beyond Eyes not only gave me a “glimpse” into the world of a blind person, but it succeeded in making me feel for Rae.  The frustration of another dead end, the confusion of thinking you hear or smell something interesting that turns out to be something completely different, the sadness of loss, the joy of succeeding at simple tasks previously taken for granted.  Beyond Eyes requires patience, empathy and a sense of exploration, but will reward you with a one of a kind experience and a charming fairytale that will stick with you long after playing.

Grim Dawn is an outstanding ARPG, if you even remotely like other ARPGs, you would do yourself a disservice not checking this one out and I can’t recommend it enough.
I prefer to start off with the negatives on games like this, more to try and keep me focused on impartiality and I'll be honest the game is not without it's flaws. 1st up is the game can be argumentative with video driver updates, only worked on Nvidia machines running this game, but occasionally my brother and I do have some issues after an update. Fortunately the devs have a nice little repair tool in the install folder to run that will fix the issue, but it is an annoyance I would like to see resolved. My 2nd complaint about the game is camera angles can be awkward in some areas like the Undercity, where walls don't go transparent as quick as they should, again this is a minor complaint as one of the games uncommon features can help with that issue, rotating the camera in an ARPG, alSo more of an annoyance but nothing too detrimental. Also online gameplay can be a little laggy depending on the person hosting the game, if the computer isn't quite up to snuff or a bad internet connection and make it pretty bad to play, maybe there is something they can do with the net code, I don't know, but when playing with a couple of my friends I usually have to host. The last complaint I have is the lack of appearance customization, you have default male and default female and that is it, not the end of the world as that does get covered up in no time with equipment, just something you would expect to see in a modern game.
Now that we got the bad stuff behind us, lets talk about what makes this game great and why you should buy it. For me this game fills a niche that lies between and above games like Diablo 3, Torchlight 2, Titan Quest and Path of Exile. The ascetics of this game is dark and gritty closer to PoE than D3 and looks really good. As I mentioned above, the game is actually 3D and not just a sprite background as you can freely rotate the camera. Another big selling point to the game is it's character customization and character builds which I think is better than PoE. You have your standard Diablo style look that can then be augmented with components you get as drops and also augments that you can buy from faction vendors. Additionally, some equipment grants you new skills that will level up with you. Your class structures are almost as varied as Diablo 2 and 3 classes (they are called masteries in Grim Dawn) and you have 6 masteries to choose from with 2 more coming in the expansion, but what really makes it shine is at becoming 10th level you pick up a 2nd class which opens up a slew of combinations for character building. And as if there isn't enough to tweak your build there is the devotion system in place, what this are is an  additional way to add perks to your character, you gain devotion points by finding and restoring shrines in the game, all characters have access to the same devotions and these can boost virtually any stat on the game with some granting special abilities that you slap onto skills that you possess modifying the way you use that skill, the possible combinations are insane and well balanced, the number of combinations is what truly makes this game stand out from the rest. You will also find features found in other games in the genre such as crafting, hardcore mode, increased difficulties on subsequent play troughs, areas you can portal in and out of like rifts from D3.
My hours played in this game should be more than enough of an endorsement to how good it is (263 as of this writing) and I am just getting started.

A very peaceful game.
It's incredible how it forces you to think like a blind girl. The game will slowly show you how everything we "see" is completely fabricated by imagination.
Now, just imagine that you are blind and that you're walking somewhere you don't know.
You can remember the way, walk with your hands stretched, feeling everything and making a 3D map in your head. That is surely the first action plan.
But...
What if part of that way was a closed space when you passed it for the first time, but the second time you went through it, it was open?
Like a door that was closed when you passed through but since then someone opened it.
What if you give the wrong face to a sound?
Like a bell that is actually someone's cellphone alarming.
What if you can feel danger ahead but can't say exactly what kind of danger?
Like the sound of an animal you don't know.
The game puts you inside all that, and in a very beautiful way.
And to everyone angry because the walking is slow, here is what I have to say about it: I loved it.
It got me really annoyed sometimes, just going to the other side of something took ages.
A blind person can't exactly run to the unknown, though. And guess what, they almost certainly didn't choose to be blind.
In this game, you also don't. If you really wanna put yourself inside a blind girl's mind, you will have to walk slow. And I think that all the annoyance it causes is part of the beauty of this game. That is just me, though.
One thing I'm sure no one disagrees with. This game is freaking beautiful. And the soundtrack to it is just perfect. The right music at the right time.

I can almost guarantee that if you liked SRTT, you'll like IV too. They brought back many, many characters from earlier Saint's Row games and it was pretty neat to see that.
They also added the idea of "romance", which are short cutscenes between the boss and their homies doing exactly what you's expect. They're really cute and hilarious to be honest, Shaundi's and Johnny's seemed to be the only ones taken seriously, Johnny's especially was heartwarming. There is absolutely no effect on the plot with these at all, and they don't change no matter how many times you initiate the scenes. That was a little disappointing because one would expect they might put effort into adding more than that because scenes like Matt's don't make any sense the second time around.
The character customization is far superior to any other game out there, in my honest opinion! The ability to play as a female character as an important aspect. The character customization at Image As Designed is fantastic, and it even improved since SRTT. The shops also had a really large amount of items that would satisfy most people. In fact, the character creation is one of the strongest points of the Saint's Row series, especially SRIV. The fact that you can change the breast size and muscularity of your saint for your preference is considerate on the developer's part.
Another important point is the diversity of the characters! The gaming industry has a monumental problem with carbon-copy, universe characters and catering to the same small audience over and over. But Saint's Row is certainly up there. With many strong female characters and homies of various races, even bring in characters who don't fit the typical image of a hypermasculine male character and are treated decently.
The small things like radio stations playing outside the car are great, the city is beautiful, and the side missions in the game are really fun(Hello, superpowers!) and there are a ton of them, and still feel pretty fresh by the time you finish. But, that brings us to the biggest problem of the game. It's obvious that it was originally meant to be a dlc in the beginning. The main quests are few and far between while there is an overabundance of side activities. The developers could have easily added many main quest line missions that fit in just fine with the rest of the story. The game never addresses what the strange floating things at the top of the simulation are. They also never physically sabotage the Zin outside the simulation, which is disappointing. They also never go beyond giving life to the Zin race outside Zinyak's love for poetry which is again, disappointing. Point being, there was a lot more potential than the final game had, with its overly linear, short plot lines. And in the end, that really detracts from the game.

Having sunk in 300+ hours and gotten to the endgame and max level.... this game is fun. Best ARPG I've played to date, and much better than Path of Exile. (I've gotten over 2k hours in PoE for reference.) The combat, level progression, non-DRM, gearing, and story are really polished. Crafting... could be improved upon, but it works and there is depth. As for character building, any pro at ARPGs will probably be able to come up with a solid build no problem. Reminiscent of Titan Quest (same makers) and Diablo 1/2/3, the character building revolves on selecting your skills, but is complemented by being able to select 2 classes for mix and matching for the the ultimate min-maxing goodness. On top of that, the devotion skill system should be familiar to anyone who played FFX/2 and PoE, and will greatly boost your character for passive skills and proc-skills. Melee, range, spell casting, it's got it all, and the balance is relatively good between the three playstyles, something that PoE fails to do due to its meta-bound nature.
All in all, a great game to sink time into whenever and wherever you want. Doesn't require top-end PCs to play, and can be decoupled from Steam syncing for a true Single-Player experience. Trading exists, and is a pain in a butt, but acceptable. I received this game as a gift, and bought the Crucible DLC which was worth the money.
Final score: 5/5

While the concept IS nice, the story leaves you feeling like you wasted your time.  When you play a game, you need a sense of fulfilment and with this, all I felt was the guess I made waaay back in Chapter One was to come into fruition, and it left me angry.
The biggest beefs I have with the game comes from several things:
* The "clues" you get to point you to your destination - with the time lapse from story intro to the impetus that drives the story, too much time had gone by to make it really feasible.
* Blind people don't just up and wander like that - even at an early age.  They have walking sticks and other safety things they keep in consideration.  This child acted waay too sheltered to be believable.
* The "true identity" concept - Hearing would be enhanced on a blind person to compensate - there is no way she would not have been able to idenify their owners better.  It ticked me off the most when going past cars, they didn't sound like either cars or road, and then when they were identified, they became the next "placeholder" for something like a lawnmower, which sounds nothing like a car, truth be told - and this is form a person with hearing problems!  The protagonist had hearing before this, and she SHOULD have been able to identify these things - including the CROWS!  Crows cawing should NOT have scared her as they did!  Going blind does not make you instantly forget how everything sounded!  You do not reset to "zero" in reality!
This last was the thing that caused me to uninstall the game.  Yes, you're trying to show someone how it feels to be in a world foreign to you, but at the same time, you need to add a bit more common sense to the concept, as well.
Again, If you like experimental and want to enjoy the concept, go ahead. but if you want a good story, I'd personally go with a different game.

Prepare for a different kind of poker night in a very different kind of club. In Poker Night at the Inventory, you'll deal with notable characters such as Penny Arcade's clever, cunning Tycho, Team Fortress 2's hulking Heavy, Homestar Runner's self-proclaimed "awesome icon" Strong Bad and the hyperkinetic "rabbity-thing" from Sam & Max. These characters come together in ways some never thought possible, in a setting few would have predicted. You'll experience a new style of poker, particularly when hands don't go the way of the other fiery competitors at the table ... because these players have left a trail of victims in their wake a mile long -- with heavy weapons, biting sarcasm and irony -- and when they sit down at the table for Poker Night at The Inventory, they're ready to go all in!
Poker Night at The Inventory features fully voiced characters utilizing Telltale’s dynamic dialog system. All the characters will talk trash, give unique tells, and react to the game dynamically as it is being played, providing a unique experience with each round played.

Before Counter-Strike won the Mod War (1996-2003), it was common for total conversions to take cues from John Woo films. Mods like Action Quake 2 (and its Action * derivatives), The Opera and The Specialists made multiplayer that wasn’t simply about running and shooting, but about doing both in style, preferably by diving sideways in slow motion through a skyscraper window while idly daydreaming about how good the Matrix sequels were surely going to be.
Those days may live again (even the Matrix bit, if you still dare to dream): some of the makers of the Specialists have released a free, standalone multiplayer shooter called Double Action: Boogaloo. Free as in free, that is; no microtransactions or free-to-play infrastructure, just a simple game of wielding pistols akimbo and releasing flocks of doves

I've been playing this game on and off for the past two years. It really gets everything down in strategy gaming perfectly. It progresses at a slow pace, but there is always something to do, and that means you can play for too long in one sitting. The Enemy Within expansion rebalances things like snipers and difficulty spikes. Also, you find nice additions like new missions and enemies; gameplay is better with it. Even without the expansion, the game has incredible expandability. I haven't tried Infinite War but have only heard good things about it. I still haven't finished the Long War mod yet as it requires 100 hours.
The setting just enraptures the strategist. You make decisions for the XCOM project, tech-tree, upgrades, research and base building. This is to me, actually more fun than the battles themselves, which get annoying. The game really requires you to think about your moves, rewarding optimizations and punishing brashness (this is even truer for the expansion). This isn't a game with in-your-face action like COD nor is it a deep story and world-building elements like Dragon Age. It is a game where you use strategic maneuvers to outplay the enemy. You do not explore worlds; aliens simply try to screw things up on earth and you just react to them to survive.
The score and the story are just decent. Graphics are very good for the turn-based categories. Addicting for anyone who likes to min/max. XCOM 2 already released, but I haven't gotten to that yet.

This is by far the greatest of what I would put into the Blockbuster category of video games alongside Metro Last Light, Mass Effect, and Fallout New Vegas. When people say, "Did you ever play Dying Light?" you do not just answer,"Yes". You look right through that man's skull and you say, "Harran? Yeah, I've been there."
The opening scene (the game being more akin to a film than a video game) places you directly into a world wide crisis of zombial proportions, there is an overwhelming sense of dread and importance. You are there for a reason bigger than yourself. As a member of the Global Relief Effort, it's your job to get in there and track down the man that will later become your nemesis. While hiding your identity from the very people you must fight to protect, you fall in love with a cagefighter as the graying ethics of the organization you are sworn to are crushed underneith your instinctual allegiance to humanity and the American bravado that paints it all in red white and blue; eagle screech, F-15 fly-by, the New England Patriots! If your panties aren't wet already then I'll just have to keep going til they are because I promised you that much the last time we spoke on the phone and I hung up on you too soon.
There is a day/night cycle that will make you dread the dying of the light. When the sun goes down the monsters come out. I haven't been this scared of something this terrifying since I was a little girl. I promise you will get so absorbed into this game for at least the first couple weeks that it will ruin your relationships with other human beings. Remember to drink plenty of fluids and get enough rest. You need to pace yourself because even though your body is screaming for the bed your mind will always be in Harran with 'Kiss Me Now Sex Face' Jade and 'Whisper to Me Again in that Voice of Yours' Brecken. "Let me out there! I gotta get that last drop before Rais' crew! There are people starving here in the tower!" that's you. That's what you'll be saying if you get this game. 10/10, would bang again.
There is in here struck the most perfect of balances between direction and open world. While you may go off a pillaging there will always be that nagging sense of dread helped on by the end of the world ambience and an erie atmosphere of a once lively city now gone dead. The storyline will keep you going on the main road, the side missions will keep you wandering down alleyways and into the gutters of eastern mediterranean slums. When people ask you for help, there is an instant sense of empathy for people who outwardly look and act just like human beings. That may sound obvious but very few games get this right which brings me to my next point. The voice acting is probably the best I have ever seen. You will realize just how far ahead the voice acting in this game is when you try playing any other game afterwards. You'll never be the same.

Tower Wars has you playing the role of the aggressor and defender simultaneously. Do you happen to know that quote from the show/books? When you play the Game of Thrones you win or you die? Do you know it? Well, if you don't it's sure as hell hammered into your skull by the end of all things.
You die and oh do you die. And not a damn choice matters.
This is a game that tries very hard to be the Game of Thrones we've all watched/read.  And it does succeed to some degree, however,  you don't really feel any satisfaction to it. When you play a game you aim to win. That's the natural order of things. When you finish a game and despite all your efforts still wind up on the losing side it leaves a poor taste in your mouth. Anyone playing this game already knows Game of Thrones and what it entails and knows that the good doesn't always win, if at all. And you feel that here, oh you certainly do,  but it's not the right thing for a game to be. You need to be able to take something from it, namely a victory. Something satisfying. And you don't. Twelve, thirteen hours everyone spent on this game, some more, and you're left feeling unsatisfied. You don't win in any area regardless of choices and that's a frustrating feeling.
Paroozing around the other comments and discussions this game seems to hold up to the old TellTale standard of choices not meaning a damn thing. Wacky Spores: The Chase is a combination of endless runner and turn based strategy. Does it run to its success or ends up failing in one of its turns, let’s find out:
“It’s the first line of the game and the developer already ran out of ideas”, that is what’s told you as the first line of the story when you boot up the game. Normally, I would tell you that it has a throwaway story that is not interesting at all. But Wacky Spores: The Chase tells the boring story by completely shattering the fourth wall and providing a lot of fun moments throughout the journey. Now that we have gotten that out of the way, let’s see how the actual running and gunning hold up.
Wacky Spores: The Chase lets you control three mushrooms at a given time who can run, shoot and perform special attacks. You are given a specific amount of time to run and dodge the enemies in your path while trying to collect coins and select which path will your mushroom be in the next turn. In the battle mode, you can choose to attack the bugs with your blaster to get them out of the way of your mushrooms or drink potions and do other stuff. Every mushroom has a different special powers like creating singularity, shooting canons and others.
These powers take some time to recharge after use and while you are waiting for these to recharge and you have enough health, the best technique is to target the bugs which are nearest to your heroes. While there is not enough depth in these turn based battles, these are fun to play through especially later on when different bosses arrive to hinder your run. By collecting coins you can unlock various characters and buy potions to use in your run. You can also complete side objectives in your run to get some bonuses.
While the combat part of Wacky Spores: The Chase is fun, the same cannot be said about its running mechanic. In an endless runner, you expect some thrills of dodging some close calls but here you won’t find it because of its design flaw. When the timer of the running starts the three mushrooms have to run at the same time while dodging and collecting coins at the same time. The movement feels clunky and since there is not much excitement during that part, it quickly gets boring and repetitive.
The game is also pretty grindy in the start and takes some time to really get going. Another flaw with Wacky Spores: The Chase is its hit detection. While your heroes can aim anywhere if there is nothing blocking it, there were times when the bullet would simply miss despite it clearly showing that it would be hitting its mark. What frustrates more is that sometimes bugs from other lanes can also hurt you and take your life quite quickly.
The majority of enemy types are bugs which come at you relentlessly but some enhanced bugs like the thief bug can easily keep you on your toes due to its tendency to steal the coins you’ve fought hard for.
While it is nothing revolutionary, the battles are good enough that you can pick up and play the game for a few runs if not for a longer time duration.

While it is nothing spectacular, Wacky Spores: The Chase is a vibrant game full of colors which gives a relaxing feel to it. The backgrounds are well done and the character models all look pretty good. It has a arcade like feel to it and does justice to its overall theme.
Wacky Spores: The Chase features different sound cues for different places. All of these are done pretty well and is a nice addition to the game. There is no voice acting as to speak of but the sound effects are nice and add to the environments of the game.
Wacky Spores: The Chase might not be revolutionary or anything but it is fun. I had fun while I running through its levels and mowing down bugs. It would help it if the devs killed the “bugs” present in the game and took time to improve the running mechanic a little more but overall, while it has its problems, it is a game that you can pick up and play for a short period of time.

The most basic question from a lot of people when they look into Tropico 4 is this: Is it any better than Tropico 3?
Short answer, In some ways yes and in other many sad ways nope. The Tropico series for those who haven't played any Tropico games at all is this. You are a Tin Pot Dictator of a small cluster of fictional Islands in the Carribean. You aim is to get rich stuffing as much money as you can into your off shore Swiss Bank Account and try and not get overthrow by the angry factions you have to appease, the people and finally the angry Cold War era Super Powers. Sounds simple right?
But anyways, Tropico 4 versus 3. The general improvements between the two games don't seem massive to be brutally honest. Some of the problems from 3 are still there (triggering Edicts still has no visual effects apart from your bank balance, same graphics and the same damn music) but 4 brings some improvements to the table. It is clear they learnt something from the DLC and Expansion of Tropico 3 as quite a few features have been ported over to the newer game. I'm sure there is  a huge amount of under the hook tweaks and additions that make it a slightly smoother experince from Tropico 3.
For one Tropico 4 has a bit more soul and is a lot more amusing. Instead of that single irritating Radio DJ with the same 6 voice clips El Presidente‎ pretty much shares his palace with his aides and faction heads who bring a new feature to the Tropico table with missions that appease your government, the factions or just a slightly easier way to help fill your bank balance or satisfy your people to some extent. And it isn't just your guys the faceless super powers from the first game have been given faces AND both the EU, China and the Middle East have joined in to squabble for your tiny Islands precious resources. This is a pretty good thing as it also gives you a reason to actually play the Main Campaign that has been tweaked a lot around these new additions. They also make sandbox games a slightly less tedious treck.
There is of course the mandatory couple of new buildings of every type and a couple of new outfits to dress up your Corrupt Carribean Dictator too. And yeah sadly that is it. Of course there is also the suspicious hefty amount of DLC packs with a lot of additional content that should really have been in the game. This game really is more Tropico: The Directors Cut The Electric Phantom Part II than Tropico 4. But hey, they added Twitter with the Facebook Social functions and new achivements if that is your thing!
I sort of wish they made the effort and a DLC that added some new Islands or Music as around the 20 hour mark like with a decent old movie you love to break out every few months to comfort yourself you eventually notice the limited flaws.
So yeah, final word. Pick it up with all the DLC during a sale if you are a big Tropico/Management game fan or want to try something new.

Half Life 2 Review Raymond KT
Summary: [Metacritic's 2004 PC Game of the Year] By taking the suspense, challenge and visceral charge of the original, and adding startling new realism and responsiveness, Half-Life 2 opens the door to a world where the player's presence affects everything around him, from the physical environment to the behaviors -- even the emotions -- of both friends and enemies. The player again picks up the crowbar of research scientist Gordon Freeman, who finds himself on an alien-infested Earth being picked to the bone, its resources depleted, its populace dwindling. Freeman is thrust into the unenviable role of rescuing the world from the wrong he unleashed back at Black Mesa. And a lot of people -- people he cares about -- are counting on him. [Vivendi Universal]
Half-Life 2 has the most varied gameplay of any shooter since Half-Life, with strikingly distinctive missions. In one, you drive an amphibious vehicle along canals, occasionally disembarking to kill soldiers guarding gates. In a later mission, you must avoid lion ants, monstrous insects that will attack anyone who walks on the sand above their burrows, by using your antigravity gun to create bridges and pathways out of scrap wood and boxes. The lion ants are transformed from enemy to friend when you gain control of them and can send swarms against soldiers.
Even elements from the original game are reimagined. Zombies with alien creatures attached to their heads now make mournful groans and hurl boxes and barrels at you with palpable anger. The barnacle, which attaches itself to the ceiling and uses its long tongue to suck up prey, will suck up an explosive barrel rolled beneath it, with predictable results.
Half-Life 2's almost photorealistic visuals are wonderfully detailed, easily beating the competition. The blades of a low-flying helicopter stir up the water beneath. Wrecked cars litter the highway, one of many signs of some great catastrophe. A powerful robot that acts like a frolic comically yet dangerously. The environment is also wonderfully malleable, allowing you to stack boxes or, with the help of your antigravity gun, grab a radiator and use it as both shield and weapon.
One of the original Half-Life's biggest achievements was the way it seamlessly provided purpose and a context for all the violence, keeping you from feeling as though you were just running around randomly shooting stuff. Half-Life 2 does the same thing, choreographing events in a way that keeps you enthralled and on track.
Yet, while Half-Life 2 offers a denser plot and more distinct characters, the story is ultimately less involving. The game only drops hints as to the cause of this grim future and never bothers to explain the motivation of your main foe, City 17's administrator. The designers did create a back story, which you can explore at
, but for some reason they chose not to include it in the game.
Yet no other game does as many things as well as Half-Life 2; I had so much fun that I can forgive the game its abysmal ending. I was continually enthralled and amazed, and would rather replay Half-Life 2 than begin a new first-person shooter. I envy those of you who are about to experience Half-Life 2 for the first time. Although I pity you for having to install it.

I've been playing this game on and off for the past two years. It really gets everything down in strategy gaming perfectly. It progresses at a slow pace, but there is always something to do, and that means you can play for too long in one sitting. The Enemy Within expansion rebalances things like snipers and difficulty spikes. Also, you find nice additions like new missions and enemies; gameplay is better with it. Even without the expansion, the game has incredible expandability. I haven't tried Infinite War but have only heard good things about it. I still haven't finished the Long War mod yet as it requires 100 hours.
The setting just enraptures the strategist. You make decisions for the XCOM project, tech-tree, upgrades, research and base building. This is to me, actually more fun than the battles themselves, which get annoying. The game really requires you to think about your moves, rewarding optimizations and punishing brashness (this is even truer for the expansion). This isn't a game with in-your-face action like COD nor is it a deep story and world-building elements like Dragon Age. It is a game where you use strategic maneuvers to outplay the enemy. You do not explore worlds; aliens simply try to screw things up on earth and you just react to them to survive.
The score and the story are just decent. Graphics are very good for the turn-based categories. Addicting for anyone who likes to min/max. XCOM 2 already released, but I haven't gotten to that yet.

Imagine that aliens are invading the Earth and you’ve been put in charge of the defense of the entire planet. That daunting proposition is at the heart of XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The absolute best aspect of XCOM is the sense that there’s never enough time or resources to do everything that needs to be done. Do you pull a trooper off of active duty to undergo psionic training or do you keep him out in the field where he can get better at his core skills? Do you spend your budget producing satellites to help locate UFOs or do you spend that same money producing interceptors to be sure you can shoot down the few UFOs you do locate? Every moment of XCOM is defined by these either/or decisions where every move involves some sort of sacrifice or compromise. When you combine that with the overall tone of the game, which emphasizes a DEFCON style countdown to a complete alien takeover, the whole experience is fantastically tense and engaging. Death is a big deal in XCOM and, by midway through the game, your Memorial to fallen soldiers, complete with bagpipe music, should have plenty of names on it. At harder difficulty levels, it can be tough to recover from the death of an experienced officer, but the tactical game virtually requires that death be a real and, more importantly, a recoverable error for you. It’s all part of that feeling of being two steps behind the aliens and frantically trying to catch up. Is it just another zombie game?
No. It is
.
This game is an amalgamation of every cliche, dilemma and trope found in zombie-related games, comics, films and culture. Though this may seem like something you've seen a hundred times, Dying Light has managed to implement and capture the core aspects of what made those devices work by adding in the right amount of survival horror and scares.
Death comes swiftly at every turn if you slip up in the night.
This game captures the intensity and tension of fast-moving zombies from 28 Days Later, adds in a horrifyingly wonderous night-time gameplay that drastically limits vision and introduces enemies that are genuinely frightening; both when they jump you and when you are trying to sneak or run past them while listening to their guttural growls and screams.
The most amazing part? YOU are in total control at every moment. YOU will understand why and how you die. YOU are definitely equipped with the ability to outrun and outlast them all. Yet Dying Light still manages to keep up the fear despite giving you every tool at your disposal once the game opens up.
And for the seasoned veterans, think the game is too easy after a while? Wear a pair of surround sound headphones, attempt it in Nightmare mode or turn off your HUD.
Good night... and have fun!

Summary: Misleading, poorly designed clickfest
Detail:
Taking a look at the cartoonish, over-the-top graphics, one gets the impression that this is a family friendly, childish (in a good way) game, great for relaxing and enjoying some simple cartoon destruction with a laid back style and maybe mild challenges.  Going through the not-very-detailed tutorial, the joking dialogue confirms your impression.  When the guidance is complete (having forced you forward so you couldn't really watch the effects of what you were told to do since the action was off the screen while the text pop-ups prevented you from scrolling), however, and you are told to defeat the AI that was allegedly designed to be laughably simple, you eerily discover that it is strangely not so easy.
Brushing it off and moving on to the first opponent AI, the real game quickly shows itself.  Still not really sure when you are supposed to use which towers and units (i.e. what the strengths are meant to be), you are left to figure it out in real-time.  A bit of delay and boring start ensues, but the pace quickly picks up.  Expect to loose if you actually try to take the time to read the in-game descriptions for each unit and tower to learn as the AI rapidly ramps up its waves.  I am quite a tower game rookie, but since the game gives the impression that it would fit well for that situation, it is telling that I lost 3 or 4 times until beating the very first AI opponent (then beating the second on the first try since the design is so repetative before giving up on the third from the stupidity).  Most annoying is the fact that there is no time to really think about how to lay out your towers, the waves come too fast, you have to memorize the map and already know what to do.  The fact that single player was an after-thought is quite evident given that, pathetically, there is nothing even as simple as a game speed adjustment.  So while the AI happily processes away at the speed of electricity, its all on you to try to out-click it - the single biggest factor in destroying the potential enjoyability of the game - it is nothing but rushing to keep up.  If you step back and think about it, though, that really is the only way to make it "challenging", since the fixed, hex based maps are so pathetically constraining, there really is only one effective way to force the path through the "maze" at a high level, all you can do is select which towers to construct where.
Which brings us to the next point.  How do you know which towers you really need?  Well it depens on what troops are being sent after you.  Do they have lots of shields? Armor? Health?  Can you watch and see how effective or ineffective your towers are?  NO!!, you can't!  When you click on a menu to bring up your options, the game forces your screen to look at a certain area.  For instance, if you bring up your castle, your screen MUST look at it, ditto your mines, etc., therefore you cannot browse through and think about upgrades while also watching the assault in the background.  If you try to go around upgrading, you will suddenly have an attacker at your castle door with ample shields and not a clue where you need to add tower strength to prevent it.  If you sit on your hands while watching the action so that you can see where your weaknesses are, you won't have time to actually implement the necessary changes.
Then there is the fact that Every. Single. Time. you launch your troops, the "king" announcer randomly picks one of 2 or 3 lame and incredibly repetitive and annoying phrases to say when you are already frustrated at yet another "strategy" game that has almost no strategy (or even tactics), replacing it with yet another round of who can click the fastest.
I could rant on, but I have wasted enough of my own life on both the game and this review already.  I have not had a Steam account very long, but this is the first game I have uninstalled without beating.  Quite surprising given the lousy 5 (simplistic) maps and 10 AI opponents you have to select between, yet another misleading indicator for this poorly designed game and its confused developers.

This would be a lot more enjoyable if TellTale made one thing very clear: your choices don't matter. Whatever you choose you will get the same result, which is really annoying so don't bother about worrying about your choices. The way Tell Tale Games markets their on the rails visual novels is very close to false advertising. Think of this as a movie where you can choose the lines, but you have no effect on anything that happens. The story is already set in stone only bits of dialogue may change. It makes sense from a business perspective when you think about how much the voice acting costs. Personally I would actually rather have a shorter and more expensive game (even with a lot less spoken dialog) that I can play multiple times if it meant that my choices really mattered like say Wasteland 2, instead of an interactive movie completely on rails which is one reason that I would never pay full price of any of TTG's visual novels.
Like Walking Dead while the story is interesting, the story is also so depressing and horrible that being able to affect and change the world really matters and it's sad that you can't do anything at all other than changing some text or a line here and there. Tales of the Borderlands can get away with the lack of true consequences for your choices because Borderlands has a funnier more lighthearted tone like Sam & Max, but worlds like Game of Thrones and Walking Dead can't. It totally kills the fantasy that we're a hero in the world when we can't change anything at all. As someone else already mentioned choice matters in the Game of Thrones universe. Both Ned Stark and John Snow got themselves killed by being too honorable. Joffrey and his non-biological father got killed by having no impulse control. The list goes on but choice matters. Not everything is by chance.
The Tell Tale Games game designers are more cruel than the gods of Westoros.

I honestly couldn't decide if I liked this game so I made a pro and con list:
Pro:
- Standard from TTG, nicely animated, interesting dialect and well presented all round with a good atmosphere.
- Seeing more of the smaller vassal houses from the GOT univerese is really interesting, they weren't discussed at length in the books.
Con:
- Unlike in other TTG series, the choices in this series seem to not affect the outcome at all. Characters have a story arc that will always lead to the same ending, the only choice is whether you take the scenic route to get there.
- I enjoyed that game linked with GOT universe, but the inclusion of characters already known to us (from books and TV series) restricts choices. Putting "choices" in the game regarding the fate of characters who we already know will live/die/whatever at a later point isn't a choice at all.
- It was too GOT. One of the biggest reasons GOT was popular was its brutally devestating dismissal of characters (red wedding/Joffrey/Ned). This series goes out of its way to fufill this, where completely unnecessary. Yes, you could kill the characters off but should you. A number of story arcs would have been better left to mature and develop for future seasons instead of being sliced early for the short term shock at the end of an episode.
- The characters are too similar to the GOT book and TV series. STARK = FORRESTER (you can match forrester family members to stark ones). Atleast the starks had more developed characters to continue the story, I have no clue where the story will go from the end of season 1 with the remaining characters, and am still deciding if I'm going to even follow this TTG series.
Concluding, if you enjoy GOT or TTG series in general go ahead, buy it. This game will keep you occupied for a while with a decent story but not much more. This game coud have been much more, with the GOT universe being so expansive its hard to think how they could make something so mediocre but if its on sale why not.

If you're thinking about buying this game, i have two words for you. RUN AWAY!
Overall rating 5/10
I'll go over why, it's a cash sink. A complete and utter ♥♥♥♥ing cash sink. There are 3 forms of currency in the game
-Silver which you earn from selling in game items on the market place and grinding
-Loyalty which you earn 100 daily but you barely have enough which forces you to either not care or spend real money
-Pearls which you get by spending real money
People will tell you it's possible to get most cash shop items in the in game marketplace, realistically it's not. The way that the marketplace works is such that one people will list an item and then the item goes into "auction", in reality it's not an action tho, it's more like a raffle. The game auto assigns a random number to the item and the person who presses bid and rolls that number wins the item. It's the most ridiculous system because you have no guarantee of getting anything, ever.
Now onto the cash shop, it's not convenience. Those who say it's not pay to win are deluding themselves. There are literally items which let you afk process longer than others, an outfit. Items which increase luck at drops. Items which increase the chance and the quality of knowledge you get. And if all that wasn't enough, you will look HORRIBLE without a cashshop item which costs roughly 34$ USD. Here's the kicker tho, you shouldn't decide on a class until you hit 56 and at that point if you bought a costume, you can't resell it or trade it. So you have to buy another.
Now let's avoid the cash sync item, as a new player you are seriously blocked from progressing. Most Guild want you to be level 58+ and have a GS of 400. The level 58 will take approximately 50 hours in total, the GS 400 tho, that will take about 400-500 million silver which is not a small amount. At this point, you're barely able to PvP and be competant. The problem is that EVERYONE who joined this game pre-server merge got their boss gear and got it higher level than the rest of us at a fraction of the cost of what we have to spend. Yet to gain these funds we have to farm but we're constantly killed by higher level players who will declare war on your guild because they can and whose guild you can't join because you don't have the money to get end game gear. Tada
Let's talk about end game boss gear, I've been killing the World Bosses for the last 3 weeks so far without a single drop and i have S rank knowledge on each, that means the highest form of knowledge on the boss. The best i've gotten now after over 2 dozen kills on each is 11 aura's on Karnada and 14 on Kzarka. You need 100 of each for a weapon. Oh and don't think about buying one on the marketplace because people will ask you to gift them cash shop items just to list the weapon of your choice for which you have 0 guarantee's that you'll get it and not someone else since there is no personal player trading.
I can keep going but this is one of the most trash MMOs that i have played in a long time. That is riddled which terrible customer support and horendous server lag.
One final note is that most end game gear with require you to use an item to repair the maximum durability of the item. Since you're new let me explain it this way, an item starts with 100 durability max and that will go down with each failed enhancement. You need a Memory Fragment to repair end game gear but it will only give you back 1 durability which as you can imagine is quite expensive. Effectively forcing you to buy a cash shop item which triples the repair, giving you back 3 durability instead of 1. It really adds up to $$$
Do yourself a favor and avoid this cancer
EDIT:
For anyone saying, you don't have to "buy" this, they are basically saying. For you to PVP you can get level 58 relatively easy in your 1st month on an exp server and that should be your focus.
After that though comes the grind be USEFUL and let me tell you. Without cash shop items to repair, it's a steep steep price for in game items and silver that requires months to accumulate. The raffle system isn't fair. It's the single WORST marketplace you will ever find in an mmo.
You weapon needs to be enhanced from +0 to +15, for that you need black stone (weapon). These are hot ticket items. You literally have to sit at a marketplace for 2-3 hours to try and get some because of how poorly designed the marketplace is. It's a bloody raffle that you're hoping you win. Then comes trying to go from +16 to +20, these are even rarer than the ones above and guess what, you can sit there for 2-3 hours and you won't get any. Anyone who bought this game before it went on steam, before the servers got merged paid a fraction of the price that we have to pay now.
To put things into perspective. ONE decent weapon needs 400 mil to buy (if you win the raffle), the end game Dande weapon needs 800 mil to buy. That's upgraded to +18 but still, that's a vast sum of money. As a new player, how much do you think you'll be making per week? If i'm actively playing (6-8hours per day) then i can currently make about 50 mil per day with another 20 mil overnight. That's about 70 mil a day. So you might think, okay. 10 days. But then you actually need 4 armor, 3 weapons and 6 accessories and that 10 days just became 4-6 months. Assuming you got the cash shop items to make processing/fishing more "convenient". Oh and let's not forget, that to make any real money in the game. The marketplace takes 35% of your profit. if you have the CASH SHOP valye pack, it will only take 15.5% of your profit. For MOST items, that's your entire profit margin right there. So you're forced into buying a value pack every month.
Do NOT be decieved by people who say this isn't a P2W game. In your first month alone, you will spend at least $10 for the game, another $15 for the 30 Day Value Pack, 35$ for an outfit so you don't look♥♥♥♥♥ because a level 58 still looks like a level 1. And you are going to need 4 pets, you have no choice in the matter unless you want to try to pick everything up yourself. Oh btw, people will kick you from grind parties for that because you're slowing down the group. A pet is about $10 and you need 4. So let's see; that's $100 just to be able to play properly.
So ask yourself this, do you have 6 hours a day to dedicate to gaming? Do you want to spend $100 in your first month and basically be forced to keep spending at least $15/month on value packs? I am still playing because i sunk about $250 into the game and trust me, the money goes fast. I just finished my first month on the game and it's a lot of fun, i won't deny that. But it has such cancerous elements to it that manage to kill it. Now if the costumes or weight increases (which you have to buy) were account wide, that would be a different story. But you're paying $40 to increase your CHARACTERS weight so you don't have to go back to your horse/wagon every 15 minutes to dump loot. You can get away with not having a lot of inventory but weight, there's is really no 2 ways about it. Either pay for the extra weight or interrupt your farming every 10-15 minutes because you're heavy. That's the end game. With the weight increases, you can go about 45-60 mins farming without having to drop excess loot onto your horse.
Sorry for the rant, if you had the patience to read through all this, i hope i managed to help you make a decision. At the end of the day $10 is to try to the game and that is worth it. But don't spend any money on it until you hit 56 and you'll soon realize why it's a cash sink and P2W.

I can almost guarantee that if you liked SRTT, you'll like IV too. They brought back many, many characters from earlier Saint's Row games and it was pretty neat to see that.
They also added the idea of "romance", which are short cutscenes between the boss and their homies doing exactly what you's expect. They're really cute and hilarious to be honest, Shaundi's and Johnny's seemed to be the only ones taken seriously, Johnny's especially was heartwarming. There is absolutely no effect on the plot with these at all, and they don't change no matter how many times you initiate the scenes. That was a little disappointing because one would expect they might put effort into adding more than that because scenes like Matt's don't make any sense the second time around.
The character customization is far superior to any other game out there, in my honest opinion! The ability to play as a female character as an important aspect. The character customization at Image As Designed is fantastic, and it even improved since SRTT. The shops also had a really large amount of items that would satisfy most people. In fact, the character creation is one of the strongest points of the Saint's Row series, especially SRIV. The fact that you can change the breast size and muscularity of your saint for your preference is considerate on the developer's part.
Another important point is the diversity of the characters! The gaming industry has a monumental problem with carbon-copy, universe characters and catering to the same small audience over and over. But Saint's Row is certainly up there. With many strong female characters and homies of various races, even bring in characters who don't fit the typical image of a hypermasculine male character and are treated decently.
The small things like radio stations playing outside the car are great, the city is beautiful, and the side missions in the game are really fun(Hello, superpowers!) and there are a ton of them, and still feel pretty fresh by the time you finish. But, that brings us to the biggest problem of the game. It's obvious that it was originally meant to be a dlc in the beginning. The main quests are few and far between while there is an overabundance of side activities. The developers could have easily added many main quest line missions that fit in just fine with the rest of the story. The game never addresses what the strange floating things at the top of the simulation are. They also never physically sabotage the Zin outside the simulation, which is disappointing. They also never go beyond giving life to the Zin race outside Zinyak's love for poetry which is again, disappointing. Point being, there was a lot more potential than the final game had, with its overly linear, short plot lines. And in the end, that really detracts from the game.

Grey Goo is a real time strategy (RTS) game with a very atmospheric introduction to the game via a campaign that features “life-like” looking aliens in video sequences. It features aspects and mechanics that make it a really good RTS game after the first look:
At the beginning of the campaign
I would recommend to start out on easy difficulty if you don´t play RTS games on a regular basis.
The game gives you all the information you need to manage your command with the help of a mini-map (featuring different filters), audio responsive units, a zoomable, turnable point of view, a resource intake/output estimation and mission objectives shown on the mini-map.
The variety in units seems to be quite large for the starting faction. As I haven´t played other factions yet, I cannot say more. It seemed quite balanced in terms of being able to counter enemy forces with the right kind of units. But that is tough to say after one session only. See other reviews for more information on that topic.
The game looks spectacular, especially in the videosequences. The music during the missions and especially in combat is really well done and one of the reasons I am reminded of older games in the RTS genre. The pacing of the game, the placing of buildings and the grouping and ordering of units reminded me very much of Command & Conquer (Red Alert), Star Craft 1, Warcraft 2 and a little of Dune 2(000)
the concrete.
If you like RTS games and want to try a game that is not Starcraft, go for Grey Goo! If you are tired of fantasy based strategy games in general, try Grey Goo. If you enjoy having nice music and visuals in a game that is nothing completely new but rather well done and 100% completed, give it a try! I definitely recommend having this game in your library!
Grey Goo is a real treasure and will be featured in the “Land Ho! with CaptN3mo” series. Join me on my

Half-Life 2 is, simply put, the best single-player shooter ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Half-Life 2 compared to other single player shooters. What Valve has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there is an excellent shooter here. Half-Life 2 doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of first-person shooters to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure here.
Before I really get into the review, you should know the background of how this game was reviewed. Valve did not want to send out copies of their game (for fairly obvious reasons) before it was released to the public. In order to play the game, I, and several of my colleagues throughout the industry, took a trip up to Seattle to visit Valve in order to have some private time with the title. I was given a little room to myself where I could close the door, turn off the lights, click my little red slippers, and pretend that I was sitting at home. It worked for the most part, largely because I was so engrossed with the game that when I came out of my trance I often had to take a moment to get my bearings. Obviously, Valve was happy to bring me into a controlled environment for ideal playing conditions.
What's particularly impressive about the game running so well is that it does so without compromising any part of gameplay or design. Environments are complex, colorful, and highly detailed; AI is certainly impressive in that NPCs work as teams, flank, react to sound and movement, and then engage with lifelike aggression. But like I said, we're going to have to wait and see what the game runs like on a more standard system after it's released. Therefore, you can look for an additional supplement to this review about how the game runs on lower-end systems after i've had the chance to check.
So I Would Give This Game A 9.7/10

Grey Goo is a very traditional RTS. No hero units or unit leveling of any kind, minimal unit micro-management, a reasonably high unit cap and proper base building. It is also rather slow paced compared to the likes of Starcraft II.
The production values are suprisingly high. Music and audio are great and campaign cutscenes are very impressive. Maps themselves are quite beautiful as well, even if most of the units and buildings look rather bland.
Gameplay itself is very traditional. There's nothing wrong with this really, not every game needs to be super innovative. Especially in a genre which is pretty much dead these days. The game copies the classic Command & Conquer gameplay formula more or less intact.
The game has four playable factions, the Humans, the Beta, the Goo and the Shroud. Humans and beta are very traditional RTS races that play very similarly to each other. The titular Goo, however, are something much more unique.
The Goo don't have a traditional base at all and instead of collecting resources, mother goo units regenerate health while on a resource node. The mother goo can then sacrifice some of its health to create new units. This is certainly the most innovative aspect of the game. Unfortunately this also leads to some tedious micro-management and I wasn't personally a big fan of the playstyle.
The shroud were not part of the original game and were added in a later patch. They only appear as an enemy in a bonus campaign mission and are also available for skirmish and multiplayer games. I didn't end up seeing enough of them to get a good feel of how they play.
For the most part the unit design is quite boring for all factions, both visually and ability-wise. The ultimate Epic units are a lot more exciting, but they take a long time and lot of resources to build and you generally use only one per map.
The user interface is for the most part quite decent and pretty much what you would except in an RTS. All the usual hotkeys are there and the controls work the way you expect them to. It's missing a few of the more advanced features, but overall the UI is decent enough.
The campaign itself is passable but again nothing spectacular. The story is quite forgettable. Surely the titular grey goo (aka runaway self-replicating nanobots) could have been used to tell a more interesting story. Missions themselves are pretty standard fare for the most part, even if some of the missions spice up things a little bit. Personally I found the campaign difficulty surprisingly high. Usually I play single-player RTS games on hard, but after the first few missions I decided to switch to normal. Part of this difficulty does come from bad mission design, however, as a lot of missions have enemy units spawning from thin air.
Personally I find Grey Goo rather hard to recommend unless you are a big RTS fan looking for a new game to play. There's nothing really wrong with the game but despite the high production values it suffers from some bland design and doesn't bring anything new to the genre. Best to wait for a sale or a bundle with this one.
I played through the main campaign on normal and also finished the Emergence DLC mini-campaign. I also played a couple skirmish games against the AI. I don't normally play multiplayer with strangers, so I skipped that part of the game.
The good:
- Solid old-school RTS gameplay
- Beautiful cut-scenes
- Great music by Frank Klepacki (of C&C fame)
The bad:
- Visual design of the units and buildings is rather bland
- Some issues with unit balance
- Some annoying campaign missions
- Forgettable story
- Goo faction is interesting but ultimately not that fun to play
- Map visuals can be somewhat confusing at times and it's hard to tell what's passable terrain and what's not
- Very strict line of sight rules are too easy to exploit
The ugly:
- Performance could be better
- Saving and especially loading take a very long time

Easily my most favorite game in my library right now. Features a great blend of tactical turn-based combat mixed with a strategy layer that supplements your combat. The basic premise is that Earth has come under attack from an alien threat and XCOM, an internationally funded paramilitary unit, is called upon to defend our planet. Manage panic between nations, intercept UFOs, and research alien technology to beat back the aliens. The base game is fun but bug-ridden and lacking in content compared to the expansion, Enemy Within. Enemy Within fixes most of the bugs of the first version and adds a new three-mission side campaign, new customization options, new enemy units, and new XCOM equipment. Two other DLCs for this game add customization options and another three-mission side campaign. It would be best to wait for a sale, when you can catch the base game, expansion, and all the DLCs for 15 or so bucks.
If you finish and enjoy the game but feel it was too easy and you're willing to mod the game, consider the Long War mod, which dramatically changes the game with more missions, a fatigue system, weaker XCOM soldiers, stronger and smarter enemies, new soldier classes, more equipment, interceptor XP and more. The mod makes the game much harder and much more satisfying to win do to your struggle. I would not recommend trying this mod without beating the base game first on classic or higher difficulty. The mod requires all the DLC to function.
TDLR: Great turn-based strategy game. Much better with the expansion, Enemy Within, and the other DLCs. Wait for a sale to get it cheap, but definitely worth 60 dollars for the game and expansion. Long War mod overhauls the game and provides a different experience for those interested in more brutal gameplay, but requires the expansions.

The gameplay feels fun and fluid for the most part (though a little repetative at times), and the fact that it has a proper COOP campaign is great (especially when most people don't bother these days). Unfortunately though, the game lets itself down at the last few hurdles.
Without spoiling anything, if you plan on playing through the story with a friend, the door that leads to the very last "level" of "stuff" boots you into single-player without choice. So if you've cried blood and tears on an awesome playthrough together, be prepared for morbid disappointment when you find your session is cut short prematurely at the end.
The ending itself is also fairly lackluster. Relying on quicktime events for the final scenes and forcing you to do a running sequence just before that'll have you pulling your hair out with frustration.
The game also has an annoying tendency to abuse the same situation for it's boss fights. It will remove all of your weapons and then force you to fight with something basic like a pipe. This would be fine for the first boss or two, but when you have a detailed crafting system and wide weapon variation, it sucks that 90% of the time there is very little point in crafting or upgrading them. I managed to complete the game with the first three decent weapons I managed to get my hands on, which seems wrong somehow.
To briefly mention, I'm not a huge fan of the climbing mechanics. For the large part they're fine, but while climbing upward is normally as expected, climbing donwards is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you're on a high crane or spire.
It also doesn't handle restoring your weapons well either. You have to collect it as loose items again from a large bag, which means if your inventory was mostly full beforehand, it's a nightmare to get everything back the way it was due to held items not taking the same storage space as your stored items.
The story is somewhat forgettable and poorly written at times (we meet characters that are supposed to die poetically and break our hearts, but only after meeting them a few missions prior, thus we feel relatively little for the loss) and there are a few plot holes or things that could have been called back to for more interesting dramatic tension or resolution (such as the ominous green zombies that never seem to really return).
The music is pretty enjoyable though, mostly consisting of 80s-style synth drones.
Long story short; the game is fun when played with a friend, but the ending and some game mechanics are a bit of a let-down (Graphically it actually reminds me more of a game from around 2009, such as the 2009 Wolfenstein game).
I'd personally recommend grabbing a copy on sale at some point and running through it with a friend. It's definitely the best multiplayer Zombie title currently around. The actual gameplay combined with the multiplayer keeps this pretty fun for the most part, but I wouldn't recommend playing it alone. It'll get old pretty fast.

I recall being distinctly unimpressed with this game upon first release.  Yes, I was one of the throng who fondly remembered the original X-COM and believed that this game was a pale, dumbed-down remake for the console generation.
However, I recently dusted it off and gave it another try.  I've been pleasantly surprised.
I'm not going to sit here and say it's a great game, because the strategic part still feels to me like it's on rails and is way more restricting than I'd like.  I also won't go in to the myriad reasons why the strategic element is a let down, because three years after release you can bet everyone else has already covered all my possible gripes.
What I will say is that the tactical element has a lot more depth than I first gave it credit for.  I don't particularly care for the way the aliens are 'activated', but that aside the battlefield abilities of the various classes and the mechanics of cover and elevation make for a rewarding - sometimes even nail-biting - experience.
If you were sorely disappointed that this wasn't a direct X-COM remake when if fitst hit the shelves, maybe it's time you gave it another chance.  If you can overlook the controversially 'streamlined' elements of the strategic side you just might find an enjoyable squad-level tactical simulation underneath.
