it's riddled with bugs and design issues. so far I've encountered:
* Object hiding is completely insane and basically doesn't work. Sloped roofs never hide. Multiple-floor buildings generally hide all at once if there's objects of interest on more than one floor, making it difficult to manage soldiers on different elevations.
* Grenade/Rocket HUD does not accurately show what environmental objects will be hit and destroyed.
* Characters can move into or out of grenade/rocket explosions in real time, because it's based on real radius and not tiles occupied. Thus, depending on what animation a character is doing, they can dodge an explosion that should have hit or be hit by an explosion they were clear of a literal second ago.
* "Missed" shots can still pass hit characters, complete with blood effects. At least it doesn't do damage!
* 100% to-hit shots can still be missed if they somehow don't connect with the enemy in question. This will fail to do damage.
* The skyranger sometimes just doesn't land at XCom HQ. It'll be shown moving on the geoscape world map, but the game will be soft-locked at this point and you have to Alt-F4. (The pause menu is not usable.)
* Combat Stims straight up do not work. Item is not depleted when used, and does not confer any benefits when used. It still takes a round-ending action to try, though.
* VIPs in escort missions can be killed before you have control of them. This is hopefully unintended behaviour.
* Soemtimes, escort missions will give control over civilians who aren't the VIP to escort. If these civilians die, the mission will fail. They are not targeted if you don't have control over them, but aliens will try to kill them if you do have control. (Oddly enough, they count as VIPs and will end the mission if you escort a body guard or generic soldier to the escape zone instead of the prescribed VIP.)
* Enemy groups don't move on lines, and just teleport from point to point. Because of this, enemy groups can teleport to closer range than where the fog ends, making for bizarre overwatch behaviours and easy flanking/point blank shots for them after being activated if you don't kill the whole group immediately.
* Enemy groups can activate such that one or more members of the group will phase through a wall. Occasionally, they will phase into normally inaccessable areas, such as the insides of shipping containers or closed rooms without doors/windows. In these cases, if you don't have explosives, the mission is effectively impossible to complete as the alien cannot leave the space and you cannot breach it to kill the alien.
* Enemy airdropped troops can land directly inside your soldiers. Oddly, shots on aliens that are occupying the same tile as you are counted as being pretty far away (but not infinitely far) and will generally have a mediocre aim chance instead of the 100% you usually get from point-blank shots.
* Destroyed cover objects generate fog of war where they were. This fog takes real time to clear; a shot that seemingly broke LOS by interfering with peeking behaviour on full-cover objects usually just made the game confused, and not doing anything for a minute or two of real time will bring the alien back into view. When this happens on alien turns, the enemy stops moving until the glitched fog clears.
* Enemies in cover who have their cover destroyed often retain the cover state they were last in when the cover was destroyed for several real-time moments, similar to above.
* Overwatch shots made by aliens have a tendency to make the camera linger on nothing of note. May also be related to above.
* Soldiers may have the HUD note that they can see an alien, but trying to select "Fire" or any similar action says that there is nothing in range. Sometimes waiting real time will fix the problem and make the supposedly seen alien able to be fired upon, but not every time.
* Left-clicking a door occasionally causes the soldier to charge through the door and stand in the doorframe instead of quietly opening the door from the side.
*The perk Rapid Reaction sometimes fails, and the Heavy will not get a second reaction fire opportunity despite hitting the first overwatch shot on an approaching enemy.
* Putting a SHIV in front of a door breaks the door forever, and makes each tile on boths sides of the door impassable terrain.
* Open doors sometimes become impassable terrain when loading a save made during a mission.
* Fire occasionally clears or spreads in the middle of a turn, making a space impassible one moment and passable again the next.
* Thin Man poison generates on the corpse in real space much like explosions, with many of the same bugs. Women are better at not getting poisoned just because their models are smaller so they have less of a chance of being hit by a random particle!
* Dense Smoke is insanely GPU-taxing for no clear reason. Several normal smokes in the same space run fine, but a single Dense Smoke tanks the framerate. Oddly, Combat Drugs smoke is less taxing than normal smoke despite having more particles to draw (it includes blue flakes in addition to the normal smoke)
* Hitting a Muton Berserker and causing it to move on the player turn makes the game stutter very severely for no clear reason.
* Berserkers rarely trigger Close Combat Specialist's free Overwatch strike, but sometimes do. Seems to do with their intent to melee.
* Close Combat Specialist can trigger multiple times. It also triggers when movement begins within the 4 tile radius, such as an enemy panicking and attempting to flee from your CCS-having soldier. Not sure if that's intended.
* Skeleton Suit and Ghost Armor grappling sometimes fails. The action is spent and the animation plays, but the charcater then teleport to their original position and the tile they attempted to grapple to becomes impassable terrain for the remainder of the round. If this triggers on the last action of the turn, the soldier gets a "free" actions back (though the HUD won't show a pip denoting the action is available), but if it was the first action, it is completely wasted. Soldiers who can fire without spending an action (e.g. In The Zone sniping, activating Run&Gun, etc) can do so normally before doing anything that would consume the action.
* Cars and other explosive objects can catch fire and explode, and then be set aflame again and explode again even though they've already exploded.
* Overwatch sometimes fails, leaving the soldier unable to use any abilities (including basic Fire, Hunker Down, etc.) but somehow retaining actions. They can move, but not do anything else.
* Overwatch sometimes fails, consuming the action and leaving the soldier supposedly in overwatch, but aliens can run directly across their view and the soldier will not even attempt a reaction shot.
*Starting the game without an audio device installed and active (i.e. your headphones/speakers are unplugged or off for whatever reason) will cause the game to never have audio for that session.
And that's just the bugs.

This game is different from other tower defense games since it lets you defend AND attack at the same time. That's about it's only advantage.
This game is below average at best. It is lacking balance, polish, it is lacking interesting upgrades, lacking transparency in numbers and stats on towers. What is the exact damage of my towers? What is the exact bonus against so and so? The game tells you nothing about the details, which is a shame considering most people who play this genre are people who like number crunching and optimising, and this game won't let you do so.
But mostly what kills it for me is the lack of a "goal". Lack of that sens of "am i doing good or bad? how good I am doing?". The single player missions seem pointless, as the game does not tell you how other people did, and gives you no score or achievement to aim for. I played the first level for an hour, survived everything and upgraded everything, yet i felt like i wasted an hour... What was the point? Againt you can't compare your performance and have no point of reference, so the whole thing is an exercice in futility no matter how well you do.
It seems the developers want you to jump into multiplayer and go against other people. But I do not believe that the system  is robust enough for multiplayer, the upgrades, towers, stats, units, nothing seems optimised, balanced, or even transparent in what it does and that is really unatractive for someone looking for a competitive game.

This is easily the best "walking simulator" I've played. I hate to be one of those people that gets pretentious about artistic video games so I'll try to remain as objective as possible but it is a very beautiful, well crafted game. More importantly, it needs to be a game. A lot of "walking sims" catch flak because some people think they would make better books or movies or are otherwise unsuited to the video game medium but Beyond Eyes has a very dynamic way of presenting the world and even though it doesn't have any traditional gameplay, it does have plenty of mechanics.
First a little about the story. You play as Rae, a young girl who is currently blind but was not born that way. You have a little orange friend by the name of Nani who happens to be a cat. One day Nani neglects to stop by to visit. After not seeing him for awhile you decide it's time to venture out and find him.
Now this is where things get interesting. Being blind, Rae's world begins as a blank slate, a white canvas. She adds things to her world by experiencing them with her remaining senses. This means things you have to touch like walls, trees, etc will only be added to her world when you're right on top of them. Things she can hear like a flowing river or a bird's song are added from further away since she can hear them before being able to touch them. It sounds fairly basic but the game has a number of mechanics that are delivered to you each chapter. If you want to know about them, read the next paragraph or skip it if you want to experience them firsthand for yourself. I'll keep from spoiling anything specific, though.
The first chapter presents you with two mechanics, the touching VS hearing one I just explained and the difference between permanence and impermanence. As Rae senses permanent objects like trees and walls, they remain in her world even when she walks away from them. They're in her mind's eye. As she experiences impermanent objects like animals that can move around of their own accord, however, they only appear briefly while making sound. The next chapter presents you with the mechanic of misunderstanding. You may hear something far away and Rae adds it to her world as what she imagines it to be but upon closer inspection it may turn out to be something else and so she may react to the difference and change the object in her mind's eye. The next chapter presents you with impermanent permanent objects. Just because an object can't move on it's own doesn't mean it can't ever move. You find out that maybe a box or gate that was barring your passage and added to your world was changed in your absence and only upon re-examining them will the change be reflected in Rae's world. There are more mechanics but you can experience the rest for yourself.
In addition to the dynamic world, though, the game also has a dynamic atmosphere. The world of a blind person could have been represented as a dull gray world devoid of features but Rae is a young girl, full of imagination. The empty world starts off bright white and as you fill it with objects, they're very colorful... while she's happy. She also has her own fears, though, especially since she's trekking out on her own for the first time. Certain encounters will color her world dark. The world literally reflects her feelings in the moment since it's all being seen with her mind's eye. It's one thing to see Rae moan and shrink away from things she fears but to see her entire world painted black because of it is rather powerful.
In summary, I think this game does an exceptional job telling the story it set out to tell. Just judging it on that alone, I'd give it a 10/10. There are a couple things people might not like, though. Firstly, you have to walk everywhere. Hey, you're a little blind girl. You shouldn't expect to sprint around the place. You have to be prepared to take this game at a slow pace. Secondly, it's about a 3 hour experience for $15 but you could probably complete it in 2 hours if you just bee-lined it to the exit every chapter. As such, the price might be a little off-putting. I highly recommend this but you might want to wait for a sale.

Hola, Amigos! It is I, your humble servant, Presidente, here to tell you about the glorious life that awaits you in Tropico... the Fourth!
I love this game. Love it. Can't even begin to express how much love I have for it. Ask me what my most anticipated game at present is, and it's not the next big AAA experience, nor some indie puzzle darling, heck, part of me might even tell you it's not the games I'm trying to make. My most anticipated video game at present is Tropico 5, and that's entirely due to the strength of its predecessor. This game's steady stream of DLC, which recently ended, always got me amazingly excited, and I always tried to buy them whenever I could. As City builders go, it's accessible in all the right ways. Simple, but not dumb.
First off, it's one of the most chill games I've ever played, not in its attitude, but in mine, while I play it. With Tropico 4, I like to sit back, relax, smile, and play. The game's script and attitude makes me chuckle--it's a humorous game, and one of the funniest titles to have been released in 2011 (has it really been that long?). There are tons of buildings that all work well together, and the new DLC buildings almost all feel as integral to the gameplay as the stuff that came before.
Modern Times, the game's large expansion, was superb, sporting a large campaign that, among other things, involved building a ton of shanties to create a mirror to reflect a giant space laser.
One thing that really makes Tropico 4 great, though, is the way choice and consequence works. Decisions you make early on in the game can prove to have incredibly positive benefits by the game's end. Or, of course, they can hurt you and drag things out. But... it's hard to lose, and that's a good thing. It's not that it's easy to win, it's just simply hard to completely fail the game. I can't even begin to tell you how many times I've hit a negative balance in my account, only to come out swinging with $50,000 and $60,000 balances quickly stacking up after. Winning is fun, and losing's so rare, it's hard to feel bad about.
The game is fun, but hey, you don't have to take my word for it, because there's a demo. Go pick it up. Kick back, relax, and give it a go. Have fun. And then realize that Tropico 4's going to give you a ton more of that, but with even more varied and diverse stuff.
Tropico is yours for the making.

Isn't it ironic that a videogame about blindness defines itself over its visuals?
Enough of being awkwardly funny, let's get to the story:
A little girl called Rae loses her eyesight due to fireworks. After that she lives a more quiet life, spends time with herself in the garden until she makes friends with a strange cat. One day the cat stops vising her and Rae leaves home in order to look for her new friend.
"Beyond Eyes" is a walking simulator that's all about the question how you would master the search if you lost your sense of orientation. That's why you stand in a completely white world and only if you're right next to or in front of something or somebody it's revealed what you're at. It also plays with sounds, for instance: sometimes Rae hears cat meows but are they really her friend's sounds? Or is a woodpecker doing that knocking sound or a traffic light? So the main challenge is to find your path to the end of the current chapter, nearer to your beloved feline friend.
I give this game a thumbs up but only for the visual experience. When you play it the first time it's quite impressing to explore an environment you can't see until everything unfolds itself right around you. The graphics are not hyperrealistic or something, they mean to be subtle and rich in colours at the same time.
Even though I wouldn't call the game a way to experience how blindness must be (after all, you'd need your sense or hearing, smelling and touching harder than this) it's an interesting experience at all.
But the downside is that this gimmick ways off very fast. I admit that I got very very tired after playing for about half and hour. This is because of three details that turn into disadvantages (in my opinion):
1. Rae walks very slowly. I get it, blind people cannot just run around as long as they're in unknown environments but this also turns the game very long. You need to explore everything around you in order to find paths (and to find scenes for Steam achievents). So prepare for a frustratingly slow gameplay.
2. Aside from the sound effects, there's hardly any music. At first I enjoyed this as I could concentrate on the sounds like birds singing and raindrops falling. But after a while I played my own selection of piano music in the background so the game would turn at least a bit less dull and quiet.
3. You get used to the graphics very fast. As I said, when you played it for the first time it's very beautiful and seems like something new. But as you progress, the game just looks nice then and you just try to get through it.
It's not really a bad game, no disaster, but it's not "Game of the Year" material in my opinion.
If you like walking simulators or are just too curious about this concept, feel free to try it out but better wait for a price discount (currently it costs about 13 Euros here on Steam).

Half Life 2 Review Raymond KT
Summary: [Metacritic's 2004 PC Game of the Year] By taking the suspense, challenge and visceral charge of the original, and adding startling new realism and responsiveness, Half-Life 2 opens the door to a world where the player's presence affects everything around him, from the physical environment to the behaviors -- even the emotions -- of both friends and enemies. The player again picks up the crowbar of research scientist Gordon Freeman, who finds himself on an alien-infested Earth being picked to the bone, its resources depleted, its populace dwindling. Freeman is thrust into the unenviable role of rescuing the world from the wrong he unleashed back at Black Mesa. And a lot of people -- people he cares about -- are counting on him. [Vivendi Universal]
Half-Life 2 has the most varied gameplay of any shooter since Half-Life, with strikingly distinctive missions. In one, you drive an amphibious vehicle along canals, occasionally disembarking to kill soldiers guarding gates. In a later mission, you must avoid lion ants, monstrous insects that will attack anyone who walks on the sand above their burrows, by using your antigravity gun to create bridges and pathways out of scrap wood and boxes. The lion ants are transformed from enemy to friend when you gain control of them and can send swarms against soldiers.
Even elements from the original game are reimagined. Zombies with alien creatures attached to their heads now make mournful groans and hurl boxes and barrels at you with palpable anger. The barnacle, which attaches itself to the ceiling and uses its long tongue to suck up prey, will suck up an explosive barrel rolled beneath it, with predictable results.
Half-Life 2's almost photorealistic visuals are wonderfully detailed, easily beating the competition. The blades of a low-flying helicopter stir up the water beneath. Wrecked cars litter the highway, one of many signs of some great catastrophe. A powerful robot that acts like a frolic comically yet dangerously. The environment is also wonderfully malleable, allowing you to stack boxes or, with the help of your antigravity gun, grab a radiator and use it as both shield and weapon.
One of the original Half-Life's biggest achievements was the way it seamlessly provided purpose and a context for all the violence, keeping you from feeling as though you were just running around randomly shooting stuff. Half-Life 2 does the same thing, choreographing events in a way that keeps you enthralled and on track.
Yet, while Half-Life 2 offers a denser plot and more distinct characters, the story is ultimately less involving. The game only drops hints as to the cause of this grim future and never bothers to explain the motivation of your main foe, City 17's administrator. The designers did create a back story, which you can explore at
, but for some reason they chose not to include it in the game.
Yet no other game does as many things as well as Half-Life 2; I had so much fun that I can forgive the game its abysmal ending. I was continually enthralled and amazed, and would rather replay Half-Life 2 than begin a new first-person shooter. I envy those of you who are about to experience Half-Life 2 for the first time. Although I pity you for having to install it.

Grey Goo is a throwback to the good old days of strategy games. It takes a lot of inspiration of the RTS's which preceded it, and that's a good thing because a new entry in the genre was sorely needed.
I only played through the single player, so I can not comment on how good this game is in multiplayer or how balanced it is. What I can say is that the single player part is very well done. There are 3 main factions and as you progress through the campaign you get to play as each one of them. One of the factions is humans and I have to say it is quite refreshing how they are approached as a faction. Usually in other games humans are presented as a relatively low tech, numerous faction. In Grey Goo the reverse is true, the spot usually occupied by humans is taken by another faction, called the Betas. And the story is more focused on them than any other faction, even the humans, which is a nice change of pace from the traditional formula of presenting the story (mostly) from the human point of view.
In between every single mission you are presented with a CGI cutscene, all of which are beautifully made. They are a bit on the shorter side, most likely due to the sheer number of them. However it feels like a real reward for when you finish a mission. In that respect Grey Goo is very much structured as a traditional RTS. There is barely any story development going on during the missions, you get most of it from the cutscenes. Personally, I like this approach, especially when the cutscenes are as well made as they are here.
I really hope there is a sequel to this game, and what I would like for them to work on is how the third faction plays, the Grey Goo. I have to say that I didn't enjoy playing as that faction nearly as much as I did the others. Although I appreciate the fact that they tried to deviate from the formula of base building which the other two factions employ. And I would really like it if they put an even bigger focus on story, with longer and more elaborate cutscenes. However I do realize this is very expensive and would only be an option if Grey Goo was a big success, and sadly I don't think it actually was.

Grey Goo is the closest thing to StarCraft II without actually being StarCraft II. The best part of it is playing as the Goo faction, because they have no "buildings" -- all their stuff moves. This makes even a moderately skilled Goo player nearly impossible to kill. Which means that the Goo faction is not fun to play against for the very same reason. Tracking down every last goo after having broken any serious resistance can make games drag on, and somewhat harms the pacing of the single player campaign, until you get to play as the Goo faction and then it's awesome.
The games feel a little slow compared to StarCraft, but the units are clearly distinguishable visually so you will be able to get a pretty clear idea of what's happening, which makes Grey Goo far above most other StarCraft clones out there. (I'm looking at you, Achron!!)
The developers of Grey Goo are real good guys and deserve your support. They added an entire fourth faction to the game long after release FOR FREE! That shows some real Blizzard level dedication to post-release support, and ultimately that's what Grey Goo seems to be at it's core: a well-executed Blizzard fan game.
So my conclusion is: Get StarCraft II. Play all the campaigns of StarCraft II. And if you are still wanting more StarCraft II after exhausting all the StarCraft II content, then Grey Goo is totally your jam, son.

-about myself and TL:DR
After passing 1000 hours in-game and still playing pretty steady, feels like I've pretty much seen it all, and have the background now to write a real review for anyone at all interested. And I'll try to touch on every aspect so TL:DR; Try Block N Load, it's fun, it's FREE, and we need more players!
-Intro
Block N Load is a block-craft style defend and attack, build and destroy, 5v5 objective based game with arenas completely destroyable for you to alter to your advantage. So you can see how creativity and innovation come into play here. Some people categorize it as FPS but take that with a grain of salt cause there's so many aspects to the game it's hard to give it a category. For comparison I'd say a fusion between the combat mechanics of Valve's 'TeamFortress2' and the build mechanics of Mojang's 'Minecraft'.
-the maps
There's a fair amount of official arenas that cycle through what's called map rotation for what shows up in online play, and in pre-game lobby you'll get three maps randomly drawn to choose from based on a vote system. The Arenas range in size and also Cube Cores(the objective each team can destroy to win.) There can be 1, 2 or 3 Cube Cores on any arena that usually coincide with the size of the map and how long the match is gonna last. What's interesting about these arenas is not all of them are official Jagex made, a lot are community made and have their own themes and playstyles. the Devs actually added the map builder tool for free use by anyone inclined enough to create their own, no catch, its completely free. I mean I have to tip my hat for that addition. There's been so many awesome maps ever since that wouldn't exist otherwise. And if your map doesn't quite cut it for online play you can still publish and play it in custom games. Refer to game guides for more information about 'Cube Cores' and map strats aka. 'map cuts' things you should know about.
-the heroes
Part 1 - buying the heroes. So the bad news is this is kinda where the free to play generates its revenue cause to unlock a hero you can either accumulate the free currency called 'gold' or you can buy 'platinum' with actual real money. The free version called gold takes forever to accumulate from winning games to be able to afford just ONE hero, let alone all of them. If youre after the full collection youre looking at months of grinding to unlock them all for free... That said there's good news about this too. There's what's called hero rotation with three free to play heroes at a time, which will change periodically like every couple weeks or something. So youre basically stuck with free rotation heroes until you have enough gold for your first owned hero. Same thing applies to perks, each hero has unique perks for that gold currency, and there's also general perks in offensive and defensive respective classifications. Refer to guides for more information on hero perks, as there are hundreds of them, and literally thousands of combinations to create here.
Part 2 - mechanics. Block N Load has three classifications for their heroes. Brawn roles have greater health and usually pack more of a punch with explosives, rockets, mortars, and overall demolition kits, and also have the exclusive ability to place radars and respawn pads. Brain roles have CC (crowd control) kits that are placements, and generally rely heavily on their placements, but have extreme area denial when used correctly, and their exclusive blocks are healthpacks and ammopacks. Skill roles don't provide much utility to their team but make up for it in kill capability, as all skill roles come with pretty low health, but extremely high damage output values, "glass cannon" if you will. And with all of this said, keep in mind each hero has their own unique primary and secondary weapon as well. Pros and cons of the classification system is it's simple and easy to learn, Brawns generally attack, and brains usually defend. So a lot of the time games depend on the pre-game lobby team composition. The basic meta is 2 brain defenders for their health and ammo packs / 2 brawn attackers for their radars and spawn pads / 1 skill role slayer for mid field control, but this almost never happens lol. So the team comp can sometimes decide the match before it even starts which can be pretty annoying.
-the gameplay
Normal online gameplay consists of entering que either solo or up to a 3 player squad. Once match is found your team has to pick composition based on who wants to attack and who wants to defend, and discuss any special strats or map cuts you're doing before the game starts. When the game starts there's a 5 minute build phase with a massive barrier between both sides as to make any contact impossible. In this 5 minute phase teams generally find large parts of the map to cut the bottom horizontally to make everything above it fall and gain that as bricks (not actual bricks) you get a wallet based on how much you farmed to be able to place things in your kit. You only start out with a little bit that's why people do map cuts or farm to max out their wallet before starting setting up defense. But not to confuse wallet bricks with actual bricks, you can actually load up literal bricks in your kit to build brick walls if you want to. There are plenty of blocks to choose from to build walls or whatever you want, but after 5 minutes is up, whether or not either side has their base set up, the barrier falls and it's open-ended from there anything can happen. The Cube Cores have a healthbar that drops as you hit it with your dig tool, deplete the cube health to zero to win.
-feelings in summary
Been a gamer for all my life and Block N Load has been good enough, on par actually for me to main with my other favorites. Hands down one of the best free to play online games I've played and it's just sad that the community's so small. Wish more people knew about it. No two matches are ever the same, meta is dependant on the players cause there's just endless possibility there's always new genius strats popping up and new base set ups you have to sit back and marvel at. I don't know any other competitive game with the complexity and freedom to build that this game comes with. Visual experience is pleasing, crisp and clean, stylistic, and original. The heroes and their respective blocks, abilities and weapons are all very pleasing and original. Very fun to play at any level of experience. As an end note I've had so much fun with this game I highly recommend it to everyone of all age groups, as it's free to play, and at least worth a try.

While I think the game is worth every dollar I spent into it for the time I put into it so far, after 44 hours of gameplay, the game did one thing that was so bad that I don't know if I can forgive it. It really made me upset to the point of questioning whether or not I want to continue playing anymore.
The game right now gave me a side quest which started out with creatures 3 levels past mine, but the hundreds that spawn in every few feet are easy to kill so long as they don't hit me, so I pushed forward, the last boss to complete the quest was up, after dying twice, I killed it and was rewarded a skeleton key, I open the door to find out there's a time limit to complete whatever is inside, and I also cannot create a rift in case I die either. So I go in to see what levels the creatures were and discovered that they were insanely high compared to mine, so I went to task manager and ended task to prevent the game from saving. I go back in the game to find out that the quest is still done, but I don't have the key and the door is locked again with no way to get the key back. Oh and it took several attempts to rush through the millions of creatures in my way so I could check to see if the door was locked, because insanely slow progress instead of balanced difficulty and ingenuity is what devs do. Why couldn't the game just take a massive dump on my face too while it was at it? I mean seriously... why purposely punish the players like that? The amount of laziness and lack of polish I see everywhere can be forgiven when it doesn't punish the players in a big way, but this... this was done on purpose.
Buy it if you don't like Diablo 3 style and miss the Diablo 2 style with a side order of other complicated stuff that isn't explained well and requires some online research to figure out. I just wish it had the budget and pride of a Blizzard game.
I will likely add a lot more to this review later when I'm a lot less frustrated.

First let me set some context:
1. I love MMOs

I really wanted to like this game, and the first 55 levels or so went quick, learned a lot and generally enjoyed the level treadmill up to that point.  There were no dungeons or instances, just some open world stuff with lots of "grindiness" toss in here or there.  I ignored most of it in favor of blowing stuff up and leveling and doing the main story quests.
Pros:
Good graphics
Fun combat
Large rich world
Cons:
You have to AFK Play to level crafting/non combat skills up.  (I only played about 50 hours, rest was AFK fishing)
You have to do boring monotonous things like walk in circles with a back pack on for days on end (or AFK play) to get things like "higher max weight" so you can hold things.
The max level equipment grind is such a grind that I LOL'd after my first night of leveling up my first good weapon and uninstalled.  You have to use stones to upgrade your weapons, but when it fails it lowers the max durability of the weapon, and you have to use more expesive stones or exact same weapon and destroy them to increase your durability back up.  This isn't something you just have to invest a little time in, the end game for equpiment is a game of grinding.  They basically made a cash sink in end game weapon upgrades and it is so horrible and silly that it ruined the game.  I spent $20-$30 on some cosmetic items, some weight increase, inventory expansion, I ♥♥♥♥♥ed about that but hey it was only $9.95, so I don't mind putting some money in for the quality of life items.  However, it was like this game was made to just annoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.  Let's fail at upgrading 20 times in a row, so now you have +20 to your next upgrade, awesome, lets use it on a really good item, nope sorry failed again.  +40?  nope failed...  meanwhile its millions of silver for each failure.  It was like someone said, how can we put in mechanics that require everyone to stop doing the fun part of the game and focus on the tedious time consuming uneventful frustrating part so they can be slightly better at the fun part?
I'm just griping now, I'm sure some will like the "hardcore" nature of the game, but I don't find it hard, just tedious and timeconsuming.  It is all about just time commitment and how much BS you are willing to put up with, the game turns into "WORK" at 55/56, and I don't have enough time in my week for gaming to spend it WORKING instead of playing.

I love Diablo clones, or aRPG as they are called. Grim Dawn however is simply BAD. I start with pros because there is a few:
PROS:
1) interesting class system - combination of classes can be powerful and anybody will find something for him/her.
2) devotion system - finding shrines and upgrading constellations for another bonuses and skills is fun.
3) not bad lore learning by finding notes etc.
CONS:
1) uninteresting level designs - almost all levels are plains or dungeons "painted" in shades of brown and black with addition of yellow and red.
2) uninteresting enemies - almost all enemies are human or human-like, most game time player will fight zombies and skeletons with some cultists, bosess are simply bigger versions of zombies/skeleton/bandits etc (with few exeptions).
3) absolutly no balance between player character and bosess - most are far more powerful than player on level when player encounters them making no fun or challenging fights, but kite around them for few blows then run or teleport to city/another location for healing then repeat whole process.
4) boring boss design - almost all boses have some skills, but mostly they summon something and then attack from distance - this pattern is used on almost all battle, be it random "hero monster" on map or level boss.
5) grindfest to the max - all equipment and craft components must be farmed - that is ok - but killing boss X-times to get another part of eg. his soul (needed 4) is boring.
6) character builds are gear dependant so grind more to get desired gear (and something really interesting drops at surprisingly low rate)
7) story is uninspiring - player do not get immersed into world he/she need to save, most time even do not remember who to kill and why.
I do not recommend this game unless discount is 75%.

Tropico 4 is a pretty standard city management sim, except it takes place on the islands of Tropico where you are free to be as dictatorial as you want. You may commit election fraud, kill protestors, create a secret police, and embezzle money into your swiss bank account. All that said, I was struck by how incredibly similar this game is to the previous one.
If you own and have played Tropico 3 and you feel like you got about all you could out of that game, there is nothing for you here. If you are new to the series, this is as good a place as any to jump in. Unfortunately this game requires you to register for yet another 3rd party service you will probably rarely ever use unless you are a big Kalypso fan.
Another aspect to mention is that the game is not very clear on how some of the buildings and functionalities work. For instance when you place certain buildings you can see the landscape is shaded. When placing a farm, the greener areas are areas where your crops will have an easier time growing, when placing a police station it shows you areas of high crime in red, etc. But for some buildings it is not clear what the colours are really indicating. For instance, should you try to place a garbage dump close to red areas, which are presumably pollution? I wouldn't think so, because they just concentrate into one spot... so why even show it? Instinctively I would place my garbage dumps away from city areas, and I'm unsure what the indication really does to help. Maybe that isn't the best example but there are others.
Also construction slows down immensely once your town grows into even moderate size. I keep building more and more construction yards but it doesn't seem to help, and some buildings will simply never be built unless they are prioritised.
Thankfully the game is incredibly forgiving so all the issues can largely be overlooked. If you ever are in need of funds foreign powers will simply give you aid, and you'll find in most cases this makes it impossible to 'lose' by running out of money (if it even is possible...).
Overall it's worth a play if you're new to the series, but there isn't a big improvement over the last iteration.

I find it utterly hilarious how people bash this game for not delivering on the ''survival'' aspect. Nobody said it would be survival, its is Farcry in the primal age and it does it well.
So, my personal opinion so far after gloriously riding my blood drenched sabertooth into battle is that its a solid and interesting new edition to the farcry franchise. A breath of fresh air in a franchise that direly needed it. The combat is visceral and hilariously satisfying. From the thumping sound of hitting someone with a club to watching your badass pet take down a person in the most merciless of ways.
Gathering is solid and for the first time to me, actually fun. I dunno if its actually different or I finally let it in but its a lot more satisfying then it used to be to me. Building up your village is somewhat meh but it is pretty fun to watch it grow and gain the new abilities associated with it.
If you like visceral combat, satisfying hunts and a decent story. I don't see why you shouldn't get this game. If you expect ARK... why not get that game instead?

This is not a game, per se, but an extremely touching experience of art. If you purchase this with the mindset of it being a game that will keep you entertained for several hours, you will be disappointed. Beyond Eyes is a story about a young girl named Rae who lost her vision to an accident. She befriends a cat she names Nani who keeps her company during a difficult transitional period in her life. One day, Nani fails to show up and Rae sets off to find Nani.
Initially, the entire is world is little more than a white backdrop. As you walk, the sounds you hear help to map out the area, highlighting walls, fences, paths, etc. based on the sounds Rae interprets. Animals that sound frightening may very well be a harmless thing, though these fears of the unknown keep Rae from continuing on her path until she finds some way to bypass that which frightens her.
I will not say much, as I do not want to spoil the short story but I will say that the art, sound and music within the game  helps the player empathise with Rae and her disability.
I would highly recommend this for those who want a touching story.

I wanted to like Beyond Eyes, I really did.  It had an original idea, with a beautiful visual style and the possibility of some interesting mechanics.
But then I started playing it, and that's when it all fell apart...
This is a very soft recommendation.  If you're genuinly curious about this game, or you got it from a Humble Bundle, then you owe the game a playthrough.  It's not a great game, or even, in my opinion, a good game, but it is interesting enough to try.
My biggest issue stems from the games central idea.  Since you're playing as a blind girl, you're unable to perceive anything in the game world unless it's making a sound, or it's directly in front of you.  This encourages exploration, and since Rae seems to have a pretty good memory, she can remember just about everything about where she has already been.  It's a lot like dealing with the Fog of War in an RTS, but from a more personal perspective.
The downside is that you often don't realize you're walking into a dead end until a wall or other obstruction appears right in front of you.  This leads to a lot of frustrated wandering.  You spend a decent chunk of the game hugging a wall or fence, looking for the gate into a new area, or backtracking because once you realize you've just spent two minutes going the wrong way.
And that's when my other major gripe with the game pops up.  It's one thing to have to backtrack, but having to do it over and over with Raes sluggish walking speed.  I haven't wanted a run button this bad since Gone Home.
The obvious counterpoint to these gripes is that the game is making an ernest attempt at replicating the experience of navigating an unfamiliar environment while blind; an effort that is both successful and admirable, yet seriously damages the overall gameplay.  Maybe there just isn't a good way to gamify blindness.
But even after managing to endure the gameplay issues, there's still not a whole lot to praise.  There's a simple story with a final emotional payoff that is both underwelming and predicable.  Replay value is almost completely non-existant; two or three hours is all you need to really need to see everything.

Grey Goo is a game that deserves a good hard look from anyone that enjoys RTS gameplay.  It's not as in depth as say Supreme Commander or Planetary Annalhation, but there is plenty of good things here to keep RTS players interested.
Each race has it's own feel to it and will be played diffrently.  While each race may have units that share roles like light fighters,  artillery,  etc.  They have diffrent methods of play and diffrent upgrades that make them behave diffrently.  They also have at a diffrent Epic unit that has it's own strengths and querks without either one being totally over powered compared to the other.
There is only one resource; catalyst.  This is placed on key locations on the map and is sure to be a point of conflict for players.
The Beta bring firepower and typical gun units to pumel their threats into submission.
The Humans are arguably (one of) the most advanced race in the game, which is a diffrent take compared to most RTS games.  They are heavly dependant on resources, but have some advanced features like teleporting and walls that will let allies fire through them while keeping out the bad guys.
The game's namesake, the Grey Goo, is a very interesting group that most RTS players should give a shot at playing if only to get a feel for a new way of playing RTS.  All Goo units are made up of the Goo and so you must decide if you want to strengthen your primary "building", build a massive light army, build a smaller army of stronger units, and / or use the mass you gain from Catalyst to focuse on creating more Mother Goo for massive expansion.  A good player will do a mix of all.  I dont recall any RTS game that I've played that is quite like this race, but I hope to see more traits of the Goo implemented.

The fact that this faction was added as a bonus as free DLC to all players later on along with a new mission raises my already good opinion of the devs.
In addition to gameplay this game has a very interesting storyline, good graphics, and fantastic voice acting.   There are plenty of plot twists that happen in the game.  Some of them are expected some not so much.   All the while presented in a nice pretty format to keep you interested.

+ Similar to games like Command and Conquer and Starcraft (yet not nearly as fast paced). I absolutely loved the pacing of the game. If you enjoyed C&C 3 Tiberium Wars or Kane's Wrath, you will likely find yourself at home with this game.
+ Amazing soundtrack with some truly epic songs
+ Very unique story setup / campaign. You actually start off playing as the alien "Beta" race who is seemingly being invaded by humans and "The Goo". You then play as the humans and find out the humans accidentally created the goo and team up with the Betas to defeat the Goo. Then you get to play as the Goo.
+ Visually the game looks excellent, rivaling other RTS games and often exceeding my expectations.
+ Great level design that are often very colorful and pleasent to gaze at while encourage exploring.
+ The 3 races you get to play as are all very unique with a variety of different units, and unique building mechanics that you will need to learn to excel in the game.
+ Every mission is story based and have unique objectives which keeps the campaign from getting repetitive.
+ Super Units, although costly you can make truly grand scale units like a flying fortress that shoots nukes, has turrets, and can manufacture units. The Beta's have an enourmous sentinel that fires a highly destructive laser.
+ Quite a lot of content. I believe there's 16 full missions + 3 DLC missions which will take around 10hours+ to finish
- The difficulty in this game is a bit too high. I found that even playing on Easy was a challenge at times, especially when trying to learn which units I needed to build as each mission is dramatically different.
- The story itself and character development is lacking in some areas. I often found myself being a bit confused on what was happening.
- The name of the game... "Grey Goo" is just silly to me, and likely caused this game to fall into obscurity far too quickly. Even in game hearing lines like "We must warn them about the Goo!!" is just laughable. I really wish they would have chosen a better name. Perhaps something like "Molecular Nanobots" would have been more fitting.
- The ending story-wise was pretty poorly scripted and a bit odd to be honest. Basically every race ends up pointing fingers at one another. The Goo basically stops at nothing to get the catalyst they need to defend against "The Silent Ones" who are planet destroying aliens you face at the end of the game. The Betas (Alien Race) are just trying to survive, and were unfairly attacked by the humans and the goo, and blame the Humans for creating the Goo. The Humans are caught in the middle trying to destroy the Goo even though the Goo are trying to ultimately defend the Humans from the Silent Ones.  (Confusing? Yeah.... )
- The DLC campaign in my opinion should have been part of the main campaign. It's sort of like they just removed a chunk of the campaign and put it as DLC, and it contains some pretty important story elements concerning Singelton which was never explained in the main campaign.
~ The multiplayer is fun, but the community is largely dead so I would not suggest buying this for multiplayer.

"Grey Goo" is beautifully produced, but ultimately disappointing.
Let's start with the positives.
This game has a grand setting and top-shelf art. The cinematics, though not having as much action as a Blizzard production, absolutely CAN compete with Blizzard in terms of character design and visual quality. My jaw also dropped for the Beta and Human mission briefings, as those often featured cinematically rendered and composited characters that were big and lifelike.
And, of course, the realtime graphics look as good as you would expect.
As a piece of art, this title stands up to the heavy hitters. I actually wish Grey Box would make a movie of this universe, because it seems like they have most of the necessary assets on hand, along with the general knowhow required. (Plus a story worth telling, naturally.)
Another aspect that earns a hat-tip is how the different factions actually have separate identities. The Humans and Betas are "external hardware" cultures that aren't completely estranged, yet the Betas have a freeform ability to plonk down structures almost anywhere. Humans, on the other hand, require a connection to their central power grid, and this has real implications for how you relate to resourcing operations and general expansion. The Goo manages to feel very alien by having a completely different take on everything. For Goo, your HQ is your resource operation, and your factory, and also a weapon. Even in "Starcraft," the Zerg distinctives don't go quite as far. This game does a great job at actually presenting the internal experience of a race that reproduces by fission, which is a feat that I will definitely applaud.
Where "Grey Goo" doesn't manage to truly compete is technical execution. Mostly, it comes down to lots of little things that aren't quite up to scratch.
To start with, the interface tries to "up the game" by being less "contextually bound" than what you would get in something like "Starcraft." Unit build information is almost always available, and that's nice, but the way you get around in the various panels isn't quite as smooth as you might like. I also found it strange that certain structure build commands aren't "sticky." That is, once you've built a structure, you drop out of the structure build command and go back to "click to select." On the one hand, this makes sense, because Grey Goo isn't really about building a giant swarm of buildings - but there are some times when it's clunky. For instance, a human player might want to build multiple sentinels (weapon towers) at a time, but there's no apparent way to do so. You either have to call up the right panel over and over, or hit the hotkey combo multiple times.
As it turns out, having an interface rearrange itself based on your selection context (and what makes sense in that context) is a better choice.
Another design choice that didn't quite pan out for me was how the "tech-tree" requirements are presented. If you can't build something yet, the prerequisites are mostly displayed as icons. This seems like a good idea in theory, but in practice, plenty of things (especially in the realm of building attachments) look pretty similar. What happens is that you end up getting a little confused, and clicking around to get another look at what that thing you need is supposed to look like.
In the same sort of track, you'll sometimes run into situations where pulling off build requirements is fiddly, or even obstructed by the natural way that a faction's builds work. Specifically, humans build on their power grid, which has an alarming tendency to block off tech-attachment slots. This causes trouble for building the "Alpha" epic unit, because various build scenarios end up preventing your large factory from attaching everything necessary. Yes, you can rotate buildings before they're constructed, but doing so never became immediately intuitive for me. Also, once you do figure that out, there's a very real tendency that the structure won't want to attach to the grid at the point you need.
I had to pause the game and go look up how to situate a factory to build the Alpha. Come on, guys...
A different problem area was the fog of war on the main map. In this game, the difference between areas that have been explored, but are not currently visible is not defined well enough. This can lead to all manner of possible confusion. A bit more contrast between those two display states would make a world of difference. As it stands, there were multiple occurrences of me having to look VERY carefully at the screen to figure out what my units could and could not observe.
...and I was pretty shocked at how underpowered the aircraft are, with limited, "plinky" munitions that have to be refilled at a landing pad every 10 seconds. (Of course, aircraft can be killer when the CPU sends them against you, but you already knew that.)
"Goo" can also suffer from some rather disappointing technical problems. As far as I can tell, the game uses a client/ server architecture for even the single player campaign. This would be fine, but my game somehow managed to lose the connection to itself(!) on a regular basis. This lead to long freezes, sound problems, and even the occasional hard crash. The final insult was during the Goo campaign, when my savegames from a long and hard-fought skirmish suddenly refused to load without crashing the client.
That's when I gave up.
I do still recommend this title, because I think its worth experiencing. Like I said, the artwork factor is really very good - but there are lots of functional things that don't seem to have worked out. I don't want to be unnecessarily hard on the Grey Box team, but dang it, they could have hit a home run if "Goo" had actually worked out as a complete package.

D.A:B is a small yet great game that had me cheering and laughing at all the overblown action and stupidity. Max-Payne-Leaping through the air to right-hook a guy is one such example. As great of a game this is, it doesn't take itself seriously, and you probably shouldn't take it seriously either. That's not a bad thing by any means, because you should go in expecting fun, stupid or otherwise. And I got fun out of it.
It's free, so there's no reason NOT to try it (though 4gb? seems large for a small game, probably uncompressed etc). Though this just means that you shouldn't expect too much or be disappointed when it isn't what you expected. It's a clunky game without doubt, but I think it uses this to add to the stupidity factor, and from there, the fun factor.
It is dated after all, source engine stuff along the lines of HL2. It's a mention of this that seemed offputting at first, but after playing for a while I was having more than enough fun to overlook the dated graphics.
There's a lack of Australian servers which kind of bugged me, especially since it means I have to play on servers with 170+ ping and force me to lead my shots, which is sort of difficult in a fast paced game like this. But then I realised it wasn't about who kills who or how many kills you rack up. Instead...
The style system awards points on what you're doing at the time of inflicting damage or killing someone, along with some temporary objectives that pop up throughout the course of the match (I've only seen 'Race' and 'Wanted' so far, not sure if there's more).
Race involves going to 3 generated points on the map in order, so typically everyone is fighting around the first checkpoint, since dying resets your checkpoint counter (e.g. you might be on your way to checkpoint 3, die, and have to start from 1 again). This was more than enough fun, dashing across rooftops on my way to the second marker with bullets whizzing past, sliding away from explosions and diving out windows into neighbouring buildings. Made harder by the fact you have a marker on you if you're the leader, in second or third place.
Wanted is a bit more simple, with one person in the match randomly elected as the target. They get buffed beyond measure, but that's only because a target is painted on them from wherever they are, leading the entire match of players to hunt them.
Let me reclarify though, these are not playlists or gametypes. These are just things that pop up during a standard match, and do not necessarily win you the match, but they give you a ton of style points which could jump you up to the point cap and win the game.
My only gripe with the game besides the lack of Aussie servers would probably be that there's no keybinding for just sliding. A mix of crouch and the stunt key don't seem like a big deal, but I just think it would be easier to have sliding as a seperate key (since it's essentially the only other maneuver besides stunt, which leaps you through the air).
If I had any suggestions besides that one, it would be that this game would be a hundred times better with a Steam Workshop. Since it ties in with source etc, I can easily imagine people using custom models besides the three default characters. Either that, or just add more characters... three felt too limited (and everyone just plays 'Eightball' anyway, which is Nick from LFD2).
Maybe this would open up the opportunity for more weapons too. If this game runs on the idea of being an overblown/corny action movie, then I'm surprised there's no katanas, .44 magnums, LMGs, sniper rifles(okay maybe not sniper rifles) and dual wieldable SMGs (there are two currently, what looks to be an MP5K and the MAC-10, but only pistols are dual wieldable).
Also, a team-play mode would be pretty great. Diving through a window with a friend and timing your slow-mo together to shred up a room of the enemy team would be awesome.
Erm, no way to mute people, so the in-game voip gets abused. A lot. This was a huge letdown, alongside the abundance of cheaters in the game. Also along these lines is the vote kicking... 4 votes to kick and 1 to keep, the vote doesn't pass. Needs to get fixed asap.
Since I write too much and most of you probably won't read this,
tl;dr, It's a clunky game and is only at 'mod' level right now if you want to rate it on quality, but I had fun at no expense of my wallet. Room for tons of improvement, and I sure hope it does, tons of potential to be amazing. Pick it up, play with friends, have a laugh: 7/10. I'd lower it further for hackers galore, but that's the players, not the game.

While I think the game is worth every dollar I spent into it for the time I put into it so far, after 44 hours of gameplay, the game did one thing that was so bad that I don't know if I can forgive it. It really made me upset to the point of questioning whether or not I want to continue playing anymore.
The game right now gave me a side quest which started out with creatures 3 levels past mine, but the hundreds that spawn in every few feet are easy to kill so long as they don't hit me, so I pushed forward, the last boss to complete the quest was up, after dying twice, I killed it and was rewarded a skeleton key, I open the door to find out there's a time limit to complete whatever is inside, and I also cannot create a rift in case I die either. So I go in to see what levels the creatures were and discovered that they were insanely high compared to mine, so I went to task manager and ended task to prevent the game from saving. I go back in the game to find out that the quest is still done, but I don't have the key and the door is locked again with no way to get the key back. Oh and it took several attempts to rush through the millions of creatures in my way so I could check to see if the door was locked, because insanely slow progress instead of balanced difficulty and ingenuity is what devs do. Why couldn't the game just take a massive dump on my face too while it was at it? I mean seriously... why purposely punish the players like that? The amount of laziness and lack of polish I see everywhere can be forgiven when it doesn't punish the players in a big way, but this... this was done on purpose.
Buy it if you don't like Diablo 3 style and miss the Diablo 2 style with a side order of other complicated stuff that isn't explained well and requires some online research to figure out. I just wish it had the budget and pride of a Blizzard game.
I will likely add a lot more to this review later when I'm a lot less frustrated.

I love Diablo clones, or aRPG as they are called. Grim Dawn however is simply BAD. I start with pros because there is a few:
PROS:
1) interesting class system - combination of classes can be powerful and anybody will find something for him/her.
2) devotion system - finding shrines and upgrading constellations for another bonuses and skills is fun.
3) not bad lore learning by finding notes etc.
CONS:
1) uninteresting level designs - almost all levels are plains or dungeons "painted" in shades of brown and black with addition of yellow and red.
2) uninteresting enemies - almost all enemies are human or human-like, most game time player will fight zombies and skeletons with some cultists, bosess are simply bigger versions of zombies/skeleton/bandits etc (with few exeptions).
3) absolutly no balance between player character and bosess - most are far more powerful than player on level when player encounters them making no fun or challenging fights, but kite around them for few blows then run or teleport to city/another location for healing then repeat whole process.
4) boring boss design - almost all boses have some skills, but mostly they summon something and then attack from distance - this pattern is used on almost all battle, be it random "hero monster" on map or level boss.
5) grindfest to the max - all equipment and craft components must be farmed - that is ok - but killing boss X-times to get another part of eg. his soul (needed 4) is boring.
6) character builds are gear dependant so grind more to get desired gear (and something really interesting drops at surprisingly low rate)
7) story is uninspiring - player do not get immersed into world he/she need to save, most time even do not remember who to kill and why.
I do not recommend this game unless discount is 75%.

For anyone who came here lost on where to start in the Hyperdimension Neptuina series, here is a brief overview on the differences between the versions of this game and whether or not this is the right place to start for you.
TL;DR: Hyperdimension Neptunia (PS3) and Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth are different games, but both work as starting points to the franchise. If you have played one of them, then you've seen the main storyline for the other and won't be missing too much (Storyline-wise at least)
This game is: Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1, is a port of the Playstation Vita game of the same name. Re;Birth1 is canonically the first game in the current canon, (albeit, some, if not most of the games take place in different dimensions) and is the best starting point for those who are interested in getting into the Neptunia games. In this game you will not encounter: Reddo-Chan, 5PB, Nisa or Gust.
This game is not: Hyperdimension Neptunia (Proper). Hyperdimension Neptunia for the PS3 was the first game in the Neptunia series and while these games have a similar storyline, characters, game play, duologue, art, graphics, etc. are all different from this game to its Re;Birth counterpart.
These two games both work as entry points to this series as they have (mostly) similar stories, but depending on what experience you want to take away from this franchise you may want to chose one over the other.
If you are looking for a better technical experience than look no further than Re;Birth1. Re;Birth1 has a unique combat system that has become the trademark of the current Neptunia games; the player will move the characters inside a instanced battle map and direct the character's attacks to hit as many enemies as possible. This can also work against the player though as the enemies can attack several of your party members if they are bundled up too closely. Re;Birth1 also boasts a better overall frame rate as it's PS3 counterpart ran very sluggishly and had a very unstable overall frame rate. Re;Birth1 also contains a new system that allows the player to unlock new, items, weapons, maps, and even characters using the Remake system. Rebirth1 also has a far larger cast of playable characters: 16 without DLC and 19 with DLC.
Hyperdimension Neptunia (PS3) Has tons of customization options not available in Re;Birth1 such as the ability to import one's own images to create custom attacks; alongside this one may also create custom attack combos that lead into custom finishing moves. On the downside, Neptunia PS3 has a smaller cast of characters 7 without DLC and 11 with, but it does feature fan favorites Nisa and Gust, neither of which you will see in any of the games on steam. The combat in this game is unique and no other game in the series plays like it; the characters do not move while in battle and the battle system is similar to that of games such as Xenosaga. Characters have three main types of attacks: Weapon, Physical and shoot (and its pretty great seeing Iffy and Nep-Nep whip out pistols to shoot the enemy with) all with their own unique properties. Neptunia PS3 also has the greatest amount of direct references to video games and gaming culture in general, so the humor is pretty great for those who like video games.
Overall they are both unique and fun experiences to be had, but if you are only going to play one of them I really must recommend Re;Birth1 as its game play and characters have a far wider appeal, and Re;Birth1 also has tons of content to play through not featured in the PS3 game. If you are a true Nep-fanatic you'll eventually find yourself playing through both games and enjoying the vastly different content presented in both.

Unfortunately the game loads so quickly that the extra bits of lore displayed on the loading screens are lost. There are plenty of maps, classes, and vehicles and they're all wickedly cool. Land combat feels pretty satisfying, especially when you spawn in as one of the famous characters, but space combat is the coolest! The campaign menu system seemed a bit underdeveloped, not that it matters but you oddly could not go back and replay completed campaign levels. Besides the campaign... Good game, definitely cannot wait for the new Battlefront!

This game at first looks like another Japanese game with no substance or thought, but it is actually quite the experience. Yes, the dungeons are a bit samey and the combat starts off very slow, but past that is a great JRPG.
An interesting setting of a multiverse where different game companys embodied as different nations are ruled over by these beautiful Goddesses. The characters are lovable and diverse, and all interaction between them (including fanservice) is always a treat. The story is somewhat basic but gradually steps up into an interesting adventure. The soundtrack is great, full of upbeat electronic battle themes and catchy field themes. The game comes in japanese or english. I preferred Jap (being weeb and all that) as it made the characters more expressive and moe. In English, instead the characters sound like typical anime dubbed characters, but with more catchy punchlines.
The combat is unique as it is "3D Turn-Based" where characters may move around a specific area during their turns before they unleash a button mash of combos and other special JRPG combat shenanigans (transformations, finishers, etc). And the enemies certainly live up to the theme of a gaming world with many traditional RPG tropes like dragons to pop culture references (there's an enemy which is literally a screenshot of a dating sim xD). Character progression is pretty simple here with typical level ups and gear crafting. Theres also a friendship system between characters where they can perform special combos and assist eachother in battle, even if on of them aren't in the party group.
Overall, a great JRPG which is one of many in it's series. I have yet to play them at this point in time, but before those, why not try out this gem of a videogame?

Games are meant to be simple experiences meant to invoke emotion in the player. Beyond Eyes exceeds that standard in every way. The game mechanics and controls are simple, the gameplay is easy to follow, the visuals are beautiful, and this is a feels trip from beginning to end.
Calling this game a "walking simulator" is not far off the mark. Aside from the occasional interaction with a ball or stile or bread, all you do in this game is navigate the big, ever-changing, and sometimes frightening world.  As a result, the controls are very simple: WASD, space bar, escape, and mouse. That's it, that's all you need.
Simple controls are helpful, though, because at times it's easy to get turned around lose your way entirely. There were a few times that I really needed to concentrate to figure out where I need to be going, and how I should get there given all the new incoming information about the environment. But that's the beauty of the gameplay here: simple to learn, but difficult to master.
Getting turned around isn't all that bad though. The art style, and watching the world form and change around you, are wonderful experiences in and of themselves. Beyond Eyes looks very much like a children's storybook, with the playful watercolor art and the short blurbs of text that pop up sometimes. I was especially impressed with how sounds are visualized, and how environment color changed to portray Rae's emotions.
The colored indications of Rae's feelings, however, did not prepare me for the emotions this game had in store. For all its bright, cheery colors, this is a very sad game-- even heartbreaking at times. I will admit it, I cried twice playing this. The sadness, though, and the way it reaches out and touches you are incredible. Not many games are able to accomplish this, in my experience.
Taking everything into account-- the simplicity, the gameplay, the visuals, and the emotions-- I most definitely recommend this game. It's short, very well done, and an experience that will not soon be forgotten. Well done, Tiger and Squid! I hope to see more of what you come out with someday.

If this is your first nep game (as it was mine) you can easily pick it up from the start and not feel like you've missed anything story-wise. Its also worth noting, to those new to the series/JRPGs, Neptunia is basically a hybrid between an RPG and a Visual Novel. In my experience with the game, about 50% of my time was spent reading text (don't use the english dub, its awful), and the other 50% was wandering dungeons and killing mobs, until the second playthrough came and I was instead grinding mobs for specific materials.
Even though the game has clear negative points, it must be doing something right to have kept me entertained for over 60 hours.

So after playing through the entirety of the season I can say this: if you played any of the post TWD:S1 Telltale games you know what you're getting into. A story driven adventure game, where most of the time the plot is flowing on its own and you're just in there for the ride, although you can splash around a bit in your own unique way and to be fair there are some huge decisions towards the end that actually impact character fates and leave a story impact, something not often seen with Telltale's usual railroading of the plot. We'll have to wait till S2 to see if the last episode's big decisions will stick or if they'll be swept under the rug for the sake of railroading the plot as is the usual practice.
For a game based on the GoT I thought the villains were too cartoonishly evil at times, doing almost everything possible to make the player dislike them or for the sake of being villains. Why does bad guy X feel the need to tell you his entire plan when he could leave you in the dark and then manipulate you further? In the end its for the benefit of the audience but it comes across as that plot point could have been revealed better in a more GoT friendly fashion.
In the end it is a good Telltale experience with the usual downfalls a very impressive performance by voice actors (including the original cast from the series), shocking twists in GoT fashion, darkness induced grief from sometimes being helpless to do anything against the illusion of choice while being stuck in a story that drags you around towards its prefered ending.  On the other hand Telltale is improving in how they handle their illusion of choice, allowing a bit more freedom than in some of their other games and even actually letting you legit decide if some characters will live to see the end of the season. Giving it a cautious recommendation for those who enjoy GoT, Telltale style adventure and being both a player and a spectator to the story.

Pros:
The characterization is great, the artistic style is quite appealing, the voiceovers are convincing, and there are numerous instances in which the story evokes an emotional response (sometimes shouting in excitement, in my case) in the player.  The developers intelligently formed a game that really is tailored to the decisions you make.
Cons:
1. Apparently, if you want to make the "right choices," you must routinely make the immoral decision.  What??
2. Some have commented that going with your intellect over your emotions will yield the best outcome...but it actually seems that you're destined to fail no matter what you choose.
3. ~SPOILERS~I get that it's Game of Thrones, a show famous for killing off characters we care about.  But some of the deaths in this game beg the question, "How did that help the plot at all?" If deaths do not further the plot or serve as a catalyst for some growth/change in an important character, then what is the point? Do those deaths not then serve primarily as shock factor? I did not grow too attached to Ethan, but I still do not see how his death helped the story at all.  Rodrik could have rolled off the cart and taken up the mantle of lord without Ethan's death, and Lady Forrester did not seem to change at all throughout the story, no matter how many of her family were slain.  In fact, the only person to change per Ethan's demise was Talia...and she really does not have much of an effect on the plot.
Some games give you a sense of reward when you play them.  Others make you feel as if you spent many hours really working at them, only to show you that failure is the ultimate outcome.  This game falls under the latter category.
But maybe that's the point of Game of Thrones series as a whole.  I think "nihilism" is the correct term.

Grey Goo is, first and foremost, not Starcraft. If you like the modern Starcraft-esque RTS that's fast paced, micro intensive, and largely based on twitch skill and on-the-fly adaptation mixed with scouting and mastery of build order, this may not be the game for you. Grey Goo is slow, deliberate, and methodical. The organization of your forces going into an engagement is going to be much more important than what you do in the middle of the fight, and for most of the factions, all of your production is going to be very, very centralized, leading to longer games that focus on large-scale battles. Grey Goo as an RTS is far more focused on the large-scale strategy to the small-scale tactics, and it can be jarring for a lot of people if they're familiar with more micro-intensive games.
The Good:
- Large faction diversity. Basic units are present in each faction, but infrastructure needs vary drastically and while the same general roles are filled by each class and their units (Light tank, light damage, heavy tank, heavy damage, artillery, seige, scout, air, etc.), how each race goes about those basic goals has enough variety to make playing each faction quite different, especially the unorthodox Goo of the title.
- Streamlined economy and tech management. Only the one resource to worry about, and tech, despite generally requiring certain buildings be built, isn't linked to them intrisically.
- Excellent UI and menu design. Once you get used to it, the hotkeys for building are incredibly intuitive, allowing for easier base management without having to set your infrastructure to 4-5 hotkeys just by themselves.
The Bad:
- A very slow game. The standard win-condition requires you destroy the enemy core, all of their factories, and all of their refineries. Even if they literally could not possibly recover, you've gotta whittle away their buildings if they don't feel like surrendering. Which the AI doesn't so practicing against the AI is going to be a bit of a long process.
- Buildings are very tanky and supply lines are difficult to disrupt early game, which makes harassment a non-viable option. Early-game can feel very same-y as you scout out the enemy and try and build your forces to counter theirs. The exception to this is the Goo, which...
- The Goo, despite being really cool and unique, are incredibly weak one-on-one. They're the only faction vulnerable to harassment because their health is their resource, and because they gain resources so slow early on, it's very, very easy for them to fall into a death spiral, especially on small maps.
