Time and time again I was recommended Hyperdimension Neptunia series but I’ve always had a problem with JRPGs and that is the fact that I tend to find grinding pretty boring and usually I leave things half way through. That said, I’m glad I was given the chance to check out
, the first part of the series to be released on Steam for not only I came into terms with grinding but it also features a storyline which takes place in a world that most of us who play videogames can either identify ourselves with or be amused by the satire and comedy that comes with it.
The game takes place in Gamindustri, a realm divided into 4 different lands, each ruled by its own CPU (Console Patron Unit). Each one of these, with the exception of one, is a reference to the 3 major consoles, Lastation - Playstation, Lowee - Wii and Leanbox - Xbox. For time immemorial the 4 CPUs, which inhabit Celestia, have battled for control of Gamindustri and its shares (the peoples faith in them). This is where the story takes off, during a battle between all the CPUs you, Neptune, CPU of Planeptune, fall down from Celestia to Gamindustri resulting in the loss of your memory but, luckely, you’re saved by your very first party companion, Compa.
The story is told as if you were playing a visual novel in the sense that you can’t change the way the story goes, you’re just pressing a button so that the next piece of dialogue triggers. The story is what kept me going through the dozens of hours that I’ve spent with this game, along with most of the combat. Still, there were moments where it felt like a cliché but sometimes the game manages to make fun of itself, for the characters become aware that they’re fictional and this creates some nice little moments in the dialogue. Overall, the dialogue is easy to understand and you’ll get a nice laugh every now and then. On the other hand, not every single piece of dialogue is voice acted, which is somewhat of a bummer to me, even if the english voice acting is not that great at times.
Besides listening and reading through the dialogue sections of the game, you’ll be spending a good amount of time in dungeons which you can access via the world map. Here you’ll also be able to visit various different locations where you can shop and talk to people which will either give you plans to craft new items or provide very small pieces of dialogue which can contain references to other popular games such as the Metal Gear saga.
Everytime you’re pursuing a quest chances are that it is at the end of the dungeon so either you want it or not, you’ll have to go through those and kill enemies. As you wander through the dungeons you might come across resources and treasures that you can pick up. Obviously you’ll also see different enemies and approaching them or attacking them will trigger an encounter but, even if you kill all the enemies during an encounter they will still respawn after a certain period of time, thus allowing you to farm for experience and loot.
As far as I’m aware, combat works like in pretty much every other Neptunia game, it is turn-based but you don’t move in squares like in most games, instead each character has this circle around them which represents the space in which they can move and attack from. Every character has the ability to use either physical or magic attacks and consume potions but the combat gets more interesting with mechanics like
and
. Depending on your lily rank with the character you’re paired with you’ll be able to use different abilities and EXE drives resort on building up a combo meter to unleash even more devastating abilities.
Of course you’re also able to equip your characters with different gear as well as craft new pieces of it. You’re also able to craft some sort of modifiers which can make enemies harder or easier, make more enemies spawn in a certain dungeon or increase the effectiveness of some ability that you might have. Looking for the ingredients to craft these is entirely optional though.
At its core, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is an extremely solid and enjoyable JRPG that made me realise how satisfying it is to finally beat that boss after spending an hour or two farming the same mobs over and over.
The overall visual presentation is pretty good, even if some of the dungeon designs are just recycled with different enemies. The only caveat I have in terms of the game audio presentation is the fact that the game is not fully voice acted, as mentioned before.
If you’re looking for an intriguing and, at the same time, silly story with various different characters and an enjoyable combat experience I certainly recommend you check this one out. If you’re a fan of the Neptunia series and haven’t played this one, chances are you’ll also have a good time here.

9/10: Telltale combined with Game of Thrones makes for a great narrative experience. Considering that this is a Game of Thrones title though, just keep in mind what the term "Valar morghulis" means.
In this season of Game of Thrones, players are introduced to the Forrester family. As vassals of House Stark, their loyalty to the north is quickly put to the test, as the game begins at the infamous Red Wedding. With the Warden of the North murdered, vassals like the Forresters now find themselves facing the machinations of bannermen loyal to the Lannisters and the Boltons, with the neighboring Whitehill family rekindling their long-standing fued with the Forresters now that their position is in jeopardy. Worse yet, Lord Forrester is one of the first to die in the ambush at the Red Wedding, leaving his family scrambling to name the next oldest son available as the new lord of House Forrester.
While the Forrester's are not mentioned in the books or show, they are granted importance in the game by being the stewards of a rare resource: ironwood, an extremely tough variety of wood that the Forrester's are especially adept at honing and maintaining. This of course brings a heap of trouble on the Forrester family as the Boltons and the Whitehill's begin haranguing and outright attacking the Forrester's.
Over the course of the game, the player plays the role of several key members of the Forrester household, starting with Lord Forrester's squire Gared Tuttle and continuing to include most of the Forrester siblings including Rodrik, Asher, Ethan, and Mira as well. Each is forced to confront impossible odds and difficult decisions, although due to the linear nature of Telltale series, it is tough to discern whether any of the choices the player makes bear any meaning. Admittedly, the choices do result in some variations to the scenes immediately following it, but even so the major scenes and character deaths appear to happen no matter what.
Even so, Telltale did a great job of putting the player in the position of people playing the Game of Thrones. With the constant challenge of trying to protect your house amidst a sea of aggression, the losses suffered by the player are felt all the more keenly for having experienced it through their eyes. While one may hold out hope that one can find a way to keep as many Forresters alive as possible, the one thing you can depend on in Game of Thrones is that "all men must die."
You will play this game and enjoy it.

I bought this game on an extreme sale not really expecting much other than some cheap entertainment, and I ended up being pleasantly surprised.
The player take the role of a South American dictator who undergoes various trials to develop the island nation of Tropico.  You can choose to embrace US-style captialism, Soviet-style communism, or a tourism-based economy.  Your island is home to various competing interests that you must work to satisfy, so there's a lot of things to juggle.  The main campaign is challenging and diverse, I chose to play through that instead of just building stand-alone islands.
One of the most unexpected positives of the game is that the campaign is just plain funny.  The banter between your dictator avatar, your advisors, the various diplomats you engage with, and the other NPCs is consistently entertaining, and is a well-written parody of Cold War era foreign relations with Latin America.
My wife and I played the game side-by-side and enjoyed bantering about the various levels and the decisions that we made.

For a zombie game, Dying Light is a surprisingly fun experience that trumps its predecessor: Dead Island.
Dying Light introduces parkour into a zombie apocalypse, and it makes the rpg experience so much fun. The animations are smooth and transition without hitches, to where you can go from running on rooftops to drop kicking zombies into spiked traps, to using the heads of the infected as a means of transportation. After a point in the game, you acquire a grappling hook, which adds an element of verticality to the game, and greatly speeds up the action in the game,
The melee system from Dead Island has been cleaned up, and feels great. The upgrade skills you get can give you unique options to kill zombies other than "wackig with bat"
The graphics are great, with amazing visual and audio feedback, zombies *feel fun* to cut and slice, and the elemental effects are amazingly visceral. The game runs pretty well, even on lower end machines.
The story is cliche and forgettable with the cast of zombie survivor tropes, and a bunch of plot holes. Fortunatly, there are plenty of side quests and activities that can increase your playtime.
Dying Light's gimmick is that you can play either in the daytime or nighttime, and these have different playstyles. During the day, you get to enjoy Harran in all its beauty. However in the night, zombies become more active and dangerous, creating a much more intense experience.
I do have some gripes especially with some of the mobs (exploding zombies in particular), which seemed to be placed in trolly locations and stop the zombie mayhem with insta-kill mechanics. Some of the later side quest these jerks are placed in closets, and will insta-kill you when you are trying to finish a quest.
Overall, Dying Light is the best zombie-action game on the market and worth checking out.

Yes, this doesn't have all the guns and explosives that we have all become too eager to expect from modern games.
Yes, this is basically Far Cry 4 with technology from 10,000 years ago.
But that is exactly what it is supposed to be. And its somewhat refreshing to be given such limited tools and equipment.
Do not compare this to other first person titles, or the previous Far Cry games as you will be dissapointed.
That being said, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing cool if you can appreciate what Ubisoft is trying to create. The whole point is to try to depict what it would've possibly been like to exist, hunt and craft 10,000 years before high tech weapons, computers and the internet. And I think they have done a fairly good job.
Don't take this game too seriously, but all in all it is very immersive and allows you to momentarily step into the life of a "primitive" human being. Life back then wasn't easy, people from this period of Earth's history had to make do with whatever they could create with their bare hands. So I think that everyone who is criticising it based on the somewhat "lackluster" features should consider the context and setting of this game. Yes, some of the crafting is hard to believe, and yes some of the dialouge is somewhat humourous, but let's not forget that this is a depiction of reality from a time where we know very little.
Anyway, I think many people who have enjoyed the Far Cry franchise will enjoy this latest installment, if you take into account the context and setting.
Happy hunting.

“Can you climb, naked man?” A point and click puzzle game, your character starts by escaping from a prison via a sewage/flood system, looking remarkably clean, if a little naked and handcuffed. He's a thief accosted by English constables, in a time where racial tensions between the Irish and English are at an all time high. When he picks up objects, they mysteriously disappear into his pants, and some of the animations are very slow ... and the character does have a slight habit of over explaining his actions during a successful “puzzle”, which could get annoying after a while. Yes smash the lock. No need to go further into it.
The character has a habit of reminding himself he can't do things or that something happened, or thinking that people are simple and how he needs to manipulate them – attributing to his thief-like character of dubious morals. Who also really dislikes hard work. Or work that requires effort in general. He's not a nice guy for sure, though entertaining in the way he interacts with people. You'll either like him or hate his guts. He seems to try and get around the game with his silver tongue. The dialogue between him and the woman who helps him out at the start is a little unbelievable, it progresses too conveniently. The accents are nice to listen to, though the main character is a little flat toned. But hey! Irish accents. It's very dialogue heavy so you'll spend a lot of time talking with characters and going through each talk option.
The environments are well rendered, they're not amazing but thought and detail has gone into it, from dirty basins to rust and pots and pans and objects lying around everywhere, giving the appearance of a run down, shabby and poor area. It's dilapidated and grimy, the less glamorous side of the Victorian style era, and this same level of detail persists in each scene you go into.
The game itself is a little too slow paced for me, things take too long to interact with, so I fast start losing interest in the adventure, despite the good environment, potential intriguing plot and interesting voice actors with their own quirks.

Beyond Eyes is a peaceful game that focuses on exploration.  You play as Rae, a blind girl who is searching for her kitty.  As you wander around, the environment changes from the white unknown to beautiful watercolor.  You can only sense what's in your immediate vicinity, leaving much to be discovered.
Walking isn't the only way to "unlock" the environment.  Sounds jump out to you and evoke color as well.  For example, when the cat meows, a brief image of the kitty will flash onto the screen, giving Rae a sense of direction and clues on where to go.  Rae uses both touch and sound to find her way.
But sometimes things aren't as they seem.  Sounds can be misleading.  What sounds like one thing turns into something different when Rae gets close enough to interact with it.  What Rae thought was clothes drying on a clothesline turned out to be a scarecrow.  The world, though beautiful, is uncertain and changing.
I've played about 17 minutes of it so far and have only unlocked 1/10 achievements.  Based on that, it seems like this game won't be over relatively quickly.  Gameplay will probably be a couple hours.
This game can appeal to a wide audience.  If you're a cat lover, you'll like this game.  If you like casual exploration, this is the game for you.  If you enjoy peaceful sounds from nature and soft, beautiful graphics, you'll appreciate Beyond Eyes.

You play as Takkar, a man on a journey to the land of Oros, who reunites with the fragments of his lost tribe, the Wenja. Oros is also home to Neanderthalic cannibals, the Udam and technologically savvy farmers/firebombers, the Izila. The Udam are stronger, the Izila smarter - by Darwinian terms, the Wenja deserve to be extinct, and if the game is suggesting that we’re descended from them, humanity got a bum deal. It’s Takkar’s job to tip the balance. His course through the game leads him to collect together the scattered remnants of the tribe, forming a strong leadership, and building a functioning village in the bucolic valley he calls home. He does so by murdering almost everything he sees.
This is different for everyone but for me the game runs excellent.
Here are my PC Specs:
i5-6500
Zotac GeForce GTX 970
16GB DDR4-2133MHz
Here is a little video of real time frame rates of 20 minutes of gameplay:
If you want guns, vehicles, rocket launchers, gernades, and a wingsuit this game will not be for you. You get 3 weapons: a bow, a spear, and a club. These weapons are able to be upgraded by progressing through the story line and getting the neccesary supplies to be able to upgrade the weapons. You are also able to craft a toolkit of traps, primitive bombs, and a grappling hook. Takkar also has a new ability that allows you to tame animals and allow you to use them to help you fight against the Udam and Izila. You are able to tame animal ranging from a badger all away to a sabertooth.
The world is just stunning from running through the jungle throughout the day and nite, to being inside a cave surrounded by animals, as well as traveling throughout the cold winter mountains. You really feel the way of a caveman sneaking up on a enemy camp through the mountains just to throw a spear straight through there head. Looking up at the stars in the night with a fire camp in place is just stunning.

I recently did another playthrough of HL2 and it holds up surprisingly well.
Pros:
- Gameplay always changes. Sometimes it's puzzles, sometimes straight shooting, sometimes you have to fight multiple enemy types, at the same time, which require different tactics.
- The story is great as are the writing and voice acting.
- It's always been a fun experience.
Cons:
- HL2 squadmates are amazingly terrible. They are constantly in the way, getting themselves killed by hazards which are easy to avoid, and are mostly useless.
- Ladders kill you less often now but getting off of them is like trying to remove superglue from your hands.
- Placing items about the ground for platforming/jumping puzzles is frightfully trying. You slide around on top of whatever surface you're on. The objects bounce around haphazardly. That part has never been fun.
Bugs and quirks aside, it's always been an enjoyable game.

Absolutely amazing game... never played an RTS as simple yet complicated as this... Men of War: Assault Squad although is brilliant, it is far too in depth for my liking... RTS games that require you to dig into your inventory is just too much. Company of Heroes the other hand is beautiful... Where other RTS games have a health system where no matter where you hit them, they will lose a certain amount of health. CoH2 (and CoH1) on the other hand, if you hit the back of the tank with an anti tank round, the back of the tank will take damage... you can destroy the main gun on a tank but is still perfectly driveable... You can even usurp enemy vehicles or use the wreckage as cover.
The Fog of War system is excellent... even if you've discovered an area, you can ONLY see the enemy if your units have a clear line of sight.. which makes for more cat and mouse games and ambushes. The only things I hate about this game is that you cannot zoom out enough, it's just that little bit too close for my liking and also the flame thrower upgrade for the engineers is a little annoying and over-used!
8/10 If you love WW2 era combat and have no experience in RTS, you might actually enjoy learning on this baby! Just dont go online... you'll get smashed!~

If this is your first nep game (as it was mine) you can easily pick it up from the start and not feel like you've missed anything story-wise. Gameplay is fairly simple even for someone new to turn-based RPGs. The humor of the game can feel beaten-in after a while, but all in all was still pretty good. As far as the content of the game, admittedly its a lot of copy and paste. Most of the dungeons and enemies are just reskins from earlier parts of the game. The characters are cute, and the animations for the EXE or SP moves can be interesting to watch the first few times. There's an offer of replayability thanks to some materials being limited to only be obtained once per playthrough, so if you wish to unlock everything in the game, you'll be playing through it multiple times.
Its also worth noting, to those new to the series/JRPGs, Neptunia is basically a hybrid between an RPG and a Visual Novel. In my experience with the game, about 50% of my time was spent reading text (don't use the english dub, its awful), and the other 50% was wandering dungeons and killing mobs, until the second playthrough came and I was instead grinding mobs for specific materials.
Even though the game has clear negative points, it must be doing something right to have kept me entertained for over 60 hours.

I absolutely recommend this game. It's not the open world space game you might hope for (look to upcoming titles like


or
for those). However, despite that, it manages to pull off an incredibly intense space experience within the constraints it puts itself in.
You're the director of the crew of a ship trying to get from point A to point B while fleeing a pursuing Rebel fleet that has all but destroyed your Federation, yet you carry vital cargo that may somehow turn the tide. It's never entirely clear what that cargo is, as the story plays pretty fast and loose, as you explore some distant reaches of space, fighting pirates, helping other intelligent species as well as being attacked by them, and coming across some fascinating anomalies as you go from beacon to beacon and sector to sector until you make it to the final, eighth sector.
Throughout all this, chances are you will die. A lot. This falls into the roguelike genre that has been popular recently, but with the great difference of being scifi amidst a bunch of more fantasy style games. Albeit, if you'd like more scifi roguelikes you may look into
for another recent scifi entry into the genre (unfortunately minus the space, but fortunately
the mechs!).
That being said, that factor alone makes it well worth purchasing in my opinion (though preferably from GOG or Humble Store), but even more than that is that with the recent introduction of Advanced Edition content, the game has only gotten even better than before. Toss in mods and the fun stories you'll get from close scrapes with death from various playthroughs, and you have countless hours of fun, many of my own not counted here from playing the DRM-free version more on the side.
Ask yourself, do you want to be able to have the virtual experience of suffocating would-be pirates or saboteaurs teleporting aboard your ship? Do you want to be saved by your enemy trying to hack an already destroyed subsystem incidentally shutting the doors to it, restoring oxygen in the rooms and allowing you to do repairs after you fend it off? Then you want FTL. Other space games may let you command fleets, but few let you manage the frantic internal affairs of the crew trying to hold everything together.

Company of Heroes 2 is just a former shadow of its predecessor, Company of Heroes 1. While one could argue that this isnt a remake of CoH1 which is true, however, CoH2 is lacks in content of its predecessor while the game felt dumb downed in so many ways where the Command Tree from CoH1 has been replaced with a system that is similar to Call of Duty's perks system. Rusians felt like a reskinned version of America from the first game in some ways. The campaign is not as fun as the previous game as it felt like the entire campaign is just a lengthy tutorial as the game does not seemed to trust you with its arsenal, unlike its predecessor.
To make things worse, Sega decided to fill the game with microtrasactions that are pretty costly that ranges from harmless cosmetic skins for vehicles to paid only commander with new units and abilities where you only can obtain it by paying your hard earned money. There isnt any way to unlock these content by playing the game. Unfortunately, this game felt like it is the paid version of Company of Heroes Online with all these microtrasactions. To make things even worse, Sega decides to hide these microtrasactions from the Steam Store while you only can find these microtrsactions inside the game, just like an In-App Purchase (IAP) in a mobile game. The only microtransactions that Sega did correctly were the DLC content packs such as Case Blue where these packs provides some pretty decent new solo and coop missions into the game. One could argue that these content are optional but having these microtrasactions are a notion by major publishers to put more and more paywall into game content to encourage gamers to pay more for lesser content.
As a conclusion, buyers beware. If you are looking for a multiplayer RTS, look elsewhere. If you are a predominantly single player RTS gamer, Company of Heroes 2 might give you a decent experience. As a Relic game fan, Company of Heroes 2 is a disappointment as this isnt the Company of Heroes sequel that most are looking for but a cynical attempt by Sega to include questionable IAPs into the game that were abused heavily on mobile. I thought Dawn of War 2 was average at best, but seemed like Relic has made Company of Heroes 2 even worse than Dawn of War 2.
I highly recommend one to get Company of Heroes 1 Complete Edition instead, then, get the Eastern Front mod to play as Rusians. Alternatively, get World in Conflict with Soviet Assault expansion or get the latest installment from the Wargame series if you want a more realistic tactical RTS.

The thing about Xcom is that the mechanics themselves are fantastic, they really are. The turn based squad strategy is fun, the overall research/building strategy is fine. The problem lies only in two elements:
1. Difficulty settings.
2. Random Number Generators.
Let it be said, if you're fairly casual with strategy and you play this game casually on "normal" setting, the game is absolutely fine. No problems there. This review is not for you then, just ignore. That's just not for me. I recommend the game on this basis, that it works fine on normal and that the basic mechanics are well done.
If you're very serious about strategy, you'll almost certainly find "Normal" difficulty too easy and "Classic" fitting in general (at least if you're only planning one playthrough). Sounds great, right? Could have been except for one thing: the variance on Classic. Everything is a roll of the dice, which is fine, but the variance is insane. You can do everything right and still lose the game in one brief moment of bad luck. I'll illustrate the problem with this one scenario that actually took place for me:
Turn 1. Your squad arrives in the woods. You move them into defensive positions just in case you're being charged right off the bat. They're all in cover, they're all in Overwatch (guarding). Three aliens attack, the squad takes down the first one. The second one uses a skill that automatically deals 1 damage, it hits one guy.
*BREAK* Let me here say that one damage is nothing, it really is nothing.
So, the guy who got hit with the whopping 1 damage rolls a dice and panics. He panics by turning to his right and trying to execute his friend standing right next to him because... well, who knows. It's the standard panic reaction in this game. He rolls another dice and misses from point blank range. Just can't hit. Well, fine you think, but alas. Behind him is a seasoned veteran, a captain who has seen many battles. He rolls a dice too, he also panics. Now, he has taken 0 damage, he has merely seen one dude take one damage. Well, he handles panic in the same way and decides to execute one of his friends. He chooses your best solider (and medic) and nails her right in the back of the head with a critical hit, killing her instantly. End turn one.
Turn 2. Bring up menu, quit game.
Things like this just happen, they just do. You can restart the mission whenever they do, but it wears you out. Or it did with me. Worst thing is, they could fix everything wrong with this game so easily.
1. rebalance panic.
2. remove critical hits.
Just those two things would limit the variance to a degree where the game would feel hard but fair. It's really all they needed to do and then the game would probably be a 10.

Short Version: The story sucks, but the gameplay is fun and hilarious.
Dying Light's mediocre, predictable story and boring, annoying characters will turn away any gamer who is looking for a story rich zombie game. When I can predict a character's death within five minutes of meeting him, then there is a problem with the writing. I don't care about the characters, let alone their deaths. I suppose I was also supposed to worry about being infected and having to get medicine to stave off zombifacation, but that doesn't matter either (only a screen effect and getting winded sometimes in story missions to remind me of my mortality) so there's no sense of tension or peril in the story, since my motivation is not very motivating.
But... I've played this game over 100 hours because I can't stop drop kicking zombies off of rooftops, slicing zombies in half with a katana, and firing explosive arrows into crowds of (probably) enemies. Running, jumping, and climbing in the game world is engaging and makes the game fast-paced and exciting. If you're going to play this game for any reason, it will be for the gameplay. Techland would have done better to embrace the silliness of the zombie apocalypse they created, instead of selling Dying Light as a gritty and dark survival horror.

A lot of other reviews focus on the mechanics, why this is better than <insert arpg here>, and other assorted gameplay aspects. Instead, I'm going to talk about what an incredibly well crafted world this game has.
This game feels lived in, as if it's "real." Everything from the area design to the in-game lore creates a sense of a fantasy world that actually exists. Speaking of lore, the way the background is delivered to you tangenitally through discovery instead of directly through exposition is crucial in creating this feeling of a deep world filled with mystery that a player can't help but want to uncover. What's more, the mythos behind this world is diverse, deep, and engaging.
Contributing to this world's diversity is the way the various enemy types interact with eachother. Mechanically, it's such a simple thing for the blood-god obsessed lunatics to wage war with the alien-like magical beings invading the world, but it really helps reinforce, from a lore standpoint, that things are bigger than you. The warring of these factions against each other is something you only see on screen, but it has a way of capturing the imagination and immerssing the player.
The setting itself, somewhat of a cross between world war 1 and high fantasy, works not because it's a good concept, but because the developers took the time to make sure that everything fit together in a pleasing and consistent way. The music combines with the art and writing direction in a way which really glues everything together so that the whole is more than simply the sum of the individual parts.
In closing, this is the finest arpg I've ever experienced from a lore perspective and I feel extremely lucky to have experienced it. Highly recommended for people who want more than just solid mechanics.

Ok, wow... I thought Dark Souls II was going to be my big end-of-the-year buy but this game blew my socks off.
Tl;DR IS AT BOTTOM OF REVIEW
Ok, that was my first impression. Now for my "Down to Earth" review. This game reminds a LOT of two of my other favorite games, Crackdown and Prototype. This is a large leap from Saints Row The Third. I played the first two games a bit when I was in my GTA phase, but I wasn't all that impressed with them. I tried The Third because it looked to be a little more wacky and wild and I thoroughly enjoyed that one for a few hours before I got bored, because with a lot of the DLC it felt like cheating, and games you cheat in (Like the Sims lol) get boring after a while. This game gives you powers which feels like cheating, but you aren't... so things still have a decent tactical aspect to them.
Pros:
--The aforementioned similarity to Crackdown and Prototype is a MAJOR plus for me.
--The references to other geek/nerd sources, like Mass Effect 3 (Keith David helps a lot for that affect lol), Star Wars ("Stay on target"), and the AC series with the usage of their version of the "Animus". Of course there are plenty more references besides those. :P
--Controller works great.
--Storyline is surprisingly fun.
--Weapons and abilities allow you to, for the most part, tackle things your way.
Cons:
--The only con I can really think of is that I don't feel like this game will offer a lot of replayability, at least for soloing. It is the kind of game where you power up, get new weapons and abilities, and that structure is fairly linear, leaving very little room for trying things differently on following playthroughs.
Other thoughts:
--I find it a little strange that you can upgrade vehicles considering that I have been playing for a while and rarely use vehicles outside of the world challenges/events that require stealing them, since you can basically jump, run, and fly everywhere you need to go lol. But just a bit into the game it doesn't cost much to max out a vehicle the way you want. Currently, I get about 6250 cache (in game currency, aka "cash") per in-game hour (not IRL hours... and it looks like you can make a LOT more than that per hour), and I think it only cost me about 7k-8k cache to make it look how I wanted with full performance upgrades.
--Weapon upgrades, at least where I'm at, seem a little pointless and expensive. Maybe it is much more important late game, but where I am, I can clear most groups with my abilities, and headshots are one hit kills. There are some "bosses" where I wish my rifle had some more damage, but that's about it so far.
TL;DR I bought this on a Steam Sale for $7.50 including all DLC, but I would have no issues if I had paid $20. At the price I paid I feel like I got a steal of a deal, but this isn't the kind of game I would pay the release day price of $50-$60. Then again, thanks to Steam, I rarely pay more than $20 for any of my games lol.

Tower Wars, what more is there to say? The game plays around the game mode made popular by War Craft III in which the player constructs towers in a maze to protect their base (or in this game's instance, their castle). Its a simple style of gameplay for a very casual game that can be both relaxing, or in more difficult settings absolutely intense. Unfortunately, Tower Wars fails to deliver on any of that excitement that made tower defence games so very popular in the years past.
A few review note this game as being easy, others stating that it is hard. Overall, the game is easy--until you hit the absolute best in any given map in which case its a waiting game for the creeps to get strong enough to make it to your castle. Games lasting an hour or more of just waiting for your maxed out maze to finally be defeated while you sit hopeless...and bored. That is the survival mode in a nutshell--lifeless and easy. Aided with a rather terrible user interface and rather bad maps it feels uninspired and a chore to get into.
There now is multiplayer too, which like one of the single player modes adds the the ability to spend gold to buy "creeps" to send to the oppossing player's maze. This verses style worked fantastic in days past--the perfect balance in deciding to spend money for either offencive play or defencive play. While Tower Wars continues on this great gameplay, some of the same reasons that make the single player so dry still exist in multiplayer making it one of those games which simply does not draw the player in.
Sure, my ideas of tower defence games is carved from the various mods from the early days of their introduction as mods for various Blizzard games, but I gave Tower Wars a chance to work with the genre to create new and interesting gameplay and build on it. It adds hexagonal tiles, which could have resulted in amazing new ways to making new mazes, alas the maps do not even permit very complex mazes thanks to their size. I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone, especially at the asking price of $8. It quite simply falls short.

My recommendation is about as weak as it gets: If there was a Null option, I would have chosen that.
I just finished this game, clocking it at 7 hours, half of which, I'm quite certain, was spent walking from place to place. At least, that's how it felt.
The game's title is in reference to the fact that the focus swaps between two separate POV characters. One is an Irish pickpocket with plans to travel to America with his best mate (with voice acting that is uniformly and bizarrely listless and monotone). The other is a new detective who is caught up in a murder investigation on his very first day on the job.
The story is intriguing and the mystery will keep you guessing for much of the game. Not that you can possibly solve it, but you can at least make wild guesses that will almost assuredly be utterly inaccurate. It's not your fault; that's how it was written.
The gameplay is very linear and the puzzles vary from snoozingly simplistic to vaguely difficult, and none of them should be particularly hard to overcome, though some are easy to overlook if you forget to talk to someone or inspect an intem in your inventory properly.
Other than the primary POV character, the voice acting is actually quite good, and the art is very well done. (well, other than the point at which the good detective is standing upon the hand of a murder victim, anyway) There is very little music other than during the cut scenes, which are not particularly obtrusive and do serve to fill out scenes between gameplay quite nicely.
There are subtitles, so you can skip forward, and nearly all dialogue during gameplay can be repeated, so if you miss something, you can go back through. However, you can't replay cut scenes or a few auto-play moments, so don't skip forward. Especially near the end. Also, there are a number of scenes where the subtitles aren't in boxes but rather are actually cut off at the bottom of the screen, making them rather difficult to read. A couple of "leave area" hot spots have that same issue.
Speaking of the end, don't blink or you'll miss it and find yourself staring at the main menu (not even credits) wondering what in the everloving hell just happened. To say that it is abrupt is putting it mildly. And even if it were longer, it would be no less unsatisfying and jarring. It looks suspiciously like there was a plan for a sequel, however the studio closed the year after this game was released, so there is no hope of the terrible ending ever being mitigated. (I don't know if they ran out of money and that's why they ended it this way, or if this game killed the studio in revenge for that ending)
I'd take the ME3 ending over this and be happy, it's just that atrocious.
The Good:
* Voice Acting is quite well done, with one unfortunately major exception
* Tone is fairly even, despite the swap between POV protagonists
* The puzzles aren't terribly difficult, though they can be a bit simplistic at times
The Bad:
* Having music during gameplay would go a long way
* Walking takes forever and there's rather too much of it
* There are plot threads and hot spots that never get resolved
* Neither of the protagonists is particularly likeable, so playing as them is kind of grating
The Ugly:
* That horribad ending... WTF?!?
Rating: 58%
This game could come in at a solid 75% or so if it weren't for the few notable flaws. It loses a full 10% for the ending alone, plus another 5% for Tim's voice actor sleeping-walking through the entire adventure. The slow pace and uneven quality on the subtitles and controls take out a few more percentage points. It had the makings of a solid, if unremarkable adventure game, and most of the time, that's what you've got. Unfortunately, it's flaws are unavoidable, and thus I can't in good consience give it more than the most tepid of recommendations. If I could give it a Null Recommendation, I would.
TLDR: It's ok enough, but you've been warned about the primary POV's sleep-inducing delivery and that ending... that terrible, execrable ending... >_<

Huge fan of the Far Cry series.  Honestly wasn't too sure about Primal, but I picked it up anyways.  Yes, you lose all you're guns and fun toys, no the story is not overly compelling, but Primal really grasps one of the best parts of the franchise, and has created a vast world where everything wants to kill you.  There are so many animals running around all at once.  I was watching two bears fight, and heard something behind me.  Turn around, and alll of a sudden I'm being mauled by a third bear!
This is one of the only series that I love playing the game on the hardest difficulty, then adding the ziggy mod to FC3, or Nightmare mod to FC4.  Neither one of them were hard enough though, because in those games you didn't have to worry about so many animals.  You could make a good assumption where the enemy was.  In Primal, the danger is EVERYWHERE.  It is unpredictable, and at night, you have to constantly watch all around you. (so many noises)
I do miss my toys from previous entries in the series, the subtitles are annoying and takes away from the immersion because if you were in this time period, you would understand what they're saying.  Just a way to get out of having to pay for multiple languages in the game.  Performance could be better,  and for a game world as large as Oros, I don't feel like I should be 18.4% complete after 5 1/2 hours of wandering around, doing the occasional quest.  Maybe bonfires and outposts aren't figured into that... I don't know.
I am also immensely dissapointed that there is no coop.  FC4 coop was fantasticly fun.  It's the reason my wife plays video games now.  It's how I taught my 5 yr old to play fps's.  But now Ubi takes it away...
Haven't run the game on my laptop (I7 w/ 980m 16gb ram) but my pc (amd-fx8320, amd 7950, 8gb ram)  runs very high settings between 40-50 fps with the occasional random dip (would probably have no issues if I turned down to high).
Ubisoft is what it is unfortunately.  Ubisoft as a Dev, I love nearly all their games, I admire the risks they take with their franchises, and they make Far Cry games.
But Ubisoft the publisher needs to step out of the way.  Quit making Devs cut corners, Optimize your pc ports, don't cut out on the creative writing, open up to the modding community, don't be like Activision and treat one game like a golden goose.
As far as Uplay,  those of you that hate on it should think twice on that.  In my opinion at least,  I like to access any and all my games from one place.  Steam.  Ubisoft still sells their titles on steam.  That makes me happy.  I hate having to use origin specificly for EA games.  It make's me really sad they control the crysis franchise.  I really wanted to play the mass effect trilogy, but I refuse to buy it on origin because I hate having my games span across so many different pc platforms.
Ubisoft, better or worse,  I still HIGHLY recommend this new entry into the FC franchise.  Ignore all the reviews about performance issues until people start posting what kind of gear they're running.  My gear is 3 years old now, and I still run all the new titles at pretty high settings, so those who cry about such terrible performance here either cry about being below their own set standard fps rate or are running gear even more out of date than my own.
I know I'll spend at least 30 hours in this game, plus whatever time my boy and my wife play on their own campaigns.  But if you take just me, $3/hr is worth it.

Beat Hazard was one of the first indie games that really stuck out and stayed with me, even after five years. It has a staying power that the likes of Audiosurf doesn't have, because unlike the aforementioned, Beat Hazard has an overwhelming sense of style with the blinding, epilepsy-inducing light show it puts out and the fast-paced carnage that plays like ADHD bullet hell on the higher difficulties, except the enemy ships are the bullets. Audiosurf is more of a pretty looking acid trip with confusing and distracting color-matching mechanics, while Beat Hazard stays true to its concept of an arcade space shooter that turns everything up to eleven and adds some bass boost in the mix. Once the hours you spend into the game pay off and you start to master the highest difficulty, all the chaos comes into place in full clarity, and you suddenly play the role of conductor in a controlled cacophony with a stupidly big grin on your face.
The result is as approachable
always thrilling as it is visually arresting and immensely replayable. A combination of classic Asteroids mechanics and procedural generation by music, included in the package are tons of unlockables and power-ups, online play and co-op, modes like survival and boss rush, great additional content, and Steam Workshop.
Simply put, it's one of my favorite indie games of all time, and the best twin-stick space shooter there ever will be, in my opinion.

I recently did another playthrough of HL2 and it holds up surprisingly well.

- Gameplay always changes. Sometimes it's puzzles, sometimes straight shooting, sometimes you have to fight multiple enemy types, at the same time, which require different tactics.

- It's always been a fun experience.
Cons:
- HL2 squadmates are amazingly terrible. They are constantly in the way, getting themselves killed by hazards which are easy to avoid, and are mostly useless.
- Ladders kill you less often now but getting off of them is like trying to remove superglue from your hands.
- Placing items about the ground for platforming/jumping puzzles is frightfully trying. You slide around on top of whatever surface you're on. The objects bounce around haphazardly. That part has never been fun.
Bugs and quirks aside, it's always been an enjoyable game.

Company of Heroes 2 is just a former shadow of its predecessor, Company of Heroes 1. While one could argue that this isnt a remake of CoH1 which is true, however, CoH2 is lacks in content of its predecessor while the game felt dumb downed in so many ways where the Command Tree from CoH1 has been replaced with a system that is similar to Call of Duty's perks system. Rusians felt like a reskinned version of America from the first game in some ways. The campaign is not as fun as the previous game as it felt like the entire campaign is just a lengthy tutorial as the game does not seemed to trust you with its arsenal, unlike its predecessor.
To make things worse, Sega decided to fill the game with microtrasactions that are pretty costly that ranges from harmless cosmetic skins for vehicles to paid only commander with new units and abilities where you only can obtain it by paying your hard earned money. There isnt any way to unlock these content by playing the game. Unfortunately, this game felt like it is the paid version of Company of Heroes Online with all these microtrasactions. To make things even worse, Sega decides to hide these microtrasactions from the Steam Store while you only can find these microtrsactions inside the game, just like an In-App Purchase (IAP) in a mobile game. The only microtransactions that Sega did correctly were the DLC content packs such as Case Blue where these packs provides some pretty decent new solo and coop missions into the game. One could argue that these content are optional but having these microtrasactions are a notion by major publishers to put more and more paywall into game content to encourage gamers to pay more for lesser content.
As a conclusion, buyers beware. If you are looking for a multiplayer RTS, look elsewhere. If you are a predominantly single player RTS gamer, Company of Heroes 2 might give you a decent experience. As a Relic game fan, Company of Heroes 2 is a disappointment as this isnt the Company of Heroes sequel that most are looking for but a cynical attempt by Sega to include questionable IAPs into the game that were abused heavily on mobile. I thought Dawn of War 2 was average at best, but seemed like Relic has made Company of Heroes 2 even worse than Dawn of War 2.
I highly recommend one to get Company of Heroes 1 Complete Edition instead, then, get the Eastern Front mod to play as Rusians. Alternatively, get World in Conflict with Soviet Assault expansion or get the latest installment from the Wargame series if you want a more realistic tactical RTS.

Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series is an adventure game by developers Telltale Games taking place in the setting of the Games of Thrones TV series. The plot revolves around a minor house from the books, house Forrester, and its family members, loyal bannermen of the Starks, as they  struggle to survive the dangerous environment around them and save their house from extinction. It's worth mentioning right of the bat that this videogame features many important events from the Game of Thrones TV series, and therefore there are plenty of spoilers from the show you may don't want to see.
Once again we have on our hands a typical Telltale videogame, so there's really not much to say about general gameplay and such. Game of Thrones has however some features that make him stand out on its own, namely:
- This time around you get to control roughly five characters in total, with you taking the shoes of a different character at each change of scenery. Also, given this game is based on Game of Thrones, nearly all the characters you play as some chances to die between the episodes, and for good
- The QTEs sequences you must face in this game are arguably more complex and require quicker reflexes than anything Telltale offered up to this point, which is rather fitting, given the game takes place in a medieval low fantasy universe where swordfights and battles are rather common
One thing that must be noted is that the engine Telltale Games is using for all their games is really becoming very outdated quickly, and it shows in a very annoying fashion in Game of Thrones above all the others (the fact the scenes here tend to be more crowded and the action sequences more ambitious don't help matters at all). It's very easy to bump into various graphical glitches during gameplay (lips not moving, lips not syncronizing with a character's speech, characters disappearing between scenes, delayed animations, characters standing still in the background, ...) that actually distract you from the experience. Also, the decision to render several backgrounds in a crayon art fashion is very questionable at best, given the whole thing doesn't mix well with the 3D models of everything else and tends to fall over onto some portions of the characters too, creating a very odd effect.
Speaking about how interactive the story is in Game of Thrones, while Telltale games have never been that much about changing the plot in any significant way with your choices, this game totally takes the cake, as the final sequences of the plot don't change at all even choosing different outcomes in past episodes, whole characters arcs turn out to be completely useless to the greater scope of saving house Forrester and some turns the story take (without your input no less) are questionable at best.
As such, while Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series is a solid Telltale videogame in its own right and can capture in the settings both the hardcore fans of the TV series and the newcommers, the enjoyment you can gain from it depends greatly on how much you are going to like the very few moments you can have control on and how much you can tolerate the story taking darker turns just for the hell of it

A lot of other reviews focus on the mechanics, why this is better than <insert arpg here>, and other assorted gameplay aspects. Instead, I'm going to talk about what an incredibly well crafted world this game has.
This game feels lived in, as if it's "real." Everything from the area design to the in-game lore creates a sense of a fantasy world that actually exists. Speaking of lore, the way the background is delivered to you tangenitally through discovery instead of directly through exposition is crucial in creating this feeling of a deep world filled with mystery that a player can't help but want to uncover. What's more, the mythos behind this world is diverse, deep, and engaging.
Contributing to this world's diversity is the way the various enemy types interact with eachother. Mechanically, it's such a simple thing for the blood-god obsessed lunatics to wage war with the alien-like magical beings invading the world, but it really helps reinforce, from a lore standpoint, that things are bigger than you. The warring of these factions against each other is something you only see on screen, but it has a way of capturing the imagination and immerssing the player.
The setting itself, somewhat of a cross between world war 1 and high fantasy, works not because it's a good concept, but because the developers took the time to make sure that everything fit together in a pleasing and consistent way. The music combines with the art and writing direction in a way which really glues everything together so that the whole is more than simply the sum of the individual parts.
In closing, this is the finest arpg I've ever experienced from a lore perspective and I feel extremely lucky to have experienced it. Highly recommended for people who want more than just solid mechanics.

So this is a surprisingly hard review to make, largely because there aren't many negative things to say about this game. It's a little old, sure, and with that can come technical problems and dated visuals, but that's something one has to expect. The awkward animations are actually a little charming, seeing how far the technologies have come since then. What is surprising though is how well the backgrounds and settings hold up. Although, yes, they tend to be a little colourless and depressing, they're gorgeously drawn and come in a crisp, high resolution. I'm kind of a stickler when it comes to 2D texture working, especially with these kinds of 3D/2D adventure games, and this one did not fail to satisfy me.
The character's are voice acted well enough; some of the lines suffer from being read from a script rather than spoken naturally, but the overall quality is just fine. Not a single character is offensive, even the ones that follow pretty blatant stereotypes. The ruffian, the evil minion, the sassy protagonist. I rather enjoyed them and the personalities they carried. Like the voice acting, the story isn't anything ground breaking or shocking. It telegraphs coming twists pretty blatantly and yet it never feels like it detracts from the game. All of this just sort of exists around the real meat of it.
That being, of course, the puzzles. This is a very genuine point & click adventure / puzzle game and I adore it for it. The puzzles are great! A few of them do follow a bizarre sort of adventure-game logic, but they never go without subtle (or overt) hinting, and when you're stuck you can always get past it just by looking around, talking to people and inspecting your inventory. My main driving force in this game was always just to solve the puzzle and get to the next one. Really, this is where the game shines, and I don't regret a moment spent playing it.
I do wish there's more I could say about it, really. I've spent hours and hours in it already and I feel like it deserves this big fat review. There just isn't much more to it, and that is in no way a detractor. If you're out for a point & click puzzler, you could do a lot worse than this. :]

is a decent adventure game. It was branded by its developer as a "dark adventure game"; I don't consider it very dark, but it is atmospheric. The game is set in Plymouth, England in 1894. Throughout the game you alternate between two characters, Timothy Moor, a petty hood seeking to find a better life, and Detective Sergeant Briscol, a rigid agent of law and order.
There are a few technical issues with the game; most notable for me was probably the discrepancy between the character models' mouth movements and the spoken dialogue. Occasionally characters' mouths would move while there was no dialogue, or there would be dialogue, but no mouth movement, or the wrong character would be in sync with the speech. Also, when a playable character reflected in thought to himself, sometimes his mouth would move even though he was only thinking, or there would be slight reverberation to his internal monologue in some environments, as if he had spoken aloud. There were occasional differences between the subtitles and the spoken dialogue, as well as at least one mislabeled inventory item
, but nothing irritatingly glaring. I think the same sound effect was employed for both walking and running, and there were a few other details-oriented issues like that which should have been polished out prior to the game's release.

as they were in
. The voice acting was competent, and didn't cause distraction. [quasi-spoiler]

,

Double-clicking on an exit allows you to leave the current screen more quickly, rather than the playable character having to traverse the entirety of the distance to the exit, but unfortunately you can't access the map whenever you choose in order to jump to a different location, first you must exit the current location. When playing, you can display the active hotspots if you abhor pixel hunting, although without using the hotspot display feature I don't recall ever feeling like I had to tediously search around, plus the cursor turns red when hovering over a hotspot. Some of the tasks weren't straightforward, not in terms of being challenging, but in terms of defying real-world expectation, and there are also several tantalizingly unfinished plotlines; however, the story makes up for these shortcomings, in my opinion. For the most part the game flowed reasonably well, although the game does feel somewhat rushed and incomplete content-wise, like the developers had more planned than they had time or budget to execute.

9/10. Nope, 10/10 after my bear ate a couple having sex. No, not in the good way. The eating, I mean. And also the sex, too, for that matter.
Although there's only 9 hrs showing, I played the hell out of this all last week on the PS4, so it's closer to 90hrs all up.
First off, I'm a huge fan of Far Cry.  When Far Cry 3 came out, I spent over 1500hrs in the sandbox in the first 6 months. I also racked up almost 700hrs in ACIII, so that was a great Ubisoft year for me (not yet repeated, unfortunately).
I'm enjoying this more.
I've seen criticisms that this is just more of the same, but it's a great sandbox, well executed, so I'm just have a blast roaming the wilderness, interacting with the wildlife, killing a bunch of stuff until I run into more than I can handle and run like hell in a panicked attempt to stay alive and uneaten.
In FC3, "interacting" was limited to hunting and killing, FC4 gave elephant rides, but with the Beastmaster aspect of Primal, there's a whole new level of play.
If you're bored by the mechanics of the franchise, this probably isn't for you. I personally am loving it.
So what's wrong with it?
Very little. Oros is stunning, the animals are as suberbly done as ever, but surprisingly there's very little difference to me between the visuals on my PS4 and with my SLI Titan X's. Normally, this isn't really noticeable thanks to the suberb art, but last night after securing my Cave Bear, the textures on his head during the petting close-ups are glaringly lo-res.
Which is a little disappointing.
And my personal pet hates in Ubisoft games - when they don't get the big cats right.
To be fair, a lot of my anti-Ubisoft feelings are only raised by my high expectations. ACIII had the best cougars ever in a game, beautifully built and realised  (even better than Red Dead Redemption, although that still has the best bears ever in a game, although tragically unlikely ever to be seen in full glory on the PC), but when FC3 released and they replaced the pre-order black leopard skin with a Puma skin, presumably as ACIII cross-promotion, it just didn't work.
They built their leopards perfectly and leopards are built very differently from mountain lions, particularly in the face. You don't put a brown skin on a leopard model and get a convincing mountain lion.
You get a brown leopard.
And leopards don't look good in brown.
When AC4 released with jaguars, the cats were perfect to look at, but they recycled the Cougar sounds from ACIII. Jaguars sound more like lions and tigers than leopards or pumas and the high pitched catamount caterwauling detracted a lot from the immersion.
Far Cry Primal has made the same mistake.
You have "jaguars" in the jungle and "leopards" in the mountains. The leopards are snow leopards, presumably re-used from FC4 and just as perfectly done as previous.
But let's be clear.
There are no jaguars in this game.
Although the heads are slighlty rounder than the leopards from FC3 and the rosettes on the fur are those of a jaguar, the cats are far too small and slight to be Pleistocene jaguars, which were modern day lion-sized, but the neck, head and limbs are far too slim to belong on a jaguar.
The mug shot of the Black Jaguar in the beast menu is clearly a leopard as well.
Although a small modern jaguar can be leopard size, they are still strikingly different in the mass of the neck and jaw. A largish modern male jaguar is the size of a lioness, in the high 300lbs, whereas a 200lb leopard is considered huge. The "jaguars" here are smaller than the wolves. They look smaller than the snow leopards and I suspect they've just put a smooth jaguar skin over their snow leopard model.
They are beautifully built and animated, but just call the damn things leopards!!
The cave lions are easily the best rendition of a lion I've ever seen in a game, but again, they are too small, looking about modern lioness size - you know, the size a small Pleistocene jaguar.
Cave lions, like most things 12000 years ago, were a lot bigger than their modern counterparts.
But if you're not a pedantic geek about big cats like me, you likely won't even notice! And I really only notice when everything else is so superb, it really sticks out to me by comparison.
All in all, I personally care a lot less about many of the "issues" raised by a lot of reviews I've read (not enough weapon variety, too much like previous installments etc), so I'd give the game 9/10. I'm deducting a point for the lack of magnificent PC graphical superiority and big cat misrepresentation.
If you couldn't wait like me and got the PS4 version last week and are expecting to be blown away by the graphical upgrade to PC, well, this isn't Black Flag. Youre not going to be floored by the visual improvement on PC.
Unless there's going to be a high res texture pack, I can't recommend graphics as a reason to get this on PC if you already have it on console.
Plus, although I ground to unlock almost all skills, but only had ~30% unlocked, I had yet to encounter any reason for the "sexual content" warning, assuming it was a story element later in the game.
Last night, however, I took my trusty lo-res cave bear companion on a little midnight stronghold raid in the frozen north. As we're creeping through an Udam cave, I could hear grunting and see movement in the distance. As I got closer, I could hear both male and female grunts and groans.
You will quite often come across Udam butchering the carcasses of your fellow Wenja to make tasty jerky, so I assumed that was what was going on. However, as I crept closer, I could see only the Udams hips moving, no arm-swinging. Closer still, I can see two sets of legs. Graphical glitch? Nope, as I moved to the side, there is an Udam female dutifully holding herself in downward facing dog position, while her standing male counterpart is equally dutifully pumping away from behind.
It took me a while to process what I was seeing, since it was so unexpected, but what else would you expect to be going on at that time of night? The grunting and groaning suddenly made sense.
Given the neanderthal modelling of the Udam, it was truly a case of bumping uglies.
So I did what any other right-thinking caveman with access to a fur-clad killing machine companion would do: had my 2000lb cave bear shred my enemies mid-coitus.
What other game can claim that?
Hang on, I'm revising my score for that alone - 10/10

Beat Hazard is one of my favorite games on Steam.  I've always been interested in the idea of music modifying a game to produce a game where you feel like you play your music.
And honestly... Beat Hazard isn't that game.  It suffer the same fate as all these procedurally generated music games, like Audiosurf, where the music doesn't have a strong connection to the game you're playing.  When you play Beat Hazard, there is limited connectability to the the music.
The Music in Beat Hazard pretty much affects the "intensity" of the game.   If you play some music with a high BPM enemies will move at a faster rate than a low BPM.  But even playing Happy Hardcore and other fast BPM music, the game doesn't appear broken, which is a good thing.  A VERY good thing, as I'd hate to see the game limit what types of music it can play.
In addition, the game comes with a built in soundtrack, something Audiosurf doesn't really do, so at least you can play exactly what song the developer was thinking of when you play the game, and the fact is... it works and by that I mean very well.  There a variety of songs chosen but slow songs have a different feel from fast songs.  That's good.
But you'll play through the 20 songs or so and then you'll have to play your music?  Right?    Well... not unless you want to, though you can.  There's also internet radio!   At least my copy (which is from the original launch) came with a few stations already set up and adding more is relatively easy, EXCEPT it requires editing a file, so steam boxes and anyone playing in a big picture mode has to go through a few hoops to make it work.  It's not awful, but it's an annoying few steps that I wish wasn't required.
However the build in internet radio works, and works well, rather than "play a song" you instead play a time battle, 4 minutes up to 20 minutes I believe (and a survival mode for when you want to see how far you can go).  And again, it's YOUR choice.  I chose an electronica station, so I was loving the music and the game, and it worked... really well.   Well except for the fact there's a little disconnect between the game and the song, but you can use internet radio, and listen to great music as you play.
So what's the game like?  It's a bit like Geometry wars.  Rather than fighting geometry shapes, you're instead blasting ships and flying dodging their attacks.  It's quite similar to bullet hell games, but there's a few major changes.  First the game isn't that brutally hard, and gives you multiple difficulty options (including a few you can only unlock through a perk system).  Second, there's power ups.  Enemy ships when destroyed can drop different items, some of them are for points, some of them are weapons you can trigger, and finally there's "volume" and "power".  Power does exactly what you think, it makes your ship strong, however Volume is different.  It increases the sound of the song you're listening to.  At the beginning your music is quite, but as you volume up the sound increases so you can hear your song at full volume.  This also affects the power of your ship (I think defensively) and when you max both you get a special mode, so both of these power ups are important.
While that disconnect from the music for the game doesn't make this the game I dream of, the fact is the gameplay of the game is fun, and there's a decent connection when you're listening to music and what's happening in the game.  If a song goes from slow to fast and back, you'll notice enemies speeding up and slowing down.  The connection could be better, if you play a song two or three times, it's random how enemies will appear and attack.   However the gameplay itself is solid, and you are able to listen to music you like and have it make a minor effect on the game you're playing.
But the game underneath is just a fun game.  I love geometry wars, and Beat Hazard I think might actually beat Geometry wars for replayability.  I recommend this game not because it's a stunning success in the world of music games, but because it's a fantastic twin stick shooter with a lot of depth.  The two DLCs (Shadow Operations Unit and Ultra) are both excellent add ons, and being able to get the whole set for under 20 bucks is a good value.

First off, at the time of writing the reviews for this game stand at Positive (1,346) Negative (695) - Mixed. This is misleading because most of the negative reviews reflect frustration over technical issues at launch. I experienced none whatsoever, and I understand that there appeared several solutions to problems presented.
That being said the game deserves a solid 8/10. It is very similar to other Far Cry games, yet it differs from Far Cry 4 more than Far Cry 4 differs from Far Cry 3. It stands out from the series in a few key ways. The setting takes center stage here, from the language, the flora and fauna, everything feels very primeval. Folks may miss the gunplay, but I found that combat can be very fast and deadly once you realize that many of your weapons are better thrown than used for melee. It is a bummer that there is no block or counter feature to combat, but if you play it right, there is never a need to. With beast in tow, there are plenty of opportunities for melee takedowns, a signature of the series. At least half the combat comes from and between the beast population, which is far more dense and deadly than in previous installments. I also like the improvements to the crafting system. Now that all your weapons can be thrown or are single use, it behooves you to keep well stocked in supplies to craft said weapons. In other Far Cry games I was let down a little in that crafting extended to only about half the game, after I crafted all my bags. Resources and crafting are more relevant thoughout the playthrough now.
All in all, very competently made. It is not ground breaking, but it is more than just Far Cry 4.5 like Blood Dragon was to 3. I would suggest, however waiting for a sale, as it is more of a $30-40 title. No regets here though.
On a side note, I know how frustrating it can be when your purchased software doesn't work properly, but that is why there is a refund system. Seeing the bad reviews leads people to believe that the product is inferior, which isn't the whole truth. I wouldn't say that a movie was bad if I was locked out of the theater. But I would get a refund and complain directly to management. Condemning the hard working artists and coders for the DRM policy of their bosses is unfair.

Kind of pointless reviewing this game in 2017, but so is my life, so whatever.
Half-Life 2 is a classic FPS that heavily influenced the entire genre. This game follows a man who almost single-handedly tries to overthrow a corrupt government in an Orwellian future.
Although the standards have changed over time and this game doesn't pack the punch that modern FPS games do, it is definitely an enjoyable experience for anyone nostalgic, any completionist and anyone with a crappy computer. Even if it's quite old for a video game, at no point in the game I was bothered by this. Some locations seemed a bit bland as they couldn't add a lot of small details with the technology they had, but this was balanced out by Valve's incredible level design.
Since the story was kind of average and the dialogue was pretty much downright horrible, the game's strongest side is gameplay. The game has neat puzzles and the platforming was absolutely incredible, but the ranged combat was great too. With plenty of weapons to choose from and plenty of enemies to fight off, this game rarely feels boring. Even though I didn't like the sequences where you use a vechile, the game has plenty of intense moments and shotgunning to the face. Nearly all my favourite parts of the game were the ones where you fight zombies, with Ravenholm being the high point for me. The zombies in this game are very well-designed, and even though the average zombie quickly became less scary once I realized how helpless it is, the fast zombies are infamously tough and scary, as it is almost impossible to escape them or hide from them. The poison zombie gave me the chills too, after a while my heart started racing every time I heard the poison headcrab sound effect. With Ravenholm having tons and tons of zombies, I was constantly on my toes, making it one of my favourite video game locations. Getting the achievement for completing it only using the gravity gun sent my heart rate through the roof.
Speaking of which, the achievements in this game make it a very good pick for a completionist. As you can see, I have more than 20 hours on record, so it does take a while to get 100% in, but it never got hopeless or tedious. Most of the achievements that you'll get later on are some challenges or related to exploration, and none of the achievements are ridiculously hard or something extremely time-consuming like "bake 1000000 pies", meaning that you just need some time (and not much of it) and you'll get them all.
Overall, it's a neat game that I recommend picking up if you don't feel like it's getting too old.

"When you play the game of thrones, you win or you die".
In Telltales take on George R.R. Martins success phantasy world, we take part while experiencing the fate of House Forrester,  a smaller northern noble house, which leads the production of ironwood, an important production material for different kind of arms and armor. In the wake of the "Red Wedding" the house, falls into disarray, facing not only their old enemies the Whitehill clan, which are in league with the cruel Boltons. But Telltales Game of Thrones story also reaches from the southern Kingdoms over Kings Landing up to the Northern Wall and beyond.
Naturally this includes quite some of the popular characters from books and tv series, which are spoken by the actors themselves.
This is only one of the points, which give Telltales game a great atmosphere, so it fits nicely into the rest of the setting.
The story itself, which quite sometimes offers surprises, in what the haunted northern House has to endure in their struggle for existence, also does not suffer in comparison. No one is safe in the harsh world of Westeros.
While regarding music and synchronization there are few points to criticise, the graphic is dark comic, not really very detailful, but ocassionally quite beautiful still.
The gameplay meanwhile is the -nowadays- usual Telltale style... quite few actual puzzles or classical adventure interactions, while the story is mostly dialogue driven, supported by the occasional quick time event (the valar morghulis death screen can happen quite often here) and told by cut scenes.
During the six episodes the player also has naturally quite some decisions to choose from, which influence the way the story goes more or less - naturally more often less, but nearing the end it get´s more pregnant.
Speaking of the end, this is also one of the main complaints, one can bring up here. Since Telltale is at the moment developing a second seasons, they left quite some open ends in their finale. This can dampen the effect for players, who naturally want a finished storyline.
Conclusio: For fans of Game of Thrones the love, with which the lore and drama is presented will bring much fun i guess. As long as you are not bothered by Telltales kind of presentation and the partly open end, it should be a clear recommendation.

Back when I was about 10 years old, all I played was Saints Row 2. I played it online with my friend Trevor and we just found it to be the greatest game. Come 2011, Saints Row: The Third comes out and I get that on the release day. I beat that game at least ten times. Then Saints Row IV came out in 2013 and I completely ignored it. I watched the trailers and I thought "Aliens? Superpowers? They destroyed the series. That game must be utter crap." I never even rented it or watched gameplay on it because I thought it was going to be so bad. Then, just six days ago, I saw that Saints Row IV Century Edition was $7.50 on HumbleBundle and I was blown away by how good that deal was. The full game and 26 DLCs for only $7.50? Hell yeah. I loved Saints Row 2 and Saints Row: The Third so much so I thought I should give Saints Row IV a chance.
Honestly, Saints Row IV has to be my favorite game in the series and my favorite game period. Not only does this game add so much to the Saints Row universe, it also reflects a lot on the three previous games. In Saints Row IV, you get to face off against the Vice Kings, Morningstar, The Brotherhood, Ultor, Sons of Samedi, and The Ronin.
Not only do they bring back many previous gangs, they also bring back famous characters from the previous games such as Benjamin King, Tanya Winters, Anthony Green, Warren Willians, Old 'Fun' Shaundi, Julius Little, Veteran Child, Maero, Phillipe Loren, Cyrus Temple, and Jyunichi. Having to go into many different simulations and fight off old gangs and old enemies is great nostalgia.
Seeing old friends and old enemies is great but finding new friends is just as good. Keith David, Asha, and CID are great help along the way (My favorite of the three are CID becuase he can be funny sometimes.) One the greatest, strongest, largest, and best new character is Paul. He's a badass.
As to the storyline, it's pretty damn good. It really ties everything together. It also sets a really nice path for Saints Row Gat out of Hell.
There's a lot I could say but to sum it up, 10/10. Saints Row IV is a fantastic edition to the series and Deep Silver did a great job making it. Some powers and weapons ('Merica) are incredibly overpowered but sometimes you need a little bit of overpowered in this game. Hacking stores instead of buying them is pretty cool and some of the puzzles can be challenging but you should get them on the first or second try.
Also, make sure to get the DLCs. Enter the Dominatrix and How the Saints Save Christmas are great story missions and I recommend that you buy and beat them. Also, make sure to watch the ending credits because all the characters sing along to the song "This Is How We Do It."
