What an awesome game Dying Light is.

Note: Haven't played The Following yet.

Dying Light takes place in a fictional place called Harran with there being two areas, the Slums and Oldtown/Sector 0. You play as Kyle Crane, voiced by the wonderful Roger Craig Smith (also does the voice for Sonic). Crane is a GRE operative sent to Harran the investigate the situation there and find a man named Rais. Now that we've got that, it's time for the pros and cons of Dying Light (in my opinion):

Positives:
- The parkour elements are very well executed and work great in the enviroment. You can climb up almost everything.
- The areas you play through are immersive, detailed, and, like I said, nearly everything can be climbed up or on.
- The melee combat is incredibly satisfying and smooth.
- There are lots of items that can be picked up and can be crafted into something else.
- There are lot of side quests to keep you busy all throughout the game.
- All of the skills on the skill tree don't feel useless and the leveling up in general is very well-done.
- The game performs pretty well and has a decent amount of graphics options (including an FOV slider).
- Most of the special enemies are cool looking and challenging to fight.
- Playing through the night is a very interesting gameplay mechanic because the enemies get tougher and very difficult to kill enemies come out. Surviving a night rewards you with a huge XP bonus.
- The finale of the game is very fun.

Negatives:
- Although the story isn't that bad, it's still kind of lackluster with not many characters getting any attributes or traits associated with them.
- The game does perform well but there are some random drops in performance in certain parts of the base game areas.
- The gunplay doesn't feel right and it isn't very fun to use guns.
- SPOILERS FOR THE END OF THE GAME:

Nonetheless, Dying Light is an incredible game if you're a fan of the survival horror/zombie game genre. I strongly recommend the game to anyone who likes zombie games or Mirror's Edge as the parkour in Dying Light feels on-par with it.

This is without a second thought, the most unique Real-Time-Stratergy game I've played since Starcraft 2 and its awsome expansions (Heart of the Swarm & Legacy of the Void). Although this game will never be as perfectly designed as what Blizzard has created, this game is epic and one of my all time favourites!
The Pros:
Four unique races that (In my opinion) are well balanced. The Humans force consisting of solely AI units. The Beta are more 'Human' like in regards to current day civilisation, with mechanised vehicles, ground soldiers with a great construction coverage of the visible map. The Goo consist of nanobots that can replicate fast and formulate into uniquely designed units. Once having established a foothold on a harder difficulty, they a near-impossible to eradicate as their expansion rate is rapid. Last but not least, the Shroud. They are a mysterious race that are hellbent on eradicating all life in the universe, as if they are trophy hunters, (In some regards, I think they are exactly that). Awsome to play as and verus.
The Cons:
Multiplayer is at times, quiet and dead, but there are thousands of active players playing by themselves.
The Frame-Per-Second can drop considerably for a short duration whilst there is large AI/User activity on curring during matches.
Conclusion:
This is an epic RTS that needs to be avalible in hardcopy for purchase to help boost the playerbase.

UBISOFT - if you are reading this: It is utterly unacceptable to launch a product in a condition such as this. $ 60 is a HIGH premium to pay for a buggy, unsatisfactory mess. I rarely take the time to review games, however with all the (I feel unwarranted) negative reviews for this game, I feel like I needed to review Far Cry Primal. I've been reading about people having issues and the game not running or looking great, but I've had literally zero problems so far.
I'm new to Far Cry, but not this type of game. So for those that say this is a rehashed version of FC4, I can't speak to that. What I can say though is that I'm having a ton of fun. The character progression with skills and crafting is fun, the questing is alright, and the combat is what I expected given the technology of the setting. The taming of beasts seems easier than I thought, which I was disappointed in, but the different beasts you can tame are cool and have their various uses.
In this game the world is alive. There are no roads. There are no cities or quest hubs. There are some allies and smaller camps scattered around, but you are left to explore basically an uninhabited forest where mostly everything is trying to kill you or something else. With every step you take, your uncertainty about what is coming up increases. You never know what exactly to expect, and it is exciting in that way. Compare it to Skyrim for example, where the world was alive, yes, but not like this. Most of your adventuring came from dungeons or discovering cities with the occasional dragon encounter. In Far Cry Primal, the whole world is teeming with danger and it's honestly really well done.
Now there isn't a ton of story (although there is a main quest line which is interesting so far) but I honestly think that adds to the games setting. It really makes you feel like a stone age man in that way. If there was much more beyond saving allies and taking over enemy camps while being in constant fear of your life, it wouldn't feel like the stone age, and I feel the developers captured that well. If you want to play a game for lore or something this definitely isn't it, but I'm not sure why you would expect it to be, and that is honestly one of the most refreshing things about this game.
TL;DR No issues for me, would highly recommend solid 8/10

This is not a yes, it's at best a "maybe". If it's discounted and/or you're a big fan of slow, linear point&click adventures of the detective mystery variety, and if you come to it with low expectations, it can offer you some entertaining hours.
It's obviously a low budget game, technically lacking, very linear, quite old-fashioned, with logical puzzles that offer zero challenge but also zero frustration. And I use the world puzzles very liberally here, most of the time you point, you click, the story moves on. It is also very sloooooow. Seriously, everything is slow: the story, the movements of the characters, the time it takes for clicks to register - this is one for people with patience, and if you can't deal with that stay well away, you'll hate it.
The overall atmosphere is probably the best part of this game. The other big positive for me is the attempt to describe the detective process in a relatively "realistic" way for the police detectives of the era, or at least their fictional counterparts. I found the characters entertaining, however they're both rather antiheroes than heroes, and not always portrayed in a positive light, and I expect not everyone will like that. The visuals are allright and fit the mood, the sound is barely there but not annoying and the voice acting is decent enough for this kind of budget. The story itself isn't good, isn't bad. Lethal League is a competitive "battle pong" that has you take control of one of six players, each with different styles of play, in a deadly game of tag-by-baseball. The fundamentals of the game are pretty simple: Hit the ball and it changes to your color and will damage every enemy player but not yourself. Bunting will send the ball upward and give you a chance to reposition for a better attack. Any time you hit the ball you build up a super meter that will allow you to perform a special attack once filled.
The majority of strategy in LL revolves around two things: hit meter/lag, and angles. You'll need to pay attention to the hit meter at the bottom of the screen to know how much longer it will be before the hit lag ends and the ball continues on in play. Knowing when it will re-enter play will allow you to position yourself accordingly and begin your counter attack. Another important factor is being aware of the angle the ball takes (or will take if you can predict it) since knowing that will allow you to take control of it with your own strike or avoid getting knocked out.
Lethal League basically has two modes spread across several categories: Versus (Online/Local/Challenge) and Strikers. Versus is the basic game mode where you have a limited number of life stocks and the game ends when you or your team run out of them. Strikers puts you in position of a goal that you must keep the enemy team from hitting with an enemy-charged ball. There is also a point game in the challenge mode which is like versus but you play until one player gets a set number of kills.
Since the game only has six playable characters, six stages, and really just two modes (only one of which seem to be played online: versus). You'll probably find yourself running out of things to do without having a bunch of friends to play with. Not to mention the online community is rather small and it can take anywhere from 5-15 minutes just to find a match, and when you do find a match, having any kind of lag between the players can make some rounds pretty difficult as the ball bounces and hit lag can become downright unpredictable. There are definitely some fun times to be had when you get matched up with a decent opponent, though.
I would recommend grabbing this game somewhere around $5 or cheaper to really get your money's worth. It's not a bad game per-se, it just needs more content.

This is the MMO I've been waiting for. I would say this is the MMO I will be playing for years as so much can change and I've been burned so many times in the past. But so far Black Desert is phenomenal.
Pros:
Combat is just so much fun. You truly feel like a bada** and the animations and effects are so cool. It will be very hard to play a tab targeting game again
Graphically there isn't another MMO that I've ever played that could touch Black Desert. It's simply gorgeous.
Crafting is enjoyable. Hiring workers to do my dirty work is so nice. I'm an altoholic and being able to command my workers on other characters is great.
Fishing, yes fishing. I'm addicted to it. Addicted to filling my inventory and filling my cart up with fish and making the trek to the trade manager to sell my bounty.
Player housing is a mini game in and of itself.
Exploration in Black Desert is quite enjoyable. From just running around exploring to crafting a boat and sailing around the world, there is much to see.
Sandbox aspects. I like the fact that you can do whatever the heck you want to do or totally avoid what you don't want to do.
Cons:
All the current alienware and trap memes. Jesus people, please stop this cancer.
No dungeons or raids. This might be a temporary issue as from what I understand the Korean version (which is ahead of the NA/EU) is starting to implement dungeons. If dungeon/raid progression is important to you this is not the game for you at this point in time.
PVP focus. Those looking for a primarily PVE focused game will probably want to look elsewhere or at least wait and see if more dungeons are implemented.
No player trading. I believe this was put in place to avoid gold sellers.
As I said earlier I like this game. A lot. I see so much potential here that I am really excited to see what's on the horizon. Unless there are factors to this game that you simply cannot get past (PVP focus, gender locks, no tab targeting) I don't see how you will get at least a couple months of enjoyment out of Black Desert. Not bad for $9 in my opinion.

For a story that's set in the Game of Thrones universe this games story is worthy of the series it's based on.   It has all the Game of Thrones trappings; brutality, betrayal, scheming, gore, and a strong setting and strong characters.  The story itself fringes on the outside of the Game of Thrones television series but intersects with characters and plotlines.  While you play various members of the Forrester family you'll cross paths with such series regulars as Cersei, Tyrion, Ramsey Snow, John Snow, and Daenerys Targaryen.  It really puts you in the Game of Thrones setting and for the most part.  Yes, this is a pretty good Game of Thrones story.
The problem, though, is in its gameplay.  About 60% of the game is nothing more than selecting dialogue options.  35% is playing out quicktime events like combat, hunting, and sneaking.  The last 5% is what little opportunity you have to actually move youself around to look and interact with objects and ultimate there is very little that is satisfying here.  While most of Telltale's games play similar this particular one even moreso lowers your freedom almost completely in favor of dialogue trees and quicktime events, leaving self discovery almost completely out which, to me, is half of what an adventure game should be.
Ultimately Telltale fails at the game aspects leaving you with minimal interaction and game elements that do nothing more than bog down a quite competent story set in the Game of Thrones universe.  This would be better off if you the gameplay was left out and you just made the dialogue choices.  Or, better het, they just produce a spinoff series on HBO and call it Game of Thrones: The Forresters.
In the end I think I am done with Game of Thrones.  Especially this game version.  It isn't about winning.  It's about making choices and seeing how bad the result of the choices are and every choice ultimately ends up being bad.  That might make for good books and compelling TV, but it is not good for a game.

I recommend this game, but barely.
This is Telltale, so "Your actions change things!" When they really don't. No matter what you choose, no matter what happens, you always have more or less the same conclusion. And in this installment, the conclusion is always you getting screwed over. Like, at all times. You always lose, no matter what. The game has a very bad habit throughout everything of doing a terrible job conveying the situation. Throughout the entire game, I was told I didn't have enough men to do anything. Yet, the enemies have plenty of soldiers, and I seem to have enough to drive th eplot forwards.
And, the source material was just too good, and they didn't do anything with it. So many characters from the show were woven in, but only to make them not important in the end. The characters exclusive to the game were nice, but I didn't really buy the game wanting something "Like Game of Thrones" I wanted more or less the same thing. In the end, the plot amounts to nothing more than semi-canon fanfiction. They had so much they could have done with it, and if they took the time to make the games more detailed, perhaps I wouldn't have this big of a gripe. But you can't influence anything! You can't start wars, you can't choose to kill or save certain people, nothing. Everyone meets the same fate at the end, and the game tells you to just suck it. Too be honest, if you want a game that changes to your choices, you're better off playing Dungeons and Dragons.
On the flip side, maybe you're not looking for a game. Not a challenge, not a way to accomplish anything, but maybe you're looking for something to entertain yourself with. If you're just looking around for a slightly interactive movie with random quick-time events, Telltale is your place to go, and this game does a great job. I didn't get the atmosphere of Game of Thrones from this game, but it gave off an atmosphere of its own, to be honest. I liked the story, despite it barely being able to call itself a "Game of Thrones" story.
In conclusion, if you want a fun thing to do, buy the game. It'll be fun, I assure you, but only if you're really JUST looking for something fun because its intruiging. If you're looking for something to do in the challenging or engaging department, I'd reccomend a Telltale game where choices somewhat matter (Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us) or just saving the money. And who knows, maybe Season 2 will be better.

The game has become a stale game that keeps being balanced to allow both the Germans and Russians to be equal. German units during the real war were hardened units with long supply chains. Germans lost over 850k while the Russians lost 7.3 million.   The game is not realistic in anyway. One German squad with LMG will be killed by a Russian squad with a flame thrower in the open. Heavy machine gun crews will not pin down a squad in the open until they get into grenade range. The tactics are the worst ever for a game. During the single player you get to conduct some scorch earth tactics. That is all lost in the multiplayer games. The feared  8.8 cm Pak 43/2 that is mounted on the Elefant won't kill T-34 tanks on the first hit. While playing the game I have used two Pz IV and one Panther set up in a blocking position only to have the T-34 take three direct hits and drive back out of sight (with one of my snipers watching) to be repaired and attack again to repeat it over. Yet during the war the Germans had a 6 to 1 kill ratio in 1942 and a 4 to 1 in 1943/44 with the major of tanks being Pz III and Pz IV. The game lacks the massive amount of cheap soldiers and tanks that were thrown toward the Germans only to be killed. Units get stuck for no reason on the maps and won't move. You tell a unit to move and it takes a while for the unit to move. The AI just runs around to where you're not and try's to steal sectors with one squad and no support. Can't get the AI to build a bridge after I blow it up and I can force it to get bottle necked. Building have almost no defensive cover. The programmers didn't like that you had to use flamethrowers or explosives to remove squads in building so they changed the balancing. It was too close to reality for them. Play the first one!! It's much better with each Army having a different style to play. I will never buy a DLC...NOT WORTH THE MONEY!!!

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a brilliant strategy game that hits all the right notes for its genre.
Pros: "Ant farm" mode is surprisingly absorbing, rather than feeling like the downtime between missions. Managing the base adds to the sensation of being a military commander. You get to decide the direction XCOM will go in and make decisions to adjust your combat style past just moving your soldiers from tile to tile. Speaking of combat, I'm a big fan of the percentage chance for hitting/missing shots. Rather than weapons dealing less damage in improper conditions or only working in a certain range, you have the chance to miss entirely. This encourages strategic play (i.e. moving your assault with a shotgun into a flanking postion rather than trying to snipe from the minimum distance). Moreover, it adds to the sensation of real combat; despite all your planning, things can and will go wrong. Difficulty is high enough so that you have to at least be trying and have some idea of what you're doing but not to the point where it's frustrating to progress. Finally, despite the non-procedurally generated maps and exact same story every playthrough, the randomness of UFO encounters and diversity of combat options adds a lot of replay value. That, and the Long War mod (but that's a whole seperate beast).
Cons: Despite what you'd expect, the game gets progressively easier as time goes on. Once you get the hang of combat and stop doing stupid stuff like ignoring council missions (give me a break, it was my first playthrough) it's just a matter of when the technology comes along and your soldiers level. Challenge is lost when your squad consists of six colonels with plasma weapons. The only thing that can really make the game suddenly harder is losing part of your team. Which is another problem; it is exceptionally easy to screw up your game. One mistake in combat can cost you all your soldiers and council nations without much you can do to fix it. I love a challenge, but save scumming often seems unavoidable with XCOM.
Overall, I'd still suggest XCOM: Enemy Unknown to almost all gamers. It's fun, addictive, immersive, and provides some of the best victories to be had in gaming. Ayylmao/10.

Alter Ego is a fantastic Point & Click game.
You play as both Timothy Moor - a thief who dreams of escaping to America, and Detective Briscol - who aims to solve the infamous murders committed by "Mad William". There are various parts to the game and you will switch between the two characters to get both perspectives on the story as it unfolds - this is the meaning behind the game's namesake, two separate points of view.
The atmosphere, voice acting and music are perfect for immersion; and the story is uniquely written - it leads you to believe one outcome, yet it turns right around and you're left with something entirely different and unexpected.
The few complaints I have are that it is a bit short, there are still a few things that are left unexplained and I wished that the ending had been left on a more positive note.
As for replay value, I can't be certain; but I absolutely loved it and it's worth the price!

Tower Wars,
It's not your average tower defence game. Sure it has a survival mode to play it that way but that's not the sole action of this game. It's a tower defender and attacker! That's right you have to go on the offence or no matter how great you planning if you only defend you will fail. In fact if your balance of attach vs defence is even a little off you will fail. The computer baddys are tough, and may even break you heh.
The real grabber with this game though is the online portion. You can battle with or against friends and strangers from across the world. Yes I used the plural, you can join with up to two other people per team (3 total) for a 6 player game! This is a fantasticly fun way to play. Mixing more than one mind into the game makes it a lot of fun, and a bit more challenging. Things happen fast, so don't plan on a extended set up period. A game can be completed in just a few turns or it can last for up to an hour (In one battle I had so far) all depending on the skill level and a little bit of luck in mine placements which are always random.
The good:
Instant fun
Decent "Cartoony" graphics
smooth, lag free play
Play with friends!
New exciting twist to the tower defence genre
The bad:
Can be a little slow to load
You don't get the option to "Rematch" and the game quits out on it's own after a match. So no chance
to ask the other player to a hosted battle for a rematch either.
The above makes meeting new people that play and growing your circle in the game a bit harder than it should be.
You can always use the steam "Recently Played" list but you shouldn't have to.

This is a very simplistic but also VERY addicting strategy game. It's simple in the fact that you can pause at any minute and walk away for hrs or days even and then pick right back off where you let off. The challenge is in the time limit to achieve your goals while finding the right combo of crew, tech and upgrades with limited resources in that time frame. It's so addicting in the fact that it's such a simple game that you SHOULD be able to beat it easily, but finding the right combo combines a good dose of random luck plus learning what-works-best-against-what. For those not able to beat it yet, dont give up as each play thru gives different turn outs of upgrade choices that also have to match up to when you havent blown all your credits. Best advice is to save for few random space port shops to get equipment (even if you cant use it yet) then build up ship to use it inbetween shopping sprees! Randomization gives to many, many different play thrus for plain game and AE adds even more content.
Only thing I'd say was missing was an infinite mode. Once you've acuatlly beat the game it almost seems severely anticlimatic to suddenly end like hitting a brick wall with the amount of effort it took to beat the final boss.

My gosh I wanted to like this game.  Red Alert 2 remains my favorite RTS experience to date, and the fact that the soundtrack is done by Frank K. is icing on the cake.  However, many of my favorite things about RA2 are absent here.  The creativity of the units, the ability of units to rank up, the humor suffused throughout the whole experience.  I played until the Goo campaign to finally make a judgment since that race seemed to be the most interesting of the three, but playing this was just a tedious and boring time.

As far as a Simcity replacement goes; it's not bad.  I have become fairly addicted but the replayability is fairly limited due to its repetative nature.  The population cap is incredibly frustrating; preventing you from constructing a real megacropolis; although that's not what this game is about. I grew up with strategy classics like Warcraft, Dune 2 and Command and Conquer, as well as earlier squad based, mouse-driven action games like Syndicate and Cannon Fodder for the Commodore Amiga. While I played earlier RTS games produced by Relic, the first Company of Heroes was an unforgettable experience in terms of tactical and strategic gameplay. The forced asymmetric balance, the recognizable roles of iconic units, the scarring of western european landscapes and the feeling of having not-quite direct control of your units - while themselves not entirely unique had not been blended this well together in an RTS before this title. If this was a review of the first game I would talk about how well it's theme and feel payed tribute to it's Hollywood inspirations.

Company of Heroes 2 had a bumpy start. The original campaign was solid but had an unfortunate anti-Soviet story line (which is distinct as the series goes to great pains to never address Nazism directly) that polarised many eastern european players. The game had a premium price tag upon release, and for the first year and a half alternated between paid single player, co-op and multiplayer expansions. Some of the multiplayer expansions (commanders) were not well balanced upon release, which cultivated the perception (and in some cases, reality) that Company of Heroes 2 was pay 2 win (although I believe this is pretty common misconception in games that frequently ship small multiplayer content). Also, the blizzard mechanics, that were one of the big selling points in the hype preceeding the release of Company of Heroes 2, turned out to be impressive visually but hardware intensive and ultimately had a negative gameplay experience (as the momentum of the battle slowed down).

The gameplay experience in Company of Heroes 2 has improved, a lot. The subsequent Theatre of War mission packs and Ardennes Assault single player campaign steer clear of controversial subject matter and give a solid mix of scalable challenge, varied gameplay and visceral theme. The game engine itself has been augmented with the addition of modding support, live spectating, improved AI, improved squad cover mechanics and small arms mechanics. This is in addition to the excellent true-sight engine, allowing you to ambush, advance and flank your enemies. Two new factions, the mobile and adaptive US forces and specialised Oberkommando West were added. The feel and gameplay of these two factions are completely unlike the Soviet or Ostheer armies from the core game - adding huge amounts of depth to the games tactics and strategy. The "war spoils" system was introduced (a method for being rewarded with a random skin, bulletin or commander every few games) and commander balance/design has improved - still not perfect but is getting better with every patch.

I pre-ordered the base package (I think the premium/collectors edition was $120 AUD or something), then picked up most of the first year's DLC in a steam sale. I picked up the rest of the DLC as it was released. I think picking everything up at full price is overpriced, but grabbing just a few at full price or waiting for a sale seems to be the best way to go (unless you get lucky with the "war spoils" system).
Multiplayer - comp-stomp, friendly and ranked games are what keep me hooked to this game. It feels like there is always more to learn and the game consistently rewards you for using tactics and abilities intelligently. The full roster of units, skills, commanders is huge and there is a lot to explore. Grab a friend and explore it. Get the hang of basic mechanics in AI mode, then play against some other players - you will get beaten a lot initially, take what you learn and use it to improve. Like most online communities there are good and bad members - listen to the good, seek feedback, discuss what you could do differently; ignore the bad.
If you enjoy RTS or MOBA games, check this out.
If you enjoy World War II themed games, check this out.
If you enjoy vanquishing skilled opponents in grueling 1v1 matchups, check this out.
If you enjoy playing with a small team, working together to outplay another small team, check this out.
If you enjoy destroying deserted farmhouses with monstrous steel beasts, check this out.
If you subscribe to a certain ideology associated with stylish uniforms, check this out.
If you hate the above ideology, check this out.
For me, Company of Heroes 2, is the RTS that I choose to play in 2013, 2014, 2015 and beyond.

Don't be dismayed by the "Mixed" rating. All the negatives I've seen are just people complaining about an error instead of looking into the forums for the simple fix.
I've not had any issues with the game on my 3.4GHz i5, 16GB RAM, 4GB GTX970 box. With my 1440p monitor, the in-game benchmark shows around 44FPS on ULTRA settings.
As for the game itself, I feel Ubisoft redeemed itself from the uter launch failure that I found FC4 was. Haven't experienced a single bug, error, or glitch. And you get a ton of UI configuration to get rid of almost all the immersion-breaking features. My only annoyance is untagged hostile animals and humans show up on the minimap and the only way to get rid of that is to disable the ENTIRE minimap.
The world is absolutely GORGEOUS! And unlike FC4, the absurd amount of animals in the world works very well, creating the feel of man being part of the nature untouched by the civilized world. The familiar mechanics received an upgrade as well. Unless you headshot a goat from your bow, it'll run away, but will soon bleed out; and you can use your "animal" vision to track it. You can use animal fat or burning things in the world to set your arrows or club on fire, increasing damage. And yes, you can set a bear on fire with a burning club, and it'll run around burning down the woods. You can also collect materials and build up your village.
You can tame animals, which will function as your attack drones. You also meet multiple characters that join your village and offer you side quests. Collecting resources and building (and upgrading) village huts for these people gives you upgrades.
If FC4 blatantly rehashed the enjoyable elements of FC3, Primal certainly makes the concept more subdued. You still have the familiar random encounters, hunts, plants, outposts, and collectables, but they feel much more an integral part of this stunning and outlandish caveman world. With FC4, I felt it was a cash grab. With Primal, I feel Ubisoft took a risk, poured some heart and soul into it, and it paid off. If you've enjoyed FC3 and FC4, you'll definitely enjoy Primal.

The game has great visuals and music, the story is decent but nothing new. It's one of those games I was pretty split on but after thinking it over I just don't think an RPG can get a recommend from me based on these elements alone. Child of Light would have made a great story-rich platform/adventure game and I know Ubisoft can make good games that fall into that category (looking at you Valiant Hearts) but this doesn't do so well as an RPG in my opinion.
I found the battle system tedious and mostly unoriginal. There are a few attempts to spice it up by adding in an interrupt system and an ally you can use to slow your enemies or heal your allies but it never really drew me in. The interrupting either slowed things down because I couldn't do anything or made the fight a breeze because the enemies couldn't do anything. The character development is pretty standard fare. There is a skill tree that is fairly limited and a rune system that involves combining gems to make more powerful versions. I was constantly spending time in the inventory trying to craft what I needed, equipping party members, and then starting the whole process over when I progressed into the next area. That's about it as far as the RPG elements in the game go. It all started to feel like a chore towards the end, which is a bit too far off since the game runs out of steam early on.
As I said up front there are some great visuals and music in the game, as well as a decent story. If I had played it years ago I probably would have liked it more but this felt like a platformer trying to be an RPG and it didn't work for me.

So the game is just your basic Texas Hold 'em, but the atmosphere is the selling point. Sitting down with the 4 characters, even if you don't know much about them to begin with, while they make interesting conversation with you and each other in a relaxing locale; that's what it's all about. Nice if you want a little break from all the fast paced do-or-die games you normally play.
You can choose how often the characters talk, and if you want to speed up the actual game you can right-click to skip dialogue. You also have two difficulties to choose from, and you can unlock a few table felts and decks to add some more variety.
There are some downsides though; you can't change the buy-in amount, how fast the blinds change, or make any tweaks to the actual game at all, so if you're a hard-core Hold 'em player this may turn you off. There's also no option for online play, and while that's mostly to be expected, having room for one friend to join in could have improved the life of the game quite a bit.
Still, you can certainly put a number of hours into this one. Myself, I was only familiar with Strong Bad, and had never played Texas Hold 'em (and don't generally like playing cards period), but I still thoroughly enjoyed my experience with it, and it's priced low enough that you don't have much to lose.

This high-priced game was bought for its unique story, told in beautiful graphics and masterful dialogues.
And, well, it has both, but not much else. The story inside the game is virtually nonexistent - you're just thrown into the battle with not explaination provided as to why, who and against whom. The campaign mode is extremely short and seems like an overgrown tutorial, a precursor for... multiplayer, I guess. Which I personally don't play, so no comments there.
The game does not give you a cohesive storyline, it provides no explaination of its events or faction motivations, and generally lacks in information, even in background one (C&C3 in-game library, anyone?).
Apart from that, it's a back-to-roots game of build a base, spam units and shoot everyone who looks at you funny. It boasts an emphasis on large-scale decision-making, but is actually completely linear and never ever deviates from a singular "spawn tanks, shoot guys" decision.
Add horrible screen tearing during pre-rendered custscenes (WTH? 0_o), and you get a game which is kind of OK... for half of its sale price.
Yes, it is better than C&C4, but that's setting the bar too low.

FTL: Faster Than Light is definitely an interesting game. (Sorry if I spelt definitely wrong :/) The game's plot is that you are the captain of a spaceship fight against the rebel fleet. You make you're way through 8 sectors (Well, really 7 because number 8 is the boss) The game is a bit like a dungeon-crawler but there are no dungeons. Everything happens is space. My issues lied within the community; I adore a good game, but if it's going to be centered around multiplayer, community is important. The Beta had only a few players who were willing to buy it, and the ones who probably got a code generator were hackers, and without any V.A.C. system or report features, this game was horrible to play and have a good time.
Now, fully fledged with constantly updated and bursting new content all the time, the community is much better. I know a lot of people may think that Free-to-Play means lots of noob-ish players, but at least their better than too few players at all, or hackers! And on top of that, anyone who DID buy the Beta, retains some of the previously available (but now unlockables) from the getgo.
As far as game-play goes, everything is pretty balanced an fair to play, it runs smooth, looks nice, controls are a bit clunky (who cares, you can reconfigure them!), but best of all: IT'S A GAME THAT IS A FREE TO PLAY AND DOESN'T FOCUS ON MICRO-TRANSACTIONS! Yeah, they have them, but they really won't get you anything that gives any sort of advantage over another player. Their also not so in-your-face about them either, almost like a thing you can do but you have no reason to do it.
All in all,

Game of Thrones as an adventure game where your choices affect who lives and who dies makes a lot of sense as a concept. And Telltale is the natural choice to do it at this point. They were probably terrified they'd mess up this hugely popular franchise. They managed not the embarass themselves, but they also didn't create anything amazing.
Focusing on a single family unknown to the books or TV show was a smart move. It allows for guest appearances from the famous characters without depending on them. And using a family from the North was also smart, as it parallels the story of the Starks.
The early episodes are fun and exciting and made me care about the Forresters. The problems began in later episodes - when the pace should have been picking up I just felt helpless to actually affect anything. The ending is truly awful. It turns out none of your earlier choices matter and most of the last episode is just sequel-bait. The problem with a game like this is that it's the sort of game where your decisions
matter and have a lasting impact. But there's no way to win any of the situations the game presents, even if you replay it with perfect knowledge. You can only lose, and that doesn't feel good. It's not the same as feeling a negative emotion, it's bad in a suspension-of-disbelief meta way.
So the game is worth playing if you're a GoT or SoIaF or general Telltale fan. But you have to play it for the journey and the experience at the time, not with the ending or the results of your actions in mind.

I think i have poured in enough hours to give a review of this game finally...(oh god what am I doing with my life)
Firstly I have avoided MMO's solely for the reason that I would get pulled into the addictive grindloop that most MMO's have, and rightly it happened as I feared. BDO suffers from the grindfest that most MMO's have, and it gets much worse around level 50, as trying to get from 54 to level 56 to get this thing called an "Awekening" weapon is one of the most teeth gritting, hair-pulling grind enduring experience ever. To put it into perspective, when I played my first character, it took me 2 days to get to level 1 to 50. This is granted that I had no experience in playing this game and having no idea where ideal grind spots were. Now I wasnt enjoying the character I was playing much and decided to roll another. Now with a little more knowledge of the world this only took me 3 to 4 hours give or take to go from level 1 to 50. After reaching level 50 it has taken me 2-6 hours over the course of 2days to get to level 54. That is a massive jump in needed EXP per level now, and this is even taking advantage of grinding hour daily rewards, combat exp scrolls and even the servers that give a 100% EXP boosts. If the combat wasn't so fun it would make grinding a lot more taxing.
Now onto some other subjects of the game, Playing ingame you will see alot of conversations about P2W, about 60% of them are people trolling and trying to start a debate, but this game is in no way P2W. This game gives daily login rewards, and even some of the login rewards are in the pearlshop (Pearlshop being using real money for ingame items). One thing that this game is Pay for Convienence, or pay to have a cool looking outfit. Sure the outfits give a little boost in combat exp, but its only 10%, and other things may give you faster knowledge gain (basically an ingame catalog of lore), or even a further vision range (which idk how that is useful). The main beef I have with the pearl shop is that outfits are character bound and not account bound, which in turn means if you buy an outfit, it is for that character alone. There is no transfering it if you decide to make another of the same class of character, which I say if you are pouring out $30 on an outfit for that much it should be account linked. Another thing is pets, they make things very easy as they pick up loot for you, and even have a few bonuses as well that benefit your character. What alot of people don't mention is you can get a free pet penguin if you login for 3 weeks. Sure it takes alot longer than just inputting your credit card and purchasing a pet from the pearl shop but in return you dont have to spend a dime on the game if you do not want to.
A huge thing that this game suffers from is lack of information on game mechanics, more than half the time I had to either ask the community or go to google to find answers on how to do certain things, like cooking, horse breeding  and even how to sell things on the marketplace (and figuring out very late that you have to collect your money from the market place too) etc. If the community wasn't so helpful and if the internet wasn't full of very indepth guides I would be very lost. Luckily the ingame systems are fairly simple and you will feel like an idiot once you do read some of the guides or as soon as an answer comes your way (as I did on multiple occasions.).
Onto the story...I will admit I was half paying attention to the intro cutscene, but so far I get a somewhat basic gist on what is going on. But from what I follow the story is all over the place and is very easy to get lost trying to follow what is going on. If you are playing this game for a story I reccomend you find a different game for story. Most of the lore must be found, and you get snippets of NPC's as you talk to them in your "lorebook" also known as knowledge. I do find it interesting to findout about the world this way and it does make it feel somewhat alive, but at times I have wandered around thinking "this black spirit thing is basically making me into a murder hobo as I cause genocide of various  ingame races to get stronger...". It left me feeling lost in this world and quickly took me out of the immersion, but I was quickly dragged back in with the various ingame activites and day to day life things you can do. Hell if you wanted to, you could solely play this game without even touching combat after the tutorial section. As soon as you get to a city called Heidel, you could live out your life as a Horse breeder, or even an alchemist, chef or fisher. The freedom of choice within this game is a huge plus.
This freedom will lead you to spend alot of time on mundane tasks that will make you feel like you accomplished a huge thing. I decided to take a crack at breeding horses, and when I sniped a tier 6 horse off the market for a cheap price, got  that thing to level 30 and decided to breed it with my tier 5 horse and a tier 7 came out, it felt like I accomplished something amazing. Or the feeling when you upgrade a piece of equipment to a +15 and get it to what is known as a Pri (fancy for a +16), it feels as if you worked hard to get there. Alot of the things I have said in this paragraph may not make sense, but as I have said with guides you will understand the lingo very quickly.
I could write a massive review of this game, and I have so much to say about it, but overall my opinion of this game is I really enjoy it even with some of the massive flaws...however those massive flaws are out done by all the good within the game. I personally would reccomend this game to those who want a fresh and fun world to explore who don't mind reading a few guides to become an experienced player.

Pros:
+ similar 8 bit still graphics, making the game optically enjoyable
+ killing zombies
+ crafting items is fun
Cons:
- Not very polished. The map just shows "quest" or other markers on certain buildings, but not why (is there a person in distress? Fuel? Supplies?). You just have to go there to find out, which is annoying if you return to a game you played a couple of days ago. In general there are a lot of things that could be improved in terms usability.
- "Permadeath" and stamina
In combat you may lose a character permanently if they die and you don't revive them. Maybe you played too risky or had bad planning - it's OK to lose someone. Except for the fact it can be easily solved by closing the game and reloading the last autosave. That's not permadeath at all.
However, if you are not in combat, and you run out of stamina (or use the retreat button), someone might die in a text based event. This can not be avoided by closing the game. Oh wow, I didn't properly count that I need 8 stamina back to the house and now I've lost half my team. That was exciting. NOT.
What makes it even worse: Some of the quest houses are so far away you cannot reach them even with maxed out stamina without running out of stamina and subsequently losing team members. Again, this is not connected to skill, good planning, or to the stats of your team members (at least i assume so), but simply the game killing off teammembers.
- green acid goo
If you kill a zombie, sometimes a puddle of green acis goo will remain in its place for some time. If you touch it, you will lose health.
This is probably even more annoying than the text based deaths. Sometimes the goo will make you chose another exit from a room because the first one is blocked, hence acting as an element of chaos and chance, but in 99% of all cases a green puddle of goo will just be in the way, blocking the only entrance or exit to a room and annoy you by being there. I really don't see how this makes the game more enjoyable or interesting.
- Low replay value.
1st game: Lost entire team, quit game.
2nd game: Figured out how to fight and how to find items. City got nuked after 15 days.
3rd game: Managed to escape city
4th game: Started with other characters, managed to escape city. Quests were slightly different, but began to feel boring.
5th game: Meh.
Overall it's a nice game, but the annoying things are a real dealbreaker.

This is a tough game to review. I have played several MMORPGs before, and this one is certainly the most diverse and vast I've played. That said, I have already noticed a few things that may be a turn off, for some and for others not so much.
TL;DR: This game is amazing, but requires you to have to do a LOT of homework, key mapping (hotkeys), and customization (which is both good and bad). But if you want to spend only 10 bucks (with in game purchases available, but not manditory) on an expansive, beautifully crafted, yet challenging MMORPG, then you'll love this game!
Now, I have only 85-87 minutes put into the game, and I am already sold on this US port of the game, and love the amount of open world to this MMO. The game offers a very large and expansive map, with tons of exporation to be had. It doesn't really feel overwhelming, unlike other MMOs where you feel like you'll get lost just looking at a map.
The amount of customization and classes is overwhelmingly beautiful too. You get to choose from over 10 classes, each with unique stats and features found only in their versions. I will say, the customization is not as intuitive, nor expansive as I'd hoped, but for an MMORPG its pretty darn impressive! That said, the only complaint here I have is the sexualization. Now I don't mean "OHHH, THIS GIRL HAS MASSIVE T*TS!" or "OH, WTF IS THIS OVER SEXUALIZED BS!?", no I'm strictly referring to sexuality being locked to the classes you choose. That's right, you can't change a Ranger from a Female to Male, or a Dark Knight (my choice) from a Female to Male. Now, this is not that big of a deal, because the gameplay is what I aim for, and MY GOD DOES IT DELIVER.
The combat system works very much like FF XV, but a hybrid with the cursor aiming system. You do not lock onto your targets (as far as I have discovered) unlike other MMOs where you lock onto the aimed target until they die, and shift targets or set(s) of targets. The amount of skills found in your character's class tree is astounding! I can tell it's gonna take me +40 hours just to clear about half of the tree, maybe even longer! However, this brings me to my next point: which is UI and Help.
You're given a very brief, but intuitive tutorial from your companion (not sure if it varies on your character choice, but mine is a black phantom), and begin doing some simple quests. Now, after you've done the very basic stuff, you're about to start relying on your UI and common knowledge of MMOs, which is slightly degrading for newcomers (I haven't touched an MMO in awhile, so it was quite daunting at first). However, if you spend time practicing combat, looting dead and broken objects and such for a little bit of time, you should get the hang of it. Now, the UI can be customized, which I love, but the default setup (IMO) is just weird. Your map is in the usual place, the hotbar at the bottom, but just about everything else seems backwards. This is all biased of course, but it remains a mystery to me.
Next, the graphics: holy crap! THIS GAME IS BEAUTIFUL FOR A MMORPG!! Now, that being said: don't be expecting your PC to be able to run everything 100% Ultra to the max. I run a R9 295x2 and it STILL can't handle a full 100% Ultra setup of graphics, shaders, etc. But, even if you have a hallf-decent GPU and setup, your game will still run a consistent +30fps (like mine) which still looks and runs very beautifully! However, be warned, if you want a non-graphical intensive MMORPG to play from a laptop and such, this game will NOT run smoothly, if at all.
So far, this game has the potential to be something I end up playing religiously (as of late, its been Dark Souls III, NON-STOP), It plays very well, the graphics are beautiful no matter what, and the world and characters are all very vast and overwhelming, like a good MMORPG brings into the realm of MMO. To be honest, this game is not the best game I've found myself playing, but if you want a challanging and fun experience for an MMO, I recommmend this game! Also, for only 10 bucks?! THAT SHOULD BE A MASSIVE SELLING POINT RIGHT THERE. You only pay once, and you're basically set for life! Now there are IN-Game transactions, but I didn't se anything game-breaking (unlike other gmaes where you can pay to win).
I highly recommend this to those who love to roleplay a character they build and create, and want to get lost in a new realm!

Lethal League is best described as "Battle Squash". Similar to the indoor sport, the object is to hit a ball as fast as you can so it will rebound towards your opponent, the only difference being that you are TRYING to hit them. It's the first fighting game I know of where player contact is actually very discouraged. The ball will gain speed with each hit, and with each character boasting their own unique 'special' moves, the game can get extremely tense very quickly.
If you like fighting games, this translates very easily, and becomes basically hardcore tennis, where the object is to get the other player 'out' by hitting them with the ball. As you can imagine, with more speed, this becomes trickier, as the frame window where you can hit the ball is VERY small and requires a keen sense of timing. Very fun, very easy to get used to, and allowing up to four players at a time, which is very rare in the world of fighting games.

Just started New Game+:
The game is overall, good. Combat is interesting and highly skill based, especially towards the end of the game; the monster damage ramps up slightly faster than the HP does, so theres a lot less room for bad technique. Power-leveling isn't really necessary if you don't avoid combat throughout the storyline, although I did feel the need to bump myself up 5 levels on the higher difficulty setting to buffer the sheer damage monsters do (1/3rd to 1/4th your player health per hit).
Some things could use some work; many of the "item" buffs are lackluster and/or barely useful, and by far the most important stats and abilities are those that affect the time bar. Pretty much the only viable tactic is to focus on abilities that knock the opponent back down the time bar or outright remove them from combat, as at the higher levels the speeds are so fast it's very difficult to actually pull off an interrupt. CC and damage mititagion are absolutely vital to finishing the game.
The skill trees really don't do much to add spice to the character as far as playstyle; each character has a particular role in mind by the devs, and that's how they play regardless of how you build their skill tree. The Healer heals, the buffer buffs, the DPS does DPS, and the "Tank" doesn't have enough health to really tank, plus his "Taunt" ability doesn't block AoE attacks so really he's just DPS.
Luckily, the game allows party member swaps without penalty. For myself, it was really hard to break the concept that when it's a character's turn it's not just their turn; it's really ALL the character's turns. You can swap that character out for anyone who has the most effective ability to use for that specific turn. Once I started doing that though, the combat ran much smoother, although buffs are per-character and really don't jive with swapping out party members on-the-fly.

I definitely recommend this game if you really like Star Wars or Battlefield. I used to play this game nonstop on my old Xbox when i was younger. The multiplayer is shut down, but you can install Gameranger and play it from their servers.
There are a ton of maps, which includes the Republic and CIS in the Clone Wars era and the Empire and The Rebel Alliance in the Galatic Civil War era and of course, you can play as Heroes, if you get enough points. The modes that are available include Conquest, where you capture the enemy control points, and Capture The Flag. There is a hunt mode, but thats only available on certain maps, such as Hoth and Endor and Naboo and Mos Eisley. My personal favorite is assault, where its heroes only, and it's exclusive to Mos Eisley. And of course, there are space battles,where you can pay capture the flag, or get into the enemy hangar and wreck havoc, and even attack the enemy ship in your space ship.
There is a single player campaign, which depicts on how the old republic fell and became the empire. There is Galactic Conquest, where you can take over enemy planets, as The Empire, The Rebels, The CIS, or The Republic.
The final verdict for Star Wars Battlefront 2 is a 9/10, my only complaint is that the AI could have been better. In conclusion, Star Wars Battlefront 2 is a great game and you should get it whether its on sale or not.

After five years since the release of the original Company of Heroes, which was brilliant and well received by critics and gamers alike, Relic dropped this turd in the bowl.
The original Company of Heroes continues to be fun and interesting because of its extensive mod community, which have produced hundreds of maps, dozens of extremely well done mods and numerous custom models for new units. The mods for CoH were a gold mine waiting to be harvested for fresh ideas, and instead Relic blundered on with their Dawn of War transformation, making CoH2 into even more of a click fest.
Instead of a Real Time Strategy game (RTS), Relic is trying to make the CoH franchise into click-spamming tactical combat. The new game systems introduced in CoH 2 (winter snowstorms and cold, and now spring mud) are gimmicky, and not even very original. The idea of ice covering rivers and lakes that can be destroyed and re-form will be familiar to any RTS grognard from the Command & Conquer franchise.
CoH2 offers less innovation than the original game, fewer customization options due to the disabled mod support (which might be re-enabled at some point in the future). The graphics should be better, but individual unit models are actually worse than CoH1 and its mods.
Five years later we get a "sequel" with worse gameplay and graphics, and an overbloated "store" to buy pay-to-win items for competitive play. Epic fail.

I never wrote a review here before and never intented to. This game changed that.
At first, a telltale game of GoT seemed like the perfect perfect fit: a great story and a terrific way to tell it.
And up to the last episode that`s how it was. Granted, you had to take a great deal of disappointment and unpleasent surprises, but it all seemed part of the GoT (or ASOIAF) mood, specially if you consider the similarities between the Forresters and the Starks. Furthermore, it all seemed like a built-up for something great. That is, some kind of grand finale where all that you had endured, all that you had visualized for you characters would come together and make sense (not unlike TWD season 1).
I guess if you read this far you won't be surprised to hear that it was nothing like that. By the end of the game, I felt like I had put 13 hours of my life and a great deal of hyping and hoping into a massive dark pit. And all that I was left with was a unifufilling cliffhanger.
But metaphores aside, the game felt throughtfully like a series of disappointments and let-downs, where you your choices, plans and schemes did not matter at all, since no matter how bold or cunning you were (I was considered a cunning strategist, by the game's final count-down), it all ended in the same crappy conclusion. I do understand why it was designed that way (to leave the open end for a second season) but I am completely tired of their way of creating a interesting and intricate situation, giving you choices of how to proceed and no matter what you did, putting you in a worse position than the one you started with, in the hopes that you'd be excited to make it all work in the next episode. That was exactly what they tried to pull in the finale, but this time I am done. I`m not excited at all for the next season and my motivation to root for the main characters was completely beaten down by the game.
The bottom line is, if you have not already purchased this game, don't.  Unless you enjoy feeling powerless and disappointed. If you have bought you and haven`t yet played the finale, don't get your hopes up.

This is a tough game to review. I have played several MMORPGs before, and this one is certainly the most diverse and vast I've played. That said, I have already noticed a few things that may be a turn off, for some and for others not so much.
TL;DR: This game is amazing, but requires you to have to do a LOT of homework, key mapping (hotkeys), and customization (which is both good and bad). But if you want to spend only 10 bucks (with in game purchases available, but not manditory) on an expansive, beautifully crafted, yet challenging MMORPG, then you'll love this game!
Now, I have only 85-87 minutes put into the game, and I am already sold on this US port of the game, and love the amount of open world to this MMO. The game offers a very large and expansive map, with tons of exporation to be had. It doesn't really feel overwhelming, unlike other MMOs where you feel like you'll get lost just looking at a map.
The amount of customization and classes is overwhelmingly beautiful too. You get to choose from over 10 classes, each with unique stats and features found only in their versions. I will say, the customization is not as intuitive, nor expansive as I'd hoped, but for an MMORPG its pretty darn impressive! That said, the only complaint here I have is the sexualization. Now I don't mean "OHHH, THIS GIRL HAS MASSIVE T*TS!" or "OH, WTF IS THIS OVER SEXUALIZED BS!?", no I'm strictly referring to sexuality being locked to the classes you choose. That's right, you can't change a Ranger from a Female to Male, or a Dark Knight (my choice) from a Female to Male. Now, this is not that big of a deal, because the gameplay is what I aim for, and MY GOD DOES IT DELIVER.
The combat system works very much like FF XV, but a hybrid with the cursor aiming system. You do not lock onto your targets (as far as I have discovered) unlike other MMOs where you lock onto the aimed target until they die, and shift targets or set(s) of targets. The amount of skills found in your character's class tree is astounding! I can tell it's gonna take me +40 hours just to clear about half of the tree, maybe even longer! However, this brings me to my next point: which is UI and Help.
You're given a very brief, but intuitive tutorial from your companion (not sure if it varies on your character choice, but mine is a black phantom), and begin doing some simple quests. Now, after you've done the very basic stuff, you're about to start relying on your UI and common knowledge of MMOs, which is slightly degrading for newcomers (I haven't touched an MMO in awhile, so it was quite daunting at first). However, if you spend time practicing combat, looting dead and broken objects and such for a little bit of time, you should get the hang of it. Now, the UI can be customized, which I love, but the default setup (IMO) is just weird. Your map is in the usual place, the hotbar at the bottom, but just about everything else seems backwards. This is all biased of course, but it remains a mystery to me.
Next, the graphics: holy crap! THIS GAME IS BEAUTIFUL FOR A MMORPG!! Now, that being said: don't be expecting your PC to be able to run everything 100% Ultra to the max. I run a R9 295x2 and it STILL can't handle a full 100% Ultra setup of graphics, shaders, etc. But, even if you have a hallf-decent GPU and setup, your game will still run a consistent +30fps (like mine) which still looks and runs very beautifully! However, be warned, if you want a non-graphical intensive MMORPG to play from a laptop and such, this game will NOT run smoothly, if at all.
So far, this game has the potential to be something I end up playing religiously (as of late, its been Dark Souls III, NON-STOP), It plays very well, the graphics are beautiful no matter what, and the world and characters are all very vast and overwhelming, like a good MMORPG brings into the realm of MMO. To be honest, this game is not the best game I've found myself playing, but if you want a challanging and fun experience for an MMO, I recommmend this game! Also, for only 10 bucks?! THAT SHOULD BE A MASSIVE SELLING POINT RIGHT THERE. You only pay once, and you're basically set for life! Now there are IN-Game transactions, but I didn't se anything game-breaking (unlike other gmaes where you can pay to win).
I highly recommend this to those who love to roleplay a character they build and create, and want to get lost in a new realm!

So I've owned this game for I think 4 or 5 days now, and sunk nearly 40 hours into it. It's oddly addicting, that's something I won't deny. I'm not an expert reviewer so I can't format my review all pretty like a lot of the folks who do on here but here's the basics on how I feel about this game:
This game is for people who have a lot of time to kill, and don't mind running their computer for HOURS AFK. (Honestly, probably about half my play time was while I was out with friends or sleeping.)
It's a fantastic looking game, there's no doubt about that, and the combat system is incredibly rewarding. I remember when I first started playing my WIzard (I always gravitate towards the magical classes like that) I found myself laughing as I slaughtered droves of enemies with a couple button clicks. The raw power of what I imagined a Wizard should be felt incredible. I wasn't the uber-squish-ball that you've come to expect a magic class to be, but that doesn't mean you could just stand still, either.
The microtransaction system is... disheartening. I wanted some pets to help me with looting since I was constantly being attacked while I was trying to run about and loot. No big deal, I had a spare $20 to drop. So I bought myself two adorable little bunnies (affectionately, and totally originally named BunBun and AlsoBunBun.)
Then I realize, crap, I have to feed these guys. Okay, cool. They provide you food when you buy them. 30 food units per pet purchased. Well, that won't last too long, will it? How do I get more? Either you buy it with more real money, or you spend hours farming materials to make pet food. Which you realize you still can't make because you now have to grind the cooking skill up. So you start to make beer, which involves MORE farming of other materials. It just seems silly to me, I guess, as someone who typically doesn't have THAT much time and effort to drop into a game. (I've been off the past couple of days so that is one of the reasons I was able to drop as much time as I have into this game.)
There's plenty of things to see and do in this game, and I definitely recommend trying the base game for just $10. It's not a lot, really, and you get PLENTY of content for that. I haven't reached end game or any of that, and I won't for probably literally years due to me leaving for the Navy soon, but I would definitely not recommend the cash shop, at all.

About me - I enjoyed all the Dead Island games I have played and am a fan of teh Walking Dead
So I got this game a while agon on the Steam sale. However, some new DLC being released got me to boot it up for the first time. I wasn't sure what to expect but had read about free running being used that I had probably only seen before in Titanfall and Mirror's Edge. This actually goes great in a zombie game when sometimes you just want to get passed and complete a quest.
The weapons are very much like in Dead Island and you can craft and upgrade them. They all have limited uses so you can't get one powerful weapon and use it for the whole game. To help you there are guns, molotovs, bows and arrows and traps etc. You will also get upgrades for your toon to allow them to free run, fight and use resources more efficiently.
You can jump into other players games or get them to join you. At night things get a lot more hectic with the ability of player invasions starting a mini-game (if activated) where they are the infected and you have to destroy nests. You will need to rely on your UV light to survive, and probbaly one or two allies.
The story will keep you interested enough, and the various sub-quests will have you running around and interacting with various NPCs. The graphics look nice and the sound is atmospheric, the growl of the larger zombies still puts me on edge.
If you were a fan of the Dead Island games you will definately enjoy this as it is ultimately more of the same, with more free running in the city but less sea and sand.

Battlefront II was a defining part of my childhood. For nostalgia reasons alone, any price that Steam has listed it at in the price is worth it.
I poured hundreds of hours into the PC disc version as a child and over 50 so far once I found it on steam. Even with the loss of multiplayer functionality, it can still be loads of fun replaying the campaign mission, or fighting against bots. There is a large libary of custom maps and mods on the battlefront II filefront website to enhance your experience. And if you still want to play multiplayer, Game Ranger has the higher player base, but Game Master appears to have more well-known battlefront II veterans.
That said the games not perfect, it is not a quintessential sci-fi shooter, the "critically acclaimed" space battles were not that complex or even well-done (in my humble opinion). The AI can provide a decent challenge but has some rather interesting quirks (I'm looking at you, Rebel soldier #11 who won't stop shooting dead stormtrooper corpses)
Despite any cons it may have, Battlefront II is a game that is great for nostalgia, and something that I can repeatedly come back to and play for a few hours at a time when I'm bored, and for that: positive review.

This is a review of Xcom EU - not the Enemy Within Expansion (or the 'Long War' mod that fixes some of it).
Microprose XCom was one of my favorite games.
This is the 'arcade version' of that game.
Good:
Very pretty.
You can uncheck the infuriating tutorial at game creation.
Bad:
1 The game randomly chooses what 'class' your agents take - and 'class' determines what weapons they can use.
2 The camera is always making you look at something.
3 One 'action' per turn
4 Kobayashi Maru is not a good game mechanic.
5 Tactically simple but extremely hard
1 - You want a lot of heavy weapons for a base assault? Need a team kitted for close combat? Want to just give a good soldier a different loadout? NOPE.  Only 'assault' soldiers can use a shotgun and only 'heavy' soldiers can use a machine gun or a rocket launcher.  Need smoke grenades for assaulting that UFO? You'll need a 'support' - the only class that carries smoke grenades - and unless they have a perk, they only have one grenade.  This might be reasonable if you could choose which classes you get. Amazingly you don't get any choice in the matter.
2 - You need to sweep a small crashsite - have a big invincible late game group? You get to watch the camera track them as they climb up the back of a bus, walk over to the side of the bus, jump off the bus, kick in the door and dash to the wall.  Presumably you enjoy taking the time to wonder why they didn't just walk around the bus and open the door.  Did you just spot your 900th SECTOID? Watch a cutscene as he notices you and scrambles to cover. NOW YOU CAN FINALLY ISSUE ANOTHER ORDER.  Frustration is why you only get 6 soldiers per mission.  Don't get me started on the grenade UI - lets just say it's a problem.
3 - Instead of spending "Time Units" in any combination you want you get 2 actions.  You can move twice, or move and shoot (unless you're a sniper) or shoot.  Shooting consumes all remaining actions so you can't ... shoot and move...  or reload and shoot or throw a grenade and ...
4 - Firaxis decided it would be good to have events... you to undertake a mission for a reward.  There will be several missions in an event.. and you get to choose one of them. The missions you can't do increase their country's panic level - which determines when they stop funding you.  Unfortunately, you only control one way to reduce the panic level and it's bottlenecked by random events (why is hiring engineers an event?). This would be fine on a game show, but we're supposed to be running an elite military organization defending the planet. The answer to simultaneous hot zones is multiple teams (which you will have) and multiple transports (which you cannot have), and deciding to hire 4 engineers shouldn't be determined by whether you to shoot aliens in nigeria or france.
5 - Xcom was amazing for number of tactical choices you could make.  You could blind fire into a hedge and hope to hit the alien your teammate saw on the other side.  You could light the battlefield on fire to negate the enemies' advantage in the dark.  You could load a rookie up with grenades and teach the aliens "how not to be seen".  Firaxis 'improved' this by eliminating all these possibilities. The battlefield is never dark.  You can't fire without a target. You can only bring one (or two in the late game) grenades...  I suppose it makes the game tactially harder when you have to give up your creative advantage but the result is closer to chess than XCom.
Finally: the AI is garbage.
Aliens
Example - I run up point blank to an alien and fire my shotgun (100% chance...).  Somehow I miss (don't ask me).  Think the alien is going to unload on my poor assault?   NOPE. Shoots at a guy behind cover a full 10-15 squares away, hits and does 2 damage.

I find this game difficult to recommend. Not because it's bad, that's certainly not the case! It's actually very enjoyable. My gripe with it is that, in almost every aspect, it pales in comparison to its predecessor. Company of Heroes 1 is still a fantastic game, one with (arguably) more content and better balance. It's also much, much cheaper than this sequel.
Company of Heroes 2 has some interesting additions to the incredible RTS formula Relic have forged. Cold weather means warmth is a new resource to be considered, frozen lakes crack under bombardment, and units are slowed during blizzards. Slight changes have been made to unit control, too, so now players can vault soldiers over cover, and split and merge squads at their will. These new elements are fun, but ultimately don't add a whole lot to the game. The same can be said for the new maps. I honestly find myself enjoying the selection of battlegrounds included from the original more than the new content. They don't have the same edge, and really, that can be said for the entire game.
Players new to the franchise will likely have a great time playing this game. Returning players may find themselves a little bit disappointed. Regardless, Company of Heroes 2 is a solid game, I won't deny that. I would just encourage anyone who reads this to opt for the original with its expansions.
