Finally someone decided to break from making generic shooter #378B and tried something new.
Story is pretty good, more or less what you would expect from a Far Cry but set in 10,000 BC. Your tribe traveled to new lands, but the warrior cannibals (there are a few other factions but those are the main bad guy so far) in those lands killed most of them. You are a warrior who got separated from your tribe and has to try and reuinite your scattered people in the new village you start.
So now you have a village that you can upgrade and grow. You not only upgrade your cave and other's huts, you have to find new people who will bring their unique skills to their village and give you new unlocks (I.E. Bring the warrior guy in to unlock new takedowns, bring the crafting guy in to unlock new gear, bring the hunting girl in to get new bows, etc). It's a well done feature that also breaks your skill tree into different blocks for each new (important) person you bring into your village. Theres also a lot of different skills and craftables now. Haven't counted but it sure feels like WAY more than FC4.
The combat is very fun. Basically the same as FC3/FC4 but without the guns. You use clubs, bows and spears to kill your enemies aside from the beasts you can tame. Each weapon has its own unique takedown animations instead of always using your knife.
There's also a day/night cycle ala Dying Light. At night, more predators and certain more rare animals come out, some of these night animal's skins are needed for crafting or missions. I approve of day/night cycles simply for the (relative) realism, but it doesn't change too much in gameplay from what ive seen. Predators are still easy to avoid or kill for the most part (save bears, do NOT ♥♥♥♥ with bears until you have a few upgrades)
Hunting is much more fun now. Instead of a camera you have "hunter vision" which, rather than tagging enemies (thats a skill you unlock) it will highlight enemies/animals in your FoV. It also highlights animals blood. So if you hit a deer in the leg and it takes off, now you can just follow the blood trail to the animals body since it will bleed out in a minute.
I like the new map as well. Large with lots of variance in terrain, the ambient sounds of all the animals are great. Sometimes you'll stumble upon a pack of wolves chasing after deer, or a bear fighting a group of Udam (the warrior cannibals you fight). Some people have said it's the same as FC4's map based on where the water is, even if they did use the old map as a foundation to build on it feels very different. Lots more vegetation, way more variances in elevation so you can sneak around above/below enemies.
The whole north half of the map is also covered in snow and can be very risky to go into early on. You get a "cold meter" when there that decreases until you die. You can either run from campfire to campfire to stay warm or upgrade your clothes so your cold meter goes down more slowly.
Also runs very well, I've had no issues with crashing and with everything maxed get a stable 40-60 fps with few to no dips. Also has a FoV slider that goes all the way up to 120 (something a lot of AAA games somehow miss)
A solid next step (or first step?) in the Far Cry series. The gameplay isn't too much different from FC4 aside from the lack of guns (you still have some of the same animations for manual healing, you have a primitive grapple hook, etc.) But the new setting combined with the lack of guns adds a whole new feel to Far Cry. The characters are all interesting with their own reasons for hating the Udam and the gameplay is enjoyable.

Since now I have the time, I'm rewriting my review to actually be more descriptive.
First of all, let me explain some of the negative reviews you'll find both here and around the Internet. When this game came out, it had several important technical issues, poor marketing and a quite big pricetag, as well as some unbalance. Most of the negative reviews come from those days. Luckly, the devs have been working very hard to fix all of that, and wow they did: technical issues fixed, pricetag reduced to normal levels permanently, free DLCs, and a 4th race also for free. Not to mention the huge dedication the devs are pouring on the community as well, by answering the forums regularly and organizing tournaments.
To put it simply: when you check other reviews about Grey Goo, pay attention to the date of those reviews. In its current state, it is more than worth every cent.
I prefer to start by the negative points, so let's go for them:
- Because of its bad start, it has a limited playerbase. Everyone could guess the current efforts to improve the game are aimed to bring more players to it, and I can understand that, given the huge amount of work dedicated to it. I guess it will need some time to grow a good playerbase, but so far it has been growing. If everything else about this game appeals to you, then by all means buy it, so that the community will grow.
- Campaign is short for a classic RTS. It is well done, but players that go after lenghty SP experienced would prefer something more. It is played with the 3 original factions, looking at the conflict from their respective points of view, and aimed to learn to use each faction. That said, the conflict in the story is relatively small-sized, so it kind of makes sense to have a short campaign.
Those are the bad points. Now to the good stuff!
- It just feels fresh, yet like a good ol' RTS. While some will see some inspiration taken from big hits like Starcraft, the whole story and its factions are very original. The whole makes a very interesting sci-fi universe.
- Gameplay feels comfortable and varied. Each faction plays utterly different from the others, especially at the base-building and unit-managing levels. Humans are the high tech ones (for once!) and focus on small, dense bases with powerful defenses and teleportation. Beta feel more traditional, and know how to garrison properly. The Goo is very mobile (they don't even have buildings, only formless masses of nanobots that spawn the actual units), and can adapt very fast. The Shroud is deceptive and its units complement each other well (even their buildings can support each other).
In addition, there is a wide variety of units for each faction, divided on ground and air units, each adapted to a role. There also are epic units, which are as devastating and cool as they sound.
- Art design is gorgeous, both in visuals and audio, both in quotes, FX and soundtrack (which btw is a free DLC).  One of my biggest dislikes of Starcraft 2 is that its art style looks too cartoonish and limited after all those cool cutscenes. Grey Goo knows how to provide some cool models.
- Steam Workshop! Used for designing maps. There has been at least one map contest, with nice prices for the winners.
The following points are very nice in my opinion, but I understand other players might not like them, so I have them separated from the previous ones.
- Gameplay is not micro-intensive, like SC2. You don't need to have lightning-fast reflexes and muscle memory to use abilities. There are no active abilities in Grey Goo. Units can be upgraded with passive abilities, which alleviates the stress on the player. For example: from the Goo, have your artillery shots heal your nearby troops.
About those upgrades: you can't have them all. Each faction has 5 upgrade categories, 3 upgrades on each. You can only have 1 from each category. In my opinion, this is a great way to encourage players to develop their own strategies.
- The game is designed with competitive play in mind. There are ranked matches aside from custom ones. By unlocking certain achievements (not the Steam ones), you unlock player avatars from the game's units and places, with a cool lore description for each.
To sum up, it's a great RTS game that while it certainly had a bad start, it has improved a lot in all senses, and has a lot to enjoy, If you are looking for a RTS game that is not a copy of SC2 and feels like an oldschool RTS, this game is for you.

Bought this game as a full release, but feels like early access.
Plenty of bugs and problems keeping it from being a great game.
To name a few problems:
- Everything requires multiple redundant confirmations. (Open backpack? Loot item?)
- Collect everything in the area? You're still forced to run around an empty map exploring it for no reason.
- Many things are unclear and/or seem to do nothing.
- It seems very difficult to last more than a few days, due to the random nature of supplies you find. You could find useless ones which makes your squad starve to death early. And if they are starving, you can't make good quick enough to save them, etc.
For a game about building a squad, they can get wiped out very easily forcing you to start a brand new save file. Roguelikes are supposed to be quick games where you can get a bit further every time. Not a game where you can develop a full party, craft things, get further to a goal, and then have your entire save file essentially deleted when the randomness of the game fails to give you items you need to survive.
I love a challenge, but this game just feels unfair, unintuitive, and as a result, unfun.

Infectionator : Survivors is a game with lots of potential but sadly doesn't deliver, it's says it's released but plays like it's still in early access. Easy to master, quick to finish, lacks replay value.
I bought this game on it's release day, it's full/gold release day. It had been in early access for quite a while before that and been on my wish list for almost as long. So seeing that it was finally completed pleased me, so I bought it.
The game is good in many ways, great even. It has nice pixel graphics and a fitting soundtrack. It is also fun to play, for a while.
The first reef barrier you hit is the frustrating random no-control insta gibs of one or all of your survivors; when on the strategical map, now and then when you move to another city block you get a prompt telling you that your team of survivors has encountered this or that, like a car on the street with boxes spread around it. Now you get pick between two choices, either leave it alone or examine the boxes.
The results? Well, it's either, A. nothing of value, B. some lesser valued stuff like twenty rounds of ammo and two food supplies, C. something valuable like a weapon (really, really rare, only found one once), or D. for Death; one to four of your survivors die, with no chance to revive, heal or mitigate damage. And the D. result happens quite often, I'd estimate about 20-25% of the times. So, you learn fast not to examine any boxes, open any doors, or doing anything besides leaving text events alone. The risk is NOT worth the reward, not at all.
But it doesn't end there, no no. Sometimes you don't get a choice. Instead, the game simply straight up tells you that one or more of your survivors have died, because "Hey, tough luck!". Could be ok if survivors in this game were like lemmings in Lemmings, or soldiers in Cannon Fodder but they are not, they are more like the soldiers in X-Com or  adventurers in Baldur's Gate.
Dieing in a hard game, a survival rogue-lite because you make mistakes, misjudge or just plain isn't skilled enough is one thing. But losing because of random events you have little to no control over isn't fun, especially not when these events are text based in an action oriented game, no booming explosions or goory pictures of zombies gorging on flesh, only a plain sentence telling you that "Mike didn't make it".
Good thing that you can press Alt+F4, restart the game and get a new random seed. Mike is alive!
So, how is the "actual" game then, when the random text events are finally handled? It's fun.
Well, for a while.
If your survivors live on long enough (more than one day), either because you chose not to take part in any of the texted events, restarted the game to get a new seed or just got lucky (I don't like this kind of luck, unvolontary russian roulette is not fun, only frustrating), you will  quickly find all you need for your team while you are out exploring the city.
Sure, you can craft alot of things in your base, like weapons, armour, grow and cook your own food to make supplies and rations, but there is no need for it really. Because you will find everything you need while you are out exploring, even food. If you have the slightest amount of brain power you will quickly find the optimal tactic to win the action sequences, whether that be the tower defence-like scouting missons or the more free-roaming exploration missions.
And then you win the game. On my first successfully completed playthrough I had owned the game for three days, played a little each day. I beat the game under nine in-game days, which there is an achievement for. You start out with a fifteen days limit in which you must repair your car and escape. That can be extended to thirty days if you spend tickets which you earn by completing runs, winning or losing.
So, after beating the game, even doing so on less than half of the required time, do I feel like play ing it again? No, not really. I mighth be going back for (some of) the achievements that are left, but I don't feel too excited about them since they are mostly "grindy" ones.
Remember how I wrote that that you don't need craft anything, because you will find everything you need? Well, guess what, several of the achievements are for crafting lots stuff. Others are grindy in the hoarding sense, either kill things in the thousands or collect ammo in the tens upon tens of thousands, or loot a couple of thous... well, you get the idea.
These "grindy" achievements might have been ok if the game had any kind of real replay value, which it doesn't. Sure, you can unlock different teams with your tickets, instead of stomping koopas with Mario you can flatten koopas with Luigi, or you can beat M. Bison with Ken instead of with Ryu (ok, maybe this is a bad analogy, ...yeah it is).
Point is, there is no replay value except for grinding out achievements; there are no special endings, no leaderboards, no functional endless/survival mode, no actual new things to explore or discover.
Apart from this there are also bugs, glitches and genereally unbalanced and unfinished elements in the game. This game left early access too early. Which is sad, because it could be a great game, and I really want to enjoy it.
Perhaps it will become updated and finally become "full" some day, I surely hope so, and that that day comes sooner than later. If so, I will update my review.

This game isn't a typical WoW type mmorpg.
This game is more like an open world mmorpg sandbox game. I feel like you can do anything you want, farm for food, chop down trees, make your own boat and go out fishing, decorate your own home and more.
Of course there are quests to do, but I never felt the pressure to do those. I've probably spend most of my time fishing and doing small side quests.
The combat is great. It has some kind of combo style thingy combat (a little bit like For Honor without the 3 stances). Even though I have no idea what i'm doing while fighting, I still feel powerful.
Some pros and cons:
+The game looks good
+Fun combat
+Cool classes
+More freedom than other mmo's
+Large world
+Very good character customization
+Bewb physics (selling point for me)
+/- Gender tied to a class (so you have an explenation as for why you have a big bewb animoo character)
-No class story (as far as i've noticed)
-No quest dialogue (npc's say random quotes that are half of what they're saying in the dialogue)
-Not very good tutorial (they give you the basics, but for things like some game mechanics you'll have to FIND the right npc that'll give you the quest, some of which aren't available from the start)
-Outfit shop similar to f2p mmo's (with outfits that can cost over 30 euros)
Overall this game is great. It has a small price tag but no subscription or anything after that.

I definitely recommend this game if you really like Star Wars or Battlefield. I used to play this game nonstop on my old Xbox when i was younger. The multiplayer is shut down, but you can install Gameranger and play it from their servers.
There are a ton of maps, which includes the Republic and CIS in the Clone Wars era and the Empire and The Rebel Alliance in the Galatic Civil War era and of course, you can play as Heroes, if you get enough points. The modes that are available include Conquest, where you capture the enemy control points, and Capture The Flag. There is a hunt mode, but thats only available on certain maps, such as Hoth and Endor and Naboo and Mos Eisley. My personal favorite is assault, where its heroes only, and it's exclusive to Mos Eisley. And of course, there are space battles,where you can pay capture the flag, or get into the enemy hangar and wreck havoc, and even attack the enemy ship in your space ship.
There is a single player campaign, which depicts on how the old republic fell and became the empire. There is Galactic Conquest, where you can take over enemy planets, as The Empire, The Rebels, The CIS, or The Republic.
The final verdict for Star Wars Battlefront 2 is a 9/10, my only complaint is that the AI could have been better. In conclusion, Star Wars Battlefront 2 is a great game and you should get it whether its on sale or not.

Okay to start this off, you have to understand that I was a die hard Diablo and Diablo 2 fan (I played the latter til it had been out for 10 years).  That being said, I avoided Diablo 3 when I saw they were pretty much bringing WoW devs in to build the game because the original Diablo franchise devs left Blizzard (and bringing in champion skills from Warcraft 3 to slap on Diablo 3 characters, ie, Warcraft champions in some ways wearing Diablo artwork).  Played Torchlight 2 and liked it but... it just got boring to grind after a while, when the classes clearly were designed to only be effective with a few build types, and you couldn't get too creative, or you'd have a level 20 character who literally was not able to hold their own.
So now that you see my personal slant, allow me to give a review of Grim Dawn.  So in summary: This game has excellent graphics, music reminiscent of Diablo/Diablo 2 (but better), questing like a RPG (and permanent game affecting decisions that make a significant difference), gear drops (and shops that sell relevant gear!) that scratch that loot itch you can never quite satiate, a real story that isn't just cobbled together quests, and a leveling system that allows for numerous amusing viable combinations.
Specifically:  Graphically, I'm not particularly picky I will admit, but the game has a nice rotatable camera and nice fine details because each area is not randomly generated.  The interface is sensical and helpful.
Musically, the game reminds me of Divinity: Original Sin as well as the Diablo franchise.  So I actually enjoy the game's muisc and don't tend to listen to something else while playing, even after playing it for 4 hours straight.
Quests and story (I'll combine these here):  I'll admit, I am not a big RPG guy.  I primarily on played Fallout 1 and 2 and then I avoided the Zelda franchise, WoW, Final Fantasy franchise, etc, but I actually have found myself saying "Maybe if RPG's could have this sort of story, I would like them..." -- this is much to my shock.  This game may have single handedly gotten me to start considering modern RPG's as playable.  Still not sure if I'm happy about that part yet... Regardless, the story doesn't feel like forced odd objectives.
< (Spoiler alert)
The first order of business in the first town is to defend it, then get the water supply, then the food supply sorted out. Kind of makes sense right?  It progresses from there and doesn't feel like just random nonsense thrown in to lengthen the game.
(Spoiler alert over) >
Gear drops!  So this is one of the two things that make or break this sort of game in my opinion.  That being said, this game consistently delivers on interesting items dropping, without feeling like you get over powered gear all the time.  In fact, I think the gear drops amazingly consistently as just what you were starting to feel your character should start looking for with the often "Oh that would go great on my other character!" item.  And the times where the drops have been disappointing, it seems like the shops have sold decent gear that makes me say "Who cares what the mobs drop, this merchant must have snuck into their camp and grabbed their best loot!"  Fact of matter, the loot drops and shops in this game rock a solid A++ on this.
Character building versatility: So this is the other thing that makes or breaks a game like this.  That being said, I feel like they went and played Diablo 2, Path of Exile, Torchlight 2 and maybe a few other ARPG style games and took the best things from them and smashed them all together to make it so you could build a different character each time and enjoy the thrills of the build working as planned (or sometimse better than imagined).
< (Spoiler Alert) My favorite right now if a character that literally lets enemies kill themselves on my character -- a damage retailiation character.  There are several suggested builds out there, and I'm making my own variant... and it is fantastically amusing to play.
< (Spoiler Alert Over)>
Oh, a final word that should be mentioned... as of now, they added with a patch a new area to the game and are further going to add 2 more classes... without making it a new thing you have to pay for.  That is pretty sweet that the devs are adding quality content this late after launch as a patch to an already awesome game.

There is a large libary of custom maps and mods on the battlefront II filefront website to enhance your experience. And if you still want to play multiplayer, Game Ranger has the higher player base, but Game Master appears to have more well-known battlefront II veterans.
That said the games not perfect, it is not a quintessential sci-fi shooter, the "critically acclaimed" space battles were not that complex or even well-done (in my humble opinion). The AI can provide a decent challenge but has some rather interesting quirks (I'm looking at you, Rebel soldier #11 who won't stop shooting dead stormtrooper corpses)
Despite any cons it may have, Battlefront II is a game that is great for nostalgia, and something that I can repeatedly come back to and play for a few hours at a time when I'm bored, and for that: positive review.

I don't usually take the time to write reviews of the games that I play, but I really feel like Grey Goo is criminally underrated. Short answer: There's a lot of meat to the multiplayer of this game if you take the time to learn it, and the game world is worth learning about.
There are a lot of people who compare this game to Command and Conquer, which they should. It owes a lot of its design to the CnC games, but I don't think that it is fair to call this a stripped-down clone. It has certainly been streamlined; unit, building, and technology production is always at hand, and you don't need to move your hand off the QWER keys to get to literally any part of it. Units are simple, too. You pretty much just right click them where you want them to go. It doesn't get much more complicated than telling Artillery to attack ground to lead shots and blind fire, or telling your aircraft to return to hanger en mass.
What a lot of people seem to totally miss out on is how focused on map awareness and harassment the game is. While it isn't as frantic as Starcraft, you are constantly moving around, trying to take and hold resource nodes from your opponent. Brush inhibits vision of where the enemy is and makes scouting units valuable even when the enemy is not using stealth tech. Because you are getting resources from 5-10 nodes scattered across the map instead of 1-3 bases, there is action going on through a much larger percentage of the map compared to other RTSs. While there is much less focus on APM to play a good game, it isn't like it will put you to sleep, either.
Everything that everyone says about the storyline is true. The cutscenes are excellent, and the world is refreshingly bright and lush compared to the grimdark war stories that most RTSs are about. The mission design is... not great, but the AI has been playing a lot smarter since the last update. It's worth the 12-15 hours to play before you dive into multiplayer.
If nothing else, I really recommend picking this game up to play as the Goo faction. There is really nothing like it in any other game that I've played. Getting to play a faction with all base mechanics fulfilled by a self-replicating super-unit with pseudo-flight and melee capabilities is just so... different from anything else. If you are a fan of the genre, you owe it to yourself to at least give it a try.

I've never played a Tropico before this, and as a fan of city-builders, I have to say it was nice. It had ups and downs. This review is kind of longer than normal.
The good is that it's easy to pick up, difficult to master. Problem here is the difficulty curve is not that high, so while difficult for a little while, you'll master it halfway through the campaign. Every island can be won by almost the same exact strategy. The good is that it's very fun to customize, micro-manage imports, exports, industry... the problem here is that almost every island can have almost every industry. I had no problem in sandbox mode doing a tourism-farming-industry-etc island. Another good is pretty graphics, great textures and detail, and music. Problem here is there isn't too much variety in a lot of the buildings, only a few are worthwhile in some ways, and therefore many cities will look the same and have tons of the same buildings. The music is great, but it's also very short, like.. >10 songs. So it repeats very often.
Considering i've spent many hours in SimCity and the like, I just feel like I've hit the end of my reach with this game much sooner. It doesn't help that there's a population cap of 1200 per island, so dreams of a sprawling, huge urban utopia are somewhat limited, and as population increases, so does system resources needed. Even a high end gaming PC can only do so much after a while and texture bugs and lag can start to occur.
Still, it was a very fun ride, and I'm sure I'll get more out of it before I'm fully through.
7/10

The fourth Tropico is a really interesting blend of city planning and political posturing, as you attempt to survive as a authoritarian Latin American Presidente through the Cold War and beyond. I really find this game and it's almost identical predecessor, Tropico 3, to be some of the most fun real time strategy games I've played in a while.
The win conditions end up being mostly irrelevant in Sandbox mode (which is honestly far better than the campaign missions), so you basically play how you want to play: is your people's happiness the most important? Or economic equality? Or the island's profitability? Or maybe you only care about skimming enough money off the top to build up a sizable Swiss Bank account? Once you ignore the guidelines the game sets up, and just play the game however you want, it's pretty neat to try and focus on different priorities for your island nation, and see what strategies you need to develop, and factions and foreign powers you need to appease to stay in power until the bitter end.
If you already own Tropico 3 (and it's awesome expansion, Absolute Power), it's hard to recommend this game for full price, as they are incredibly similar. If you do not, or you are still interested, I recommend picking up the DLC, Modern Times, as it adds some much needed options for the late game which can become pretty tedious. Also, unless they are very cheap, ignore the small DLC packs: they are pretty underwhelming, and don't add much, if anything, to a typical game.
10/10 would buy again.

This game deserves a lot more praise than it's currently getting. It's a beautiful game, which may have some 'minor' optimisation issues in its current state. But looking past that, it's a great concept and I love these action filled prehistoric genre of games which often require a lot of stealth to get out of some harsh situations, and this certainly doesn't fail to satisfy that convention. In all honesty, the style of the game is quite similar to Far Cry 4, as many people have complained about, but then again it is a f*cking Far Cry game, which means that it's intentional and is purposely the style of the game, so what do you honestly expect? But nevertheless, it's unique in its own way and very different to other prehistoric games of the sort. The game menu and start-up screens are beautiful, as are the scenery and animals.
However, some people are saying that you should hold off on purchasing the game right now until some bugs get fixed and the game gets optimised better, which may be true in some cases, but if you're anything like me then I'd purchase it right now as it is and play the game until these optimisation and bugs get fixed. Quite frankly, the game is entirely playable and extremely enjoyable as it is right now and I have no complaints with it thus far. With all the complaints about this being too similar to Far Cry 4, I think what most people seem to be forgetting is that this is a Far Cry game in the Far Cry series made by Ubisoft and so similarities to Far Cry 3 & 4 are to be expected immediately after reading the title of the game and long before you purchase it, so these complaints about it being too similar to Far Cry 3 and/or 4 are complete bullsh*t. On another note, I have no idea why people are saying that they have errors when loading up the game since my game ran perfectly fine the first time I opened it and is continuing to do so.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the Far Cry series or prehistoric games, as this is a good addition to both the genre and the game series. I like what Ubisoft have done with this game and I commend them for it. Although it is very basic at parts, there are a lot of things to keep the user playing for a long time, even after the story is complete. For example, you can tame 'beasts' (canivorous animals - such as a panther, wolf, lion etc.) and have them fight by your side which is a lot of fun and there are many beasts to tame and so a lot of time can be spent searching for the different beasts and attempting to tame them. As well as this, you (*POSSIBLE MINOR SPOILER*) lead a group of tribes-people and build a colony while fighting to survive against a common enemy group, known as the 'Udam'. You're able to build and upgrade your own base and your tribesmen's huts as well which will keep you busy gathering supplies. Upgrading bases and huts give you extra skill unlockables and crafting recipes, for example.
I won't go much further into the details of the game as I know most people like to experience it for themselves, but that is just a basic guideline of what the game has to offer (bear in mind that at the time of writing this I only have 5 hours of game time (3 hours of me actually playing the game, so f*ck knows what I was doing in the other 2, but that's what the game says on the main menu)), so there may be a lot of things I have yet to discover. I may update this review in the future, however, I feel this is a good enough description of the games details and features for you to decide on whether you want to purchase it or not.
As a guideline in terms of how well you may be able to run the game, here are my specs and the games graphics settings along with my usual FPS in the game;
-My Rig:
GPU: NVidia GeForce GTX 760
CPU: Intel Core i5-4690k CPU @ 3.5 GHz
Memory: 8GB RAM
OS: Win 10
With everything on 'High' graphics settings with the following turned down to 'Normal'; shadows, terrain, water, geometry.
V-Sync; on,
Anti-Aliasing; SMAA.
I get around 35-50 FPS (42 on average) with ocassional drops of frames and lag spikes during graphically intense situations, such as a huge fight between 15(ish)+ people and/or animals, or a large wild fire etc.
So far, I'm thoroughly enjoying this game and rate it the following:
Graphics: 8/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Story: 5/10 (I am so early into the game as I mainly free roam and hardly ever do story missions, so this story rating may not be accurate, but so far the entirety of the story is that there's two different tribes of people who loathe eachother and constantly fight and kill one another because of this hatred)
Overall:
7/10
-Review to be updated in the future when I have a better idea on the story line and features of the game-
EDIT: I have recently discovered that the Far Cry Primal map is an almost identical copy of the Far Cry 4 map. If you don't believe me, look it up. A lot of people are incredibly disappointed by that, but I honestly don't see the issue. Had there never been any map comparisons, nobody would have ever been able to tell that this game has the same map as the previous one in the series, so what is the issue here? The map size and layout itself may be the same, but the scenery and environmental layout are completely different, so it's not like it's noticeable at all. I agree that it would be nice to have a completely fresh map, but keeping the same general layout of Far Cry 4's is fine in my opinion as, as I said, it is honestly not noticeable in-game at all, even after looking at a map comparison. So just look past that small issue with the game and enjoy what there is, as it is still stunningly beautiful.

All right. Here is a review in a few catagories. Let me start by saying I've never played a Telltale game, So there is no fan boy here. Though I do love Game of Thrones.
*SPOILERS*
Graphics: Bad
people are claiming that fallout 4 is bad? I get the game is supposed to look like a painting, And it launched a while ago, But it's terrible. The game can look downright ugly in some areas. In the desert where you controll Asher(One of the main characters), the graphics felt like Prince of persia: Two thrones. Remember that game? From 2005? it's that bad. The digital artwork for it, And I mean the digital paintings, are great though. It's a shame the 3D models and textures are so low quality.
Sound: Average
The cast in the game didn't do a bad job. If there is one REALLY strong point of the game, It's the original cast from GoT. They do a great job, And when they are in the scenes, It feels like a GoT episode. Other times the audio can be....off. I noticed several points where the dialog was cut short, Or there was a microphone pop when the actors got too close to the mic, Or sounded like they might have bumped it. No joke. happened twice alone with Beskha(Asher's companion). The music is pretty good, Also helping fit the mood just right for tense moments.
Gameplay: Below average
My first playthrough, I really enjoyed myself. I though the dialog sucks you right into the moment. After finishing my first go, and almost being complete with my second, I feel differently. Quite a bit I wonder why I'm even being forced to take three steps before it throws another cutscene at me. This happens quite a bit, And it feels totally not needed. majority of the action takes place in quick time events. Which felt fine for the game. Since there really isn't any gameplay other than that, and controlling the dialog, Aside from some bow shooting( I'll mention that below because there were issue with it), I'll end the section here.
Verdict: Deception
The game I really wanted to like. And I did my first play through. After just about finishing my second, My view has changed. People are saying that "Your choices don't matter". And sadly they are true. Not much about the game from what I've seen has much of an impact on the story. Everything feels on rails, And that I can push the minecart but not change it's course. Right in the beginning of the game, It gives us a character named Ethan. I thought "This will be interesting seeing him take command and be a lord at a young age". And on my first playthorugh he was killed a mere 30 minutes after introducing him to us. I though" Ok when I finish my first I'll start over and save him". It's not possible. He was killed again on my second playthrough. Only after looking it up, Did I find out there was no way to save him. All the choices you are given are small, and literally in the end meaningless. The game ends in the exact same position with different actors in their places. Same setting and all. So that was pretty disappointing to say the least. Another gripe I have is that the game has issues. In a type of comical matter, only when you actually have to controll the characters directly. What I mean is when you shoot a bow/crossbow. For me, I run multiple monitors, and trying to shoot the crossbow/bow was impossible, As the mouse cursor isn't locked to the game window, tabbing you out when you need to shoot. I unplugged my other monitors and restarted the game because I was sure it would help, But to no avail. This time, the cursor couldnt go far enough, As if there was an invisible wall preventing my mouse from moving any further.
TLDR?:
The game gives the illusion of choice, But really has none, And all for a cliffhanger ending so you can buy the next season. Poor graphics, Iffy audio, And zero closure. They could continue this for 5 seasons if they want. No thanks. I'll wait to see how season two ends, And if it's any better. I wouldn't recommend this game as a whole.
Thanks for reading if you took the time. Just my honest thoughts.

If You like something you can play Casually with the option of Challanging, this game is going to be a winner for you.
This game is a Bullet-Hell, plain and simple, but unique in the aspect of Music being the determining factor of how fast your game will go. Mixed with the Seizure-Inducing Visuals (warning btw) that can be boosted all the way to 200%, this game is made to be more for the Rock/Techno fans.
You Control a Ship and play through songs pre-installed in the game's Album. As stated before, the Music is the Determining Factor on how fast the game will go and stop, as the music used will also Determine the Length of the level you need to survive in, if it's the Standard Mode. The Music controls just about everything, including your Ship's Gun Strength and Movement Speed, as well as Bullet Speed. The Faster and more Intense/Loud the Music is, the faster and stronger everything is.
Multiplayer is a Mixed Bag of good and bad however. If for Friends, then Multiplayer can be good. If for the Public Multiplayer, then it's not great. There are barely anybody wishing to play this game Public Multiplayer to begin with due to DLCs making some players better than others, in a bad way, but i'll get to those in the next section. As long as there is an Even Playing-Field for all players, then Multiplayer can be fun. However, that can Rarely happen, resulting in the lack of Public Multiplayer Games atm. This is more of a Singleplayer game to begin with regardless, so don't have Multiplayer be one of those reasons for getting this game.
Now that the main, Overall General Game is taken care of, ONTO THE DLCS! This Section is PARAMOUNT to how much fun you want in your Beat Hazard Experience, so Read up! The best to least needed DLCs shall be listed in order from top to bottom.
First and Foremost, while a situational and very optional DLC, the $0.99 DLC of the Ability to Put extra music-type files into your Beat Hazard Game. TL;DR, For Single Player, and with the very low price of $1 to do it make it the most Highly Recommended DLC to get, unless if the files it's allowing support over you don't use. Even With the Ultra DLC, the game only has 23 Songs, so if you really want to get maximum Enjoyment, The Ability to Stack on Loads and Loads of songs to play on will give Beat Hazard MUCH more Replayability. Again, this DLC will vary from person to person because some may use .mp3 and .wav music files, so it's not needed, but for people who mainly uses iTunes files and what-not, it's a must for them. Something to note, however: the only way you can play Multiplayer with your songs is if everyone else has A: The Same Song name, and B: The Same Song FILE Type (.mp3, .ogg, .wav, etc.) Unless it's for Friends, Multiplayer utilizing this is as unlikaly as you winning the lottery. As stated before, you'll usually want to stick to Friends-Only for Multiplayer, as from what I've experienced in Public Multiplayer, It's not the best.
Secondly, the Ultra DLC. This is the Pack you need if you are looking for all of that Challange you may/may not be yearning for. While it's $4.99, and for a small game like this, the Ultra DLC is quite Game-Changing. This unlocks the Perk System where, if you level up, you can now pick from a variety of Perks to unlock such as ones made to increase Score, obtaining new Weapons such as Micro Missiles and Reflect Shields, and even getting unlockable difficulty levels, which are all VERY useful if you do not plan on getting the Shadow Ops DLC, which will be later. This also gives New Enemies, More Bosses, and Boss Rush Mode. While Boss Rush Mode can, sorta, kinda, a LIIIIIITLE bit be abused to level up fast (which I do Not Condone, nor like, the use of doing,) The new Mode can be quite the experience, and can become Hell-on-Earth, or, in this Case, Hell-in-Space, VERY Fast if you cannot keep up, making it a good challange the longer you survive. This also adds in Co-oP, and Head-to-Head, which is Competitive for whoever can get the most points. While this IS second, it is nearly as needed of a DLC as the Custom Track DLC explained first, with the only 2 reasons of that being Price and Player Skill needed for Ultra.
Now comes the worst of them, and this time an Un-needed DLC that I Do Not Recommend if you get Ultra, and that is the Shadow Ops DLC. The Shadow Ops DLC is, in my theory, the main reason Public Multiplayer is Lacking. From what I have seen from Multiplayer, many of the ships are a Much more OP Version of the Standard Version of the Ship, with the downside of a Larger Hitbox the Majority of the time (exception is the Mosquito Ship). While it may give the game a sense of Completion, it gives Unnessessary Ships that would Kill the purpose of the Ultra DLC, and with a $5 Price tag as well, I cannot recommend this DLC over the Ultra DLC, for 2 main reasons; Bad Synergy, and Less Needed out of the 2. The Reason why the Shadow Ops DLC mixes bad w/ Ultra is that the Shadow Ops DLC makes the game more Easy, as it gives better firepower, killing many of the reasons to even GET Ultra in the first place. If you're good enough, you can, Like me, and potentially many otjhers, complete Tracks on Suicidal only needing the Standard Ship. Even if it DIDN'T make things easier, it sure as heck not making it harder for you. I've seen games where i see people using a few of the Shadow Ops Ships and other Custom ships from the Steam Workshop, and only Rolls with the Reflect Shield, because their ship is so good they don't even NEED the Micro Missiles or Ultra Beams the Ultra DLC Gives, which are two VERY Useful Weapon Perks. If it makes the game that much easier in the higher difficulties, you shouldn't be playing on the higher difficulties to begin with if you wanted a more Casual Play of Beat Hazard, even IF the missions of obtaining the Ships are very Tough, making this DLC not needed if you already have Ultra, which i Recommend Much Higher than this.
TL;DR: Great Game Casually and Challenging, but not in both worlds for DLC. If need-be, Immedietly get the Custom Song Track DLC ASAP. Do not get Shadow Ops if you're wanting a more Challanging Feel to the Game.

Grim Dawn is the best ARPG I have seen. It has it all - atmoshere, replayability(through many class combination, differens skill and devotions build). And though it can be quite long, especialy for busy people, it's length actually can be shortened by just ignoring special dungeons and some missions and go straight to next level(where most high level items will drop). This game especially fun with the party and at high levels can really test your build and prove yourself quite rewarding.
Though game isn't without some problems:
1) Items sets. Even with quite large items database some builds can prove themself more relevant for exisisting item sets in the game than other, for e.g. bombs throwing build is not bosted with high level legendary item sets. This game needs more items variaty in future that will even more incorage experementing even with most crazy builds.
2) Devotion composition. Some devotion paths can be more beneficial than other. What I mean is that it is much easer with a warrior going on top-right devotion sector to get more high level constellations(two with the same number and type of affinities points) than for e.g. as Demolitioner that concentrate on fire and burn damage when he goes in buttom-left devotion sector(when he can only grab one castelion with the same number and type of affinities points).
3) There are almost no range weapon physical base damage castelions so it's hurt some build ideas too. What I mean is that most abilities from castelations that improve your physical and trauma damage strictly requires you to have a melee weapon equiped. This problem combine with developers sometimes changing how some abilities work, e.g. Granado skill starts to deal trauma damage with it's shattering blast improvement instead electrocute.
4) You will receive less components and aether crystals(rare component required for crafting and devotion redistribution) if you play with the party. In my opinion it should drop depending on how man people are playing.
Although it may seem that I mentioned many problems above it's actually nothing game breaking and you still will get a lot of fun from this game (though I highly recomend to find people to play with before you start). There actually so many good in that that I just can't actually list it all and you can see it for yourself simply looking how many hours I spent on this game.
So just buy it and hf! :)

Star Wars Battlefront II improves upon the original game's single-player experience with open-ended, mission-based objectives inspired from all six Star Wars films. The compelling storyline spans more than 12 new locations, many from Episode III, including volcanic Mustafar and the space battle above Coruscant. All-new classic movie moments complete the Star Wars Battlefront II experience, as players battle within the interior of the Death Star and visit Princess Leia’s blockade runner, the Tantive IV, as seen at the beginning of Episode IV A New Hope. In addition, at certain key moments within the battles, players can feel the Force as a Jedi. For the first time ever, Star Wars Battlefront II players can engage in space combat and, during the same battle, board enemy ships to attack from within. Starting on foot inside a capital ship, players can enter the spacecraft of their choice and travel into space to dogfight with the rival faction. From there, they can dock within the enemy’s capital ship, overtake the ship’s command posts, man its turrets to disable its shields and destroy it from within! Or, they can simply stay inside their own capital ship and defend it from attacks and enemy fire. The choice is theirs. The stellar online play that marked the original Star Wars Battlefront returns even bigger and better for Star Wars Battlefront II. Players can locate their buddies and track their stats as they battle alongside more players than ever (up to 24 on PS2, 32 on Xbox, 64 on Windows).

This is not a game where you are going to be single handly saving the world. This is not a game where you are the great hero that brings humanity from extinction. In fact, at the start of the game, the intro even tells you that we are no longer going to win the war, but rather this is now about survival.
Survival with enough items to kill it with fire.
Let me start that if you have played Titan Quest, you've played this game in many ways. Same idea of a duel levling system which allows you to mix and match characters. Both main quests and side quests to track progress, and many characters with exposition on what this world is now like. And a relic system/components system that allows you to upgrade your items with other abilites.
Where the game improves upon this is the details. Lore books filling in even more stories of heartbreak, despair and humor in desperation. A reputation system giving you access to bigger items and schematics (Though, the game doesn't do enough to play off the reputations enough where you can♥♥♥♥♥♥off one faction when you help another 'good' faction like deciding to help either Homestead or Death's Vigil). And♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the enemies enough will force them to send out nemesis groups after you to make a mess of your day.
The graphics are a bit muddy, but the fact you can rotate the camera is something different and unique, and they do use it to full advantage hiding entrances to side areas and challenges. Finding a special boss by turning the camera just enough to see that glow of a cave will give you a case of the squeals. The areas are not randomly generated (for the most part. I've heard the new Port area is, and that the lower levels of the Steps are random as well. Also, some entries into dungeons do change, even if the layout inside does not). They also reward noticing the fact that there's a chest in an odd place by doing a bit of research to find the hidden entry to retrieve that loot as well.
To put it mildly: this is a worthy entry into the ARPG canon, and a setting we've not quite seen before in an ARPG. I feel they can do more with the steampunk ideas they have here, but I am looking forward to seeing what Crate can do next in this game.
Have fun, and loot on!

So after reading thru several reviews, and seeing all the acclaim this got, I decided on buying even tho it was on a moderate (30%) discount. I played past the 2 hours limit, hoping for the game and pace to start picking on and... never really got into it.
Sure the dual classes system looks novel and potentially endless, until you realize all classes burn thru mana (well, energy) and the only difference between a demolitions guy and a sorcerer are the fact that one throws canisters of fuel while the other calls down firebolts, but spells are functionally the same, spend the same resource and accomplish roughly the same effect. Opening cinema was great, but rest of the game so far has been a letdown.
The game pieces itself together out of several RPG basic elements and clichés (zombies, lizards, skeletons, mutated fauna), and delivers a world that does next to nothing to diferentiate itself from ten thousand other RPGs. No revolutionary combat system, no enemies that deviate from your garden variety zombies and giant rats, no innovation to world clearing, leveling up or resource conservation, everything's based on your usual fetch/kill x quests, but most of all, it fails like so many other RPGs, to engage the player; a good game hooks you in by the 30 minute mark, this one does absolutely nothing innovative for itself (you're the blank slate noname that happened to stumble upon the power to save this world, surprise surprise).
Overall my veredict to this game is a solid meh. Sure I'll get to finish it (and if anything changes I'll be sure to alter review) when I have nothing better to play, but I would not recommend it for any RPG fan, it offers absolutely nothing that sets it apart from dozens of other mediocre RPGs, and the story isn't even that good, nor it feels like your choices and actions impact the gameworld or story whatsoever.
6/10 don't buy unless discount is 60% or greater.

I'd say this game requires a decent bit of patience, but is otherwise amazing and well worth the money. The finest comedy game I've played in a long, long time.
Game of Thrones follows the bumbling Forester family in the wake of the events of the Red Wedding. You will take this collection of playable nitwits on a journey through six episodes of trying to find a way to save their house and having every hope crushed one by one, in a series of events that redefine the classic trope of the 'Trauma Conga Line'. In true Song of Ice and Fire fashion, we have a group of protagonists centered in the north, and then isolated figures scattered in remote locations who are either irrelevent to the main plot or don't get involved until near the end of the game.
This game is certian to evoke an emotional response from you. You will cheer for the obviously evil and hammy Whitehills! You will laugh as some guy's love interest is cut down in front of them and they have a derpy face! You will rage alongside House Forester after you play the final episode and realize the whole game was ultimately pretty pointless!
In short, while it is by far the worst Telltale game to date, it is nonetheless the most amusing one. Highly reccomended to anyone needing a good laugh

The first time i saw Hyperdimension Neptunia on Steam i told myself: what the ♥♥♥♥ is this♥♥♥♥♥♥ The only anime i ever watched was pokemon and i usually don't play anime games except the Persona series. Because i like the scenario of this game i decided to give it a try.
And this is the strongest part of this game, the fresh scenario. In a land called gamindustri, 4 goddesses fight against each other in the console war to gain shares (you can say followers) and to rule over gamindustri. These girls are called CPU's. Neptune, the protagonist represents Sega (Planetune), Noire the Playstation (Lastation), Blanc the Nintendo Wii (Lowee) and Vert the X-Box (Leanbox). The entire cast are girls.
This game offers this cool scenario, many jokes, lots of game references, good english voice acting, likeable characters and an amusing storyline. Its the perfect start for everyone to get into the world of Hyperdimension Neptunia.
The game itself is 50% visuel novel and 50% dungeon crawler. It plays like Persona 3 portable without the social links and a lighter, carefree story. The fights are turn-based with an easy combo system. The first bosses can be hard so you need to grind a few levels every now and then.
To date, i played every Neptunia game on steam. Its now one of my favorite game series. Don't be fooled by the colourful look and the cute little girls. This game is a lot of fun and you dont have to be a anime loving little kid to enjoy it.
Fantastic game, still a marvel in 2017.

Is this game good? Yes it is. Though it's a special game so it might not be everyones cup of tea. So why the negative review? Because they lock game features beind paywalls and other nonsense i will be bringing up in this review. Don't be fooled by the positive rating this game has, this game do have their skeletons in their closet.
Amazing graphics and it even has character adapting their feet to the ground so they stand "natural" and not stand straight at 90 degrees because you stepped on an angled surface. In my opinion an important detail because it tends to break the immersion when you see your character being... "Special" again.
Horse game mechanic is so in-depth and broad that it's amazing. The mount is legitimately a separate entity, it doesn't just disappear and reappear on a key click. This means that you can't be stupid when you park your horse and go off questing because mobs might attack your mount.
You yourself is responsible for your mount and if taken with great care it can be an amazing mount. There's tiers, levels, breeding and skills your horse can learn so you tend to wanna park your horse on a safe place before you go out and adventure.
I feel like this is the game's strongest and unique game mechanic you wont find anywhere else. This MMO did mounts best of them all.
You can invest money in banks, hire workers to do labor work which ranges from mining to crafting. You can fish, hunt whales with your boat, buy houses and even become a merchant by buying a carriage and strap it onto your horse. Buy wares from one town and sell them in another town. Though being a merchant is really boring, but just that it exists as an option adds to your freedom to do what you want.
A brilliant game menu that has everything you'd look for all in one place.
If you ever wanted to find a specific NPC in a town you've never been to before, there's an NPC finder that will mark the NPC for you and guide you to them. There's video tutorial of ability combo's in-game so it's easier to learn them and you get a cute tutorial dark spirit as your guide.
This game is cruel towards new players. You get bombarded with notifications and UI interface buttons all over your screen and it keeps throwing enormous amount of information and expects you to remember it all. A really hard learning curve.
There are still buttons and Icons I'm not sure what they do.
This game doesn't explain stats, what type of gear you should look for etc. Gear in this game is very,
different from other MMO's so you have nothing to compare with to grasp what is better or not.
In-game currency inflation is through the roof. If you thought Soviet Russia had it bad, ooooh boy...
They have autoloot but this feature is locked behind a paywall in the form of Pets. Tier 1 pet can autoloot once every 10 sec to once every 4 sec if you level them. Notice "them". You can have up to 4 pets and a pet costs 10 euro a pop.
This is a big deal because in this game you cut through mobs like butter and leave a trail of dead bodies behind you. Now looting is a real hassle since it's looting one guy at a time and if you experience server lag due to high influx of people then that looting will suffer enormous amount of delay. So it's inevitable that you'll miss loot unless you cough up 40 euro.
They have "costumes" to make your character look pretty/sexy/cool - which is always nice! Buuuut they have stats, so they are no longer costumes. They are cash armor that will give you an edge over others that haven't invested money as well.
They give new players a laughably small inventory and hide 1 single inventory slot unlocks behind quests. The game also gives you free inventory slots sent to you in your mail along with other free cash items like costumes for your character or horse costumes to deck out your horse. It gives you a free color palette to customize your colors on your gear and your horses gear. You also get a free ticket to edit your character's looks, hairstyle and hair color etc that you did when you created your character. It even gives you a coupons for your first purchase, discounts ftw. Why is this on cons?
It's marketing psychology.
What you get is temporary cash costume and cash horse costumes that expire so you get a
of the premium life. They give you temporary color palette so you wanna take advantage of fixing your preferred colors on your cash costumes before it expires so that means you have to buy the costumes now while you have the free temporary color palette. They give you coupons that expire within a week to give you a real incentive to buy it while you still have the discount and you will have to buy cash inventory slot unlocks and inventory weight limit unlocks eventually.
It's a marketing strategy to make you act without thinking rationally because it's on a time limit and they bloody know it. It's really dirty tactics.
30 euro for costumes, 20 euro for horse costumes, 40 euro for 4 pets, around 40 euro for a decent inventory and weight limit increase. If you actually want to customize your gear with colors, thats 10 euro. Wanna remove a color? 0.5 euro per color you remove. Edit your characters appearance? 10 euro. That's a lot of money you could spend on different games that doesn't treat it's customer this disgusting.
Now you don't have to buy horse armor, color palette, edit appearance and remove colors. you can simply endure looking like a peasant - but the rest you will have to buy. Otherwise you'll endure suffering through limitations that are there only to punish you.
If your horse learned a bad skill, pay money to remove it and reroll your chances to the RNG gods that you get the skill you want.
Wanna increase the chances of you getting a specific skill for your horse? Pay cash to increase the odds of receiving that specific skill.
Can't be bothered to train your horse skill? Pay cash so the stablekeeper will train your horse for you.
Can't be bothered with waiting 2+ hours for breeding your horses? Well you have a wallet... Open it.
You probably get my point.

Obligatory 100th hour review:
Average Score: 8/10
Gamplay (8/10):
Easy to use battle systems and skills which are not complex, yet not basic. Highly enjoyable battles for an RPG, with detailed animations and graphic art for skill executions. Movement is fluid when remapped logically to the keyboard, allowing all the versitility of a joystick. Game does not get boring after several dozen hours, which is a major plus for any RPG game.
Plot (6/10):
Good length story, around 40 hours of gameplay by just following the story. Plot is fun and easy to follow and remains rather interesting. It's no masterpiece, and not very impressive. Far too much 4th wall breaking for my liking, but at least it doesn't affect the plot. Could use more drama and suspense. It's mainly a typical story which introduces a conflict and then resolves it at the end.
Visuals (9/10):
Outstanding artwork and animations, even for a JRPG. Makes the game worth playing on it's own, just to see kawaii moe-chans fight to the death. Graphics are good for the time this game was released at, and is far superior to your average RPG.
Audio (9/10):
Excellent music. Various themes are dedicated to this game and the BGM is outstanding. RPG games are generally mediocre in their music, however Hyper Nep 1 stands out for being an exception. Voice actors for most characters vibrantly exemplify the relevant personalities
Things that need improvement:
> Dungeon Design: Is severally limited in it's variety. The same dungeons are recycled and reused multiple times with only the enemies inside being different
> Erin Fitzgerald was a poor choice of voice actor for Noire. Noire is an introvert, constantly labelled 'loner' throughout the story by Neptune. Fitzgerald on the other hand is a voice actor well known for her extremely lively + bubbly voice. You might know her from Persona 4's Chie Satonaka, Danganronpa's Genocide Jill and knights of Sidonia's Mozuku Kunato. A more reserved voice would be appropriate for this character, but this is likely me being pedantic. Most players probably don't care.
> Skills: Too much end game emphasis on the EXE drive. This is basically a mechanic where performing any attack will fill a meter guage. Rush attacks fill the gauge 3x faster. Once the gauge reaches levels 1 and beyond, an EXE attack can be performed, which is far more powerful than any other attack. Boss fights generally become all about filling that EXE drive, to the point where normal skills are all but forgotten about. Furthermore the normal skills are rather... boring. There's not much to them other than their existence, and a tad more complexity about their nature, such as prerequisites for acquiring them would make their use more rewarding.
Final thought:
> Is it worth the price it's sold at? Considering everything, Yes. The price reflects its enjoyability. I would recommend.

Bullet Heaven 2 puts you in the shoes of either Matt or NoLegs from Epic Battle Fantasy, with the rest of the heroes and three bonus characters being unlockable as you play the game. As the title implies, the game is a bullet hell, and will throw walls of bullets you're expected to dodge through. The only handicap that doesn't boost your score is the Pacifist one, where you simply get a very good rank at the end of the stage instead.

Great Game. 9.5/10
There is some real polish to this game, the graphics, animations and sound are solid, as are the unit and camera controls.
Xcom lets you customize your soldiers, upgrade them and reward them accordly.  This forms a kind of bond and makes you really feel the impact of permanent death and adds real consequences to your choices.
The difficulty of the game seems to plateau at about 1/3 of the way thru.  Early on soldiers will die if an alien lands any kind of a hit on them, this makes the first handful of missions very challenging and critical.  If you fail an early mission you are out men, money and your terror level will increase, which can easly snowball into losing Xcom councel members and funding.  Once you get past this stage in the game, you should have things on lock to the point where losing men and being short on funds will not directly lose you the game.  The difficulty does rachet up later as new aliens, weapons and ablitlies are introduced however never to the point of the early game.
The ending of the game seems a little abrupt, thankfully Xcom is more about the journey than the destination. I do wish there was a dooms day clock or some mechanic that forces the player to move quicker and make harder choices near the end.  As it stands, at the end game you can sit on your hands finish off your research, engineer anything you want and level up soldiers until you have the perfect squad to send out.
The AI is just smart enough to catch and kill you if you're not paying attention.  However after a while you can easily predict how it will react to a situation and use that to your advantage.
I appreciate the "Ant Farm" base building, dispite it being fairly simple.  I really wish the base assault mission used your base's layout, (Old School Xcom) instead of just a generic base map.  Being able to zoom in and look around is a nice touch.
The technology tree is alittle weak and pretty linear, it does and has just enough to get by.  You will find some items you can skip completely, while others are forced on you to progress the story.  That's not really a problem, it is what it is.
Multiplayer is flat and boring.  There is a point system you use to select troops and a handful of map to play on.  I really wish there was a CoOp option.
The DLC adds some nice additions to the game, more maps, couple missions, Mech and Cyber Soldiers and more customization.
Solid replayablity, some combat maps can become repedative; achievements, DLC, difficulty settings, and a little combat RNG helps.
Xcom is what I expect out of my turn based strategy games, it sets the bar.

Grim Dawn is the best ARPG I have seen. It has it all - atmoshere, replayability(through many class combination, differens skill and devotions build). And though it can be quite long, especialy for busy people, it's length actually can be shortened by just ignoring special dungeons and some missions and go straight to next level(where most high level items will drop). This game especially fun with the party and at high levels can really test your build and prove yourself quite rewarding.
Though game isn't without some problems:
1) Items sets. Even with quite large items database some builds can prove themself more relevant for exisisting item sets in the game than other, for e.g. bombs throwing build is not bosted with high level legendary item sets. This game needs more items variaty in future that will even more incorage experementing even with most crazy builds.
2) Devotion composition. Some devotion paths can be more beneficial than other. What I mean is that it is much easer with a warrior going on top-right devotion sector to get more high level constellations(two with the same number and type of affinities points) than for e.g. as Demolitioner that concentrate on fire and burn damage when he goes in buttom-left devotion sector(when he can only grab one castelion with the same number and type of affinities points).
3) There are almost no range weapon physical base damage castelions so it's hurt some build ideas too. What I mean is that most abilities from castelations that improve your physical and trauma damage strictly requires you to have a melee weapon equiped. This problem combine with developers sometimes changing how some abilities work, e.g. Granado skill starts to deal trauma damage with it's shattering blast improvement instead electrocute.
4) You will receive less components and aether crystals(rare component required for crafting and devotion redistribution) if you play with the party. In my opinion it should drop depending on how man people are playing.
Although it may seem that I mentioned many problems above it's actually nothing game breaking and you still will get a lot of fun from this game (though I highly recomend to find people to play with before you start). There actually so many good in that that I just can't actually list it all and you can see it for yourself simply looking how many hours I spent on this game.
So just buy it and hf! :)

TL;DR - Excellent game with minor issues, even when supported with fanboy nostalgia. 9.3/10
Man what
been said about this game? For your multiplayer shooter Star Wars experience, this is the end-all be-all, and probably still will be even after DICE's Battlefront hits store shelves.
I've played this game since my babysitter brought it over for us about ten years ago, and while I may be fueled by nostalgia both for this game and for the movies, it's arguably one of my favorite games of all time.
The graphics have not aged the best (Although still looks good for a game that's a decade old), it takes so many good concepts and throws them together in this sci fi orgy for the eyes and for the hands, whether grasping a controller or rapping away at a keyboard. Sound? Do I even need to bring this up? The entire John Williams soundtrack and narration by Jango Fett. Need I say more? Although you're going to be hearing "We've lost/gained the command post!" a lot in big battles, which brings me to my next point.
The gameplay is nearly flawless. The beautiful lovechild of Battlefield 1942's class-based open map battles with vehicular combat and the aesthetic, story, and design of Star Wars. You get a handful of gamemodes at your disposal, including Conquest (Similar to Battlefield's capture-and-hold spawnpoints, whittle down enemy numbers system), Capture the Flag (A staple of shooting games), Assault (Essentially deathmatch, except space battles where you destroy frigates and integral ship systems), Hunt (Play as different Star Wars aliens; Sand People, Jawas, Geonosians to name a few), and others.
I only have two large qualms about gameplay. Due to the Gamespy shutdown a year ago, standard online compatability no longer exists, forcing the use of a third party client called GameRanger. Now while GR does help link Steam games with other games that suffered from the shutdown, it does have its issues, mainly latency and server stability. The second is with AI which can range from average to running-into-walls dumb (E.g. on Hoth, in the XL mode, getting into an AT-AT and laying waste to scores of Rebels is feasible because a lot of them just stand there and do nothing. Lambs to the slaughter). Even on Elite difficulty they're not a head trip to kill. Much more exciting when you're playing online.
The campaign is good but only goes to the Battle of Hoth. Covers the 501st Legion as one of the most elite Clone regiments which then becomes the ultimate main fighting force under Darth Vader. You'll get a few hours of playability out of it.
Galactic Conquest is amazing; combining the conquest system with turn-based strategy as a Risk-like game of buying units and supplies to try and take over the whole galaxy. Will have you playing for hours.
Overall, even when I gush with that Star Wars nerd nostalgia, it's definitely an excellent title and one of my favorites, even with it's issues.

This is not a game where you are going to be single handly saving the world. This is not a game where you are the great hero that brings humanity from extinction. In fact, at the start of the game, the intro even tells you that we are no longer going to win the war, but rather this is now about survival.
Survival with enough items to kill it with fire.
Let me start that if you have played Titan Quest, you've played this game in many ways. Same idea of a duel levling system which allows you to mix and match characters. Both main quests and side quests to track progress, and many characters with exposition on what this world is now like. And a relic system/components system that allows you to upgrade your items with other abilites.
Where the game improves upon this is the details. Lore books filling in even more stories of heartbreak, despair and humor in desperation. A reputation system giving you access to bigger items and schematics (Though, the game doesn't do enough to play off the reputations enough where you can♥♥♥♥♥♥off one faction when you help another 'good' faction like deciding to help either Homestead or Death's Vigil). And♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the enemies enough will force them to send out nemesis groups after you to make a mess of your day.
The graphics are a bit muddy, but the fact you can rotate the camera is something different and unique, and they do use it to full advantage hiding entrances to side areas and challenges. Finding a special boss by turning the camera just enough to see that glow of a cave will give you a case of the squeals. The areas are not randomly generated (for the most part. I've heard the new Port area is, and that the lower levels of the Steps are random as well. Also, some entries into dungeons do change, even if the layout inside does not). They also reward noticing the fact that there's a chest in an odd place by doing a bit of research to find the hidden entry to retrieve that loot as well.
To put it mildly: this is a worthy entry into the ARPG canon, and a setting we've not quite seen before in an ARPG. I feel they can do more with the steampunk ideas they have here, but I am looking forward to seeing what Crate can do next in this game.
Have fun, and loot on!

So after reading thru several reviews, and seeing all the acclaim this got, I decided on buying even tho it was on a moderate (30%) discount. I played past the 2 hours limit, hoping for the game and pace to start picking on and... never really got into it.
Sure the dual classes system looks novel and potentially endless, until you realize all classes burn thru mana (well, energy) and the only difference between a demolitions guy and a sorcerer are the fact that one throws canisters of fuel while the other calls down firebolts, but spells are functionally the same, spend the same resource and accomplish roughly the same effect. Opening cinema was great, but rest of the game so far has been a letdown.
The game pieces itself together out of several RPG basic elements and clichés (zombies, lizards, skeletons, mutated fauna), and delivers a world that does next to nothing to diferentiate itself from ten thousand other RPGs. No revolutionary combat system, no enemies that deviate from your garden variety zombies and giant rats, no innovation to world clearing, leveling up or resource conservation, everything's based on your usual fetch/kill x quests, but most of all, it fails like so many other RPGs, to engage the player; a good game hooks you in by the 30 minute mark, this one does absolutely nothing innovative for itself (you're the blank slate noname that happened to stumble upon the power to save this world, surprise surprise).
Overall my veredict to this game is a solid meh. Sure I'll get to finish it (and if anything changes I'll be sure to alter review) when I have nothing better to play, but I would not recommend it for any RPG fan, it offers absolutely nothing that sets it apart from dozens of other mediocre RPGs, and the story isn't even that good, nor it feels like your choices and actions impact the gameworld or story whatsoever.

TL'DR: This is a Farcry game, for good and bad of it.
Pros
- The graphics and gameworld, npcs and models are really well made. The game is immersive.
Sound follows suit, the language is something that i deemed positive, some ppl don't. (most a matter of opnion).
- Gameplay is responsive, you move, run and fight (combat is a mixed bag) well
- The story is okay, the pro here goes for the npcs of your tribe, they are really interesting characters.
- Your tribe and village.
- The beasts that you control adds a interesting layer of gameplay in a Farcry game.
- Some enemies are brutal, Mamoths and bears are going to kick your♥♥♥♥♥
- Tossing a spear and having a headshot with it, it's really rewarding
- One of the lamest things that turned farcry 3 and 4 a borefest for me, it's how boring the gimmick of towers were . Good thing is that here in primal, there isn't. While you go conquering areas and bases, the fact that you don't need to do something to reveal your objects (they appear naturally when you explore the map) helps a lot to quell the sensation of rince-repeat.
Cons
- Game is too streamlined, the survival is lacking, you don't really feel you need to keep yourself up with vital suplies. No hunger meter, no need to sleep, most of the things you gonna gather are materials to keep yourself armed, wich is constant. This isn't really a gamebreaker, but i've wished that we could have a more hardcore survival experience in a game where the focus is surviving in the stone age.
-The biggest letdown in my view: Melee combat, be it using clubs, be it using the spear, you have no “punch”, no combo, no skill involve, you just spam attacks, the enemies have no phisics while receiving blows, melee is really bad in the game, and it baffles me that these devs ignore this. For shame.
- Crafting is too streamlined in the farcry way, it's okayish, but i can't help to feel that this could be more deep.
Some events spam too often, killing patrols with prisioners over and over and over again.
Final thoughts:
This is a farcry game, for good and bad. If you play Farcry 3 and 4 and are bored of the gameplay, you will be bored here.
I for once played a little of both, only to know how the “mechanics and systems” of these games works. Here in Farcry Primal it's almost the same with a twist.
The greatest thing in this game is how immersive it is, i really enjoy the tribal theme here. 	Different from it's predecessors, you're not a outsider stuck helping people, here you are a member of a tribe, a important one, who helps your people to grow. Your tribe grows while you help and complete missions, wich provides materials and perks for you.

Perfomance it seems to be a hit-or-miss, here in my cpu, i've encountered zero problems, the game runs well.
This game is good. There is production value here, the world is beautiful and detailed, the sound and effects helps a lot with immersion. (nights are scaring!)
The animals are gorgeous, their animations are really well done. The facial animations of the characters you met are really good as well.
Is it worth 60 bucks? That depends on you. A good game yes, not the best you going to play, but it's far from been crap.
