Technical problems bring this game down to a "Not Recommended" zone. Grey Goo's gameplay makes for a fun, if not outstanding RTS game. However, even after a hardware upgrade and exceeding the recommend specs, the game just tanks in FPS.
First off, my specs:
Windows 8.1 64-bit
Intel i5-4590 Quad Core
Geforce GTX 760 (driver version 362.00)
Samsun SSD 850 PRO 512GB (primary drive)
WDC WD5000 (secondary drive)
I run this game on medium-low settings.
So, the big problem I have with this game involves major FPS loss when a significant amount of units are onscreen. I believe this is due to how the more units are onscreen, the model models need to be rendered and shaders (special effects essentially) have to be calculated. I'm guessing the models lack optimization, especially when FPS starts to dip into low 20's. I am unsure if the maps in the game are unoptimized as well, but I think the units are the major problem.
The gameplay was enjoyable, if a bit slow paced. I very much appreciate the modular building style of the Beta and Human factions, as well as being able to quickly select units to build/ buildings to make/techs to reserach with a MOBA-style QWER hotkey system. I haven't run into many balance issues, but that could be from inexperience. The campaign boasts nicely rendered cutscenes and some actually challenging missions, even if the story is forgettable.
Overall, even with the generally decent gameplay, my technical issues stopped me from enjoying this game. I imagine if I had a 970 or a 980 (or their AMD equivalent), my game would run a lot better. If you didn't purchase a new CPU and/or GPU in the last 3 years, it's likely you will struggle with FPS like I did.

Dont usually do reviews for games but feel that this game has received far too many negative and unfair reviews (imo) which have resulted in making it harder for people to decide on whether to get the game. From what i have seen, a lot of the poor reviews are from people that are having problems due to their own computer issues and thus it is often easier to just blame the game. I struggle to see why fans of the Far Cry series would not like this game. It is stunning in every way.
I have played all of the Far Cry series and after playing just 2.9 hours of this one so far, i am completely blown away and addicted. Graphics are breathtaking and i have had no issues at all so far. Game is being played with all settings maxed out (Ultra) @ 1920x1200 and it is smooth as silk (i7 4790K @4GHz OC'd to 4.7, 16GB Memory, R9 390 @8Gb).  In the 3 hours i have played, i still havent even hit 4% of the game yet. The map is massive and the beauty of it compels you to explore and take in the scenery and explore some more. Easier to give you an example of what i mean. I was wondering across the mountains and decided to find a nice spot and sit and wait for some birds to fly across with Bow and Arrows at the ready. To my left, a huge Elk came wandering by. Me being a bit itchy fingered i drew back the bow and fired an arrow into the Elk. Unsurprisingly it ran away and so i continued in wait to line a good shot up on some birds. 5 Minutes later, i received a pair of huge Elk Antlers up my back side. It had circled and flanked me and attacked me savagely. While i was trying to back away and react, a Wolf jumped on the Elk and tore it to shreds. I waited till the Elk was dead and then killed the wolf and skinned them both. Then i continued on with my bird hunt and eventually got a couple. At this rate i am going to have many hours of breathtaking fun. Money well spent and anyther great Far Cry game. Possibly even the best of the series.
That is what Far Cry Primal brings you. Unique experiences, beauty and complete freedom. Would definitely recommend. Abolutely love the game.

Tropico 4 is one of those games where you start playing, look up, and have a nasty shock when 5 hours are gone in 5 minutes.
A smaller-scale simulator than a Sim City. Tropico 4 puts you in charge of a small Caribbean banana republic and lets you have at it.  You have a surprising amount of freedom in how you'll run your show - are you an assholish venture capitalist, whose citizens live in squalor to support a tourism industry?  Are you a corrupt socialist, arresting your political rivals and propping yourself up through cult of personality and military bribes?  Are you a democratically-elected whitebread ruler carefully avoiding the cold war?  All of these options and more exist in how to run your island.
If the game has a flaw, it's that it's not particularly challenging, and that some of its mechanics are poorly-emphasized.  Garages, for example, are vital to getting your people to move about most of your city, but the game doesn't draw a line under how important it is to have a wide-spread network.  The DLC is cheap but you don't get too much for your money, and I have aesthetic qualms with Modern Times, personally.  If you've previously played Tropico 3, Tropico 4 plays almost more like an expansion pack, though there's no question that 4 takes what 3 did right, refines it, and expands upon it.
That said, this is a fun city-builder game with a cheeky sense of humor and a rather impressive amount of control in just what you can do.  Despotic parasite or benevolent statesman, Tropico 4 has something for you.

It's a korean MMO, meaning it was designed around the korean aspects of internet cafés and per-hour internet usage. That being said, it is far more tolerable than something like old MapleStory or Archeage. It tends to feel like a single player game up until you hit max level, where you can then (maybe) put together a guild and go fight other re­tar­ds for land. The game hands out money to you, and every day you get EXP boosts so grinding doesn't feel so bad. Farming is fun, but getting your skill levels up to actually make stuff is tedious and requires dedication (like in Runescape, and maybe World of Warcraft to some degree).
All-in-all, good time sink, pretty looking game, poorly optimized (cities will lag you out regardless of how beefy your rig is), extremely expensive microtransactions (you can buy real clothing at a 1:1 ratio with the amount of money it takes to purchase cosmetic items in-game), but not a bad MMO for the $10 price tag. Catch it on sale for $5.

TLDR this game is great, get it.
Long version:
Bullet Heaven 2 is a pretty amazing (or, well, at least SLIGHTLY amazing) danmaku game that accounts for both newbies to the genre and veterans. The game is built around bite-sized stages that can be replayed at will, so getting a game over never means you lose progress, and it's the perfect thing to pick up when you want to have fun for 15 minutes... but with almost a hundred of them, you still get a lot of bang for the buck! The harder difficulty settings give you a real challenge, and get so hard I've not managed to clear stage 1-1 on the hardest difficulty yet despite years of casually fiddling with danmakus.
The game also has some nice customization options to let you tailor your experience for your taste... money dropped by enemies can be used to unlock cheats to make the game easier, handicaps to make it harder, and lots of customization options like alternate weapons and characters; each has slightly different play style and switching up characters or weapons to suit the stage you're going to play has a big impact on your experience. You can play co-op with up to 3 friends for an easier or harder time depending on how well you coordinate your attacks, too.
The game doesn't punish you for using cheats and playing it safe, but it rewards you for playing well. Each stage has 3 extra-difficult optional bonus waves accessed if you get enough Perfects on the normal waves, which offer huge score boosts and extra cash for the unlockables; you can unlock hidden bosses and stages in each world, and all the game's achievements also rewards you with a substantial amount of unlockables cash giving you an incentive to achieve them. There's also a bunch of achievements awarded for very silly or stupid-to-attempt things encouraging you to take the game less serious and try things outside your comfort zone, and before you know it, it'll become second nature.
Bullet Heaven 2 combines the best parts of Jamestown's co-op and Touhou's tight bullet pattern design with a small pinch of roguelike elements, and it's pretty unique in the amount of polish and quality it has, but the best parts of it is how accessible it is. You'll probably only play in short, intense bursts, but it feels like you've had fun for hours.

Anyone who knows me knows that anime is my jam. This game seemed a natural extension. I came into it knowing about the “bad” localization. Yes it was meme heavy, but so was the original Japanese. They were just harder for most non- Japanese speakers/culture experts to catch, much less fully understand. Even I caught maybe half. Nep talks damn fast.
So all in all, I didn’t mind the script. Could they have given the option for a more direct translation and maybe a translation notes encyclopedia? Yes. Would I ever expect any game licensing/localization company to always do such a thing? No.
As far as the actual plot, it was fun enough. I didn’t buy this game looking for another emo/dark/grim/agnsty etc RPG story. I wasn’t looking for a fantasy of the usual Final or Tales style. I just wanted some fun, not-so deep game that I could just play and not have to analyze every plot moment. I got exactly what I was looking for.
The gameplay (DUN Dun dun):
You will grind and grind and grind and grind. Just like any Shin Megami Tensei game. The enemies are hard and the battle can take time if you don’t have any grasp of the mechanics. But like all grinding RPGs, the battles get repetitive, as does the reused dungeon layouts. This is probably where I say, “A few more map designs and level styles would have helped.” So I said it.
To speak a little bit more on the grinding, so as to just♥♥♥♥♥♥off the bad reviewers who hated it because it takes up so much time. Or the many, many quests that are just hour padders. The first RPG I really ever played was FF7, and to get to Lvl 70 for all my party members and maybe finishing half of the side-quests, it took me 60 some odd hours and I barely beat the final boss. The difficulty of Neptunia was not that hard to deal with.
Lolis anyone?

Anyway, yes there are some and yes there is service. Was that a problem for me? Yeaaaaa…… Nope! If it was, I wouldn’t have bought the game, even on sale.
The final:
If you can handle meme, both English localized and Original Japanese; lolis in swimsuits and maid outfits, and panty shots with a camera mod; grinding lvls and learning the battle system; repetition of scenery; and just want some fun- This game might just be for you.

I'm a big fan of bullet hell STGs, one of the first that I played being Bullet Heaven 1. While I look back at that game with nostalgia, and BH2 is an improvement in every way, I still have a hard time recommending it having played the likes of Touhou, Crimzon Clover, or Cave's stuff.
There's admittedly a lot to like here. The boss levels are all pretty good. There's a lot of fun bullet patterns in every difficulty, so you can basically dive in no matter your skill level. This idea is taken further with the "cheats and handicaps" system which is supposed to let you further customise your difficulty. The cheats being an interesting alternative to the continues you would get in most STGs, bringing the idea into an arcadeless era. There are achievements and lots of unlockables.
But the game is really let down by the non-boss levels. There are very many of these and they quickly start feeling like a slog. While there are quite a few enemies, they tend to just spawn in big rectangles and either throw bullets directly at you or everywhere. I guess it gets the defense right, as weaving through bullets feels good, but not really the offensive side. If feels like enemies can either be spawn-killed or are tanky to the point where killing them doesn't really feel good.
There are also problems having to do with how the game is in flash. That means you might need a more powerful machine than you might expect to run it smoothly, and running an STG smoothly is paramount. I also couldn't get it working on Linux and so had to boot up my rusty win7 install, which I don't like to do.

the game is overall straightfowards, you have a ship versus a near infinite amount of enemy ships in fast paced laser-gun combat at the beat of whatever background music is playing.
while the above sentence could easily apply on many other twin-stick shooters out there, it stands out on this game in particular due to it's core mechanic:
Gameplay powered by YOUR Music.
there are many twin-stick shooters out there, but all restrict the player on whatever powerups you may pick what levels you play and at most provide you with a few catchy tunes along the way,
this game however manages to go the extra mile and provide support for your music and even better base it's entire core mechanic around it, how so?
the strength, intensity, speed and visuals of nearly all elements on the screen while you play are directly affected by the intensity of your music.
if your music library consists of heavy beats, then the game will crank enemy spawns and spazz-inducing visual effects like there's no tomorrow, the downside to this however is that having a mellow music library does the opposite, reduces enemy spawns, light intensity and overall speed of the game.
(which by itself, isn't so bad if you're looking for a break in the action or cannot handle strobing lights)
The fact that this game uses your very own music library is also it's best point, as if you're one of those guys that cannot help but have more than 20 GB of music stored on their hard drive, then you've basically given yourself hours and hours of free DLC, in the end, it's up to the player to decide how active or dull their experience with this game is.
moving on to the ships,
as of the last update (shadow operations DLC) the player can now change between different ships, now to be honest, this is merely just an extra for those who wish to give the default ship a break, these newer ships provide either greater mobility or firepower and sometimes even auto-fire or auto-pickup for items. all in all the extra ships are made for people who are either having a tough time on the regular game or want a self-imposed challenge by selecting (or creating) a weak. slow. ship. You're not missing out on much should you play with the regular ship.
which brings me to the next point. Ship Crafting.
If you're one of the players who just doesn't want to customize the music, but the ship as well, you now can with the previously mentioned DLC. you are given a set of "points" that you can use to spend on designing your ship.
you can go for heavy and strong or light and nimble. you're pretty much given a good set of options on how to build a ship, the kicker is, PNG support, what makes your ships unique is that you can in a way draw your own ship, customize it, THEN play with it, all in all, a pretty cool feature if you have the patience for it.
FINAL VERDICT: If you're into shoot-em-ups, and love music-based gameplay, this game is for you.
AS A BONUS: This is one of those games that actively benefits from soundtrack bought from other steam games such as TF2 or Half Life. if you by any chance have any game albums downloaded, give them a go with this game you might be surprised how some tracks play out.

The compelling storyline spans more than 12 new locations, many from Episode III, including volcanic Mustafar and the space battle above Coruscant. For the first time ever, Star Wars Battlefront II players can engage in space combat and, during the same battle, board enemy ships to attack from within. Starting on foot inside a capital ship, players can enter the spacecraft of their choice and travel into space to dogfight with the rival faction. From there, they can dock within the enemy’s capital ship, overtake the ship’s command posts, man its turrets to disable its shields and destroy it from within! Or, they can simply stay inside their own capital ship and defend it from attacks and enemy fire. The choice is theirs. The stellar online play that marked the original Star Wars Battlefront returns even bigger and better for Star Wars Battlefront II. Players can locate their buddies and track their stats as they battle alongside more players than ever (up to 24 on PS2, 32 on Xbox, 64 on Windows).

If I had to give this game a tagline, it would be "very fun, but really only if you have friends to play with".
Really, this game has the potential to be very fun. In the most basic game, you hit a ball back and forth; if it hits you, you're out for the round. And it gains speed at every swing. So pretty simple, really. And hilarious. You can play local multiplayer or online multiplayer, and there's also a single player mode ("challenge mode") which is a set amount of matches against set characters and combinations. The game modes are free-for-all (just hitting the ball until only one player remains), team play (works best for four players, obviously) and strikers (hit the other team's goal instead of its players).
The problem with this game is that if you're playing alone, there really isn't much to do besides challenge mode - which, honestly, I didn't find it as fun as multiplayer. You can try to search for matches online, but most of the time it's just unfruitful, and the online mode has quite a few connectivity issues, especially if the match has more than two players. The game also gets repetitive quite fast, and while leveling up does unlock new things, they're mostly skins for the characters (there are 6 different in the game) which are purely cosmetic and honestly not that rewarding.
Still, if you have a couple friends willing to engage in some pong-esque shenanigans, maybe over a skype call or even some pizza at your house, I can recommend getting a multi-pack of this game and bash away.

Child of Light pairs gorgeous graphics with simple but effective music to create a storybook adventure that transports.
The animations and the settings are lovingly crafted. Exploring the landscape reminded me of the best illustrated storybooks I devoured as a small child. I wouldn't just read them again and again, but I'd also study the tiny details. In the visual story telling of Child of Light, background characters or far-off scenes, paint a picture, in water color style, of a larger world built on a mythic scale.
A nicely employed gimick turns your cursor into a firefly, an elemental spirit that you can use to interact with the environment remotely. The glowing blob acts as sort of a Swiss (well, Austrian, since that's where Aurora hails from) Army knife by lighting up dark areas, blinding opponents and even healing you and your companions.
As Aurora, you assemble a motley crew, some of which are more complex or interesting than the others. These characters often have exchanges that do not include Aurora and add more depth not just to the companions, but also to the greater story and their larger world. So much of Child of Light is about growing up, letting go of the past, good or bad, and letting it die so that the new can be born and the future embraced.
In addition to the various folk you encounter along the way, there are quite a few enemies to trounce. Strangely, your growing team of comrades, each with their own special skill trees, is always limited to one representative at a time on the battle field. There is facility for switching characters out, but I found it cumbersome and the fights generally easy enough not to bother with trying to stack together too many buffs or debuffs by swapping in different guys.
The combat, though adequate, is one of the two stumbles in Child of Light. By use of your cursor's blinding ability, it's possible to skip many of the fights; however, I wonder if the boss fights might be much more difficult without grinding out some experience. The fighting revolves around timing, how long a wind up takes and interrupting enemy attacks. It's not a bad system, but it feels conventional and focuses on violence as the only solution.
A game like Renowned Explorer's Society (as an example) employs a tactical rock/paper/scissors that allows for victory by charming or frightening/intimidating foes, as well as by beating the crap out of them, if you so choose. I think Child of Light could have benefited from a variety of minigames or some other challenge that would allow for alternate forms of advancing your character's growth and the story. It's not that I don't think that Aurora shouldn't fight; rather, limiting so much of her interaction outside of towns to fighting misses opportunities for more story telling. There are a variety of well drawn and interestingly animated bad guys, but only the bosses get any lines.
The other stumble, this one on the story-telling end, was in the choice to write the thing entirely in verse. Many reviews pan the game solely for the endless rhyme and the resulting awkward language. The game must have been a nightmare to translate. I often find even one character the speaks entirely in rhyme to be exhausting in most games or stories, so I worried that having the whole thing written that way would spoil the experience.
Since I expected nothing from the poetry, it surprised me by working, if only in fits and starts, here and there. Putting all the narrative, the dialog, and even the exclamations and interjections, into rhyme was an ambitious undertaking. I applaud UBIsoft the effort, but felt that the relentless poetry detracted, if only mildly, rather than added to my overall enjoyment of the game. YMMV
I was surprised by some genuinely touching moments in Child of Light, as well as some subtle visual story telling, backed by restrained, but sweetly, sadly haunting music. It used its fantastical characters as metaphors for facing the challenges that we all face in growing up and, eventually, becoming parent to the child. Poetry aside, Child of Light is a memorable, imaginative and satisfying fairy tale.

TL;DR - Excellent game with minor issues, even when supported with fanboy nostalgia. 9.3/10
Man what
been said about this game? For your multiplayer shooter Star Wars experience, this is the end-all be-all, and probably still will be even after DICE's Battlefront hits store shelves.
I've played this game since my babysitter brought it over for us about ten years ago, and while I may be fueled by nostalgia both for this game and for the movies, it's arguably one of my favorite games of all time.
The graphics have not aged the best (Although still looks good for a game that's a decade old), it takes so many good concepts and throws them together in this sci fi orgy for the eyes and for the hands, whether grasping a controller or rapping away at a keyboard. Sound? Do I even need to bring this up? The entire John Williams soundtrack and narration by Jango Fett. Need I say more? Although you're going to be hearing "We've lost/gained the command post!" a lot in big battles, which brings me to my next point.
The gameplay is nearly flawless. The beautiful lovechild of Battlefield 1942's class-based open map battles with vehicular combat and the aesthetic, story, and design of Star Wars. You get a handful of gamemodes at your disposal, including Conquest (Similar to Battlefield's capture-and-hold spawnpoints, whittle down enemy numbers system), Capture the Flag (A staple of shooting games), Assault (Essentially deathmatch, except space battles where you destroy frigates and integral ship systems), Hunt (Play as different Star Wars aliens; Sand People, Jawas, Geonosians to name a few), and others.
I only have two large qualms about gameplay. Due to the Gamespy shutdown a year ago, standard online compatability no longer exists, forcing the use of a third party client called GameRanger. Now while GR does help link Steam games with other games that suffered from the shutdown, it does have its issues, mainly latency and server stability. The second is with AI which can range from average to running-into-walls dumb (E.g. on Hoth, in the XL mode, getting into an AT-AT and laying waste to scores of Rebels is feasible because a lot of them just stand there and do nothing. Lambs to the slaughter). Even on Elite difficulty they're not a head trip to kill. Much more exciting when you're playing online.
The campaign is good but only goes to the Battle of Hoth. Covers the 501st Legion as one of the most elite Clone regiments which then becomes the ultimate main fighting force under Darth Vader. You'll get a few hours of playability out of it.
Galactic Conquest is amazing; combining the conquest system with turn-based strategy as a Risk-like game of buying units and supplies to try and take over the whole galaxy. Will have you playing for hours.
Overall, even when I gush with that Star Wars nerd nostalgia, it's definitely an excellent title and one of my favorites, even with it's issues.

are you looking to get into rpg's, but all the rpg's terrify you because of their length and the ridiculous difficulty spike that goes along with managing stats, managing equipment, managing party members, doing the combat dance and generally worrying whether you're making all the right choices?
if this is the case, i'd like to introduce you to child of light.  child of light is a very simple "first" rpg that you can finish in 10-12 hours [my playtime is excessive, because i play games slowly and i tend to try and find ALL THE THINGS.]
child of light's framework is that of a storybook.  the minute you start the game, it recounts a simple narrative that takes place in a fantasy world that feels exactly like those bedtime stories you used to hear as a child.  "there was a princess" "she saw many strange things" - i'm sure you know exactly what i mean.
in this framework, you slowly collect party members that help you on your quest.  each party member has their own personality and their own strengths.  there are magic users, but each magic user does a different job.  there are physical characters, but each one tackles being physical in a different way.
combat is turn based and largely stress free, but you can only ever have two party members on screen at any time during combat, where the enemy almost always has three [this is somewhat mitigated by the easy drop-in/drop-out nature of the fights:  when it's your turn, you can easily swap to one of your other party members.  you can also flee at the drop of a hat if it's your turn with no serious repurcussions.]
there's no actual items to manage:  you get dust, which makes you better and jewels which you can forge into stat-boosting trinkets that do different things based on which equipment slot you put them into.  anything else you pick up is a part of the story.
in the same vein, conversations are scripted.  you don't need to worry about getting things wrong in conversation trees, because everything that is said is "the right thing at the right time to the right person."
with all this going for it, it's easy to make a case for this as your first rpg if you're even a little on the fence about the genre.  the visuals are charming, the music is beautiful [if repetitive - it's one of the very few downsides] and the story is sweet [though quite trope-y.  you'll spot many of the story beats coming a mile away.]
if you've never tried a rpg, i can heartily recommend this one.

This is perhaps one of the most refined indie games on steam. Just based on that only, this is definitely worth your penny. These indie developers spend years developing and refining the game so giving up your lunch money for this game really nothing huge compared to what you're getting.
Graphics: 7.5/10
PIXELS!! Pixels are back! Pixel art are never out of season. There are various kinds of pixel art, but the pixel rate on these graphics are quite high and although you can still get the pixel feeling these are definitely top of the art pixels. Although you'll see some of these gets repeated throughout the game but believe me - the graphics on this game I can only say 'its an art'.
Audio: 7.5/10
The sound of the multiple gunshots is somewhat addictive, gets you pumping, and the beautiful sound when the zeds drops dead. When the sound stops and your ammo runs out you know you're in trouble. The sound effects are well... effective i guess.
The developers really know how to match the audio and the atmosphere of the game really well. The BG retro music suits well with the graphics of the game. I don't know how else you can improve the audio on this game. Just watch the trailer you know what i meant.
Gameplay: 8/10
You can definitely spends hours playing this game. It'll definitely give you a run for your money. It's very addictive and may seems very hard at first. I'm quite a hard core gamer so I can easily adjust to the game quite fast. For casual gamers the game dificulty can be quite hard.
The game does requires tactic, but cmon peeps the game is set in a zombie apocalypse world, of course if you run around like an idiot without any tactic in both exploration and scout mode you'll get yourself killed. Positioning, check perimeters, hit and run, divide and conquer, use your sun tzu art of war knowledge on surviving. some battles are won or lost before it's ever fought. If you don't work on your supplies for healing and getting by the days of course you'll get doomed. Even researching at your HQ and thinking ahead which work needs done and assigning which members to work are part of the preparation.
I really enjoy the gameplay. It's part RPG so there is role playing involved, and putting yourself in the game is really easy to get your head around what choices to make. There are random events and quests in the game which keeps you well motivated and adds variety throught the game.
The permadeath on characters really adds the reality in the game. You don't get second chances with life. Sometimes you just have to move forward. It's challenging, but it depends on the players makes of this feature of the game. Luckily there're no 'personality' for the characters so the RPG stops right there and you don't really get attached to them except for the exp and levels you had racked up.
Mechanics 8/10
It's hard to explain all the game mechanics, because it is rather a rather in depth game system. But in simple term the game is really about surviving a zombie apocalypse. If I really have to give a simple explanation, perhaps this might be the easiest way to explain the game mechanics through genre:
Missions/World Map
Scout - Tower Defense / Action RPG
Exploration -  Dungeon Exploration / Action RPG
HQ Base
Research, Craft & Upgrades - Simulation
Character Stats, Levelups, Equipments - RPG
It is a well mixed genre for the game, which makes the game mechanic sort of a mini game within a game, but having them built as such, makes the game well versed and so interesting. The fact that the developer chose to develop the game built around a variety of mechanics for the different tasks in order to reach the goal of the game is highly commendable.
Story: 4/10
The bit that is definitely lacking in the game is story. The game has a high potential in having a good story telling put into it. The random events are all nice and all, but a stong storyline is missing in the game. The game could really use it as a sort of milestone checkpoint to motivate the players as you proceed into the game. Some people might find repetitive quests and exploration to be a bit grinding at the late stage of the game. A story with a main protagonist and background story could really be impactful.
Overall: 7/10
I'm giving this game a solid 7. Understand when you buy this game, this is an indie game, don't expect full featured game from big game developers with unlimited budget. I'm giving the reviews above with consideration that this is an indie game. Nevertheless, this is definitely one hell of a game. It's addictive, fun, and very indepth. I'm definitely recommending this one.

Regardless of what classes you pick, you can further customize you class with extra skills you can get both from the items/weapons you equip as well as the components you can use to augment said items/weapons. With over a dozen equip slots, you can essentially add up to more than 2 dozen additional skills/abilities to use in combat. When you add in the fact that there are 50 devotion points you can get by restoring desecrated shrines around the world and that you can use those points for even MORE customization, this game is amazing and has a ton of depth.
I would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the hack and slash genre. Considering it has full controller suppport, tons of customization, a wealth of interesting enemies to fight and an engaging story to go along with its incredible gameplay-getting this game is a no brainer. Legitimately though:
Simply, this game is phenomenal.
There are very few games I would list as 'Masterpeices', by which I mean that they not only define but alos entirely a genre or theme. To this date my only other 'Masterpiece' is Red Dead Redemption. This game is exactly everything you could ever want from a game about the struggles of primitive man. The prevelent themes of which I mean the importance of the alliance between Man and animals (primarily man and wolf but thats less important given story elements), the presence of Neanderthals in the evolution of man (their defeat/ultimate integration) and the importance of religion in the development of mankind. I'll admit I have a level of bias given my personal preferance to the major themes and their design choice of trying to adhere to history (or prehistory as it might be) as much as possible for example referring to linguistics professionals for the language and likewise for how weapons and clothings and such resembled what they had back then. So as to be expected the plot is simple though it is more than enough fleshed out by the backstory of the cultures involved and as such I found it very fulfilling (despite and including the nuances) in the plot department.
That being said (spoiler warning kinda) there are only three catagories of weapons the Club, the Bow and the Spear though all three of which are versatile and varied enough to be satisfing in their own way. Clubbing someone and wantching them ragdoll away is just as satisfying as watching someone cop an arrow to the face and collapse to the ground. And that all separate from watching the tamed animal takedowns or the owl kill people.
If your looking for Far Cry 4 then perhaps look elsewhere as more than a few people have mentioned the lack of weapons and vehicles make them unhappy, though riding animals was more than an adequate replacement and the weapon variations was more than enough to keep my attention and interest. If you want as accurate an experience as you'll ever get to an engaging experience of what it was like to be primitive man then this is exactly what you should buy. Personally, the weapons, gameplay, mission and animals were all very exciting and fulfilling including the very tongue in cheek character Urki. That all being said its very much a Far Cry game, if you like pulling your thumb back in place then with a satisfying snap and pop or a varied cast of weird and interesting characters and their subsequent development then you'll be more than pleased.

The idea behind the game is a solid one and I do feel that if I gave the game some serious time, picked up some decent players for a team and started playing matches against opponents that are deeply familiar with the game, this would be something deeply entertaining. However, my experience with the game was more of the opposite. Of the 8 or so matches played, both my and the enemy team simply sat in their bases for the first 15-20 minutes of the game, attempting to build objects that would ultimately serve no purpose.
Each match, which lasted roughly 25-40 minutes, degraded into fighting in a small tunnel underneath the map whilst placing radars in as many locations as possible to spot and counter the next branching tunnel into the base. Typically assaulting bases above ground lead to slow chipping away of various turrets and makeshift defences only to be sniped or smashed by 3 base defenders. As an attacker, the currently established role is to basically sneak across the map and find a clever place to slap down a spawner and a few radars whilst your team slumps around in the base staring at the enemy doing the exact same thing across the map.
As it's free, there's no harm in giving it a try and should you be able to talk a few friends into playing the game with you, this could be a very entertaining game. However, if your friends are like my own, finding the general idea behind the game 'Dumb,' you're in for a slow and painful experience.
In summary:
Play the game with at least 2 friends and you'll deeply enjoy what the game has to offer as it's built around teamwork. Play it alone, meaning with a full team of strangers and you'll deeply regret wasting a few hours digging holes and placing landmines, over and over and over and over and ov...

As a sucker for MMORPGs I had it on my 'to play list' for a while and finally decided to check it out.
The good:
- The graphics are really great
- Very fun action game styled combat system
- Lots of great mini systems implemented like map nodes, expanded crafting system, trade routes, etc.
- Lots of small things that make it overall much more of an enjoyable experience to play in this world, for example actually bumping into people, climbing high obstacles
- Contribution points system which lets you buy houses, workers, etc is really great
- Really great character creation system (lots of customization)
- Different classes have really diverse playstyle which makes them fun to explore and experiment with
The meh:
- Classes bound to character genders (not a problem for me and it lets for some more character customization and diversity to happen)
- Quests are: mostly boring kill 50 boars stuff; you outlevel lots of the early ones pretty fast making them obsolete (but since some of them carry good reward you either have to check online tutorial to see which ones are worth doing, or you end up doing all of them anyway (potentially wasting your time))
- The story is meh to say at least, it lacks any kind of narrative that would make sense of all the pushing around you get
- Rng based item progression system. Base of it is the oldschool by now, common especially in asian MMORPGs, system of applying +x upgrades to items. Because of it it's not just the good players that have engame gear but mostly those that got lucky with upgrade rolls/invested much more money and time. Best gear for everyone, even when all they do is gathering
- Some classes have great default keybinds, others have really bad default keybinds (but you can change them somewhat easily)
- Energy system is stupid
- The grind is real but it's a MMORPG so it shouldn't be any surprise, personally I don't mind it
- Huge number of minor and major bugs; considering the 'scale' of the game it's to be expected,  the fact they hapen fairly often remains
The bad:
- Market is absolutely atrocious (I've never thought it's possible to have worse auction house than PoE, quite an accomplishment)
- Weight limit exists only to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, XL life potions weight 2.5lt each forcing you to carry 40 at most (if you want to loot anything) and that doesn't last for too long; your option is ofc to drop $$ to increase the weight limit
- No trading between players, in a MMO, in 2017 (I guess the technology is still not there)
- Cringy, overly jiggly boobs and♥♥♥♥♥physics on female models; they should at least remove it from the plate armor where it's stupid as ♥♥♥♥
- The market system
- Very few default item models that mostly look bad; in the end to make a character that doesn't look like a complete plebian failure that happens to have high level you must get a costume (seriously overpriced $$). Those tend to look plain or just bad leaving you with very limited cosmetic options for the character's outfit
- A fair part of the community is pure cancer; it's impossible for any global channel to go for longer than 5 minutes without autistic screeching about traps or alienware
- Pets and Value Pack provide utility that should have been base game feature, but are instead gated behind $$ (you can in theory get them on the market, but as we already know, market is garbage)
- The point above can also be applied to other things in the coin shop, it's not only buy-to-play but also drop-even-more-to-get-base-account-setup-that-won't-make-you-want-to-kill-yourself-while-trying-to-play
- Swimming is... terrible, really terrible
Overall the game is in my opinion a 5/10, some great ideas that are especially fun to explore, but after you're done doing that there's not much left the game has to offer and the cons start to drag it down way too much, just like the major inconvenience.

I had fun with this game, though there are actually quite a lot of issues I had that were quite frustrating to deal with. I played through the entire game on only Heavenly difficulty and it took me around 15 hours to get all the achievements. I have a lot of bullet hell experience and this game still managed to challenge me, but not always for the right reasons... in spite of these complaints I did enjoy the game and the lower difficulties make it quite accessible.
My first major issue was the constant lag spikes I was getting. I haven't had these since my first playthrough of the game, and so this issue isn't one any more.
My second issue is that some of the waves are completely unreasonable or require a perectly choreographed path to complete. Most enemies shoot additional bullets on being killed, but they also flood the screen if not killed. So you'd think you just balance that by killing a few, dodge what's left... but that rarely worked. The only feasible way to handle most stage waves is to speedkill enemies. Further, some enemies (especially in world 9) have really dumb patterns. My preferred shot type was Matt with either the Titan Blade or Holy Swords, and neither of these have spread coverage. The homing shots in this game felt pretty weak as well, and can't keep the stronger enemies off the board. So overall some stages are designed so that different waves are nearly impossible for different shot types. That's not exactly great, but it's an unavoidable side effect of 24 different shots available. But when a lot of them are forward focus only, it's not unreasonable to expect forward-focus to be able to manage the waves and seeing that many waves couldn't be reasonably done was a little disappointing.
The next issue I had was the diamond system. This is more of a personal nitpick than anything else, but you only get diamonds for killing all enemies in a wave without bombing while at full health. If the first 2 requirements are met, a heart is dropped instead, and if an enemy escapes or you bomb, nothing is dropped. Hearts and diamonds both refill both the primary and secondary gauges, allowing the next wave to be speedkilled easier. Bombing costs 1 diamond but losing a life costs 2: that wave itself plus the next one which becomes a heart. This makes any early mistakes immediately catastrophic for a rank, which was especially annoying on bosses or when I got hit as a resullt of a lag spike.
Building on the previous, the survival levels are quite fun...until you get dealt a ridiculous wave nearly impossible for the shot type you went in with and die. It turns what would otherwise be a nice test of skill into an RNG-fest. Again, world 9's enemies are either well balanced or absurd, and the absurd waves can end an attempt just by appearing. The item drops range from helpful to useless depending on when they're randomly dropped, as well. These levels were still fun, but could have been much stronger. And that's true of much of the game as well.
Finally: the bosses. They, like the rest of the game, lack a real difficulty curve. Past the first stage I felt like the difficulty stayed overall constant, with random absurd spikes. The bosses fall into this as well with some patterns being trivial, and then immediately followed up by nearly impossible waves. The final boss takes this almost too far, with my star approach being capture the first 3, carefully choreographed wave 4 with 1 bomb, capture the nearly absurd wave 5 and 6, bomb 7 and 8, capture 9 (which is trivial once you realize it's just vertical streaming), and dodge wave 10, which is absurd. I'm sure the balance is better on hard, but that doesn't mean that the highest difficulty should be unbalanced.
So in conclusion: Bullet Heaven 2 is a good, fun bullet hell held back from being great by balance issues. If you like bullet hells, you'll like this game, but may find it frustrating in places.  When it's good, it's amazing (World 6 bosses especially). Just be mindful of the schizophrenic curve.
edit, 2 years later: my biggest issue was lag, as mentioned above, and on my current setup I haven't had that problem once. That alone boosts the game quite far, but doesn't help the schizophrenic curve.

When I started playing this game, I didn't really like the weapon system. Your main weapon gets a lot weaker with continuous fire and you have to wait a moment for it to recharge to full strength. You can also equip a sub-weapon which is more powerful, but takes a lot longer to recharge. Not being able to attack constantly felt awkward at first.
After a few worlds, things started to click because the game's design meshes perfectly with the weapon system. Taking out large groups and dangerous enemies with full firepower, then pursuing stragglers while my sub weapon recharged soon became second nature. And then there are the bullet patterns, which are among the best I've ever seen. The spider boss alone is a marvel to behold. Then you get plants shooting lilypad-shaped bullets, or clouds shooting raindrops and snowflakes. The visual design is simply outstanding. The soundtrack is also great and comes as free DLC with the game.
Bullet Heaven 2 may look daunting, but the game is actually very forgiving. I was able to finish Hard mode in 4 hours without hitting a wall. Most of the challenge comes from score attacking and the optional Heavenly difficulty, which is fine. I did encounter some rather extreme glitches, but nothing that a quick restart of the game wouldn't fix.
Overall, I'm really impressed by how well-designed this game turned out to be. Truly a hidden gem within the Steam library.

Half-Life 2 is a first-person shooter video game developed and published by Valve Corporation. It is the sequel to 1998's Half-Life, and was released in November 2004 following a five-year, $40 million development phase... Half-Life 2 is, simply put, the best single-player shooter ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Half-Life 2 compared to other single player shooters. What Valve has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there is an excellent shooter here. Half-Life 2 doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of first-person shooters to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure as a PC Gamer.

Dying Light is a fun, open world zombie adventure game that is fun alone, and even better with friends. Download the Demo before buying.
Dying Light, at first glance, is your average zombie slayer/survivor experience. Looking for supplies, weapons, and a rudimentary crafting system. Adding free running into the mix makes for a whole new experience, and unlike some other games of it's kind, it emphasizes the difficulty of zombies, making it much more appealing to run away rather than to just shoot & slash your way through a horde of zombies
Running, Jumping, and combat are all very smooth. The new 'Parkour Fever' mode really illustrates how smooth this mechanic is. Zombies (biters, whatever they call them) are challenging instead of just simply being able to mow down hundreds with a few clicks of the mouse. Most all of the storyline missions (except for the very beginning and the very end) can be played with a friend. This game is fun enough by yourself, but playing with a few friends can really get the game to come to life. I've played the majority of the game in singleplayer, and killing zeds whilst jumping from rooftop to rooftop and along skyscrapers just never seems to get old for me.  Side-Quests have a small amount of story in them, and they really do motivate you to complete them. Capturing safe zones may get a little dull once you get the hang of it, but it's a necessity if you plan to roam the game at night, where tougher zombies that are faster than you come out and seem impossible to kill.
Co-op multiplayer isn't a necissity, but it isn't a requirement either. The instant challenges are a great way to occupy yourselves and get a few extra survivor points while you're at it. I do not recommend allowing your game to an open, public lobby until much later, after you have gained some serious equipment yourself. Otherwise, More advanced players tend to join your game and drop a lot of highly advanced weapons that make the game way to easy to kill zombies way to early. There is the chance you may find someone at your skill level, but its unlikely unless you open your lobby as soon as you get the opportunity.
Dying Light on Steam has Workshop compatibility, and I have seen some really great multiplayer maps, both co-op and directly PvP arenas come out from this, and I can't wait to spend hours with friends in these community made maps and mods.
The story in Dying Light wasn't terrible, but it wasn't anything special either. There were a few twists here and there, and the voice acting was really well done, but overall its nothing that stands out. There was one part
that felt completely out of place and over used, but it didn't ruin the overall experience

I find that there's a fine line to walk when it comes to a setting and story being airy and whimsical. Child of Light's dialog/story are presented as poetry, and it came off to me as very dismissive of anything being all that important. The game doesn't appear to be made for small children, but the dialog sounds to me like a bedtime story an adult would read to a small child in a soft tone, completely devoid of substance or sincerity; just trying to get the little rugrat to fall asleep rather than to actually entertain.
The music is charming, and the art style is rather pretty, which I feel are the game's biggest positives. The combat is alright, though it's clearly at a level of difficulty higher than what a small child could handle, so this further evidences that the story was meant for more mature people capable of winning its battles.
Unfortunately, the whimsy of its story completely obliterated all sense of urgency or interest I had in the game. With the gameplay not being terribly entertaining for me, despite the fact that I like turn-based RPG combat just fine, I needed characters and story that would keep me interested and wanting to go on. I certainly don't demand really mature themes or grittiness or anything of that sort, and find some whimsy fun. However, everything felt
inconsequential and airy to me in Child of Light that I could not feel even the least bit compelled to continue, despite paying for it at launch and sinking 10+ hours into it. I honestly don't know how I got the will to play that long.

Grim Dawn is a Diablo-Clone hack and slash action adventure that will be very comfortable to anyone who is used to this genre. All the basic mechanics and gameplay are there without much deviation.
Graphics-wise, like it's title, this game has a much darker and grimer feel then Diablo 3 and feels closer to Diablo 2. Environments look appropriately apocalyptic and monster designs are very well made with few recycles. A little disappointing are the character models, but maybe I expected a bit more flair for a game in 2016.
Sound design is appropriately gothic and moody with very nice atmospheric effects. Music is a tad generic however and I didn't exactly pay close attention to any tunes that I particularly enjoyed. Voices for the NPCs aren't over-the-top but they are also aren't particularly memorable.
One thing to note, is that the game map is really huge. There is so much to explore that if you just rush headlong the main quest and finish everything, you will be missing out quite a few sub-quests with good rewards and experience. Take your time to explore every nook and cranny.
Speaking of quests, this game offers choices in how you can undertake or complete some quests. Example: If you were to act like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and kill indiscriminately, some paths may be forever locked to you, while some others may open up. There isn't really a wrong or right choice, and the player can feel free to choose what he / she wishes. The only downside I can see is that you may miss out on some rewards that may be more to what you want.
Skilltrees for this game feels alot like the system in Titan Quest in that you can multiclass. Not surprising since most of the game developers used to work on that game. Almost anything other then character attribute points can be respec quite cheaply.
Downsides, this game is VERY STINGY with its loot.
I played as a caster in the game, and after 40 hours, I got my first legendary loot, and .... its for a different class. Yes I know, thats what people normally call "A Near Miss" but c'mon man. While playing, items that drop are usually of about 5-10 levels higher and is quite rare to find a significant upgrade that is close to your current level. Maybe i'm playing the game wrong, but as a caster, my focus is on DPS, and it is so rare to find an item that gives me good dps. Its always an item that has good side-attributes with Bad DPS, or a Good DPS item with below-average side-attributes.
From what I read in the forums, apparently the game encourages multiple alts with multiple playthroughs. So unless you are willing to invest hundreds and hundreds of hours in creating alts for farming, you would be disappointed in the quality of loot the game offers.
Another disappointing thing I encountered was the ending.
Here I am having just defeated the final boss, and the next thing, I meet an NPC who congratulated me.....and then....Nothing. No end credit screen, no penguins dancing on the screen. Just a simple in-game quest NPC saying thanks and I continue with the game. Is it really that difficult and expensive to code a simple end credit screen? :\
Overall Rating: 7.0 / 10
A very well made Diablo-Clone that will scratch the itch for anyone looking for a good hack-and-slash ARPG. I've been a big fan of the Infectonator games since I first played them on Kongregate way back when.  Toge Productions showed a lot of promise and potential with their games and ideas.  I like what I see so far from Survivors, but it's obvious that the game still has its flaws and feels incomplete in a number of places.  In no particular order, I'm just going to pinpoint some notes I had while playing the game.
1.  Experience - It appears that my "travel team" never really gets experience.  As I bounce from location to location in the map, my efforts are not reflected against my team's experience.   Only when I get back to base does XP appear to be tallied, and even then it appears that I only get credit for the last fight I was in.  On the other hand, if I stay at the base and use my guys to plant or build something, then they get experience for doing those activities.  In the end, spending 10 minutes fast-forwarding time while planting veggies and other things granted my team more XP than the hours upon hours I spent going through and collecting tons of items across a long expedition.
2.  It's a little difficult to determine what you're supposed to do when a location has a symbol over it.  Do I go into Scout mode or Explore mode to resolve the issue at the location?
3.  In the begining while trying to build the car, you can use one of your quest items to build something else, thus losing that item forever  (the electronic module seems to also go into making advanced turrets).  Be careful with this, it sucked when I had to restart my game.
I'll add more to this as it comes to mind, in the hopes that it will help the devs with feedback.  I think this game is definitely one to keep track of and watch for any fan of Greenlight games.

Writing this review at 9.4 hours in. So far I have really enjoyed the game. All I'm gonna talk about are the elements of the gameplay. It isn't very inovative gameplay wise, but they took a big risk by making a FPS, in a way, set in the stone age. I think the lack of guns make it challenging. Far Cry is Far Cry after all, the usual running around and taking outposts for towers to take over an area. The set amount of resources you can carry does make the crafting interesting. You have to run around and search for different sources in different areas of the map to upgrade your village huts, weapons, resource bags, etc. The resource hunting is endless. The hunting is a bit more challenging because of the limited amounts of weapons you have. To move to different areas you must upgrade your weapons and clothing to be able to survive against harsher elements and the dangerous animals in the different enviroments. The map is a nice size although I haven't explored all of it yet. The missions aren't too mindblowing but they provide entertainment.
If you want a game that will change your life, this isn't it. If you just want a game to entertain yourself until something different comes out, or something to keep the boredom away, then this would be a great game. I can't say anything about the crashes because I haven't experienced any of those yet. It has been fun. Wait for a sale and then pick it up.
In the end the game is entertaining and will keep you busy running around hunting, doing missions, side objectives, and resource gathering. Buy it or don't buy it. Watch some gameplay first. With the whole steam refund thing it makes it much easier to buy a game and try it out. I give it a 7 outta 10. Not the most amazing game I have played but definitely something different. The whole stone age thing really is a cool idea and it would be interesting to see if other developers try it out. Sorry for the long read.

MacGuffin's Curse is a puzzle game where you push and pull boxes in order solve puzzles. What makes this game special is you get a medallion from a museum that allows you to transform into a wolf. This wolf form is the only way to move objects within the world, however your human form, which you can switch to and from in moonlight, allows you to hit switches swim and open doors. The story is ok but what really shines is the world and all of the side quest within it. The game has a lot of optional content and even more is made available after you complete the story. In certain areas you can unlock safes that have comic books pieces in them that when put together make a nice visual story. You can also find money that can be spent on improving your house or unlocking music and art. The puzzles start out easy but get challenging quick. Luckily there is a hint system that gives you two hints and the option to skip the puzzle and come back to solve it later. The game length really varies on what you want out of the game. If you try to tackle all of the tasks in the game you could easily get 12 hours out of it. If you want to try a block pushing puzzle game you really can't go wrong with MacGuffin's Curse.

Telltale's adventure game tells the story of the Forrester House, a dynasty that allies itself with the Stark and find itself in danger after the Red Wedding. This 6-episode long story parallels with the TV series from the end of season 3 till early season 5.
Checking the trailers  and pictures one can already guess how much detail Telltale has put into this. It is just superb - we have all our favourite characters returning from the show including Cersei, Tyrion and Ramsay Bolton or even Jon Snow. You recognise the actors from the show and shiver when hearing their texts are spoken by the same voice actors. I particularly liked the oil painting effect that was applied to many backgrounds - it is something very neat and makes the game look pretty cool.
The formula is the usual considering it is yet another Telltale adventure: you mainly pick responses when in dialogues and you also have fight sequences. QTE events now occur more often than in previous Telltale titles and also expect the game to be very violent. I mean VERY violent. And expect a lot of sacrifices - if you hated Martin for some of the things that transpired on the TV show you'll hate him even more for some of the choices you have to face in this game. I believe so far this game has offered the toughest choices of all the Telltale titles.
It is an emotional ride that superbly accompanies the TV show. A must for all GoT fans but remember to prepare yourself for the game - if you think you have seen everything you'll be mistaken as the game has some nasty surprises for you. The game has a nice story build-up but once reaches its conclusion it does not really offer a satisfactory ending. Since there are some questions unanswered expect a Season 2 just like in case of Walking Dead.

But after episode three I started seeing the hands behind the puppets so to speak. The plot devices became very transparent and some of the hard choices forced upon the player make actually no sense from the point of view of the player. Episode 5 has you choose something, not as making a hard choice as one of the characters, but more like the player is now assigned the role of the hand holding the puppets.
Now after episode 6 has been released it is revealed that episodic gaming has reached a new low, no doubt thanks to EA pulling the stings of Telltale these days.
You may think you get a full game in 6 episodic parts, but this is no longer the case. The sixth episode is now full of cliffhangers, trying to get you to buy season 2. We all know where this is going. This will continue as long as it sales. Even if season 2 will be exceptional, we know it won't end there. I would say especially then it won't end there. We will get a season 3, etc, until writers run out of steam, players stop buying it and it will be quickly wrapped up to put an end to it.
So, no, I don't recommend this standing on its own and I especially won't recommend anyone going along with EA's new money cow.

The special little things this game does to differ itself that make me very happy.
MAIN SIMPLIFIED "SPECIAL LITTLE THINGS"
Hyperdimension Neptunia is a fresh take on jrpg where three big differences arrise. For one, the take on dialogue where it jokes about sequels, unbeatable bosses, and other picks at jrpg games. Then there's the gameplay, the gameplay works on a hitbox like system where any enemies inside your hitbox will take damage from the attack. These things called plans can spawn dungeons, create items for the shop to sell etc.
THE SPECIFICS OF THOSE LITTLE THINGS
Now I will speak of the hitbox system. This system allows certain weapons have different hitboxes making stats not the only attribute of a weapon. There is nothing else I can say about dialogue other than it's amazing. The plans can, as I mentioned, create dungeons and things for the shop to sell. Plans require certain materials to be created, also theres is a memory system where if you run out of memory, you can't make plans. Each plan takes up certain amounts of space and this space can be upgraded through finding items.
EQUIPMENT
There is of course, armor, but lots of it is just cosmetic. One of the main armor parts is the "disc" or whatever you'd like to call it. Essentially when fighting you can pick up items that you can burn on to a disc, these items are different levels. The discs themselves can only have certain attributes burned into them, such as only a level 3 yellow attribute. The discs can only (at least from what I've seen) be collected from interacting with characters. Then the previously mentioned weapon hitboxes being different.
THE MENUS
At first these menus such as the main map, the shop, and the guild are a bit confusing but you easily get the hang of it after a short while.
THE BATTLE SYSTEM
The menu is the basic SP attack, normal attack, items, block, and run. The menu also includes HDD transformation, EXE attack, and combos during the normal attack. HDD first, this is a technique where any godess gets a crazy stat boost for a small cost of SP during the battle. The EXE moves are moves that utilize your EXE gauge which fills overtime. Once filled to a certain point the attack is usable. These moves are DEVASTATING and once the opponents shield is down they may take down a tough enemies health heavily. Now for the combos. These combos are set up in your menu. You can customize these combos and you are unable to just choose the best and leave, you have a limit and each move takes up a certain amount of cp and they either specialize in destroying shield or just damaging. Now on to the HP system. Before you can go all out and melt the enemies HP you must destroy the shield to deal max damage. after each time the monster's shield is depleted it will recharge after the monster's turn. This can get very annoying but that's why you need to tactically plan moves for the situation. Very few monsters recharge their HP but when they do, it is very hard to deal with them so find out your maximum damage dealt in a short time.
THE MONSTERS
These monsters will highly vary but the main thing is the "tough" monsters. This doesn't signal that it's too strong for you. it signals it is much much stronger than anything in that dungeon. During battle monsters may also become "Viral". Once Viral they will regan all of their hp and be comparable to the strong monsters.
FINAL NOTE AND RATING
Mind you I have not finished this game and it was  on a large sale so I can't determine if it's worth the $30.00 price tag but for the $5.00 I spent this is damn good. My "final" rating will be a 10/10 for hilarious dialogue, great battle system, and perfectly crafted dungeon system with plans. The only downside I can spot is the regening shield but it just adds to the difficulty.

BLUF:  If you have not played the original XCOM, then thsi game is a must have.  If you played the original and spent hours talking with your friends about memorable battles you had, then this game will be a let down ....and you need to get a girl or boy friend.
Pros:

On the one hand, I was very emotionally invested in this game start to finish; not quite as tear-jerking as Telltale's The Walking Dead, but definitely close at times. Unfortunately the whole "illusion of choice" thing that Telltale games do doesn't really work as well with a game about political intrigue as it does with something with an inhuman outside threat like zombies, and the emotion you'll most often be feeling is rage and frustration as things go from bad to worse to humiiliating time and again. There really isn't a great way to explain how truly meaningless all of your choices are in this game without going into spoiler territory... but basically you'll just find again and again and again that when you're given choices between who to pledge loyalty to, or whether to uphold commitments you've made, or whether to play ruthlessly or with honor... none of it ever matters. NPCs never have your back, always assume the worst about you, and there is almost never a dialogue choice provided for you to even attempt to protest. And you'll find that the game is rarely graceful in the way it railroads you back into the path of its plot when you attempt to deviate, the game is not shy about having NPCs behave in a completely insane and irrational manner in order to ensure that you're getting betrayed at all the right times.
I've read before that in Telltale games you shouldn't approach them expecting that you can controll outcomes, only control the sort of person that you're playing as, and that's certainly true... but you don't even really have control over that in Game of Thrones, the decision to bounce around between so many different point of view characters means that very few of them are written with the sort of depth that leaves you feeling there's really enough room to to flesh out anything approaching a personality or set of values.
I've read a lot of reddit snark calling this a "submission simulator," and that really is the most apt descriptor possible. Then again, if you can find it on sale.... it'll give you feels, just not the good ones!

Imagine the weird offspring of Smash Brothers, dodgeball and Pong. Cover it in an art style similar to Jet Set Radio. Add quirky characters and you're all set. Lethal League is one of those games that's difficult to describe. Though there have probably been similar games before it, this one does enough new things that make it unique.  You start out in an arena hitting a ball around. If you hit the ball, it turns your color. When you hit an opponent with the ball, they die. Last one standing wins. Last won standing after ten lives is declared the winner of the match.  To win, the game requires you to have cat like quickness. Each hit that the ball takes from a player it speeds up. The more players hit it, the faster it will go. Matches are usually five minutes at the most, so this game is great to kill a few spare minutes if you have a busy schedule. I would highly recommend this game to those who want to try a unique take on some well-known game mechanics. The game is fast, competitive and hell of a lot of fun.

I've been a longtime Starcraft fan so I was a little suspicious of this game when I first got it. I'd tried a few other sci-fi RTS games in the past and none of them held my attention for long... boy was I in for a surprise!
Grey Goo is one of the most creative and beautifully animated games I've played in a long time! The cutscenes and pre-mission briefings almost look real when I'm watching them, the audio is damn near perfect, and the gameplay is fast enough to keep up a good pace, but also encourages thoughtful preparation and decision making.
So, lets go down the list of races first, as is always important with an RTS game:
The Beta: A race of four armed humanoid aliens who have been on the run from something they refer to as "The Silent Ones" for generations. They're a sort of warrior race by necessity, having to constantly worry about their adversaries catching up to them as they're the last of their species. All three races get an 'Epic' unit, one that can be built by combining several buildings and spending a lot of resources. Their epic unit is the Hand of Aruk, a mobile weapons platform with a cannon that launches missles for massive explosive damage. Its slow and the cannon takes a while to recharge, but all around the cannon are little slots where you can have your other units ride ontop of the platform to add firepower to it. Outfit it with a few tanks and you've got a holy terror for your enemies to deal with.
The Humans: Oddly enough WE'RE the super-advanced race this time around! Humanity went the Star Trek route in Grey Goo, becoming a spacefaring colonization race. As war has been rendered unnecessary for centuries all the human units are rather weak drone-robots that were mostly used to deal with aggressive wildlife on various planets. Infact, the leader of this expedition is one of the only two actual humans in the game! The other two units are a humanoid robot and a relic from the last war humanity ever had and MUM, their main computer. The Human's epic unit is Alpha and, well, this is also probably a relic from said war. Lemme put it this way: remember Power Rangers? Well you get your own space-age megazord!
The Goo: This is the game's namesake and while it sounds silly its actually one of the most creative things I've seen in a while. The goo is a giant amoeba-like mass of nanomachines that can split itself off into smaller units which then morph into the more traditional units. While in amoeba form it can climb up walls and literally EAT buildings and enemy units, consuming them to heal itself and give you resources to make more units! At time of writing I haven't gotten to their epic unit yet, but I'm definitely intrigued to see how this all ends.
There's one more species, but it's in the DLC expansion and I haven't played it yet. Its called the Shroud and is apparently the "Silent Ones" that were hunting the Beta.
As for the game overall:
What I liked:
- Some of the most creative species concepts I've seen since I first played the original Starcraft.
- Gorgeous animation, I can't believe this is an indie game!
- Gameplay that encourages a thoughtful approach to enemies rather than the ol' standby of the 'zerg rush'.
What I'm meh about:
- The controls can be a bit awkward at first since all the units that you can build are tied to the keyboard in the menu, making it easy to select something by mistake.
What I didn't like:
- A couple of the missions can be pretty frustrating. I had to repeat one of the human ones several times when you're trying to find a downed spaceship and if the opponent finds it first it gets blown to bits within a few seconds, causing the mission to fail.
Overall: With Blizz winding down Starcraft this is a definite way to scratch the RTS itch. I wholeheartedly recommend buying this game!

Grey Goo is a fantastic RTS set in the far future and populated with a diverse set of characters and factions.  It also features  an incredibly interesting take on faction infrastructure and upgrading technology.
To start, as of now there are four factions, the Beta, Humans, Goo, and Shroud.  The Beta use 'hubs' to create structures anywhere that they have vision, and can set up forward bases pretty much anywhere with relative ease.  Their units can also mount on wall pillars providing an additional defensive bonus.  The Humans on the other hand have a single massive base built using 'conduits' (think of roads) and can teleport any structure along the conduits for easier defence and more efficient use of the space that they have.  The Goo dont have any structures at all! Instead they have 'goo mothers' that roam around the map and use health as a means of production, splitting off pieces of themselves to create units.  The Shroud are relatively new to the game, and use amplifiers to increase the effectiveness of their buildings.  They also can 'evolve' their buildings for different purposes as the situation dictates.
The story of GG is pretty well done and has an interesting twist at the end.  Mission Types are pretty diverse and let you understand the fundamentals of the major races before you set fourth in the multiplayer.  Also, the cinematics are GORGEOUS, honestly they beat out blizzard's own department in realism and quality.   Additionally, there is the 'emergence' mini-campeign that tells the story of one of the more significant characters after a certain event had happened.
The way technology works in GG is actually very novel.  Whenever you meet the requirements for an upgrade you can pick only one tech out of three.  Each upgrade is unique and you never really feel like you are losing when you do an upgrade, which in my mind is a pretty good achievement considering you are spurning other possibilities for the match.
Despite the factional diversity each faction is pretty well balanced, and the team does a good job of putting out balance changes on the regular whenever an issue pops up.  The game had kind of a rocky release as well, but since that point and through the effort of Petroglyph the game keeps getting better and better with each content release and balance update.  The last update featured an ENTIRE FACTION FOR FREE.  That NEVER HAPPENS (at least what I've played) in RTS.  I have nothing but praise for Petroglyph.
Honestly, if you like the "90's style" of RTS then you are doing yourself a disservice by not getting this game.  Personally its one of the best games I've played in a long time, and even with the release of XCOM 2 I can't seem to get away from this game.  It just has a special charm that will keep pulling you back in if you give it a try.
TL:DR, If you like RTS in the "90's style", balanced gameplay (with diverse factions), great cinematics and rediculously committed developers, then buy this game.

Child of Light is a pleasant fairy tale-like RPG. Its main strengths are its beautiful aesthetics and music, and its particular turn based combat. Not an instant classic, but still good.
- We must acknowledge that Ubisoft did an excellent job with the watercolour style and the music. The soundtrack is beautiful, tragic, but encouraging.
- The main form of movement in Child of Light is flying. The flying feels very responsive and smooth.
- Large amount of party members with different strengths and weaknesses. Very nice that you can switch between them mid battle.
- Each character, including your own, has different skill trees. You can choose to play your characters in different ways.
- You are accompanied by Igniculus, a glowing ball of light. I enjoyed that he can be used both in and out of combat. In the overworld you can use him to blind enemies you want to avoid. In battle, he can be used to slow down your enemies’ actions or heal yourself.
- The turn based battle system has a twist where you can interrupt your foe’s actions depending on your timing. This makes battles more interactive and skill based.
- I don’t really like that opening the game on Steam forces you to use Uplay as well. It’s not such a big deal though.
- I didn’t find the game particularly difficult or challenging.
- Segments where you must fly a lot can be dull. The game is quite slow paced.
Ubisoft often gets a lot of bad press. I agree that Ubisoft has made numerous mistakes when developing and releasing games, but Child of Light is well made and pleasant to play for the most part. Child of Light not a personal favourite, nor will I play it again any time soon, but I think that the positive aspects of the game outweigh the negative ones. If you are unconvinced, I suggest you try the demo before buying the game.
