I initially enjoyed this game, but now that I have finished the first season, I can't recommend it. Designing this type of game is tricky: they promise that one's choices will matter, but the narratives must converge in order to make designing the game manageable. Telltale managed to strike this balance in The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us. It failed in Game of Thrones. By the end, I felt like I might as well button mash my way to the fated ending. Of the four threads, only two interact with each other and have visible if minor effects of one's choice. The other two seem like they could have been cut out of the game entirely without the player noticing. One of these also suffers from putting the revelation of the stakes in the next season. Rather than enticing me to see more, it left me wondering what was the point of the hours I put into the game.

If you're thinking about buying,  don't. It has way too many bugs to be enjoyable. Believe me, I tried.
Maybe it will become a decent or even a great game in 2018.

MacGuffin's Curse is a gem of a puzzle adventure game. You steal this amulet that gets permanently attached to you which allows you to change into a werewolf using moonlight. Using that ability, you then maneuver through a maze of puzzles in which you must move a battery into a slot which powers the door to the next location. The puzzles range from simple to challenging. You have certain abilities and restrictions in wolf form such as moving objects which you can't do when in human form. But in human form, you can use terminals and move through water which you can't do in wolf form. The shape shifting element plus the different puzzle rules for each character really makes for a great mental workout.
On top of the great puzzles they throw in a cool story and a few side missions to keep things interesting. Some of the later missions seem to end up being fetch quests, but they weren't excruciatingly painful to deal with.
The game is really well balanced and has a decent coat of polish on it. It has great music too and offers a lot of attention to detail. Puzzle lovers can't go wrong here. Check it out.

With the release of X-Com 2 on the horizon, now is a time to write a review of the most brilliant squad-based management crew in the history of mankind. In fact, my favorite game of all time.
As can be said of Dark Souls (my second favorite game), it is rare a game beats the nostalgia of childhood to become one a gamers greatest games of all times. Even more rare, when it becomes a gamers #1 game after 20+ years of gaming. It. Is. That. Good.
At any price tag, do not neglect buying it.
A few points:
-After 2+ hours, I had to stop playing. It was so fun my brain was imploding.
-It is difficult to describe why this game is so good, but it is just as good an RPG as a TBS game.
-Money is scarce. Spend wisely!
-Narrative presentation is spot-on, as is story delivery. It is like a mix of X-Files and Independence Day.
-Action has a cinematic flair.
-As others have pointed out, you really get attached to squadmates. They even start taking on a personality in your head, after a time.
-Engine is highly optimized, and runs even on my 4GB laptop swimmingly well.
-IGN coined the term post-X-Com syndrome for anything after X-Com. They are so right. This is a trainwreck to all other games you will ever play afterwards. Save X-Com 2.
Overall, 5/5, and if I could give it more brownie points, I would.

Imagine somebody tells you that they're going to cook you your favourite meal. You pay them and sit at the table waiting patiently for almost a year as it's delivered, piece by piece. Finally, the entire meal has arrived and you've forgotten what you ordered. Turns out it doesn't matter anyway because your choices mean nothing. Also it's cold, full of token cameos and the original characters have no flavour. Dessert is also an underwhelming cliffhanger. Actually ♥♥♥♥ this metaphor, it's not worth it.
I loved The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us and Tales from the Borderlands, I've even played Telltale's Back to the Future, Wallace and Gromit, Sam and Max, Monkey Island and Poker games and they were of so much higher quality than this. I'd rather re-read the first half of Feast for Crows than play this again. I want to list all the things I hate about this series but I just can't be bothered. Anyway, here are a few:
Animation is jerky, the writing isn't up to standard, certain character's motivations make no sense, while others can lose an eye and turn up with 20/20 vision a month or so later to gloat and kill your family, who I can only assume were named after Forrest Gump, considering their collective IQ.
Daenerys is there only because somebody decided she should be there. Same with Jon, Tyrion and Ramsay. While Ramsay is indeed a formidable villain, the fact that his plot-armour is stronger than valyrian steel means that his appearances carry little to no tension after the first meeting.
What's more, the game requires very little of you except for your time (with the exception of your money.) The quicktime events that so many Telltale critics detest are incredibly easily executed and failure only means that you have to retry. You have very little power to alter the path of a character's story. This isn't new in Telltale games but it's felt much more acutely in this series, when a 'wrong' decision that seems perfectly reasonable to the player can lead to a GAME OVER screen.
It seemed like a perfect match - the 'anyone-can-die' universe of A Song of Ice and Fire in the hands of the developers that brought us The Walking Dead should have been a no-brainer. I made the mistake of purchasing after good reviews for the first episode, but I won't be paying for season two.
I just wish I'd spent my money on Tales From the Borderlands first instead.

Lethal League is a fighting game where opponents fight in the vein of dodgeball. You smack a ball at each other and whoever gets hit with said ball is knocked out; you usually have several stocks to lose before losing the game.
Just the first 2 senteces should provide an accurate look on how original and interesting this game is. Lethal League is possibly one of the best video games I've played in 2015, and it's a shame to know I could've picked it up last year. It provides an easy premise with simple controls that allow the newest of PC gamers to enjoy the game, but it also gives space for more dedicated players to learn the game and play on a new level of skill. Similar to Super Smash Bros. in the sense that there's room for casual play but also room for intense combat. There's never a shred of time when I feel like the game is bad or boring. There's a multiplayer function that works well allowing you to host a room or join quick matches with others. There's also a single-player tutorial and challenge mode (similar to Classic mode for Smash Bros.)
The Soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in some time and provides a meld of hip-hop beats and electronic funk to heighten the intensity of battles between others.

I've found myself growing more and more frustrated with traditional bullet hell games, but this one is excellent. It defies genre conventions in subtle ways, and in doing so produces a game that is enjoyable beyond the usual niche scope of this sort of thing.
The most important thing for me is that it provides you with plenty of things to do besides endlessly repeating the same six levels for score. There's a lot of content! 70 levels, and the non-boss waves are an interesting challenge on their own instead of being a pointless grind. Plus there's a variety of characters and modes to unlock, and in-game achievements covering a wide range of potential activities.
The other big difference compared to other danmaku is that the game is rather forgiving. The actual waves and patterns are as hard as any bullet hell, but you can recover life in a stage and can always start from any stage you've unlocked -- no endlessly repeating the first few areas in search of a one credit clear here. To me, this makes the game feel far more fair and approachable. I find myself wanting to put in the effort to learn the harder patterns, since the game makes them available to practice as much as I need to.
As for the rest, it's a very solid entry in the genre. Great music, cute art and character designs, and amusing party banter at the start and end of each level. Controls and interface are solid, and it's refreshing to play a danmaku that properly uses widescreen resolutions.
My thanks to Matt Roszak for another great release -- looking forward to EBF5!

I'm pretty crappy at writing up all the pros and cons of a videogame, so I'm just going to say this: I have never felt as satisfied in a video game as in this. It is as hard as you want it to be, and it's really easy to set goals and mileposts for yourself.
I literally shouted at the top of my lungs and did a happy dance as I beat the final boss on hard with the "1 life" modifier on. I had been trying to do that for about a week or so, and through practice and learning the bullet patterns, I finally managed.
In that, the game is VERY fair. If you lost, it meant that you did something wrong. That your reaction time was too long, that your movement to react to an incoming bullet was too fast and you hit something else. That you messed up in dodging attacks and found yourself cornered by bullets unable to escape. It'll never throw ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t at you that was impossible to dodge. If you get hit, it means you need to get better, you need to learn how to dodge the patterns that those specific enemies throw at you. And believe me you will. The learning curve is very well done, and the unlockable handicaps and cheats help in finetuning that process.
As you graduate from normal to hard or heavenly, you'll have a bit of things to adjust to (suddenly all enemies explode into bullets), but just playing through the worlds again is equally satisfying as the first time on normal.
In short, if you have any interest whatsoever in the genre, buy this, you won't regret it.

Bullet Heaven 2 is a SHMUP. It's made by Kupogames, an indie game dev that has made the beloved (to me, at least) Epic Battle Fantasy series.
And Bullet Heaven 2 is freakin' cool.
It's a game with flexible difficulty, that never challenges you with more than you're ready to tackle. But that doesn't mean it's easy. No, no, the game is rather deliciously hard! I've spent a few hours agonizing over character configurations and what options I could afford to turn on or off in order to get the best result possible.
That's one of the key points of the game: It has options, purchases, and other such things, but none of those ever make the game easier to master. It just gives you more options to attack the problem. Turning on "cheats" will give you various benefits, but decrease your score. Turning on "handicaps" will make the game more difficult, but boost your score. And scoring is universal- every difficulty and every option is posted on the same scoreboard. There's no "wrong" way to play.
And that's what I love about the game. It's a shooter that's not punishing you for being "hardcore" enough. It's a shooter that's there so that you can have fun playing it. It's a shooter for you.
If you have any interest in shooters, give Bullet Heaven 2 a try!

Child of Light is a pleasant fairy tale-like RPG. Its main strengths are its beautiful aesthetics and music, and its particular turn based combat. Not an instant classic, but still good.
- We must acknowledge that Ubisoft did an excellent job with the watercolour style and the music. The soundtrack is beautiful, tragic, but encouraging.
- The main form of movement in Child of Light is flying. The flying feels very responsive and smooth.
- Large amount of party members with different strengths and weaknesses. Very nice that you can switch between them mid battle.
- Each character, including your own, has different skill trees. You can choose to play your characters in different ways.
- You are accompanied by Igniculus, a glowing ball of light. I enjoyed that he can be used both in and out of combat. In the overworld you can use him to blind enemies you want to avoid. In battle, he can be used to slow down your enemies’ actions or heal yourself.
- The turn based battle system has a twist where you can interrupt your foe’s actions depending on your timing. This makes battles more interactive and skill based.
- I don’t really like that opening the game on Steam forces you to use Uplay as well. It’s not such a big deal though.
- I didn’t find the game particularly difficult or challenging.
- Segments where you must fly a lot can be dull. The game is quite slow paced.
Ubisoft often gets a lot of bad press. I agree that Ubisoft has made numerous mistakes when developing and releasing games, but Child of Light is well made and pleasant to play for the most part. Child of Light not a personal favourite, nor will I play it again any time soon, but I think that the positive aspects of the game outweigh the negative ones. If you are unconvinced, I suggest you try the demo before buying the game.

Child of Light is without a doubt one of the games I've most enjoyed playing in a long time. Although this game is already 3 years old, I still very much have wanted to make a review of this game. Also, English is not my main language, so sorry if there is a grammar mistake or something sounds weirdly redacted.
Personally, I liked everything from this game, though I know there are some aspects that might not be as liked by others, and it is completely understandable. Let's get into that.
- The story: It's not the most outstanding aspect of the game, but it's not something terrible that brings the whole game down either. It's very confusing if you do not pay attention to the dialogue of the characters, and that isn't always too easy since the narration in this game is always "poetic", which isn't bad but can really get unclear or confusing. It's the way that everything is written in a verse that makes the story interesting, because it somehow makes it pleasant to read or listen to. If you have trouble understanding poetic elements such as metaphors, then I highly suggest paying attention to the dialogue if you don't want a confusing ending.
- The characters: The character design is one outstanding element in this game, they really reflect the fantasy theme the game features, and each one of them have their very own interesting backstory. The characters is one thing that you'll remember after playing the game.
- The gameplay: It is fairly balanced, there's nothing that will be incredibly overpowered, and if there is it's because you're probably not preparing yourself enough. This is not simply a turn-based game, there is also a feature in the combat system which is a meter that indicates the order in which all entities in a battle will perform an action in every turn, which is a really cool mechanic in the game. The combat system allows you to use 2 characters at the same time (of course you can also swap them out with others). It might sound weird, but if the 2 characters that are currently in the field are dead it counts as game over, even if you still have other alive members in your party. This is actually pretty great because it encourages you to play strategically and swap out between characters when you need to.
- Role distribution: Each playable character is highly different from one another. You have your all-round class whose stats vary depending on how you build their skill tree; you have a mage that excels in magic damage and magic resistance who also has access to elemental attacks; you have several supportive roles, but each one of them offers different supportive abilities (heals, revives and status condition defense / provides buffs to allies / provides debuffs to enemies); you have your high-reward high-risk class who can dish out a lot of damage, but is also pretty squishy, its higher than average crit chance and dodge chance makes up for that; and finally you have your tank class with considerably more health who is all about taking the hits for the team.
What does this all mean? You're never gonna feel a character exactly the same as other, which means they have good gameplay design.
- Other features: This game has something called Occuli, which basically are fragments you can give to your characters to boost a specific stat or add a little tweak to their resistances and attacks. I like and dislike this feature at the same time. The game hardly gives any explanation on to how they work or what even they are for. You constantly rely on them, which isn't necessarily bad but I can understand why some people might hate that.
- The music: Last but not least, the music. If there is anything you slightly didn't like from the game, the music will surely make up for it. I found myself repeteadly listening to the soundtrack after finishing the game. They fit the scenes and ambients in which they play.
Do I highly suggest this game? Absolutely. If you like turn-based RPGs with interesting characters, music and combat mechanics, then this game will not let you down. And if you're up for a bigger challenge, you can try out the expert mode unlocked after finishing a normal playthrough.

To start, I've played just about all of the major ARPG's. Diablo, Diablo 2 and 3. Titan Quest and expansion, Torchlight, Torchlight 2 and Path of Exile.
I saw numerous reviews prior to purchasing this stating the game was easy and had no difficulty. They either played a different game, or only tried the lowest difficulty. I just finished the main game on Veteran(2nd difficulty), first playthrough. I had at least 100 deaths. The game brings a huge challenge on higher difficulties, especially if your gear is behind and your build is not optimized.
Which brings me to my first gripe. You picked 2 classes of the bunch as your character. The max level is 85, which equates to around 228 skill points I believe. Each class has 20-30 skills with ranks going from 1 to anywhere as high as 12. So to rank 1 skill to max you have to use 12 skill points. For me, I have never been good with theorycrafting so this is a big challenge for me and a stresser. There aren't a ton of builds out there on the web to go off of, so you kind of have to make good choices or your character won't have enough resistances or skills to kill the bosses. If you love theorycrafting and TONS of different options for builds, you will love this. It's not as complex as Path of Exile, but there's a ton of build variety.
My next few gripes I will lump together. There's a weird level scaling system in place. Some areas have a max level for scaling while others seem to not, or have a higher threshold. If you find yourself getting slaughtered by a boss, and go level 4 or 5 times and come back, the boss will still be 4 or 5 levels higher than you. It makes it hard to want to keep going sometimes, because you feel like youre on a stairstepper that doesn't end. I occasionally had crashes/freezes. There is also some line of sight issues with ranged abilities. I also found the navigation to be buggy sometimes when dealing with areas with multiple platforms or levels.
As this game was made by the people who did Titan Quest, this game throws mountains of loot at you. 99/100 pieces of the loot will be useless, but it's good for making money. Which you'll need to buy lots of potions, and some nice gear upgrades from the reputation vendors.
The game has reputation factions which you gain rep with and each rank of rep has different rewards. It's a nice side grind/progress checker. The music, level design and art is great. I found the main theme to be very nostalgic of Diablo.
I finished the game in just under 30 hours on my first playthrough and managed to get to level 50. I found myself wanting to keep progressing each time and keep finding those upgrades and getting that next level so I could get a new skill or new buff. If you enjoy ARPG's, you really can't go wrong with this game. I am glad I bought it, and expect to try to get a char to max level and try the harder difficulties. I do not regret buying this what-so-ever, and fully recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the genre. There's a ton of stuff to do, the areas are huge, there's tons of loot, great music, great build diversity, and it's quite challenging.

Straighten up and get in line!  Tower Wars is a unique tower defense game with a heavy emphasis on technique and planning.  This isn't your grannies Bloon Wars, babies! The learning curve is high, but those who perservere and learn the ropes march towards glory.  Be warned:  You WILL get your backsides handed to you your first few rounds in multiplayer, but not to fret.  The community has done a great job of creating guides and videos that are easily available to get new players up to speed, and the guy who just slaughtered you in six rounds will also more than likely be totally willing to give you a practice round or two to show you how things work.  All that said, my favorite part of this game is actually the audio and voice acting.  Skillfully put together, it matches the art in theme and energy, and the voices of both the King and the troops are amusing even when you're on a losing streak.

In 3 weeks, I will probably forget all about Infectonator and Toge Productions, as I will have a much better computer, and it will allow me to play better games. Infectonator Survivors is by no means outdated or outclassed by other prettier games, but it loses in responsiveness as an early access game that claims to be headed towards completion. When I say that I had a great time playing The Organ Trail, that is my genuine review of hours of satisfying gameplay of a retro game that has had someone's care and attention given into it's development. Respectively, for Infectonator Survivors, what I have taken away from many hours of gameplay is also drawn from various other aspects and small details that I've observed. The conclusion I've come to is that the developers do not care to fix the bugs, bad english, small details or mechanics. Honesty is a big part of success, but naturally people are afraid to face others objectively and they lie, just like how the developer who relays updates to players can't honestly say that updates actually take 3-4 weeks on average and continue to insist that they'll be back in 2 weeks with another update. Personally, this trend has made me have doubts in the back of my mind about how serious the developers are about  fulfilling the promises that they have set forth and even leaving their own mark on the game industry. I feel that the sheer heart that other developers have toward their games will outpace Toge; when you then add graphics and inspiration to a passionate developer, the disparity will become even more noticeable, until everyone notices that the developers behind Infectonator Survivors is not as responsive as other teams.

Sometimes I am really surprised by an indie game. This is definitely one of them:
I hadn't heard of the game before and was just a bit curious what it was. I expected to be bored very soon - but couldn't stop playing until, four days later, I had not only completed the game, but also collected every achievement.
MacGuffin's Curse is puzzle game made by some witty and talented Australians. You navigate MacGuffin, an anti-hero-turned-werewolf, through lots of boxes, occasionally pushing them around to open exits and such. The story is well-crafted and offers a lot of funny as well as some touching moments. The environments are fantastic, too, and some lunatic even took the time to write a seperate description for every chair, lantern, picture or other item you come across. Needless to say, I had to read every single one so I wouldn't miss anything. The puzzles hardly ever become boring or frustrating. Another thing I really liked was the developer commentary. It is always interesting to get a little glimpse into the process that went into making a game.
Overall I have nothing negative to say. Unless you really don't like puzzle games or indies you should give this one a shot!

TLDR
A mediocre/budget softcore porn JRG that has about a 66% repetative gameplay without any gimmicks (like a steath section), and 33% "story", which consists of the characters talking to eachother in the form of animated 2d artwork.
This game is very similar to the other JRPG hyperdimension games (rebirth 1,2,3), including that roughly 80% of the gameplay, models, animations, item models, monsters, music, formats, character abilities, characters, 2d-artwork, ETC are ripped from or are reused for their other hyperdimension games, indeed playing one is like playing them all.
PERSONAL PLAYSTYLE/INFO
-Played as a western gamer, who can only read/speak english.
-Played with the expectation that it will be a lower quality version of rebirth 3.
-Played with the goal to get all of the achievements.
-Played in a bit of a rush due to wanting to get achievements.
-Played on it's easy "setting"
Now, if one comes into this expecting something of the quality of eternal sonata, or of the final fantasy games, don't, you will just set yourself up for disappointment, indeed treat this game as an "ok/good" quality indie game, little else.
When starting up the game's campaign, one will be greeted with what could be seen as the developers best work, the "fight" cutscene while not bad, it isin't something like the intro to "vermintide" or "diablo 2" it feels like it was a rather good quality animation done in MMD, in that the animations are stiff (linear movement, and static poses), and that the audio is copy/pasted from the various combat dialog that they use in the rest of the game, giving a disembodied sense to it. If you assume that this quality is repeated throughout the game, well you guessed right but I'll give the devs credit, at least each character has it's own animations, to give distinct personallity.
The story is mildly interesting, but I felt it somehow too "conventional" and definantly more "escalated" than rebirth 3 in that there is some great threat that must be defeated, whos implications are vast, and the medium in which it is being conveyed is somewhat reinforcing of the intensity. Yet there is plenty of pettiness in their dialog, like how "angry daria" (blanc) gets angry at "fully grown woman" (vert) for leveraging her breast size in an failed attempt to get a guy to do something for her (an example of the softcore porn in the game) to keep the game fairly relaxed and cartoony. Though is a techinical flaw with the way it is conveyed, not in the animated 2d artwork itself, but in how it's animated the mouth movements were for the japanese version, not the english version, of which only 50% of the dialog is voiced (so if you wanna hear mouth noises throughout, you gotta switch to the higher quality but unintelligible japanese version).
The gameplay situation is indeed as if playing one is like playing them all, it's very similar to the other games, with the enemies having a separate defense bar with it's own "hit points" that while active mitigates damage, with buffs and debuffs to each of the 7 stats, with the same debilitating debuffs, with "energy" being aquired for hitting enemies repeatedly (regardless of damage dealt).
Indeed it worked, the gameplay is ok/good (which is better than other parts of this game) but there is minimal change in the overall formulas with most of the complexity it coming from a greater variety of items and abilities on the part of your characters, all bosses come in singles (or at least the ones I found) and there is no need to change elemental types, (just use the stardard attacks mostly), and the rather minimal alterations there are is the enemy that passively disables your abilities/item use as long as it's alive. Don't expect much change between the beginning and the end (other than stats of course).
However my ambitions...
As an achiever, (I have 100% achievements for this game) the game was rendered less enjoyable since I'm also the kind to worry about missed content, forcing another playthrough, and the planning phase of achieving (where you plan out how you are going to get the achievements on your playthrough) hurt the immersion into the story making the game feel as if I was min-maxing an MMO game instead of playing a JRPG, there is also the issue of the grind needed to get a couple of them (the 100 million money achievement) which absolely drains any enjoyment you have of the game, and any positive sentiment you might have had about it. I my opinion this is one of the greatest blunders about the game especially since it invalidates the positive sentiment generated in the scene where all of the characters congratulate you over finishing the game, "Cuz you know it ain't over yet" and you gotta do another playthrough. However one could blame me sensibly by stating "why not ignore achievements?" which I feel to reply "why should the game screw over a portion of it's playerbase on the whims of some egocentric developers" (since they think their game is crazy important, and you better get all those stupid things).
But there was one great mitigation to the second playthrough, the game is like 33-66% dialog, so if you skip all of that, (there is a button for that) you can save a bunch of time. I also "rushed" through the game on easy mode which helped cut down the amount of time.

Half-Life 2 is a first-person shooter video game developed and published by Valve Corporation. It is the sequel to 1998's Half-Life, and was released in November 2004 following a five-year, $40 million development phase... Half-Life 2 is, simply put, the best single-player shooter ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Half-Life 2 compared to other single player shooters. What Valve has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there is an excellent shooter here. Half-Life 2 doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of first-person shooters to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure as a PC Gamer.

Do you like shooting enemies?
Do you like dodging tons of bullets?
Do you like collecting coins, gems and unlocking stuff?
Do you like a quirky, amusing cast of characters that are incredibly genre-savvy?
Then you might like Bullet Heaven 2! For the reasons why I like and recommend this game, keep reading!
======
Like most people, I started getting into Matt Roszak's games through the Epic Battle Fantasy RPGs. Eventually, I was surprised to learn that Roszak expanded into other game genres, particularly the Arcade-style vertical Shooter. Yes, I played Bullet Heaven long before the sequel was released. While I enjoyed the game quite a bit, I didn't feel like it stood out that much amongst the other flash-based shooters I played (sorry Matt).
Thankfully, Bullet Heaven 2 cuts out the bits that held the original game back and tightens its gameplay to a laser-focused point. BH2 is a true arcade shmup to the core, for all the right reasons.
The main thing that was dropped from Bullet Heaven 1 was the Upgrade Shop. You could buy powerups for your characters using the gold gained from defeated enemies. While this is nice and all, it made the game play out entirely differently from BH2. Your upgrades dictated your skill level, not your actual skill itself (though in BH1's defense, some of the levels are super hard even with upgrades). Axing the Upgrade Shop was a very smart idea and I feel BH2 benefitted heavily from the change.
That being said, how
BH2 play? Well, like a typical score-based shmup, as one may expect. You dodge bullets, you shoot enemies, you collect the point items you drop, and that's about it. You can control your character through either the keyboard, mouse or controller, though I honestly prefer the mouse. The amount of control and precision offered with the mouse is incredible, and I wish more shmup games like this had mouse (though maybe they don't for that reason, sometimes the mouse is TOO accurate at times, at least when the game isn't lagging).
You will probably need this precision quite badly in Bullet Heaven 2, because as the screenshots show, it's one of those Danmaku-style games where bullets fill the screen, creating claustrophobic patterns for you to weave through. Games like these can be intimidating at first, BH2 gives you many options to change the difficulty. aside from the three difficulty levels that adjust the number of bullets the enemies fire, there are cheats and handicaps to adjust your attack power and bullet speed, give you more health/bombs and temporary powerups. If you don't care about unlocking high-end stuff or high scores and just want to blast things, feel free to use the Cheats as upgrades to make things easier.
If you DO want to chase high scores and three-star rankings, however, the game has a simple yet effective scoring system in plae. Cheats lower score, Handicaps increase it, as does the difficulty itself. Clearing an enemy wave without getting hit, running out of time or bombing gives you a diamond, which boosts your score multiplier. Therefore, getting a high score mainly relies on clearing waves quickly, though you can also gain some extra points by collecting the coins enemies drop. And since this is a bullet hell game, you earn points for grazing bullets and clearing them from the screen too, though depending on the difficulty they may or may not be worth the effort.
In addition to chasing Medals and High Scores, the shop in this game adds alternate sub-weapons and costumes for each character, changing their play style. I honestly prefer using a costume that increases my item-grabbing radius, as I love collecting coins and increasing my score with them. When I'm not chasing achievements, I usually use Phrynna in her Fairy Wings outfit, she has amazing damage output against most bosses and enemies (I use Dry NoLegs for things like the robotic wasp boss).
Speaking of weapons, each character has a sub-weapon in addition to their main shot, which can be fired off once their subweapon gauge is full. You can also charge up an attack with your main shot to deal extra damage, but I rarely use it. Each smart bomb also acts a little differently and does damage depending on the character and mods you are using, but you can only carry so many per level, so use them wisely!
In terms of content and story...Well, there's not too much of a story. Monsters start attacking Matt and friends out of the blue, so they travel across ten or so worlds to try and figure out why they're being targeted.
The story is told through dialog between the party members before and after each stage, and it is pretty funny most of the time. Matt's the dim-witted warrior, Natalie's the sarcastic magical girl, Lance is the somewhat serious tech-head (whom has a serious crush on Natalie), Anna is the nature girl, and NoLegs...Is the team pet, not much else to say there, heh.
Each world has seven levels; four normal story levels, a boss level, a tougher boss, and an endless level.
In terms of presentation...The game looks great. Roszak's cartoony anime-ish art style really fits the setting for this game, yet he also does a fine job of making some truly detailed and intimidating monsters and backgrounds. There is also a gallery where you can choose the sidebar graphics, main menu backgrounds, and even listen to the awesome music Phrynna made for this game! The game can run at a smooth 60 FPS, or it can be locked at 30 FPS if you feel your computer can't handle 60 FPS for whatever reason. Lots of graphical options and screen sizes exist as well, so tweak them to your liking. I didn't have that many visibility problems while playing this game, aside from getting hit by a bullet that was hiding behind another bullet or something dumb like that.
And yes, like most arcade shmups, there is Multiplayer, but I feel it gets in the way of pursuing high scores since you have to work well with your friends to get said high scores. It's good for a laugh, however.
I apologize for this being a lengthy review, but I hope it's been helpful regardless. If you enjoy these kinds of arcade shooters, then Bullet Heaven 2 will be right up your alley, and I highly recommend purchasing it.

In terms of graphics, performance, gameplay, and the DLC's such as "Shadow Operations Unit", the game is great. However, the one major flaw that gives me reason to not recommend this game is due to the repetition in the gameplay.

Now, a month or two after I initially downloaded Beat Hazard, I never open the game anymore because it plainly becomes boring-- the gameplay is always the same: shoot and survive. Yes, there's goals such as those with the Shadow Operations Unit, but that doesn't change how repetitive the gameplay gets after a very short time. The gameplay is designed well, but it needs more variety, options, gamemodes and so on to prevent it from getting old as quick as it did for me.
I personally find the game very boring now, due to how incredibly repetitive this game is. In my opinion, the $9.99 I spent on it was not well spent, and unfortunately due to my 3.7 hours on record I am unable to refund the game. If the developer were to add more gamemodes and variety to the gameplay so it isn't the same old thing, I would love to get back into this game again. I could also settle for a lower price assuming the repetition in the gameplay does not change. But until any of that happens, I probably won't be spending much if any time on Beat Hazard.
Thanks for reading my review and I hope any possible viewers take it into consideration before purchasing this game.

This game is amazing, to put it simply.
Movement mechanics for running, jumping etc are nearly flawless. The keybinds may be odd at first, but aside from the melee key, it's doubtful you'll want to rebind anything with some practice.
The maps are simplistic to put it lightly, but there is still a decent amount of detail to them, and they incorporate a lot of features that work well with the jumping and sliding mechanics.
The guns have insane recoil, which only adds to the intensity of the firefights in the best way. However, if you feel like it, you can steady your aim with the Shift key, though this limits your mobility and makes you an easy target for all the pros jumping around and making swiss cheese of people. In short, practice. A lot. At jumping and sliding. A lot.
There's also a skill system, and no, I'm not talking skill trees and unlocks. Once you pick your playermodel and your weapon of choice, you get to pick one skill, each with its own benefits. For instance, there's a skill card that allows you to reload faster, reduces recoil, etc, all in one package. When you find a combination that's good for you, the game will get a lot easier.
And let me just say, I haven't played a game that made me laugh so hard so fast in ages. Some seriously funny crap can go down in this game, and it's just beautiful when you're a part of it.
So, in short, this game is amazing because:
A.)  It's got great movement mechanics.
B.) The gunplay is fast and tense, and easy to learn.
C.) It's got some comedy value to it, such as when you shoot someone and they rocket across the map and helicopter over a parked car.
D.) It's completely free! No microtransactions, no DLC, nothing!
It's awesome, it's free, DOWNLOAD IT!

To start, I've played just about all of the major ARPG's. Diablo, Diablo 2 and 3. Titan Quest and expansion, Torchlight, Torchlight 2 and Path of Exile.
I saw numerous reviews prior to purchasing this stating the game was easy and had no difficulty. They either played a different game, or only tried the lowest difficulty. I just finished the main game on Veteran(2nd difficulty), first playthrough. I had at least 100 deaths. The game brings a huge challenge on higher difficulties, especially if your gear is behind and your build is not optimized.
Which brings me to my first gripe. You picked 2 classes of the bunch as your character. The max level is 85, which equates to around 228 skill points I believe. Each class has 20-30 skills with ranks going from 1 to anywhere as high as 12. So to rank 1 skill to max you have to use 12 skill points. For me, I have never been good with theorycrafting so this is a big challenge for me and a stresser. There aren't a ton of builds out there on the web to go off of, so you kind of have to make good choices or your character won't have enough resistances or skills to kill the bosses. If you love theorycrafting and TONS of different options for builds, you will love this. It's not as complex as Path of Exile, but there's a ton of build variety.
My next few gripes I will lump together. There's a weird level scaling system in place. Some areas have a max level for scaling while others seem to not, or have a higher threshold. If you find yourself getting slaughtered by a boss, and go level 4 or 5 times and come back, the boss will still be 4 or 5 levels higher than you. It makes it hard to want to keep going sometimes, because you feel like youre on a stairstepper that doesn't end. I occasionally had crashes/freezes. There is also some line of sight issues with ranged abilities. I also found the navigation to be buggy sometimes when dealing with areas with multiple platforms or levels.
As this game was made by the people who did Titan Quest, this game throws mountains of loot at you. 99/100 pieces of the loot will be useless, but it's good for making money. Which you'll need to buy lots of potions, and some nice gear upgrades from the reputation vendors.
The game has reputation factions which you gain rep with and each rank of rep has different rewards. It's a nice side grind/progress checker. The music, level design and art is great. I found the main theme to be very nostalgic of Diablo.
I finished the game in just under 30 hours on my first playthrough and managed to get to level 50. I found myself wanting to keep progressing each time and keep finding those upgrades and getting that next level so I could get a new skill or new buff. If you enjoy ARPG's, you really can't go wrong with this game. I am glad I bought it, and expect to try to get a char to max level and try the harder difficulties. I do not regret buying this what-so-ever, and fully recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the genre. There's a ton of stuff to do, the areas are huge, there's tons of loot, great music, great build diversity, and it's quite challenging.

It's everything you look for in a role playing game with a balance of classic zombies with a balanced pinch of super zombies.

There are a few that are downright frustrating because it takes so long to get to the objective, which then requires a bunch of jumps and acrobatics. One mistake or slip and you're back at the safe house starting all over again. There's no ability to save or at l;east have the game save part way through a difficult mission. I highly recommend this game for in general and RPG'ers, and strategy types may also find this game an interesting distraction. If you liked Batman, Arkham City, you'll find some familiar parallels. I particularly like the grappling hook use and the true 3D environment of this game.

DEFINITELY one of my top ARPGs (thanks to them supporting the Steam Controller) ... just some thoughts, not all ...
***Great detail on environments, monsters, effects, lots of beautiful stuff
***Abilities have impact (as in monsters go flying)
***FANTASTIC Steam Controller support (although I heavily modified mine and I've been using one since they came out so I'm very familiar with custom profile tinkering)
- I was able to put my default attack on a soft pull of right trigger, and then a slew of abilities (3 at the end - primal strike, forcewave, super slam item ability, and then of course it would use default attack cadence when the three were on cooldown)  staggered to fire off one after the other continuously even when held down when I pulled the trigger the full click down... felt REALLY cool to play that way because soft pull for little stuff, big pull for big groups and stuff
- I'm glad it had really good Steam Controller support, I was able to customize tons of other stuff that made playing a breeze.  I would still switch back to mouse interaction when I was in town of course for buying/selling/talking/etc and for inventory management.  It doesn't have any other directional movement support outside of controller, though, which is sad.  I was hoping it had WASD movement option for combat tactics while mixing in mouse movement and combat at leisure so that combat is tight and other types of things (like buying selling or going long distance with mouse) are easy too, but Steam Controller did great (with mouse switch for town stuff).
***loved playing the Warden - a mix of Shaman and Soldier, you can mix any two base classes, really cool, I had a few pets too, LIGHTNING ZAP and TOTEMS (I didn't think I'd like the totems, but it's pretty cool to position them properly and dance around them).
***didn't like that you couldn't save whenever you want ... it DOES always save your progress, but all the mobs respawn and there aren't that many rift checkpoints ... I learned to live with it because everything else was so cool, but not being able to drop and pickup the game when I wanted made the game less enjoyable (just a fact of life when you don't always have lots of time to sit down in one sitting).  I think at least your personal portal should stay between game shutdowns so that you don't have to slog all the way back.
***There was definitely enough good story elements to frame the combat well and make me feel like I was in the world.  Nothing super awesome, no cutscenes, no emotional animation for characters or anything like that, but there is some voice acting and the titbits you pick up make sense for what you're doing on quests without sounding too blandly fetch-or-kill-quest like. You can definitely tell that the action/combat is the focus, and the story doesn't doesn't detract from that.  I did liked some of the little extra written stories you pick up in the environment;  I remember one about a family slowly becoming cannibal zombies from the perspective of the mother.  Only funky part of the story was the ending.  The game ended after boss fight and that's about it, no cutscene, no fanfare, its just kinda done (I'm not sure what I was expecting).

I think to begin with, I am a bit biased because I deeply enjoy Hack&Slash genre and I feel there isn't quite enough of this kind of games in general. Having said that, Grim Dawn overall comes across as an extremely well put together piece of software, with a gritty setting (but not obnoxiously so), balanced mechanic and plenty of class combinations and loot to acquire. As a spiritual successor to Titan's Quest it does remarkably well, expanding and streamlining on almost every concept from the original. The new loot is exciting to find, the new abilities alway fun to try out and see how these combine together. My only gripe is that the storyline ends somewhat abruptly - I understand that the developer will release story DLC not too long from now, but all the same it feels like clearly there was more to be done. The lenght of the game is not an issue, understand - there is good 40 - 50 hours worth of gameplay in a playthrough, and you have the different difficulty setting and roguelike dungeons on top of that, but the storyline could have been somewhat more fine tuned rather than leave you hanging like it does. Other than that, it is definitely a great game, worth of recommending to anyone, and a must buy for any gamer who enjoys Hack&Slash but feels like Diablo 3 was too expectably consolized - though I don't have an issue with progress happening to games, Diablo 3 lacked something, and I find that somehting in Grim Dawn and Titan's Quest Anniversary.

Hello fellow explorers. I say that primarily because that is what most people who play sandbox games are though some of us like to shoot our guns/bows or swing our swords/clubs more than others. Ubisoft Montreal has crafted a beautiful land for you to explore and conquer. It's filled with danger at every turn, until with a little time and a few prehistoric beasts; you can stride the land like a confident apex predator. The abilities of all the critters vary and give you ways to spice up what has become a standard in the Far Cry series; taking outposts. There are dozens of ways to occupy your time in Oros apart from that standard, and a large variety of mission types can be played or not just like FC 2, 3, and 4. Ubisoft continues to polish this series and find ways to add to the variety of options in which you can conquer your stone age world.
I have read a number of reviews that bemoan the lack of multiplayer and a cohesive compelling storyline. I have told a friend, that for myself I would have loved there to have been a coop campaign like FC4, but alas instead we get a highly polished singleplayer game instead. I prefer that dedication to honing the SP experience over trying to mash in a multiplayer mode and both SP and MP suffering for it, I wish more companies would take note of what Ubisoft has been doing with the Far Cry series.
As to the story. A stone age era is exactly that. Stone age. Languages are not overly expressive, there is no wealth of history for characters to rely on, only oral histories. Human interaction at that level of development would be just as infantile and primordial as the technology said cavemen are using. I mean the wheel hasn't even been invented yet and cannibalism is rampant, so what makes people think there would be some super complex emotional rollercoaster of a narrative?
I've played all the Far Cry games, and the stories have never been "OMG make a movie out of that!", but they have been entertaining, and so is the simplistic tale of a tribe's struggle for survival and the need to evolve that was presented in this game. For me this title fires on all cylinders and delivers exactly what one would expect. A great romp through the year 10,000 BC with a plethora of weapons, tools, and tactics at your disposal to make any style of playthrough possible.
8/10 for me, with the minus two points for no multiplayer or announced plans for it.
A word to the wise Ubisoft, take what you have done and make a DLC that adds something of merit for once. A multiplayer campaign expansion that is unlocked after you beat the game in singleplayer that features a whole new tribe invading the land of Oros.

I'll start out by saying the game is gorgeous visually, but what else would you expect from this series.  The major problem I've had so far is not being able to distinguish friend from foe at a distance.  The animal skins work too well as camouflage and everything becomes a jumbled mess unless you're already aiming and let the cross-hair tell you what you're about to shoot.  Yes that is part of the challenge of the game but it can still be annoying to not know there's an enemy around until the gauge that alerts you to being spotted flashes on the screen.
The audio is excellent.  You really get the feeling that you're the one being hunted in Oros, partially because the animals never seem to shut up around you and it becomes a challenge determining which noise means food and which growl means you're about to be food.
Menu interface is counter-intuitive, the same as the other far cry games. The weapon wheel could benefit from being more simplified, and the crafting / character perk menus are overcrowded with icons that are just a tad too small to be useful.  Honestly I don't have a problem scrolling on a perk tree menu if it means I get a little more detail without having to select each individual icon and read it's description.
Traveling can be slow but fast travel is available when you're ready to start hacking away at the game, and there's an actual reward system for helping other people during escort / rescue sidequests so you'll be less likely to ignore their cries for help.
Really, Far Cry Primal is solid, and the complaints I have are in no way deal breakers.  The experience is unique and will more than make up for the game's few flaws.

-- 4 Classes (+ a 5th class with Enemy Within Expansion) that each have their own Skill/ability tree
--- classes are: Sniper (Long range, uses sniper rifle), Heavy (Demo and area control expert, uses LMG and Rocket launcher), Assault ( High Crit/Short range/Multi-shot unit, uses shotgun or Assault rifle), and Support (Healer/cover unit, uses Assault rifle)
-- Lots of ways to customize the look of the soldiers
-- Many Armor Types, 3 weapon tech levels, 5 base weapon types (6 with EW expansion), and lots of items that can be carried
- Interesting, varied enemies, many of which can be captured -> Interrogated -> autopsy for new technology
- Customizable base, which makes up the "Strategic Layer"
-- Interesting facilities which you can build in the base, including:
--- The Foundry, where you can build cool things, invent new tools, and improve existing weapons (better crit rate, more ammo space, etc...), though it is a little bland compared to the amount the Enemy WIthin expansion adds
--- The Officer Training school, which betters your troops in various ways
--- the Labratories (Where you research cool things)
- Good Tactical Gameplay
--Well Designed cover system, with destroyable cover of varying durablity
-- Accuracy System and Flanking system (The names are kind of self-explainatory) where height, distance, and line of sight matter; and can effect damage, crit rate, and accuracy
Con's:
-Story is very predictable
-No Steam Workshop/Mod Tools, though there is a sadistic mod called the "Long War"
-While the game does have a large amount of maps, which have decent variety, you will still end up going thru most of
them in a playthrough, and will definitly start feeling repetative by the second playthrough
- Overwatch action wasn't implemented in the best way, and everyone will fire on the first alien that comes into view instead of taking turns (In case there are more aliens, which there always are)
- Once you get good at the game, you'll realize that there is one strategy which is signifigantly better than all the others, which makes the game start to feel bland after awhile.

Disappointment utter disappointment!
has been the most frustrating & dull game I have played from Telltale to date. Starting stronger than it ends
, it's story across six episodes is cliché, lacking interesting characters other than those already established in the TV series.
brings little that is new to the table. The parallels between the Forrester's story & Stark's story arcs are uncanny, leaving me with a strong sense of déjà vu. After the first couple of episodes the pattern becomes clear, & as such becomes predictable. It lacks the twists or shock value that the TV series/books are renowned for, instead it compensates by using excessive violence & swearing.
world is brutal
, but this is not the brutality surgically used to emphasise the emotional impact of a scene that is done so well in the TV series.
The entire game sets you up for failure, regardless of the choices you make. Its one painful scene after another, leaving you feeling bullied & powerless to make a difference. This left me angry throughout most of the experience. In some respects you want a strong emotional response to the antagonists in such a story, but to put it simply the Whitehill's
are simply one-dimensional assclowns where every single line of dialog comes off as obnoxious. They lack any charisma needed to be memorable villains. It's almost like the writers said, "ok, what is the most insulting & horrible thing we could say at this point" .. lets write that! None of the subtly or cleverness seen in the scripts that makes the TV Show so compelling.
There were also many parts of some of the story arcs that just didn’t seem to have any meaning/motive/link to the overall story. Senseless. Spoiler:
Overall quality of the production is sub-par compared to previous Telltale titles, from the animations to the facial expressions. Lips are often out of sync, emotions are not communicated clearly
, & often see odd things like character smiling when its a dead serious situation. Character 'popping' is semi-frequent, where they would just disappear, or jump to another location or miss a few animation frames. Texture mapping also left 'holes' in the characters where you could see right through them. Also many of the characters look very similar & in later episodes you can clearly see the same models being reused blatantly. If you fail a scene several times, music &/or some audio elements would stop triggering.
It is possible in many situations for you to not even press any button
when prompted & still get through the scene. Other times it took me several attempts despite pressing the button quickly/on queue. Felt very hit & miss, no pun intended.
One of the most annoying things though was the blurriness from the 'oil painting' effect used, that you simply cannot turn off. In a still screenshot it doesn't look too bad generally, but in motion the edges flicker badly; it is really distracting. It varies from scene to scene too, where some sections actually look pretty good, then others where the entire view looks like I am playing without my prescription glasses on. Other times parts of the screen are impacted & others are not, has such a random feel to it. On top of this there is a blurred 'halo' constantly seen around the characters. Nothing graphically is sharp & frankly looks horrible much of the time - it was a bold design choice from Telltale that regrettable doesn't work for me. Anti-aliasing also doesn't seem to work nor does running the game in 4k using DSR seem to help. Overall, this just diminishes the richness & beauty of the locations & the individual objects created in the world. An option should have been provided to disable this!
There is also some good aspects to come out of
. As with previous Telltale episodic adventures, the camera work & direction is great! The actual textures look vivid & detailed, as is the multiple locations which span most of Westeros. The multiple protagonists of the Forrester family are used well, changing often giving the same feeling/flow as the TV Show following several story arcs. There were the occasional scene or one-liner that did give me a good laugh too. The animals & beast animations are fantastic from the horses to the dragons. The voice acting is high quality & actors do their best with the script given, plus it includes the original actors from the TV series which is a bonus for fans.
Despite the few positives I can take from this, & my previous issue explained with the story, dialog, choices & technical issues, by far the worst part of
is the ending. There is no closure, & my cynical self simply sees it at an attempt to sell a sequel. It is atrocious to be honest!
Unlike
seasons, which do come to a natural conclusion (yet leave it open enough to continue) you are basically left wondering what you have wasted the last 12 hours doing! Lots of death, lots of blood, too many loose ends & a lot of guff.
Seems I will need to buy Season 2 to find out what happens...
No thanks Telltale, no thanks... I'll stick with the TV series.

XCOM is a nice combination of the RTS and Civ-style genres. I get to build my resources up as I see fit. Enemy attacks can either help or hinder depending on how I've built my forces and expanded my tech abilities. And I'm not going for global domination. Instead, I'm defending the planet from aggression. It's a refreshing twist.
Research seems to be a main function of the storyline. I've dead-ended myself in the first game to the point that I really only have entry-level units for what's ultimately going to end in a party-wipe mission followed by widespread panic. Having this firmly in mind is making the frustration-induced second go-around much more enjoyable.
Speaking of party wipe... The turn-based action makes me happy for my DnD experiences. It's basically table-top combat and storytelling. Might have something to do with why I enjoy the game so much... The experience is like a combination of being the GM/DM and the party, all at the same time. As the player, the storyline is given to you at your own pace. You also micro-manage characters during combat. And you have NPC interactions, though limited.
That being said, your research choices give you a degree of DM control. The more you understand the game, the more you can orchestrate your own tale. Not to mention you get to build your party the way that a DM would plan out their combat encounters. Again, the more you know, the better you can plan.

Each sector has randomized waypoints and one point that leads to the next sector.  A waypoint can have a store, another has a beacon projecting a distress call, yet another has a rebel scout ship. When you enter battle, you allocate power to various sections of your ship: shields, weapons, oxygen, etc. At the same time, you attack the opposing ship, which is also rerouting power and scattering its crew to its best ability. You also scavenge resources in order to make your jumps, you repair your ship, you replace your crew. It’s basically [insert your preference: Star Trek/Babylon 5/Farscape/Cowboy Bebop/Firefly] in indie game form.

Can't say I am very thrilled with this. I know it is Early Access, but it is in version .9 now and should have most of the bugs worked out. I KNOW IT IS SUPPOSED TO BE HARD. Here is a list of bugs I came across not even mentioning the horrific balancing and game mechanics:
1. Villager instantly died from illness, then when I revived him with faith, he kept insta-dying.
2. I bought "Reinforcements" from the nomads, 8 to be exact, but nothing showed up, no one came. I spent all of my wood on them for nothing.
3. I "declared war" on the Nords. I selected 6 soldiers to go, but nothing happened. No war happened at all.
4. My villagers were going to sleep for like 20 hours a day. They would wake up and I would task them, then walk about 10 steps before turning around to go back to sleep. Happened with multiple villagers.
Those are just what I would consider "bugs" so far. There is a laundry list of unintuitive gameplay controls and mechanics. It took me 2 hours of play to figure out how to get villagers to do stuff. The combat it horrific, random villagers seem to run into battle and throw themselves in the line of fire instead of staying behind the hero or well armed villagers. You can't really control villagers(especially in battle), you cant position them very easily, you have to issues them a tasks(chop wood, hunt, gather berries, "guard here", etc) to make them do anything so combat is very difficult to control. All combat involves is people standing next to each other swinging repeatedly. That is fine, but it is very difficult to get anyone to fight the right enemy, so everyone dies when they didn't need to. Nords are stupid OP. They come demanding resources from you every couple of days, if you can't pay then they attack you. Usually if you can't pay you aren't going to be able to defend against them either. I went to attack the nords and they had an infinite supply of soldiers to keep throwing at me. I killed like 10-15 of them, but they kept coming, even after I destroyed the two houses they were getting all of this population from (wtf). The skeletons come every night. These are just some of the gameplay mechanics that are awful. The balancing is up to interpretation as this is supposed to be difficult. The problem is when the difficulty is amplified by the shoddy controls and UI. Really, I haven't seen many games with this bad of a UI. Half the time I am in a menu and have no idea how to get out of it or get to a different menu. There are losts of clunky problems involving tasking the villagers and getting the right ones to do the work you want. I would be okay recommending this if the devs were able to streamline the UI and controls more and get rid of some of the bugs. I can't recommend it until then though.

To me after having played the campaign, which was really short, this felt like another generic 3 faction RTS, with a bunch of gimmicks to make it want to be interesting, but fail at it. Nevertheless, it was fun while it lasted.
And I'm saying: generic 3 faction RTS, because I will admit I have been spoiled with stuff like Red Alert 2's countries unique units and Generals ZH's Generals unique armies. I was hoping that Grey Goo could bring some of that.
Basically this game was like the old school RTS: Build 1 blob of the same unit and attack move.
Human faction, aren't human at all. The only human driver is the Alpha pilot, the rest is AI, plus it felt too limited in building space and thus ability. but perhaps there's just something I missed.
The Goo, while an interesting concept, fell short in implementation. I've already posted my thoughts on what the Goo was lacking on the forums, but I came to that conclusion after only 2 missions of me playing as the Goo. There is just so much more that could've been done with the Goo.
The Beta was the most fun for me to play as, since I personally like map-control. Be everywhere at once. And with their Hub system, I could really do what I wanted.
As for the multiplayer: When I talked to Ted at Gamescom 2014 I expressed how important it is for and RTS t o have Replay and Observer mode in at launch, especially if the developpers want to work with the modding community and really push the PvP forward.
At launch, there was neither. We had to wait a few months, but by then, I completely lost interest in this game. Otherwise I would've probably be streaming some PvP as observer.
I am not going to recommend this game, because I personally feel it missed so many opportunities,  For me it fell off the radar as quickly as it came onto the radar.

Disclaimer: I played all of Matt's games and was a big fan of Bullet Heaven 1.
Bullet Heaven 2 is an incredibly pretty Bullet Hell game full of content, and it comes packed with features to adjust the difficulty for any player.  But at the end of the day, it is still a Bullet Hell game.  If you don't derive any enjoyment from moving your tiny hitbox (it's one pixel) through intricate patterns of near-death, then this will game will quickly wear thin for you.  If on the other hand you have even a passing interest in this genre or SHMUPs of any kind, you will definitely enjoy this game.
Gameplay:  Many others have listed the numbers, but there are a crap ton of stages with 3 difficulty levels, and each world has two bosses as well as a random survival level.  The game's characters all have minor differences and 3 subweapons each, with no two subweapons being exactly the same.  You will definitely find something that suits your playstyle in this bunch.  There are optional cheats and handicaps to tweak the difficulty both ways, but nothing in the way of permanent upgrades like in BH1.  This game is more "pure" than that; your character does not improve over time, only your skill does.  The high scores are heavily influenced by difficulty, meaning that the only way to compete for top scores on the leaderboards is to git gud at Heavenly difficulty.  This provides a nice incentive for players to get better, while in no way locking out casual players from completing the game on Normal.
Controls:  Responsive but not without caveats.  The Mouse and Keyboard setup is clearly most ideal, as mouse movement gives you a huge advantage in precision.  It also supports controllers including properly analog stick control, which when combined with other features can yield enough precision to even beat Heavenly difficulty without resorting to mouse.  There is a "focus" button to slow down your character while held, but you can invert this option to always move slowly and use the button to gain a sprint mode.  Highly recommended as the setup for controller, but redundant for mouse since you can just move the mouse less.  Unfortunately, you can't remap or rebind almost any of these control options.
Graphics:  Overly cutesy with soft lines and pleasant, but obviously flash, animation.  The character art is something I'm used to and is true to Matt's usual style.  It's a huge step up from BH1 though.  Conversely, the bullets themselves look highly professional and the boss patterns match up to anything else on the market.  The game has performance issues for some people, but playing in windowed mode instead of fullscreen seems to fix most FPS issues.
Soundtrack:  Unbelievable, 11/10.  Halyconic Falcon X (Phyrnna) is the composer and is even a playable character this time around.  You get the entire OST FOR FREE when you buy the game, and can listen to any song in-game in the gallery.  The SFX are mostly decent.  Some are really good, but some of the enemy shot SFX are kinda grating and annoying to me.  Fortunately the options let you turn off these sounds (among other things) if you so desire.
Finally, this game has some sort of mysterious power to be HIGHLY addicting.  I get that way with new games a lot, but everyone I personally know who owns this game, has a really hard time putting it down.

Game of Thrones - A Telltale Game Series is an enjoyable cinematic experience. The game is more interactive cutscene than game proper, albeit given its strong focus on narrative its the better route. The story is tied into the lore of the Game of Thrones HBO series, and incorporates many of the crucial cast, albeit alongside House Forrestor and the Whitehills the main cast of characters actually seems one dimensional. The ironic twist, and I'll avoid spoilers, is that you are basically introduced to house Forrestor....a house which shares much in common in character personalities with the Starks of Winterfell...yet they explore a different means to an end. Returning to technical standpoint, the game is underwelming in this regard and seems like a budget title given the options (although it clearly wasn't).
As many have noted, and as is par for Tell Tale games....the plot is on fixed rails, you are given the illusion of choice, but it is an excellent illusion...people seem to struggle with the concept that true freedom in a heavily narrative driven story isn't feasible  in modern games, unless said game exists in an open world (Skyrim seems to be the poster child for this), yet the narrative suffers as a result. You can't have both, you either have a concise and well thought out plot with choice of illusion or an open world free to explore world where the main plot seems somewhat vague (although that being said, Skyrim is one of the few games to actually have some level of tight narrative, albeit fragmented by progression).
In conclusion I give a full recommendation for this game for both fans of the HBO series and fans of player choice games (ex Dragon Age, Mass Effect etc.), although it definitely does benefit when you have knowledge of the lore of the Game of Thrones universe.

Overall Beta provides you with a great variety of units and structures to give you a high winning % with a low learning curve!
//Humans -
Sci Fi-like units and tech, Drones are the primary make-up of vehicles. Teleportation gives you the ability to teleport units to a certain "visible" location. Also, teleporting structures across the conduits gives flexibility and many strategic options. Units deal decent damage and the Epic is all-around quite powerful and can quickly shut down the opposition when played correctly. HQ is the central point of your expansion in which you can only extend so far with, sadly. Great defensive capabilities but expanding is rather difficult. Overall Humans give you a slightly harder yet satisfying experience. The diversity of the Humans makes them deadly when you learn the curve.
//Goo -
A complex algorithm which evolved into a deadly consolidation of nanites that are extremely adaptive. Unlike the other 3 factions the Goo do not have a set HQ, instead an exceptionally mobile "Mother Goo" in which can split itself (Meiosis) into smaller proteins in which form units. The Mother Goo is also able to countlessly split and form into additional Mother Goo's that give you easy expansion over the entire map. The Goo are easy to play but hard to master. Goo are primarily illusive and are extremely hard to pin down which give them versatility. The unit make-up is interesting and can leave you favoring only a few for mulit role functions. No air units! Damage and health are not quite as good as the Human and Beta faction, Instead utilize quantity of quality. Having only the need for "Spigots" (appear as steam from resource pools) the Goo can indefinately produce units and over time wean down the other factions when they become resource drained. The Goo are dangerous when using "Zerg-like" tactics to overwhelm the enemy. The Epic can be had quickly and is deadly in more than one way, able to heal Mother Goo and consume targets (not for health) as well as pulverize from a distance. Overall The Goo are IMO the most fun yet challenging of the 4 factions which require a decent amount of awareness.
//Shroud "Silent Ones" -
Ancient race that coincidentally resemble the Protoss from Starcraft and are equally as powerful! The Shroud is the newest playable faction and shake up the roster a great deal. Able to evolve, overcharge, mimic etc.. The Shroud can easily overcome an opposition's tactics. Unique characteristics for their units which can give them high damage and armor if upgraded properly. The base units can seem a bit underpowered early game. The Shroud has amplifiers which obviously amplify and can evolve into spikes which give you great adaptivity. Unfortunately you can not go back once evolving amplifiers. While not able to set base anywhere from the start like the Beta, The Shroud can however expand when placing structures and exctractors down to provide a larger radius in which to place structures. The Shroud has the most devastating air units IMO and can easily change the tides of a battle especially against the Goo. The Epic is by far the strongest of the 4 factions and as a result needs to be evolved to stage 3 which can take a great deal of time after building. Overall The Shroud are not easy to learn but once understood IMO are the strongest of the 4. (My favorite race)

Stripped-down, real-time strategy that becomes more difficult with each FTL jump. You hop from location to location outrunning rebels and attempting to reach a point multiple sectors away. Each sector has randomized waypoints and one point that leads to the next sector.  A waypoint can have a store, another has a beacon projecting a distress call, yet another has a rebel scout ship. When you enter battle, you allocate power to various sections of your ship: shields, weapons, oxygen, etc. At the same time, you attack the opposing ship, which is also rerouting power and scattering its crew to its best ability. You also scavenge resources in order to make your jumps, you repair your ship, you replace your crew. It’s basically [insert your preference: Star Trek/Babylon 5/Farscape/Cowboy Bebop/Firefly] in indie game form.

Riddled with problems, not the best RTS around. Other reviews have already covered the main ones - similar factions, lack of unit abilities, odd and univesting story, balance issues here and there. With the price drop, however and with the deal you get out of the Definitive Edition, it is actually quite worth it. It is far from bad, but it was nowhere near the price asked - the drop was already enough to justify a recommendation.
However, another bit of good news to consider is the Shroud, the fourth faction. In short, they are an example of Petroglyph finally realizing the issues their game has. Having a fourth faction already fixes a significant amount of issues with the game, having two rather similar non-Goo factions for one. However, they are also clearly different without being... weird like the Goo. They are, gasp, a decent RTS faction, which it seemed Petroglyph had forgotten how to make.
That you get them with the Definitive Edition is already good, but another point in Petro's favor is that previous owner get it for free. For a game that underperformed as this one did, it's reassuring to see bold decisions such as this massive price drop and non-half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥DLC. Sure, it's because they're desperate, but they didn't give up, and they went on to make it far more consumer-friendly.
As for the other elements of the DE - Emergence is not an improvement on the shrug-inducing original campaign, actually, it's worse. The OST is now fully worth it (Frank Klepacki, if not at his most metal)  because they fixed it because they somehow broke the OST for close to a year. The Shroud is the best thing to happen with the game so far, it really elevated my own opinion on the game. You do as you will, but the new price makes it worth it for any RTS enthusiast.
