First of all, I played the hell out of the first Bullet Heaven (which, sadly, never made it to Steam), so, needless to say, I've been waiting for BH2 with bated breath. And it certainly delivered.
If I were to describe the game with one word, it would be
. It took the very best features of the original and made them even better. More characters, more weapons, more BADA** BOSSES, longer levels
But let's look at things in a bit more detail.
We have 8 playable characters, each with a different play style and a bunch of weapons and costumes (those provide some minor bonuses) to boot. My personal favourites are Matt, Phyrnna and NoLegs (that kitty is OP as hell, btw). Making use of their strengths and avoiding their weaknesses is ESSENTIAL for surviving on difficulties other then Normal (though the final set of levels  may argue with that - those are quite nightmarish even on Normal).
Speaking of difficulty, there is a lot of ways for the player to customize it. Enabling certain cheats and handicaps gives a chance to those of us who are not well-versed in bullet-hells AND can satisfy even the toughest of hardcore players. My personal favourite handicap is pacifist mode. It leaves the player with no ways to damage enemies, forcing him/her to survive through waves by waiting for them to end. Also that makes some levels hard as b***s. Even on Normal. Luckily, only one pixel of the character can take damage making things fair.
Next, the BOSSES. Yes, all caps, they deserve it. The patterns of bullet-hells they tend to generate can and will leave you speechless. They look amazing and are deadly enough to push you to the very extent of your abilities. Keep in mind, btw, some of their shots bounce, so if you are like me and prefer to keep your distance, you can get some surprise
attacks from behind. My personal favourite is the Wicked Weaver. Seriously, look at that thing and try telling me you don't want this adorable monstrosity as a pet.
Also the final BOSS.
And last, but not the least, the soundtrack. Phyrnna (the composer) outdid herself. Every tune fits the level
, especially boss themes. Those will make your blood boil, trust me. Also catchy as hell. This is where I struggle to name a personal favourite as all the tracks are worthy of the title.
To summarize: awesome action, incredible music, smooth controls, cute visuals and customizable difficulty. If you played BH1 than this is everything you ever dreamed of. If not - it's easy enough to get into so hop on. Buy it, I can guarantee that you won't regret a single penny.
P.S. And now, if you'll excuse me, I'm off to try and finally do that pacifist marathon. I'm so dead.

The devs seem to find it perfectly acceptable that players run second accounts that they keep at low levels by giving their points to other players. These low ranked accounts then end up getting matched against players that are playing at their true ranking. Since the scoring is handicapped, this leads to the honest players not gaining anything much when they win, but they will end up losing more times than enough and will have large amounts of points taken away.
On paper, they will be losing to a noob and so get penalised, but in reality they are losing to players with skills that place him in the top 10.
So, even at the bottomm rungs of the ladder, expect to find excellent players who will take great delight in making sure you end up frustrated and hating this game.
Since the game is predominently multiplayer (the bots are fun for a while), what you are paying for is to be meat in the grinder.
Avoid.

I think this has to be the most overhyped game I've played in a long time. People are so nostalgic for old ARPGs, when a new one comes along from a fresh development team, they tend to jump on the hype train. Add to that people following the game and becomming committed from a very early stage and I guess thats where the massive hype has come from.
Diablo II was one of my first online gaming experiences. I picked it up on release and played long before Lord of Destruction came along and pushed it slightly mainstream. I followed Path of Exile from paid beta and I absolutely love a good ARPG. Grim Dawn falls slightly short, and I'd call it 'quite good'. The thing with this genre is that it's supposed to be mightily addictive. You're supposed to sit at school or work thinking about this game and what you're gonna do next, what boss you're gonna fight when you get home; what character you're gonna try next; what you're gonna do with that unique item you found. You're gonna spend hours upon hours with a game in this genre so it has to be addictive. Unfortunately, I just don't feel that addiction with Grim Dawn.
I thought at first maybe I was the problem and that I was a different person since playing Diablo 2, but then I thought to PoE. PoE captured that feeling for me and still does to an extent. It's exciting, and when I'm playing it, I'm thinking about it when I'm offline. GD doesn't do that for me.
Is it because it's offline? Maybe. There's a psychological effect for me that I'm not competing with anyone and that nothing I find really matters because it's not "WORTH SOJS" (or Chaos Orbs). But I think it goes deeper than that still. The skills (that I've tried so far) seem utterly dull. Basic ranged attack goes pop pop pop, but pick up this skill and it goes pop pop pop but now it's red. I've not experienced any exciting skills like Diablo 2's whirlwind, meteor, hydra, etc and the tons of brilliant skills in PoE. The unique items seem pretty cool but again, unless it's the rare case where it's something useful to my character right now, it's difficult to care about it when it drops. The enemies also seem rather plain with no real buildup to boss fights. No Diablo, Mephisto or even Andariel, just some punk bandit captain. At this point, I have no idea who the end of game boss or even the end of act boss is going to be, just that I'll kill them and they'll drop stuff.
For me this wasn't a waste of money. I picked it up for £11 in the sales and if you're thinking about doing the same, I'd probably recommend it. However, I'll be lucky if I finish the game on normal difficulty, never mind the second or third time on higher difficulties, as is the bread and butter of this genre. I just don't feel that attached to the game or my characters and for that reason I overall do not recommend this game.

If you're looking for an intriuging and challenging audio-synchronized experience, you won't find it here. Beat Hazard is instead an isometric space/arena shooter that paces everything, from the intensity of your fire to the pacing of enemies to the seizure-inducing screen effects, to the intensity of your music.
It's a pleasant game for when you want to zone out and enjoy sound and color. There's not a lot there, but it's a pleasant enough game. You're more likely to die in many cases from having trouble determining which bright flashing thing is going to kill you than from legitimate in-game challenges.
"Shadow Missions" and perk unlocking add a mild sense of progression to the game, but otherwise no storyline or plot exists. I enjoy the game as a sensory experience, rather than an immersive otherworldly indulgence or hyper-challenging gameplay quest.

Summary:
This was a frustrating and flawed game, but utterly engrossing. You'll doubtless see plenty of harsh criticism of this game, and a lot of that is legitimate, but you'll also be hard pressed to find any game that will emotionally engage you like this one, especially if you are as much a fan of this setting as I am. I absolutely recommend any fan of Telltale or of A Song of Ice and Fire to play this. The North remembers.
Negatives:
Doesn't deviate much from the Telltale formula - Much has been made of the fact that Telltale has been making the same types of games with the same engine for a while now, and Game of Thrones isn't much of an exception. If you're bored of these types of games, you might want to look elsewhere.
Buggy / Clunky - Moreso than other Telltale games I've played, this one seems to have lots of weird little graphical errors and bugs and occasional crashes.
Reactivity - Sometimes it feels like your decisions in the game have an impact, but other times it feels like there's a sort of canonical outcome that happens no matter what which doesn't really jive with the decision you made. It can be a bit jarring. Also, if you do a bit of research, you may find that in the grand scheme of things the story ends a certain way regardless of your choices. Personally I don't mind a linear story because it gives a skilled writer (and make no mistake, Telltale's writers are very skilled) more power to tell a great story effectively. If you're not like me, you might be a bit disappointed.
Story - I found one of the main story threads to be fairly boring, especially after the beginning. I felt similarly about some of the characters in the books though. It's hard to avoid this when you have several different characters that have very distinct styles of story unfolding around them.
Visuals - They were going for a very distinctive art style, and I'm not sure their engine was perfectly suited to the task. Some of the characters looked really weird at certain times, and some of the scenes looked a bit off.
Body count - One very good criticism of the Game of Thrones tv series is that it relies too much on shock value. A similar criticism could be made of this game. When GRRM kills a character, I don't get the sense that he's doing it just to shock me, but rather to create interesting situations, put other characters to the test, or to make good on previous foreshadowing, etc. This game kills a *lot* of important characters, and it gets a bit tiresome. They needed to give you a little bit more to be happy about in the end. The catharsis wasn't *quite* there.
Positives:
Emotional impact - Despite what I just said about body count, some of those scenes were legitimately gut wrenching. I was furious at the things that were being done to the characters I'd grown attached to. I'd built up plans for how I was going to play things, what kind of person I wanted certain characters to be, and then had to watch those dreams being crushed. It felt so good to get a chance to cut through some bad guys in the end. I was literally shouting the House Forrester words.
Visuals - Despite the problems I mentioned before, some of the scenes are almost breathtakingly beautiful. They really look like moving paintings. I don't know what the issue is that makes the visuals so inconcistent, but you can see what they were going for, and it was almost a great triumph.
Story - Telltale writers really are some of the best in the business, and they seem to have a very good handle on the setting and the kinds of stories the setting is suited to. A Song of Ice and Fire is very dear to my heart, and I'm glad that it is in such capable hands. In a world where Peter Jackson is allowed to♥♥♥♥♥♥on one of the most beloved stories in the English language with his CGI pseudo-Hobbit garbage, it's nice to see that it isn't impossible for a great author to have the spirit of his work respected. (Okay, I'm a little bitter about The Hobbit movies, you'll have to forgive me.)
Voice Acting - Several members of the cast of the show voice their characters for the game and do a commendable job. The voice actors cast for the new characters were universally quite good, I thought. Sometimes the way they deliver a line isn't quite how you imagined it when you make your choice, but that can't really be helped.
Overall: 8/10
I'd love to rate it higher, but there are legitimate problems with the game that shouldn't be ignored. I've heard that Telltale are making another season (the story is very much set up for one), and I will certainly be playing it. I hope Telltale can step up their game and bring this series to the next level.

There are elements of Telltale's Game of Thrones that are good, but overall it's kind of a convoluted mess. The main problem is that it's got the worst narrative elements of the show--having to balance multiple POV characters in varying locales, making it incredibly difficult to feel any particular emotional connection to one character or another. This makes some of the choices you're presented with feel rather empty, and it prevents the game from even approaching the emotional intensity of The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us.
With regard to choices, a lot of folks seem to be complaining that their choices don't "matter"; that is, they don't change the overall plot. This doesn't really bother me, because I don't expect them to. This is an adventure game afterall. What I do expect is that the choices are difficult and emotionally affecting. As noted above, the narrative structure of the game can work against the choices feeling profound, but there are a number of decisions through the series' six episodes that do really stick with you.
While the game does a pretty good job of fully fleshing its POV characters, the villains are one-dimensional and cartoonish, and the guest appearances from series regulars largely feel forced. The game has interesting implications for the GOT?/ASOIAF universe due to some of the events of the last episode, but of course there's always the question of whether the story will even be considered canon. (That said, it does seem to be canon in the universe of the TV show.) Ultimately, I am interested in seeing if the North Grove shows up at any point in either the books or the show.
It's hard to say whether I recommend this game or not. I feel like it was an interesting experiment on Telltale's part, but it's one that's largely unsuccessful. Hopefully they will learn from their missteps here and the inevitable sequel will not be such a mess. Still, I did enjoy playing it, even as I found the endless POV changes a bit gruelling. I could see fans of the show going either way on it--it expands the show's universe in a potentially important way, but it can be a bit of a slog to play. Telltale diehards will likely be disappointed, but will get a lot out of seeing what works and what doesn't. In the end, it's a pretty big disappointment after the highs of The Walking Dead seasons 1 and 2 and The Wolf Among Us. I wouldn't recommend buying it for full price, but if you catch it in a sale, it's worth your time.

As a strategy game Life is Hard already offers a decent complexity of choice -- updgrade the settlement, craft items, explore, gather resources, and defend from skeletons by night and norse raiders by day. All activities are limited by availability of free settlers to carry out orders. From time to time help your settlers with spells at the cost of faith points.
All this sounds nice and undoubtedly will make for an engagind and difficult strategy game, however at the moment it's mired by a very poor user interface -- in terms of form, accessibility, as well as the amount of information available. Other reviewers mention this too, and some dismiss this criticism arguing that players can learn and adapt to the interface with time. True, but we should not have to.
Most of the orders are issued by clicking on an object -- building, resource, etc -- and the nearest free settler will take care of it. Some orders can be set to repeated -- chopping trees, minig, gathering rocks -- by clicking again on the resource. This can be a bit finnicky as sometimes the click areas don't seem to overlap with the object in question, or clicks don't register. Elsewhere the clickable buttons lack tooltips to clarify what action ca be performed. There are menus to see status of each settler and issue resource-gathering orders quickly, however these don't work properly -- cannot click on settler to jump to them, and clicking the issue order button doesn't always work.
Players also have a Hero unit to direct, a stronger attacking unit with skills. Controlling the hero is a pain though. The hero is utterly lazy -- monsters can be destroying building and killing settlers next to him yet he won't do anything unless ordered (or attacked directly). There is a button to select the hero but it scrolls the camera to him as well. The world is a very, very, very long horizontal map and TONS of scrolling is required to navigate it. There is a 'minimap' which can be used to quickly scroll over vast distances but it less helpful when navigating medium distances (like from one end of your settlement to the other). This gets in the way if your Hero is chilling while skeletons attach from the other end of the settlement as you have to scroll for several long seconds while your settlers are being killed. There should be an option to order the hero to a particular location without moving the camera. Oh, and if the hero dies there is no indication of this. Yeah. Clicking on the 'center on hero' button does nothing.

Stripped-down, real-time strategy that becomes more difficult with each FTL jump. You hop from location to location outrunning rebels and attempting to reach a point multiple sectors away. Each sector has randomized waypoints and one point that leads to the next sector.  A waypoint can have a store, another has a beacon projecting a distress call, yet another has a rebel scout ship. When you enter battle, you allocate power to various sections of your ship: shields, weapons, oxygen, etc. At the same time, you attack the opposing ship, which is also rerouting power and scattering its crew to its best ability. You also scavenge resources in order to make your jumps, you repair your ship, you replace your crew. It’s basically [insert your preference: Star Trek/Babylon 5/Farscape/Cowboy Bebop/Firefly] in indie game form.

Playing off the genre that the game is inspired from, Bullet Heaven 2 has a few tricks up its sleeve that makes it stand out from the rest of its competition. It's art style has a cute yet striking appearance that does the job, despite the fact that it can get in the way of combat at times. But you are here for the shoot em up gameplay, which focuses on action and dodging with the amount of bullets on the screen. Great amount of choice for score chasers out there in getting the most out of each run, while still providing comfort for those who need a bit of help.
What's interesting here is that Bullet Heaven 2's wave based gameplay feels accessible for newer players in the genre, and yet its weapon charge system will have those veterans of the genre take notice with it's slight differences in gameplay.  It's what you want if you're looking for another game in the genre to refresh your pallet: something twisted a bit so that it stands out, but keeping its core components the same to still make it feel like the genre in question in the end. Definitely worth the time, especially if you're looking for game to chase high scores in.
The game is available on Kongerate without the expansions, but the game is worth your time in any form, and it's a good experience regardless of the expansion or not. I can recommend to support the developer in question, and those who don't want to spend the money can go play it on kongerate.

As with most games I get, I bought this on a complete whim. High reviews, and the low price drew me in, but it was the gameplay that kept me going.
Life Is Hard is yet another survival simulator, but one of a totally different breed. You start off with four villagers, each of which are capable of gathering every resource you need, and a chosen god, which allows for various features during the game. For instance, one god allows you to gather extra faith, which allows you to heal your villagers, deal damage to enemies, and plant trees necessary for wood.
It operates much like an RTS (Real Time Strategy) game, similar to Starcraft and Age of Empires in terms of 'build trees' and various buildings that produce various resources. One building allows you to make bread, which provides food, another is an armory to build weapons and armor, etc. Due to this feature, the game is a constant balance of resources.
I'd say the main selling point of the game is that it's so goddamn charming. You can tell that a lot of work went into it, and the passion behind it is palpable. I've played my fair share of survival sims, but it's rare that I replay them at all. With Life Is Hard, I finally found a nice sit-down survival sim that allows for quick one-off runs while still maintaining it's charm and overall fun.
VERY high replay value, although initially, it's a lot to adjust to. In time, when you get more used to the game, different gods allow for all sorts of different builds. You could be a warring tribe, a peaceful tribe, farmers, merchants, etc. With all of this quality and attention to detail, as well as the high replay value, this is shaping up to be a beautiful little game.
At the moment, the game is marketed at $7.99. While I think this is absolutely worth the price, I might wait for the sale if you're unsure. Overall, if you enjoy survival simulators, and want to support indie developers, this is a great little game.

After a year and a free expansion I think I can safely say this was worth the purchase. Here is the rundown.
Pros:
- Not two, not three, but FOUR asymmetrical factions! Each with their own base building, units and epic unit.
- A very traditional RTS with a healthy balance between micro and macro. You will need strategy and tactics to be the best.
- Amazing detail to individual units, both in animation and sound design.
- A competent single player campaign with pretty CGI cutscenes.
- An AI that, after lots of tweaking, is fun in Skirmish with lots of dynamic responses.
- Astounding soundtrack by Frank Klepacki with an in-game jukebox! (The OST DLC now includes all songs as well)
- THEY JUST RELEASED A FREE EXPANSION-UPDATE! The publisher Greybox have been nothing but amazing with supporting the customers with patches and content.
Cons:
- A somewhat unoptimised engine can tax systems on ultra settings.
- Aforementioned engine means that 4 players is the max limit. Personally I like a minimum of 6 players in my RTS games.
- Not many people playing anymore so don't expect an active multiplayer community. Grab a friend or three for PVE and PVP.
- Balance for PVP is an issue. Though they are still patching.
If you like Command & Conquer, Starcraft, and even lesser known games like Perimeter then you'll have fun with Grey Goo!

This is possibly the best flash game I've ever seen. The game has a huge number of levels (70 total) and even after every level is completed, all the medals and leaderboards are enough to give you a push to do even better. The patterns are gorgeous to look at, and there are a good number of patterns that offer decent challenges. Most patterns feel completely unique, and learning how to beat them all (usually) doesn't end up causing a great deal of frustration, and remains generally fun. There are 19 huge bosses to fight, 40 regular stages to conquer and 11 survival stages to test your abilities with. Beating hard levels is most definitely satisfying, and it's always good to go back and challenge levels time and time again for high scores. All of that added together makes for some of the best times I've had with a bullet hell game, or just games in general.
EDIT: Having now beaten the game and having obtained every achievment in the game, I think I should do a small update to this review. While the game is definitely a lot of fun, it's worth noting that some of the later achievments are only worth attempting if you have a lot of experience, or a lot of patience.  It took me a good 24 hours of gameplay to unlock and beat every level, and another 11 hours to unlock the rest of the achievments I had left. Putting everything this game offers into consideration, I'd definitely say it's worth picking up. The game does sometimes become frustrating, but it feels rewarding to beat a tough level. I genuinely had a ton of fun with this from start to finish.

I've been playing for over 10 hours now and would definitely recommend this game. I've found that sound is very important in the game because sometimes my vision is blocked by grass/bushes/etc, even with hunter vision. I've had a bear get me twice now because I didn't see or hear it. And outrunning them is a joke. They'll catch up and rip you apart unless you kill them.
Fire is your friend. Lots of predators are afraid of the fire and will keep a safe distance until they see an opportunity. Your tamed animal is another deterrent for some predators.
I like how they really tried to be realistic with the wolves and how they hunt. They're always in packs and they use tactics to try and attack you. I've had it where one has rushed me so that my focus is on that one then 2 others flank me while the first runs to a safe distance. It's also kind of sad that if they run, they'll come back and howl for their fallen wolves. Also, their eyes reflect the light at night which is just awesome.
There's definitely some things that they need to work on with the tamed beasts. Sometimes my beast will be stuck somewhere while I'm getting my butt kicked by enemies. Other times, my beast won't disengage from enemies so it ends up dying because it won't come back for me to heal it. It's a bit annoying and frustrating, especially when you're trying to take a bonfire...but it's not a deal breaker.
Yes, it's annoying that they speak a different language and you have to read the subtitles...but you get used to it after a while.
The graphics aren't bad...but they're also not the best. I'm also running it on "high". I could probably run it higher than that, but it doesn't really matter to me. Again, not a deal breaker.
There's plenty to do in the game to keep you occupied. Right now I'm just capturing various bonfires and hunting/gathering so I can upgrade my camp.

At heart, it is a city-building game with a sense of humour.  You have to plan around the geography and resources of your island (as well as your leader's special quirks), raise money and resources to build with, while trying to keep your population happy and growing.  All while receiving hilarious news reports, side goals and commentary from the game.  The campaigns are easy to get into and have an enjoyable, light story line.  It's easy to pick up for a couple of hours and then stop - and just as easy to spend an entire day building up your island, and the night dreaming about that next move...
If you've ever wanted to build an island paradise...or a tropical prison...this is the game for you.

I'm not the biggest fan of Bullet Hell or Shoot 'em Ups in general, but I'm a big fan of the developer and was willing to give this a shot; and it really surprised me.
This is an incredibly accesible Bullet Hell game with a wide range of difficulty, if you or someone you know wants to get into the genre this is a great place to start. The game is also a very good Flash port with multiple control schemes (Including controller support) and a wide range of option, including the ability to use high contrast bullets, hide things like score numbers, or cap the frame rate lower for lower end computers.
The game is responsive and has a surprising amount of depth focused around the scoreboard; handicaps, bonuses, and a variety of mechanics can be used to alter your score to get higher and higher on the very well intergrated scoreboard (something most steam games fail miserably at).
The art style may not be for everyone, but the bullet patterns are very aesthetic. The music on the other hand is, like Matt's other games, very good with a large variety to match different areas and bosses. The sound design is also nice and work well to punctuate actions like slain enemies and grazed bullets allowing you to focus elsewere.
Where the game really shines is the sheer amount of content: 3 Difficulties, 8 Characters (Each with multiple costumes and sub-weapons that are all unique to each character), over 70 stages with dozens of bosses. If you were to start on Normal and play through every stage on each difficulty you'd see well over 300 unique waves.
Oh, and it's got 4-Player local co-op too, which is really neat.
I suggest this to any Bullet Hell fan looking for something to play and especially anyone looking to get into them.
Now get to work on EBF5, Matt.

Genre: ARPG, Loot
#Worth/NotWorth: #SortofWorth
BSERC - (Borderline Sardonic and Extremely Reductive Comparison): Every ARPG ever. Diablo/Victor Vran/Torchlight/Van Helsing and the like but namely Titan Quest
Exposition, Concurrence and Summation
Now, Grim Dawn is an APRG. Should you not be familiar with this genre tag it basically equates to a dungeon crawler wherein you control one character, kill monsters then apply skill points into a specific tech tree or build of a certain style of play. All the while trying to land some, and please excuse my verbiage, “sick drops and hawt loot” in order to kill stronger enemies faster; rinse and repeat.
Grim Dawn is from Crate Entertainment which is comprised of old members of the now defunct Iron Lore Entertainment who are responsible for Titan Quest. The remnants of that system are still quite apparent.
To be upfront, I'm slightly dismissive of this game because the way I see it. It's a very good “one of those”. And doesn't really do a ton to stick out above the rest.
Here are some complaints in comparison
Often, the argument I hear against what I'd considered to be the most recent and prominent ARPG, Diablo III: Reapers of Souls is that it takes away proper character building. Allowing the changing of abilities and runes at will with no cost. Well, I'd argue that Grim Dawn does the very same; re-specing is basically of no cost (should you not posses the iron bits or aether crystals, it's nothing a few moments of grinding can't fix) and can be done at any time back at devils crossing which you can return to at no cost and at will stay from Chthonic Rifts which are rare.
An additional thing about classes is that in Grim Dawn the classes are chosen after starting a few levels into a new playthrough. Each class uses a spirit gauge regardless of what you decide to level into; Dual class or not. As an example, in Diablo 3 the Demon Hunter alone has 2 gauges to pull from and must be managed throughout play and style of build for the abilities chosen to be effective. This isn't a real complaint, it just is sort of antithetical to this idea of proper classes being something that you need to build and somehow the ability to change that build quickly negates it's enjoyability. Another thing is that is takes a very long time to even remotely level deeply into one class.
I also had an issue and this is another small complaint but I feel it should be said, there is very little direction for objectives to be completed. By the end of the game I had so many side quests I was unable to locate and had leveled past that they were literally spilling off screen. A little direction would have gone a long way.
But I digress, Grim Dawn is again a very good “one of those” so if ARPG's/Dungeon Crawlers aren't your thing this will not change your mind. However the game does have full gamepad support. So during your tenure of monster slaying you can get real lazy bones about it. Additionally, through the weapon sets and control schemes you can essentially have four hotbars at your disposal.
The art style is very nice looking, the environments diverse. There is some faction play which is relatively interesting but doesn't hold a ton of interest in the long haul unless you become deeply involved with the narrative. It seemed very “not Diablo” to me. I wish there were more cut-scenes to be honest. They adopted this sort of Darkest Dungeon look, a sort of Gothic cartoon that I'd have loved to see more of.
THE GIST
Grim Dawn is a good game, I just don't think it's as inspired as it has been made out to be by Diablo 3 detractors. If you are looking for a Torchlight replacement that's a bit more “adult” and dark. This is it.

I got a review code for this game and had no idea what to expect. I saw it was a shmup which was a plus, a Bullet Hell which was another plus, then I saw it was ported over from Kongregate and I thought like many formerly Flash games, that it'd be a lousy port of a weak game. I couldn't have been more wrong.
I'm terrible at shmups and worse at Bullet Hell games but I love them anyway. I love the thrill of the score chase, the art of the bullet patterns and figuring out the best path through brutal levels. This game has all of that plus an absolutely insane amount of depth, both to the scoring system and to the amount of customisation that's available for your characters and weapons. There are three difficulty levels which can make things accessible to new players but the level of brutally hard you expect from this kind of game. Most arcade shmups are only a handful of levels but this one has over fifty which is crazy, even if they are each rather short. You'll quickly reach a point where things get very tough, even on the lowest difficulty setting so repeated play is encouraged and indeed necessary.
Succeed or fail, you'll earn different amounts of in-game currency which you can use to buy new characters, new weapons and costumes for them which all have benefits and even cheats and handicaps which impact your score when used. This has the major advantage of you still being able to qualify for the leaderboards if you use them. The leaderboard integration is very slick and while it would have been nice to see each difficulty level get its own roster, each level does have its own and you can sort by a variety of means. You're also shown your current position before starting a level and right after you complete it, assuming you're online.
Bullet Heaven 2 has a very cutesy/twee aesthetic which really doesn't do much for me but in Bullet Hell games, you don't really have a lot of time to pay attention to the art. If you are, you're kinda' doing it wrong.
This game is an incredible value for shmup fans and if you are one, you should pick it up without hesitation. It astounds me that this was made by only one person. There are many well regarded shmups with a fraction of the content this has and when I see games like Darius Burst CS coming out for an insane $40+, this is a no brainer. I didn't expect this game to be good and it could very well be in my top 10 this year. Seriously, get it, it's that good.

Disclaimer: I have only ever played Beat Hazard Ultra, since I got this in a bundle. I will only be speaking about Ultra and the Shadow Operations Unit DLC. It’s possible most of this review will only be relevant to Beat Hazard Ultra.
Also, if you have a history of epilepsy/seizures or anything related, pass on this game. Seriously.
Beat Hazard is an extremely visually intensive shoot em’ up music game. You pick a mode, pick a song, either your own or from the supplied ones in the game, and then you play it. Enemy ships spawn, with some accordance to the intensity of the song. You shoot them with your incredibly flashy weapons. If listening to your music and shooting enemy spaceships while lights flash a ton sounds appealing to you, then great. This might be your game. There’s also controller support! (I recommend controller if you can. It’s very nice.)
There are a pretty decent amount of options when you play a song. You have three initial difficulties, Easy, Normal, Hardcore, and you can unlock Insane and Suicidal later on. Visual Intensity can be set to 50%, 75%, 100%, 150%, and 200%. (These do affect score, but honestly 200% is very difficult to look at, with only a 20% bonus.) Finally, there are perks. And there are a lot of perks. Score boosting perks, item perks, and sub weapon perks.
The four game modes are…
Standard: Playing through one song
Survival: Playing for a long as you can while the game cycles through songs
Boss Rush: Fighting bosses on a timer before more spawn, as long as you can, while songs cycle
Chill Out: All perks unlocked, infinite sub weapons, infinite lives, no score, no currency earning, casual playing
The Shadow Operations Unit DLC is an alright buy. You gain access to more ships, including Steam Workshop ones, and you can make your own as well. Each ship plays differently, and it’s a nice change of pace. However, I will say the Shadow Missions are incredibly… irksome. Death penalties can be difficult to overcome depending on the mission, and some missions are just difficult to begin with. You can absolutely opt out of the missions, since they’re just there for achievements.
A few people call it a rhythm game, I strongly disagree. In my opinion, rhythm games are defined by a strong correlation of the song with the gameplay. For example, in Crypt of the Necrodancer, your movement is meant to be linked with the beat of the song. Beat Hazard isn’t really like that. The closest you’ll get is if the song intensity dips down into nothing, and then comes back up. It’s not really related to the beat.
Do I recommend this game? Yes.

+ The new Commander System, makes the game more fleshed out; giving the player the complete choice of what he/she wants as the commander of the his/her army.
+ Worskshop support, gives this game even more fun, with new maps and some old (From CoH 1) and Tuners which are similiar to mods.
+ The ability for troops to vault over cover.
+ + Prosttruppen... Prosttruppen everywhere...
Cons:
- Lag in Multiplayer is horrid in some cases, unless you've got the Computer of All Computers.
- Patches by SEGA have ruined CoH 1's Mutiplayer in regards of CoH 2; which is wrong for any company to do.
- The Campaign's Narrative is annoying in the sense that it constantly bashes the Soviets rather than seeing them as Heroes; I know they want to make the whole "War is Bad" and "Dictators are bad" but it gets annoying fast.
- Some of the Commanders in the new Commander system, have the exact same abilities as others and some worthless ones, while most of the Premium Commanders are Fresh and Awesome to have.
- The Campaign feels like a large stretched out tutorial, rather than the player doing their own thing plus some side objectives, he/she is constantly doing what the magic Bad Russian accented voice in the sky tells them to do.
- The Unit's skins in game are sometimes amazingly inaccurate often sometimes wearing uniforms that didn't even exsist or what not used by that army (Looking at you Whermacht Grenadiers).
Do I recommend this game? Yes, but lightly so; simply because this game still has the Company of Heroes gameplay we all know and love, and that the developers try their best to make the game like it's predecessor. However with glaring bad side effects like Lag and the slander of the first installment of CoH I do this recommendation lightly.

If you look for an easy-to-learn but difficult-to-master Turn Based Strategy game, go no further.
Sid Meier's Civilization V includes the most flexible and quick mechanics to control your Civilization I have ever seen in a game of each genre. The battle mechanics are very simple, but cannot be that easily Min-Maxed, something that leaves space for a lot of tactical choices and, thus, a lot of outplays. The Science-Culture-Tourism-Religion and Espionage Systems are all quite simplified, however, their variety means that you'll have to choose which you will specialize in your every go, making the game extremely re-playable. Finally, the Map generation and the Exploration part are for me the smoothest and most fun aspect of the game, especially when it comes to selecting the place to settle your City. Trying to find the Mountain-Coast-River Combo to settle your City is an enjoyable "frustration".
Overall, if you seek for a cheap but epic game to spend your hours solo, or with friends, grab this one. Unless the price of Civ VI comes down, which it will, but not soon enough to SURVIVE WITHOUT PLAYING CIV :P

I'm going to start this off with a little background on my relationship with JRPGs.  Feel free to skip ahead if you want.
I didn't really like JRPGs growing up.  I first tried Dragon Warrior as a kid, and it was just confusing and boring compared to games like Zelda.  JRPGs seemed to require a certain amount of attention and commitment that I, with my childhood ADHD, simply did not possess.  All through my childhood and teenage years, friends would speak highly of Final Fantasies and Xeno-whatevers and Grandias and Something of Manas.  I would give them a shot once in a while, but nothing ever stuck.  My response was to shrug and simply remark that JRPGs were not my thing.
I did like RPGs though.  I liked the depth and the story and the characters they offered.  I played Planescape Torment and Baldur's Gate a lot.  I would gush endlessly about Morrowind.  Still, something about Japanese made games in the genre was an instant turn off for me.
One day, a friend of mine informed me that Dragon Quest VIII was awesome, which I dismissed, and that it came with a demo of Final Fantasy XII.  I dismissed this as well, but he said "No, dude.  This is different.  I think you'll dig it."
I humored him, and sat down for a playthrough of the demo, and you know what?..
He was right.
This game was fantastic.  The art style, the music, the gameplay, everything hooked me.  There were no random encounters to annoy me.  In a way the game reminded me of the western made PC RPGs I enjoyed, but there was a certain fantasic, stylized quality to it that intrigued me.  This quality is what puts the J in JRPG.  Final Fantasy XII had it's hooks in me, and with it a whole world of Japanese STUFF opened up.
I re-approached older JRPGs with new eyes that I can only assume to the outside observer would appear as oversized and stylized with way too many glossy highlights.  Turns out Dragon Quest VIII IS awesome.  Chrono Trigger is a masterpiece.  And something about the slower pace of a turn based battle system invites a certain amount of strategy and ponderous gameplay.
But you know what?  ADHD never really goes away.  It's just that as an adult, you learn to cope with it better, and certain elements of it become muted.  I don't have a problem with holding still for extended periods of time anymore, for example, but sitting and watching an ENTIRE MOVIE that I'm not ABSOLUTELY ENTHRALLED by is still pretty difficult.  It's for this reason that while I enjoy really big RPGs, I had never actually finished one.  Until Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1.
If you were looking for where I actually talk about this game, this is where you can start reading.
Hyperdimension Neptunia re;Birth1 is not a particularly deep game.  The combat is grindy and repetitive.  The dungeons all seem copy-pasted from each other, and none of them are very large.  Enemies are varied up until a point, then they're just more powerful color edits.  Exploration involves just checking off every icon on the map.  Equipment seems more focused on costuming and looks rather than actually changing the strategy in the game, with the skimpiest outfits being the most expensive, naturally.  The story progresses via Visual Novel style sequences that are minimally animated and full of memes and they don't always make a lot of sense.  My JRPG hating past self would NOT have liked this game.  If you are not a fan of this kind of Japanese STUFF, you will not like this game.  I would say it's a niche title.
That being said, I really, really liked this game.
The story is all over the place, and Neptune herself has the attention span of a squirrel, so naturally I automatically felt right at home.  I found myself actually caring about the characters and what happened next.  It helped that I am already fully indoctrinated into the world of very Japanese STUFF, so if you're not, your mileage may vary.
In playing this game, I found that I would pick out between one to three current goals, then slowly grind my way, zen like, toward them.  These goals might be affording a new weapon, leveling up a certain amount, completing a certain quest or six.  It was never complicated.  The path to these goals was always clear.  Only a few times did I need to look up which enemies give the best chance to drop some rare item.
Playing this game became like a ritual to me.  I would sit down, slip into my weeaboo trance, then emerge because I have to adult and get enough sleep to be able to function at work tomorrow.  I did this a lot, until one day I was deep in my big-glossy eyed trance when I noticed that the credits were rolling.
I had just completed a JRPG, and it happened to be an extremely niche, fanservicey title that I'm a little embarrassed to tell people that I enjoy.
So do I recommend this game?  Well, I liked it, but anyone who would enjoy this already knows if they will like it or not.  For me the only thing is I now have to play through to completion Final Fantasy 3/6 or Chrono Trigger or something because I'm hesitant to brag about beating Re;Birth1 in polite company.

Telltales Game of Thrones actually manages to capture the spirit of the tv series very well. There are some interesting characters and some truly shocking moments which could be compared to some scenes in Telltales Walking Dead Season 1.
BUT there are some major problems with this series:
- there is no real ending, it pretty much ends on a bunch of cliffhangers. Season 2 is already announced, but there's no guarantee that you will actually see a final conclusion there
- the visuals just aren't up to date anymore. Animations are clunky, lip sync is shoddy at best. Models and textures really show that this game is also made for mobile devices. The worst offender in this department is the "oil painting" filter they use, which makes everything look worse instead of stylized.
- like always, your decisions barely matter. After playing games like Until Dawn and Life is Strange, this just feels cheap.
Telltale really needs to up their game.
All in all, i wouldn't recommend it except for really hardened fans of the TV show who are willing to commit to buying the second season as well when it comes out. If you're looking for an engaging, story and decision focussed adventure game, you're better off with The Wolf Among Us or Life is Strange.

Half-Life 2 is the superb sequel to 1998's critically acclaimed Half-Life. The sequel sticks very close to the blueprints set by the original, but also surpasses it in nearly every way. The game has its fair share of problems, but these are overshadowed by the game's many, many strong points. Basically, I can't think of a game I could recommend more than Half-Life 2.
STORY: 9.5/10 The game starts you off at the train station of City 17; where it becomes very clear that something is not right. You have obviously been placed here by the G-Man for a reason, but as of now, you don't know that reason. In the beginning of the game, you have no means of defense for yourself, so the Combine, an alien force of some kind, can attack you however they please. But this just gives you more of an incentive to get your payback; and you shall get that payback very soon. The story itself is good and intriguing. You will be captivated from the very beginning to the end. The only problem with it is that the game leaves a bit too many questions unanswered. The ending is a little bit too much of a cliffhanger. There is a positive aspect to this, though. It means that Valve will almost certainly make a sequel. It would have also been nice to have even more run-ins with the game's excellent characters, as they were very memorable. Overall, though, the story is truly great.
SOUND: 9.0/10 Half-Life 2's sound is not the game's strongest point, but that's not to say that it is bad. In fact, the sound in the game is anything but. The voice acting in the game is top-notch, and you will surely be impressed by it. The characters in the game have a very nice script and deliver their lines very well. The sound effects in the game are also, for the most part, exceptional. The weapons pack a very punchy sound and are very nice. The soundtrack in the game isn't around all that much, but when it is, it is very apparent. It only plays about a dozen times during the game, but it makes those moments very memorable. The soundtrack itself, though, is only pretty good. It just doesn't seem all that fitting, but it is nice none-the-less. There are also same sound glitches every now and then, but they are not too bad. All in all, the sound in the game is very, very good.
GAMEPLAY: 9.5/10 Even if everything else in the game was great, if the gameplay wasn't good, the game wouldn't be good. But gameplay is another place where Half-Life 2 stands above the rest. In most ways, the gameplay of Half-Life 2 isn't revolutionary or innovative, but it sure is fun. The amount of variety in the game is also pretty impressive. The most interesting item in the game is the Gravity Gun. You are able to pick up objects and throw them, both in combat and in use for the game's several puzzles. The puzzles in the game are pretty simple, but are a nice change of pace. It would have been nice to see some more puzzles in the later stages of the game, though. There are also two rather lengthy sequences in the game that involve vehicles. The vehicles in the game are a little awkward to drive, but are, however, fun. The weapons are pretty well balanced, for the most part. The only real balancing issues are that the pistol can be a little too useful at times, and the last weapon given to you in the game feels very overpowered. You will go up against a variety of enemies in the game, from the menacing Combine soldiers, to zombies, to antlions. The Combine are the most advanced enemies in the game, from an artificial intelligence standpoint. The zombies just tend to lumber over to you pretty slowly. The artificial intelligence in the game is great. The game's length is also more than satisfactory; coming in at close to 20 hours for the average player. There are three different difficulty levels to choose from in the game; easy, normal, and hard. Easy will definitely be too simple for the vast majority of players, but hard should suit even the better players. You will be fighting alone for most of the game, but in the later stages you will sometimes have allies. The allies in the game are not as helpful as you might have hoped, but they are still a nice gameplay addition.
GRAPHICS: 10/10 From a technological standpoint, Half-Life 2 stands above all else. The graphics in the game are truly stunning, and are some of the best, if not the best, graphics out there. Everything from facial animation, to shadowing, to textures is astounding. The game also holds up at an impressive frame rate, even on older computers. The art direction in the game is also a sight to behold. Everything about the game conveys the look that was intended; and the result is nothing short of spectacular. All the explosions in the game are also great. Lighting and shadowing is also beautifully mastered in the game. The superb facial animations truly bring the characters to life like no other game has been able to do. But what is even more amazing than Half-Life 2's graphics, is its incredible use of physics. Graphically, the game is virtually unsurpassed.
Overall Score : 10/10

This game is fun, for a little while. Early on you feel like an unstoppable god face rolling groups of 15-20 npcs at a time, no problem.
Here's where the game starts to lose me. All bosses are summoned by scrolls, weekly. There are no traditional "dungeons". The quests are boring as anything.
Here's where the game REALLY loses me. You dont really find better gear by progressing in the game. You upgrade lower level gear with "stones". When you get your items to a certain level, you fail upgrades at an increasingly high rate. The stones can be looted or given from quests, but not nearly enough, so you have to grind for cash to buy them on the MP. The most effective way to upgrade higher level gear is to fail upgrades on purpose on low end gear to increase your chances of succeeding on the piece you actually want to upgrade. At the end of the day, this adds up to more grinding.
You grind you grind you grind, start to finish. Nothing cool happens, nothing cool is going to happen. Not my jam.

Have you ever imagined you were Piccard commanding your crew in the heat of battle? Now you can, without the hassle of attending skirt-wearing ceremonies for visiting species inbetween each skirmish.
Lead your spaceship and power up your FTL drive to hop from beacon to beacon exploring sectors of space; encountering Pirates, distress beacons to challenge your morality, different species that can become part of your crew, all for the ultimate goal of defeating the Rebel Flagship.
This games focuses on strategic combat. Prioritising you and your foes ship-systems in a battle to outwit each other gives a rewarding test that definitely keeps you on your toes. Encountering stores and gathering materials to upgrade your ships abilities and weapons builds ample depth in the diferent systems for you to micro-manage. Each playthrough is different enough not to be too repetitive aswell as being challenging enough that it requires sufficient concentration to properly strategies your run. FTL provides extremely satisfying, bite-size chunks of play that can last from 15 minutes to 50. It's not something you need commitment to playing, pick up and play perfectly defines it.

Things XCOM taught me:
1) "Streamlined" means: devoid of any meaningful strategy (i.e. dumbed down)
--The "strategy" you work out in the first few missions will last you the entire game. Everything that follows is upgrades to keep up with the aliens.
2) 0-70% = 0%; 71-99% = 85%; 100% = 100% (but I already knew that one)
3) Scientists >> Engineers because it takes 30 engineers longer to construct 60s-era space tech than it does 30 scientists to reverse engineer alien tech.
4) It's acceptable to be sinfully ugly when you've casual-ized a genre known for its depth
--Considering I continue to play games from the mid 90s, I'm not normally one to harp about graphics...but am I the only one who found XCOM difficult to look at? It's on par with Halo 3 (which was also ugly for its time and released years before XCOM).
The first point renders any others irrelevant since, without a need for dynamic strategizing, this game will get stale faster than thin-sliced bread left outside in Arizona. It made me want to play Starcraft...1. Yeah...I recommend you play that any number of times before purchasing this. Better yet, just don't.

I like god games.  I enjoy RTS games that deviate from the norm.  This does both, and I really wanted to like it but I don't.
Let's get the "early access" stuff out of the way first: sometimes your game is too early in development even for early access, and this game is a prime example of that.  The UI is hideous, hard to use, barely functional and sometimes busted.  Actually managing anything is more of a chore because of the UI, and keeping track of things is difficult.  Moving the camera around in the world is cumbersome at best.  Too many things require ridiculous micromanagement where it feels like things could be much more readily automated.  Placing buildings and trees is spotty, I'm not convinced that the game itself even knows what a legal placement is.  Casting spells is hit or miss, as sometimes you wanna cast a spell on someone or something and end up selecting them instead.
As it is now, this build is nothing more than a prototype or proof of concept and, in my opinion, has no business being sold for money right now.
I see potential here, I do, but as of writing this I can NOT recommend this to anyone.
Gripes not about early access: resource scarcity and discovery is frustrating and annoying.  The game description says it is 2D, but it feels more like it's 1-dimensional.  If you think about it, even games like Black & White are fundamentally 2D, just using 3D graphics.  I don't really like the idea of a god game in a side-view one-dimensional space such as this, but it is unique and some people may enjoy the change of perspective.  Resource costs are just ridiculous.  It takes like 15 logs and 10 stone to build a building, yeah okay cool that makes sense, but it takes 5 logs and 2 whole bolts of cloth to make a single bow.  That's just silly.
The title screen music is VERY nice though.  I just wish there was more music throughout the game, as it just disappears when you actually start playing.

I don't have a lot of experience in the bullet hell genre, as I've only recently gotten into them. I've missed many important entries and don't have much to compare this game to (I haven't even played Ikaruga yet, but I plan to!), but I can definitely say I enjoyed it. When I first saw the screenshots for this game, my immediate reaction was one of abject horror and revulsion. But, the screenshots don't do it justice, even videos don't quite translate. It feels incredibly smooth to play!
I've only gotten as far as completing the first of ten worlds, and most of the second. The first world - and I assume, the others as well, - has 2 extra bosses you unlock by clearing levels at a certain rank. I've only beaten one of these optional bosses so far, - the very first one - but I can assure you, they're hard as balls. The game has three difficulty levels; normal, hard, and heavenly. These up the game's pace a bit, and change enemy's bullet patterns, which is most apparent in boss fights.
There are also various cheats and handicaps you can unlock to customize the difficulty even further, which lower and raise your score by an arbitrary percentage. These include changing bullet speed and damage, but also a few more interesting ones. My favorite was one that keeps bullets persistent between waves, and gives a whopping 20% score boost. I actually found that this handicap improved my performance, as it kept me on my toes at all times.
The replayability is definitely there, hence how I managed to play until 8 A.M. while only completing one world. Experimenting with the eight different characters and each of their three unique sub-weapons, testing out new cheats/handicaps and difficulty levels, or just trying to up your score to earn new ranks or climb the leaderboard keeps old levels replayable for a very long time.
The game also supports 4-player local co-op, with keyboard and gamepad controls. It also lets you controls your character by guiding it with the mouse, which works quite well.
All in all, I found this to be game very fun. If you want to try it out, there is a version on Kongregate. Don't worry if the game is jerky and gives you migraines like it did to me, the Steam version runs much nicer.
As an added bonus, this game includes its 20-track soundtrack and some wallpapers for free, which is pretty cool!

What is this game?
Essentially, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a turn-based battlefield tactics/base management game, where you command a small group of elite military operatives against an invading alien force, killing the attackers, rescuing civilians, and blowing things to Hell and back.
What's good?
Pretty much everything. With the exceptions of a few flaws I'll get to later, almost everything about this game is brilliant. The two main gameplay elements, turn-based military strategy and base managment, both work well, each standing up on their own two feet, but combining together in a brilliant way. What you do in your base affects your troops in the field, and vice-versa, so the game really rewards you for clever tactics and strategy in both areas. The graphics, while less than perfect, are as good as they need to be, and since the joy of this game comes less from spectacle and more from the reward of good strategy, the lower-end graphics don't let the game down.
The combat system works beautifully, and while there's random number generation to keep it tense, you have enough control over the shooting that you never feel like it's completely up in the air (unless you're playing badly). The four classes are unique enough in their own ways to each be highly useful in battle, and this game has one of the greatest modding communities I've seen in years. This game is phenomenal, and if you enjoy more thinky, strategic games, you should absolutely pick up not just the base game, but the DLC as well.
What's bad?
As much as I like this game, there's a few things that bug me a little bit. Some of these are extremely subjective, though, so take them with huge amounts of salt, as they may not bother you in the same way they bother me.
Most of the choices in this game are either absolutely pointless, or ridiculously contrived. Let me give you an example. At random times in the game, aliens will invade and attack three different cities. Panic will rise in the countries they attack, and I can only defend one of the cities. WHY? I have 20 troops twiddling their thumbs back at the base while 4 of my soldiers go to defend one of the cities, so why can't I go and take care of the others?
From the other end of the spectrum, you spend a portion of the game upgrading weapons and armor for your troops. But  the issue I have with this is that any new weapons you get will always be better than your old weapons in every single way. You go from ballistic to beam to plasma, but plasma guns will always shoot more accurately and do more damage than beam weapons, no matter what. Personally, I would have liked a bit more of a difficult decision in what weapons to equip my troops with, but that's just me.
All that being said, these issues were fixed in an absolutely beautiful mod called "Long War", but since this mod is also extremely difficult, you'll need to do at least a couple playthroughs of the vanilla game before moving up.
Don't take away that XCOM is bad, because it's absolutely amazing, and between the time I've spent playing on here and on my old Xbox, it's easily one of my most played games of all time. There are a couple issues, yes, but they can be fixed when you're good enough to handle Long War and even before that, they're never dealbreakers. Please get this game, you owe it to yourself.

TL DR version: great game to get into the bullet hell genre, has a lot of content for newcomers and veterans alike
Full review:
The bullet hell genre is very a niche genre (one of those love or hate it cases), most people are afraid of playing these kind of games once they see the barrage of♥♥♥♥♥♥flying everywhere in the screen (most people i know call me crazy for liking these games) and its exacly where this game shines.
Bullet Heaven 2 has a lot of features to help newcomers with get used to dodging bullets, greasing, paying attention to patterns and etc without being overwhelming, its very forgiving and holds you by the hand (if you want), it starts of pretty easy and with each level introduces you to new concepts and slowly ramps up the difficulty, it also has other in game mechanics to ease things like the counter bomb (instead of losing a life when you get hit, you counter bomb to wipe the screen and lose only the bomb, not the life), 3 lifes before you die and has to restart (with heart drops being possible after every wave) and all enemy bullets becoming slower if you only have one heart left.
All that plus "cheats" that you buy in the game store, things like attack power, item drops (double attack, shields, bombs etc), increased max. life, increased item grab ratius, even more drops and others. of course with each one that you activate you give yourself a penalty in your score but if you are learning or just wanting to have fun that probably wont bother you.
You, my friend who also enjoys bullet hells, must be thinking: this game only for "filthy casuals" and I´m happy to say that its not the case, the game has 3 difficulty settings and in the last one, heavenly, it gets pretty crazy (don´t worry, you don´t need to beat the game or anything to get it) and same as the "cheats" we have the "handicaps", no item drops, counter bombing or anything that I mentioned above, but we get faster enemy bullets, decreased attack power, only one life and whats probably the most entertaining mode, the "pacifist" mode (where you don´t shoot and have to time out every wave and give you a high score for clearing it), as the cheats they modify your multiplier but in a positive way, so more handicaps = 1.30x / 1.50x / 1.70x etc (with regular steam highscore updates)
With all that out of the way we only have a few features to talk about like the big roster of characters ( 8 characters with 4 skins that grant different bonuses, 3 main weapons and 3 sub weapons each), survival mode mode (only one life, one bomb and no cheats or handicaps) and the coolest IMO 2-4 player mode ( get your friends and enjoy the mayhem)
well thats it, hope you find this review useful and give this game a shot if you are interested in getting into bullet hells or liked them already.

The most underrated game this developer has ever published. If you're looking for a good beginner-level Bullet Hell game, this is the one.
A proper Bullet Hell game has the player character shoot a bunch of enemies from a top down perspective, with progressively more (difficult) enemies and progressively more bullets on the screen at once. The player has their hitbox (the part that actually takes damage) visible at all times, and the actual size of their hitbox is always exactly one pixel. So you're actually playing a pixel dodging a bunch of other pixels.
What makes this game accessable to everyone is the difficulty. The difficulty scales from pretty easy to unbelievably difficult, and if thats not enough, the ingame "cheats" can make your game even easier or even harder.
While most Bullet Hell type games force you to use a controller or keyboard with a "slow down" button, Bullet Heaven 2 allows users to use a mouse, which makes the game considerably more intuitive especially for beginners to the genre.
Your more skilled friends can join your local co-op game with a controller or with the keyboard. While the campaign is pretty short, playing the campaign again with friends is pretty fun, no matter how skilled they are.
The biggest downside with this game are it's characters. Bullet Heaven 2's characters come directly from the Epic Battle Fantasy series, and unless you're familiar with that game series, the character dialogs will probably sound a bit cheesy. I do recommend reading the dialogs, as they sometimes contain essentail gameplay information, but if you're interested in getting to know the characters, I recommend playing Epic Battle Fantasy 3 on steam, which is a free game.
Another downside would be the game engine. Bullet Heaven 2 was built in Flash, which is an excellent engine for the animations in the game, but otherwise very poorly optimized for games. Steam has absolutely no issue running flash, but you might encounter framerate problems if your laptop does not support at least entry level graphics.
To recap;
+ Very adjustable difficulty, accessable to everyone
+ Good starter for those unknown to the Bullet Hell type games
+ Good support for mouse, controller and keyboard
+/- Characters aren't properly introduced in this game
- Runs in flash

The first bullet heaven was the first bullet hell game I had ever played, although now I've played so many. I liked it so much that I went to the creator's youtube page and asked for a bullet heaven 2. 4 years later, I'm browsing through steam and I see that bullet heaven 2 came out! Imagine my excitement! Thanks for making a second one!
Now to the review: So overall, this is a good bullet hell game. It's especially good, if not perfect, for those who are new to the genre. But there are many unorthodox things about this game which separate it from all other bullet hell games. A few of those things are having a currency to spend things on, the entire stage design, collecting gems, and so forth. It's what would be expected from japanese bullet hell meets american online game maker. Normally in bullet hell games, there's the stage where you fight through countless little guys and then you face the big boss. And there's about 5 or 6 stages which get exponentially more difficult. This game's design is that you fight through many little guys and a few levels of them which are composed of 13 stages each (including bonus stages) until you get to a boss level. It's not arcade-like as in when you lose your lives you have to start all over. The difficulties range from normal to hard to heavenly. And there's room for the absolute beginner all the way to seasoned veteran. There are many things I like about this game such as the scoring mechanism, PRETTY BULLETS!, extra bosses, extra content, online high scores, the music, and all the love that went into perfecting the game.
Now here are a few minor criticisms. The shooting mechanic can drive me a little nuts sometimes. I use keyboard because that's what I'm used to with bullet hell games. And I would absolutely love if I were able to shift+z+x. But I can't. And then if I do x+z and fly around sloppily, it only lets me move right and left. I don't know if this was done on purpose but I don't enjoy that one bit. I was thinking it's possible that maybe that's just my computer so if that's the case, ignore everything I just said. Secondly, going through stage after stage after stage of little guys can get a bit repetative. I don't think there's necessarily a way to avoid that unless a solid mini boss was put in at the end of each level. That would be so much more fun.
Overall, I really love this game and it's so addictive. I would give it a 9/10. Its replayability is much higher than most arcade shooters and I can really see how much attention to detail and effort went into this awesome game!

BSERC - (Borderline Sardonic and Extremely Reductive Comparison): Every ARPG ever. Diablo/Victor Vran/Torchlight/Van Helsing and the like but namely Titan Quest
Exposition, Concurrence and Summation
Now, Grim Dawn is an APRG. Should you not be familiar with this genre tag it basically equates to a dungeon crawler wherein you control one character, kill monsters then apply skill points into a specific tech tree or build of a certain style of play. All the while trying to land some, and please excuse my verbiage, “sick drops and hawt loot” in order to kill stronger enemies faster; rinse and repeat.
Grim Dawn is from Crate Entertainment which is comprised of old members of the now defunct Iron Lore Entertainment who are responsible for Titan Quest. The remnants of that system are still quite apparent.
To be upfront, I'm slightly dismissive of this game because the way I see it. It's a very good “one of those”. And doesn't really do a ton to stick out above the rest.
Here are some complaints in comparison
Often, the argument I hear against what I'd considered to be the most recent and prominent ARPG, Diablo III: Reapers of Souls is that it takes away proper character building. Allowing the changing of abilities and runes at will with no cost. Well, I'd argue that Grim Dawn does the very same; re-specing is basically of no cost (should you not posses the iron bits or aether crystals, it's nothing a few moments of grinding can't fix) and can be done at any time back at devils crossing which you can return to at no cost and at will stay from Chthonic Rifts which are rare.
An additional thing about classes is that in Grim Dawn the classes are chosen after starting a few levels into a new playthrough. Each class uses a spirit gauge regardless of what you decide to level into; Dual class or not. As an example, in Diablo 3 the Demon Hunter alone has 2 gauges to pull from and must be managed throughout play and style of build for the abilities chosen to be effective. This isn't a real complaint, it just is sort of antithetical to this idea of proper classes being something that you need to build and somehow the ability to change that build quickly negates it's enjoyability. Another thing is that is takes a very long time to even remotely level deeply into one class.
I also had an issue and this is another small complaint but I feel it should be said, there is very little direction for objectives to be completed. By the end of the game I had so many side quests I was unable to locate and had leveled past that they were literally spilling off screen. A little direction would have gone a long way.
But I digress, Grim Dawn is again a very good “one of those” so if ARPG's/Dungeon Crawlers aren't your thing this will not change your mind. However the game does have full gamepad support. So during your tenure of monster slaying you can get real lazy bones about it. Additionally, through the weapon sets and control schemes you can essentially have four hotbars at your disposal.
The art style is very nice looking, the environments diverse. There is some faction play which is relatively interesting but doesn't hold a ton of interest in the long haul unless you become deeply involved with the narrative. It seemed very “not Diablo” to me. I wish there were more cut-scenes to be honest. They adopted this sort of Darkest Dungeon look, a sort of Gothic cartoon that I'd have loved to see more of.
THE GIST
Grim Dawn is a good game, I just don't think it's as inspired as it has been made out to be by Diablo 3 detractors. If you are looking for a Torchlight replacement that's a bit more “adult” and dark. This is it.

Yes I would recommend this game. Not for its great game play though. It feels incomplete. When fighting enemies using a club or your bow it isn't satisfying to simply strike them. I want to feel the impact. This doesn't provide that at all. Quick pros and cons
Pros
-Beautiful landscape. STUNNING!
-Beast companions? I DIG IT!
-The look and feel when you throw a spear into a mans chest? Priceless.
-Village building system.
-Memoriable characters..ish
-Your movement. At one point I jumped off a ledge and stabbed some one in the chest with my spear. Oh it just felt right. Of course the spear didn't penetrate so He just sort of fell over and died from his lack of wounds.
-Predator vison. This allows you to see enemies, collectables, animals, friends and blood in a different color. ( sure I've always wanted Eagle vision from Assassin's creed in Far Cry.)
Cons
-Subtitles. ( I know. Freaking americans hate watching movies in subtitles because we are uncultured D-bags :/ ) no but really, the fact this game is not in english ( as a native english speaker) really subtracts from the beauty of the design. I can't watch this curiously cute half bald lady for facial cues when she is talking to me, because i'm too busy reading.
- Combat is like combatlite. You don't feel the impact. Unless its a ranged projectile. Ranged feels solid. LIke you have just hit this person with a sledge hammer, but really who wants to throw spears all day. Oh that is right I DO.
-Spirit quests. Screw these so much. Farcry 4 made me hate it when the Character got high. Controls were sloppy and it was hard to see. Well they brought it back people. Now I get to get tanked under the guidance of a Shaman! In all honesty though this really prompted me to write this review.  *SPOLIERS!!!!!!* So The second spirit quest you take you get transported into the body of a Wooly Mammoth. Yes it looked sweet at first. Until you notice that attack and rally call have the same animations and sounds. They both have different buttons taking up space on the mouse. Then the movement problems came. It felt like you were riding on the back of a wooly mammoth and it was standing on a platform on wheels. I could run backward and to the left at the same speed as forward. I made extremely tight turns. Then of course the challenge came. Fight a bunch of rhinos at once. SCREW THIS. Seriously screw this. 20 minutes of my life I will never get back. You know what I don't want to do with my time? Fight 8 Rhinos at once while dodging boulders in a drunk fake elephant. At one point I died and I wasn't even mad I just calmy said If I die once more I don't care I just spent $64 on this game. It will be uninstalled. Yay I didn't die again.
TLDR: This game has some serious flaws. MAJOR flaws. It is still fun though. Hunting baddies and killing them with a spear is satisfying. I would recommend this game, but know that going in You won't be invested in the characters. Do your self a favor, get a beast companion and enjoy being the silent killer lurking in the dark of night. This should have been a DLC.
Edit: Played a few more hours and It does get better. Upgrading your weapons is satisfying. They do much more damage/break less. The animations are still pretty basic. No blocking/ no great flourish moves. Just down and dirty stuff. Saw something on reddit today. An overlay of FC4 map and Primals map. They are the same one. I find this extremely lazy. This seems like a better DLC instead of a full priced game.

Most tower defense games put you in charge of building towers to defeat waves of enemies sent to your base by the computer. Tower Wars however takes this idea and makes it a two player competitive game. Not only do you build towers, but you yourself also send waves of units to attack the other player's base while he sends waves of units to attack yours. All the staples of tower defense in competitive mode. It's so brilliant a concept I find it hard to believe it's not used more. Of course you can also play classic tower defense alone in an included mode if you want, but that defeats what makes this game unique.
