Ah, Company of Heroes 2 a big Budget sequel to everyone's favorite RTS, WWII game; its become a large Giant in the RTS gaming industry, much like it's predecessor... can it live up to it's CoH name and roots?
Pros:
+ The Game plays much like the first one, so those who have played the first can get used to this one fast.
+ The campaign is much bigger than the First game (In my Opinnion) and has a more Historial feel to it in a sense.
+ The Addition of Western Fronts, much like the two DLCs from the first game add more factions and action to the table
+ Unlike the first one, you can mix factions. In other words you can have Soviets fighting AMericans and Wehrmacht fighting OKW and vice versa.
+ The new Commander System, makes the game more fleshed out; giving the player the complete choice of what he/she wants as the commander of the his/her army.
+ Worskshop support, gives this game even more fun, with new maps and some old (From CoH 1) and Tuners which are similiar to mods.
+ The ability for troops to vault over cover.
+ + Prosttruppen... Prosttruppen everywhere...
Cons:
- Lag in Multiplayer is horrid in some cases, unless you've got the Computer of All Computers.
- Patches by SEGA have ruined CoH 1's Mutiplayer in regards of CoH 2; which is wrong for any company to do.
- The Campaign's Narrative is annoying in the sense that it constantly bashes the Soviets rather than seeing them as Heroes; I know they want to make the whole "War is Bad" and "Dictators are bad" but it gets annoying fast.
- Some of the Commanders in the new Commander system, have the exact same abilities as others and some worthless ones, while most of the Premium Commanders are Fresh and Awesome to have.
- The Campaign feels like a large stretched out tutorial, rather than the player doing their own thing plus some side objectives, he/she is constantly doing what the magic Bad Russian accented voice in the sky tells them to do.
- The Unit's skins in game are sometimes amazingly inaccurate often sometimes wearing uniforms that didn't even exsist or what not used by that army (Looking at you Whermacht Grenadiers).
Do I recommend this game? Yes, but lightly so; simply because this game still has the Company of Heroes gameplay we all know and love, and that the developers try their best to make the game like it's predecessor. However with glaring bad side effects like Lag and the slander of the first installment of CoH I do this recommendation lightly.

Poker Night at the Inventory:
It is a Texas hold 'em single player only game featuring: Strong Bad from Homestar Runner,  The Heavy from Team Fortress 2, Max from Sam & Max, Tycho from Penny Arcade and you.
The NPC players play similar to their personalities. The Heavy is very aggressive frequently going all in with poor hands etc. Another interesting aspect the the NPC players are not of all the same skill level with players like The Heavy often being one of the first ones out and Max being one of the last two. At the beginning of a game each there is a chance one of the NPCs will bet a Team Fortress 2 item which is a nice touch and adds an incentive to continue playing the game after the first three or four games.
The game attempts to draw the player in by having lots of back and forth talking between the NPC players and it does this quite well with enough dialogue to keep it from getting repetitive too quickly but after several games it will get repetitive as you start to hear the same things for the fourth and fifth times. Games also take a while to play out due to the amount of talking during the games. You can click to skip past the speaking which helps sometimes but also gets old after a while. There are options in the settings menu to prevent them from triggering speech scenes that delay play until they are complete or turn off speech completely but doing so removes the main focus of the game. If you are going for the Team Fortress 2 items it may get frustrating as winning is not enough to get them. You must be the one to knock the NPC betting their item out of the game and often none of the NPCs will bet an item resulting in some reloading if you just are only after them.
Overall I found it a fun experience. The dialogue was amusing but does get repetitive. The poker play was solid and the NPCs having different play styles combined with the Team Fortress 2 items add some replayability. As of writing this the list price is $5 and at that price I felt it was worth the cost.

is a visual novel that has dating sim elements and stat raising.  You play as Marcel, who has arrived at Lord Sandor's mansion in order to meet his father.  Lord Sandor abandoned Marcel and his mother to a life of poverty, and Marcel arrives at the mansion (under the guise of working as a servant) to confront him.  However, events take a turn when Marcel and Lord Sandor meet face-to-face, and Lord Sandor recognizes Marcel.  Even though Marcel only wanted to meet his father and then leave, he is given an offer.  Become worthy and Lord Sandor will name Marcel his heir, as he has no other children of his own to do so.  It sounds a little too good to be true, right?  Well, Marcel thinks so but he decides to stick around to see if he has the skills worthy of becoming the heir and along the way, he may form a romantic relationship with one of four possible choices: Kamal (the ex-gladiator now turned gardener), Vincent (the butler who always strives for perfection for himself), Borges (the local doctor who is determined to find a way to save Lord Sandor-I forgot to mention but Lord Sandor is dying, so thus, the challenge to Marcel), and Eloy (the mischievous elven lord).
Now, I'll briefly describe the gameplay and then get to my critique.  As I stated,
is a visual novel so you do make choices.  The choices affect how well Marcel gets along with the romantic options.  (Another thing I forgot to mention but this game only has malexmale romances.)  The main part of the game is the stat simulation.  Basically, for Marcel to be named Lord Sandor's heir, he'll need to work hard and well as his servant, and this means that he'll need to pass skill checks.  For example, Marcel may need a certain amount of strength to be able to carry a guest's luggage by himself inside the mansion.  There are 8 different stats.  You will need certain amounts of each stat to pass various skill checkpoints.  Each of the romance options are associated with two of the stats but if you only focus on those two to get closer to Marcel's love interest, there is no way to win the game.  That's basically how the game works in a nutshell.
Ok, it's time to get to the critique part of the review so shall we?  ;)  First, I liked the writing and how well the story was told.  I found myself sympathizing with Marcel.  He is certainly not a perfect main character.  He has his flaws and a less-than-reputable past, but I like characters like him.  I did notice grammatical errors and typos here and there that could have used some polish, but they weren't too huge of a distraction.  The gameplay was fine.  I didn't mind the stat simulation part although the only thing that bothered me was that there is no way to anticipate what stats you would need to pass, how much of each you'd need, or when the checkpoints would pop up.  The only way you would know is either to play the game once and make note of those checkpoints or to use the developer's walkthrough.  The art was fine as well and I liked the CGs, as I always love viewing CGs in VNs.  ^^  The music was appropriate and placed well.  Oh and also, I liked that there was a cast of characters.  Aside from Marcel, Lord Sandor, and the four main love interests, there were plenty of side characters (NPCs) as well.  I thought that the introduction of Lady Rosalynn, Lord Sandor's cousin, added some interesting element to the game even though I totally detested her.
Overall, I enjoyed
and liked getting to play out Marcel's story.  It was great to play a VN with malexmale relationships, and there really should be more games like this on Steam, as they are so few and rare.  Now, is it worth the asking price?  I suppose it depends on preferences.  If you like VNs and don't mind stat simulators, then yes, it is worth it.  However, if you don't like the stat part of the game, then you may want to wait for a sale.  There is no option to play only in visual novel mode so you have to play stat simulation part.  (Oh and gosh, I do keep forgetting to mention some things.  lol  I liked how there were references made from
, another one of Winter Wolves' games.  My eyes would light up every time a character from
was mentioned.)  Nevertheless, I enjoyed this game and as I said, if you like VNs and such, then you'll enjoy it, too.  ^^

Look, if this is your favorite game, that's totally fine. Good for you. The industry has different genres for this exact reason - different strokes for different folks (pun entirely intended). With this in mind I ask that please, do not take this the wrong way, but I personally cannot in good conscious recommend this game to anyone.
Visually, the best way to sum up
is "softcore loli porn: the JRPG". And again, if that's your thing, that's totally fine - but if it isn't, you're not going to enjoy the visual novel aspects of the game, which include 'animated' fanservice sequences where literally only the characters' breasts are animated. Within the first minute and a half of the game, the primary characters are introduced in armor that is not only impractical for battle but impossible to wear in real life, while the dialogue referencing their centuries-long war over who deserves to be
devolves into an argument over whether breast size should be a factor in determining who has control over literally all of creation.
As a number of other reviewers have pointed out (and I hate to recycle the words of others here), it's a very niche brand of humor, and unless you're a hardcore anime fan - and again, specifically the loli genre - you're not going to get a lot of enjoyment out of this title from a writing standpoint. Everything is designed to be 'cuteness overload' while somehow simultaneously completely oversexualized, and that really just isn't going to appeal to everyone, which is why the 'Overwhelmingly Positive' rating on Steam feels both baffling and completely unjustified.
Regardless of your softcore porn preferences, moving past the visual novel aspects (which are about 50% of the game), the gameplay itself aims to be a mix of a traditional turn-based JRPG while combining elements of a basic tactics system in which you have to physically move characters within range of their opponents, which presumably opens them up to attack. However, given the range of movement afforded characters from the start of battle with most low-leveled monsters, this system doesn't appear to make much sense because both you and your opponent will easily be able to close any starting gaps within the space of a single turn. Perhaps with the addition of long-ranged characters later on in the game, the tactics aspect will actually begin to shine, but for the beginning levels its inclusion is more mildly confusing and frustrating than anything else, especially considering that visually the system actually looks nice. Aside from this, however, the combat boils down to your basic JRPG fare, and there's nothing really special about it - because, again, the combat is really only half the game anyway. I'm not sure if the combat improves in the game's sequels, but I'm far less tempted to shell out any more money to even attempt to try them given my experience thus far with
.
The greatest setback of them all, however, is the game's controls. As the store page says, for a long time this game was exclusively available on consoles, and it is made abundantly clear from the very first dungeon that
was not designed with PC gamers in mind. The keyboard controls are abominable, even with keymapping, and it turns the entire experience into a taxing, joyless, tedious affair. I don't think I'd recommend anyone even attempt to play this game without a controller, unless you have the miraculous, nigh-inhuman patience required to alternate between using the mouse and having both hands on the keyboard just to be able to navigate the first dungeon. It's just that infuriating, and this problem persists into the combat sequences, where you will often find yourself having to once again alternate between using the mouse and having both hands on the keyboard within the space of a single turn, just to be able to select more than one target. It is absolutely mind-boggling that there isn't a warning on the store page that a controller is recommended for this game. Oh, and by the way, every single key prompt is designed with a controller in mind, which makes memorizing the keymapping even more difficult.
The game's writing, meanwhile, is an entirely different source of frustration. The plot is a thinly veiled parody of the console war between Microsoft, Sony, Nintendo, and Sega (?), and in this reality all four are middle to highschool-aged girls guilty of more fourth-wall breaks than Deadpool himself. It's an interesting premise that gets heavily bogged down by the 'cutesy' anime dialogue of our loli protagonists, and it's a shame, because the concept of playing as characters who are aware they are in a video game is one that is seldom used. Unfortunately,
fails to utilize its basic premise to its full potential.
I'm sorry if this all sounds harsh. Again, obviously this game appeals to some people. I sure as hell don't know why, but if this is your kind of game, hats off to you. I'll never judge you for that. But the point of this wall of text is that this game really isn't designed to appeal to the average gamer - or, hell, most gamers in general. And people deserve to know that, given that this game still has an 'Overwhelmingly Positive' rating. If you absolutely have to try
, get it on sale - but it definitely isn't worth the retail price tag, and I cannot recommend anyone spend $29.99 on this.

Half-Life 2 is the superb sequel to 1998's critically acclaimed Half-Life. The sequel sticks very close to the blueprints set by the original, but also surpasses it in nearly every way. The game has its fair share of problems, but these are overshadowed by the game's many, many strong points. Basically, I can't think of a game I could recommend more than Half-Life 2.
STORY: 9.5/10 The game starts you off at the train station of City 17; where it becomes very clear that something is not right. You have obviously been placed here by the G-Man for a reason, but as of now, you don't know that reason. In the beginning of the game, you have no means of defense for yourself, so the Combine, an alien force of some kind, can attack you however they please. But this just gives you more of an incentive to get your payback; and you shall get that payback very soon. The story itself is good and intriguing. You will be captivated from the very beginning to the end. The only problem with it is that the game leaves a bit too many questions unanswered. The ending is a little bit too much of a cliffhanger. There is a positive aspect to this, though. It means that Valve will almost certainly make a sequel. It would have also been nice to have even more run-ins with the game's excellent characters, as they were very memorable. Overall, though, the story is truly great.
SOUND: 9.0/10 Half-Life 2's sound is not the game's strongest point, but that's not to say that it is bad. In fact, the sound in the game is anything but. The voice acting in the game is top-notch, and you will surely be impressed by it. The characters in the game have a very nice script and deliver their lines very well. The sound effects in the game are also, for the most part, exceptional. The weapons pack a very punchy sound and are very nice. The soundtrack in the game isn't around all that much, but when it is, it is very apparent. It only plays about a dozen times during the game, but it makes those moments very memorable. The soundtrack itself, though, is only pretty good. It just doesn't seem all that fitting, but it is nice none-the-less. There are also same sound glitches every now and then, but they are not too bad. All in all, the sound in the game is very, very good.
GAMEPLAY: 9.5/10 Even if everything else in the game was great, if the gameplay wasn't good, the game wouldn't be good. But gameplay is another place where Half-Life 2 stands above the rest. In most ways, the gameplay of Half-Life 2 isn't revolutionary or innovative, but it sure is fun. The amount of variety in the game is also pretty impressive. The most interesting item in the game is the Gravity Gun. You are able to pick up objects and throw them, both in combat and in use for the game's several puzzles. The puzzles in the game are pretty simple, but are a nice change of pace. It would have been nice to see some more puzzles in the later stages of the game, though. There are also two rather lengthy sequences in the game that involve vehicles. The vehicles in the game are a little awkward to drive, but are, however, fun. The weapons are pretty well balanced, for the most part. The only real balancing issues are that the pistol can be a little too useful at times, and the last weapon given to you in the game feels very overpowered. You will go up against a variety of enemies in the game, from the menacing Combine soldiers, to zombies, to antlions. The Combine are the most advanced enemies in the game, from an artificial intelligence standpoint. The zombies just tend to lumber over to you pretty slowly. The artificial intelligence in the game is great. The game's length is also more than satisfactory; coming in at close to 20 hours for the average player. There are three different difficulty levels to choose from in the game; easy, normal, and hard. Easy will definitely be too simple for the vast majority of players, but hard should suit even the better players. You will be fighting alone for most of the game, but in the later stages you will sometimes have allies. The allies in the game are not as helpful as you might have hoped, but they are still a nice gameplay addition.
GRAPHICS: 10/10 From a technological standpoint, Half-Life 2 stands above all else. The graphics in the game are truly stunning, and are some of the best, if not the best, graphics out there. Everything from facial animation, to shadowing, to textures is astounding. The game also holds up at an impressive frame rate, even on older computers. The art direction in the game is also a sight to behold. Everything about the game conveys the look that was intended; and the result is nothing short of spectacular. All the explosions in the game are also great. Lighting and shadowing is also beautifully mastered in the game. The superb facial animations truly bring the characters to life like no other game has been able to do. But what is even more amazing than Half-Life 2's graphics, is its incredible use of physics. Graphically, the game is virtually unsurpassed.
Overall Score : 10/10

This is a review for the base game, played in single player.
If I had to describe Dying Light in one sentence it would be "Dead Island meets Far Cry 3 with a smattering of Assassin's Creed". This is a compliment as it combines some of the best parts of each game.
In the game you play Crane who (for reasons I will leave unspoiled) finds himself rampaging around a zombie-infested city using parkour to move around the environment and any metal object he can find to slaughter the undead. The parkour is very natural and fluid and ties together well with a very physical and satisfying combat system.
The game is genuinely tense as even the basic enemies do not go down easily and, if you lose concentration, you can easily become mobbed and die. The enemies appear to level in a smart fashion - normal biters gain health as you get stronger but special enemies appear to gain health more slowly. This means you feel as though you're always under threat throughout the game whilst still feeling the benefit of that new weapon when you face a larger, deadlier version of the infected. At night the game is scary as even the best-equipped character cannot stand toe-to-toe with the enemies and must run. This leads to some very thrilling moments where you are trying to avoid detection or trying to escape the horrors of the night.
As you level up you gain access to more powerful weapons but, more importantly, you gain new skills to use in combat and whilst traversing the city, widening your tactical options. This feels very organic to begin with a provides a well-paced learning curve. After the mid-game I felt as though I had most of the skills I wanted and was taking filler skills I'd decided to skip earlier on, but this is a minor complaint.
Crane is very well voice acted and I mostly enjoyed listening him interact with the city's inhabitants as he could be forceful, witty, disgusted or panicked and often reacted in the way I was reacting as a player. The NPCs are also fairly well voiced and fleshed out, although the main antagonist may feel a bit too familiar if you played Far Cry 3. Side quests were also a pleasure to complete as they included some truly memorable and interesting characters and situations. The main plot is not as strong and seems to lose focus and cohesion on occasion but is still enjoyable.
Death is fairly well handled. On death you lose some xp towards your next upgrade but otherwise you aren't punished harshly. This is just as well because misjudging a jump can lead to instant-death falls (this adds to the tension of running around the rooftops of the city) and human enemies with guns can put you down quickly if you don't use your skills, the environment and inventory wisely.
Finally, the game is very pretty and weather, lighting and so on used to great effect.
Overall, this is a fun and pretty action game with enough depth to hold interest and strong enough characters, stories and voice-acting to be memorable.

***EARLY ACCESS REVIEW***
Genre: Adventure, Indie, Simulation, Strategy,Early Access
Developer: Pirozhok Studio, Timur Shakirov, Vadim Pushkarev  Eugene Rezantsev, Vitaliy Ruzankin
Publisher: Pirozhok
Release Date: 3 Nov, 2015
Completionist Gameplay: 20+ Hours
is a very complex strategy and resource management town builder. You control a tribe, your ‘minions’ (no, not the annoying yellow things we’re all sick of), and need to fight skeletons, barbarians, swamp people, sometimes tribesmen and the inevitable starvation that we all put our townspeople through whenever we play these kinds of games. You’ll need to build housing to expand your population, pay tributes to the barbarians you’re at war with so they don’t flatten you the next day, mine for stone and ore, grow food, build portals and explore the surprisingly large world for those diminishing resources. It slightly reminds me of Kingdom, so if you liked that, you’d probably also really like
.
You’ll also have to keep your villagers happy with a steady supply of beer, made in a tavern. Keeping inter-village relations friendly is also a great idea. Occasionally, a caravan trader will stop by and you have the option to trade with him or loot his goods (which will damage your relationship with him and his village). You can also send out your own cart to gather resources, although it will occasionally break, requiring resources you’ve gathered at home to repair. It may also get looted itself, so it’s up to you to decide if it’s worth the expense and the risk.
The game offers multiple bonuses at the start to help customize and diversify each playthrough, adding hours of replay time. You can pick one god out of six at the beginning of your township and each god gives you extra resources, damage, or faith. Damage bonuses are particularly useful against the nightly mobs and later on in the game barbarians, faith is used to cast healing spells or special attacks for your paladin, and extra resources are very, very helpful. Believe me when I tell you, you’re going to be counting every single resource you have.
At this stage, the game is still in Early Access and still has quite a few bugs. Currently you cannot save your game at all, which is both a blessing and a curse. The steam overlay is currently a little funky, although it works perfectly fine. The tutorial pictures will sit on top of the text if you’re not playing the game full-screen with a higher resolution, although this is easily fixed by doing the aforementioned. I really love the hot keys that are available for each of the building, spell and tribe menus, as well as the menu’s themselves. While they’re mostly easy to understand, you’ll come across one or two buttons that don’t seem to have a clear purpose, but again, it’s not too big of a deal. The developers first language is not English, and while all the text is completely understandable, you’ll definitely notice.

Disclosure, Kupo/Matt sent me a free key a few days before the official release for one of those fancy
things. Amativ.
Anyway, I quite liked this game. That said, this is a very different game from the regular EBF turn-based strategy games. This is a bullet shooter, think "1945" or Touhou or Crimson Clover. If you're not a fan of that genre I wouldn't rule this game out entirely, but do play
for a few hours - more on that below.
As for the game itself: it has quite a bit of depth, for just having two or three main mechanics. You can shoot stuff, and you can use a wild card "bomb" attack to clear (or almost clear) the screen of enemies. Despite that, almost every level manages to feel distinct thanks to the variety of enemies and bullet patterns. Most of the enemies are making reappearences from past EBF games, and a lot of them have made the transition pretty well, from obvious things like Gunslingers shooting stuff at you to Fire Monster Things blowing burning ash in your face.
You get eight characters to play:
; each of them have their own unique attack methods and Bomb designs. There are also a couple different "costumes" you can give the characters, and a couple different secondary attacks they can use.
It would be hard to talk about an EBF game without making note of the writing. At the start and end of pretty much every level the main characters exchange a few lines of dialogue, which is usually completely off-the-wall and decently helpful at the same time. The descriptions of achievements and whatnot also tend to be quite colorful. Expect fourth wall breaks. True to form, the writing does not take itself too seriously. (Also, it's available in a bunch of different languages.)
Difficulty . . . if you're a Touhou veteran you probably won't have too hard a time with this, but on higher difficulties it's quite easy to get yourself into spaces where you only have one or two pixels where it's safe to move without getting hit. If that's too much, or not enough, you have quite a bit of control over the difficulty: there are three tiers of bullet density, and a bunch of bonuses/handicaps you can buy with in-game money and enable and disable to make the game way easier or way harder.
The art style. It's pretty. It's . . . really pretty. Scroll up to the top of the store page and look at the screenshots.
You can even grab a friend and play local co-op with up to four people, but those aren't something I have a whole lot of so I'm going to assume that feature's really good, too. Regardless of whether or not you have any IRL friends, you can control the game with the mouse, the keyboard or a dedicated game controller.
Performance: a few people have reported lag, but I'm basically running this on a college essay machine (see below) and so far, I've seen no lag even with all of the graphical effects turned on and bullet density set to Heavenly. The optimization is amazing, if you have any performance issues they should be decently simple to fix.
- All "premium content" is automatically available, with the base game, no microtransactions, no questions asked, no nothing. Unlock it the same way you'd unlock any other character or stage in the game. Seriously,
- Leaderboards. You can now see how your scores stack up against everyone elses' scores
.
- Steam Achievements that unlock in parallel with the in-game achievements. Again, if you're a completionist . . . these are not easy, some of them you can grind out but a lot of them rely on a considerable level of bullet shooter skill. You have been warned.
- Steam trading cards. Come on, those things look adorable.
- Better performance. Like, WAY better performance.
- The OST as a free DLC. If you've listened to more than about three minutes of the in-game music, I don't think I have to explain this, but
is my review on that anyway.
Intel i7 @2.6 GHz
8 GB RAM
Intel HD Graphics
Windows 8.1
Again, no lag even with the graphics on full blast. Edit: Dropped momentarily to 40-ish fps for a few seconds on later bosses while recording, but that's about it.

The game instantly reminded me of Castle Fight - a Warcraft 3's mod map. Unfortunately it's still lacking many things, including but not limited to Good AI, more campaign maps (solo play) and missions. Would've been a good one if it was released from the start so as the game would have been more popular than it is now.
There's only three or so missions/maps for solo play including one tutorial. If you expect to play alone... don't think about it too much.
UPDATE: There's now single player content. Horrayyyyyyyyyy!
Multiplayer aspect is pretty much dead. Arrange a match with friend before you jump into multiplayer. If you can find someone with same skill level, well, I guess it's fun.
Learning curve is surprisingly not that hard. There's still a learning curve, but from what I can see, not as steep as Castle Fight. Also there's little teamwork required unlike in Castle Fight so yeah... You just need to send your units (controlled by AI after you launch them) into enemy's castle and simultaneously defend you castle by making maze (hello Sanctum 1). When engaging enemies, you earn points that you can use to hire workers to obtain more gold, upgrade your tech trees to obtain more units and make them stronger. Rinse and repeat - don't forget to keep creating maze.
Typical tower defense stuffs, heh.
All in all, a promising game but lacking execution and less polished. Despite the workshop implemented already, there's little to none content in it. Sad, but that's true. Maybe with longer developer supports and a few sales here and there the game can be improved and has bigger player base.
Do you hate music? Do you have epilepsy? If you answered no to both of those questions, buy this game.

Definitely not worth the price of admission... it seems like an interesting concept but it's just excuted very poorly.
The game becomes a monotonous grind out of collecting wood, fibers, ammo, fuel and food to stay alive.
All you do is wave after wave of zombie hordes in a small confined area... you then move on to clear a building full of zombies and salvage some items, maybe meet a merchant (which is where the real progress beings)
You have so many moves to jump around and scavenge the map, what happens when those moves run out? I'll never know, I was too scared to find out... probably death... I always retreated early and got penalized for doing so by losing some of the supplies I had gained... yet another flawed and idiotic design to go with the rest of the game.
It's rogue like, so expect to have either great luck or terrible luck... if you have the latter, expect many restarts. I fixed the car twice and travelled to two different areas... nothing different from the first two... I think the game might be endless until you finally can no longer survive... so a game that never ends... lame.
Death is also perminent in this game, there is no way to revive your team mates if you leave them behind. You can only resuscitate them in a battle but if they die from starvation, that's it. Also if your entire team is wiped, your save file is erased and you must start from scratch again.
I didn't really understand the crafting system either... you place your team on a work bench, then speed up time, wasting a couple days just to upgrade a turret or craft a shotgun... it's kind of ridiculous. Everything is a domino effect... you have to have ammo to progress the game and find food so you can survive all the while collecting components for upgrades so you can make your life easier. If you run out of any one of those things, the game is basically over.
The farming aspect of the game is really silly as well... it takes a full day just to harvest food and the amount of food you harvest is good enough for an entire day... so it just becomes redundant to even bother harvesting food... if the gains were better and you earned 6 supply or 8 supply for wasting a day harvesting, then you could get somewhere.
You can however upgrade your ability to catch food and even though it takes a day, you'll get a perminent +1 to supply per day that passes... thus securing survivability for a single team member... that makes more sense... There's just a lot of weird and quirky things with this game I didn't like. The HUD and interface is abysmal at best... it feels like a cell phone game.
The only redeeming quality of this game is that you get to play as the Left 4 Dead squad, which is what kept my appeal going, however this is offset by the inclusion of the highly obnoxious Pewdiepie and his girlfriend Cutiepie character which I rolled my eyes at and cringed at the sight of.
Either way, it's early access and I doubt it's going to get any better really... so far the upgrades are basic and there's room for improvement on those, other than that I think the game is pretty much finished in terms of game play... you just keep doing the same monotonous boring thing over and over again until you either die or get fed up and uninstall it like I have...
Cheers.

I really loved this game. The art is beautiful, and the control mechanisms are easy to use. The story is complex, and you get to meet a variety of unique characters with different skills and personalities. While the choices you make may not do much to impact the overarching story, they can impact which characters you can have as allies. The oculi system in the game is a great mechanism for complicating battles and making you think strategy. Without the proper oculi to give you an edge, certain battles can be hard to win, but the wrong ones can put you at a disadvantage. Really, the only less than positive thing I can say is that the story (especially the ending) feels a bit rushed. The whole world is scattered with lore, and it sort of feels like this game was designed with a much longer, more complex story in mind than what it was eventually actually given. (Maybe they their development was rushed towards the end, and they had to cut stuff out?) Regardless, if you like fantasy worlds, gorgeous art, unique characters and a meaningful story with turn-based battle mechanics and plenty of opportunity to explore the world, I would highly recommend. I, for one, will be replaying, and hoping for more stories set in this colorful, complex world that Ubisoft has created here.

Games have changed tremendously since I was a child in the early 90s. Then was a time of experimentation, freshness, and a lack of corporate handlers ready to strangle the life out of anyone who dared to be a rogue. I could chalk these recollections up to nostalgia and my young age at the time, but I don't think so. It was really different.
Today we've settled into a stale rut of standard genres: RPG, FPS, Sim, etc, and they all rehash the same principles, the same ideas, over and over. It's a stinking pile of zero innovation, a soulless churning out of reskin after reskin where gamers are forced to eat up the latest iteration of crap distributed by *insert mega publisher here.*
But X-Com is different. It feels new. Unique. And above all, it feels fun. After sinking a few hours into the game and becoming absorbed in its intricacies, I realized how I had almost forgotten that word in gaming. There hasn't been a game like it since the originals on floppy disk. And chances are if you're reading this than you're too young to have played them back when they were a big deal. So pick this one up.
Sure, it would be unfair to say that games never attempt to innovate anymore, but the vast majority of those that do just aren't GOOD. This isn't a bad thing- anything that deviates from the status quo will be met failure more often than success. But X-Com is the outlier. In recent years (read: the last 15 or so), the only games that have accomplished similar sentiments on my insides are gems like Eternal Darkness or Total War or MechWarrior when they were first released. Games that felt entirely different and had never before seen mechanics that just worked. Take note, that is some good company to be in.
X-Com's one drawback is the cheesiness. It runs so rampant throughout the game that I not only smell it, but taste it. But we all enjoy a little bit of cheese every now and then, and like a good Frenchman, the game manages to erase its stench with the cologne of absorbing gameplay.
I won't get in to the nuts and bolts of the game. I don't want to ruin it for you. Especially if you were too young to play the first. In a world of jaded gamers, sometimes the best route is to hear a game is awesome and then play it yourself. That way, you can be surprised once again. Take it. It's an experience rare enough in gaming these days.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game.  I bought it on sale figuring that there would be SOME gay (male) options but they are all gay male options!  Usually, these visual novels are fairly heterosexual.  There is sometimes one bisexual male character which doesn't give you many options if you want to romance a dude...  I've seen lesbians fairly often in these types of games as well as bisexual women.  It's refreshing to finally see a game that caters exclusively to gay men.  Anyone can play it, by all means, but you are going into the game knowing that there is only gay romances.  Some people complained about that which I find fairly ridiculous taking into account that there are SO MANY visual novels that cater to heterosexuals and that this is the first exclusively gay one that I've ever seen.
The plot isn't horrible but it could be better.  The only ''issues'' are typo's and a believable ''gay reality'' at times.  One speaks their ''peace'' for example and not their ''piece''.  It doesn't ruin the game, obviously.
Your character is fairly prudish so don't expect much action.  This didn't need to turn into a bad pornographic visual novel but you don't even see any characters kiss.  A bit of a let down.  There isn't enough romance to make up for it either.  I wonder if you had any gay writers work on this or if you kind of took a heterosexual model and changed the characters that would be females into males?  It doesn't entirely feel authentic to me.  Even when the characters couldn't like each other more in the romantic way, they remain cold and distant.  It's almost as if you wanted to make a gay romance game but not really go too deep in order to avoid angering some people.
It's still the best entirely gay visual novel that I've seen out there due to lack of choice.  I encourage my fellow gaymers and those who support the fact that there are people like me who make a viable enough audience to warrant making more exclusively gay visual novels to encourage this game and maybe we can get more and better content.

I really enjoyed Heirs and Graces.  The writing and story are excellent, the art is good (especially the backgrounds) and even the music fits perfectly.  The actual "game" part of the VN experience was innovative, too, and I appreciated the effort to make the skills line up with what you might be doing as a servant.
I might have chafed at the fact that I had a "schedule" confining my options, but combined with a helpful guide (provided by the developer, no less) to make sure I got what I wanted out of the game, it turned out to be a good way to keep the story moving.  Yeah, I might have liked to be more carefree with my time, or even to romance multiple characters at once, but the tradeoff was excellent pacing and keeping me invested in what was happening from start to finish.
Most of all though it was the story I recommend.  Marcel (that's you) is not the most likeable protagonist, but his development through the story (and through the romances) is worthwhile and meaningful.  Even if you aren't into the "game" part (the schedule and skills and stuff), you can use the guide to sort it out and then focus on the tale.
The romances themselves were all different and enjoyable, and I liked the fact that they developed over time.  The incremental experiences built up a more sincere conclusion than the typical rush to love.  If there's anything I
like about them, it would be that I felt forced to choose too early (at just 20% affection).  I would have liked to see more first, and it was a little strange to have my options fighting over me when things were only just beginning to bloom.  But as I said earlier, I think that was to keep the pacing strong; the balance between the main story, a romance and the forward march of time seemed just right.
Finally, I'd like to personally thank the developer for taking a chance on a BL-only game.  That's not to say the game would have been less appealing with more options (I'm all for inclusivity, especially with romances), but since it
exclusive I felt like it was made just for fans like me.

So, I've been on a BL dating sim kind of kick, and have been searching everywhere. Heard about this one and was happy to see that it was on steam. This game was an absolute treat to play, and I've played it multiple times since, despite exhausting all the choices. So, let me get into the pros and cons of the game.
Pros:
Characters- The characters were all beautiful in their own way. I really got into each of their routes, tearing up a bit a few times. My roommate even got a kick out was first my least favorite character turned favorite character...A certain preppy, perverted know-it-all elf prince. Anyways, the characters were very well thought out and I enjoyed watching my character growing along with the character he chose to romance. Even the minor characters that become friends were wonderfully thought out.
Setting- I enjoyed the setting, despite the lack of choices on where to go. Everything kept with the time period and nothing seemed out of place. Though I thought it was funny when we would be making a cake or sandwhich or something and suddenly BAM! carrying soup and bread. It'd be nice to see a change in certain drawings, though I understand that can be difficult.
Plot- The plot was wonderful, if not a little heartbreaking. I don't want to say too much, because I don't want to spoil anything. This is just something you have to play and find out for yourself.
Cons:
The Schedule- This game is based on a weekly schedule where you perform jobs to gain experience. They kind of just throw you into it. If you don't see the help button, which I didn't the first time I played and failed everything.  You also get  a chance to turn off the other characters, making sure any and all points you receive will go to your choice and not bother with the random inputs of the other choices. I just wish it was a little more informative when you first start.
Reputation- I hated this the first time I played, and continued to stress about it throughout the game. Besides your man, reputation is the most important thing in the entire game. This is going to decide whether you're going to get the bad ending or whether you'll be the sole heir or not. I also didn't like stressing to get my reputation to 90, where you'll see the sexy scene or your man.
Choices- I don't mean the men in the game, I mean the choices that will affect your relationship. I notice this in almost every game. The choices seem to be fairly obvious in most instances, if you actually pay attention to the one you choose.  I like to  have a little difficulty when I see the choices. I want to sit there and think. I just didn't get that with most of the choices.
Overall, I loved this game and recommend it to anyone who enjoys BL games with a wonderful story. 8/10, still playing every chance I get!

Summary: I enjoy this game but this is clearly a work in progress. If you were hoping to buy early access to an almost finished game than these aren't the droids your looking for.
Pros:

Cons:
♦Crafting system is more like a 'research' system because it takes forever even with 4 guys helping. Seriously from a design standpoint this should be broken down into 2 seperate things and crafting should be more instaneous and item based. Researching should be more time and skill based. Example: I spent 1.5 days learning (researching) how to craft armor. Why does each additional armor take 1.5 days, why not just take my materials and make it instant?
♦There are some tough spots that might kill you, but right now it's very 'grindy' without much tension. If you go play their ArmorGames flash version I think that version had better tension.

Tips as of v0.54: Start waves as a fast as you can, spam where the button appears even. This will help you build up 4000+ ammo. Don't wander too far from base, just go out 1-2 and then do 1-2 more buildings on your way back. Goto buildings with (!) above them, rescue the guy and then put him to work on the crafting table. Level up 4 guys as crafters and 4 guys as scavengers. Give lots of HP to the scavengers.
Have fun and good luck.

Tower wars is a steampunk, competitive, Tower Defense game that challenges the preconceptions of the genre by putting you in control of not only your towers, but the lemmings that throw themselves at the defenses of your opponent.
It requires maintaining a delicate balance between building your towers and upgrading (and purchasing) your troops.  Focus too much on your towers, and your enemy will overwhelm you with a superior economy; but focus too much on creating an army and your defenses will fall to even the puniest wave.
The ecnomy of the game requires two currencies:  Gold (used to purchase troops, unlock new troops, and build and upgrade towers) which is mined through randomly placed mines that must be upgraded, and Battle Points (used to upgrade toops and mines) which is gained through sending troops into battle.  The interdependency of these two currencies further requires maintaining a delicate balance between offense and defense.
Battles can be decisive and quick if the skills are mismatched; but if you find a good opponent, then you'll find yourself in for a campaign of attrition which could take upwards of two hours.  It's a high stakes tower defense game that offers a high amount of replayability; but the lack of map content (three total) leaves a lot to be desired when it comes to diversity of content.

Really great foundation. Interesting gameplay and awesome potential for strategy. I know it's early access, so I'm not complaining, but it's definitely lacking polish. I think it's a solid beginning and has a lot of potential to grow into a very well developed strategy game.
Here are the issues I feel need to be addressed:
1. Difficulty. The game starts out great. But after a few hours of play, it becomes repetitive. There needs to be a sharper increase in difficulty. Faster zombies, more resilient zombies, more zombies, new types of zombies, that throw a curve ball at you. As is, once your characters are leveled up a bit and have good equipment, there's not a lot of need to place them anywhere specific, you can just walk into a room and clear it.
2. Harsher limit to actions per day. The timed system in place right now takes all need for supplies or sending specific characters on runs. Instead of splitting the group to hit two buildings in a day and risk having your smaller teams be overrun, You can almost hit as many buildings as you want before your group "uses" supplies. By the time the supplies are deducted, you have such a huge stockpile it's basically a non existant feature of the game. There's no threat or danger to running out of supplies. This ties in with the difficulty increase.
3. More Random encounters. Obviously there is more coming as this is still a work in progress. This suggestion is more me looking forward to interesting situations being introduced into the game. My two cents would be to include aggressive zombies. Have the base camp be under threat of being attacked so players need to keep "guards" there as well as send some characters on runs.
Overall, great work so far, but I'm looking forward to what will be coming!

I played this and the original Battlefront on PS2 and I just had to get a Steam copy. I wanted to see one of my favorite Star Wars games with better textures and mods to enjoy it all over again.
There is nothing like choosing a faction and conquering the opposing faction while doing so as different battle units and heroes/villains; playing as Darth Vader slicing and force-choking rebel scum never gets boring. You can pilot AT-ATs and TIE Fighters along with several other vehicles including those from the Clone Wars era. There is a campaign based upon the story of a clone trooper all the way to the transformation of storm trooper.
Galactic Conquest is an exciting mode where you choose an era and a faction and then attempt to conquer the galaxy; you must earn points to purchase new unit types and bonuses to help you dominate each planet.
Engage in space battles over different planets; you can choose to attack other units in space or try to bring down the mother ship from the inside and/or out. I always found landing inside the enemy's hangar to be an interesting feat where you can attack units before they board their fighters and destroy the insides of the ship.
Instant Action is another mode where you can choose from several maps with different factions where some battles might not have taken place. There is a battle mode called "hunt" which usually allows you to control the planet's indigenous tribes like the Jawa, Tusken Raiders, Wampas, Ewok, etc.
This is a must for any Star Wars fan and anyone who enjoys a good FPS/TPS hybrid. Upon getting this, check out the mods available. There is one that adds the KOTOR era including its heroes/villains like Revan, Darth Malak, Darth Traya, and many more. I recommend playing this before the new Battlefront developed by DICE is released.

Games have changed tremendously since I was a child in the early 90s. Then was a time of experimentation, freshness, and a lack of corporate handlers ready to strangle the life out of anyone who dared to be a rogue. I could chalk these recollections up to nostalgia and my young age at the time, but I don't think so. It was really different.
Today we've settled into a stale rut of standard genres: RPG, FPS, Sim, etc, and they all rehash the same principles, the same ideas, over and over. It's a stinking pile of zero innovation, a soulless churning out of reskin after reskin where gamers are forced to eat up the latest iteration of crap distributed by *insert mega publisher here.*
But X-Com is different. It feels new. Unique. And above all, it feels fun. After sinking a few hours into the game and becoming absorbed in its intricacies, I realized how I had almost forgotten that word in gaming. There hasn't been a game like it since the originals on floppy disk. And chances are if you're reading this than you're too young to have played them back when they were a big deal. So pick this one up.
Sure, it would be unfair to say that games never attempt to innovate anymore, but the vast majority of those that do just aren't GOOD. This isn't a bad thing- anything that deviates from the status quo will be met failure more often than success. But X-Com is the outlier. In recent years (read: the last 15 or so), the only games that have accomplished similar sentiments on my insides are gems like Eternal Darkness or Total War or MechWarrior when they were first released. Games that felt entirely different and had never before seen mechanics that just worked. Take note, that is some good company to be in.
X-Com's one drawback is the cheesiness. It runs so rampant throughout the game that I not only smell it, but taste it. But we all enjoy a little bit of cheese every now and then, and like a good Frenchman, the game manages to erase its stench with the cologne of absorbing gameplay.
I won't get in to the nuts and bolts of the game. I don't want to ruin it for you. Especially if you were too young to play the first. In a world of jaded gamers, sometimes the best route is to hear a game is awesome and then play it yourself. That way, you can be surprised once again. Take it. It's an experience rare enough in gaming these days.

This is a review for the base game, played in single player.
If I had to describe Dying Light in one sentence it would be "Dead Island meets Far Cry 3 with a smattering of Assassin's Creed". This is a compliment as it combines some of the best parts of each game.
In the game you play Crane who (for reasons I will leave unspoiled) finds himself rampaging around a zombie-infested city using parkour to move around the environment and any metal object he can find to slaughter the undead. The parkour is very natural and fluid and ties together well with a very physical and satisfying combat system.
The game is genuinely tense as even the basic enemies do not go down easily and, if you lose concentration, you can easily become mobbed and die. The enemies appear to level in a smart fashion - normal biters gain health as you get stronger but special enemies appear to gain health more slowly. This means you feel as though you're always under threat throughout the game whilst still feeling the benefit of that new weapon when you face a larger, deadlier version of the infected. At night the game is scary as even the best-equipped character cannot stand toe-to-toe with the enemies and must run. This leads to some very thrilling moments where you are trying to avoid detection or trying to escape the horrors of the night.
As you level up you gain access to more powerful weapons but, more importantly, you gain new skills to use in combat and whilst traversing the city, widening your tactical options. This feels very organic to begin with a provides a well-paced learning curve. After the mid-game I felt as though I had most of the skills I wanted and was taking filler skills I'd decided to skip earlier on, but this is a minor complaint.
Crane is very well voice acted and I mostly enjoyed listening him interact with the city's inhabitants as he could be forceful, witty, disgusted or panicked and often reacted in the way I was reacting as a player. The NPCs are also fairly well voiced and fleshed out, although the main antagonist may feel a bit too familiar if you played Far Cry 3. Side quests were also a pleasure to complete as they included some truly memorable and interesting characters and situations. The main plot is not as strong and seems to lose focus and cohesion on occasion but is still enjoyable.
Death is fairly well handled. On death you lose some xp towards your next upgrade but otherwise you aren't punished harshly. This is just as well because misjudging a jump can lead to instant-death falls (this adds to the tension of running around the rooftops of the city) and human enemies with guns can put you down quickly if you don't use your skills, the environment and inventory wisely.
Finally, the game is very pretty and weather, lighting and so on used to great effect.
Overall, this is a fun and pretty action game with enough depth to hold interest and strong enough characters, stories and voice-acting to be memorable.

I'm going to be honest, this game is a double-edged sword.
In the beginning when I first started playing this game (the first 3 chapters or so) I absolutely loved it. I appreciated controlling three different characters that emphasized the main points of GoT. There was political intrigue, there was war, there was venturing out into the wilds of the North; ultimately it was great.
However things started to change. The choices got more dramatic, but ultimately didn't do much for the storyline. While I understand that GoT isn't necessarily the happiest of shows, when I play a video game I still want to try and succeed or beat the odds. When I finished the game, I did not feel satisfied. I felt like I wanted to go redo the entire thing and try and change things. But then I realized it didn't matter anyways. No matter what I did, the outcome would be the same. In a game where making choices is the ultimate goal, I need to know that my choices will make a difference. That they will matter. Not that they will be brushed under the rug and used to create a set-up ending for the second season.
Overall, did I enjoy myself? Yes. I can't say I hate the whole game just because of the ending. The story was intriguing, I played each episode in one sitting because I was so consumed by it. But, at the same time, I don't feel good about it. This game leaves you unsatisfied and frustrated, and I guess if you are prepared for that from the start, then be my guest and purchase this game. But if you have any hesitation, I'm warning you now, be prepared for what awaits you.

I have an ongoing love-hate relationship with FTL.
On one hand, it's a brilliantly designed semi-strategy roguelike game where you take control of a spacecaft and it's crew. You'll visit star systems, fight enemy spacecraft, upgrade your ship, and make little "do you help this person or that person" kind of decisions. The music is FANTASTIC and the learning curve is very mild. The storyline is very simple, but it gives reason to the way the game plays, why you have to be picky in what systems you visit, and such. And the game gives me the vibe that the designers didn't want to make a best-seller: They just wanted to make a fun game, regardless of profit margins.
On the other hand, it's a roguelike, which means that you'll suddenly be completely overwhelmed by enemies and lose. And it's not one of those losses where you think "maybe if I did this differently.." No, you just get completely blown away with no chance of escape. And I swear this game "cheats"...I'll be attacking some lowly enemy craft and my maximum experience gunner will miss with a missile. Then another. Then another. Meanwhile, the enemy shoots my ship twice with a junk weapon and blows two holes in the hull.
A friend used a cheat and gave himself a ship hull that could take unlimited damage and maximum money (called "scrap"). He still lost because the game found some other way to overpower his ship and crew. I've come close to beating it, but only by a thread.
Yes, this game makes me want to break my keyboard in half. Then I'll have to buy another because I'll want to play again a few hours later.

I will say that I loved most of the Telltale games and I'm still thinking they are good. But I can't say that this one is as good as I expected. It had potential but I think it's the worst telltale game I've bought so far.
I don't recommend this game for two reasons mainly: 1) you're choices are often meaningless and in this kind of game is a very big downside; at first you may think that if you had acted in a different way maybe things could have been different, but that's not true for most of the important choices that define your story. 2) the story/plot is full of holes. I personally didn't like the finale that I find ridiculous, but that's just my opinion. The fact is that it's actually incredibly stupid how the ending turns out, that no matter what are your choices things will go in the same way (only small things change). Regardless of what you chose to do there will be always an excuse for something to happen despite all of you preparations. [Pressing Q or E it's useless most of the time]. Moreover I found boring and annoying the fact that the bad guys win most of the times in absurd ways, often you don't even get to know the process that led to their win. Good guys find themselves striving to achieve even for the smallest success while their enemies seem to have already everything and to be one step ahead. So I found the story to be quite unbalanced lacking a realistic approach depending on the situation (in my opinion there is only a character [Tuttle] that seems to have an acceptable and balanced storyline).
Don't get me wrong, I didn't expect a fairy tale with an "happy" ending (I know how GoT works), anyway I felt the game as an unrealistic experience in terms of plot. Of course good guys can't always win (I would have disliked that as much!) but I find also absurd that the good guys are always unlocky or held back by some sort of problems while bad guys seem always to have good luck and they find their plans turning successful (you'll never find them failing 100% in any situation). Often it feels like the game leads you to failure no matter what you do. Even if you like diehard games I think this it's quite disappointing.
As I've already said this game had potential and it's not a complete failure, but if I knew how it was I wouldn't have bought it. (4/10)

Another solid entry in the Romance VN genre from Winter Wolves. I applaud them for making a BxB exclusive title. It was refreshing to see something new.
The plot is straightforward – you are Marcel, a young man whose mother was abandoned by her titled lover while she was pregnant. Marcel takes a job as a servant in his father’s household, but is quickly found out and his father offers him a deal; if Marcel can prove himself worthy, he can inherit the estate when the old man dies. This is where stat building comes in – you perform tasks to gain skill points. There are skill checks as a part of the story, and if you pass them you gain Reputation. Tasks also help you gain relationship points with the four romanceable characters. With enough Reputation points you can become the heir and end up with the man of your dreams.
I’m not usually a big fan of skill building in VNs (takes too long, I’d rather be reading!) but they do a good job in this of not making it feel too grindy. The story scenes are plentiful, and almost every one of them comes with a dialog choice (the best part of playing a VN : )
I wish the “sexy scenes” had been a little more sexy. I was expecting something more explicit (based on having played Heileen 3) and the most you get here are a few kisses and some (very attractive) bare chests. I did like that the focus was very much on the relationship between the characters – they choose to be together because they love each other (not just physical attraction) but I still wish it had gone a bit further.
All and all it’s a solid romance VN with a unique subplot where the main character gets to know the Father who abandoned him. If you like other Winter Wolves titles, or romance VNs in general, this is worth picking up.

TL;DR: boys love visual novel with interesting characters and overly simple game mechanics. Recommended for yaoi fans and fans of other Winter Wolves games.
The story is structured around a simple stat-raising simulation with a weekly schedule and scripted events. The main plot around Marcel's relationship with his father is the same no matter what romance you pursue, and the romance is more of a side plot. Raising skills is necessary to pass skill checks.
Events occur on certain days no matter what you have scheduled (e.g., you don't have to be in the library on Monday of Week 14 to trigger an event with Eloy; you'll just show up there). Skill checks are the same for each playthrough, as well, and so the strategy is very simple:
These design choices make the game friendlier to fans of pure visual novels, but they also make it kind of annoying to play through the game multiple times to see everyone's romance. Failing a skill check just gets you a few different lines, and the bad endings (other than
) aren't very interesting, so once you know how to "win," there's nothing new mechanically or strategically, and the simulation parts are just dull busywork. There's also no "successful" romance ending if you don't inherit, which doesn't make sense for characters who aren't tied to the estate.
The art is nice, although it seems like the artist has trouble drawing hands. (Marcel's seem oddly small, and most other characters have their hands behind their back, in gloves, or otherwise hidden.) The sprites have different costumes and a good variety of expressions. For some reason the sprites don't show blushing when it's mentioned in the text, though, which disappointed me, because blushing sprites are the cutest. I'd also have liked more than two CGs per character route, especially since Borges and Vincent's "sexy" CGs seemed very out of place, more an explicit reward for the player than something that makes sense in the story. Winter Wolves games typically just have a kiss CG at the end, so I didn't really expect more, but I think it would add a lot, especially considering the game's price.
The story is set in Aravorn, a vaguely medieval fantasy world, and mentions characters and events from
and
. However,
isn't an RPG adventure with epic battles, and instead is confined to a noble estate and a small town. Elves exist and the doctor uses magic spells and potions to treat patients, but other fantasy elements don't come into play. I actually like exploring how "normal" people live in a fantastic world, and look forward to seeing more of the setting in future WW games.
All the romances are BxB, which is a first for WW. Sexual preference isn't a major theme or source of conflict, but one love interest is explicitly bi, one is explicitly gay, and the protagonist might be gay, so the "straight except for you" yaoi trope is avoided. Marcel, the protagonist, has a developed personality (and a bit of snarky narration) and isn't just a player self-insert. He's inexperienced in relationships, but not shy and passive about it. The romances all have an open sort of "let's see where this goes from here" ending, rather than a conclusive happily ever after, but I like the realistic awkwardness of that, and it fits with Marcel's character. If you're avoiding the game just because
don't want to romance guys, I'd urge you to give it a chance. (There's a
at Winter Wolves' website.)

The game is really good, but I have a couple of suggestions:
- I think at the moment it's way too easy. I'm able to hold off a block at "Dangerous" level including a boss zombie with only 2 survivors with no problem at all. I now have something like 15,000 ammo and 300 supplies and an insane amount of weapons and building material. Also, I don't know about anyone else but I've never had the need to build turrets.
- Going through blocks that you have already cleared is incredibly tedious... you're needed to hunt zombies in the building even though you have done it already? I don't see the point in having to do it a second time, especially if there's one zombie left and you're out on a wild goose chase to find it is pretty agrivating. Maybe after a random amount of days those blocks can become repopulated with zombies again?
- I really dislike that you have to always return back to your HQ in order to save progress. I think there should be an option to set up camp at the block that you have just cleared, maybe have a limit per in-game day that you can do this.
- I hate that you can switch equipment mid-clearing. It should be that the weapons that the survivors are already using to shoot zombies just stay that way until it's clear.
- Just a glitch I've come across when clearing zombies in the merchant block. I headed to a merchant block that I had already cleared and found that there were two merchants?? I couldn't talk to the second one or anything, it was just his playermodel standing there. No guards, just the merchant.
- It'd be great to see more variety/customisation in the survivors. Maybe like weapon specialisations, such as rifles or shotguns. Or even talent trees.
All this being said, the game is really good and would recommend playing this game, and any other Infectonator games, it's just a couple of things that I think could be improved.

I can kind of understand why everyone is sooooo in love with this game. The graphics are amazingly beautiful, the soundscape is marvellous and there is a pretty little story going on. Oh yes, I heard so many positive reviews about this game – basically everybody is enchanted by it! But I am not.
As a player, I do like lovely art in a game and of course a good score brings it to life. In this game all this just was wasted: the gameplay itself was so boring that I didn’t enjoy exploring the beautiful world after the first hour or so. You just basically walk (and later fly) around pretty aimlessly. You can find treasures, carry out little quests and do some fighting alongside the main storyline. And the fights were the worst, because they were painfully manual and boring. Same thing over and over again. Thank god you didn’t actually have to fight that much if you didn’t want to. Because oh yes, there were battles everywhere.
Usually I’m all for exploring and doing all the quests and finding all the items. This time I just wanted the experience to end as fast as possible. This time I didn’t do all the side quests and didn’t find all the items and didn’t fight almost any battles. I just didn’t want to bother. I’m sad to admit this, because this game had so much potential.
Let’s talk about the music. It fit perfectly well to the game world. It was as pretty as the graphics in the game, it created lovely atmosphere. Piano and violin sounded so beautiful in the score. But it was getting very repetitive: after some time you just got very numb about it. It didn’t offer anything suprising or new. The same thing just went on and on and on… And the same thing you could say about the whole game.
So, in conclusion. I do understand why so many are enchanted by this. It has a good combo of things and it is not a game with horrible quality. Sadly this just wasn’t a game for me. For me this game was just plain boring.

Double Action: Boogaloo is a fun little shooter. The game is very fun, and can be addictive, it's rapid pace, and utter moments of hilarity will keep you entertained for some time. The game offers 1 mode on 7 maps. The game mode itself is pretty standard you shoot people, and you get points, however you get more points for how "stylish" you are. Another way the game keeps itself from being boring is the objectives that randomly pop up on screen, whether it be you racing to certain points, or collecting a briefcase. Of course you can just ignore them if you want, but going after them makes it all the more satisfying when you win, and gain a bunch of points. If you really want to jump around all over the shooting at people, this is the game for you.

Wow, this thing is almost 13 years old now. I can't believe I never played it before.
Even as a "retro game" it beats most of the games released nowadays.
Graphics is old, but for a game released in 2004 its way better than expected. One thing I noticed straight away is how good facial animations are. I don't remember any other game had that at the time.
As a first person shooter there is so many little things this game does great. Starting with a physics engine, I can easily say that never have I ever played something on this level. Gravity gun (weapon you get in-game) allows you to kill enemies in huge amount of ways with various objects. Other than that, you can interact with almost any object in-game and use it in some way.
All of the levels are designed with great attention to detail. You can never get bored exploring all of the corners looking for supplies and ammo. It is not just "run and gun" as most FPS games are today. Some of the levels require you to use a boat, buggy, crane etc. There are also small physics puzzles you can stumble upon that require to be solved in order to proceed. All of this just shows how powerful this game engine is. It's a shame Valve doesn't make more games like this.
Even though Civ VI is already out this is a perfect cheaper option if money is tight. Great for beginners to those of this genre but still complex for said beginners.

Worst community in a game I've ever seen... and I just came from League of Legends - now that says something. It seems as though every player just doesn't care about anyone. If you're grinding at a decent location, you're either going to get karma bombed by a lower level (who even if you kill they just come back because there's no real punishment by being PK'd) or get killed by a higher leveled/more geared player who thinks they're a saint because they're more powerful than the majority in a video game. It doesn't matter if you were there first, if you're new, or you have daily grinding hour on - no one cares. Let's say you can defend your grinding position... more than likely the opposer(s) are simply going to declare war on your guild so they don't lose karma by slaughtering you and your people. Guild wars are a joke and consists more of pathetic drama than you think. Here's the question: How do the creators expect the weak to become stronger if the strong keep taking from them? Morally, this is wrong and pathetic. It's all fun in games for Olvia servers (safe servers for those who just started), but when the time is up, you have to face the real world in the real servers where the weak scatter around to pick up scraps like starving scavengers and most of the strong feed off everything they can because they're greedy selfish♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I understand I'm going on and on about this, but I'm trying to paint an image. Yeah, I know there's a lot more to the game other than grinding but if you want to become stronger, grinding is the way to go.
I'm merely writing this review not in hopes to review every aspect and feature of the game (because there's already enough reviews for that), but to bring light on this topic and expose the terrible community.
As my recommendation stands, I do not recommend this to the average gamer. Don't waste your time. Although, if Black Desert Online really peaks your interest, then go ahead and prepare for the worst on the road of growth where RNG may also deterimine your fate. May RNGesus be with you.
**EDIT - I feel like I need to add in the fact that Black Desert Online is still quite new, especially to North America. There's a lot of upcoming content and changes, so it's safe to expect the game will become better through time.

I recognize that you can't get the full sense of an MMORPG after just a few days of playing. However, if a game fails to capture interest after the initial days, what is the point of continuing?
The combat in this game is visually stunning. It reminds me of dynasty warriors - great combo moves, lots of sparkles. But the fact that I haven't even come close to dying in 30 levels (I haven't even had to use a potion) is not a good sign.  The enemies you fight are all one-shot-kills - I've heard that it gets harder at level 50, but I shouldn't have to grind boring inconsequential enemies for that many levels in order to get to a challenging part of the game.
The questing is... confusing. There are waypaths which point you to your destination... but it becomes unclear which quest you are tracking, and often times the paths don't update when you surpass a certain stage of the quest.  Moreover, MOST of the quests I have been on have not been combat related at all - dozens of quests later, I've picked some corn, chopped down a couple trees... and killed some boars for meat.  Of the few combat quests I have had, none have led me to interesting areas, just chunks of mobs clustered randomly in the world which I immediately demolish with a single hit.
It feels like there is no consequence to level - I've updated my main weapon maybe twice, the last time being probably around level 10, and I haven't noticed at all. Everything dies in one hit.
The crafting is also boring. And I've played runescape - I'm used to long repetitive grinds. But at least it felt like I was getting somewhere in that game, all those years ago. If you asked me what my crafting levels are in Black Desert, I couldn't tell you - because it doesn't seem to matter at all.
I thoroughly enjoy how my toon's breasts bounce unnecessarily when the model loads in on the login screen, though. After all, where would we be without every single character looking like they came straight off of a dakimakura pillow (males included).

If you have ever played the original XCOM then you already have this in your library. And you should, because it's the best adaptation of the original since Terror From the Deep.
If you've never played an XCOM game before, here's a brief description:
The world is getting invaded by aliens and you're the commander of the team of soldiers from around the world sent to stop them.  This is a turn based strategy game, meaning that you'll take a turn and then the computer will take a turn.  You'll control a squad of up to six varied soldiers taking on a variety of mission types, all with the eventual goal of stopping the alien threat. Each soldier has one of several classes (like a Sniper or Support medic) with special skills for that class that make your job easier the more you level up.
