Actual review.
-Yes the engine is a bit... tempermental, but as far as I'm aware the engine is based on similar grounds as the Titan Quest engine, though admitedly more updated, but when it plays smooth and doesn't suffer micro stutters, oh god, it plays like a goddess of beautyy's silky smooth, freshly shaved and moisturised legs.
-Dual class or Pure class, is an absoloute joy, warriors in heavy armour kitted with an eldritch hound and crow is the most horrifying idea every to grace the ARPG genre. Personaly play an absoloutely destructive Warlock who's magic missiles tear through undead flesh like a newly sharpened blade through spider silk.
-Devotion, whoa baby, this idea should be in more games, clearing shrines awards 1 devotion point which allows you to further tweak and augment with your character with percentage increases and some amazing passives and abilities. Never before has a foe been so fearful to strike as the spear of the heavens smites the last demon who struck you.
-Graphicly, it's not the most impressive, it's grimy, it's dark, but it is GRIM dawn after all, the general art style is simple, but effective, each class archetype has very thematic armour sets and each looks fitting for the setting and the classes.
Enemies also explode very, very satisfyingly, so let your murderous side reign as the blood and gibs cover the ground beneath your feet as you cleave, cast and detonate your way through Grim Dawn.
-Sound design is beautiful, it fits wonderfully and is incredibly immersive compared to other ARPGs on the markets overly charicatural sounds, music is incredibly thematic and fits the setting amazingly.
-World feels relatively large, BUT for those too lazy who don't want to wade through corpses, demons and brigands, there is a system of portals traversing each area, but they must be discovered beforehand, they aren't usually very far from the main road and main quest areas.
- DLC is not a required purchase as characters are utterly seperate from characters created in the ''story mode''.
- Lot's of replayability in terms of class combos, BUT seems limited, would really benefit from a dedicated mod scene and steam workshop in future to allow for new classes / zones/ quests/ limits etc with easy installation provided with the workshop,...

How am I going to write a review without mentioning Diablo (I & II) and Torchlight? Probably not. Being a huge fan of those franchises, Grim Dawn felt both familiar and refreshing at the same time. It starts off as a pretty straight-forward experience: slay monsters, level up, choose a class and some skills, repeat. At level 10 you choose a second class, forcing you to spend your hard-earned skill points more carefully. Then you start discovering shrines, relics and augmentations, enabling advanced character customization. After messing up my first character, I am now adventuring as a dual-wielding gunslinger Demolitionist-Soldier that specializes in Fire and Poison attacks. Grim Dawn is my favorite game of 2016 and I'll probably be playing it for a long time!
+ Great atmosphere and graphics
+ Simple, yet deep character customization through skills, gear and devotion.
+ Four-player online multiplayer
+ Rogue-lite dungeons for the occassional challenge
+ Difficulty setting is perfect: challenging without being punishing, Hardcore mode is optional.
+ Huge amount of loot, including Legendary items and craftables
+ Interesting classes and NG+ for high replay value
- Pretty standard story
- The occasional FPS-drop, even on high-end machines
Whether on discount or full-price, I wholeheartedly recommend buying Grim Dawn if you're a ARPG-fan!

Far Cry Primal is an action-adventure video game.  The game is not a sequal to Far Cry 4.  The game is developed and produced by Ubisoft.
I really have enjoyed the story so far.  The game is set in 10,000 BC, during the beginning of the Mesolithic and Epipaleolithic periods.  Players take on the role of a lone surviving hunter, Takkar, who makes his way to Oros and sets out to build his own tribe.  Takkar learns to tame animals in his quests.  He eventually rises to power and leads his tribe.
I should note that the game is in subtitles for the fictional language used.  At first I was not too enthused about the use of subtitles, but after playing the game I really did not mind.  Although I have to argue that by taking on the role of Takkar, I shouldn't need subtitles to understand what I am saying.
The game is designed with difficulty levels in mind.  The April 12 patch to Primal has introduced Survivor Mode for those that want something much more difficult to play.  Elements, stamina fatigue, permadeath for trained beasts, more difficult taming process for the stronger beasts, skill trees reworked for difficulty, and the option for permadeath for your character.
The crafting system is very similiar to Far Cry 4.  The system is easy and in no way overwhelming.  It is simplistic yet ample enough to provide plenty of items such as weapons, equipment, medical items, and food to help you through your adventures or Oros.  Players must craft weapons using the materials scavenged while playing such as wood and stone.
The gameplay feels very familiar to anyone who has played Far Cry 3 or 4.  The controls work very well with most keys able to be bound. I could not bind my Cap Locks Lock key which was disappointing but I think I can manage another bind.  The player can dirrectly control the owl which beocme a very useful tool to scout enemies.  Transitioning into the animal controls is fluid and works well.  The owl feels very similiar to flying a helo in FC 4.  The gameplay is very smooth and I really do not have any complaints with the controls, at least in terms of using a keyboard and mouse.
FC Primal was built on the Dunia 2 Engine which was used for Far Cry 3 (2012), Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon (2013), Far Cry 4 (2014), and now Far Cry Primal (2016).  While the engine looks good, it is dated and the visuals suffer for it.  Although aestheticly pleasing in many ways, the enviromental fidelity suffers as does the character models.  Why Ubisoft did not pass the AnvilNext 2.0 game engine which Assassin's Creed Unity (2014), Assassin's Creed Syndicate (2015), Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Siege (2015), and For Honor (2016) are built on or perhaps even the Snowflake Engine which Tom Clancy's The Division is built on is dumbfounding.
The game initially had no SLI/Crossfire support.  My fps would double if I force my system to run on a single GTX 980 rather than in tripple SLI.  The patches and Nvidia drivers have resolved this issue, although there is not true sli support that benefits using multiple cards.  But at least sli is now running as good as a single card.
The April 12 patch introduces a HD texture pack for those that want to run Primal on Ultra & 4k.
I really enjoy playing Far Cry Primal and do recommend it if you are a fan of the series, even with the changes such as the time period, weapons, and the lack of vehicles the game stands on its own and is very satisfying to play.

For me, Dying Light is hit-or-miss.
I have completed Dead Island/Riptide several times and I've preordered the Definitive versions. I was extremely excited to play DL after thoroughly enjoying DI and I thought it would be one of the best games I'd ever play. I was very disappointed. Techland described DL as the game DI was meant to be.........not quite.
PROS:
- Melee combat is upgraded and is quite fun. I have mildly more fun chopping the undead down than I did in DI/Riptide.
- Graphics are an improvement over DI/Riptide. It's certainly flashier-looking than the original DI/Riptide.
- Modding support is included, although actual quality of said mods is negligible. If you're looking for zombie masterpieces, you're better off sticking with Left 4 Dead 2.
- The "sound attracts zombies" feature adds a bit of "realism" and increases immersion, reminiscent of The Walking Dead. I liked that. You have to be vewy, vewy quiet! They're hunting wabbits!
CONS (where do I even start???):
- While the parkour can be fun and you'll get meatheads praising it nonstop, it is an "extremely overrated" feature which does not even belong in a ZOMBIE game. You're supposed to shoot/chop them up, not run away from them. What is the point of having such an elaborate crafting/weaponry system if you parkour away from the zombies 90% of the time?
It's a waste of dev time & resources to create all those weapons & crafting system if everyone just jumps over the zombies most of the time. The parkour itself is far from polished.
- It's one of the worst-optimized games I've ever played. It's not mid-low rig-friendly. Certainly not an ideal setup for a game where you have to rely on quick reflexes to survive. And don't even get me started on the ghastly Chromatic Aberration which people had to wait for over a year to be removed.
- After everything Techland learned during the production of DI/Riptide, you'd think they could come up with better melee combat features than just the running dropkick. Seriously, how many of those can you do before you get sick to death of them?
- The firearms combat system is watered down and vastly inferior to DI/Riptide. While playing the originals, I enjoyed nothing more than finding a shotgun and just blasting everything in my path to pieces. The guns in DL look like toys and handle even worse than toys. A recent patch has practically castrated them as well, rendering them almost useless.
- You're stuck in the same city for the duration of the entire game (excluding DLC). To me that's extremely boring. DI/Riptide wins hands down on this matter with 4 awesome acts & different regions for each one. It kept the pace fresh & kept you engaged with awesome visuals & varying detailed environments as opposed to the same old boring slums of Harran for the entire main storyline.
15% into the story and I was already forcing myself to continue due to the visual boredom that is Dying Light. Making it worse is the fact that I have nothing new to look forward to. If I got bored with the Resort, I knew I'd be heading to Port Moresby soon enough and I could speedrun past Act 1 in subsequent playthroughs. From there to the Jungle and to the Prison Island ---> Palanai.
But utter blandness led me to quit playing DL for at least a month. After a Walking Dead marathon I got the itch again......only to make it past a couple sidequests that I had half-completed over a month earlier. And that was it for me again.
- You're stuck controlling the same bland character throughout the whole thing. The early teasers showing various different characters implied that you'll have multiple choices. That is NOT the case. You're stuck with a bland government stooge playing Mata Hari (without the kinky stuff). Crane SUCKS.
ON THE FENCE:
- I would've enjoyed a proper day/night cycle. The only gripe I have with this one is that time flies far too fast for my liking. I hear Mass Effect: Andromeda will have a time cycle as well. Let's see how that one turns out.
CONCLUSION:
Build yourself a maxed-out rig before attempting to play this one. If you enjoy speedrunning through a game, then this is the game for you as the parkour system will allow you to complete all quests without needing to kill a single shambling corpse. If you're looking for a proper zombie game, give Dying Light a miss.
As for me, I think I'm finally done with the game at around 20% story progress. There's only so many zombies I can chop in half horizontally & vertically with my modded katana before I'm overwhelmed by the visual blandness that is Harran. Overall it's a significant downgrade from Dead Island/Riptide. I did NOT get my money's worth.

+The "world" design is spot on

The negative:
-Choices don't matter for the most part, the dialogue is slightly changed and the game literally forced me into a choice I didn't pick because the story had to roll on
-The graphic fidelity is below average which makes characters seem made out of plastic
-no conclusion to most of the story so there is set up to a sequel

FTL: Faster Than Light describes itself as a
. Now, while I don't like that word to be used lightly - as many indies are doing lately -, I'll have to admit that it really fits this game well.
The premise and goal are simple: you're the captain of a Federation space-cruiser, and you have to deliver critical information that will allow your faction to vanquish the Rebels once and for all. Sounds simple.
I can't say I was really good at this game when I first began playing: it took me a shameful lot of hours to achieve a victory on Easy. But if there's one great thing about FTL, it's the replay value. Game after game, loss after loss, I understood more and more of the mechanics. Then I unlocked more ships. Then I beat the game employing a wide range of different strategies. There's no stopping the fun, and if there is, a decently-sized modding community will do its best to help.

Pros:
-The game is hilarious. The amount of jokes in this game is extensive and the timing for them are excellent.
-The characters in the game are interesting, especially Penultimo. The local and foreign leaders are much more fleshed out then the previous game and have their own personalities.
-Tasks are added. Occasionally you will be asked by foreign powers and the local factions to do something for them. These allow you to get greater support from your political parties and economic benefits you otherwise would ignore.
-RPG features are added. The Swiss bank account rolls over and the traits for your Presidente become progressively better as you start to finish islands.
-Imports are added to the island’s economy. This takes a considerable amount of strain off of your island as you’re able to get raw materials that you may only have a limited supply of. I particularly found this to be useful for importing cheap corn as an alternative to creating more farms.
Cons:
-Most of the game is just like Tropica 3. Most of the buildings, the character models, the edicts, and the world in general are exactly the same.
-You’re going to replay the same islands over and over. After a while you notice that eventually you stop playing on unique islands, which gets annoying if you don’t like doing things twice. Basically it reeks of l
-The soundtrack is still extremely limited and this time there’s no Juanito as radio DJ to spice it up.
Overall: Tropico4 is a lot of fun. It takes what’s good about Tropico 3 and only adds onto it. However, that being said, it’s basically Tropico 3. I felt a lot of the time that there was a lot of laziness in the game, between recycling islands to be played on again and again and the fact that there’s not a lot of new buildings or edicts that are even available. It just feels like the same game with a lot of lazy add-ons 7.5/10

A very nice upgrade to the franchise!
The new gameplay mechanics that COH2 offers change the game drastically and for the better. The ability to vault over walls with your infantry together with True Sight (which means that your units line of sight is affected by obstacles like tall walls or buildings) changes the way you engage the enemy in the battlefield, it is easier to set up proper ambushes with MGs but remember it works the other way around :).
Tanks can be abandoned, which means that you have to be that extra carefull with your Panther or you could be facing him soon in the hands of your enemy!
Flamethrowers can be dropped by infantry! So barbecue time!
ColdTech, some maps have blizzards and frozen rivers where your units can cross, or die if someone blows the ice!
The Teather of War packs are interesting and add a little more campaign missions if one is interested in them, the main campaign itself is fun but maybe too easy even in General difficulty.
Multiplayer is interesting, but be sure to master all the new things vs the AI first or you might get frustrated :), all the commanders available add some flexibility to the MP because you never know what you will find against you!
EDIT: My only complaint about this game at the moment is the huge amount of PREMIUM commanders available, mainly with those that add units to the game that are not available for free (yes I am looking at you Tiger Ace, KV-1, KV-2, Assault Grenadiers...) and some other abilities too. These start to make the game a bit like Pay to Win and must be addressed! Ideally, the commanders should be built by the player from a pool of abilities and let us fine tune the commanders to our liking and to suit our game style ( not to different from COHO really).
Regarding the skins, I dont really care, they dont change the game other than visually.
So my recomendation is not YES or NO, it can go both ways.

There's an easy way to recommend this game: did you like Tropico 3? If yes, you'll dig this, if not, pass. This game's called Tropico 4 but it's nominally an expansion pack to Tropico 3, though a large one at that. Tropico is a nation-building game in the vein of the Anno series, though not nearly as in-depth and with a sense of humor. It features a few new buildings and edicts and some new mechanics, as well as an entirely new campaign. A few of the added structures make things a little easier- like the salt mine, a mine that never runs out, and the chemical plant, a factory that requires no input. The mechanic improvements serve to streamline the gameplay and the added buildings are interesting. The campaign is quite good and about 40 hours long, a decent amount of play can be had. There is of course a sandbox mode if all you wish to build is an island. I very much recommend this game if you enjoy city or nation building games.

How am I going to write a review without mentioning Diablo (I & II) and Torchlight? Probably not. Being a huge fan of those franchises, Grim Dawn felt both familiar and refreshing at the same time. It starts off as a pretty straight-forward experience: slay monsters, level up, choose a class and some skills, repeat. At level 10 you choose a second class, forcing you to spend your hard-earned skill points more carefully. Then you start discovering shrines, relics and augmentations, enabling advanced character customization. After messing up my first character, I am now adventuring as a dual-wielding gunslinger Demolitionist-Soldier that specializes in Fire and Poison attacks. Grim Dawn is my favorite game of 2016 and I'll probably be playing it for a long time!
+ Great atmosphere and graphics
+ Simple, yet deep character customization through skills, gear and devotion.
+ Four-player online multiplayer
+ Rogue-lite dungeons for the occassional challenge
+ Difficulty setting is perfect: challenging without being punishing, Hardcore mode is optional.
+ Huge amount of loot, including Legendary items and craftables
+ Interesting classes and NG+ for high replay value
- Pretty standard story
- The occasional FPS-drop, even on high-end machines
Whether on discount or full-price, I wholeheartedly recommend buying Grim Dawn if you're a ARPG-fan!

This game is a tad bit fun. It might even be worth your hard earned monies. But not at the price of 12.99. This is a 2 to 3 dollar game at best. I can easily, off the top of my head, list games that are in the same genre and beat this game hands down: Project Zomboid, Fort Zombie (even with all the bugginess), and rogue survivor. What I expected, from the description of this game, was Fort Zombie+UFO: Afterlight-lots of things due to it being alpha. What I got instead was essentially a more spiffy web browser game (even the graphics reinforce this notion of the game).
Pros:
+Solid semi-fun mechanics
Cons:
-No challenge (you don't even need turrets half the time and you would be hard pressed to lose any survivors)
-Limited tech tree
-Oversimplified mechanics (for a zombie game that's 12.99)
-Unintriquing story
-Pretty much no content that justifies the current price even for an alpha
This may all change as the devs continue to release material for the game. However, until they do I highly recommend those of you looking for a rogue zombie game to check out Project Zomboid, Rogue Survivor, and even Fort Zombie if you are considering this game. If you haven't played Rogue Survivor it is FREE to download and play, and it offers a good challenge for those who like games in the rogue genre. On the other hand, if you want a good rogue-like game that combines RPG, strategy, and tower defense there is also Dungeon of the Endless which is absolutely fantastic (and very challenging).
More in-depth analysis:
I recently replayed this game. While the tone is much more apocalyptic many of the issues I had with the game haven't been addressed. Primarily, the issue of getting me hooked and wanting to continue to play the d*** thing. I'll divide this up into several sub-sections.
1. Failures on the zombie survival game level.
Again, if you're looking for something to fill the void of being eatten alive by the undead (wait, what?) there are plenty of other titles out there. This game fails on this premise simply because supplies are too plentiful. It is too easy to acquire absolutely everything that you need to survive. Most zombie survival (and rogue-likes) turn every move into a time vs ammo vs hunger sort of mechanic. IE, if I engage that horde of zombies how much ammo do I waste to get the supplies they're guarding? That simply isn't the case here. The issue becomes simply one of finding enough food and resources, which are too plentiful. But that's partially due to design. Because you *have* to clear each level there is no room to design the levels around players making strategic decisions (rather than just tactical ones).
2. Failures on the level of tower defense.
The towers/turrets are still just over-simplified fluff. I didn't get to (and I didn't want to either) play long enough to see if we see towers/turrets evolve. Are they even really necessary? Well, they could help someone who doesn't know how to manuever characters in the middle of combat. I could see that, but I still don't feel that we need them. At this point in time they're just feature creep.
3. Semi-successful on the management side:
With getting rid of the rest period between fights we actually do see a useful element of management occuring, however this is undermined by the fact that the game is still way too easy. In a 1-2 hour play through I ended up with enough characters to both send out into the field and to research/build stuff (and I choose a 2 character start). If the devs manage to make the game challenging the current management part of the game might become more important and less feature creep.
4. Still just a way too easy RPG tactical:
We still don't see the game improving to the point of really having much promise. It is mildly fun for a 1-3 hour play through (though boring to come back to). While the devs talk about a lot of exciting improvements none of the changes they're proposing will actually fix the main issue with the game: Making people want to (continue to) play it.
I think what has to absolutely be addressed is either developing a decent story to make us want to play through the cities or to ratchet up the challenge (preferably both). The later of which doesn't necessarily have to come from overhauling combat, just rebalancing how players get resources. Specifically, redoing drops from zombies and forcing most of our resource gathering to be from scavenging the mission sites. This might make both turrets (as a way to deal with really difficult waves) and management (as a way to balance injured personel) more important and less feature creep-ish.

The game takes a similar tone to the Diablo franchise, while making use of all the things learned from the Titan Quest franchise and from The Chosen: Well of Souls, and does it at least as well, if not generally better than most of those that preceeded it.
The game is can be taken at a range of paces, from careful and methodical to a hyper aggressive blitz, plentiful with the loot, and has a huge variety of little tricks.
Every class combination has merits, and even within a single specialization there is a huge variety of ways to play, multiplied massively by the interaction between classes. The devotion system lets you either enhance your own specialization, or shore up positions where your build might have weaknesses (for example, on my glass cannon of a character I grabbed one that throws up an ablative force field at 40% health).
One of the best things about Grim Dawn, especially compared to many of its recent competitors, is that crowd control is amazing, and every last class has some form of it. Each method of crowd control is great, and varied and useful in a wide variety of situations. The recharge times on the abilities are pretty fast too, which lets you use them often enough to REALLY work them into your style.
Of course, for as powerful as your character is, the enemies don't pull their punches either. Difficulty has a good ramp to it, letting you get the hang of your character and the game for a little, then working its way up to high intensity battles. If you find normal too easy, turn on veteran difficulty and you will not find yourself wanting for a challenge.
Unlike many other games in the genre, you don't have long between fights, and often while defeating one group of enemies, you'll draw several others. All of these drop wonderful, wonderful loot. Of course, there is no way one hero can use all this loot themselves, and you will find that your shared stash has ample room for all your "foisting off on the rookie character" needs.

SHORT SUMMARY:
It is fun for several hours. For $5 ($2.49 during the Steam Autumn Sale) it is EASILY worth the money.
LONG SUMMARY:
I found this game to be easily worth the 5$ I spent. Had I waited for the Steam Autumn Sale, I could have had this game for $2.49. Fans of wanting to play fun casual Poker will probably get the most enjoyment as the characters are fun to play against and listen to their playful banter. The interface is very simple and easy to understand.
The main criticism which many have pointed out is that after several hours, the dialogue gets old and repeatable. Although it is a valid criticism, I was still able to overlook this factor as I was so focussed on the game that I was able to tune it out. If players find it too difficult to tune out, there are actual audio controls that let you decide how much dialogue you want or players can flat out turned off the dialogue. Although the game could have used more dialogue, Considering that this was TTG's first attempt at a Poker game like this, I can find this shortcoming forgiveable.
This is a game where the unlocks are a fun challenge. The Steam achievements are also equally fun to acquire. These both combined is what made the game really fun for me. They are both hard to acquire, but not in a unrealistic or frustrating way. It makes you want to get them all no matter how many games or hands you have to play.
Depending on how good of a Poker player you are, if this game is played on Normal, it should not take too many hours to unlock all the game features which can cut the lifespan of this game. However, I found that if I play this game on Hard difficulty, it really extended the life of this game. On Hard, I felt like I was playing against smart poker players that were able to mathematically make smart decisions while also making bluffs or even calling your bluffs. The Hard setting is the perfect difficulty fun wise.
This game lacks on-line multi-player. However, knowing that I only paid $5 for this game, I definitely was not expecting that feature. To be honest, I was quite fine with this exclusion as I found this game to be more fun that way. Since this game does not use real money, human players can often not take the game serious and make ridiculous decisions.
Beyond the unlocks and achievements, this game has a longer life span than people think. No 2 games are ever the same (aside from the dialogue). Overall for 5$, I got more than my money worth from this game and enjoyed playing with characters from various media genres. There is no question Tell Tale will only improve on this fun unique Poker concept.

I have an ongoing love-hate relationship with FTL.
On one hand, it's a brilliantly designed semi-strategy roguelike game where you take control of a spacecaft and it's crew. You'll visit star systems, fight enemy spacecraft, upgrade your ship, and make little "do you help this person or that person" kind of decisions. The music is FANTASTIC and the learning curve is very mild. The storyline is very simple, but it gives reason to the way the game plays, why you have to be picky in what systems you visit, and such. And the game gives me the vibe that the designers didn't want to make a best-seller: They just wanted to make a fun game, regardless of profit margins.
On the other hand, it's a roguelike, which means that you'll suddenly be completely overwhelmed by enemies and lose. And it's not one of those losses where you think "maybe if I did this differently.." No, you just get completely blown away with no chance of escape. And I swear this game "cheats"...I'll be attacking some lowly enemy craft and my maximum experience gunner will miss with a missile. Then another. Then another. Meanwhile, the enemy shoots my ship twice with a junk weapon and blows two holes in the hull.
A friend used a cheat and gave himself a ship hull that could take unlimited damage and maximum money (called "scrap"). He still lost because the game found some other way to overpower his ship and crew. I've come close to beating it, but only by a thread.
Yes, this game makes me want to break my keyboard in half. Then I'll have to buy another because I'll want to play again a few hours later.

There’s a kind of poetic irony in remaking a game designed to poke fun at the game industry, considering all the remakes and reboots already flooding shelves. To both its credit and detriment, Re;Birth1 carries that identity struggle throughout.

Sometimes the in-jokes and references are spot on, while others fail to critique and instead repeat old mistakes. What could have been a new start for the series instead becomes a merely average role-playing game that just doesn’t fit together completely.
It’s lighthearted, and sports some fun, giant-anime-weapon battles, but its lack of challenge causes it to grow stale quickly.
The best part of the Hyperdimension Neptunia games is inarguably the concept: Four goddesses, each representing a different game system, are waging a “Console War” against one another in a cutesy, high-octane anime fashion.
Following this idea, Re;Birth1 is filled with meta, fourth wall-breaking humor, and a good bit of charming self-awareness. Pretty much every character and party member you encounter along the way fits into some sort of anime or gaming archetype — Neptune, who represents the fourth (imaginary) console, is the high-energy, childlike protagonist, while Iffy is a smart tsundere who can get quite flustered at times — and Re;Birth1 actually does a good job of balancing character versus caricature. That's about where "good balance" ends, however.
One cheeky addition along the same self-aware vein is the “remake” system, which changes aspects of dungeons like enemy difficulty and the types of items that appear. It’s good in theory , but in practice, it’s not all that fun to go through old dungeons again just to get new items. I didn’t think grinding was at all necessary, either, so “remaking” a dungeon to increase the challenge didn’t make a whole lot of sense.
Grinding is made unnecessary, by the way, due to the relative ease of combat. It’s of the basic turn-based, open-movement variety, and I found it functional, yet underwhelming.
The only strategy I really needed was to have my healer heal between attacks and kind of brute force my way through things, though a few harder fights were more satisfying. A partnering system that allows one party member to loan her battle perks to another while staying out of harm’s way adds another dimension to battle, but it’s not really necessary, and ultimately, it just made battles easier, not more exciting.
The story and dialogue both suffer from the same identity problems that permeate every other aspect of Re;Birth1, being simultaneously irritating and endearing at times. If a monster was clearly too hard for the area, I realized it before the characters sassily pointed it out, and I don’t need a dozen mentions of the word “tsundere” to realize which characters fit the archetype. Again, the ideas were there, but they were either too shallow or too frequent, rendering them moot. But I also found it adorable and loved playing as a group of dorky girls, at least for a while.

I remember playing the original one on my ps3 I liked it well enough but as things came out my attention got divided between this game and the other ones that came out around the same time. It has fan service written all over like just like all compile arts titles; and just like compile arts titles they have their own unique charm now enough of the intro let’s get to the review.
Graphics: This is where I am the most critical. The game looks great the art is fantastic the character models look excellent and really good work went into every aspect of the combat.... HOWEVER, in 2016 there is NO EXCUSE for recycled assets and don't give me that limited technology bs either. The assets in this game such as the environment and enemies do look very good they are creative and fit the feel of the game however it losses its luster when I see the same thing 10 times with different color schemes and it losses it FAST enemies are the same enemies except with pallet swaps and the fields are recycled 10 times before something new shows up and then the new field is recycled 10 more. The hub world aka the world map can only be explored by selecting tabs sure this is a compile heart staple but still in a generation of true open world games you have to have more than this.
Sound: The music and sound effects are very good a hit sounds very satisfying when you landed it and the music is really up beat and fun to listen to.....however the voice acting. Oh God the voice acting The English voice acting is very good for the most part its clear inflections are fine and their voices match the character and personalities well but the combat quotes are grading as hell to listen to not because they are bad but because they are so frequent and there are so few choices you will hear the same 5 quotes EVERYTIME you do almost any standard attack or skill and is just better in Japanese so my advice when grinding if that is your thing choose Japanese when doing the story choose English.
Story: I mostly like every character here they are fun and full of personality they work well off each other and do a fantastic job satirizing themselves from making fun of pop culture references to making fun of everything about gaming and you will recognize the parodies instantly and will get a good chuckle every time they make fun of clichés and tropes even making forth wall breaking jokes that I find entertaining every time I hear them however some comedy does feels a bit forced but it is defiantly far better than its predecessor also the story itself is very fun.
Game play: This game has one of the biggest character rosters I have seen to date each character plays and feels differently with their own unique skills and abilities that have a synergy with every character. The combat is over the top flashy and genuinely enjoyable though I can see grinding becoming draining and you might want to take a break every once in a while if you are one of those people that want EVERY character to be equally leveled because that will take a very long time to accomplish.
Overall: I give this game a 7/10 it's a good game and I think an improvement over the original though there are a lot of recycling in game assets the characters voice acting outside of combat is very good despite these flaws the game play hold it up and make it well worth the time and money and though the music is very good I don't see myself getting an OST for it and listening to it in my car the music fits the game but that is where the music shines IN GAME. Compile Arts I love you I really do but more variety please I eagerly await your next project.

The new gameplay mechanics that COH2 offers change the game drastically and for the better. The ability to vault over walls with your infantry together with True Sight (which means that your units line of sight is affected by obstacles like tall walls or buildings) changes the way you engage the enemy in the battlefield, it is easier to set up proper ambushes with MGs but remember it works the other way around :).
Tanks can be abandoned, which means that you have to be that extra carefull with your Panther or you could be facing him soon in the hands of your enemy!
Flamethrowers can be dropped by infantry! So barbecue time!
ColdTech, some maps have blizzards and frozen rivers where your units can cross, or die if someone blows the ice!
The Teather of War packs are interesting and add a little more campaign missions if one is interested in them, the main campaign itself is fun but maybe too easy even in General difficulty.
Multiplayer is interesting, but be sure to master all the new things vs the AI first or you might get frustrated :), all the commanders available add some flexibility to the MP because you never know what you will find against you!
EDIT: My only complaint about this game at the moment is the huge amount of PREMIUM commanders available, mainly with those that add units to the game that are not available for free (yes I am looking at you Tiger Ace, KV-1, KV-2, Assault Grenadiers...) and some other abilities too. These start to make the game a bit like Pay to Win and must be addressed! Ideally, the commanders should be built by the player from a pool of abilities and let us fine tune the commanders to our liking and to suit our game style ( not to different from COHO really).
Regarding the skins, I dont really care, they dont change the game other than visually.
So my recomendation is not YES or NO, it can go both ways.

I have played all infinity engine games; played Arcanum, Pillars of Eternity, Tyranny Divine Divinity and Path of Exile. Having said that my expectations for Divinity Original Sin, after reading the overwhelmingly positive reviews, were very high, expecting to experience something new and exciting. Alas, it is just another isometric rpg that works well. Divinity Original Sin is a good game if you have not played any isometric rpg before. If you have however, it may or may not be your kind of rpg.
The game has its charm, building on the experience of Divine Divinity as a hack and slash rpg with some kind of a story. DOS has a more fleshed out story this time around, but it takes time to build up, and the beginning seems to drag a bit.
Gameplay: You choose two characters to begin your quest. Select between female and male, and from an array of the classic fantasy classes: wizard, rouge, knight, warrior etc. A rudimentary system allows to somewhat customize your characters' looks, voice and underwear with a very limited set of options. There is a preset skillset for each, but you can also fumble around to "customize" them. As I said, if you have played rpgs since Baldur's Gate, expect nothing new here. In fact, it is far from the “build the character and party that you want” promise, since the available choices are very limited.
Controlling your characters is easy as point and click. There is also the option to set the camera to accommodate your taste. With WASD you can span the screen around without moving your characters. You have a quick bar for each character to use spells, items and potions as you see fit.
The selling proposition of DOS was the "interactive environments" to play and solve combat situations or overcome the standard array of rpg puzzles. Well if moving a barrel or setting oil on fire is mind-blowing to you, then it is, but there have been games doing that before DOS. Yes, it works but as to say that you can have a "blast" of a game with “a fully interactive environment” is just a bit exaggerated.  Is it as "promised" by marketing and PR? No.
Another element is the rock paper scissors mini game as a system to persuade another character in conversations. I found it humorous the first two times, but after a while it just gets in the way of the role-play. In Tyranny, for example, your skill level in subterfuge or athletics play an important part in conversations and some quest situations; you actually use your skills and talents; and even your stance towards other factions (loyalty, wrath, fear) serve a purpose in conversations and quests.  In DOS you do not "win" a conversation through talent, but rather due to luck in the mini game. For example, whether you try to use charm, or intimidation, it all comes down to the mini game, leaving you at the mercy of lady luck.
One element that annoys me is the NPCs constant repetition of what they say when you are not interacting with them. Remember when you entered a bar or an inn in Baldur's Gate? There was music and the sound of chattering of the people there, all made you feel in a place which was alive. In DOS the NPCs repeat the same line over and over in short periods of time, wearing them off very quickly and making you wish to just shut them up or leave.
Story: well you start the game as a Source Hunter who was sent to solve a murder and as predictable as it is, it is not a simple murder… yawn. It is nothing to be amazed of as it starts slow and soon you will be distracted with a bunch of side quests. If you want a game with a more solid story, go play Planescape Torment, Arcanum or even the original Baldur's Gate. If it was not for a bit of humor, I would say the story is forgettable.
Graphics: well it is a game from 2013 and looks ok for the most part. Textures are a hit and miss, being detailed in some environments, while some objects and places being less so. Characters do not look good. One could argue that the "humorous" tone of the game excuses the characters for looking a bit cartoony.
Animations: I guess Larian Studios had to work with a very limited budget, more so since the game was funded with Kickstarter,  and it shows. The character animations are not that fluid, more to the stiff side. But since it is an isometric rpg, that may not be much of a problem.
Magic effects look ok and there are some lighting effects here and there that help with the atmosphere of some places in the game.
Music and sound: The music is overall nice. Sound effects are, in my opinion, bland compared to other rpgs. The voice acting is not bad but forgettable and, as I said before, NPCs can annoy you to no end repeating the same line over and over.
Combat: It is turned based. As in Fallout and Fallout 2, you have action points at your disposal. Wearing certain armor or weapon can affect how many actions points you have. Use magic, melee and range attacks,  and"interact" with barrels of water, oil or poison to defeat your enemies or be defeated.
Aside of your two starting characters, you can add up to two more to your party. As always, you have to “balance” your party to be able to see the end credits after a play through.
Divinity Original Sin is isometric rpgs which was highly regarded by critics and players alike. I for one, already getting old and having played so many games, was disappointed, not because the game is bad per se, but if you have played older isometric rpgs, this gameswon’t bring nothing new to the table.
I recommend Divinity Original Sin if you are new to isometric rpgs or just have played a couple. If you are an experienced player, I do not recommend it unless you are one who wants to experience every single isometric rpg out there.

The game takes a similar tone to the Diablo franchise, while making use of all the things learned from the Titan Quest franchise and from The Chosen: Well of Souls, and does it at least as well, if not generally better than most of those that preceeded it.
The game is can be taken at a range of paces, from careful and methodical to a hyper aggressive blitz, plentiful with the loot, and has a huge variety of little tricks.
Every class combination has merits, and even within a single specialization there is a huge variety of ways to play, multiplied massively by the interaction between classes. The devotion system lets you either enhance your own specialization, or shore up positions where your build might have weaknesses (for example, on my glass cannon of a character I grabbed one that throws up an ablative force field at 40% health).
One of the best things about Grim Dawn, especially compared to many of its recent competitors, is that crowd control is amazing, and every last class has some form of it. Each method of crowd control is great, and varied and useful in a wide variety of situations. The recharge times on the abilities are pretty fast too, which lets you use them often enough to REALLY work them into your style.
Of course, for as powerful as your character is, the enemies don't pull their punches either. Difficulty has a good ramp to it, letting you get the hang of your character and the game for a little, then working its way up to high intensity battles. If you find normal too easy, turn on veteran difficulty and you will not find yourself wanting for a challenge.
Unlike many other games in the genre, you don't have long between fights, and often while defeating one group of enemies, you'll draw several others. All of these drop wonderful, wonderful loot. Of course, there is no way one hero can use all this loot themselves, and you will find that your shared stash has ample room for all your "foisting off on the rookie character" needs.

Would I recommend this? Yes. On one condition: when it is on sale.
Why the condition? Well I'll get to that...
The good:
- The title faction, the Grey Goo, is the most interesting faction I've played for years in an RTS. The unit designs are simple but appealing and the faction's overall design philosophy is as far as I know unique. It has several units that are truly distinct, there are no counterparts in the other faction's armies.
- The presentation in this game is lovely. The Goo, as mentioned above, are stellar standouts but the rest is still very competant.
- The cutscenes are beautiful. I really wasn't expecting them. Iirc there is a cutscene in between every mission, all of them quality CG (as opposed to in-engine) ((Not that there is anything wrong with in-engine, but this is damn good CG work))
- Music is pretty competant, I believe Frank Klepacki (of C&C fame, among others) is involved. Nothing as stand out as Hell March but there are a few tracks that caught in my mind.
The grey:
- The game does not have a long campaign. There are 3 factions, 15 missions overall meaning 5 missions apiece. You'll play your first 5 missions as the Beta, an unremarkable faction whose only saving grace is awesome accents. The second 5 as the Humans who use drones built by Apple. The third 5 as the Goo, who are awesome. Your mileage may vary depending on your buying price, interest and patience. I'll get back to this one...
- Most units from all factions fall into specific roles with little deviation. For the most part each faction will have 3 light units and 3 heavy units. 2 factions also have 3 aircraft, scouts, fighters and bombers. The Goo outshines the other factions here because of it's different approach but still has the light/heavy formula weighing it down somewhat.
- Some of the unit designs are so generic as to be boring to look at and boring to use.
- I'm not particularly versed in balancing, I don't know all of what goes into balancing decisions. Bearing that in mind, I found one or two of the Goo's units underpowered. Actually all of their heavy units, as cool as they are, seemed to be flawed. The heavy tank seemed fragile and the artillery seemed weak even in massed groups.
The bad:
- The Goo has a unique unit with no attack whose sole purposes are to block line of sight and taunt enemies. It's a great concept. The trouble is they are slow and when moving a mass of units they are not always in the front line when needed and unit pathing/collision would not allow them to move. Good, predictive micro helps this somewhat.
- Let me phrase that last point another way, units of the faction whose army is made up of puddles of nanobots grouped in certain formations cannot move past each other. Conceptually they should be able to flow around each other. Gameplay wise, there is an upgrade to let the above unit start a rampage when critically damaged. A far better upgrade would be to have them charge enemy units. A missed opportunity.
- The AI is not the best. This works both for and against you. Enemy units will sometimes not retaliate to your attacks. Your units will not retaliate while a nearby enemy attacks them. This is unrelated to the gameplay of stealth units and units in bushes.
- Unique to the Goo, every once in a while you will find your Mother Goos (the mobile HQ/factory/so much more of the faction) randomly moving. You will not have told them to do so, will not have had them even selected. But they will move. And you will curse.
Now the crux of the matter, why the condition? If you've looked this far, you know why you want to play 'Grey Goo'. You want to play the Grey Goo. The other factions aren't anything remarkable. You've seen the Goo and thought you'd like to get your hands on them. You're also probably not new to RTS games, you know that you only get the good stuff, the 'cool faction' at the end. You're right: the Goo is the third campaign. You're going to have to sit through 2/3rds of the game to get to the part you actually want to play. The positive is that each faction has only 5 missions so it won't take that long to reach the 'Good' bit. The conditional 'Yes' recommendation hinges on the fact that on sale, this isn't too big of a pill to swallow. But at full price? You're paying £30 or the equivalent in the knowledge that £20 is a chore you have to get over to get to the fun.
Now this is all subjective, my opinion only. I didn't even mind playing as the Humans as much as I thought I would. The Beta are terrible in their blandness though. But I can only think back to my thought process as I played through: 'Get this first bit over and done with and then the fun starts'.

At it's core, I really love Child of Light. The gameplay is interesting, everything is very pretty and aesthetically pleasing, and the story is fairly well done. However, a few awful missteps made me immediately drop the game with zero motivation to ever finish it.
My major issue with the game is a spoiler, so if you wish to play through the game unspoiled, I will just say this: Story is important, but not when you absolutely punish and cripple the player for no reason if they make certain choices.
Here is my complaint put more specifically:
Remember all those good times you had playing Tower Defense maps in WarCraft III?

This is a great RTS that keeps true to most of the classical elements of the older games like War Craft 1-3, Star Craft, Red Alert, etc.  It does a good job keeping things interesting though by introducing the unique Goo race, and race defined limiters like the power conduits for humans.  The one down side that I have found is a very short single player campaign.  However, I found the story and universe to be compelling.  This is a great buy if you find it on sale, or perhaps if you are a big RTS fan and do not want yet another EA or Blizzard game.
Warning!  I do not ever play RTS games online or even in multiplayer.  I enjoy the great challenges presented by the unique scenarios and puzzles inherent to good RTS games.  To me solving an seemingly impossible puzzle is much more rewarding than training myself for years to micro-manage units only to lose to some 10 year old who is using a hack IT did not even make.

What is this game worth? Probably about $10.

What to say about this game.
Despite its' simplicity there's an undercurrent of planning and forethought that is all but required. Squandering supplies or fuel is death, and if one of your Survivors is killed, their weapon, equipment, levels and skills are lost with them. Every Survivor is an investment.
Yet things can go wrong so quickly, and without warning, that it feels unfair at times. Survivors can't reload and move at the same time, so prolonged waves of zombies all but require that someone take the fall. They can seldom be outran or outmaneuvered in the landscapes.
In addition, while the lack of anything other than autosaves makes the game seem unfair, punishing small mistakes with the abject loss of considerable time and effort by killing off your last, desperate survivors as their guns click dry and they find themselves faced with a horde, it doesn't offer enough opportunities to refill those numbers, and when your survivors are dead, there's no "game over" screen, it just returns you to your most recent base camp, and sits there. You have to exit the game yourself. As if being defeated isn't bad enough, you must exit the game manually, erase the save file that now contains nothing, and start over.
The game has potential, and I've enjoyed the previous Infectionator titles, but I feel this game has a sense of artificial difficulty that keeps nagging at me. If you give your survivors the best weapons, then they quickly run out of ammunition. Apparantely it costs more ammunition to reload a 30 round rifle than it does a 30 round submachinegun. If you give them more modest, economic weapons then they are swamped, crying out their lack of ammunition.
The roguelikes elements are extremely well done, the skills management is effective, and levelling up is just difficult enough to make each skill point seem valuable, yet I feel the game could do with a tweak in the difficulty curve, particularly given that there is only one city, and yet the maximum level of difficulty is not impossible to find in it.
Recommended, but only for those with time, patience, and a voluminous vocabulary of colourful language.

Back more than 10 years ago, I was fond of RPG games, especially the Japanese ones (Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, Golden Sun, Secret of Mana, Chrono Trigger, ...). When I moved to Steam a few years ago, I started to play different kinds of games that did not require to invest a lot of time (platformer, shoot'em up, puzzle, ...). But I felt that something was missing ...
So I looked at my games, and amongst the thousands of games I own, I found Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth1. I also own a lot of the FF games, but I wanted to try something new, that is why I checked the comments on this game, and I was in !
I grabbed my pad and quickly, I was immersed in the game : I liked the characters, the story, the soundtrack (Japanese voices available !), the animations for the special attacks ... but overall, I really loved the gameplay ! Between the combos, the standard skills, the EXE skills, the HDD forms, and a lot of characters, you have almost infinite ways to fight !! Do not worry, it is easy to understand how everything works. In order to enable that, you have access to A LOT of dungeons, and in each dungeon, there are some bosses that are waiting for you to defeat them.
Moreover, there is a craft system with the plans, it will keep you busy for a long time, because you can, as expected, craft both weapons and armor, but you can also unlock special assets that have a direct implication on the fights (more loot, more money, more xp, ...).
I do not own the DLC, but I believe that being able to reach level 999 means a huge content !
However, the game is not perfect : even if I liked the story, I found that, sometimes, dialogues were too long and childish, focusing on things that could be funny the first time, but not after (pudding, breast, ...). You can almost skip them by using the quick speed, but you feel like you are missing something ...
If you want to unlock a lot of plans (for the gameplay or for the achievements), you are forced to replay the game a second time after you completed it (New Game +, you still have access to a lot of things you had at the end of the first run) : indeed, you need memory to craft, but memory is a limited ressource. This is kind of annoying since you cannot fully skip the dialogues, as mentionned above ...
To put it in a nutshell, I had a great experience with this game that I highly recommend if you like J-RPG ! With the upcoming summer sales (tomorrow ... !), I may be tempted to buy the other Neptunia games ... wait and see !

Has Minecraft gotten boring for your 12 year old self? Do you want something different than Team Fortress 2 or Dota 2? Do you want to blow the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the enemy base? Then Block N' Load is for you!
Not only is it free, but it's actually good! This is one of the few games that shine in the Free To Play section of Steam, which really says something when almost everything in the F2P section of Steam is complete garabage.
In Block N' Load, you and 4 other teammates must destroy the enemies base (Cube) to win, while your opponents try to do the same. Before each round, you choose to defend or attack. Next, you pick your class (You start out with 3 and can buy more with in-game cash which you get from matches) and select your perks and blocks. Before the fighting begins, there is a small setup round which allows you to build defenses or traps around your base. Once that's over, you get to work with your team to defend and attack, blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up along the way as the map gets ripped to shreds. Most of the map is fully destructable, and it's always a great feeling to destroy structures or bring down buildings with explosives.
The community isn't too bad, and many seem to be helpful towards new players. Although you`ll still get a fair helping of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in the game. It's very easy to start playing and even easier to get addicted to this drug of a game. Preformance wise, it runs alright on my computer (My computer isn't meant for gaming).
This game isn't Pay 2 Win, although paying allows you to get Heros faster, get perks faster, and allows you to buy skins. I seriously reccomend this game, I`m loving it more than a Happy Meal with a Neo pet inside. Go get youself somthin' nice and play Block N' Load.

I don't understand the sheer vitriol this game seems to be generating in reviews and comments. This is a fairly short game, and the puzzles are pretty simple. The plot seems a bit off the rails, but that's kinda typical for a PnC game anyway. Some people seem pretty put off by the voice acting but although it was fairly bland I didn't find much else to fault it with. But I'm not a great judge of acting of any sort so take from that what you will.
My biggest gripe with the game was the slightly clunky controls. Having to click on "view" or "use" in the inventory before interacting with an item is old-school, but in a way that makes me sort of glad most newer games have given up that minor annoyance. And the walking controls seemed really clunky, with the PC stopping randomly and not recognizing certain parts of the screen to move forward.
Some things are worthy of praise. I thought the backgrounds were lovely, they had a sort of storybook pastel cutout look that's neat. They looked hand drawn (although again, I don't actually know). The music was pleasant and on theme too. Catchy, I'll easily have it in my head the rest of the night. And it is original music, written just for the game.
I think those two major points show a bunch of care and effort went into thise game, which is the developer's first. The way the developer has been engaging on the discussion boards and incorparating suggested changes to improve the flaws of the game is also really nice to see. I look forward to seeing more from this developer.

This was a nice short LucasArts style point and click adventure game. It only took me 37 minutes to beat the game, but I also only paid $1.25, so I can't really complain about the game's length.  You can tell the game was made by a single person, with both the good and bad that comes with that. The puzzles are the usual old school inventory pieces, most of which are fun for what they are, save for the fuse box combo, but it's easy enough to get around that. I never found myself stumped by any of the puzzles, but I also never found my self disappointed or not enjoying the experience. The voice acting is a little rough, but it is an indie game AND the game is fully voiced acted, which is a nice touch and something most higher budget adventure games don't even do. The game's ending is a bit abrupt and I was surprised to see "The End" appear after a line of dialogue, but I still found myself entertained with what was here for the price tag. When you're paying a dollar you can't expect something to be AAA quality or a JRPG in length. I got my money's worth out of this game and that's all I can ask for.
The developer shows promise and I'd probably buy his next game as well.

As far as I can tell, this is the last Tropico installment, at least for now. Collectively, the “new” Tropico has been a great series and has born again a classic game and genre. However that is as a whole. Individually, these games feel incomplete. That is especially true when the DLCs are not included. I’ll just say that as for Tropico 3, the Absolute Power DLC is a must. And the Modern Times DLC is the same in regards to Tropico 4. Yet Tropico 4 amazingly improved on Tropico 3. Despite the fact that the core is unchanged, the small and subtle changes are more of refinements. I honestly feel like these two games are actually very different, despite the vast rehashing of graphics and copied game play core. Tropico 3 was about island nation development, and Tropico 4 is about Presidente’s development. And yes, that is drastically different. If you’ve played Tropico 3 and liked it, I see no need to get this title. If you played Tropico 3 and loved it, then grab this game too. Considering my first 5 minute test run of this game turned into a 40 minute shoot fest, I have to admit this game is pretty downright addicting!
Pros:
-Simple Gameplay mechanics so it's quick to learn
-No longer having to decide between listening to music or playing games
-As both the enemies and your guns are affected by the music, there is always a very fluid balance
-As many levels as you have music
-Plenty of growth with bonuses, unlocks to keep you interested
Cons:
-VERY visually overpowering (I have it set to 50% and it's still pretty mind numbing so take the siezure warning seriously)
-3/4 time songs are a pain to do.... Death Waltz has new meaning!
-Any song that goes quiet for the bridge is DEADLY
-The money system is not quite intuitive.... I end up with less money than I collect over the level (this is probably me being dumb though)
-Not so much a con but it would be nice to be able to link youtube videos or music websites the same way we can do internet radio
Final thoughts:
This game is awesome! The level generation based on music is done beautifully making it difficult but never impossible. It is visually overwhelming but in the most beautiful way. Give it a try and I hope you find your 5 minute game sessions bursting into hour long adventures as well!

"What would Heavy Weapons Guy have to say to Strong Bad in their off-hours?"  Not a lot as it turns out.  Telltale took a chance and made a poker game by licensing characters from other properties, and it works... for a while.  The dialogue is interesting and entertaining for the first couple hours, but loses its lustre as you hear the same things over and over.  Though once in a while, you'll get a new one and the surprise of new dialogue will make it extra funny.  If you're an achievement perfectionist, you'll end up with a lot of time in this one as the odds of some of the hands are 1:64,000.  Part of where this game stumbles is the choice of more obscure characters (Strong Bad, Tycho from Penny Arcade) which not everyone will be familiar with, though that's a minor point (and the characters in Poker Night 2 are more mainstream).
Verdict:  Fun for a while, but recommend waiting for a 75% off discount.  After you're tired of the dialogue, play it in a window and watch Netflix, Hulu, or YouTube in another window.  Or pick up Poker Night 2 for the same price and have options for Texas and Omaha Hold 'Em instead of just Texas.

First impressions are huge for me when I look at games. Even if a game has overwhelmingly great reviews, if I'm not impressed within the first 20 minutes I tend to put it away. I know I may miss out on a few things, but that's just who I am.
That being said, at first glance, this game seemed like a cliche alien invasion story (which in some ways it is). Little bug-eyed humanoid aliens with no discernable facial features just seemed too basic from a design perspective. I never even gave this game a second look after the trailer, but up came a free weekend deal and I decided to give it a chance.
I didn't expect much as I started it up, but as I progressed through the first few minutes of the game my attention was immediately caught by the VERY well designed strategic gameplay and the wealth of customization options for each of my soldiers (personalizing my characters is HUGE for my tastes). I started growing very attached to my squad from the get go and throughout the game I've always loved the feeling that this was my very own personal squad that nobody else had.
Gameplaywise, it's a very engaging game of strategy! The cover/flank mechanics in the game really force you to think about positioning as if you were playing a game of chess. Positioning at the corner wall of a building gives you more cover than ducking behind a counter, which is still much better than standing out in the open. If you sneak up behind an enemy, you will get a massive flanking bonus to aim and damage. The enemies also follow the same rules. And to add to that, the varied maps give you a myriad of unique situations to adapt to. Forests are generally open spaces with only a few trees and rocks to serve as cover which can benefit a squad built for mobility and range. City maps tend to have tall rooftop nests for snipers and a lot of cover/flank play within the small crevices in the indoor hallways. There are also city street maps where the majority of your cover will be cars and trucks. And as if that wasn't exciting enough, almost all of these map elements are destructible! Your enemies can destroy the wall you're hiding behind leaving your soldiers open. Cars can be set on fire and the explosions cause a great amount of damage. You'll have to be constantly adapting your strategy to fit the ever-changing environment.
No matter how strong your soldiers and equipment are, running in blind will almost always get your squad killed (which is devastating since personalizing them makes you feel so attached).
Overall great game! I'm glad I paid the weekend sale price of $10 because I honestly think it's worth every penny of the original price.

This game was a hard one to review. I
wanted to love this game, but in the end it just felt a bit average.
The story is decent. You play as a goddess who has lost her memory after being attacked by the other three goddesses, and you travel around making friends, fighting monsters, and eventually trying to save the world.
Most of the characters are likable, but I found some of them
annoying (
). Some of the voice actresses felt a bit "plain", but I was surprised to hear the voice of Tosaka Rin (from Fate/Stay Night) coming from one of the main characters. I also loved the voice of  one character (
), and Neptune was a pretty good main character. The design of most of the characters were great, and they all felt very distinct and different from each other.
However, one thing that was
annoying was that whenever two or more characters spoke at the same time I would get this really annoying static that would just rip my ears.
Another minus was that the English translations were often very off or just plain wrong. I played the game with Japanese audio and English subtitles, but I got annoyed a couple of times because the subtitles were so completely different from what the characters were saying. That said, there were a few times when the English subtitles were different in a good way, and I actually laughed at some of the jokes that (probably) weren't in the Japanese version.
The fighting is turn-based, but in between turns you can position your characters on the battlefield to be able to attack multiple enemies at once, dodge area-of-effect attacks, keep your healer safe, etc.
In between fights you can decide what type of attacks your characters can use in combat (one hit/multiple hits, physical/magical, rush attack to build "super meter"/heavy attack/guard break attack), pair together two characters that get along well to gain benefitial bonuses (or make them fight together so that they will get along eventually), equip/create weapons and armor, etc. In short, there's alot of stuff to do here, and if you want to do well you have to master all of it.
The game does require you to do some grinding, since if you (like me) try to play through the story without leveling up in between boss fights you will get
. You have to level up alot and make good use of all your weapons, combos, pairings, and so on to get through the game.
There are several areas in the game, but some of them are almost exactly the same. The only difference is that the monsters have changed. I wish they hadn't used the exact same map/terrain for several areas, as it makes the game feel a bit "cheaper" than it is.
I also, at one point, faced a game-breaking bug. During my second playthrough I had the game on auto-skip to get through the cut scenes faster, and suddenly the game just went dark. I could see the "skip" icon in the top right corner, but the game just froze even if I turned off the skip function. The same thing happened at the same spot a second time, and I had to turn off the skip function
I reached that point if I wanted to get to the next area. Not a major bug, but still something that should be fixed.
I
enjoy this game, but I also thought that there were a few negatives, and it didn't live
up to my (high) expectations. All in all, I
recommend this game, but you might be better of waiting for a sale, as the regular price seems a bit steep.

After playing all 6 episodes, I'm disappointed. By the end of the final episode, I didn't really care what happened to House Forrester.
You play various characters of House Forrester, a House not really mentioned at all in the novels or the HBO series. They're Northerners, allied with the Starks, but with little power. The family is spread out across the world, so you get to see places you will recognise if you've followed the series at all - King's Landing, Meereen, etc. The timeline you play in is between the Red Wedding until slightly after the Purple Wedding.
+ You get to meet familiar faces from the series - John Snow, Tyrion, Cersei, Daenarys, Ramsay
+ They got the real actors to voice their counterparts in the game
+ Interesting history behind House Forrester
+ Characters of House Forrester are pretty well designed and developed overall
+ Some nice plot twists, but nothing mind-blowing
- Your choices don't really matter. Most deaths and events in the final episode are not preventable, no matter what you do in the first 5 episodes.
- The graphics aren't good, especially the backgrounds. Trees and ground textures look strange and not detailed.
- The opening theme song/animation, which was so-well done in the HBO series, looks weird and poorly rendered in the game.
- It's a shame you can't meet more characters from the TV series.
- Events in the novels/TV limit what the writers can really do for House Forrester. For example, options like trying to attack or offend Ramsay Snow will never turn out well because he's a main character, so you know there's no way to really do much against him.
- A few story points that are mentioned in the game, especially the North Grove, are never properly explained.

Waited until the final episode to write my review. Though I enjoyed the story I find it very frustrating that no matter you do, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. Without getting into spoiler territory I'll say one thing. No matter what you do, it's wrong. If you're given option A and option B, A is definitely wrong while B is very wrong. It's all wrong. Once you realize that the tension for the game is gone. The joy of Telltale games is the heart wrenching decisions. You sit there and go 'Oh jeez. I hope I did the right thing...' It's just doesn't matter in this game. A seemingly extremely important decision will have the same result, albeit very minor differences. And at the end, when you make what seems to be an extremely important decision you don't get to see how it plays out because that's the finale. Won't surprise me that in Season 2 (assuming there will in fact be one) that the decision doesn't matter anyways.
On a more positive note, the game's story is quite good in my opinion. If you just want to see the story unfold and don't really care about the impact of your decisions then I think you would really enjoy this game. I, however, think that a decision based game should have meaningful decisions. I'd give it an 'okay' rating or something on those lines if that was an option. As is though, thumbs down from me.

Here is a snapshot of a post that I wrote in the forum:
. As you can see, the thread is now removed -- by the developers, I assume. In the post I was focusing mostly on issues that I hoped could be improved. The developers' response was to remove the whole thread, obliterating the four comments from other people in that thread as well (update:
). Here I'll do a more proper review.
70 minutes is the time it took me to complete the game, even though I was stuck for a while on one puzzle. The game has about 9 small locations with 3-4 interactive hotspots in each location.
Most of the puzzles are inventory-based. All manage to be cliched and absurd at the same time.
standing in the same room with another person to cause a distraction and to make that person walk away in the opposite direction. Gluing
with
and then using the glued
to
. Adventure games get some artistic license on the credibility of the puzzles, but there are limits to everything.
Same as the puzzles, the characters and the plot also borrow bits and pieces from many different sources and fail to produce anything coherent. Given the length of the game, it's hard to expect any in-depth character development, but the plot is just nonsensical.
The animations are very poor, even the simplistic speech animation, which usually doesn't draw any particular attention, here looks jarring.
The interface is very awkward. Skipping dialog lines can be done only by clicking on the Skip button. The Use button is needed to use an item, but not to combine two items. There is a button to highlight all hotspots, but when using an item on a hotspot that's hard to identify visually (one small piece of floor that doesn't stand out), you cannot be sure if you're clicking on the right spot, because the text identifying the hotspot appears only after the click. That explanation was probably confusing, but it's a confusing system.
The speech playback begins about half a second after the subtitle appears.
And of course the "Gold is extremely magnetic" bit deserves to be a meme and is the symbol and the essence of the whole game. With just a little more thought it could be changed into something workable, something like "Curses, they sold me a fake tiara!" (as it's magnetic).

The game is what you would assume a stone age simulator would be like. It's fun, but they could have worked on the graphics a tad. I'm running an gtx 980 and it's just chewing through it on ultra settings. The screenshots look amazing but the game doesn't.
