No boats were harmed in the making of this review.
You play a cruise ship captain named Chris that somehow arrived at this mysterious island. How did you get here? Where is your boat? Explore to find various odd ball characters and items to find out.
As you talk to the other residents, learning that this island is named Bayou Island, you learn what goes on in the first area. Everyone here seemed to have washed up on the shore not knowing how they could of. There is also a correlation with boats disappearing as well. However Chris is a different story, having another passenger with him.
There is not much ways to grab hold onto the plot, as a lot is mysterious and questioning, especially the ending twist. As the price tag suggests, Bayou Island is a short. But the second half seems rushed compared to the first half, especially how the ending is so abrupt. There are a lot of questions other
With the ease of point and click mechanics, it is very easy to play. A wheel of options shows what you can possibly do. The only thing you might have to get used to is selecting the "use item" before clicking on an item. With the game's short stay I was not able to remember to use it every time, but I do see why it was made like that. Combining items is used by dragging an item to another so perhaps it was to not confuse the game.
On the puzzle side most of them were easy, taking no time at all. Some requiring you to just talk with the residents as the others needs items that are just laying around for anyone to steal. One had you playing an instrument, but it did not make sense what the character did in result of it. I do know that if you play an instrument behind someone inside a building, it will sound like it's inside the building. Not outside, especially when the person saw you coming inside. Other than this, another puzzle did not make sense at all. It is a combination but getting it is full of red herrings. It's not something obvious, it's not something based on the amount of certain items (which I initially thought), but based on time. With the descriptions of the objects not being useful till now, it's very weird considering the clue you get. The main red herring seems to be for something else that was originally planned but was scrapped.
The music accompanying each area goes well with the surroundings. The music in the Day of the Dead store, and the area behind it, has a Latin flare to it. Making it seem like Chris did get washed up on the Day of the Dead, which is possible but no decorations are shown outside of the shop.
The voice acting can be better. There are some that did well, such as the bartender, but the one for Chris is not as much. Sometimes it gives off a sarcastic tone while other times he pauses where it seems it should not. There are parts where it works of course, but not throughout the whole piece.
The art style is pleasant to look at, with the Day of the Dead area is the best. Backgrounds having some sort of color pallet depending where the area might be. While they do tell you boats disappeared, why can one be seen in the background? Some areas have weird proportions in the backgrounds, such as the bar's counter looking taller than Chris even though the bartender is the same height as you.
The characters do seem to have time put into them to make them unique. However one design is not on the store page, which also only has the side perspective.
Bayou Island runs well, not putting pressure onto your computer. The only options you do get is volume and you can go into windowed mode by hitting escape. Though I could not find a way to exit out of the game without going to windowed mode and closing out of that.
Of course with point and clickers, the only reason to really replay is for achievements or seeing the different choices you could of made if able to. Bayou Island currently has no achievements and no trading cards so replayability might not be there. You can go back and see all the hints towards the ending twist, but that’s about it.
+ Appropriate music
+ Art
+/- Voice acting can be better
+/- Puzzles spike in difficulty at the end
- Ends abruptly
Looking more into it, I do see that this is the developer’s first game. Originally going to be a two parter, with the first part having a different system in interacting. I will recommend a few things. The subtitles may work better on the bottom of the screen, and perhaps being able to skip by just clicking than having to press a skip button. Putting in a few animations can help, such as putting a 'waking up' animation instead of having the drunk man sit up and go to sleep immediately. Is Bayou Island so horrible that you shouldn’t buy it? No. With the problems it has, it still has all the aspects of being a good point and clicker. There are things to learn from and I hope this developer continues making games.

I would suggest the game has been heavily inspired by Grim Fandango and the Monkey Island series and that's not a bad thing right?...
It's better than most of your independent point and clicks (which are mostly just screen transitions borderlining hidden object puzzles rather than containing animations).
I would expect that this is perhaps the developers first project on this scale as there are some minor issues;
- The voice of the protagonist is annoyingly delayed compared to the subtitles, it feels like there's a 1 second load time on each line of dialogue.
- Most of it is pleasantly logical, however 1 puzzle I found unnecessarily abstract.
- The lack of a menu is disappointing and with no obvious auto-save feature it makes you reluctant to close the program for fear of losing what you have done so far.
*SPOILERS**SPOILERS**SPOILERS**SPOILERS**SPOILERS**SPOILERS**SPOILERS*
The code for the fuse box is unnecessarily complicated, based on everything which preceeded it, the solution (being the actual numbers on which the hands of the clock was located) seemed out of place.
It's like asking someone what's 2+2, 2x2, 4+4, 5+5 and then just once throwing in 'recite pi to 14 places'.
There are a few other numbers in the room (such as a date above the door) that based on the general level of difficulty made it seem that you were doing something wrong rather than it being a red herring.
*END OF SPOILERS**END OF SPOILERS**END OF SPOILERS**END OF SPOILERS*
There is only 1 instance in the game where an item combination in inventory is used, making the mechanic almost unnecessary.
There is 1 instance where a character has a chain dialogue which doesn't occur before, the removal of 'unhighlighting' of used dialogue would have made this a lot more obvious.
Didn't take me long to complete, but then I'm a seasoned hand at point and clicks, I did enjoy it and would recommend it, however I think there are lessons to be learnt from this which I have no doubt will lead to a much more impressive and stronger product next time around for the developer.

Grim Dawn is a dark and interesting isometric action roleplaying game. The voice acting is good. The graphics are alright, personally I don't like bright cute characters and these characters are far from that. Combat is good, the class system does have an impact on the way you play, so choose carefully.
Grim Dawn has fun and detailed environments and there is quite a lot to explore. The environments have some nice details, portraits on walls, fauna, people cages, signs hanging, etc. I could go on, but best to check out the screenshots above, none are misleading.
The loot is good, there is plenty, although progress is slow and rarity of loot definetely follows your level, some people might like that. The weapons are chunky and brutal looking, the armour is detailed, varied and more worn than shiny, in a good way.
Crafting hasn't really grabbed me yet, just started, have to see, but I do like the way you can add strength or abilities to weapons and armour through picking up stackable scrap like items, seems like a complex but accessible system for those with patience. Looks like there is a bit to craft, I've noticed a rune slot, a blacksmith requiring recipes and there are lots of bits and bobs dropped constantly.
I'm enjoying the progression, leveling up, getting better gear. The dual class system is good and placing points does matter, but don't worry you can speak to this lady who gives you points back if you want to alter your build. I haven't found a way to completely change my class, as she won't reset mastery points, but she does allow me to alter points placed for passives and active abilities within my chosen classes.
If you like isometric action roleplaying games, particularly for exploring, I would say this is a very good choice. You can play it solo offline, enjoy the story and it's not expensive.

Grey Goo is a Real-Time Strategy game made by veterans of Westwood, the studio responsible for Command and Conquer (before EA bought them and hollowed them out).  Featuring three interesting, asymmetrical factions, the goal of the game is to harvest Catalyst, the one resource in the game, and use it to create units to beat up bad guys.
Pros:
+Namesake Goo faction is a unique faction that does not construct buildings, opting to instead produce its units from Mother Goos
+Unusual movement options combine with a large scale to create a game with an epic scale as well as interesting micro options
+Interesting takes on various units; no unit is a direct comparison to the similar-niche unit from another side.  For example: Beta artillery leaves behind mines, Human artillery can fire on the move, Goo artillery leaves a pool of corrosive acid that heals units
+Good graficks
+Awesome cutscenes and story delivery, nice fluffy universe that makes you want more
Cons:
-no extremely interesting units aside from the epic units; mostly standard fare for an RTS
-short campaign (15 missions, 5 with each side)
-Other reviews report poor multiplayer balance
-only 4 players on a map

There are a lot of things going on with this game, so I guess I'll just break it into parts. I'll start with the gameplay:
This game has a two-dimensional overworld. Enemies are shown on the overworld, and can be engaged or avoided. Combat takes place in a separate battle screen. From a gameplay perspective, the combat system is probably the most interesting and novel thing about the game. There are a number of options for slowing enemies down, and striking a foe at the right time can "interrupt" them. Of course they can also interrupt you if you aren't careful. This can often make combat feel like you are juggling enemies, which I liked.
On to story and writing: The story is very much a straight-up fairy tale about a princess coming of age and saving her kingdom. The characters are fairly colorful and varied. Also, all dialogue is written in rhyme, which could be a positive or a negative. I personally found it endearing, but I can see how others could find it maddening. Overall, it's a fairly light-hearted adventure.
I liked the visuals too. They were fairly simple, and high-contrast, which I thought worked well with the story.

When this game was first announced, I thought, "strategy game is on BOTH consoles and PC? I'll pass, thanks." Indeed, looking at games like Halo Wars and the recent C&Cs, I was under the impression that the console version would compromise the quality of the PC version. After watching a friend play it, I realized I was so wrong. I seized upon a $16.99 sale at GameFly and began an epic saga.
Having never played previous XCOM games, I have no baseline to compare Enemy Unknown to. It really feels like a genre of its own. The combat is like Ghost Recon meets Total War. The base-maintaining (including research and equipment) in between missions is like SimTower meets Civilization.
The game first begins to just mold itself with your life when you select your squad. You can choose the name of every member in your squad, and I personally chose to name them after my real-life friends and myself. When some of them inevitably die in battle, you will feel the anguish, especially if you've poured untold resources into making them top-tier fighters. When one of them gets impaled by a Chrysalid and then becomes a zombie, you will feel rage as your other squad members are forced to gun down one of their own. Or sometimes, you can feel proud of your friend as he heroically sacrifices himself with a close-range explosive to save the rest of the squad.
Despite being a turn-based system, the combat really sends adrenaline through your system. Move a trooper forward and suddenly a few Mutons make themselves known, and you go "oh s**t" and scramble your remaining squad to tactical positions. Select an enemy to target, only to see that the chance of hitting is 30% with your pistol while the main weapon is dry... do you risk that shot? Equip that Arc thrower because you need to salvage those alien weapons... only to have it miss while your trooper has only one health bar left. No two missions play out the same way, and you'll also want to be strategic about mixing rookies with veterans when you pick your squads, because you need to make sure everyone gets experience.
When everyone's back at base, the stakes are no less high. You don't have infinite money (really, if governments are so stingy during a real alien invasion, we deserve to let them kill us), so you will be forced to choose between a rock and a hard place. Do you launch that satellite so China doesn't panic and withdraw support from XCOM, or do you invest in a thermal generator to power an essential facility? Do you risk that last remaining Interceptor on that newly spotted UFO, or do you let it go and cause panic elsewhere or shoot down a satellite? These decisions can make or break your XCOM saga. Choose wisely.
On the technical side, Firaxis proves that it knows its stuff. Graphics aren't going to blow minds away, but they also aren't going to make your rig chug if it isn't the latest and greatest. My ultrabook's Intel IGP can handle the game at 720p on medium, while my desktop's GTX760 obviously runs it at a buttery smooth framerate with everything cranked to the max. This is one game I can actually play while flying on a plane.
The controls are properly structured for a mouse and keyboard. The interface adapts if you plug in a controller. I have tried both and surprisingly both feel equally smooth. I still stick with the keyboard and mouse to make it easier to type in names for my soldiers.
I sank over 150 hours into this game and will continue to sink even more!
P.S. After your first playthrough, if you want to spice things up with some cheats, name your troops Sid Meier, Ken Levine, Otto Zander, Joe Kelly, Chris Kluwe, or William Carter :)
I can't wait for XCOM 2. In the meantime, here are my minor criticisms:
- The probability system for scoring a shot during combat is sometimes frustrating, especially in a seemingly ideal situation where there aren't any physical obstacles between the soldier and the alien. If you're looking at a review to decide whether to buy this game, you probably like the anime aesthetic, so this review will mostly cover gameplay.
The combat itself is pretty good, character movement, attack ranges, areas of effect, elemental weaknesses, knockbacks, and charging the EXE Drive allow for a decent amount of strategy if you are so inclined. Bank EXE to perform more powerful finishers to your basic attacks, or expend it to deal massive damage.
You can customize your characters stats with equipment(although the game isn't very clear about which stats do what, you can probably get a general idea, though I looked at a guide to be sure), even allowing you to choose between STR or INT-based attacks on several characters. In addition to weapons, armor, and ornaments, there are also the largely cosmetic accessories and costumes, which typically provide only tiny bonuses to stats, so you can use whatever you think looks good if you so choose. There is even a customizeable equipment piece, the disc, which you can load with abilities you find the most useful.
I'm a bit of a grinder, so I'll mention a bit about grinding here. The grinding is pretty tastefully executed: rather than running through the most recent area to senselessly smash monsters' faces in, I often found myself choosing areas based on monsters' item drops in order to complete Plans, which could add items to the shop, slightly change mechanics, or unlock new dungeons. These Plans also require Storage (in MB), which is mostly found in boss battles in the main storyline, or from NPCs on the map as the story progresses, which encouraged to stop grinding and get back to the story. The combination of a direction to focus my grinding energy and a factor to limit meaningless grinding I found to be a very classy method of executing grinding.
The story is pretty simple; don't expect to be blown away by a new development, or to be particularly impressed in general; the game seems to focus on presenting a variety of characters and have them interact in a largely slice-of-life fashion, rather than provide a serious emotional or intellectual experience.
My largest problem with the game, was it's reuse of assets; many dungeons are reused in their entirety or pieced together from similar dungeons, and creatures are reused constantly, often without so much as a retexturing. It seems their budget went more to character visuals and voice acting(the weeaboo in me quickly changed the spoken dialogue to Japanese, where I was pleasantly surprised to hear many pretty big names from anime) than environmental or creature art.
Overall, it's not a bad game at all, and if you're on the fence to the extent that a review is gonna make or break it for you, I don't think you'll be disappointed.

Divinity: Original Sin (Classic) is an outstanding game. But it is not a game for everyone.
I have achieved 100% achievments on this game because I absolutely loved playing it over and over.
The game is a prequel to the Divinity series (Divine, Beyond, Divinity 2, Dragon Commander) so technically the 5th game released. It is based as a CRPG. So players whom remember Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights and such will immediately feel a sense of familiar top/down gameplay without the Isometric style.
The game mechanics are surprisingly new and very interesting. It takes a while to get a handle on how it all comes together but the fact all the rules are blind makes it more interesting.
First thing is this is a true RPG in the sense it's not all about combat. In fact you can bypass most combat in this game and finish it (a little salty there was no achievement for that). You can just fight your way through the game but you will miss out on a lot of XP and will be quite lost without some essential NPCs.
The downside to this; is the newer generations will have little to no idea how to progress. There are no quest markers, no easy to follow navigation, it's all up to you and your intellect. Which I guess is why there are so many bad reviews from players who can't deal with 'how hard' it is.
It reminds me a lot of the older Ultimate games where you are popped into the world and just have to figure it out. If that doesn't sound appealing then best avoid this game.
There are no classes in this game. You do get to choose a starting class if you want or you can just customise but either way it doesn't mean much since it's about just allocating skills & some attribute points, ultimately there is nothing stopping you from playing any number of solo or hybrid fighting/sneak/mage styles.
The sound engineering is sadly the weakness thing about the game. While the music is great and is a throw back to many of the original Divinity games it is a little buggy and can be either repetitive or just stops. This is weird in combat especially in an epic boss fight and sudden it's just quiet except for the voice lines or sound effects.
The story isn't anything to scream about. It's not new and original but it is interesting and fun for those that are interested in Rivellon's lore and history especially regarding  SOURCE and why it's tainted.
The process of playing 2 main characters is fun but it's no different from having a party of four in the ultimate series and the teleport pyramids are a fun way to get around some puzzles as well as call in for an immediate assist when one party split ends up in combat.
I highly recommend it to CRPG veterans but I would recommend the Enhanced Edition for brand new players.

I'm going to preface this review by saying I'm a huge fan of TellTale Games. However, I am appalled at the lack of quality involved in the production of this game. I don't even know where to begin.
TellTale Games usually has a bad track record of having choices that don't actually matter. I totally see this in every one of their games that I've played. But the choices don't just not matter in Game of Thrones - they're downright stupid. Many times, characters within the story strong arm you into having to make a decision that doesn't need to made. For instance, and without spoiling too much, Character 1 suggests Character 2 leaves for Character 2's safety, but Character 2 wants to stay or else Character 2 will get upset with the Player. BUT CHARACTER 1 IS COMPLETELY IN THE RIGHT AND CHARACTER 2 IS A COMPLETE IDIOT! What to do, what to do, you may ask yourself. Well, don't worry - if you're anything like me, then by the time you have to make this decision, you won't care about the well being of the characters around you anymore.
Next up - voice acting. Yeah, at first, I thought it was rad they got some original cast members to voice their characters.  Kit Harrington as Jon Snow FOR REAL?! Emilia Clarke as Daenerys Targaryen FOR REAL?! PETER DINKLAGE AS TYRION LANNISTER FOR REAL?! However, by Episode 2, I was asking myself if it was worth it. The characters from the show are barely featured in the game at all, and the characters you are exposed to for a majority of the game have incredibly unconvincing voice acting. There's such a blatant lack of detail that it makes dialogue's appear forced, like something out of a really bad B movie. Additionally, something I noticed specifically in Episode 6 was that a lot of dialogue from three specific characters would cut off halfway through the sentence.
The characters themselves are simply boring. Even the characters from the show have little depth, and they're characters we know already. The only character that matches her TV persona is Cersei Lannister. Jon Snow is almost a completely different character. Margaery Tyrell is an overly emotional train wreck. But I blame this on the writing. Because every other character not featured in the show is boring, as well. There is no definite main character, but the characters you play as have no depth and are completely unrelatable. Mira Forrestor is the worst TellTale character I have ever played as. Gared Tuttle is the blandest. Really, the only character I found to be interesting at all was Asher Forrestor, the exiled second son of the Forrestors.
Now, the real meat of the game: The story. Usually, in a TellTale game, the story really draws you in. Obviously, the first that comes to mind is The Walking Dead, but TellTale has shown story telling prowess through The Wolf Among Us and Tales From The Borderlands, as well, all four being incredibly fantastic games in their own amazing ways. The Game of Thrones story is awful in so many different ways. It feels like the story goes nowhere until Episode 5. I personally gave the game the benefit of the doubt after I finished Episode 1; maybe it's just some exposition. But by the end of Episode 2, I got worried. And by the end of Episode 3, I was real worried. And by the end of Episode 4, I knew I'd wasted my money. But the end of Episode 5 was something else - it featured many interesting elements of the story that actually moved the plot forward. I was ready for a kickass finale episode. But as I sit here, typing this out, I know that Episode 6 has confirmed that I really did waste my money. The ending, without going into too much detail, features "cliff hangers" that set things up for a Game of Thrones Season 2. There's an epilogue sequence that, admittedly, does intrigue me and leaves me wondering where the story will go. But I think back to the rest of the game and remind myself - save the money and watch a playthrough online if you get interested. TellTale seems to have taken George RR Martin's grim portrayal of the "A Song of Ice and Fire" series and tried to emulate it in the game - instead, they leave you with a game that leaves you feeling unfulfilled. Your heroes aren't going anywhere - where's the incentive to care anymore? In the book series and the TV program, the story and characters are engaging, and there are constantly plots being made to get back at the "villains" of the series (the best part is, there are no villains in either of those mediums). However, in the game, there are clear lines between good and evil, things that George RR Martin tried to stray from in the source material because that is the way life is - everything is gray, there is no black and white. With these two aspects of the source materials blended in this way, the player's experience is guaranteed to be unfulfilling and feel like a waste of time.
I highly recommend you watch a playthrough online if you are interested. Save your money for The Walking Dead Season 3, or The Wolf Among Us/Tales from the Borderlands Season 2. This game is not at all worth any amount of money, save maybe a dollar or two.
Yeah, maybe I'm a little salty, but wouldn't you be too?

I'm going to leave the recommendation at no for now, since it is difficult to come to a yes/no conclusion. If you can suffer through reading my review, the game has pros and cons that can be interpreted differently by different players.
>Played during development stages, got to top 30 in 1v1 by playing goo.
>Felt bad for playing an overpowered race (2 minute rage quit wins, or massive map expansion)
>Took a break to see if they would adjust the races.
>A big patch finally nerfs goo early game, commandos, and gladiuses (gladi?)
>Goo is still OP (imho), can still end the game in very early stages, but beta have a chance at stopping them (not sure on humans b/c I don't play them much)
The biggest problem I have- The resource areas deplete after a while (usually a long time at least), forcing expansion, but also expansion is very helpful in the game overall. Humans have never discovered how to counter the enigma of the sloped plane, so if there is a hill they can't expand out of their initial area. Beta have easy expansion, but they are vulnerable during it. These are well-balanced. However, the goo can expand easily without being vulnerable early game, and they can dominate the map. Unless the goo player has poor micro skills, it is rare that they lose.
Overall, I'd recommend people to give the game a try while it is on sale, NOT for full price. The campaign is fun, and sometimes challenging. I'd also recommend to play with friends, rather than getting frustrated in ranked against different exploits.

I would recommend ignoring my rating for this review. I have to give the game something and I'm not willing to vote it down but neither am I comfortable with the vote up. Steam really needs to add a middle ground option.
Grey Goo is a Command & Conquer styled real-time-strategy game centered around three races with their own unique playstyles. The game comes packed with features including Steam workshop support, single & multiplayer modes, ranked/unranked matchmaking, custom game support and player profiles. Grey Goo’s main campaign features high quality cutscenes and a reasonable story arc for each race. So, there’s the Beta who are considered the “balanced” race in terms of offense and defense with their bullet and missile weapons. Their unique features include being able to deploy buildings anywhere on the map without directly tied to the main mother base and walls that can be manned by units. The Humans are the technologically advanced race and are generally more defense oriented. Everything about them is tied into one core base, with any of their buildings requiring power coming directly from said base. Finally, there’s the Goo, the most unique race both in presentation and playstyle. This race of nanorobots is a collective intelligence that use large formless units that can split off to create other types of units. They generally tend to be more aggressive than the other two races as their formless units can do significant damage to enemy units if in close proximity. Some of their strengths are offset but their complete lack of air units. All three have their own unique attributes while sticking largely to the core of Grey Goo’s mechanics.
The Beta and Human races play out very similarly to each other. Both have a single base they are tied to, build generally the same buildings and have the same type of units. Each builds resource collectors that have harvesters transport resources from the collector back to the harvester. Both races then use these resources to carefully build more resource harvesters, tech buildings or factories. Technology buildings grant access to more advanced units and tech upgrades that can further enhance certain units. However, these tech upgrades are restricted to one change per type of unit. They tend to be helpful in certain situations but are otherwise not going to massively change how you play. When a player has lost all of their production buildings and main base, it’s game over. The Goo race on the other hand is unique though they ultimately have the same types of units and win/loss conditions as well. Instead of constructing buildings, they use Mother Goos to build up their forces. These giant formless masses can attack units, go to resource points and split off other Mother Goos or Proteans. They must stay on resource points as long as possible in order to build up mass which leaves them vulnerable to harassment. Proteans are smaller formless units that have a higher speed than Mothers, enabling them to attack or create light/heavy units depending on which protean they are. which can then be transformed to light or heavy units depending on the player. Once all Mother Goos are destroyed, they lose.
Performance in Grey Goo is disastrous despite months of patching and promises from the developers that it would be fixed. The entire main menu has severe lag, only managing to get somewhere in the realm of 20-40FPS. Why it’s so poor is unclear but it seems to be an engine issue. Cutscenes also have the same framerate problems and it’s really too bad because they are quite well done. It’s quite irritating to see this too when my CPU is only 45-50% consumed when Grey Goo is running. My GTX 970 should be able to easily handle this title but the framerate counter seems to indicate otherwise. The in-game situation isn’t much better as the framerate will go from a solid 60 to a mere 30-45 when a base is under construction. Turning every graphics option down to minimum helps things but it doesn’t fix the menu framerate lag and games can still bring the framerate down. It’s unclear why Grey Goo continues to suffer performance problems despite months of work but it’s definitely a problem worth considering if you’re interested in the title. It’s certainly frustrating enough for me to now want to play it. I could be much more understanding if the CPU/GPU was near max while playing Grey Goo. But it’s not. I did consult with their tech support over the course of several weeks in order to identify the issue but they didn’t have any suggestions on fixing it. Instead, they insisted that that my computer wasn’t up to the task. A computer that meets or exceeds the minimum required specs stated on the Steam store page.
During the campaign, you’ll be able to experience the three races in the following order. Beta, Human and last but not least, Goo. Each race is given five missions each for a total of 15. All three races have the same gameplay arc. You’re first given a very small army and no access to the race’s tech tree. The next three missions gradually unlock units and upgrades as you go along. The missions getting gradually more difficult as well. The fifth mission is the big event of the campaign, allowing the player to use the race’s Epic unit and all technology available. Overall, the campaign feels short even though it’s about 10 hours long. I’ll admit, I didn’t particularly enjoy the campaign either. Mostly because I did the same things to win mission after mission and the three race buildup starts creating a very samey feeling. It also doesn’t help that it feels like content has been cut from the game.
I think Grey Goo is a reasonable modern take on the C&C formula established so long ago. There’s a decent amount of strategy involved and each race feels uniquely its own and fairly well balanced. Unfortunately, the multiplayer has been falling apart since release and doesn’t seem to be showing signs of returning any time soon. The 20min+ long queues at this point make it even more of an anti-recommendation at this point. The story narrative also has multiple problems and I don’t really think the game is worth getting for it alone. At the very least, it’s questionable value for money, especially the DLC. Credit to the devs though, they have supported Grey Goo pretty well over the past year with multiple balance updates, new features and minor content additions. I think they’re pinning a little too much hope on it becoming a e-sport though. It’s just a pity that the engine problems and the expensive price haven’t been shored up during the course of this year, as I have no doubt that’s what has kept the multiplayer community from growing. Ultimately, while Grey Goo as an RTS is possible to enjoy at times, I have trouble recommending it due to the performance problems, shrinking multiplayer community and multiple story issues.

This has the soul of what I loved about the original X-COM. No it's not the same--just like it's not 1994 anymore--and I can happily embrace the UI and UX improvements while quietly missing some of the things discarded along the way (goodbye multiple base coordination, free-targeting cover, alien raids, going to mars, etc).
What you get is some fantastic action camp, soldiers you still care about, a progression system that makes soldiers more individual (and makes your more attached to them), and some really f'in-spectacular set pieces. In losing random generated maps (boo) we've gained boatloads of spectacularly crafted maps with some real depth and personality of their own. Do yourself a favor and get Enemy Within -- and sit tight for the "Whale Map."  Anyone whose played it will never forget it.
Oh, and when you're done, go explore the very large modding community that will put some of those things in the game that you missed.

While being a sequel, Company Of Heroes 2 offers less content than the original game and has many holes that scream to be filled with future DLC releases. Many of the units simply feel like a re-skin; the Russians take the exact role the Americans did in the first game. All of the Russian units have a similar counterpart in the first game and yet CoH2 still manages to offer less variety in units than that first game, leaving certain battlefield roles completely missing.
On CoH2's day of release it already had a gigantic collection of twenty six DLC packages totaling a whopping £42. Costing more than the game itself, the downloadable content added vehicle skins and access to five unique commanders which could have simply added to standard release. Downloadable content implies you are actually paying for something, however Company Of Heroes 2 manages to charge and give nothing in return. The five commanders that can be bought offer no new abilities, just remixing the existing content within the game, only changing the orders of abilities players can spend hard earned cash without adding a single drop of new content to the experience. For pre-ordering I had access to the new co-op “missions” known as theater of war; instantly I was unable to access most of this since it will be released as future DLC. These missions are meant to have a unique co-op focus, however they did little to bring anything fresh to the game: most of these simply being a skirmish with one or two unique abilities and a smaller unit variety then a standard skirmish.
The main campaign does little to inspire beyond the first game. Consisting of fourteen missions about an hour each, they simply feel like a skirmish game except offering unique units, upgrades, and abilities which are not available during any other game mode. I found myself questioning why all of this had been removed from the other game modes. With poor dialogue, story, and boring missions that simply feel like tutorials you will feel little incentive to return for a second play-through. Multiplayer does little to improve as an unfair matchmaking system frequently creates unbalanced teams as well as giving players no choice in what they would like to play. If you want to play with random players, you lose choice over the map played as well as only having access to point control mode. Creating your own custom game denies you access to other players, and only allows you to invite friends which feels unnecessarily limiting.
The new winter maps add new mechanics to the game in which infantry become exposed to the cold and risk freezing, while random blizzards limit speed and visibility that can quickly turn heavy skirmishes into silence and small raids. This welcome and unique design can really change the battlefield while making players adapt to the new low sight conditions however it soon loses its novelty after a few games. After a few maps I soon found that blizzards simply seem to slow the game down and add to unnecessary micromanagement of units. After hearing “Your men are freezing to death” I  moved my camera to see an infantry squad stood one meter too far from a fire where they simply stood allowing themselves to freeze to death. After this happened a few times while I focused on the battle it just made winter maps soon feel like additional and unneeded “busy work.” With no other new game mechanics besides additional “busy work” it brings into question, “why should I choose Company of Heroes 2 over the first?”
With the combat mechanics remaining the same of the first game I expected to find myself playing an almost identical game to the original but with additional content. However, after playing against the AI on many skirmish maps I soon realized that my choices were significantly more limited. All of the maps are very open, with little to no choke points to really plan any defensive tactics: I soon found myself getting slaughtered if I ever tried to play defensively.  Defenses soon become useless as they are now easily flanked by speeding armor or even basic the infantry squad which pushes all players to play aggressively and use almost identical tactics. Do you like to play defensively and push forwards inch by inch? Tough luck. Want to focus mostly on support infantry? Tough luck. The only way you can win is tanks, immune to most damage and with all anti-tank weaponry so easily flanked. Every match becomes a race to build the first tank and with Germany armor being superior to the soviets in every possible way, except mobility, the Germans have a significant advantage on all maps.
During a match you will eventually earn your first command point, giving you access to your custom selected commanders with each having five traits. At least one of these will be a passive ability that will add little to nothing to the battlefield. Two points will often give you access to unique units, with only two semi-unique units per commander it hardly changes how you decide to play against your opponent. Often these unique units are shared between many possible commanders further removing any roles or unique identity on the battlefield. Everyone builds the same units, everyone is forced to play the same aggressive tactics and as a result every game ends up playing out like the previous one. Losing teams do not have any chance to retake the battlefield against aggressive players and the winning team within the game can be seen within the first five minutes.
Pros:
+good campaign length of around ten or more hours
+action focused RTS appeals to those who are not interested in most RTS games
+weather elements are impressive for the first few game
+cinematic combat provides impressive sights
Cons:
-a complete downgrade of the first game
-high system requirements
-overpriced and unnecessary release DLC, with more to come!
-winning with defensive or support roles is impossible
-the new commander system makes every battle the same
-poor multiplayer system, removing all choice from players
-predictable campaign story does nothing to entice the player
-no reason to ever replay the campaign missions
-content available for campaign but denied in all other game modes
-skirmish and multiplayer maps offer no chance for a losing team to fight back
Company of Heroes 2 remains a good game, the fun action-orientated strategy game remains satisfying and intense while able to appeal to players that are not familiar to the RTS genre. Though still an enjoyable experience it is a complete downgrade from the first release back in 2006. Seven years later fans are left with an overpriced game. DLC, and less content than the first release for a small graphical update. For these reasons I would not recommend CoH2 to those interested as the unique gameplay the game has to offer should look to the original Company of Heroes instead.

I walked into this game expecting literally nothing but disappointment.
Thankfully, I could push my innate hate for fanservice only anime stuff aside for a few hours and walked out pleasantly surprised with this game.
It's, well. Not the best JRPG, but it's certainly unique and charming. I personally couldn't force myself to care enough to pay attention to the story, but I think it's got something to do with four anthropomorphized consoles fighting for... something. Anyways the main character gets theirself beat up and gets... yeah amnesia that trope's been used alot.
Something something makes friends and goes on a journey to beat up things. Typical RPG stuff that I'm probably missing 99% of. Yeah personally the story didn't really do it for me.
However, the gameplay interested me. I'm guilty of mindless grinding and this game has plenty of that don't worry there, but if you're an insane person who likes watching stats rise such as me, you may enjoy that part of it. The gameplay is an RPG style game where you take control over your character in a defined area, and highlight your little attack square over and enemy and you whack them.
While I know this has probably been done numerous times before, this is the first time I'VE personally seen it, and I really like it. It opens up realms of possibility for cheaping out attacks and hitting every single enemy when you obviously should not have.
There's also (apparently) many character outfits. Which I personally always thing is a good thing.
The characters themselves are unique enough for me to give them a pass on "are they humans and not robots" test. So that's also a pretty good thing when compared to OTHER games of the similar Visual Novel/JRPG style.
Overall, I'd rate this game an "Alright" out of five. Pick it up on sale and see if you like it.
Beware of the memes though, this game has plenty of those strewn about there. At least I didn't see any 2005 memes.
Also I forgot to mention the devs of this game are actually pretty active with updating their games and keeping them working, which I can respect.

I don't want to do this... review this game negatively. Really I don't, because it's an amazing Telltale game, very fun, with a very good and intriguing story. But there are two major issues here, two things which force me to say No :

Yet another game for which I wished there was a "neutral" review option. Child of Light is not a bad game, however it has many little defects that prevent it from being the real gem it could have been. I'll briefly explain what are the pros and cons of the game in my opinion.
+ Beautiful visual style and art direction.
+ Simple but effective combat system, which is an interesting variation of the classic ATB-based system often seen in JRPGs like Final Fantasy; the player has the possibility to influence in real time the speed of his enemies, thus making combat more dynamic.
+ Tactical boss battles; bosses are pretty smart and strong and you'll need to plan your moves carefully when facing them if you don't want to be defeated, especially when playing at the higher difficulty.
+ Good variety of playable characters and skills.
+ Nice soundtrack.
- You can only deploy two characters in battle at a time, which limits a lot strategy and often makes you feel like you have too many characters and too little space. Most boss battles require a continuous change of formation in order to be able to use the proper skills at the proper time, which often leads to waste more turns than necessary.
- Some characters are rarely useful and towards the end of the game you'll pretty much always use the same ones.
- The game is fairly short for an RPG (the 20+ hours I've spent on it were way more than enough to finish it, and I lost a good amount of time trying to farm gems and exp until I got bored) and there's no real need to exp your characters to the full extent of their skill trees in order to progress. There's also no real need to craft all the perfect gems to be equipped, also because finding all the necessary ones would require a lot of grinding. The longevity can be extended by playing a New Game+ but since there's no real change or reward for doing it, most people won't bother.
- The story is very basic, despite the interesting presentation and the peculiar rhymed narration, and that's just awful for a RPG like this. Yes, there is some lore (god I'm starting to hate this word) to be reconstructed by finding confessions, but it's nothing particularly detailed or deep. Most of the backstory is left to the imagination and all focus is on the simple main plot.
- Not a defect of the game itself, but it requires a Uplay account to be played. It wasn't a problem for me to create one but I really find stupid to use two DRMs for a single game. If Ubisoft didn't want people to play this anywhere else than on their platform, they shouldn't have allowed Valve to sell it on Steam. Period.
Considering all I think that Child of Light is a flawed little gem that could be worth a play but only if picked at sale price and only if you're not looking for deep gameplay or story. Otherwise you'll be very disappointed. I honestly expected much more from this title considering its fame and the enthusiastic reviews, but I guess that nowadays people are just too much inclined to see all the positive aspects of something they knee-jerk like and forget about objectivity.

While being a sequel, Company Of Heroes 2 offers less content than the original game and has many holes that scream to be filled with future DLC releases. Many of the units simply feel like a re-skin; the Russians take the exact role the Americans did in the first game. All of the Russian units have a similar counterpart in the first game and yet CoH2 still manages to offer less variety in units than that first game, leaving certain battlefield roles completely missing.
On CoH2's day of release it already had a gigantic collection of twenty six DLC packages totaling a whopping £42. Costing more than the game itself, the downloadable content added vehicle skins and access to five unique commanders which could have simply added to standard release. Downloadable content implies you are actually paying for something, however Company Of Heroes 2 manages to charge and give nothing in return. The five commanders that can be bought offer no new abilities, just remixing the existing content within the game, only changing the orders of abilities players can spend hard earned cash without adding a single drop of new content to the experience. For pre-ordering I had access to the new co-op “missions” known as theater of war; instantly I was unable to access most of this since it will be released as future DLC. These missions are meant to have a unique co-op focus, however they did little to bring anything fresh to the game: most of these simply being a skirmish with one or two unique abilities and a smaller unit variety then a standard skirmish.
The main campaign does little to inspire beyond the first game. Consisting of fourteen missions about an hour each, they simply feel like a skirmish game except offering unique units, upgrades, and abilities which are not available during any other game mode. I found myself questioning why all of this had been removed from the other game modes. With poor dialogue, story, and boring missions that simply feel like tutorials you will feel little incentive to return for a second play-through. Multiplayer does little to improve as an unfair matchmaking system frequently creates unbalanced teams as well as giving players no choice in what they would like to play. If you want to play with random players, you lose choice over the map played as well as only having access to point control mode. Creating your own custom game denies you access to other players, and only allows you to invite friends which feels unnecessarily limiting.
The new winter maps add new mechanics to the game in which infantry become exposed to the cold and risk freezing, while random blizzards limit speed and visibility that can quickly turn heavy skirmishes into silence and small raids. This welcome and unique design can really change the battlefield while making players adapt to the new low sight conditions however it soon loses its novelty after a few games. After a few maps I soon found that blizzards simply seem to slow the game down and add to unnecessary micromanagement of units. After hearing “Your men are freezing to death” I  moved my camera to see an infantry squad stood one meter too far from a fire where they simply stood allowing themselves to freeze to death. After this happened a few times while I focused on the battle it just made winter maps soon feel like additional and unneeded “busy work.” With no other new game mechanics besides additional “busy work” it brings into question, “why should I choose Company of Heroes 2 over the first?”
With the combat mechanics remaining the same of the first game I expected to find myself playing an almost identical game to the original but with additional content. However, after playing against the AI on many skirmish maps I soon realized that my choices were significantly more limited. All of the maps are very open, with little to no choke points to really plan any defensive tactics: I soon found myself getting slaughtered if I ever tried to play defensively.  Defenses soon become useless as they are now easily flanked by speeding armor or even basic the infantry squad which pushes all players to play aggressively and use almost identical tactics. Do you like to play defensively and push forwards inch by inch? Tough luck. Want to focus mostly on support infantry? Tough luck. The only way you can win is tanks, immune to most damage and with all anti-tank weaponry so easily flanked. Every match becomes a race to build the first tank and with Germany armor being superior to the soviets in every possible way, except mobility, the Germans have a significant advantage on all maps.
During a match you will eventually earn your first command point, giving you access to your custom selected commanders with each having five traits. At least one of these will be a passive ability that will add little to nothing to the battlefield. Two points will often give you access to unique units, with only two semi-unique units per commander it hardly changes how you decide to play against your opponent. Often these unique units are shared between many possible commanders further removing any roles or unique identity on the battlefield. Everyone builds the same units, everyone is forced to play the same aggressive tactics and as a result every game ends up playing out like the previous one. Losing teams do not have any chance to retake the battlefield against aggressive players and the winning team within the game can be seen within the first five minutes.
Pros:
+good campaign length of around ten or more hours
+action focused RTS appeals to those who are not interested in most RTS games
+weather elements are impressive for the first few game
+cinematic combat provides impressive sights
Cons:
-a complete downgrade of the first game
-high system requirements
-overpriced and unnecessary release DLC, with more to come!
-winning with defensive or support roles is impossible
-the new commander system makes every battle the same
-poor multiplayer system, removing all choice from players
-predictable campaign story does nothing to entice the player
-no reason to ever replay the campaign missions
-content available for campaign but denied in all other game modes
-skirmish and multiplayer maps offer no chance for a losing team to fight back
Company of Heroes 2 remains a good game, the fun action-orientated strategy game remains satisfying and intense while able to appeal to players that are not familiar to the RTS genre. Though still an enjoyable experience it is a complete downgrade from the first release back in 2006. Seven years later fans are left with an overpriced game. DLC, and less content than the first release for a small graphical update. For these reasons I would not recommend CoH2 to those interested as the unique gameplay the game has to offer should look to the original Company of Heroes instead.

To be honest, I really have mixed feelings about this one.
On one hand, this is a very well realized classical isometric RPG. The mechanics are quite well done, which put it one notch above Pillars of Eternity, which, at some points, is simply a chore to play.
On the other hand, I am a story freak. I love games with good and cohesive stories. This game doesn't really deliver on that field.
It's a pity because I really enjoyed the stories of the original Divinity games. That's why I had high hopes coming into this one. However, I didn't manage to even finish this one - simply because I lost interest. The storyline drags a lot with not really many interesting twists and not enough happening to keep it going.
So, if you enjoy a decent world and good turn-based mechanics, this RPG is for you, If, like me, you enjoy a good leading story and characters, than I would wait for the sequel - hopefully it will address the storybuilding flaws.

Divinity: Original Sin is a really interesting take on a turn-based strategy system, with a charming world and some nice storytelling. It does have a lot of clunky features, but I only played the Classic version of the game. It's possible that some of these were fixed in the enhanced edition.
Pros:
-Diverse strategic and characterisation options for your characters, with some nice banter moments between them.
-Really engaging roleplaying system: you can choose whether your playable characters agree or disagree with one another's decisions, which affects their personality trees (and gives stat bonuses),
-Charming, expansive open world with some nice story and humorous moment. Don't expect to finish this quickly!
Cons:
-So, so much RNG dependence. No matter how much you try to strategize, there's so much of this game that boils down to hoping the rolls go okay. Even the roleplaying/storytelling aspect has this horrid fake rock-paper-scissors system that comes into play far too often.
-Has an inventory management system that's even worse than early Bioware games. You loot an item, the item gets sorted into one charater's inventory (inventory isn't shared between characters). But you probably need to transfer it to another character with high loremaster skill, so that he can identify the item and what class the item is for, so that he can send it to that character so that you can change to that character for them to equip the item. Ugh. The trading system is also very tedious.
-The game doesn't do a very good job of giving you direction. You'll probably find you're heading to areas out of sequence, and hitting enemies that are too strong for your level, but the game won't give you any hint that you're not supposed to be in an area yet, or give you any kind of clue about the route you're 'supposed' to take first. It's just trial and error - will this route lead me to winnable combat? Maybe this one?

Block N Load is a Freemium First-Person Shooter created by Artplant and Published by Jagex Games Studios on the Unity Engine. This game was originally in Early Access Beta for about $5 as a Premium game in late 2014, but has become Free-To-Play in May 2015. The game features eight Blockheads / classes to choose from, a base preparation period for those that want to build a massive death trap for any foreigners, and a completely different 5v5 experience that you might not have felt in other Freemium games.
According to some of the community, this game used to be set for a higher premium price during its Early Access Beta stage, and has claimed to accommodate these users with all the classes along with premium skins when they have announced the game to become a Free-To-Play game. With that in mind, how does this game stand as a Free-To-Play?
This game does not offer much - if any - kind of lore in the whole "blockhead" universe. The classes themselves can fit into some strange archetypes as well. You have Sergeant Stone, which is your No-Nonsense Blood-thirsty brute of a drill instructor, the nearly insane scientist known as Doc Eliza that shoots globs of acid to slow people down, or the Yeti, the Russian abdominal monster that crushes anything in his wake.
For a game built off the Unity Engine, I'm somewhat surprised in regards to the graphical options based off experience. Block N' Load offers resolutions supporting from potato resolutions like 640x480 to more average resolutions such as 1920x1080. There is an option to select which monitor to run the program on, but not one that supports multiple screens.
if you really want to get the most bang for your buck. The main drawback I see from seeing these options are that they're not detailed enough, as most of the options listed above are a toggle, not which one you want to do.

For a bit of context, I am running an Intel i5-4460 at 3.2GHz with an MSI Geforce GTX 970 with 8GB of RAM. If I am not putting out enough information, then please do comment below, but I am running everything at the highest specs I can set in the game, with no particular experience editing the game's files to make it look "prettier". I made sure to turn off Vsync, and it strangely feels like my framerate caps at 70. I guess I was expecting a smoother experience since this didn't seem to be a game that's very graphically intensive, but I digress.
The Aesthetics in the game can be a redeeming part though. The map design themselves don't fit my tastes, but your mileage may vary. The User Interface design itself is a personal soft spot that I have, so if you like a more compact, cozy kind of design, this would not appeal to you. I did find some minor problems with this, and it was that it took me some time to figure out what the exit window was. I can't imagine it to be some kind of culture-shock kind of thing for me, but the icon next to the gear image gave me the association that it was to pop-out, and not to close the game.
All of that said, I came into this game under the impression that other reviewers generalized it to be, that the game is a mix between Minecraft and Team Fortress 2, where obstensibly the fort-building part and main aesthetic comes from Minecraft, whereas the classes and overall atmosphere felt like Team Fortress 2. And boy, did they hit a bulls-eye
on this one.. but the one thing irking me about this statement is that
In fact, it's leading me to believe that this game just wanted a mash-up of every popular game out there.
When you start up the client, the game introduces you to three prompts -- One to introduce the player to the FPS genre and eventually Block N' Load, One that gives a quick overview over what Block 'N Load is for FPS players, as well as a prompt to directly jump into the game. Of the three prompts, only two actually reward you, and they're both the ones that encourage you to jump straight into the game, even if you don't understand the basis of the game.
Guess that's something new I was not expecting.
When looking for a match, you can choose to either head into a match-making system or head into a dedicated server list. If you're planning on using the matchmaking system, you are able to invite your friends, but it can only be up to two, or so it seems from the User Interface. From there, I've only been able to play one mode, which was essentially a 5v5 destroy the other base kind of mode. From creating a match on the dedicated server list, I remember being able to change the number of bases, the building phase, among other mutators, but I unfortunately was unable to find any other mode.
The controls to the game from time to time are unresponsive, and I want to chalk that up to not understanding the controls very well. At least the net code is for the most part on-par with other shooters. Now, unless you are facing a player who mistakenly comes to your region and teleports across every five seconds, it's mostly been a fun experience so far. I haven't really met a lot of laggers to say the least, and while I have made a fair share of dumb mistakes while I was playing, I at least felt like I wasn't terribly hindered by more technical issues. Still, changing from building to shooting was a problem I had while providing the video review.
The most shameful part I see in this whole prospect is that there seems to be a lot of premade maps to start building and fight from, but there are only two maps you could choose when you get into the game. I was pretty grateful to see a handful of the maps I played in, but only being able to choose two out of the other premades in the list was upsetting.

I cannot recommend this game enough. Although it's different that the traditional Far Cry game with it's lack of meme-heavy villains and grenade launchers, it makes up for all of that with setting alone. The sound design is just incredible, and the world is just stunning. I don't exactly have a high end graphics card but it looks pretty solid at high settings.
This is arguably one of the nicest looking games to come out in the last year, and as a fan of the Far Cry formula I cannot recommend this enough. They removed the tedious radio towers and replaced them with bonfires that serve as a sort of smaller outpost. You can use them for fast travel just like any other outpost, too. The beast master mechanics really seem to balance out the gameplay. It's difficult to worry about the lack of machine guns when you have a bear that is just tearing people apart. Sometimes tamed beasts will attack hostiles even without the player's command, which really makes them work more like allies than weapons.
The best part though, is that I've barely scatched the surface. I've tamed brown bears, but I've never seen the larger cave bears that are in the game. I've found so many camps, caves and hidden areas in my journey but I've been so busy reaching new outposts that I haven't stopped to appreciate them. But they are on my map and I can return to them at any time. A lot of the outposts have similar enemies, and maybe require similar strategies to take them down, but in no way did I ever feel that this game was repeatative.
I know the other reviews for this game seem to revolve around technical issues people are having, and I believe that is justified. However I have not encountered a single error screen in the time I've played this game and the game runs just fine. I would however recommend that you dismiss any non-bug related reviews from people with less than two hours of play time.♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't get real until you tame honey badgers.

Grim Dawn is one of the best ARPGs since Diablo 2: Lord of Destruction and Torchlight. I cannot recommend this game enough, especially if you're starved for an ARPG that offers a lot of replay value. It is an essential buy for fans of this genre and you should stop reading this lengthy review and play it now!
There are a lot of good things to say about Grim Dawn. I absolutely haven't felt this way about an ARPG for a real long time. It scratched that itch for me that Diablo 3 and Path of Exile couldn't. The game is not without its faults, however, since the pros heavily outweigh the cons I'll start with the bad and follow up with the good.
The music/soundtrack is incredibly limited and it's something where I ended up turning it off to play my own music or podcasts over instead. To be completely honest, a large majority of the music sounded like someone practicing guitar for the first time... and you're hearing it over and over
It's really not good and you'll quickly grow to hate it the longer you play, which is unfortunate because a decent soundtrack with a ton of variety would compliment such an already awesome game even further! The music is just so detached from the wide variety of environments you'll venture across.
The only real other complaint is the story seems to progress in a weird way that it kind of completely forgets about what you've done in the starting act as well as the NPCs in the first town area where your journey began. The story is not bad and it definitely moves forward without dragging on. It just felt weird that after all I did to help the people in the first town - or even convince stranded NPCs to join said town - it became an afterthought.
Other than that there are a few QoL improvements which I would really like to see that ostensibly could be changed in a future patch. One of them being the color indicators for loot. There are gems, or "components", in the game and the rare versions of the components share a nearly identical yellow as magic level items (akin to blues in Diablo). I could name a few more but this review is already getting long and I would just be nitpicking.
Grim Dawn does a fairly good job setting up the world you're in. There is a good reason - several, in fact - why so many people say that this is how Diablo 3 should've been. One of those reasons is that you feel like you're a part of this one big cohesive world when traveling from area to area. It all meshes in seamlessly and if you venture too far ahead too soon, you'll come across enemies far too tough for you to handle at the present time.
Enemies have their own levels, much like you would have in a Diablo 2 or Borderlands. They also have a variety of elemental strengths and resistances (as do you) that you need to be aware of. Fortunately, you have the ability to create dual-class characters and with the combinations of classes and skills at your disposal, you become pretty flexible on being able to handle enemies. You don't need to choose a second class for your character but the option is there by level 10.
Being able to create a variety of builds is a part of the game's replay value. You'll eventually come across certain items like relics or armor, for example, that enable your character to dual-wield pistols which is one of many exclusive skills you can only get from gear rather than from a specific class' skill tree. This game has a lot of loot and it's incredibly satisfying when you finally find a rare/epic/legendary piece of gear that's an actual upgrade from what you've been using for a while. There are also a wide variety of gems called "components" which can be used for crafting but also share a similarity with gems in Path of Exile. Certain components when attached to certain parts of your gear can either give you a buff in stats or entirely new skills, such as a Fireball skill.
The game's story is pretty long and will take you a few days to complete all the side quests and main story the first time through. The game also has elements of choices and consequences. Doing stuff for (or aligning with) one faction might♥♥♥♥♥♥off or lock you out of another rival faction. You may come across a random NPC that may or may not be evil af that could take advantage of your kindness (if you choose to be). When you have earned enough respect and trust within a faction, you can start taking on an endless loop of optional Bounties (side missions) that'll earn you new stuff and more respect.
There are also roguelike dungeons which require keys to enter. I found these dungeons to have a very Dark Souls-y vibe to them, as it really changes the way you play inside them and they are incredibly challenging. If you can survive through them, the reward is usually worthwhile. These types of dungeons are limited in quantity and are pretty tough. Some seem to be intended as end-game content in order to survive through and complete.
All in all, there is likely a bunch more I left out but if you want the TL;DR, then as I already mentioned off the top of this review, if you like ARPGs buy this game right now! It's an original thing that meshes a bunch of similar concepts/good ideas from other ARPGs like Path of Exile and Diablo 2. It's actively being supported by the devs plus the online community is active and largely friendly.

Very much a high quality old-fashioned RTS with a blissfully modern interface and a really rare dedication to worldbuilding. The campaign reflects the basic gameplay properly and provides a genuine challenge and the cutscenes and voice acting are exotically good for an RTS game. The campaign does have a couple of strange difficulty spikes and a few things that could've been used more but I've enjoyed it more than pretty much any of the gimmick-laden stuff that has predominated in RTS campaigns since probably Age of Empires 3.  I've been dipping my toes in the multiplayer and think the blend of a more Total Annihilation production-style economy with the conventional RTS resource pools makes for some very interesting options and the way the factions balance against each other is quite interesting. Looking forwards to playing more.

A twin stick shooter not only powered by music, but powered by YOUR music! Beat Hazard takes your songs and puts you into a world of intense, twin-stick shooter action. The music you play really impacts the flow of the game from the enemies that spawn to how fast and frantic movement on the screen is, especially when taking into account the wonderful, very bright visuals.
The game alone, "regular" Beat Hazard is awesome, however for the TRUE feel of the game purchasing the entire set of DLC is worth every penny. The "Ultra" DLC adds more ranks, new enemy, higher difficulty and improves the game all round. Then, to add to this chaos, the "Shadow Operations Unit" DLC adds a VERY nice element of challenge that adds a new ranking system along side the normal one which rewards the player for completing challenges. This, however, is not easy as a death during a challenge will set you back. Be it that the current song does not count towards a total of songs completed on 'x' difficulty, or that you lose ALL (yes, all) progress in that challenge, deaths are even more unbearable than usual.
Please note: In order to use songs from iTunes you will need to purchase the "iTunes & m4a file support" DLC. It's cheap, and I understand why they've done it. You're best off buying the mega bundle anyway as all the DLC is worth it.

It's tough to thoroughly appreciate a game when it's still in Early Access, but the fact that there's nothing preventing you from playing continuously (as there's not now, nor do I ever think should be an official "end") and amassing incredible stats and weaponry, is extremely telling. This game was complete a few months ago when I purchased it, and it's added a lot since then. It's simple to pick up and play, and it's tough to master (especially when you take a break for a month and come back to new game mechanics!) which is a great feature of this game. The developers are trying to get the updates out, and usually focusing on major, imperative facets.
Slight things have happened since I purchased this game (not the least of which is an increase in the price!) so there are bugs to occasionally look out for, but they've been dutiful in weekly updates (it'll be bi-weekly now, but I don't see that as a problem) and even updating in-between when bugs are noticed.
The developers are taking notice of what the community wants and responding by prioritizing that, and actually returning the feedback with in-game changes!
It's a very complete game, despite there still being a lot to add. And I don't see a reason not to purchase it, unless you want to truly wait until it's released.
I can't see the price going down much, though, so you may want to purchase it while you can.

First of all, I think this is a must have for any Turn-Based RPG fan, almost everything about it is perfect, it’s simply very charming.
The artwork, the atmosphere, the characters, the gameplay mechanics, the music, they are amazing, especially the music it’s so beautiful and emotional it makes a great memory for me, although I wish there were more tracks, sometimes they tend to repeat a little bit.
I enjoyed the combat system so much, I stand to be corrected but I think it’s one of kind, I mean the way it handles the turn is so immersive, the way you can gain advantage and disadvantages based on the way you attack enemies (normal, getting ambushed, or surprise attack) is unique as well, the way you collect wishes to replenish HP and MP is nice and fun too.
The way the story was written is again so beautiful, the way the text rhymes is one of a kind and I disagree with people thinking that it gets old, actually it’s so well written and perfectly woven from start to end, kudos to the developers for such an artistic touch.
I lost count of all the thing this game does perfectly, but there are a very few minor cons as well even though they didn’t affect my experience at all, for example most of the potions you collect are useless, you have them as spells, also why can’t I use three protagonist instead of two? It feels like this game was designed for three anyway, also the leveling tree felt a bit messy sometimes, and I can’t help but to notice a balancing problem, and without spoiling anything, the way you can abuse the paralyze system end game makes the game too easy as you can literally freeze your enemies the whole game and win flawlessly.
All in all this is a great game, a must have in my opinion even full price, I finished this game in 24 hours, but half of that time was just grinding to level up (I love doing that in RPG’s), it felt hard to say goodbye to this one after finishing it, I give this game an excellent 9 out of 10.
