Grim Dawn is one of the best ARPGs since Diablo 2: Lord of Destruction and Torchlight. I cannot recommend this game enough, especially if you're starved for an ARPG that offers a lot of replay value. It is an essential buy for fans of this genre and you should stop reading this lengthy review and play it now!
There are a lot of good things to say about Grim Dawn. I absolutely haven't felt this way about an ARPG for a real long time. It scratched that itch for me that Diablo 3 and Path of Exile couldn't. The game is not without its faults, however, since the pros heavily outweigh the cons I'll start with the bad and follow up with the good.
The music/soundtrack is incredibly limited and it's something where I ended up turning it off to play my own music or podcasts over instead. To be completely honest, a large majority of the music sounded like someone practicing guitar for the first time... and you're hearing it over and over
It's really not good and you'll quickly grow to hate it the longer you play, which is unfortunate because a decent soundtrack with a ton of variety would compliment such an already awesome game even further! The music is just so detached from the wide variety of environments you'll venture across.
The only real other complaint is the story seems to progress in a weird way that it kind of completely forgets about what you've done in the starting act as well as the NPCs in the first town area where your journey began. The story is not bad and it definitely moves forward without dragging on. It just felt weird that after all I did to help the people in the first town - or even convince stranded NPCs to join said town - it became an afterthought.
Other than that there are a few QoL improvements which I would really like to see that ostensibly could be changed in a future patch. One of them being the color indicators for loot. There are gems, or "components", in the game and the rare versions of the components share a nearly identical yellow as magic level items (akin to blues in Diablo). I could name a few more but this review is already getting long and I would just be nitpicking.
Grim Dawn does a fairly good job setting up the world you're in. There is a good reason - several, in fact - why so many people say that this is how Diablo 3 should've been. One of those reasons is that you feel like you're a part of this one big cohesive world when traveling from area to area. It all meshes in seamlessly and if you venture too far ahead too soon, you'll come across enemies far too tough for you to handle at the present time.
Enemies have their own levels, much like you would have in a Diablo 2 or Borderlands. They also have a variety of elemental strengths and resistances (as do you) that you need to be aware of. Fortunately, you have the ability to create dual-class characters and with the combinations of classes and skills at your disposal, you become pretty flexible on being able to handle enemies. You don't need to choose a second class for your character but the option is there by level 10.
Being able to create a variety of builds is a part of the game's replay value. You'll eventually come across certain items like relics or armor, for example, that enable your character to dual-wield pistols which is one of many exclusive skills you can only get from gear rather than from a specific class' skill tree. This game has a lot of loot and it's incredibly satisfying when you finally find a rare/epic/legendary piece of gear that's an actual upgrade from what you've been using for a while. There are also a wide variety of gems called "components" which can be used for crafting but also share a similarity with gems in Path of Exile. Certain components when attached to certain parts of your gear can either give you a buff in stats or entirely new skills, such as a Fireball skill.
The game's story is pretty long and will take you a few days to complete all the side quests and main story the first time through. The game also has elements of choices and consequences. Doing stuff for (or aligning with) one faction might♥♥♥♥♥♥off or lock you out of another rival faction. You may come across a random NPC that may or may not be evil af that could take advantage of your kindness (if you choose to be). When you have earned enough respect and trust within a faction, you can start taking on an endless loop of optional Bounties (side missions) that'll earn you new stuff and more respect.
There are also roguelike dungeons which require keys to enter. I found these dungeons to have a very Dark Souls-y vibe to them, as it really changes the way you play inside them and they are incredibly challenging. If you can survive through them, the reward is usually worthwhile. These types of dungeons are limited in quantity and are pretty tough. Some seem to be intended as end-game content in order to survive through and complete.
All in all, there is likely a bunch more I left out but if you want the TL;DR, then as I already mentioned off the top of this review, if you like ARPGs buy this game right now! It's an original thing that meshes a bunch of similar concepts/good ideas from other ARPGs like Path of Exile and Diablo 2. It's actively being supported by the devs plus the online community is active and largely friendly.

is a (slightly-grindy) JRPG developed by Idea Factory and the remake of
released for PS3.
The four CPUs of Gamindustri are in a bitter fight for the title of the "True Goddess". This battle however has been fought for several hundred years already. When a mysterious voice appears to three of the CPUs, they team up to defeat the remaining one - Purple Heart, Neptune - and knock her down to the main land...
If you have already played other main-series titles of this game, the gameplay is pretty much the same as always.
For those who don't know, there is a generic overworld from which you access the dungeons, shops and other instances, the dungeons themselves where you can walk around, collect items and fight monsters.
Encounters are - rather than being random - based on "symbols" which are enemies on the dungeon map.
For combat you can set 3 characters to fight at the same time. During each character's turn, they may move and choose an action (attack, item, etc.). The CPUs still retain their transformed state, HDD, which increases their stats.
And then there's even more stuff you can do, but that's nothing worth noting here (and nothing that would change your mind).
The grinding isn't as bad as many people make it out to be; a little tactic can help you out. And there's fan-service. Nothing all too significant, but it's definitely there.

Far Cry 3 was a very, very good game.  With Far Cry 4, Ubisoft took a 'it isn't broke, so don't try to fix it' approach, taking 3, transporting it to a more mountainous area, and giving it a new story and new protagonist, plus one or two other little tweaks and features.  Primal is a little bit more of a departure, with the lack of vehicles, a beast taming function, and a basic village building bit that ties into an expanded crafting and skill set, but it is Ubisoft doing this again, so it's basically what you'd expect from Far Cry in 10,000BCE. First of all, I think this is a must have for any Turn-Based RPG fan, almost everything about it is perfect, it’s simply very charming.
The artwork, the atmosphere, the characters, the gameplay mechanics, the music, they are amazing, especially the music it’s so beautiful and emotional it makes a great memory for me, although I wish there were more tracks, sometimes they tend to repeat a little bit.
I enjoyed the combat system so much, I stand to be corrected but I think it’s one of kind, I mean the way it handles the turn is so immersive, the way you can gain advantage and disadvantages based on the way you attack enemies (normal, getting ambushed, or surprise attack) is unique as well, the way you collect wishes to replenish HP and MP is nice and fun too.
The way the story was written is again so beautiful, the way the text rhymes is one of a kind and I disagree with people thinking that it gets old, actually it’s so well written and perfectly woven from start to end, kudos to the developers for such an artistic touch.
I lost count of all the thing this game does perfectly, but there are a very few minor cons as well even though they didn’t affect my experience at all, for example most of the potions you collect are useless, you have them as spells, also why can’t I use three protagonist instead of two? It feels like this game was designed for three anyway, also the leveling tree felt a bit messy sometimes, and I can’t help but to notice a balancing problem, and without spoiling anything, the way you can abuse the paralyze system end game makes the game too easy as you can literally freeze your enemies the whole game and win flawlessly.
All in all this is a great game, a must have in my opinion even full price, I finished this game in 24 hours, but half of that time was just grinding to level up (I love doing that in RPG’s), it felt hard to say goodbye to this one after finishing it, I give this game an excellent 9 out of 10.

Kill

kill
buy guns
buy food
kill
buy food
If you don't exploit the game, it's really hard to survive...almost impossible with an odd diffuculty curve which randomly ranps up nearby locations to frantic and dangerous in the first 20 days. TRY THIS GAME.
Summary: This game is an appallingly funny game and a really fun time!
Good: Normally, I'm not an FPS gamer, but this game has me making an exception. The stunt and slide system, while a little unrealistic (you can slide up stairs like you're made of rocket propelled olive oil) is EXTREMELY engaging, and leads to some hilarious moments in gaming. The first time you follow an opponent who has jumped off a roof to prevent him from denying you style points, you'll be utterly and irrevocably hooked. Having an aerial gunfight is more fun than I can possibly explain.
In the middle of your match, randomized objectives will spawn, and while they are pretty familiar tropes (check point racing, kill the target (who gets super powers until killed), deliver briefcase to specified point), it's presented in a whole new way. Instead of each of these being a dedicated game type, it's just an objective that can give you a pretty substantial bonus to your score.
Bad: Grenades are pretty damn OP. This game is scored on style points, not kills, and not only do grenades give you a lot of them, in most maps you can pretty much just fire blindly and forget. The majority of the time, you'll nab some points. While the mechanics are fun and engaging, they still seem glitchy and inconsistent, but not enough that it detracted from my experience. Also, the game doesn't give a good enough reaction to damage. A small red tint creeping in to the screen would be nice.
Ugly: In every match on the servers I played on, before you can get fighting, you have to watch a rather loud commercial for a video game or console. I don't mind developers monetizing free games, but I would gladly pay to have these ads removed.
All in all, you NEED to try this game. It may not find a permanent home in your library, but you will thoroughly enjoy the time you do put in to this game.

Half-Life 2 is one of those games that is often labled as the best game ever created, is it true though? In my honest opinion yes, absolutely yes! The first game which came out in 1998 already changed everything we knew about FPS games, some may say that Doom was far more influencial for the genre but it was Half-Life that showed exactly how far a simple shooting game with modest graphics can do and now years later the long-awaited sequel did exactly what we wanted it to do, it surpassed our expectations. So is HL 2 the best game ever created? That is greatly subjective, for me the original will always hold a special place in my heart and I'm sure for most of you other more successful games might take that place but let's be real, HL 2 is the pinnacle of gaming experience no matter if you played it when it came out or right now years later when many other similar games came out.
In short, Half-Life 2 is what every game developer should play before considering to make a game that will be a success!

Telltale, you keep breaking my heart.  You do it to me every time.
And I kind of love it.
Game of Thrones isn't likely to win any converts, though if you haven't experienced Telltale's brand of storytelling you probably should, post haste: this game, both seasons of The Walking Dead, and The Wolf Among Us (sequel plz!!!) are all awesome narratively and stylistically; beautiful and intense experiences centered around storytelling and relationships.
This one's definitely got the most punch for fans of the show and/or novels, and like most TTG offerings the narrative choice executes primarily in shifting tone, characterizations, and relationships through the story rather than dramatically divergent series of events.  Gameplay consists of reflex QTEs and targetting/timing exercises for the action scenes alongside the periodic (usually exceptionally simple) puzzling or stealth to do.
Past the caveats, what I found here was a heartwrenching and complex tale of politics and pride, justice and pragmatism.  An examination of the dark and dangerous side of feudalism and the nefarious machinations of man and magic that this series has always evoked on full display with gorgeous art and heraldry that have quickly become iconic, in my opinion, to the setting.  House Forrester's days have never been bleaker in recorded history, I should think-- and what a rollercoaster that nightmare becomes.  If you like Game of Thrones or dark fantasy in general, and can take all your best laid plans coming to naught but blood and tears and the promise of revenge, check this one out.

Lethal league's core gameplay loop is the some of the most fun I've had since I started playing games on PC. It's a very basic game about hitting an anti-gravity ball at opposing players to kill them. Each round involves up to 4 players in a 2d arena hitting a ball at each other until only one player is left standing. The ball's speed increases with every hit so the game can become particularly intense when you and your opponents are all frantically trying to hit a ball that is travelling so fast that it appears to be in 6 places at once. Being hit by the ball after it has been hit by another player (not in your possession) means instant death; so reaction times and skillful plays are key.
The matches last around 10 rounds and can take place in a variety of different arenas each with it's own theme and great soundtrack.There are 6 different characters to play as and each of them feels very distinct in playstyle due to each having different hit animations, mobility options and a unique special ability that can change the tide of battle in an instant.
I won't lie to you, this game is extremely repetitive, but if you find the core gameplay principle of hitting a ball at ridiculous speeds into another player's face extremely satisfying like I do, then you will be able to put a respectable amount of hours into this game; especially if you bring freinds along for the ride. as such I would definitely recommend this game at its current price.

Divinity: Original Sin is good, but overrated. The visuals, music, combat system etc. are all solid, but there are a seeming myriad of little annoying design choices that bring the overall experience down.
Inventory management gets very messy. In-combat click detection is done in a weird way, which often results in misclicks. Around 1/3 of available skills are useless or barely useful. Character customization is respectable, but the portraits that represent your character in dialogue and combat are all premade. So if you decide to make a character with a bright blue afro (which is possible, btw), there isn't any portrait that is going to match your creation. It kind of defeats the purpose of character customization; they may as well have you select from a pool of premade appearances...
Even so, none of these issues are deal-breakers, imo. Despite all of its flaws, Divinity: Original Sin is a good game. If you like rpgs in the vein of Baldur's Gate, then in the worst case scenario this game will still likely be enjoyable to you.

This game wasn't on my radar when it came out so I picked it up during a sale and OMFG... this game is so much fun and is very VERY underrated.
Story: The plot is good that can give fun little twists that you weren't expecting. Though the only good character and the one  with the only good voice acting is the main character who is voiced by Roger Crag Smith (Chris Redfield and Ezio Auditore). Although my biggest issue is that the story just feels very cliche at like every big action moment and they don't try anything creative. Also the antagonist was being way too serious that it became very annoying to listen to him... Clearly he wants to be a Vaas character but fails so bad.
Gameplay: Best part of this game is how much variety there is in the gameplay. This is a survival game and you have to search throughout the city for items to craft your weapons and other items. There is even a leveling up system for both your weapons, agility, and survival abilities to unlock more perks, best perk of all is the drop kick. You can find blueprints throughout the game to help make even more interesting weapons and add boosters to them more powerful. The parkour system may feel wierd at first when your doing the tutorial mission based around it, after a while it becomes very fluid and responsive that you can pull off some very cool moments with the parkour. Melee weapons do have the same animations over and over again but killing zombies with them just never gets old that you just want to go through multiple killing sprees of zombies. Gunplay is honestly only ment for human enemies since the sounds of the gunfire will draw in zombies but the weapons are very well designed for either situation. At night time the game turns into a horror game that you have to run away from certain zombies that will almost instantly kill you. Side missions are more interesting than the main missions and you will spend a lot of time with it. The only problem with the gameplay is at the beginning of the game you don't have the most powerful weapons so they just degrade fast and takes forever to kill zombies.
Conclusion: Dying Light is a very well made zombie survival game and should be played by every fan of these genres. The story isn't really something you will remember or you probably are gonna careless about but it still offers a thrilling experience. At the start of the game it may feel harsh on you for having weak weapons and stats but later on it pays off. If you have a group of friends to play with this game would be a good option since it is co-op and you can play through the whole story together.

Let's be perfectly clear: It's obvious to those whom played Saints Row: The Third that Saints Row IV is just Saints Row: The Third with a slightly different skin. The price should have never been that of a brand new game. ”Deep Silver” Volition   seems to pride itself on being “out there” and have went out of their way to stray from the original concept of Saints Row since “The Third”.
Season Passes, DLC and other things cut out of the game to sell you later are also still a disturbing trend.
That said, Saints Row IV does stand very well on its own via the very fun new age and retro mini games included.  The material, which is mostly just humorous parodies of other franchises, is fun to engage in but can at times make you wonder if there is anything original about Saints Row IV at all.
Your character is super powered pretty much the whole duration of Saints Row IV which makes all the vehicles such as cars, boats and airplanes “virtually” useless to say the least. You are basically Neo in the Matrix (to give you a little perspective) and Neo doesn’t drive cars. So if you were one of those people that enjoyed customizing your vehicles, driving around town and racing with the police, it’s still there but why would you do it when you can run faster than cars now?
If you can FORGET that Saints Row was about driving, gangs and drama with humor on the side, you will be fine. If you can’t forget that, you will probably hate Saints Row IV.
I personally feel that Saints Row IV is the worst in the series but it has its good moments. I, however, would not like to see the series become more “wacky” than this or I fear “Saints Row” might as well be called “The Animaniacs”.
I suppose you should give this game a try if you are into the Saints Row series but I would recommend you buy this game only when it is 50 to 70 percent off so you do not feel ripped off because most of the missions are just repeated with characters giving you "different reasons" for doing the same things over and over.

Grey Goo is great concept, but suffers from bugs, crashes and lack of content.
The best way to describe this game is "incomplete".
There are only five missions per race in the single player campaign. The story is disjointed and not very well presented, despite beautiful cutscenes and decent mission briefings. At the end of the campaign, you find out this game, which is billed as a full game, is only a precursor to an actual storyline. The Emergence mini-campaign only adds three more missions (total; not per race) which take place during the regular game's campaign from a different perspective, giving no additional story.
Unit types are mostly what you'd expect (light units, scouts, medium units, artillery, air and anti-air). Note the distinct lack of heavy units. Instead, you get epic units, which are extremely overpowered monstrosities. Putting aside the controversial epic units, the basic units are limited and poorly balanced. Artillery and aircraft, for instance, do very little damage. Artillery can hardly even dent walls and structures; medium units do a much better job. Medium units, while doing decent damage, can't take much, and so are easily destroyed by static defenses.
Despite all this, the game manages to be pretty fun for a limited time. Until the bugs and crashes strike. For instance, on the final campaign mission, if you save at all during the mission, the win conditions are negated. No matter what you do, you can't win. The bug was acknowledged and had a supposed fix in a patch, but the latest patch still contains the bug. And while I had no crashes during the campaign, nearly half of the skirmish matches I have played have experienced game crashes.
As for multiplayer, there are so few official maps available and the unofficial maps are mostly unbalanced, with none of them offering much more variety than amount and placement of resources, that it's really not worth playing for more than a few rounds.
Overall, the incompleteness of the game makes it a disapointment.

FTL: Faster Than Light
In this review I'm just going to call it "FTL".
So, let's get to the actual review...
At first I thought this game looked kind of boring. But after making some research I found it to be quite interesting, and when it showed up as a daily deal on some Steam Sale which I can't remember, I bought it, cheap! It turned out to be worth it. I haven't put in that many hours into this game, but the hours I've played have really convinced me. I'm quite fond of these games in which you spawn in a world that is randomly generated (Some other examples; Super House of Dead Ninjas* and Binding of Isaac**). I think it's way better for a game to have lots of replayability than a superb story. One exception is Brothers: A Tale Of Two Sons*** which is just perfect. Simply.
FTL is an action/strategy game in which you take control of a spaceship, wanted by the rebels. The game has a goal, and that is to destroy ("kill" if you prefer that term) the Rebel Flagship, who is kind of a Boss in any other game. To get there you must travel through 8 sectors. A sector consists of a map with small dots in which you can travel between using your FTL jump. At some of these dots you will find merchants, enemies, quests and just loot. I find the combat system rather amusing with a lot of different weapons to choose from and different tactics to try.
Overall this game is quite amusing with lots of potential replayability and good combat system. The unlocking system can be a bit unfair since you can only unlock  some ships throughout random events in the game. I would recommend this game for all kinds of players.
I would give this game 9/10 since it has great combat system and overall game mechanics although it can be a bit challenging and unfair sometimes.

Saint's Row IV brought with it a lot of skepticism coming on the heels of Saint's Row: The Third. The Third was so much fun and absurd, it did everything GTA IV forgot to do with its self-serious plot. Saint's Row IV continues the Open World insanity and ups it with the use of Super Powers. To be fair, it really is nothing but a reskin of the last game, but it does play and feel incredibly different while keeping all the attitude. The big let down of this game is that after exploring Steelport so much in the last game, you're put right back in a "virtual" version of it in this one. It's not a bad world to hang out in, but it just shines a light on the games roots as a DLC. In the end, if you like the last game, you'll like this one too if for no other reason than the same style of writing is present and the mission set pieces are still as fun as they ever were. It's an excuse to hang with the Saints again, and as long as Volition is at the helm, I don't see that ever being a bad thing at all.

Child of Light is a fantastic game with a fairytale aesthetic, using classic storybook tropes, but using them effectively enough to make them enjoyable. The mechanics of the game are clean, borrowing ideas from JRPGs like Final Fantasy, with turn-based combat that simultaneously has real-time elements, and other tools like crafting and skill trees.
Yes, the ending is rushed, but it isn’t terrible; the plot elements would likely have remained the same had more time been afforded to the development team. But there are other games that rushed or less than ideal endings that are still considered classics, such as Obsidian’s Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic 2, or Bioware’s Mass Effect trilogy. Video games by their nature should be more focused on giving joy in the journey, and this is exactly what Child of Light does.

Wow, okay this will be my first legit review for any game ever. please keep in mind that these sort of games are my favourite kind to play, so althoug imperfect, i may be a little biassed towards it.I was very cautious when considering whether to buy this game or not. The Steam reviews have not been so good so I really fought with myself for two days before crumbling under the pressure and buying it. I mean what's the worst that can happen? I paid $6. After playing for a little bit over the span of two days, i have quickly realised that this game has consumed over thirty hours of my life. I realised that Steam reviews can't always be trusted, considering that this game has less than perfect reviews, but I do know this type of game isn't for everybody. Everybody has their tastes, and I STRONGLY suggest you at least give this game a try. You get a free two hours afterall. I will warn you though, you may easily waste two hours creating a character so i suggest you use a base character and go straight into the game to really get a feel for it. I'll also say that you should NOT go into this game expecting an RPG game. it is NOT an RPG. I would consider this game closer to a Sandbox MMO, due to the fact that you'll find yourself not really roleplaying all that much like you would in games like Skyrim or Runescape even. You can be a fisherman in this game or a trader, but you'll feel the same way doing both of those activities, although they are so diverse. so now that we have that out of the way, I will say that this is one of the best Sandbox games that I have played in ages.
First impressions: I will admit that I still have no idea what Im doing in this game and there are all sorts of items and little things that buff your items that I have no experience with. Google hasn't been able to really help me always, but so far 99% of the players in the game are more than happy to assist me. I have barely explored the world, so there will be all sorts of features probably left out of this review, but after thirty hours, i feel that a review is appopriate.
Pros:
-Epic combat
-Beautiful graphics
-A dozen of skills to spend hours training
-Massive open world
-Decent servers (mostly)
-Autorun feature (no quick teleport so this feature is a godsend)
-An interesting Node system that allows you to own properties (I haven't fully explored this feature so please Google it if you're interested in learning more)
-A marketplace that allows players to trade universally with each other
-Guilds/ Clans allow you to interact with other players and become a part of the community
Cons:
-you need to pay real money to really make your character look any different
-The game can stutter at times
-servers are sometimes unstable during the day
-Sometimes the chat can become a toxic mess (can disable)
-The UI can get a little spammy (can disable)
-Sometimes it really feels like there's too much to do and might become overwhelmed
-Once you get to a higher level, killing enemies becomes very very easy
-Can't do individual trading with other players
All in all there really is no need to ever pay more money than what you paid in the original price. most things that can be bought with real money can be aquired from a few days of grinding. This game is not perfect, but it has been such an enjoyable experience for me. The best advice i can give anybody considering buying this game is to not expect an rpg like WoW or Runescape, but instead expect an openworld Sandbox style MMO. Another thing to keep in mind is to not take this game too seriously. I have seen countless people complain over "the grind" in the game istelf. yes there does involve a bit of grinding, but if you play this game somewhat casually to have a fun time and waste some time, then the grind feels much more enjoyable. For people who have played Runescape (Specifically Classic), the grind in that is much worse than the grind in this so it shouldn't be a problem for those people. Players will definitely need to invest some time in this game to get far, but so far after thirty hours, it has not once felt like a chore to me. I STRONGLY recommend that anybody buy this game and give it a try for $6, but i do believe that once this game is no longer on sale, The price is still very much worth it. The game normally is $10.99. Even investing a mere twenty hours into this game means you've gotten your money's worth, and I know that for me, I can easily put 100 more hours into this game. After casually playing for thirty hours, I have ONLY discovered 8% of the world. This game truly has so much content in it. Im so pleased that this game has been brought to Steam because before that, I had never heard of it. i would love to see this community grow bigger in the future. I strongly advise you to at least give this game a try. You may be strongly pleased, and if not, that's perfectly okay too! This review definitely isn't very well thought out or written, but after over a day of constant enjoyment, I figured that I had to write a review for this game, because I strongly believe that this game is of higher quality than what the overall rating for this game displays. After 100 hours i might realise there's a fatal error in this game, and if there is, I'll be sure to update the review. For the time being I know there are many many people on the fence whether to buy this game or not, and i hope I helped a few people make a final decision.
*Update* Sorry for any confusion when I list this game as a "Sandbox MMO" I know it's sort of vague, but I believe that calling this game an RPG is a little misleading because you'll find that you don't really do any real roleplaying in this game. There is a roleplay chat, but people just use it to casually discuss certain things about the game. People with a good imagination can easily roleplay in this game, however. ie. Fisherman,trader, lumberjack, cook, ect. I'll try to find a better thing to call this game. A fantasy Sandbox MMO? It definitely has Rolep-laying potential, but I don't think many people see it as an RPG. The reason I define it more as a "Sandbox game" is because you can run around for hours doing nothing of any importance and you can have fun. I love wandering around without an reason similarly to how i would in minecraft. All in all everybody might have a different genre to consider this game, but I do apologise if I caused any confusion by considering it simply a "sandbox MMO"

A couple notes because I'm not sure where else to put them and I feel like constructive criticisms are an advantage of going public early:
I think survivors should get XP from working on projects in the garage. Not as much as from a battle of course, but I think it makes more sense to have one person man the garage than have people constantly taking turns being the mechanic so they can rotate who gets XP.
I know it's like a satire that the only girl in the game (not counting Zoey from L4D) is just called Blonde Girl and has no background of note, but until there are more girl survivors to choose from I think you should give her something compelling. Having survivors with backgrounds and proficiencies is always more interesting and I feel like you're alienating people by having the sole representation of females be a sexist joke.
A little more time at the end of a round to finish scavenging would be good. It seems intentional to keep up the pace and difficulty, but it strays from real world logic a little too far for me. Maybe have a place you move to to complete the level instead having the survivors leave automatically?
That said, really fun game! Can't wait for updates with more events and characters.

Anyone who has seen my reviews elsewhere knows my opinion on Early Access games, but heres a quick recap for those who are first time readers/viewers:
1. Early Access games that charge money should be considered a finished game
2. Content missing at time of review is still considered content missing, regardless of "promises to put it in"
Simple enough, right? Let's move on to the review.
I like this game. It has a particular charm that tugs at my nostalgia strings and panders to my every whim. A zombie survival game with a cool soundtrack, featuring old school stylistic visuals and RPG management elements. What the game does well, outweighs where the game is currently lacking. The most annoying feature for me is the inability to select multiple survivors for movement, you have to panstakingly move each survivor one at a time, and there is no pause hotkey button, although the game can be paused by clicking the options tab on the top right of the screen.
I think more hotkeys ingame, for example a reload, heal and search hotkey, rather than having to click the appropriate tab when under attack. Although I like the idea of a randomised world, it can cause situations that are impossible for the player to rectify, for example - if you start next the game next to no trader and find no supplies in the tutorial map, your party will begin starving after the first day, which then makes the game very difficult, throw in the fact that you can only move to an adjacent building may cause issues when resupplying, unless you were lucky at the beginning. I also don't understand why I am given 3 mortars if I enable tutorial, but get nothing if I switch it off. The player should get consistant equipment before day 1, whether they want to on screen help or not. Also, a few events don't work properly (at time of writing) - such as the bandits attacking survivors, you offer help, you jot down on the map the location...the event ends. No bandits, no additional supplies, no extra map, nothing happens. Also, the character portraits of certain characters are not present, my researcher doesn't have a character portrait, just a black box. Some of these issues may be restricted to myself, but after playing through the game with and without the tutorial more than once, this is based off my experience.
Also, I've noticed the game doesn't like me right-clicking, makes the screeen freeze for split second. I also don't understand how easy the game becomes once you've acquired a level 3 weapon, like the SAW, I can literally let 1 survivor run through a map with just the SAW, letting me cover a minimum of 4 maps (well, not counting the builder because of his poor aiming ability).
I believe a better tutorial would go a long way to making this game more enjoyable for people, but so far, I've enjoyed it.
Most of the issues I have do seem to revolve around things that may be patched in the future, let's hope so, because so far, I've thoroughly enjoyed this experience with a few features missing (perks).

I played the flash version, loved it. I was excited for this early release and have not been disappointed. This game is simple, addictive, and (surprisingly) thought provoking.
Pros:
-Weapon range
-Character builds
-Random events
-Research system
-Characters actually loose life when they don't eat
-Weapon knockback feature
-Replayability
Cons:
-Reloads and/or heals not completing on level transitions
-Map navigation makes portion of the game slow and tedious
-Level length (would love to see some 3 or 4 transition buildings to add to difficulty)
-Supply/Weapons are never obtained where they should be (gun store/police station never have any guns). Would be cool to know exactly where to expect to find certain types of items. Would make map navigation more strategic.
-Supplies are maybe a little too scarce (while I realize this meant to be a zombie survival game, 2 to 0 supplies per building make it almost impossible to keep the basic 4 character team build from starving each round after a while). If you want to have more than four players to focus on research, forget about it. I very rarely keep more than 6 players on my team for this reason.
-Not being able to walk and reload at the same time. increases difficutly, but not very realistic.
Best Feature:
The "random events" system at the end of some levels is what completes the game for me. After a few hours, the game can become fairly stagnent. Difficulty increases, but if you get the hang of weapon combos (2 ar's, 1 shotgun, 1 melee) and creating choke points, you can breeze through most of the levels with little difficulty. And then, once the game starts to become mechanical and get boring, it throws an uncontrollable  wrench into your system: "You hear moaning behind the door...A zombie horde is onto you, you manage to get away but now all survivors make it." All of a sudden, you loose your best weapon, you loose your best player, and you have to completely reevaluate your approach.. Do I need to go find a merchant?. Do I need to go find a survivor?, etc.. BRILLIANT game mechanics to spice things up in a no-going-back zombie game.  I would love to see further development in this portion of the game.
Worst Feature:
My biggest complaint about the game mechanics would have to be with the map navigation. As the cities get bigger, only being able to move to adjacent buildings makes the game progression very slow and tedious. At certain points in the game, you just want to move across the map quickly, especially when you have alreayd cleared 98% of it. It would be nice to be able to move to any building that you have already occupied, no matter where it is on the map or how far you are from it. This would expediate th e most tedious portion on the game and let you get into the core gameplay quicker.
All-in-all, a very good game. For the price, I would recommend it.

Grim Dawn, to me, is the spiritual succesor of Diablo II. It has an interesting story, a beautifully detailed and designed world to explore, a metric butt ton of items, and really engaging gameplay. Leveling and development have a great balance of challenge and reward. The pace of the game is nigh on perfect, and the classes are actually interesting enough that I want to replay the game to try out different builds.
This is the game that I've been looking for; Titan Quest, Dungeon Siege, Torchlight I & II, they were all good games, but they all failed to pull me in and really catch my interest. Some of you may disagree but in my opinion Diablo III was just dissapointing. Grim Dawn, however, has managed to do what none of those games has been able to. It gave me something to sink my teeth into, and brought me back to that feeling I had nearly 20 years ago when I first played Diablo II. Quite the feat since no other game since then has been able to do that.
I love the game, and the Crucible expansion. I'll be buying another copy of both so that I can play it with my Step-Daughter, and I would happily pay full price for it. The developers have easily made a game that could sell for more, but instead are only asking $25. It's a steal.
And speaking of the developers, if you really want to know how cool they are, google Praetorian Zedlee.

*This review does NOT contain spoilers*
Wow! What a game!!
I was looking forward for the last episode for a long while. And there it was.
So... let me give you a short story of my experience.
To begin with: I read the five books of A Song of Ice and Fire and I watched the series trice.
I know quite a lot about the world of Westeros and Essos and its houses and relationships.
This game was great to expand the meaning of that world.
- The immersion in the game was great. I, myself, got really sucked into it.
- The artwork is brilliant. Good quality. Sometimes a bit blurry, but nothing to hate the game for.
- Characters are great, just like their voice-actors and character-progression. (I didn't like Ethan though, his voice was annoying)
- The overall progression through the game was amazing. I had the feeling that my choices had quite a lot of impact. Not so much as I thought it would be before I started playing it, but that's probably just me.
- The story was easy to follow. Not too many characters like in the series and books where you get overwhelmed by the amount.
- Controls were easy to handle. Just Q-W-E-A-S-D and the Mouse.
- Time to pick your choice was sometimes a bit short.  And I would say my english is pretty decent. Easy solution was to press 'space' to pause the game and read the different answers.
- Great to see the percentage of how many people made the same choice as you.
- Prepare to a (in my experience) somewhat open ending with many questions still floating around in your brain.
- Prepare to make hard choices.
- Prepare to feel miserable after you regret you choice
- Prepare to feel more miserable after you realize it was probably the best choice.
- Prepare to feel even more miserable after you realize the story was able to become more miserable.
- Prepare for the night, which is dark and full of terrors!
- Prepare for Valar Morghulis!
- Prepare for Winter is Coming!
- Prepare for Iron from Ice!
- Prepare for the ending of my review of which I spent way too much time on.
To sum things up:
Game of Thrones - A Telltale is a great game if you are willing to feel miserable afterwards.
The game can be played without having seen the series or read the books or whatsoever.
Though, it is not recommended if that's the case.
It is an immersive experience with a great story. Definitely a 'must-play' if you're a fan of Game of Thrones.
It's more like watching an interactive story than playing a game.
So.... buy it, if you haven't already!
I recommend to buy it in sale tho. Paid about €9,- instead of the normal €28,-

Let's be perfectly clear: It's obvious to those whom played Saints Row: The Third that Saints Row IV is just Saints Row: The Third with a slightly different skin. The price should have never been that of a brand new game. ”Deep Silver” Volition   seems to pride itself on being “out there” and have went out of their way to stray from the original concept of Saints Row since “The Third”.
Season Passes, DLC and other things cut out of the game to sell you later are also still a disturbing trend.
That said, Saints Row IV does stand very well on its own via the very fun new age and retro mini games included.  The material, which is mostly just humorous parodies of other franchises, is fun to engage in but can at times make you wonder if there is anything original about Saints Row IV at all.
Your character is super powered pretty much the whole duration of Saints Row IV which makes all the vehicles such as cars, boats and airplanes “virtually” useless to say the least. You are basically Neo in the Matrix (to give you a little perspective) and Neo doesn’t drive cars. So if you were one of those people that enjoyed customizing your vehicles, driving around town and racing with the police, it’s still there but why would you do it when you can run faster than cars now?
If you can FORGET that Saints Row was about driving, gangs and drama with humor on the side, you will be fine. If you can’t forget that, you will probably hate Saints Row IV.
I personally feel that Saints Row IV is the worst in the series but it has its good moments. I, however, would not like to see the series become more “wacky” than this or I fear “Saints Row” might as well be called “The Animaniacs”.
I suppose you should give this game a try if you are into the Saints Row series but I would recommend you buy this game only when it is 50 to 70 percent off so you do not feel ripped off because most of the missions are just repeated with characters giving you "different reasons" for doing the same things over and over.

This game wasn't on my radar when it came out so I picked it up during a sale and OMFG... this game is so much fun and is very VERY underrated.
Story: The plot is good that can give fun little twists that you weren't expecting. Though the only good character and the one  with the only good voice acting is the main character who is voiced by Roger Crag Smith (Chris Redfield and Ezio Auditore). Although my biggest issue is that the story just feels very cliche at like every big action moment and they don't try anything creative. Also the antagonist was being way too serious that it became very annoying to listen to him... Clearly he wants to be a Vaas character but fails so bad.
Gameplay: Best part of this game is how much variety there is in the gameplay. This is a survival game and you have to search throughout the city for items to craft your weapons and other items. There is even a leveling up system for both your weapons, agility, and survival abilities to unlock more perks, best perk of all is the drop kick. You can find blueprints throughout the game to help make even more interesting weapons and add boosters to them more powerful. The parkour system may feel wierd at first when your doing the tutorial mission based around it, after a while it becomes very fluid and responsive that you can pull off some very cool moments with the parkour. Melee weapons do have the same animations over and over again but killing zombies with them just never gets old that you just want to go through multiple killing sprees of zombies. Gunplay is honestly only ment for human enemies since the sounds of the gunfire will draw in zombies but the weapons are very well designed for either situation. At night time the game turns into a horror game that you have to run away from certain zombies that will almost instantly kill you. Side missions are more interesting than the main missions and you will spend a lot of time with it. The only problem with the gameplay is at the beginning of the game you don't have the most powerful weapons so they just degrade fast and takes forever to kill zombies.
Conclusion: Dying Light is a very well made zombie survival game and should be played by every fan of these genres. The story isn't really something you will remember or you probably are gonna careless about but it still offers a thrilling experience. At the start of the game it may feel harsh on you for having weak weapons and stats but later on it pays off. If you have a group of friends to play with this game would be a good option since it is co-op and you can play through the whole story together.
Rating: 8/10

The fourth installment of Tropic introduces a few new things, that was not available in Tropico 3. Aside from more buildings, the political climate has changed slightly. Now you will have to appoint a cabinet of ministers, if you want to issue edicts, for example. There are also more foreign powers (EU, China, Middle-East).
Perhaps the largest change, is that there are way more smaller missions you can acomplish in the middle of the game, "e.g. export 500 bananas". Some of them are fun, but at a point you simply start ignoring most of them, except for plot missions and things which already fit in your game plan.
At the end of the day, Tropico 4 is still a good game, but it's a bit of a stretch to release it as a standalone game instead of a DLC. It is very much the same as Tropico 3, so read my recommendation of that game, and save your pennies if you already own it.

The big let down of this game is that after exploring Steelport so much in the last game, you're put right back in a "virtual" version of it in this one. It's not a bad world to hang out in, but it just shines a light on the games roots as a DLC. In the end, if you like the last game, you'll like this one too if for no other reason than the same style of writing is present and the mission set pieces are still as fun as they ever were. It's an excuse to hang with the Saints again, and as long as Volition is at the helm, I don't see that ever being a bad thing at all.

In Telltale's Game of Thrones, you play as multiple members of house Forrester, staunch Stark loyalists, who are facing total annihilation after the Red Wedding reverses their fortunes. Their Ironwood is coveted by the now stronger and bitter rivals, house Whitehill, who are backed by the new lords of the North, the Boltons.
The story stays true to the source material, as it is extremely brutal, with an unforgiving and depressing tone. No character is ever truly safe, and everything is unpredictable. This could make the game fall flat on its face, but the characters are extremely well put together and well written, so it adds to the tension. Some well known characters also appear, adding authenticity and weight to the story.
If you aren't familiar with the Game of Thrones universe, you can still enjoy the game, but it will feel unfamiliar and you will miss some references. Otherwise, If you intend to read the books or watch the TV series, I recommend only playing the game after you have read the third book or seen the fourth season, respectively, as it will spoil some key events.
In terms of gameplay, the formula is very similar to previous Telltale games, so you either love it or hate it by now. It plays out like a point and click game, but with little focus on puzzles, and more on the story and the decisions you make. There are also quick time events for the action packed sequences. Even though the core plot line will play out more or less similarly, you still have a serious impact in it. This is definitely the most ambitious Telltale game by far, with significant different scenarios based on your choices. The decisions themselves are well designed, there isn't a clear right or wrong, making you will feel conflicted about your actions.
The graphics may not be cutting edge, but they fit the game perfectly and the sound design and voice acting are flawless, which add to the immersion. My only grievance with the game is that it isn't a self contained experience. Even with six episodes, many story arcs are left unfinished and it ends with a cliffhanger. After all the build up to the final episode, the ending feels rather unsatisfying with little to no closure. Nonetheless, everything else about the game is solid, so it's still a very positive experience overall.
In the end, Telltale's Game of Thrones is a storytelling masterpiece and I highly recommend it. Iron from Ice!

Half-Life 2 is one of those games that is often labled as the best game ever created, is it true though? In my honest opinion yes, absolutely yes! The first game which came out in 1998 already changed everything we knew about FPS games, some may say that Doom was far more influencial for the genre but it was Half-Life that showed exactly how far a simple shooting game with modest graphics can do and now years later the long-awaited sequel did exactly what we wanted it to do, it surpassed our expectations. So is HL 2 the best game ever created? That is greatly subjective, for me the original will always hold a special place in my heart and I'm sure for most of you other more successful games might take that place but let's be real, HL 2 is the pinnacle of gaming experience no matter if you played it when it came out or right now years later when many other similar games came out.
In short, Half-Life 2 is what every game developer should play before considering to make a game that will be a success!

Personally, I love far cry primal.I LOVE primitive or medieval gameplay and I think this game was more tailored to people that enjoy that, versus gunplay and explosives, which was what far cry was about before. The game FEELS like far cry 4, you can definitely tell it's the same engine. There is also a lot of the same ideas you're used to from far cry 3 and 4, such as hunting for crafting upgrades, capturing towers, i mean bonfires/outposts,  but there's just enough that's unique to make is work perfectly, unlike between for far cry 4 (for me personally at least).
There is just something "primal" and savage about bashing some dudes face in with a fiery club, or watching your arrow sink into someone's eye socket as they rush you with a spear. Or speaking of Spears, watching your freakishly strong arm ragdoll them back when you throw your spear into their gut is also quite satisfying, I swear I'm not a serial killer... There's numerous upgrades for most of the weapons and inventory types, probably due to the fact there is not a huge selection. Your primary weapons are the bow (of which there are 3 I've found so far, the fast beginning bow, a slow, powerful longbow, and a double arrow bow with aim assist), the spear, three club types (regular, Apex club, and two-handed), shards, which are throwing knives, and thats about it aside from traps, and a sling that makes your distraction rocks lethal. Despite the limited arsenal, it is extremely satisfying to use, at least for ranged weapons. The longbow is especially op due to the extra range and power. However, melee just lacks interaction in my opinion. You basically just sit there and swing and hear impacts, but don't really feel it, the fight doesn't really have a ton of immersion I guess and feels like hack and slash but without satisfying kills. However, with how great ranged is you won't really notice it, especially as you upgrade takedowns and unlock more bows. You can clear a squad in two seconds from a distance or surprising them.
The story is not really what I would call enthralling, but moreso the world that you are in is and makes you interested in what's going on. The non-spoiler version from what I've seen so far (I've mostly done all the side/crafting quests for the village) the Udam are a cannibalistic tribe attacking you initially, and the other people that are blue which haven't been introduced as in conflict with the Wenja yet, but they're the ruling southern tribe, whereas Udam are northern, and you're♥♥♥♥♥♥♥from both directions in the middle xD You have to swell your tribe after you find the first crazy Wenja and keep them safe from the neighboring tribes while you swell your territory. More population provides extra bonuses like; the passive resources you receive each day increases, you unlock upgrades for structures which in turn unlocks new quests, skills, and items/weapons, and at higher population an xp bonus ( as by the time you have like 80 population you should probably have most of the weapons and tools unlocked so skills are your main grind left to you)
Minor complaint but  I would say the world kind of blends together at times due to how prevalent earth tones from the era, which forces you to use hunter vision for everything, which wouldn'y be that bad if it wasn't a hideous low res matte, yellow overlay on anything important, but is necessary when your'e sniping archers in bushes and dark huts. However, I also am playing with only the reticle on for immersion, which I would reccomend because the game is gorgeous.
I'll update as I actually get into the story but as long as you can run the game, you're off to an amazing start. Also since I've seen people complain about the Division, I played the beta with no issues, no crashes, and on ultra, basically the exact same experience I'm having with Primal right now... You can look at my specs on my profile (although I have 10 now not Windows 7) and how they match up with yours, anything similar to mine shouldn't have any issues, although I cant help you with your firewall, only apologize you're missing out on some fantastic, primitive badassery.
My opinion: 9.5/10

Gameplay-wise, this might very well be my favorite RPG ever.
No worst-of-both-worlds, real-time-with-pause nonsense here. No samey filler battles, either. Each battle is a tough, interesting tactical challenge that can be dealt with in a variety of ways, depending on how you customized your characters. Character customization is great too: the "classes" are just suggested default builds, you can ignore them and just mix and match the available skills however you want.
The story is... entertaining. Nothing special, but the dialogue is lively and quirky and creates a fun atmosphere. It doesn't try to be more than what it is, which is a pretty big plus. Still, this is definitely a "gameplay" RPG rather than a "story" RPG. The fact that you control two characters and can roleplay the interactions between them does a lot to keep cutscenes and choices interesting, though.
If you're in the mood for a few interesting, tactical battles in a fun fantasy land, you can't do much better than this game.

An unworthy successor to BG1.  I liked the tweaks to the skill system, but this game was not as interesting as BG1, and it still has serious bugs over two years after its release.
I bought BG2 for just few dollars on sale because I had enjoyed the original.  The thing is, it's not about the money but the experience.  Having finished the game, I wish I'd spent the time playing something else -- something more fun and less frustrating.  Unexplained quirks and bugginess spoiled the experience.
If you want to save a certain sympathetic NPC, you must sacrifice something important before the final battle, just to keep that option open.  I did that, but had to replay the final battle because the first time it simply would not not end.  One enemy unit had been permanently petrified and could not be killed.  I restarted and was careful not to let that happen.  The battle still would not end unless I killed the last surviving enemy, which I had to keep alive or that sympathetic NPC would die.  When the battle didn't end, I thought maybe I had to "subdue" that enemy by taking him to zero health.  No, that triggered the end but also cost the life of the person I was trying to save.
The epilogue was buggy too.  Naurim was alive at the end of the final battle, but conspicuously absent from the epilogue, and I did not get the achievement for his survival.  Somehow I got both the achievements for Zurburan being evil AND good, even though I'd only chosen the good options (it's not like he flipped during the course of the game).
Character development choices were also unclear.  Apparently unlocking an NPC's potential, such as fueling Naurim's rage to gain combat bonuses, counts as turning him evil.  I figured a little fire in the belly would be good for a warrior, but no that's "evil".
Some battles chain right into another battle without a chance to re-equip.  That's fine, but you never know when that will happen.  Should I use my poison in this fight or save it for a possible chained-into battle?  I ended up hardly using expendables because I kept saving them.
Too much frustration, too little satisfaction.

Yes, yes, we know all the jokes "you lose your life, your friends, you become a loner, a weirdo, a pervert, a phedophile" blablabla. Those "reviews" are hardly a review. So let me give you my subjective unbiased and totally unfunny review of HyperD Nep Rebirth1. It's a JRPG through and through. What kept me interested and playing was the gameplay. Believe it or not.
What are you doing in this game? You play as teenager girls having an adventure by visiting dungeons, fighting monsters while they break the 4th wall more than enuff to make fun of popculture and videogames. The game follows a simple pattern: Follow the story as visual novel, go to dungeon, fight monsters, beat a boss, continue following the story as visual novel. Repeat. What spices it up is the sheer amount of items, dungeons, monsters to craft, visit and customize. You constantly meet new interesting characters with their own style of combat, abilities, items and weapons that will join your party and help out in combat.
Combat seems not very interesting at first, but the more you play, the more you progress, the more diverse characters join your party and the more weapons and items you create, the more combat opens up to you and makes you realise how complex it actually is. I couldt explain it here in a very long wall of text, but I suppose finding out yourself is what makes it fun. As a quick summary, let me just tell you that you will meet a ton of characters for your party, each with their own style of combat, skills, strengths and weaknesses. The game allows you to have 3 members in the front and 3 more in the back as well as giving you free reign over which characters you want to pair, which abilities you want them to use and more. This leads to countless combinations that will keep combat fresh and exciting.
Combat too got its downsides. Status Ailments (poison, paralyze, etc) hardly get applied, element types (fire, thunder, ice, etc.) don't really make much of a difference and sooner or later you will find equipment that simply ignores guardpoints and deals heavy damage to HP anyway. (Keep in mind I haven't played the additional content that increases level cap to 999 and adds super enemies to dungeons etc. yet. If the downsides dissappear because of that I will update the review accordingly)
Is this game grindy? Yes and No. Level Progression is fast and returning to previously visited dungeons isn't boring since you will be able to alter the monsters/items in each of the dungeons separately. You will find lots of new Plans for new Items  to craft constantly that makes you want to return to dungeons. You maybe reach a point in the story where you have to fight a boss that gives you a bit of a hard time, but you don't need to level up much to be able to make the odds even unlike other JRPGs.
Who should buy this game? If you don't mind slight but not too extrem grinding, its for you. If you like an interesting and entertaining story with many diverse and distinct characters, its for you. If you like videogames and popculture then its for you! If you like anime? Yeah its for you! If you don't like anime but a deep and interesting comabt system, give it a try!

I'll simply start by saying that Dying Light is -- hands down -- the best open world game I've played in my entire gaming career. In fact, it's fast becoming one of my favorite all-time games (and I've been gaming since the '80s).
As opposed to others in its genre (Assassin's Creed, Sleeping Dogs, Red Dead Redemption, Skyrim, ...), this game does not propel you from one mission to the other, having you grab for fast travel at every opportunity. No, you'll be crawling through the streets or jumping across roofs to try to get to your next mission alive! The in-between is just as much fun -- if not more so -- than the actual missions.
Which is not to say that the story is bad, far from it. You'll find yourself engrossed in the unraveling story line, meeting interesting and colorful (and every now and then comical) characters, with voice acting well done ... finally!
Add on top of that a seamless parcour gameplay, four completely different parallel RPG-style skill trees, a crafting system that finds the perfect balance between having to search for new material and using awesome weaponry -- until they are broken and you either repair it or build something new --, fantastic mo-capped animations for monsters, a tense and exciting day-night cycle, and to top it all off -- the lush cherry on the delicious whipped cream -- an unbelievably stunning graphics engine.
Oh, and the zombies are sufficiently creepy and so very believable! This game has my heart pumping with fear, excitement, and relief dashing for the nearest safe zone while a viral or hunter is chasing me down. Something that hasn't happened ever since I played Thief in '98.
Another thing I need to mention: every other game I've played like this is only really exciting for the first couple of hours. After that, I rely on save games to get away with recklessness and, given enough tries, complete whatever task I'm undertaking. Not so with Dying Light. Death is not permanent and you'll respawn in the nearest safe zone, but you will lose plenty of survival skill points, making you fall behind on that skill tree. That's incentive enough to be careful and make for a continuously tense and exciting game.
Just one piece of advice, though: turn of the minimap and take your time to try to learn the layout of the city by heart. There are plenty of landmarks that help you find your way. This greatly improves on the immersion and gameplay.

Saints Row IV is a buggy piece of trash that I have too much fun with and I highly recommend that you buy it.

Fun, but I think I still like Saints Row: The Third more.

DivOS is a solid, fun, and often funny CRPG with some pretty unique mechanics for environmental interaction that will greatly change how you approach combat in almost every encounter. It takes some unique twists on standard fantasy storytelling, and has a very relaxing "stop and smell the roses" pacing that nonetheless drives its story forward without derailing too often.
The graphics, while fairly humble in fidelity, are vibrant, clear, and lovingly crafted, with each environment displaying personal effort in making them look believable. This is doubly valuable in combat, where areas of danger (or benefit, depending), are easily defined and the positioning of enemies is likewise.
Playing with a friend in co-op is a blast, allowing both your PCs equal purchase in conversation, and even the ability to disagree or argue with your friend. Outside of fully leaving the current map, which requires you to gather your party before venturing forth, you don't even have to always be together which creates some fun moments of parallel travel and risk to complete objectives simultaneously.
DivOS' weaknesses are mostly technical and balance related.
Technically, there are just some polish and functionality weaknesses in the product; personally the volume sliders were always binary for me. 1-100 was "on" and 0 was "off," meaning my voice chat with my friend was often fighting for audio supremacy, something that would often balloon into a bigger problem with certain NPCs whose audio-leveling-out was wildly inconsistent, either shattering my ears or being imperceptible. On top of this most of the voicework is ugly or weird; it's clear there was a reach for comedy here, but it's way off the mark--the writing is better by far in this case.
Balance-wise, the game is all over the map. My personal experience, with a melee-heavy party (two two-handed weapon users, both focused on Man-at-Arms skills), my friend attempting a rogue, and a single wizard, was that melee is incredibly bad in the beginning of the game. Hit chance is very, very low, leading to lots of big wiffs and encounters that SHOULD be simple becoming complex and difficult. While this slowly improved, it took a lot of investment in skills and gear to do so, and even then my character was still inconsistent. Similarly, my friend's Rogue was wholesale useless, and he took a turn into making his character into a support mage, which was what helped propel our party forward.
On the other end of the spectrum, magic-users are incredibly powerful. Some exceedingly good spells that can deal big damage AND stun/root/control enemies have a one-turn cooldown, meaning our wizard character could dominate the battlefield with damage and status effects every time his turn came around. This NPC became the linchpin of our party, creating openings for the rest of us to deal damage.
So, is it worth it with these issues? What's the good news? All of the above weaknesses were fixed with the Enhanced Edition, which rebalanced combat (especially in the early game) to be less punishing for melee players, gave Wizards better weapons (wands), but fairer cooldowns, and fixed all the technical oddities like the audio bugs. On top of this, they polished the visuals up and, near as I can tell, re-recorded ALL of the voice work for the game to remove the more grating VO and give many NPCs full voice-acting. Even better: if you own THIS version, you can get the Enhanced Edition for free, and it is ABSOLUTELY worth your time, even if only to see the work Larian put into this re-freshing of an already solid game.
This is an excellent game, and almost more importantly, Larian Studios is an excellent developer. Few companies would be willing to spend the time to improve an already-released title wholesale, even fewer would be willing to give it to you for free. Support developers like this, let the gaming world know this kind of players-first behaviour should be rewarded!

How do I even describe Child of Light? It's a gorgeous side scrolling platformer adventure game with RPG elements and turn-based combat. I enjoyed nearly every second I played it. It's usually a good sign when I lose track of time while playing something.
Pros:
- Strong female protagonist? Sign me up!
- Beautiful world. Child of Light is absolutely stunning. All the drawings are so well done, and it made the game as a whole delightful.
- Cute, easy to follow story. It wasn't overly cheesy or too serious. It had a good balance.
- The combat was done so well. I'm not big on turn based combat, but this game's combat was perfect for someone like me. It was easy to follow and relatively easy to get the hang of. By the middle of the game, I knew how to utilize the oculi/potions/elixirs and which party members to use when. I was guilty of hoarding my inventory though. By the last battle, I had tons of unused items.
- There was a lot of combat, but I liked the fact that you could flee at any time or use Igniculus to avoid enemies. It gave me freedom to play the game as I wanted.
- The length was great. I finished the game with most (if not all, I'm not sure) of the side quests completed in 13 hours. I always appreciate lengthy.
- Full controller support

Cons:
- The rhyming got old after a while. Actually, I'd say the dialogue mostly was dull. I did like how Rubella never rhymed though.
- Robert's character was useless. His whole little story was a yawn, and he wasn't a strong party member. This isn't really a critique on the game though. I just really didn't like Robert.
- I wish there was more voice acting beyond the voice over during the occasional cutscene.
- The soundtrack seemed repetitive at times.
I got Child of Light on sale, and I definitely got my money's worth. I could see myself paying more for this game too. I'll maybe now give other games with turn-based combat another look. I absolutely recommend!

Let’s face it; most people buy this game purely for the items you can earn for yourself on team fortress 2.
If that really is the only reason why you are on the store page, then there are ways of getting those items relatively quickly.
It took me around 3 hours to get all 4 of the items, and I personally don’t think that is too shabby, the AI in this game is pretty bad… and easy to manipulate, or at least that is what I thought. All I did was start up a game, if one of them puts their item up, great, carry on, if not… I restarted the game until one of them did. And from there, went all-in every hand in a complete gamble, because sometimes they call and you knock them out and get their item right there. You can do it any way you like, but if you are lazy like me and can’t be bothered, it’s a fairly easy way to “earn” those items. And hey hoe it only left me around $600,000 in debt.
On the other hand, if you are looking at this game, not for the items, but for actual gameplay… there isn’t really much you can say,
as mentioned before the AI in this game is terrible, it is repetitive and you can start to sus out patterns that the characters have. Their dialog you can tell is trying to be laid back, friendly chum-to-chum talk with one another, and in all fairness some of it is amusing… the first 5 times. The dialog is so frequent and repetitive that after a little while, I really started to get annoyed with what they were saying. I don’t play many poker type games with the gambling and whatnot, but the feel from the game isn’t what I would imagine a real person interested in poker would be looking for. It doesn’t feel like real poker… or a real game… it seems dumbed down.
Now that I have gotten all the items, I really don’t think I will ever be playing this game again.

Bad slow grindful online Scifi/fantasy RPG.
The premise is cool an a bit like Star Wars: you are a
Guardian whose job is to defend this star system from an approaching
huge evil space station by upgrading your own space station and fighting on the planets below; oh, and you're also allowed to play as
evil Dominion. Unfortunately, the actual game is bad. The writing is bad. The interface is bad. The level design is bad. The grinding is bad. You need to walk everywhere, even to the next planet (even if you have wings), and while you can "run", if you did it any slower it'd look like the moonwalk. The glitches are bad (had to quit the game 4 times). The NPCs are bad (there's an attribute NPC you have to seek out when you level to upgrade your stats; it's not a skill trainer, just gives you a choice of upgrading Att/Def/HP/Mana). The quests are triple bad ("bring me 10 rats" means you have to kill the 2 actual rats in the level 5 times each -- and you have to walk there - and there's no point to kill other mobs on the way there because you can only have one quest open at a time). There's no main quest line to advance, only mission points, and you grind them; you can actually advance by running around your base repeatedly opening the same boxes (they even have a visible cooldown) and then crafting with the stuff you found and turning the result in. Did I mention the crafting is bad (twice so because of the interface)? You can't craft any equipment, and none drops.
The developer is friendly and posted a nice reply to my original short review, which is why I put in the hours to create another character, played to complete the first zone and then some more to peek into zone 3, wrestle with the end boss of zone 2, and and get my first set of wings. I feel I have a pretty good grasp of the game by now. However, the execution is such that it suffers from bad design decisions everywhere. I haven't found a single aspect of this game that didn't have something wrong with it, except maybe the soundtrack and the way potions scale as you level (via your pharmacy skill). In all of my hours playing, I saw one other player (the game's on a bundle that sold well over 1000 copies), so I can't comment on the party system or the chat.
I have to admit this game has all of the fascination of a pileup on the motorway. As with a clicker game, you can get into it and go through the motions thinking "wtf" all the way, knowing you're playing a bad game and still continuing precisely because it is so predictable and requires little thought or skill. But why would you want to when you could play other RPGs that outclass this one in just about every respect?
Don't.
