I played Diablo 1 back in the day. I loved Diablo 2, and I welcomed Titan Quest into my game cabinet, too. Diablo 3 looked underwhelming to me and to this day I continue to ignore its existence.
Somewhere along the time-line, Path of Exile arrived and changed everything in the ARPG genre. It's free to play; it reinvented the standard game mechanics, and introduced a rich and deep character building experience; and offered an innovative and rewarding 'integrated' currency and crafting system.
The downsides it brought along (in my opinion), was a lack lustre story, and the seemingly 'forced' play-though progress from the three standard difficulties (from Diablo 1). The majority of players in POE dwell in the hardest difficulties and have incredibly contrived systems for moving quickly into the last difficulty mode, where I'm told 'the real game is'.
Now, all of this prelude to my review of Grim Dawn isn't just random, it is vital. All of these games pre-date Grim Dawn, I would have expected more development into new systems and mechanics than I was presented with.
I like the class based system sticking to the Diablo 1 system; the game offers slightly deeper character development with a skill tree of sorts, with a dual-classing option. There are 6 classes, giving a large combination of dual classes (optional), allowing perhaps a wider range of character types… in theory.
My issues with this game begin here. I found two huge disappointments with the character system and the equipment system, both feeling incredibly underwhelming and, frankly, tedious.
Why? Well I went for a Demolitionist with 'guns' as my weapon of choice. Throughout the entire campaign (in standard difficulty), I changed my weapon maybe 6 times, at maximum. There are not enough item drops, or useful items in the stores, to change to.
In 41 hours I changed my main weapon 6 times! I looked up online and I'm not alone in thinking this, apparently several thousands posts mention this problem, including an official forum poll from the development team asking about the drop balance. Apparently the majority vote of 'it is well balanced' is something I literally can't agree with and provide my own evidence that this is awful.
First and foremost, this is a computer game. Let me have some fun, please? Why do I have to spend another 10 hours to find a new weapon to use? This is more annoying when you see so much junk dropping. I see the 'crafting system', and it is utter rubbish.
Another random lotto-generator is accessed via a blacksmith, who somehow arbitrarily combines three 'scraps' (an item of its own) to create a random magical item. Please go and review POE, which is FREE, and take notes how a crafting system can be done.
The character progression is extended slightly with the 'Devotion' system which allows you to spend points on a celestial pattern of constellations linked into the games attack and defence systems. Think of a cut-up, disconnected, and smaller version of the Path of Exile's main character progression system. Now if you are going to lamely imitate and copy a mechanics of POE, this is not the one to do.
The system feels awkward and disjointed compared to the main character skill trees, and really feels tedious to use, however I did enjoy finding the 'devotion' points by activating the shrines around the game world (giving an exploration reward).
Back to the game world, I barely had any interest into the cartoon flash style intro sequence. The NPC characters are bland. There wasn't a single one in this game that I remember for standing out, or having any character traits what so ever. Yet somehow I can recall Decard Cain, or Wirt the Peg Legged Boy from Diablo 1, released about 20 years ago.
The main quest is limp. The side quests are go here and kill x. There is no 'story' here that I was absorbed into. In fact, thinking about it the story is almost a carbon-copy of Path of Exile, literally the same areas, and the same boss types.
At the 7 or so hour mark I started to feel the game lost all pace, became a grind-fest, and I took a look at the over-world map and it is clear what is going on. At this point the map sequence is a linear path all the way north to your final destination. The boss (some sort of living wall, a clone of the thing from Borderlands 1 final boss) is dispatched with ease and… nothing. I get a text box telling me how awesome I am and then I'm free to wander around, here I suppose the development team expect me to run the game in the newly unlocked 'Elite' mode and do the whole thing again...
I could stomach doing that in Diablo 1 and 2, and I tried to do this in POE. But here I draw the line. This game is fundamentally flawed with the horrible outdated loot system spewing thousands of trash items onto the floor. A system perfectly taken apart by 'Total Biscuit' who points out that with these 'looter' titles: lots of prefixes and affixes and random components doesn't make the game more interesting, or the weapon more useful, instead it just created hundreds of thousands of junk items that bog down the game interface and wastes everyone’s bleeding time.
The development team are so lost in understanding how awful this system is, are then somehow ironically self aware as they include a 'filter' toggle button on the main game UI to prevent trash items from appearing on your game screen. What the heck is going on here? If it is so horrible, then bloody fix it, don't give me a button to hide it and pretend it doesn't exit in the first place!
After an hour or two I was enjoying the visual realness of the world of the game. The sounds effects are serviceable. The maps were sometimes too long, sometimes too short; a repeated problem of lack of pacing in the game (along with the 'story' and the equipment drops). I now appreciate what Diablo 2 (and what POE) does with it's side quests as part of the UI, which when completed unlock skill points for your character.
I found moments of this game very easy (1 hit kills), then I come across a random hero who will kill me. There doesn't seem to be a reason or rhyme for this other than the consistent theme of this game of lack of pacing and lack of competent game design.
I pushed myself to finish this game because I predicted that the linear aspect of the second part of the game would force an end soon. I was correct in my read, as the last act was clearly rushed out. In my 41 hour run, I found every area possible, however clearly the second half of the game has next to no additional content to explore (it is rushed).
If you do a straight run, the campaign is probably 12 hours long. I explore a lot and tried to fulfil the incredibly frustrating and grind-fest 'faction' system where the developers expect you to grind to earn the ability to buy items from the factions. By the time you unlock the high level requirements, the items look to be average and useless, begging the question 'why ****ing bother'.
In a sentence: I went from enjoyment, to boredom, to disgust.

When I first found out about this series almost a year ago, I knew that I had to try this game, and so I did. I got this game along with the second one, which was the only other one out at the time, and told myself that I would not the next game in the series until I had unlocked all the achievements in the previous title. With the recent release of the fifth game, Hyperdevotion Noire Goddess Blackheart, I'm starting to regret that decision since I'm still working on the achievements of Re;birth 2. However, that does not matter, what matters here is whether or not Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth 1 is a good game.
In short, yes, this game is amazing. I didn't know what to really expect when I started playing this game, but the game surpassed any and all of them without any hesitation. I'm not sure how a well written review should be formatted, but I'm not looking to write a formal review anyway. All I can really say about this game is that it was wonderful. The art style was amazing, the story was a wonderful mix of comedy and seriousness, and the gameplay was fantastic. Although, like almost every RPG in existence, there is a bit of grinding that will need to be done, I found that grinding to be fun and entertaining. With the variety of characters to choose from, there is so much to do in this game. I've put in just over 200 hours at the time I wrote this review and there are still things that I haven't done in this game!
In the end, if you're looking for light-hearted and cute RPG series to get into then look no further than this series right here.

In ‘Child of Light’, you play as a young girl named Aurora, who one day falls asleep and dies. She finds herself in a strange land called Lemuria, which she finds is cast in darkness by her stepmother Umbra. Aurora then embarks on a quest to find the sun, moon, and stars to restore light to the land of Lemuria. On your quest, you meet a firefly named Igniculus, who becomes your main sidekick in your journey across Lemuria. You also meet a number Lemurians from different factions, some of whom eventually join your party for different reasons. You traverse the game world in a side-scrolling manner, and combat creatures of the dark in a hybrid turn-based/real-time system. You progress in the game by discovering new areas and leveling up Aurora and the characters you meet along the way in an RPG fashion.
The game was very enjoyable to play, since I found both the combat and crafting systems very easy to pick up. The combat system was easy to understand, but may take a while to master. You will need to utilize your sidekick Igniculus well to ensure you get the edge in battles. I played the game on Normal mode and found the game sufficiently difficult, since I didn’t try to grind the leveling up of my characters. The ability to choose your battles definitely helped in this regard, and allowed me to focus on other aspects in the game, like the story and the artwork. The crafting system was straightforward, and the buffs offered to your party members were easy to keep track of. For game completionists, there are side quests that you can complete and collectibles to, well, collect, that will keep you occupied with ‘Child of Light’ longer than what the main quest alone can offer. The side quests are short and give life to the NPCs you encounter. The collectibles give you a reason to explore the nooks and crannies of Lemuria’s regions.
In terms of the game’s aesthetics - the art design lends to a dreamy, picture book-esque atmosphere. Despite this though, stages and enemies can evoke the haunting and eerie. The soundtrack in general was very pleasant and relaxing to listen to, and reminded me of the tiny music boxes that you play by turning the crank. The use of piano added a melancholic touch to the music. The music during boss fights added a lot to the tension and excitement, therefore making boss fights feel more ‘epic’.
‘Child of Light’ was good, but was not without its faults. One of the things that I felt didn’t shine so much was the dialogue. Throughout the game, expect to read dialogue that rhymes, or written in poetry-like manner. At times, the rhymes felt forced, and therefore awkward to read. Another thing that I felt was quite weak was the fleshing out of the characters that join your party. Because of the scant glimpses offered on each character’s history, I didn’t get particularly attached to the characters. Interestingly as well, you get a character quite late in the game, who I didn’t really get to utilize because I was already invested in the other characters’ abilities. Lastly, the biggest gripe I had with this game was of a technical nature. Unfortunately for me, the game could never close properly via the “Exit to Main Menu” option on the main game screen. Whenever I tried to use this option, my computer would just get stuck on a black screen, which I couldn’t get out of by any means. This meant I had to restart my computer. I eventually found out a way to close the game without needing to restart my computer by pressing Alt + Tab, and then closing the game window from the taskbar.
All in all, this was a beautifully made game that I think different types of gamers will enjoy. The simplicity in story, combat, and crafting made the game very enjoyable to play, and the art and sound definitely contributed towards making the game a delightful experience.

I'll start this review by saying two things, 1) you really should play Blackguards 1 before playing this; it helps understand the characters and the mechanics of the game. 2) I've only been playing it recently and have experienced no bugs or crashes, which suggests that after a year in the wild they've fixed a lot of issues
That said, this is quite different to BG1 in a few ways, the simplest comparison is that BG1 was Dragon Age: Origins and BG2 is Dragon Age 2; not in terms of story quality as I think they are quite comparable but in terms of mechanics. BG2 has been streamlined considerably (to some people's annoyance) and so if you've played BG1 it is at first a bit of a shock, but it is essentially the same system just more Spartan / focussed.
I completed BG1 and went straight on to this game; the first game had a horrible learning curve and was restricted by the fact that in most fights you only had 3 - 5 characters against usually many more. In BG2 this is resolved in quite a clever way. In BG1 you jumped around points on the map trying to find out if a new side quest had popped up with someone you had previously talked to. Whilst in BG2 the map is laid out before you and you can see exactly what each place will offer. In BG1 you spoke with your characters only at specific moments, always initiated by the game. In BG2 you have a camp where you can interact with your party, but only after an encounter.
They are different games but there is one constant, all battles are resolved on a hex grid with turn based combat; in BG1 you had to juggle using potions and resting in between fights; in BG2 you start every fight at full life (and mana) meaning that every fight is more of a challenge between you and the AI. Both games can punish you if you have selected the 'wrong' skills or, more often than not, failed to improve a skill to the right level (I'm looking at you cure poison).
If you enjoyed BG1 then I would pause and consider what parts did you really enjoy? If you liked bits that I say have changed maybe wait until an 80% sale, if it still sounds good then just go ahead.
At the end of the day if you like turn based combat games you'll probably be entertained, for a little while.

It is an incredible shame that this game isn't highly rated, as the first game gets great reviews, yet this game is actually better, albeit shorter. I would recommend playing the first game first because it eases you into the way the game works, and also the extremely challenging combat. The first game was one of the best games I've played in a little over 30 years of gaming, but it had some shortcomings which this game amazingly manages to fix head on.
These Blackguards games are basically typical RPG's on paper, but they play differently. There is a story which is actually better than most RPG's I've played (and I've played probably 100), and the characters are exceptional. They are all voice acted too, and well. Combat is the highlight and focus of these games, and it is slow paced, turn based, very strategic, very tactical, and very challenging. Every battle can be won if you play well, but even experienced RPG gamers will likely need to attempt some missions twice. If you like deep and tactical combat, this is the best game I have ever found, and if anyone knows anything better, please send me a message! The nearest equivalent I can think of was Final Fantasy Tactics, in that each battle is very finely tuned to be challenging, and movement and positioning of your team is just as important as the spells and abilities they use on each turn. FFT was very popular and really well respected and one of my favorite games, but this game is better in every way.
The only thing these games don't have that the average RPG gamer might want to know about, is exploration. There is no 1st or 3rd person walking around through forests looking for enemies or anything like that, instead you get a battle map of a country with various regions and cities, and you travel to them and get battles either in the cities or whilst travelling to them. I suppose if games like this could get the kinds of budgets the Elder Scrolls games get, there would be some exploration too, but this is an indie game so it can't have everything. But it still manages to have a lot, and what it does have it does extremely well. The itemization is fantastic, not so much in the first game but definitely in this sequel. There is a large variety of armor and weapons and there are sets you can wear which give bonuses. There are also dozens of usable items, not just potions but various traps and tools you can use in combat. Also the way you build up your characters with stats and spells is as good as it gets for RPG's. It uses an old rulebook which is an alternative to D&D and it is really deep and really good, and the game allows you to get really involved with lots of abilities and spells. The first game had a bit more customization as this sequel simplified one layer of this, but I don't think anything was lost with that, because you still get to focus on the various moves, spells and abilities, just without having to waste time tweaking stats to allow whichever ones you want to pick.
Story, characters, dialogue, itemisation, and especially combat, this game is as good as any other game out there. It would probably be horrifying to the average action RPG player that dont want to try something different, but if you are someone who likes tactical RPG's, this is a must have game. I've loved Baldurs Gate 2, TOEE, all the Icewind Dale games, Summoner, Wizardry, Might & Magic, etc. but this game is my new love and comparable or better than most of those games.
The first game is too, but the battle maps were just ok, the enemy types were repetitive, the itemisation was too limited, and hunting down needle in a haystack skill trainers was an unnecessary chore. This game improves all of those things significantly, the battle maps are bigger and more interesting here, and the enemies are too with huge bosses with great graphical touches. There are loads of items to choose from, and the tedium with trainers and finding gear etc. is all gone.
I am aware most of the negative reviews these games get are because of the terrible bugs they had at release, and when I played the first game, even a long time after release, I suffered through a lot of really bad bugs. I even regularly had corrupt savegames which meant my last few saves would die and I had to recover one from further back which meant I had to replay an hour or more of the game... Really bad bugs, worse than most games, yet I still loved the game. I don't know what state it is in now, I assume pretty perfect by now. This game however I only played very recently and I didn't find ANY  bugs at all. I am sure there are some somewhere but it is a slick experience for me, so don't be put off by the negative reviews, they were surely very valid early on, but if you play the game now it is a great experience.

If I were to sum up the game simply, I would say "Imagine if Jet Set Radio and Street Fighter 3: Third Strike were one game, but instead of hitting each other, you were hitting balls."
However, I am not summing up this game (that) simply.
Lethal League is definitely a must have game for anyone that is a fan of fast-paced action, hype, or good ol' fashion fun in general (so everyone). It's an easy game to pick up, but a difficult one to master, so practice makes perfect.
Gameplay-wise, the game is pretty simple. Z is used to hit the ball, X is used to bunt, Space is jump, and A is "expressions", so each character's unique taunt, and A with a directional button will display a different phrase. The game is tight, and everything from moving to hitting the ball feels good. The more the ball is hit, the more energy is picks up, meaning each round, or "burst", picks up the pace as time goes on.

Atmosphere wise, the game is slick. The graphics are phenomenal, and the music is amazing (hence the JSRxTS statement I made above). As well as playing great, LL looks and sounds great as well, with the voice acting and sound effects all on point as well.
All in all, it's a great game that is definitely worth the cost. Multiplayer is fun too, and regular single player matches and the challenge/arcade mode are good practice for the real deal against other people.

AI is not very difficult to defeat, but the most difficult AI provided is kind of a step to possibly winning a good PvP match.
Overall, very fun but requires a bit of knowledge and RTS experience. Slower players that are interested should definitely buy it, but only if the price is right. It's not hard to learn. I love Company of Heroes 2, the first game will always have a place in my heart as an amazing RTS and I still play it all the time, but this really was a fresh update on the series. It is not some extreme tactical realistic RTS but neither is the first one (ex. troops standing right next to eachother in the open point blank and still miss) if you are looking for that then go for the Blitzkreig mod, but for what this game offers you get your money's worth. I do see the occasional balancing issue but this game is still in early phases in a few months to a year I think it will be just as acclaimed as the first one. The winter combat is great and the blizzards can offer some peace and rebuilding or for others a chance to reclaim some territories without a shot fired. The summer fighting is fun as well with colorful landscapes that you turn to burned out rubble, the campaign is not the best in terms of story but it still had me mildly interested and the missions were decent but the first game is still better on that but the multiplayer is great. The commanders are a nice addition along with the bulletins they can give you even a small edge on the battlefield which is nice. The tank skins are cool to see, I would love to see infantry skins as well but I doubt that will happen. Just the game overall is great for a RTS, if you want realism buy the first and download blitzkreig instead but if you want a good RTS on the Eastern Front then go for this.

Half-Life 2 is a first-person shooter video game developed and published by Valve Corporation. It is the sequel to 1998's Half-Life, and was released in November 2004 following a five-year, $40 million development phase... Half-Life 2 is, simply put, the best single-player shooter ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Half-Life 2 compared to other single player shooters. What Valve has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there is an excellent shooter here. Half-Life 2 doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of first-person shooters to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure as a PC Gamer.

This game is phenomenal and awful at the same time. The campaign is great but the multiplayer is very difficulty to get into, especiall for the non-goo factions. I have no editted this review 3 times in different states - joy, rage, and now neutrality. At first i was blown away by the sleek design and well organized maps and the unique feel of each team. The secon time was after being soundly defeated by the goo which - which at the time, felt like an over-powered team. Now after watching twitch and replays I was not only able to play better, but defeat the goo player that had decimated me so many times I almost uninstalled the game. The one beef I have with goo is that they have so many detectors, not because i rely on my stealth units to do damage...as daggers are rather weak, but it mkaes it very hard to keep eyes on the goo moms - which is what wins or loses games. Either the small proteans or the goo moms should have detector, not both. Only because the goo also have their scout/detector unit which means that goo has more detection than any other faction.
TL'DR there is balance in multi-player, you just need to really learn the game to see it. The goo have a slight edge over the other teams, but that edge- the abilit to quickly control the map, is also their greatest weakness, if you can exploit it.
The human team is slightly under-powered. Concidering a few of our units are signicantly harder to get out than the other 2 teams I would like to feel a bit more punch behind my units. I would like to see the Gladius becoming slightly faster - but that may just be me wanting a stronger unit.
Is the game perfect? No - but it is a damn good effort, and if you can get passed screaming at the screen when you get beaten once again by goo or one of the top 10 players it is a fantastic game.
Pros:
- simple easy to use UI
- by not requiring to constantly moniter unit production you are free to really play tactically and out maneuver your enemy.
- the teams are very diverse and allow for specific exploitation.
- the AI is intelligent and challenging even in the campaign. Can honestly that hasn't happened to me in a long time.
- despite not being a AAA company, the cinematics, music, and voice acting are top notch and very well done.
Cons:
- High learning curve for new players getting into multi-player the reason for this is con number 2
- small player base. Wait times for a match can get up to 10 minutes. Because of the small player base you often play the same people over and over again and those who play the game most often at the top 50 players. Which can be very frustrating for new players, i know I got slaughtered a few times. But beating that one goo player after losing 15+ matches to him... that's a feeling i cannot describe.
This game needs more sales and a lower price tag. The free weekend is what got me into it, and a few more events like that might just get more players involved.

I just can't stop playing this game.
The base, unmodded version of this game gave me a good 100+ hours of play.  I'm not one of those types to get to the end and beat it as quickly as possible - I drag things on, get a good group of experienced soldiers, etc.  In one game, I actually had a group of soldiers with kill counts in the 900s.  That should give you an idea of how long I like to play a game!
Ultimately though, even on Impossible Iron Man Mode (hardest difficulty, only one save), I could get through the game with hardly any losses at all.  When the expansion dropped, I beat the entire thing in IIMM in one sitting.  After you play the game for 50 or so hours, you start to understand the patterns of how the aliens function in battle.  It becomes all too easy to lure them 1-2 at a time into a kill squad, without your guys taking a single hit.  There are also various glitches (I'll let you figure them out) that make the battles completely one-sided - certain angles that really give you the advantage, for example.
Then, I discovered "The Long War".  It's a mod on Nexus that breathes new life into this game, and boy does it.  I tried doing an IIMM run in Long War, and got my rump handed to me!  I've since logged another 100+ hours in TLW, and am still playing new games in it.  I highly recommend installing this mod!

If you enjoy PVP this game may be good for you, I am not interested in PVP and have no comment on it. If you want to get the game hoping to have some fun with the quests and combat, I highly recommend avoiding this game.

For the first hour this felt like a badly developed version of the first game, which itself was decent but not fantastic by any means.  But once the story got going it became surprisingly addictive.  The story feels unique, it really feels like decisions you make impact on both how the story develops and on the gameplay (I'm not certain it does, but think it's very likely and either way it really pulls you in).
The 3D-ness is slightly more distracting than impressive and combined with frequently having too many characters on a map the game can feel sluggish.  But again, the massive size of the battles and potential for strategem, perhaps initially frustrating, turns out to be really addictive.
And where the first game did shine, this one does too:
* In the range of abilities and effects available, with multiple ways to develop characters and multiple abilities that often play out very differently.  It includes a huge range of spells (if you consider in that levelled up spells are often quite different from the initial versions, and levelling up gives you access to each version), a decent range of melee abilities, a decent range of archery abilities, plus traps and throwable items.  And because you can usually combine at least two types of build in one character (eg. a melee character could turn out to be melee + archery, or melee + thrown weapons, or melee + traps, or melee + magic; etc), there's plenty of scope for variety and for just playing it your own way.
* And, to a slightly lesser extent, in some of the unique differences between maps.  It's not all just a wide hex field - there are different kinds of interactive objects, barrels and traps, narrow corridors, switches, hidden entrances, and more.  Some of the switch based maps are a little annoying, but they're rare.
Where the first was terrible, this made leaps and bounds of improvement:
* Powerful voice acting, particularly the narrating, and cutscenes.
* Maps, battles, and in-town interactions that really feel like part of the story.
Overall, slightly less variety in maps, and considerably shorter in gameplay than the original... but fully made up for in the epicness of both the maps/battles and the story and for really engaging you in that story.

tl;dr 8.1/10 where I would give the previous game 9.4/10
Normally, I would hold a grudge against having a completely repackaged version of a previous game thrown at me with a few improvements, remixed mechanics, and slight map additions posing as a new game.  The mainstay of this game is essentially the final mission of the "Weird Science" DLC missions of the previous game where you have super powers.  I thought that mission was one shot at best and when I sunk into this game realizing that the mechanics were similair, I had some reservations.
But those reservations were dispelled after spending more time in the game.  The additional superpowers, interesting weapons, numerous amounts of side missions, the satirical (sometimes serious but funny still) commentary we got used to is still good, and the additions of main missions without the use of superpowers mix the difficulty well to keep you on your toes.  The game gets better with co-op as well.  Add in an excellent selection of weird but awesome weapons and you got yourself the trademark Saints Row Experience, just barely fresh but sustaining enough for you to enjoy it still.
Pros:
-Trademark Saints Row action with an interesting mix of superpowers
-Still great co-op
-Great customization options from the third game remain with a few adjustments
-Many side missions  and plenty of content to tackle
-Humorous commentary about various aspects of society and media
Cons:
-Can't really shake the feeling of it being recycled in some form in a really obvious way
-Might get repetitive for some players
-Some elements of the game seem to clash, such as driving and the super speed.
Afterthoughts
You will be playing in Steelport again with some minor additions, but the overall map shape is the same.  Take this how you want it.  It would probably be best to describe this game as more of a super content packed expansion to Saints Row: The Third to play after you finish it.

I really enjoyed Saint Row III and spend a lot of time playing it. It was a good game, it was taking itself way less seriously than GTA, the story was ridiculous (Zombie? Check! Cowboy Mayor? Check! Wrestlers fight with chainsaw? Check!) and kinda full of holes but it felt intended. Hell the characters were joking about how their choice made no sense and that everything looked like a parody.
Now Saint Row IV is a different beast. It does not has the "we are not taking ourself seriously" atmosphere; everything is in a serious tone but it makes no sense being serious with a story of alien and virtual reality crap. The story is full of hole that are never quite explained and ends up feeling cheap and rushed out. The jokes characters along the path are not funny unless you are stuck in your pre-teen years. It ends up being quite dull.
Now the play mecanics is a bit better. The super power are interesting and add fun to the game. Unfortunately, it also ruins what was a fun part of the game in Saint Row III : the vehicles. Why would I search around trying to steal new vehicles when I can run faster than a car, run higher than a plane and run on water? Car or helicopters are useful in the first 15-30 minutes of the game assuming you found some. But after that you don't care / don't need them. Weirdly enough the missions still reward you with those until very late in the game... Worst, some late mission force you to ride car although you would be better off running. It really feel like the developers didn't think this whole super-power balance through.
The game has some minor bugs, like scene not loading, achievements not being rewarded, some guns offered has reward in two different missions. There is also a certain number of places where I was wondering "wtf am I suppose to do" as some mecanics or mission really lacks explanations... Overall, the bugs and the lack of explanations are not that bad but it makes me feel the game was rushed and not quite tested.
It feel like the game was just rushed out. They took an old engine, they used the old characters, hell they even took the old city map of Saint Row III. Then they added some aliens, some unconvincing virtual reality crap and they called it a new game. But in the end it really feel like a big DLC. Not even a good one or a funny one.
If you were a fan of the serie, wait until it gets around 5$, this does not worth 22$ at all.
If you are new to the serie... go buy yourself Saint Row The Third. It is the same map, the same engine, the same characters BUT it is funny as hell, well made and it is fun to play.

Rather short (in the review it says I played 10.8h last two weeks out of a total 22h. I can assure you this must be idle time. Every episode took about 2h to play for me with perhaps a total of 2h checking alternative scenes... a total of 14h for the entire "game"). and as usual without any game changing choices to choose from. It's an animated spinoff tale of the Forresters (not present in Martins Books or the TV-series) in Westeros with references to different places in the Game of Thrones world.
It was nicely made with animations and voice, although that in itself is the main reason why any real choice isn't present. It would simply be too expensive to animate many different outcomes based on user choices, and change future situations based on it. Instead we get single changes in animations for every choice, mostly cosmetic ones, that has no influence in future happenings.
This makes the game less of a "game" and more of a short movie where you need to click now and then. But the interaction and "moral" choices do give feeling to the story. The lack of relevance of the choices also give freedom to choose whatever you feel is right without bothering that much about real consequences. This is both good and bad in the sense that it gives casual freedom, yet it means less intellectual depth to dilemmas as you know that if you choose to save someones life, that person will die quickly for other reasons shortly after for the game creators to get rid of extra work.
Is this a bad game? Not if you realize that it's a little movie in 6 parts more than a game and that your choices doesn't really matter in the sense that it will change any outcome of the story. If you are a fan of Game of Thrones and want to experience a spin off where your interaction gives more feeling it it worth it on sale or (if money isn't a real issue) for entertainment. But if you expect it to deliver on Telltales usually slogan that your "choices matter", it will disappoint you.
I also found the ending (last chapter) disappointing in the sense that there were no real ending. If you view it as a season of game of thrones, then it was perfectly alright. But it gave closure to nothing so if you see this 6 chapter game/story as a product of it's own, the cliffhanger type of ending is very unsatisfactory. It also seem to me that the creators might not anticipate a second "season" for the game, allowing some last minute choices to actually seem to have a possible impact for the future. But we all know that they never will, which means that IF there would be a second season, they would have to bend over backwards to make the last chapter choice not matter (as always). Annoying.
And for the dishonestly in marketing and telltale practice of letting each choice that should matter have no relevand for the outcome of the story... I will not recommend the game. If there were a "shrug" option I would use that instead, as I don't mean to say that playing the "game" wasn't entertaining to a degree. So read the review and make up your own mind :)

I will start by saying for a fan of Telltale and of Game of Thrones/A Song of Ice and Fire I would suggest checking this out. Overall the experience wasn't on the same level as say Telltale's The Walking Dead Season 1 & 2 but was enjoyable and a good way to spend a few hours every couple of months. Now that the full season has been released I feel obliged to give my experience of the game.
The game started off really strongly, with the first few episodes having me on my toes just waiting for what happened next but the excitement and compassion I felt for the characters in the story slowly declined as the season progressed. The illusion of choice is still present from previous Telltale games, as is the formula, but this time I was really disappointed to see some of the major choices the game presented me with having little to no major effect on the story, especially when it should have been impactful.
This leads me to the ending of the game. Here the endings start to verge off from one another, much like at the ending of Season 2 of The Walking Dead, but the cliffhanger it ends on gives no resolution to the entirety of the game. I view this as a blatent money making opportunity on the behalf of Telltale. I do however understand that they are a company and their goal is to make money but I would be happier to purchase a continuation of this season if they had executed the ending better.
(I'll also mention the length of the wait between episode 5 and 6 was ridiculously long, which helped to lose a great deal of tension in the story. at least for me it did)
Despite the ending and the long wait I will give Telltale credit where credit is due:
- The visuals were fantastically suited to the style of game
- The story, while slow in places, was pretty enjoyable
- The cast of characters, both playable and non playable, really made the game for me and were thrilling and never dull
- Actually getting actors from the show to voice act their character in the game made it feel so much more engaging and authentic
- The length of each episode, hence the entirety of the game, was very much appriciated and made for an enjoyable experience.
Overall the game has it's ups and downs but still managed to give an authentic feel to the world of Ice and Fire.
Recommeded for fans of Telltale and/or Game of Thrones

This is one of Telltale Games' bad, stereotypical, games.  They
capable of making good games, as
proves.  Their bad games have only the illusion of choice, and unsatisfying endings.
Like their other bad games, the possible paths through the plot take the shape of a diamond necklace (like so ◀▶◀▶◀▶◀▶◀▶◀▶).  Within each episode your choices fan out for a while (like this ◀), but they all converge to lead to the same result (like this ▶).  This is particularly harmful in games with the gameplay theirs always seems to have; only timed decisions and quick time events.  There are no puzzles, unlike most other adventure games.  What you are left with is a movie with awkward pauses where you have to press the right sequence of buttons to keep it playing.
This game occasionally goes the extra mile to destroy any impact of your choices, even within-episode.  For example, at one point I had guessed that my character was likely to die, and I wanted to make sure that I took a certain evil ƅastard with me.  To achieve this I had separated him from the majority of his army, only allowing him within my walls with a small escort, and placed troops in the corridors leading to my throne room, who were instructed to kill him if he attacked me.  Apparently the writers found my decisions
, so I was treated to the same scene someone would have gotten if they had allowed the entire enemy army inside and made no preparations.
Perhaps an ‘awkward movie’ could still be enjoyable, if the plot was good…  No such luck.
Daenerys Targaryen is portrayed as haughty, selfish, and perpetually angry and threatening for no reason.  I do not know who this spoiled brat is, but they are not the Dany I know.  There is also a laughably inappropriate quote from John Snow in the ending about not breaking vows.
The writers only half-understood the style of the series.  They managed to grasp that bad things often happen, even to good people, even if they are cautious.  They did not grasp that both good and bad events should cause the situation to progress, and that bad events (like the death of a hero) should feel meaningful, not just cruel.  This shaggy dog story begins with House Forrester in peril from the Boultons and Whitehills, and the pursuit of the North Grove MacGuffin.  It ends in
the same situation.  No loose ends are tied up.  Nothing is explained.  The path is strewn with the broken bodies of any characters you might have gotten attached to, most of which die without achieving anything of significance.
In the future I recommend only buying Telltale Games' products after all episodes are released, and reviews show them free of similar problems.

Another month, another Telltale finale is upon us. This time it's Game of Thrones and we see whether Telltale learned a thing or two from their years of making these interactive games I hesitate to call adventure games but feel comfortable enough stating they have indeed carved their own niche at this point, niche even other developers have decided to dabble in.
While it is not necessary to be familiar with ASOIF as such, probably better known as Game of Thrones these days thanks to its namesake TV show,  it certainly helps and game references as well as heavily adheres to visual style of the ongoing series. Perhaps even a bit too much, in my opinion. So much so that House your characters belong to, House Forrester, at times feels like merely a stand-in for better known Starks and all the shenanigans that ensue can certainly be used to draw some clear parallels between the two. Yes, you read that correctly – characters. Taking up after their recent Borderlands game Telltale has opted to once again go for multiple-playable-characters-tied-together scenario, probably in the vein to emulate source material's multiple POVs structure as well. I have to admit I like the idea, but its execution simply wasn't that great because, for the most part, stories don't really tie together until the very end  and even then only for some while a good half still remains standalone without many ties to the rest.  Game is also perfectly content to re-tread a lot of the same ground, beat-by-beat, that was already covered in the books and, by proxy, the show itself. Yes, politicking in King's Landing, for example, is all nice and good but we've seen it all before and done better.
What I'm trying to say is game could've done its own thing, perhaps following in the footsteps of the Game of Thrones RPG, but it largely chooses not to in order to play on familiar imagery. It was entertaining to see how they played up signature shock factor when certain key characters keeled over, but I can't shake the feeling this was yet another game that suffered from lack of cohesive vision over what to do with it and some events that were built up as major never really amount to anything and end up simply left somewhere on they wayside forgotten because, in now standard formula approach, you dance to whatever tune Telltale ultimately decides they want to play.
I imagine this may come off as exceedingly negative opinion, but I assure you I was really torn on how to thumb the game in the end. It's not a bad game or anything, but following after Tales from the Borderlands it's clear Telltale's heart wasn't in this one and just comes off as a B-grade product in comparison. And I would consider myself a fan of the source material. Telltale simply needs to step up their game at this point or shake up the formula a bit because it's getting stale and this one had none of the personality or atmosphere to really sell it to me.
It's a Telltale game.

My initial review was after about 20 hours of gameplay and I have since decided to change that review now that I have near 100 hours logged.  From the start this game falls flat on its face due to the outrageous price and loaded DLC that Relic claims is for "continued support".  What a load of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  Never until this decade has DLC gotten so out of control.  Companies out there that make games with no DLC charge less for some of their games and patch them for years afterwards.  But, enough about the horrendous business model that has lost my money and more about the game.
Company of Heroes 2 takes what the 1st one did and makes it bland.  No longer are you able to approach a situation from multiple vectors of possibilities and are now forced to be aggressive.  Trench wars, defensive positions, and the general concept of holding a point and inching forward no longer exists unless you build a custom map with a specific choke point that is designed to do just this.  Commanders do very little other than offer a few units that you can't build or offer some weapons you normally wouldn't get.  Don't think for an instant this is a direct equivalent to the doctrines in the first CoH because it isn't, not even by a long shot.  T-34 85s are called in units and not build versus the 76s that are built.  Tigers are called in and not built.  Population is capped at 100 unless you manually change it in the map editor.  No V1 rockets or other cool special abilities like calling in a King Tiger, JagdPanther, Pershing Tank, etc.  Just a few fragmentation bombing runs, and plane strafes with some other abilities like camo, tank smoke, etc.
The game does do well graphically, I will give it that but I do not believe that is anyhwere near sufficient to call this a second game.  Sounds are just as realisitic as they were in the first one but pathfinding seems to never have been improved.  I guess they wanted to focus on vaulting over sandbags and walls instead of fixing critical issues from a game that suffered the same issues 7 years ago.  Buying barbed wire cutters for engineers because they don't come with them, you know....cause engineers don't work in situations like that...or something.....
I really hate to fill a review with constant negatives so I will put a few of the things that this games does manage to do well.  First, I like the concept that Germans and Russians can play on the same team.  This slightly alters the single strategy concept that this game has embedded into its core.  I also like that you can repair bridges if they are partially damaged instead of waiting until it is completely gone.  Another great aspect of this game is that the physics have been improved.  Tanks feel more like tanks as they rock when they shoot and get hit and actually have a reverse button so you arn't spam clicking or queueing your tank backwards like you had to in the first installment.  Finally, capping points by standing near them is great.  I no longer have to make sure my units are capping, all I have to do is get them within the area of effect for it to begin capturing.
Unfortunately, that is really all I can think of that makes the game look decent.  All of the improper balancing due to a new and whiny community is holding this game back.  I wish Relic would just balance the game as they see fit, it worked great for the first installment.  Gamers are entirely to whiny and shed tears when something doesn't go their way, but then again that is the way most my country is.  People will whine because they can't play, don't understand a concept, or simply just don't get their way but a game like this shouldn't be altered because of those reasons.  Single minded strategy, a massively cheating AI, and horrendous balancing with laregely missing content make this game a no purchase unless you are either bored or get it during a massive sale, and by massive I mean 75% or more.  Do yourself a favor, don't get burned.

Beautiful game in terms of style but don't expect too much from it in terms of writing. Pleasant, relaxing experience for when you need to retreat into an uncomplicated fairytale world, but this is not the game to blow you away and capture your imagination for years to come.
Pros:
- The art style and music make for a great aesthetic, you feel like you're caught in a living watercolour painting.
- Combat can be quite fun. There is no real 'one size fits all' combat strategy as different monsters require different strategies to defeat, and figuring out the best strategy for a new monster or boss fight can be quite fun. Its up to you if you seek out every encounter to gain XP or avoid all encounters but the necessary.
- The level design is quite nice and there's something very pleasing and relaxing about exploring it, especially with Aurora's flight ability.
- The worldbuilding is quite fascinating.
Cons:
- Levelling is too quick and easy. In terms of difficulty, I found 'normal' mode too easy once you got the hang of the game. Thankfully you can change modes mid-game.
- All dialogue and narration is in rhyme. While the developers likely felt this created a certain feel, too often the rhymes are forced and cringeworthy and it comes at the expense of the dialogue.
- The story is very... formulaic, in depth, and plays the 'good vs. evil' tropes very straight. There are some attempts at layers with the implication that The Whole Thing Might Have Been A Dying Dream (can it be a coincidence that the first companion you meet is named Rubella? Which is also the name of a disease.. maybe I'm searching too hard for something that isn't there) and all in her head, but they're not explored and won't give you any satisfaction. The protagonist changes from a little girl to a teen seemingly spontaneously mid-story and that's not really explained either beyond the vague understanding that it's meant to be symbolic of her personal growth or something.
- On a similar level, though the game tries to create a sense of strong camaraderie and Friendship(TM) between the ragtag group of heroes and treats it as a given in-story, the short snippets of intra-pary dialogue feels like little more than lip service to it. Not helped by the fact that you as the protag can never actually choose what you say, so there's a sense of bystander rather than participant in all interactions with the NPCs. As such, I feel like you never really get fully invested in identifying with the protagonist.
On the whole I'd say this is a game of style over substance. Good enough for the price I bought it at, but I consistently felt like I was expecting to like it more than I did. It's like all the elements were there separately that woke up my nostalgia and conditioned me to like this game through reminders of older and possibly better-written games, but none of it came together into anything meaningful. So it was okay, but it could have been great.

tl;dr 8.1/10 where I would give the previous game 9.4/10
Normally, I would hold a grudge against having a completely repackaged version of a previous game thrown at me with a few improvements, remixed mechanics, and slight map additions posing as a new game.  The mainstay of this game is essentially the final mission of the "Weird Science" DLC missions of the previous game where you have super powers.  I thought that mission was one shot at best and when I sunk into this game realizing that the mechanics were similair, I had some reservations.
But those reservations were dispelled after spending more time in the game.  The additional superpowers, interesting weapons, numerous amounts of side missions, the satirical (sometimes serious but funny still) commentary we got used to is still good, and the additions of main missions without the use of superpowers mix the difficulty well to keep you on your toes.  The game gets better with co-op as well.  Add in an excellent selection of weird but awesome weapons and you got yourself the trademark Saints Row Experience, just barely fresh but sustaining enough for you to enjoy it still.
Pros:
-Trademark Saints Row action with an interesting mix of superpowers
-Still great co-op
-Great customization options from the third game remain with a few adjustments
-Many side missions  and plenty of content to tackle
-Humorous commentary about various aspects of society and media
Cons:
-Can't really shake the feeling of it being recycled in some form in a really obvious way
-Might get repetitive for some players
-Some elements of the game seem to clash, such as driving and the super speed.
Afterthoughts
You will be playing in Steelport again with some minor additions, but the overall map shape is the same.  Take this how you want it.  It would probably be best to describe this game as more of a super content packed expansion to Saints Row: The Third to play after you finish it.

Black Desert Online... Is it really worth your time and money?
--------------------------------
PROS -
Large, beautiful living world with plenty to do everytime to login
Classes seem fairly balanced in PvP
Node system is a nice touch for those wanting something else to do aside from the main Black Spirit quests (plus you earn a ton of cash on the side)
Lifeskills are fleshed out and fun to do when you have the time to master them
Grinding doesn't feel repetitive. It feels fresh everytime
Large Guild PvP wars that span across the entire map
Sandbox elements are a welcomed change to the world of MMORPGs (we could really use more)

Game isn't P2W at all. Yes it has a cash shop, but mostly everything from the cash shop can be bought on the marketplace with silver (ingame currency)
--------------------------------
CONS -
Sometimes cash shop items are needed, unless you don't mind grinding
The game has no instances, Instead the whole entire world renders at once. Can be very tasking on weaker CPUs
Serverlag is common. However this can be fixed by swapping to less crowded servers.
--------------------------------
In total I've really enjoyed my time on BDO. Sure it isn't the "perfect MMORPG" that some people make it out to be. But that doesn't mean it isn't a good one. Give it a shot if you have 10$. It's worth it, trust me.

I really enjoyed Saint Row III and spend a lot of time playing it. It was a good game, it was taking itself way less seriously than GTA, the story was ridiculous (Zombie? Check! Cowboy Mayor? Check! Wrestlers fight with chainsaw? Check!) and kinda full of holes but it felt intended. Hell the characters were joking about how their choice made no sense and that everything looked like a parody.
Now Saint Row IV is a different beast. It does not has the "we are not taking ourself seriously" atmosphere; everything is in a serious tone but it makes no sense being serious with a story of alien and virtual reality crap. The story is full of hole that are never quite explained and ends up feeling cheap and rushed out. The jokes characters along the path are not funny unless you are stuck in your pre-teen years. It ends up being quite dull.
Now the play mecanics is a bit better. The super power are interesting and add fun to the game. Unfortunately, it also ruins what was a fun part of the game in Saint Row III : the vehicles. Why would I search around trying to steal new vehicles when I can run faster than a car, run higher than a plane and run on water? Car or helicopters are useful in the first 15-30 minutes of the game assuming you found some. But after that you don't care / don't need them. Weirdly enough the missions still reward you with those until very late in the game... Worst, some late mission force you to ride car although you would be better off running. It really feel like the developers didn't think this whole super-power balance through.
The game has some minor bugs, like scene not loading, achievements not being rewarded, some guns offered has reward in two different missions. There is also a certain number of places where I was wondering "wtf am I suppose to do" as some mecanics or mission really lacks explanations... Overall, the bugs and the lack of explanations are not that bad but it makes me feel the game was rushed and not quite tested.
It feel like the game was just rushed out. They took an old engine, they used the old characters, hell they even took the old city map of Saint Row III. Then they added some aliens, some unconvincing virtual reality crap and they called it a new game. But in the end it really feel like a big DLC. Not even a good one or a funny one.
If you were a fan of the serie, wait until it gets around 5$, this does not worth 22$ at all.
If you are new to the serie... go buy yourself Saint Row The Third. It is the same map, the same engine, the same characters BUT it is funny as hell, well made and it is fun to play.

Short: This game offers nothing new to the RTS genre, nor does it even come close to even matching many others in it's price range. C&C, Starcraft, Planetary Annihilation.. ect.. All vastly outmatch this poorly executed game (which in my opinion is a starcraft rip-off)
If you took starcraft, made the protoss into a 4-armed race of pathetic cry-babies with a nearly incoherant west-australian accent, the Zerg into an AI race, and the terrans into a.. well just about the same story for them down to the letter; Then removed the interesting storyline, unit diversity, and creative map design.. You get Grey Goo.
I experience this game in the aspect of, I want it to be good, I want the story to pick up, but after playing half the campaign, I feel bored, like I am just shoveling past the fluff to try to find something interesting. I often quit after each map of the campaign and look for something less mind-numbing in my library.
On the hardest difficulty I often just find myself spamming the same units every map, the only difference is each map I have to spam a bit more  and harvest a bit more than the last time to win. There is very little offered in the way of different challenges. Just a collect-spam-win game.
Pros & Cons
Pros -
-  Decent Narration and cut scenes
Cons -
- Unininteresting / often choppy storyline. It starts out as if this game was a sequel, as if you should know what they are talking about, like picking up a book and starting to read at the center of it. Without any character development, and no true depth to the ongoing story, there is no immersion into the story or connection to the characters. You're just an outsider looking in and expected to care.
- Voice acting for the "beta race" has a heavy accent, (guessing west-australian? south african?) which can make them hard to understand at times. This detracted from immersion for me, as instead of listening to a story, I was more focused on trying to understand what they were saying.
- 0 replayability, getting to the end started feeling more like a chore just to see how it ends, I have no interest in playing again, and given the horrible unit diversity and little strategy required, I have no interest in playing multiplayer as it most likely will be, who can bind their keys to spam the most.
- Graphics, while the cut-scenes and mission intros are very well made, and modern, the graphics in-game and the map designs felt worse than the original 90s version starcraft. Which was a confusing contrast that left me going into the graphics settings multiple times to see if I didn't have them at max, when in fact, they were.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 is a JRPG that throws away any serious story for nothing but references and jokes yet still manages to be somewhat enjoyable.
Now the story is as generic as you can get; the main character Neptune is a goddess that fell from the sky, hit her head really hard and has amnesia. Along the way she meets other characters that join her party trying to help her get her memory back, some of these characters are other goddess's that before they met Neptune all hated each other but they learn to get along. There's a bit more to the story than that, but that's basically the gist of it; Neptune literally takes any serious tone and throws it out the window every chance she gets and at first it's funny but eventually it just gets old.
This game is broken up into eight chapters; typically the order of events goes story, look at new items at the shop, view world map events, go to newly revealed dungeon and repeat all of that. What helps to shake this up a bit is when you're in the dungeons you can freely roam around and instead of getting into random battles you see the enemies roaming around just like you are. When you come in contact with an enemy it starts the encounter, but you can also attack them instead of touching them to get the advantage and have your party members start off the fight. When you're in combat you'll notice right away you can freely move around within the specified circular area, this is the combat zone and you're enouraged to keep your party spaced apart because enemies can hit multiple targets but so can you. Though you can move each character around individually the combat is turn based, so once you move you have to attack or skip your turn; there are three types of attacks that all build your .EXE meter (Which is basically your super meter). Each attack type has different properties, rush type attacks generally do little damage but hit a lot of times in one action and they're used to build the .EXE meter, power type attacks do tons of health damage in usually one swing and don't build .EXE meter very well nor do they do a lot of guard damage, and lastly break type attacks are used for destroying your opponents shield and don't do much health damage nor build .EXE meter that well. You'll also unlock special abilities like heals, spells, or buffs that use SP as your characters level up so you can have defined rolls for each party member like healer, damage, support. Aside from healing when you're low on health there really isn't a lot of strategy involved in the combat, build .EXE meter when you don't have any to use super moves at the end of combos, destroy enemy shields with break attacks than spam power attacks to finish the fight. This game also has a ton of plans you can complete and if you go after all of them it'll take a considerable amount of time, they generally add a new piece of equipment or an accessory you can purchase from the shop but some of them change enemy types in a dungeon or give you more experience/credits from fights.
The soundtrack wasn't that bad, I wouldn't say it's anything memorable; but it really fit the game and some of the tracks were quite catchy.
Though it might have an alright soundtrack this game's graphics aren't anything worthy of praise, the character/enemy models look alright but the environments are really uninspired. Each dungeon has a "theme" and each of these "themes" has about 3 layouts that don't change and look identical to the others in the same "theme".
I would recommend a purchase to any fan of JRPGs that really enjoy grinding because that's honestly all this game is, a massive grind fest from leveling up to farming materials for plans to get stronger items or unlock optional dungeons. If you're not a fan of JRPGs or if you're not into very grind heavy games than I'd say either get this on a very good sale or skip it all together because there honestly isn't an intriguing story to keep you hooked if that's what you're after.

My initial review was after about 20 hours of gameplay and I have since decided to change that review now that I have near 100 hours logged.  From the start this game falls flat on its face due to the outrageous price and loaded DLC that Relic claims is for "continued support".  What a load of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  Never until this decade has DLC gotten so out of control.  Companies out there that make games with no DLC charge less for some of their games and patch them for years afterwards.  But, enough about the horrendous business model that has lost my money and more about the game.
Company of Heroes 2 takes what the 1st one did and makes it bland.  No longer are you able to approach a situation from multiple vectors of possibilities and are now forced to be aggressive.  Trench wars, defensive positions, and the general concept of holding a point and inching forward no longer exists unless you build a custom map with a specific choke point that is designed to do just this.  Commanders do very little other than offer a few units that you can't build or offer some weapons you normally wouldn't get.  Don't think for an instant this is a direct equivalent to the doctrines in the first CoH because it isn't, not even by a long shot.  T-34 85s are called in units and not build versus the 76s that are built.  Tigers are called in and not built.  Population is capped at 100 unless you manually change it in the map editor.  No V1 rockets or other cool special abilities like calling in a King Tiger, JagdPanther, Pershing Tank, etc.  Just a few fragmentation bombing runs, and plane strafes with some other abilities like camo, tank smoke, etc.
The game does do well graphically, I will give it that but I do not believe that is anyhwere near sufficient to call this a second game.  Sounds are just as realisitic as they were in the first one but pathfinding seems to never have been improved.  I guess they wanted to focus on vaulting over sandbags and walls instead of fixing critical issues from a game that suffered the same issues 7 years ago.  Buying barbed wire cutters for engineers because they don't come with them, you know....cause engineers don't work in situations like that...or something.....
I really hate to fill a review with constant negatives so I will put a few of the things that this games does manage to do well.  First, I like the concept that Germans and Russians can play on the same team.  This slightly alters the single strategy concept that this game has embedded into its core.  I also like that you can repair bridges if they are partially damaged instead of waiting until it is completely gone.  Another great aspect of this game is that the physics have been improved.  Tanks feel more like tanks as they rock when they shoot and get hit and actually have a reverse button so you arn't spam clicking or queueing your tank backwards like you had to in the first installment.  Finally, capping points by standing near them is great.  I no longer have to make sure my units are capping, all I have to do is get them within the area of effect for it to begin capturing.
Unfortunately, that is really all I can think of that makes the game look decent.  All of the improper balancing due to a new and whiny community is holding this game back.  I wish Relic would just balance the game as they see fit, it worked great for the first installment.  Gamers are entirely to whiny and shed tears when something doesn't go their way, but then again that is the way most my country is.  People will whine because they can't play, don't understand a concept, or simply just don't get their way but a game like this shouldn't be altered because of those reasons.  Single minded strategy, a massively cheating AI, and horrendous balancing with laregely missing content make this game a no purchase unless you are either bored or get it during a massive sale, and by massive I mean 75% or more.  Do yourself a favor, don't get burned.

Child of Light received a lot of praise from critics and gamers alike for its unique approach to story-telling and graphics. While I enjoyed it, I wouldn't say I was quite as taken in as many seem to be.
Its strongest points are undoubtedly it's unique visual aesthetic and beautiful piano-based soundtrack which perfectly matches the mood of the action on screen.
It's fairy-tale story serves well enough, and I appreciate it for its attempt to be different, but at times the iambic pentameter rhyming was a little forced and somewhat tiresome.  It may be that I'm just not that crazy about turn-based combat, but I also found the combat in-game a little repetitive after 6-7 hours. From what I understand the turn-based combat in this game has more real-time elements than most turn-based games, but they weren't enough to really hook me on the moment to moment gameplay.
Is this a good game worth playing? Absolutely. Is it a 9 or 10 out of 10 as many feel it is? In my opinion, no. What you get out of it will depend on your enjoyment of turn-based combat, your interest in a fairy-tale style story, and your appreciation of its beautiful hand-drawn graphics and elegant soundtrack.
My overall rating: 7.5/10

Child of Light's story and gameplay offered a solid 15 hrs of entertainment. The whole game is told as a poem which got to be a little annoying towards the end but I do commend them for putting the effort into doing so. The gameplay is turn-based with 2 characters put up against up to 3 enemies with the ability to swap out teammates on the fly. This allowed for some neat strategies where I would swap out characters for a certain buff or ability they had then pound with hard hitting melee or magic characters depending on the enemies. You also have control of a firefly who can either slow enemies or heal individual teammates (though I never really used it in that way since the heals are tiny). Finally, the game separates "wait" times and "cast" times and allows interruptions if hit during your casting phase. All this leads to a ton of variation from fight to fight and kept the combat somewhat fresh throughout the game. Although the game as a whole isn't very difficult, there were a couple of encounters where I either died or struggled to scrape out a victory.
Definitely worth the <$10 price tag.

What can I say about Star Wars Battlefront 2?
Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. Super Mario Brothers. Halo: Combat Evolved. The Simpsons: Hit and Run!
This is just a small list of the amazingly fantastic games that Battlefront 2 should be associated with. Whether being played on a console or a computer this game is a classic. Such an improvement from the original, and in comparison, very basic first Battlefront game with the introduction of the space battles, greater range of infantry based roles and the playable Heroes and Villians.
The gameplay is smooth and flowing, through the 50+ hours spent playing this PC version (and the uncountable number spent playing the console version) never once has this game crashed or bugged out.
The controls are simple (point and shoot - well point and clicking the left mouse button) and easy to pick up; in no time you can go from runing head strong into the heat of battle, disabling droids as you go on the dry desert world of Genosis, to piloting a Tie Interceptor and blowing up Rebel scum in a battle above the barren ice world of Hoth!
The single-player campaign following in the footsteps of the brave men of the 501st legion is a fantastic part of this game. It fully immerses you into the Star Wars story as you play through missions based on the events from Episode III through to Episode V. Only slight downside to these missions is that they seem slightly too short for my personal taste, but a very small fly in the ointment.
This game is simply incredible! I do believe that the new Star Wars Battlefront game, being released later this year (November I think) will have to be quite something to out do its predecessor. The bar is exceptionally high.
Would I recommend this game to anyone? I don't think I even have to write my answer, do you?

I really enjoyed Saint Row III and spend a lot of time playing it. It was a good game, it was taking itself way less seriously than GTA, the story was ridiculous (Zombie? Check! Cowboy Mayor? Check! Wrestlers fight with chainsaw? Check!) and kinda full of holes but it felt intended. Hell the characters were joking about how their choice made no sense and that everything looked like a parody.
Now Saint Row IV is a different beast. It does not has the "we are not taking ourself seriously" atmosphere; everything is in a serious tone but it makes no sense being serious with a story of alien and virtual reality crap. The story is full of hole that are never quite explained and ends up feeling cheap and rushed out. The jokes characters along the path are not funny unless you are stuck in your pre-teen years. It ends up being quite dull.
Now the play mecanics is a bit better. The super power are interesting and add fun to the game. Unfortunately, it also ruins what was a fun part of the game in Saint Row III : the vehicles. Why would I search around trying to steal new vehicles when I can run faster than a car, run higher than a plane and run on water? Car or helicopters are useful in the first 15-30 minutes of the game assuming you found some. But after that you don't care / don't need them. Weirdly enough the missions still reward you with those until very late in the game... Worst, some late mission force you to ride car although you would be better off running. It really feel like the developers didn't think this whole super-power balance through.
The game has some minor bugs, like scene not loading, achievements not being rewarded, some guns offered has reward in two different missions. There is also a certain number of places where I was wondering "wtf am I suppose to do" as some mecanics or mission really lacks explanations... Overall, the bugs and the lack of explanations are not that bad but it makes me feel the game was rushed and not quite tested.
It feel like the game was just rushed out. They took an old engine, they used the old characters, hell they even took the old city map of Saint Row III. Then they added some aliens, some unconvincing virtual reality crap and they called it a new game. But in the end it really feel like a big DLC. Not even a good one or a funny one.
If you were a fan of the serie, wait until it gets around 5$, this does not worth 22$ at all.
If you are new to the serie... go buy yourself Saint Row The Third. It is the same map, the same engine, the same characters BUT it is funny as hell, well made and it is fun to play.

Beat Hazard (Ultra) is a music-based game that centers around music, primarily your own playlists, often via iTunes or other media libraries. The game itself has you piloting a ship (or one of many with DLC) whose goal is to score as many points as necessary within the length of any given song and to avoid dying. You'll face enemies ranging from stray asteroids and basic enemy ships, to mines and even bosses in the form of large monsters or battleships with a multitude of weapons at their disposal.
The game rewards you for staying alive by supplying you random powerups and score multipliers that dropped from defeated enemies. If you die, which you can by being hit just once, you lose some  of your powers and score bonuses. At the end of the song, your score is tallied and as you score more points, your piloting rank will increase. Increasing your rank gives you the option to select bonus perks, weapons or even extra lives based on your play style.
The difficulty can be adjusted based on two parameters: The song you play and the base game's difficulty. Since the game's pace is based on your music's pace, speeding up and slowing down as the music does, creating a different play through for each song. You can also ramp up the challenge by selecting "hardcore", "insane" "and suicidal". I found "hardcore" to be a nice base for causal playing if you're looking for something that won't stress you out. "Insane" is great for a challenge and "Suicidal" is, well, suicidal. If you're looking to test your reflexes, it will show you no mercy.
In my eyes, the visuals are what make this game so enjoyable. Even with roughly 40 hours of game play done at the time of this review, the visuals have yet to bore me. The visuals, much like the pace of the game, will fluctuate between slow and erratic, constantly changing colors. Players can adjust how strong they want the color effects from the ingame menu, helpful for those with sensitivity issues or that have a difficult time determining enemies from balls of light in the background.
While your overall enjoyment and replayability may differ, the game is well polished and provides comfortable atmosphere and challenging game play. I've enjoyed every moment of this game.


Overall, if you're a fan of music-based games, then I'd highly recommend looking into Beat Hazard.

The bow that most people liked in the previous Far Cry titles (3, Blood Dragon, 4) have been worked on and you now have 3 different kinds of bows. Short bow for quick, weak shots, longbow for sniping off people and a bow that fires 2 arrows at once. The melee weapons have a nice flow and consistency as well with clubs, spears and your shards for takedowns.
It plays like a standard Far Cry game with takedowns, crafting and a little bit of basebuilding, similar to that of the Ghale Homestead in FC4, though it's not about money this time around but rather resources and population...
All in all, if you enjoy the previous Far Cry games or if you're interested in the formula or even the setting (which is really freaking awesome, the game looks absolutely gorgeous and the world feels huge) then go for it. It's pretty dang good.
