Okay the final episode is out, so I finally played through this game and I guess its therefore a good time to review.
"Too Long, Won't Read" - Typical modern Telltale game, with a few minor annoyances. Not as well put together as some of their others and suffers badly from actually wrapping up very little. Enjoyable to play through, but the ending is desperately disappointing. Tentative recommendation, but be aware that the end of the game is very much sequel-bait and it has a few small annoyances overall.
Longer version:
Telltale's Game of Thrones plays quite analogously to how the books read. Unlike in TWD or TWAU you play as several members of House Forrester, a noble house hailing from the north. As bannermen to the Starks the game opens with you playing as Gared Tuttle, the nephew of the Castellan of Ironrath, seat of House Forrester, and squire to Lord Gregor Forrester himself. You, your Lord and his men are celebrating a wedding. Specifically the wedding of Edmure Tully and Roslin Frey at the Twins and...well I'm sure anyone who knows ASOIAF can fill in the rest of that.
From there the story spirals out into the different members of the house and their efforts to save their house in the aftermath of the fall of the Starks, in the face of their bitter rivals House Whitehill. right the way across Westeros. Gared is sent to the Wall to take the Black amidst rumours of "The North Grove"; the third-born son Ethan Forrester, in the absence of the eldest son (who was also at the wedding) and the second born (exiled), becomes Lord Ethan and has to deal with issues that he is ill-prepared for but must handle; eldest daughter Mira Forrester down in King's Landing as a handmaiden to Margaery Tyrell learns to play 'the game' and weaves a political web to help protect her family; meanwhile Asher Forrester, the second born son exiled across the Narrow Sea, gets news of the slaughter at the wedding and resolves to somehow gather an army and return to Westeros to fight for his family.
Its a very compelling story and the jumping between viewpoints works surprisingly well with the scene switches being typically well placed and each part being nicely paced. However it does suffer somewhat for being seemingly even more careless of your actual choices than Telltale games usually are. Some choices you make seem to have literally zero impact, even in terms of extra dialogue or not. If you don't mind that, however, you'll likely find a lot to love about the story and the characters are engaging and endearing.
More annoying is the actual choosing of decisions and the QTEs themselves. When conversations are going on you cannot see the mouse cursor and, rather than allowing you to choose an option by pressing a number corresponding to that option you MUST click it. Which means all too often when I first started I was sitting back and enjoying a scene when suddenly the game would throw a choice at me with a rapidly decreasing timer; leading to a frantic scramble to hit the space bar to pause the game. The countdown is, in many cases, far too rapid for the procedure of firstly taking in what was said, then reading the options and making a decision on which one, then finding where on the screen the mouse cursor has wandered off to and finally hitting the right option. It was a rather frustrating experience until I got into the habit of regularly pausing the game, which had a rather negative effect on the flow. The QTEs suffer similarly in some cases, for many it was a simple case of pressing the appropriate WASD button and/or using Q and E (although they did tend to rather spring them on you sometimes); but some of them required using the mouse either to click on a highlighted spot fast or to use the mouse to perform some other action, frequently only explaining what you needed to do on that specific screen only. My particular annoyance with this was a brief section in a later episode where you have to use a bow to shoot a rabbit; you have probably less than ten seconds to do it, your mouse is likely off-target, the instructions pop up in the top left corner (if I remember rightly) but if you take the few seconds to read you'll probably miss your chance, and the whole thing required a rather lengthy "hold the button to draw, aim, let go to release" action which is fine if you know its coming but when thrown at you all of a sudden can be a little jarring. Especially since your only piece of archery to that point had been with a crossbow which was literally point and click.
In terms of looks my only complaint is the 'oil painting' thing they've gone for the backgrounds of scenes. In some cases this is fine and actually feels pretty good but for a few scenes, particularly in King's Landing, it makes the game look ugly in parts. Though on the whole the game does look very good and the characters are well designed.
Finally I come to probably the most damning part of the game: Episode 6 and the ending. Without wanting to give away any spoilers this game suffers BADLY from 'sequelitis'. As the most mild spoiler I can think of: I mentioned "The North Grove" earlier and it is a central part of Gared's story and you do indeed find out more about what it is...however it is never explained WHY its important. Even worse it seems totally isolated and unrelated to the main focus on the struggles of House Forrester. Similarly for Mira's story down in King's Landing; although all of it ties into her trying to help her family the lack of any real connection between that story and the story of the rest of her family leaves the whole thing feeling limp and largely irrelevant outside of one or two minor references. Which was disappointing because I found it to be a quite compelling part of the game. Ultimately anyone hoping that the disparate threads of all the different stories would be tied together at the end for a big climax will be bitterly disappointed.
Overall then? I can't help feeling a little cheated by the ending. Personally I'd deliberately waited until the final episode was out before playing this and to play it through and basically be confronted with a "To Be Continued" on so many key issues was a bit of a let down. However on the other hand the simple fact is I DO want to see what happens next because I greatly enjoyed my time with House Forrester and want to continue with all of their stories, for good or ill.
Given this is Game of Thrones...its most likely going to be ill. But despite that, I still want to see it through to the end. And I guess you can take that as something of an endorsement.

Fantastic, very replayable game: A micro-management of fully customisable starship systems and operations during your quest to get to the last level and destroy the rebel flagship or die trying, permanently.
Upgrade your initially basic starship to amass an array of weapons, ship systems and crew.  Unlock new starships and initial configurations by completing in-game quests and achievements - alas, these are not tracked on Steam.
Use a variety of methods and tactics:
- Negotiate with neutral ships, avoid conflict where possible or blast everything
- Win starship combat by destroying the enemy ship or killing the enemy crew (if it has one...)
- Flee combat if the odds are against you (and the enemy doesn't kill you first...)
- Stop your enemy from fleeing to alert the rebel fleet
- Target enemy ship systems, crew and hull with energy weapons, beams, missiles, bombs, by starting fires or board the enemy  ship and fight hand-to-hand
- Defend and enhance your ships systems by manning them with crew members from all over the galaxy, each type has it's own strengths and weaknesses and can enhance their skills through experience
This is a value for money must-buy for any age group and achievement hoarder.

Meh, just not any good.  I've been a big fan of the book series for a long time and liked the first season of The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, so I was interested to see how this would turn out but still had modest expectations based on season 2 of TWD and the end of TWAU.  Take note the game fully expects you to have knowledge of the series coming in and doesn't work well as a stand-alone experience.
It has all the typical railroading you'd come to expect from a Telltale game and the writing and characters aren't good enough to counter it.  It tries to do too many things and ends up not doing any one thing particularly thing well.  It wants to make the the main cast important by having them meet up with a bunch of major characters from the source material and suffers from it since it feels so forced.  It tries to take a handle on the book POV style and have a bunch of viewpoint characters but you end up splitting a 90-minute episode between four different groups and none of them feel fleshed out.  The main cast is also supposed to be the not-Starks to a puzzling degree and would of been much better off with some personality.
The visual style is really sub-par and character models are all over the place in quality.  There are jaggies everywhere and backgrounds and any type of detail work stands out in how poor they look.  I thought Telltale did a great job with TWAU  stylistically so it's disappointing to see them put out such a bland-looking and technically ugly game.
It's still the same old Telltale engine and gameplay where you're going to be hitting q and e a lot with the occasional "hold down the forward button to walk for five seconds" segment.  No simple puzzles or anything.  Telltale also desperately needs to work a line-skipping function into their games.
Finally, it's not a self-contained story and I'm sure a second season will be announced soon, so don't expect this game to serve as a stand-alone experience.  I probably won't bother since I have a lot of doubts whether Telltale is capable of any type of nuanced writing at this point.  Most of the game just feels like they're trying to get a reaction by having stuff happen.
In short, Telltale's AGoT is more of  the same, but unlike their recent adaptions, AGoT expects you to have knowledge of the series coming in so it doesn't even work well as a potential attraction for non-fans.  A "maybe" purchase if you dig their narrative games and a not recommended if you're on the fence.

Oh this game...how to describe it...
Well I guess I'll open saying that I am both a huge GoT fan, as well as a telltale games fan, and I feel that it is because of both of these facts that I was unable to enjoy the game to it's fullest. Allow me to explain, and fair warning, this review will contain major spoilers.
On the game of thrones side, the setting and timing was great. It takes part just after the red wedding, and puts you in the place of a family whos entire life was turned upside down from this. Stroke of genius. In one fell swoop we have our conflict, and fits damn well within lore. But from there we start to slip. we're introdced to the importance or ironwood, our main commodity. We're told how important it is, and because of it just how important our family is. Every character in the game treats us with some level of respect because of this (or at least will lend us an ear), but often in ways that make little sense. We encounter many characters from the books/show, but they feel weird, and often their power doesn't gel with their position. For example, john snow has seemingly way too much sway at the wall for the time period, or Ramsey just outright being untouchable (though this is as much a fault of the show as it is the game. Difference is here I have control)
And here is where we get to the telltale side. I understand with these games, to an extent you're always on rails, but it feels agregious here. Far too many times it doesn't matter what you do, the outcome will be the same. And the game isn't even subtle at times about this, with some very weird transitions that left me yelling angrily at the screen (My favourite one being "I made specific safeguards to make sure this DIDN'T happen! Where the ♥♥♥♥ did they go?"). This unfortunately left me feeling cheated, and all my actions cheapened by the end (I even tested it, you big choice at the end of chapter 5 actually maks suprisingly little difference, just a few scenes get swapped around). This may be because I've played a fair few of telltale games, and recognise the formula. But it's never been this obvious to me before. And that's the sad part for me.
Another major issue is at times you don't understand the weight of certain actions. The biggest example being (and this is a massive spoiler comming, you have been warned) when you finally get to the north grove. You spend 5 bloody chapters finding it, and when you do, all you're told is it has "Power", and all you see is a dozen or so people defending it from wights. I played the final chapter 3 times now, and I have no idea why the north grove is important. I don't understand what the power it has really is, and as such I am incapable of making informed decisions involving it. Now this was the worst example of this, but there are many more in the game.
Overall though, do I recommend this game? Yes. It is a flawed game, no doubts there. And at times you may feel frustrated or cheated. But the story and characters are interesting, the scenarios you're forced to deal with get you genuinely thinking, and when it hits the mark, boy does it hit the mark. Just a bit strange that I feel I recommend this game more the less you know about GoT or telltale.

An interesting mix of a building sim and diplomatic strategy game.  The campaigns are fairly straight-forward in that, in order, to complete them you really just need to fulfill the main quests.  Each campaign has a unique island (20 total) with a different element to make it interesting.
For example, one level you are caught in the middle of the Cold War with the US and USSR ready to bomb one another at a moments notice.  You have to keep the DEFCON level up otherwise the world will explode.  In another level, you might have a resource rich island where exports of raw goods will make you rich and in another you might have a resource-lacking island where industry and imports or tourism are your only way of making money.
The game contains lots of humorous content including a frequent radio show (some jokes repeat after some time) and really funny voice acting with some inching-on-racism stereotypes.
I picked this up for $8 and I've gotten more than my money's worth without any DLCs.  I highly recommend this game as a respite from the frustrating multi-player games out there.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth1 has a story that is as subtle as a punch to the face.  The land of Gamindustri is being divided by a war, called the Console Wars, between the areas of Planeptune, Laststation, Leanbox, and Lowee.  Despite the game's blurb saying it has trope-demolishing dialogue, this game is ridiculously cliched.  You do meet several characters throughout the game and they are all one-note spanning from your "lol so random" to a tsundere.  There is an absolute ton of dialogue in this game when its plot and characters are so ridiculously simplistic.
Moving on into the combat.  The regular encounters are nothing special.  Just power attack them (as long as you aren't underleveled) and be on your way.  The bigger enemies last longer but require only the barest of tactics.  Just spread out your characters to avoid any potential aoe attacks they may have while increasing your EXE bar through your own attacks (the damage you do here is negligible).  When your EXE bar is full (or high enough), unload on the enemy and you win.  Stay with power attacks before you get your EXE attacks works for the early bigger enemies.
The areas you travel through are nothing special the first time around.  Sadly, the game copy and pastes the areas you go through.  Multiple times.  It is a wonder that late game cave looks identical to that early game cave, just with different enemies.  Speaking of, the enemies don't fare any better in that regard.  They get copy and pasted just as much which is even more annoying when just about all of them have unique drops to be used in the game's crafting system.
Go out, kill enemies, hope they drop their item, and craft the thing.  The crafting system is as basic as that.  These can be items for the shop, "new" areas/enemies, or various abilities to make the game easier (one makes it harder).  This is where grinding comes into play.  Ignoring the crafting system will end with you getting into areas underleveled so you may as well go ahead and do it.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth1 is ultimately a very shallow, simple game for both the story and combat.

I’ve happily been chipping away at Original Sin for the past year now with two mates (using 4-player co-op mod). It’s definitely one of my fondest gaming moments in the last couple of years. This is no doubt thanks to the whole co-op experience. I’m so glad they’re focusing on 4-player and more user creation for the sequel.
We’ve taken our time and boy it’s been good! While we’re sometimes having trouble making sense of the plot the world the combat and adventure makes up for it ten fold. We’re playing on the harder difficulties, and trying new and silly yet creative things out in a battle is just so much fun.
The game doesn’t have set classes, but rather a big pile of pre-sets of your characters early skills. After that you can shape your character whichever way you want. I find this rather nice, since I can still decide to go the Stealthy Two Handed Axeman-route with my otherwise very much wizard-like character a couple of levels in.
The beauty of Original Sin is the sort of chaotic and often random turn based fights, that’s hard to predict. These can result in hilarious or frustrating situations, based on how you approach the game. These things can happen more often, if you choose to use more Area of Effect Spells, where you, say, accidentally freeze, poison or set fire to your buddy. A bit like a turn based Magicka, come to think of it… Experiment with different combinations of elements.
That said, it’s always handy to have some shields and healing in your skill list.
I believe, we reached the finale last night after ~100 hours, so we’re still looking forward to put and end to it – and spend some time in other games for a change – but we’re already discussing the possibility of revisiting Rivelon in the Enhanced Edition sometime in the future.

Beta:
I put 20hrs into the game during beta testing, despite constant character wipes.
Now that the game has released:
I put another 50 hours into it just trying to beat normal difficulty. Now sure I could have just skipped straight to the end... but then you miss the story and all the side quests and what makes Grim Dawn so fantastic! This is a beautiful game, with a lot of quality content to deliver.
~PROS!~
One of the best parts about the game is that the replayabiltity is also there, which isn't something I get from a lot of games anymore unfortunately. (i.e. Diablo 3 was terrible to re-play until the Rifts came out and Season Leagues, etc.; I haven't hardly touched Skyrim since I beat it either...)
The ability to design your character however you'd like is also an amazing feature. The mass amounts of weapons and armor that you pickup through your journeys only allow you to customize your character that much the more by deciding if you want to focus on melee or ranged/magic combat, raining destruction upon your enemies or making a miniature army of pets, or even focusing on being a complete retaliation warden and letting everything kill itself why trying to kill you! You are practically only limited by your imagination... as well as the level cap and skill points you can earn obiously!
~CONS!~
One of the biggest things I (and my buddy) disliked about the game, is the map structure. You don't have a clue where anything is, and there is no real way of tracking your quest (or other POI) through it unless you just so happen to stumble close enough on the mini-map to see the golden star (or the POI icons.)
Another feature that I wasn't so keen on was that during gameplay, little books/journal entries would drop on the ground. (This in it of itself wasn't a bad idea as they told some of the Lore that went into the game. Please keep reading to see the issue!) I played my first official playthough (since the live build released) with my buddy, and he would occasionally receive these entry pages that would grant him Lore Experience - yet I wouldn't receive the experience. Every so often this would happen, and we could never figure out why. Normally you wouldn't gain the experience if you already had the journal entry, but I have never played solo this far into the game (meaning I shouldn't have it,) so we don't know the issue with this.
~RESULTS!~
Sure I could have nit-picked a lot of things about this game, but this game is very much so perfect in its design. It has so much replayability with it, and it is a complete game all the way around. I would love to see more content added, new places to explore, higher levels to obtain, and so on and so forth... but this game is a complete package the way it is. It is definitely worth the $24.99 price despite some minor flaws, and you will definitely get your money (and time's worth) out of this masterpiece.
~TL:DR!~

Very Content
Buy!!!

Are you a fan of a creative shooter that is fun to play?
Do you like the team-based, class-based combat that exists in TF2?
Do you like building PVP bases in Minecraft?
If anyone of those questions are answered with a "Hell to the Yes!", Block N Load might be for you.
BNL is an interesting mix of class-based combat that is featured within TF2 and the building and destroying aspects of Minecraft. You start out with 3 heroes, each with nice beginner rolls, but cover nice areas of combat. You can purchase additional ones with in-game collected gold or with Steam Credit bought Platinum. This is the only bad thing about this game so far. If you just want to try out a class but don't want to waste your hard-earned gold, you can't. Thankfully, that is the only thing this game is bad at.
The goal of the game is simple. Within the battlefield, there are 2 cubes; one belongs to you, and the other one to the other team. Your goal is to destroy their cube. Simple enough. Each team is given 5 minutes in the start of the match to fortify their base with traps and other objects. Once the 5 minutes are up, the forcefield splitting the 2 teams dissapears, allowing each team to come togeather. There are 5 players per team, so that means 10 player games.
If the other team was stupid enough to not make any defenses and focused on complete offense, their Cube would get trashed, making them lose the game. Nicely enough, if the opposing team has a good enough defense, it can keep you busy. You must focus on complete offensive pushes while still keeping a solid defense, and this is where the game turns from good to great. Your team must know when it's time to hunker down and defend for a bit, or go on a complete Cube destroying run.
Because theoretically every block can be destroyed, this allows for pretty flexible games. You can either fly over the map using Speed Pads and Bounce Pads, or you can tunnel under the ground. You contain 1 primary weapon, 1 secondary weapon, 1 melee weapon to contrust and deconstruct blocks, 6 block choices, and a usable ability. Ablities change between players. For example, Tony's ability allows for faster construction of blocks. Classes also have passive abilities that don't need to be activated to be used. Using Tony as an example again, whenever Tony builds, he takes less damage. Blocks are interesting as well. Each class has a class-specific block, several role-specific blocks, and a couple of general blocks that can be used by anyone.
This could be described as a bad thing, but it doesn't really bother me. Once you get within a game, it will take a while to finish the game, depending on several variables. Some games are 10 minutes long while others can be a half-hour long if there is a lot of struggle. If you leave during the game, you will be penalized, sort of how in CS:GO you don't earn the XP for that round if you leave early.
All in all, BNL is a great game that everyone should play. Ever since this game turned Free 2 Play, there is no reason to not play this. Download it right now and play!

This game is nothing but the worst kind of excruciating ♥♥♥♥ing pain. I've been playing a bit recently because it went free and it has drawing aspects, but 70% of my matches are unmatched pain from broken mechanics, and having a team of snipers all being played by what I presume are five year olds. Buckle in this will be a long one.
Pros:
-Pay model is fair on free players and doesn't seem to provide any real advantage other than you can select other heroes who will eventually appear on free rotation anyway.
-In concept the gamemode is nice, building a fort and trying to break into the enemies can offer interesting strategies and meta game.
Cons:
-No time limit and players rarely doing anything asides from sitting at base killing with no attempt to hit the objective leads to games that last for well over half an hour which is absolute hell.
-You can't change classes, while this isn't an issue in mobas which this takes some ideas from, the classes are so unbalanced and heavily countering that certain strategies being enacted by the enemy will prevent you from doing anything productive if you didn't pick the right class for the situation. In other words expect to be locked in long frustrating deadlocks that you can rarely escape from unless your teammates assist you.
-They won't. They won't even attempt to destroy the objective 90% of the time.
-No class limitations, this means it's not uncommon to see every other player on your team lock into a half an hour or longer match playing as nothing but the sniper class. For a game that has such an attempted focus on the objective this pretty much guarantees that you will lose the match after a long grueling deadlock.
-The community is mostly children. Most people who you play with in a class locking objective centered game have no strategic thoughts going through their heads, they will not pursue the objective, they will rarely help defend if you need it, they will float around, often go afk and block a respawn point, and prematurely leave the game part way through regularly. When they do stay, they will not listen to you if you ask them to attack the core or defend.
-Squad size is limited to two players, so you can only bring one friend with you to endure the cesspool of other people who will make up your team.
-Sentry spam. If you are up against a semi-competent engineer this will make life hell if you are the wrong class, they will plant sentries inside your base, all around theirs, and all throughout the map and choke points. Without a good team (see previous points) you will most likely not be able to stop the spam from progressively getting worse. Sometimes an enemy team may have two or more engineers so getting through their defenses (since you will be doing this alone) will be next to impossible.
-Children like Snipers. Most of your team will be snipers. The enemy team will often have multiple snipers. They do what you'd expect, camp, do a lot of damage, they're everywhere and they are frustrating to play with and against when there is more than one. Also if you get into close quarters with one and say, minigun them in the face, they will sprint away at full speed with zero speed impediment and go camp a healing station.
-On that last point, walking speed is fairly slow, but many classes (sniper included) move at warp speed when they sprint, so many people will camp, chip off your hp, you'll lower theirs faster, and they will then warp out of a fight to go camp their health station right next to all of their turrets, or they'll hide in their base. (yeah, it's one of THOSE games.) If you pick the wrong class, expect to be encumbered the entire game without the means to pursue these people.
-Enemies will get a health pack when you die so you cannot knock down their hp that much for teammates because they will heal right up and continue camping their sentries or any other number of annoying things that they will continue to do for over half an hour.
-If you want to dodge an enemies shots, stand as close to their gun as possible. This works in reverse when enemies come right up to you because due to the shoddy way this game is designed it becomes abnormally difficult to hit targets.
-The voice acting will drive you insane. (at least you can turn it off)
Tl;dr, Reach into your♥♥♥♥♥right now, and pull out a fistful of your hairs, this is a much more painless and fun filled experience than playing this game with its community. Why? Because it's quicker.

I heard some stuff that didn't sound too great when it came out, so I held off on getting it.
Beat the campaign recently and am delighted to say that some of the criticism was unfounded(Particularly that about uninspired unit design).
I must say, this seems to be Frank Klepacki's best sound track yet. Although the Goo's orchestral dubstep mostly lacks the things I consider the best of both worlds. The Beta and Human tracks, however are by far my favorites yet.
This certainly feels like a slower more deliberate game than your starcrafts or C&C titles, and I like that about it. There's still that feeling that certain situations are "supposed" to be solved with particular rock-paper-scissors combos, but this game has a nice way of mixing it up with the tech system, allowing some wiggleroom for your favorite units.
The Goo as a faction are unlike anything I've ever played in an RTS before, the closest facsimile I can equate are the Heirarchy from Petroglyph's innovative yet ill-fated Universe at War: Earth Assault, but even that doesn't describe it adequately. They aren't such heavy hitters, and rely heavily on hit-and-run tactics to attack effectively.
Overall, if you're aching for a new RTS, pick it up, I wouldn't recommend it if you have a personal favorite right now you couldn't go without.

Soon in the first minutes of the game, powers like super jumps and bursts of ice will be unlocked. Although they seem a little too strong at first, time balances the strength of the character with that of the enemies, making combat immensely fun and enjoyable.
Following the open world pattern with missions marked on the map, the game offers a scandalous variety of content, backed by a lack of commitment to realism and seriousness, which are the trademark of the series.
If you play in cars, shooting people and vehicles in the air and running after robots are just some of the bizarre tasks proposed by the game, which also offers a plethora of optional side missions.
The game works as a great satire, going from popular games like Call of Duty and Mass Effect to pop culture icons of the Matrix and Armaggedon caliber. They are purposely crude jokes, but they have their charm there.

So first purchasing the game, it seemed to be quite a refreshing buy from my norm, and it's good to get out of one's comfort zone, but not like this. I cannot sit through these kind of visuals, it's unimaginably bad. Big random particle effects are not fun, they strain the eyes. But when you turn them off, you see the games dull interior. Stock ships and static icons to go around. I tried playing the hardest mode to see if the ships really could be differentiated, but alas, no. Even if the artists of the game make each ship a different color, they would still look the same.
That's on top of the fact that they use the same ships over and over again. There is one scout ship design, but there could be 30 of the things on the screen. It just looks ugly. But when you get to a boss, that's the really kicker. They start to shed hundreds of the same little yellow and red triangle looking thing, until you get to the gross interior of this thing. It makes it even worse by the very black background. Puke green on black, awesome.
The meat of the game comes from it's one gimmick: your music fuels the game. Yeah right, more like background music to boring game play. I put in one of the most techno songs I had, it had a base drop and everything, and the game didn't even follow the beat of the damned song! You put in "Marry had a little lamb" and you still wouldn't know how the song and game play correspond. The ships come in at random, and you shoot them. I thought the lasers would of had a beat to follow the song, but no. Nothing of the sort came my way, only disappointment.
This game is nothing but a bunch of static images shoot particle effects. This game should be for like 2 bucks, but it's 10. Plus, it's necessary DLC, Shadow Operations Unit. That. unlocks the steam workshop and missions. It might of done something else, but not as far as I got. The first thing I looked at before even playing the game was a logo that looked like it was made in MS Paint. It was an unskippable text cut scene that felt like 15 minutes.
I was genuinely surprised that some of the most basics things to a game were DLC, which made me wonder when the DLC came out. Turns out Shadow Operations Unit came out 4 YEARS after the games initial release. What? It took these smucks 4 years to add missions and a leader board? That's horrible. M4A file support wasn't even available at launch. (just as a side note, there is an option to play the game in classic mode, but I couldn't even get that to work)
But wait! There's more! The game didn't even work for me for the first hour after buying it. It kept crashing, so I had to go find the file, and change it's properties, and then create a different file to put in the roaming folder to make it windows and HOLY CRAP. I should not have to do this much computer work to make a game work properly. Even after that, the game still crashed during game play. I am running win8.1 and even games that ran on XP work, so this is inexcusable.
If you skipped down to the bottom to get my verdict here it is: it's bad, eye straining, and doesn't even work properly. Everyone should treat this game like it's a hazard.

So now that the game is officially over, I feel like I can give a good spoiler-free review.
First of all, it's a Telltale game. You know to an extent what you're getting. Like all the others I've played, they capture the world of the books/series perfectly. Everything constantly feels desperate, and you wonder if you'll be able to maintain your integrity or start selling out your closest friends to save your own skin. You also get to visit a large variety of locations in Westeros (although this can be both a plus and a negative, see below), so you can get the entire experience.
It's not all perfect, though. For starters, the graphics look really ugly. I noticed a lot of blurring and stuttering, and it kept taking me out of the game. Also the fact that you control so many characters in so many places led me to a lot of frustration. It felt very unfocused, and it was more than a little silly how many characters from the series I encountered. A tighter focus with fewer main characters would have made the drama more real, the game more meaningful, and the plight of the Forresters more urgent.
That being said, I'd still give an overall recommendation. While it's not my favorite of the Telltale games by a long shot, if you're a fan of both series and their games, you'll enjoy it just fine.

Divinity: Original Sin is the most fun multiplayer experience I have had in quite a while. You play as two characters that you create known as "Source Hunters" in a turn-based RPG game. You have free roam of the world around you filled with story and enemies at every turn. You can play co-op, as the other player creates and takes the role of the second source hunter.
STORY:
You arrive on a ship to Rivellon. A place filled with Turmoil, under the threat of source. Evil mages are plotting against the world, and it is your job to stop them. As you travel, you will come accross countless side quests for leveling up.
Mechanics:
It's a free roam game until you spot and or spotted by enemies. Once spotted, imedient turn-based combat begins. this is really fun for working with the other player and formulating a good srategy. Generally I find myself reloading saves quite often because of how difficult the game is. There is such thing as making the "wrong party" and screwing up your leveling, each time you level up, you get an attribute (strength, Dexterity, Will, ECT) and rofficiency is weapons, armor, ect.
The map is fun, although I will say that for how "Free" you are, the game is pretty linear. Anyone who will say otherwise isn't totally wrong either though. You can do whatever quest you want, go where you want, but go anywhere that the enemies are 2 levels above you and you will get *DEMOLISHED*
Resistance to stun, poison, prone, and pretty much everything is important in this game. all negative things are deadly. During combat you can use the environment to your advanage. See a puddle? Electrocute the enemy standing it with a shock spell. See a poisonous cloud? Shoot a fire arrow, and it explodes! Is the ground of fire? Break that barrel filled with water to put it out! Is the enemy attacking your mage? use his spell to teleport the enemy on the fire that the water barrel missed. So much strategy in this game. You can learn to abilities by purchasing skill books, and teaching your character new abilities.

Worshippers looks and feels like a 4x built around a CCG. An interesting and unique mix that while solid, does miss the mark on depth and freedom.
Video:
Text:
Lets get the Early access bits out of the way first: Outside of a (severely) limited set of options the game runs smooth, stable and steady with (almost) no bugs, and no performance or other issues that I've encountered. For an Early Access title that is noteworthy in itself.
From a visual perspective the artstyle is fairly unique, and while not "high fidelity" it still has enough detail and nuance between the tiles and cards not to bore to quickly.  audio is unremarkable and only noteworthy in that it doesn't annoy, but neither does it enhance.
The technical things thus aside, lets talk gameplay depth and some of the issues... because while i love the combination of a 4X-Lite and deck building to get cards you then play as buildings and units and build from there, which creates a layer of planing with a little bit of "luck" thrown in, the experience feels to directed and lacking in depth to often.
You might get the idea that you have a lot of freedom, but the constraints of every mission require a "objective only" approach much like a tactics or puzzle game, and less like a 4X where the objective is a recommendation and the road you have to pave yourself. Here often the road is set and your choice is limited to how efficiently you want to build it, not if you might want to approach it from another direction or method.
For me personally, that is the biggest flaw in the title: It looks like you have a lot of freedom to experiment, expand and "mess about" in terms of a 4X... but the reality is that you have to play it like a puzzle game with limited moves and that makes the rest of the experience a lot less fun for me.
Note i less lot less fun, not boring. Because this is a solid title, that only requires more content, more depth and more freedom to the player. Which is where early access comes in.

I was curious about JRPG games and had been wanting to give one a try. I investigated this one because the title sounded like they named it by picking random words out of a bag and didn't quite know when to stop. I then looked at the Steam store page and was left with no idea what the game was about but I suspected it was probably something to do with breasts.
When I started playing the game the plot was introduced through the medium of text boxes and fan service. My first impression of the gameplay was how poorly the controls had been ported to the PC, specifically how I couldn't configure the mouse movement to control the camera movement as would be most natural for me. I soon gave up on using a keyboard and mouse and plugged in a controller. Once I did that I found the gameplay was pretty solid. It has a good turn based combat system, a range of fun characters, amusing fourth wall breaking dialogue, loads of customisation and upgrades, dramatic cinematic special moves, a range of cute monsters and bright colourful environments. After a couple of hours I was really enjoying this game.
So why am I giving this game a thumbs down? Well if your experience is anything like mine sooner or later you will run into a boss that will utterly destroy you, you will then have to go and repeat the levels you have already completed until you level up sufficiently to take on that boss. You can then go and take on the boss again and scrape through. The game will then reward you with an even tougher boss who will instantly kill you again with no opportunity to save. So you have to go off and grind again. And that sets the tone for the rest of the game just grinding through the same monsters over and over again till you can progress. The game likes to♥♥♥♥♥♥with you further by occasionally giving you boss fights you are supposed to lose so you will burn through all your best items in a vain attempt to stay alive. You can unlock more dungeons and tougher enemies to help you level up. There are a couple of problems with this, firstly there is absolutely no indication as to which monsters you will be able to defeat, this means you have to save whenever you get the opportunity. Secondly as if this game was not repetitive enough pretty soon you will realise there is only a handful of environments that are reused throughout all the dungeons and the monsters are reused with slight colour variations over and over again.
If the game was just flat out too difficult I would have abandoned it but my desire to finish what I start combined with knowing I could defeat the next boss if I carried on got into my head so I couldn't stop playing. If this game was stripped of all the grinding it would probably be a very enjoyable 10 hour game but instead I am left resenting this game for wasting 45 hours of my life.

At the very beginning I couldn't understand much because it was hell breaking down and there was a lot of running and shooting.. At the same time i couldn't stop emphasizing on how atmospheric the game was. When things calmed down, characters appeared and storyline started making sense.. Amazing!
A town that lacks of green, made of worn off buildings with rusty vehicles that don't work anymore. This is the first place we ended up first. Afraid civilians don't talk to each other and remain silent and scattered, while CivilProtection serves and protects the crap out of us all with taser clubs. Men and women dressed in full body suits, speaking through a voice distorter to sound unnatural, became one with the tyrant system just to ensure a better meal.
..
The distorted voices of the CivilProtection and the Overwatch Soldiers and the heavily mechanized radio chats/dialogues, the hot deserts and wet sewers, the dark buildings and the empty highways affect the gameplay really heavily. Half Life 2 was the only game that made me forget to blink, thanks to its ability to totally mesmerize me and make me think that i really was out there surrounded by danger!
Characters are so sophisticated.. They were not made to look pretty (damn these cinematic mods), but their personality and actions earn your admiration and soon after you start to care about their well being.
On the other hand, teams of rioted civilians that form around you are not that smart AI and end up serving as meatshields for you to survive, which is sad.
Despite the real life weapons (TBH crowbars never looked so badass!), there are weapons like Gravity Guns, Pulse Rifles and Bugbait seeds. Bugbait seeds are seeds that help you manipulate and use against the enemies a specified species of monster (Antlions) that would otherwise attack you. Enemies have sniper rifles, but we never got our hands on them.
While the enemy humans are after us, many nightmare fuel monsters turn against us too as we get in their way.
The notorious headcrab'ed zombies that slowly hunt us down and the skinny taller ones that run - or even climb - towards us and let out a haunting scream as they jump upon us! The barnacles hanging from the ceilings, the toxic headcrabs and many others make their appearance throughout the game.
Half Life 2 is one of those games where there is only one way towards the end of the stage, that is tricky to find out. Moving on requires thinking of ways to move obstacles or to raise gates etc. It won't fit to players who want a game just to kill time. You have to deal with puzzles here!

The review below is only a part of the full review. Due to spacial constraints, I cannot post my full review here. therefore I posted it as a Re;Birth 1 guide. I hope this does not cause any inconvenience to anyone. It's neatly devided into subjects with their own grades/scores, so that everyone can easily find whatever they want and read however much they want.
Still, I decided to post a bit here, so you can all see at least the tip of the iceberg.
Hello everyone, DiaborMagics here. For those who like short answers, I’ll just go ahead and answer your questions right away:
-	Am I new to the Hyperdimension Neptunia series? Yes, Re;Birth 1 was the first Neptunia game I’ve ever played.
-	Is the game worth your money? Yes, it is.
-	Would I recommend this game to my friends? I already have.
-	Would I buy it as a birthday gift? I already have.
-	Does this game have any flaws? Yes, all games do.
-	What rating would I give this game? I give it a 7.8/10 overall.
Now, if you’re still with me, that probably means you wish to know more. If so, I encourage you to read on. I will try to stay away from any spoilers, but since everyone has their own definition of a ‘spoiler’, this could be quite difficult to do. Therefore, I will tell you something is or could be a spoiler, if I try to explain something that begs for an example.
I will rate and explain every aspect of this game separately and at the very end, I shall give you my conclusion. Happy reading, I hope this review will prove to be useful.
Story: 6/10
Let us start with the story. Since I’m new to the series and haven’t played the original game, I cannot compare these two. As a new player, I enjoyed the story, but I also thought it was lacking.
The story in Re;Birth 1 is not to be taken seriously, as it does not even take itself seriously and characters will often break the fourth wall, just to make that fact perfectly clear. I thought there were funny moments, only slightly emotional ones and it had enough tension to keep me entertained. However, it was full of plot holes and I was left with a great many unanswered questions. That might be me taking the game too seriously, but once I was done with the story, I felt like there should’ve been more. More things should’ve been addressed and explained.
Now, possible spoilers:
Characters: 9/10
The characters are, for the most part, great. They are lovable, funny and interact well with each other. If one says something cheesy, chances are the fourth wall will be broken to tell you they know how cheesy it sounded.
I believe there to be at least one character that’s to anyone’s tastes, only you will not find any playable guys in this game. Is that a problem? Not for me, but if it is for you, you might be more interested in Fairy Fencer F instead.
Without DLC, there’s a great number of characters to choose from, should you unlock them all: 16 of them. 19 If we include the DLC. This is a big number for RPG games and for that reason, I think they’ve done an outstanding job. All characters look as unique as they need to, there are clear personality differences, combat styles, you name it.
My only real problem is how all mages are pretty much recycled versions of each other in terms of combos.
I also have to note that the main character, Neptune, does not really appeal to me as the main character. I would rather have seen any of the other CPU’s as main characters. I only like Neptune’s

Having almost completed every accomplishments, I think that giving a review for fresh players should be a good thing to do, lets put features of this game into a summary:
+ Long, funny and shallow storyline, 2 endings for us to choose, 20-30 hours for a walkthrough.
+ Unbeatably cute characters which can instantly make you addicted on this game.
+ Features different types of weapons, items and crafts, making players stonger constantly.
+ Cute CGs.
+ Immersive soundtracks.
+ Reasonable training system.
- The only little flaw is that there are too many items players can miss,mostly important for achievement accomplishments, the only cure is to start a NG+ or to reload a saved checkpoint, and the only way to prevent this is to read achievement guides. Of course, if you do not care about the achievements, it’s fine, but for those who do care, they have lots of works to do.
I will hereby try to cover as many aspects and features as I possibly can:
This product is also called HDN re birth 1 for short, as a tactical role-playing game, players take control of 3 characters in the front line while keeping 3 others as reserves in the rear. With different combinations players can create their own strategy, when facing challenging foes or bosses this can evidently prove helpful. However, you can defeat the bosses that are powerful more easily if you just train your characters, augmenting several levels. But a strategy is still recommended as it entertains your intelligence, this is also the point of playing games with identic genres.
Now let us see its in-game equipments, including weapons, items and crafts. Weapons here varies a lot, this keeps upgrading your character’s attack output in general. As to items, the system of HDN re birth 3 also keeps track on your level and gives you different items that you might need in different situations. Healing potions for instance, varies from 1000-10000 points and 30-100% of healing, these potions can be used for high level or low level characters depending on their efficiency, as far as I’m concerned, this feature is also found in other role-playing games, but since I haven’t experienced many so far, I still pointed it out. Furthermore, crafts, or plans as named in this game, are very important features, plans are your best friends, they can unlock powerful weapons, useful items in addition to many dungeon maps.
About CGs and Soundtracks, both are well designed, although nothing extraordinary, they do make the players immerse into the game. Especially CGs, they actually did point out the funniest and important events into a more specified way.
Thank you for reading this review up to here, I hope that this helped you a bit, however, if you find anything interesting in any of my explanations or introductions, I suggest you to give this game a try ^^, be aware that you might get addicted very soon …… ^.^.

What can I say about Star Wars Battlefront 2?
Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. Super Mario Brothers. Halo: Combat Evolved. The Simpsons: Hit and Run!
This is just a small list of the amazingly fantastic games that Battlefront 2 should be associated with. Whether being played on a console or a computer this game is a classic. Such an improvement from the original, and in comparison, very basic first Battlefront game with the introduction of the space battles, greater range of infantry based roles and the playable Heroes and Villians.
The gameplay is smooth and flowing, through the 50+ hours spent playing this PC version (and the uncountable number spent playing the console version) never once has this game crashed or bugged out.
The controls are simple (point and shoot - well point and clicking the left mouse button) and easy to pick up; in no time you can go from runing head strong into the heat of battle, disabling droids as you go on the dry desert world of Genosis, to piloting a Tie Interceptor and blowing up Rebel scum in a battle above the barren ice world of Hoth!
The single-player campaign following in the footsteps of the brave men of the 501st legion is a fantastic part of this game. It fully immerses you into the Star Wars story as you play through missions based on the events from Episode III through to Episode V. Only slight downside to these missions is that they seem slightly too short for my personal taste, but a very small fly in the ointment.
This game is simply incredible! I do believe that the new Star Wars Battlefront game, being released later this year (November I think) will have to be quite something to out do its predecessor. The bar is exceptionally high.
Would I recommend this game to anyone? I don't think I even have to write my answer, do you?

I just started playing Grim Dawn in the last week or so and I already have some things to say:
Character level progression -
I love the customization in making characters. You have normal ability upgrades, but then you have the class abilities and devotions... all of which leads to some insane combinations of customization. I'm currently building a close combat Shaman that uses a pet and if I build the character wrong, or it just doesn't feel right, I can remap my abilities... which I did have to do early on for taking a skill I did not need.
Boss level progression -
I made the mistake of thinking I could out level the cult boss in the locked area to the east of Act 1. I did not really realize that all the creatures scaled based on the characters level, and bosses were set levels above that. That being said, I at first thought that bosses gained XP from defeating the hero since I was getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me so efficiently. I'm not sure if I like the scaling difficulty, only time will really tell.
Purple items -
Brilliant, simply brilliant having items in game that can be either be task specific quest items, or usable in item crafting. I was wondering at first why I was getting so many drops of a certain type and there was my answer. All of a sudden, I can use dynamite and royal jelly in multiple locations.
Overall you guys did an amazing job on Grim Dawn. I like the gritty artwork and the leveling system is unique and has such utility in character build. I also enjoy the fact that every character can use any item in game... regardless of how poor they will be at using it. HIGHLY recommended if you like games like PoE or D3 and want to take it to the next level.

A great game despite minor flaws and frustrations. This is a gorgeous MMO that has so much content to offer. You can grind, do lifeskills, just like you would irl. You can gather, process food and materials, make items, and perform alchemy. Many of these can be done AFK minimized in your PC so as to consume less resources.

The character customization is filled with options.
A lot of people have complained about this "P2W" or "micro transaction" game. I disagree. You can certainly see microtransactions, but these are all QoL perks. The marketplace is on a BID (rng) system where everyone rich or poor had the same chance of getting an item. You do not need to purchase extra inventory or weights as there are easily workarounds. As stated above, these micro transactions are purely for quality of life.
The loyalty shop for those playing F2P is already quite enough. Progress can be slow, but that's what makes this game playable after a hundred hours. It's still fun.

I LOVED the first Blackguards game, and was looking forward to this one for a long time.
It is NOT the same.
First, there are some definite improvements to the way the game plays on a technical level.
It is far more clear what you will get for putting points into skills, and the equipment is a little easier to make use of as well.
And it starts off soooo promising -- the jilted protagonist, twisted by solitude and lead by fate into a monster-ridden nightmare. Should be amazing.
But the game doesn't draw you in the same way the original(BG1) did, and the flow of the story is too disjointed and meandering.
Worse still is that the combat is VERY repetitive.
In BG1, you could make half your units mages, or refocus everyone to melee -- there was immense versatility, despite very limited choices and a very clunky character sheet.
In this game, you mostly fight using NON-MAGICAL generic units, and the battles don't really weave into the plot much.
They just seem to be "fight the stuff to move forward" and it just gets boring quick.
Unless you REALLY like the big fights with generic units, just play the first one and hope the next brings together what is good about BG 1&2.

The overall story might be good, but I'll never know: the forced rhyme-speech of every character in this game (at least, the handful that I encountered in the prologue + first hour of play) is simply unbearable.  That is to say, every character in this game speaks in rhymes (not riddles or anything, just rhymes).  It would be slightly amusing if executed well, but unfortunately the dialogue between characters is butchered to an unreal degree all for the sake of the pointless rhyming.  Seriously, the "poet" behind this game should stick to handing in assignments to his or her third grade teacher.
But if you don't care about characters breaking versimilitude by occasionally slipping into Yoda-sentence-structure to piece together yet another forced rhyme with a thesaurus-sourced vocab choice, you might like this game.
One thing that you might want to know before buying this game (I didn't realize it) is that combat isn't executed in the manner traditional to side scrollers: unlike Trine, Dust, or Bastion, combat in this game plays out like a JRPG.  Like in Chrono Trigger you can approach an enemy, then the game will cut-scene into a small arena where you play the battle out in a turn-based manner.
This isn't necessarily a detractor from the game if you enjoy that kind of combat, but I have to admit I was a little disappointed since I happen to prefer side scrolling battle (jumping around, aiming, choosing correct weapons, etc.) over the JRPG style (conserving your mana until you need it, spending a turn to use a potion when necessary, etc.).
I hope you found this review useful.

While the story is, at times, DEEPLY engaging, the game is ultimately unsatisfying for two reasons: (1) every decision is a Morton's fork, where it makes no difference what choice you make; and (2) none of the storylines is given a satisfying conclusion.
A Morton's Fork is a fallacy where all options lead to the same outcome. In this case, make a smart decision and end up in bad situation. Make a foolish decision and end up in the EXACT SAME bad situation. It makes it very hard to care about individual choices when they do not effect the ultimate outcome. This is an especially big problem when the whole point of the game is that it allows you to "choose" what happens.
The second problem is that the storyteller seem, in true GRRM fashion, to be incapable of writing a satisfying conclusion to a storyline. When only bad things happen to characters no matter what they (or you) do, it instills a sense of hopelessness in the narrative that makes the reader stop caring what happens to the characters.
Maybe this was supposed to be a setup for further games, but I can find better uses for my money. After playing this season to its "conclusion" I honestly don't care what happens to these characters anymore.

In short: The only good parts of Tropico 4 is what hasn't changed from Tropico 3. This makes it a good game, but disappointing. I would not recommend this unless Tropico 3: Ultimate Power somehow cost more money than this, which I'd have a hard time believing is going to happen.
This strikes me as a creatively bankrupt sequel, most noticable in how they have adjusted the shaders and bloom to make all the content look different, but 99% of it is the same content as in Tropico 3 Ultimate Power and it now just looks uglier.
Speaking of DLC, there is a lot of it for this time, but none of it seems to offer any improvement to the game. The game as it was in Tropico 3 was already fairly complete in terms of options for its setting, and I would attribute the choice of what DLC to create more on marketing decisions and not creative, design decisions that would actually make the game any better. I have a hard time figuring out why else there is no worthwhile DLC.
One irritating new feature are the advisors. They don't appear to actually have any effect on the running of your empire, their only function is that they unlock the usage of policies. Tropico 3 did not have this requirement, and there aren't any new, valuable policies that would necessitate an increase in start-up cost. All in all this 'feature' is a downside-- it's one more hoop that you must jump through on every single session. If your choice of advisors meant something, this would be one more wrinkle to make every island unique, but as implemented it just makes each island take longer.
Voicework has been redone entirely for this edition of the game, but the lines are all the same. The difference is now the accents and mannerisms are much more muted, much more subtle. Improvement? I guess if you took the voicework in Tropico 3 very seriously and felt it was insensitively broad, then this would be an improvement. Personally I really missed the energetic, light-hearted and boisterous character-line delivery, and the words haven't even changed so if they wanted to be more politically correct this is a half-measure at best; a compromise that pleases no one.
If you've tapped out Tropico 3 and its expansions and just want more missions, then by all means, get this game. If you're wondering which Tropico to get, or want the most value for the dollar, get Tropico 3 + its expansion.

The game system is the BEST among first person shooter games I have ever played, and this is why I recommend to play this game.  You are now not blocked by irrational surroundings, like other games, in the quarantine of Harran.
However, the main story is the WORST.  You cannot choose how to behave through the main storyline.  The main character does not behave as an experienced agent, a professional, but an ignorant ten-years-old boy.  The last fight was the worst moment in my some decades computer gaming experience.  There is no feeling of accomplishment or satisfaction when you defeat your nemesis.
However, free-running in the urban settings is a totally new experience, and in overall, there is no doubt that you can enjoy parkouring the city of Harran.

As many people have it doesn't hold your hand, but it goes beyond that, it gently lures you the edge of a cliff, which it ices before-hand. What i mean by that is that it's possible to screw up even during character creation, leaving the city early on will definitely get you killed.
Having said that if you do manage to get the some beginning difficulty (or restart and do thing a lot more optimally)  it is actually a really good game. The lack of hand holding means that when you investigate shenanigans, it actually feels like investigating (remembering clues, trying to figure out what they mean etc), instead of just going to the next map marker.
The battle system is simple enough to understand but there is a lot of complexity that can brought into it, like combing spell effects, using the weather and so on, and while I've seen this in other games, often you just overlevel you characters and ignore all that complex stuff for the most part, here, especially at the start the odds are not ever in your favour, so you are forced to use all sorts of dirty tricks to get the job done. But that makes it immensly satisfying and really gets you to learn the combat well, so later as you get more spells and such you can wreak a lot of havoc on the enemies while they can barelly reatliate.
Also while some puzzles took me a while to figure out, Ididn't have to look up any of them online.
Overall the game is pretty hard (especially at the beginning) but it's the good kind of hard and for every frustrating battle there is a great sense of accomplishment and when you do manage to kill a bunch of enemies easily by some underhanded tactic it doesn't feel cheap, it feels earned.
Played it for about 100 hours, highly recommend it

Context: Played this during the recent free trial weekend (and accompanying 60% off). I am also a fan of the C&C series and currently have C&C 3 in my library. Just so you know my basis of comparison. I would rate my interest in the RTS genre as moderate, with an interest in base building. Very singleplayer focused; no interest in multiplayer beyond skirmishes v CPU.
GG is a solid entry in the RTS genre, harking back to the days of C&C. The presentation value is high, with really detailed cutscenes and well presented menus. The battlefield and unit/structure graphics are good, better than C&C3 but not by much. Sound and music are top notch with a nice synth theme during missions and skirmish.
Gameplay wise, it is what you would expect of an RTS with a heavy focus on resource extraction and management and unit production. If you keep the flow of inputs you can keep pumping out units. The hotkey system is a nice touch, something I wish more RTS' would do. Allowing you to quickly select a unit, building or technology to queue with a quick button combination. The base building is nice (hey hey, we got walls!) with each race (of which there are 3) managing it differently. The Goo don't really base build at all, and have a completely different play style. Not one I could get used to in the time alotted. The humans / beta play rather similar, each constructing structures of nodes. But essentially are the same in terms of units just with a different skin.
Battles are slower paced than in C&C3 with unit mixing a must to make sure units don't get outmatched. The use of trees as a cover system is also a nice touch. You can easily ambush enemy units from the safety of the trees hidden across the maps. The story of the campaign seems compelling, although i really didn't get that far (4th mission) to gauge it properly.
Overall I enjoyed the experience but besides the nice touches I mentioned, it is just too similar an experience to C&C to warrant a $20 price tag on sale let alone a $50 one RRP. I am interested in the story, but I think since I have C&C3 already, I might just stick with it for now and wait for a heavier price drop (~$10).
So its a recommend from me, when the price drops.

I sincerely dislike this game. I wanted to like it as a reboot of the franchise, but it pulls only mild strategy elements from the older games. The problem is that when I think X-Com, I think pure strategy from every aspect. Base placement, radar coverage and range management on a planetary scale, full building demolition, proper incindiary characteristics from a battle perspective, using your engineers to provide saleable components to the world market at a profit. All of these things have just gone away, and been replaced by a simplistic interface, with a story line pushed ahead like it's on rails.
Soldier classifications was a waste of effort on the developer's part. In previous X-Com games, there was no specialization. People don't operate that way. They are all soldiers, mostly equally capable of doing the same things. Some have faster reaction or aim scores, but all of them can weild a rocket launcher or shotgun.
The true successor to the Xcom series is Xenonauts, and even that missed the mark.
If someone were to look for an uncomplicated game in the genre, I would point them towards the new Shadowrun series. It has most of the same elements, but doesn't adulterate any old franchises by removing much of the complexity of the system originally created.
I realize that I will never see a better version of X-Com: Apocalypse, and that really disappoints me.

Blackguards 2 plays quite differently from Blackguards 1.  While I preferred the first game's character customization with the stats, the battles in 2 were more intense and included many more combatants.  The random number generator was significantly less frustrating.  It's hard to pick a favorite.  Both are amazing TRPGs.  Some believe this game feels like DLC for #1, and while I understand how you can get that impression (most music tracks in #2 are from #1), the world map and battles play quite differently.  There's enough content here to justify the sequel status, in my opinion.
What I liked about Blackguards 2.
* Battles were very intense.  The player can't always win with brute force (in fact, a great deal of battles will result in defeat if the player opts for brute force).  I took ONE LOOK at the field during the fight against the druid, my group surrounded by the treant chimearas, and didn't think there was any hope of success.  I ended up succeeding on my first attempt with the help of 2 well-placed fireballs (they unexpectedly grouped together).  A lot of battles had me thinking "What the heck am I going to do to win this?!" and occasionally required a second attempt.
* The return of Takate, Zurburan and Naurim from 1 was appreciated.
* Huge battles.  The number of combatants in #1 (the unit portraits) never exceeded my screen's capacity, but the majority of the battles in #2 wrapped around.
* Contains multiple endings.  I think if I had played differently, the main character survives.  (I'll be back, just you wait #2.)
* The ability to have a magic-user wearing armor without penalty potentially allows for some very interesting hybrid options for Zurburan and the main character.
* I felt there were more than enough character points to complete what I wanted for all of my characters.
What I didn't like.
* Stats were dropped completely, dumbing down character customization and nearly completely removing the table-top RPG feel that the first game had.  This loss of stats affected the spells a lot.  The creators decided to hold on to every spell from #1 and alter them to keep them relevant.  I don't think it worked.  Many spells became nearly useless.
* I prefer an adventuring party with mercenary assistance over a conquering horde.  Having to defend territories already claimed was a nuisance.  I hope it wasn't added just to increase play time.
* The narrator's voice annoyed the snot out of me.  I found myself pressing multiple buttons trying to shut him up, as I had already read the words.
* The story was there, but it was narrated more than acted out with the characters.
Overall, this provides more of what I'm looking for.  More tactical RPG awesomeness.  I'm glad I didn't pass this series up.

Put it on your "catch-it-on-sale" list.
Pros
- 1080p 60 fps, native controller support, no crashes in game, borderless windowed support (1080p upscaled to 1440p in my case), and none of the usual console port problems.
- Skill system felt enjoyable to mess around with, and there weren't many skills that just felt so good or broken that they were the only viable strategies for certain portions of the game.
- Hilarious dialogue, lots of gaming culture references, superfluous amounts of satire/puns. With terms like HDD/CPU, names of the cities (Leanbox/Lastation/Lowee aka XboX/PlayStation/Wii), numerous characters/dialogue a character who's entire existence is to contain references to Steins;Gate, and incessant 4th wall breaks, I was endlessly amused at the writing. The humor is quite cheesy, but I like cheesy humor.
Cons
- Very unimaginative dungeons. They are not randomly generated and some of the later ones are literally copy-pasted with some different mixes of enemies. There is literally zero puzzle solving and the exploration might as well not exist. It's also impossible to know the leveling of the zones/dungeons aside from just kind of "remembering" the recent ones to gauge the leveling potential.
- The menu is a huge pain to navigate. Items aren't sorted alphabetically or aren't in many logical orders. You can't do something as simple as buy a weapon and equip it on the same screen, etc. Most of the out of dungeon UI navigation is very cumbersome.
- Have to be sure that my controller is on when I start the game
- The game consistently crashes when I start it up if it isn't the first thing that I open on Steam. This might have something to do with the fact that I consistently play with a controller? Anyway, I always had to quickly exit Steam if I wanted to play.
- Large lack of information in-game. It took me a long time to even find out what the stats do! A lot of mechanics are not transparent at all, which can get quite annoying.
- The "plan" system is pretty necessary for item advancing/crafting, but some of these parts have a large chain of item hunting that gets really tough to keep track of due to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ menu. Break out that pen and paper, I guess.
I'll add a neutral point that the save system is very similar to the ones from older games. You can save during the menu outside of a dungeon and at other save points prior to boss fights and such. It might take some time to get back into the habit of saving as often as possible. You can easily lose some progress if you enter an event and it involves a boss fight, which is very annoying the first few times.
Overall, the game feels like it should have come out in the early 2000s. It reminds me a lot of a 2001 game called Dark Cloud. I enjoyed Dark Cloud a couple of times, but i definitely became more aware of its glaring flaws/shortcomings as I got older and played better games. Additionally, the road blocks in the game can't be overcome by many skillful execution or innovative ideas; instead, you just grind to get more levels. In that regard, it's extremely similar to Pokemon. Since I grew up enjoying both of those games, I think that's the only reason I really enjoyed this one.
At the end of the day, I'd give it a 6.3/10.

Seeing so many negative reviews, I had to contribute something positive despite my minimal playtime. I apologize if this review is lacking, as it is my first. Long story short, it's a Far Cry game. It has stealth kills, basic crafting, animal hunting, karma events, outposts, collectibles, all the bare bones stuff that has become the basis of the Far Cry series. That's where most people will complain, but Primal is more than it's skeleton.
Good Stuff
- Great setting. Running through the environment is awesome.
- Language is pretty cool, though I've had a few laughs at how it sounds sometimes (Think male Twi'lek from KOTOR. You know the one).
- Limited base building. You can't choose where it goes, but I like seeing the village being built up over time.
Hit or Miss
- Taming system is basic, but there are plenty of animal choices.
- Melee is simple, but fun.
Bad Stuff
- Open world elements are the usual Far Cry filler.
Without guns, the pace of combat has changed quite a bit. Sure, Jason/Ajay could charge someone swinging a sword wildly, but in Primal you're far less likely to get suckerpunched and shot in the face. The melee combat is simple, but effective. I haven't had this much fun bashing things in an FPS since Bioshock and Half-Life.
The taming system is about as primitive as it gets, throw meat and press the button. I dislike this, but beating a sabretooth tiger halfway unconscious with a club while it tears you limb from limb probably isn't as fun as it sounds in my head. We can't all be Drago Bludvist, I guess. The animals themselves are fairly varied, with different stats and abilities between the species. It's pretty fun comboing them together - start attacking from stealth with your leopard, then call on your lion/tiger/bear (oh my) to finish them off in open combat.
The major complaint about Primal is going to be that it's just more of the same. And I suppose in a way it is, but if that's the attitude you take then you'll miss the forest for the trees.

This game is a fantastic Zelda II/metroidvania adventure.  It was lots of fun to play, very addictive, and it only became a drag at the very end when trying to beat the superbosses.  I 100%ed this game (well, I didn't get all the coin chests or all the endings, but I don't think that counts) and I have to say, I enjoyed it quite a bit!  I did not use guides for most of it; I did get lost at one point and used a guide there, and I also got guidance for the superbosses and the final crystals, but other than that, a careful explorer can get pretty much everything.  So:
Things I liked: the metroidvania gameplay, obviously, is the main draw.  It's not a straight metroidvania: each area is self-contained.  Basically, there's an overworld map filled with impassable areas raising exclamation points, and you go into these places to cross the map to the other side of that impassable area.  These areas often have challenges requiring the use of upgrades or spells, so you may not be able to cross them at first but have to come back with better stuff.  The game also has a nifty story told in flashbacks, a karma meter (which I never got to move), EXP and level-ups (it would have been nice to know what's actually important to have late-game, because you get 1 skill point at level-up and with the level cap you can only get some of the upgrades).  Also, every new thing on the map is exciting to explore and discover!  I guess that's what kept me playing for so many hours.
Things I didn't really like: the lack of direction.  The game is deliberately designed with a "retro" feel.  I honestly wish developers would stop doing that.  I buy the simplicity in graphics, that's fine, but the game could well have explained more.  For example, at one point you can find a blue book.  It goes into your upgrade grid.  What does it do?  The forums aren't sure.  The game sure doesn't tell you!  I think, for the most part, you can kinda figure out where to go by just looking around on the map, but maybe also someone in the towns could kinda say something to point you in the right direction too?  You also collect crystals -- why?  What's the point?  Turns out they open doors if you have enough of them, OK.  So they're... door counters?
Other things of note: the game is pretty hard.  There are lots of puzzles, lots of challenging platforming, etc.  There's a very nice Hell-Temple-esque challenge area that's quite a bit harder than the rest of the game.  And then there are... the superbosses.  MASSIVE DIFFICULTY SPIKE, even compared to the Wizard's Tower.  They're not required, of course, but yeah.  My last week of playing this game was spent getting frustrated against one of these guys for a bit and giving up for the night.  On the other hand, it felt damn good to kill the last one and open the door they were guarding!
Anyway, I had a lot of fun playing Elliot Quest.  Other than those superbosses, the challenge level is great, though you may want to look things up on occasion in case you missed something big (I missed a crucial game mechanic, for example, that nobody bothered to tell me about in-game).  Enjoy!
