Child of Light is a fairytale-inspired RPG with modest exploration and puzzle-solving elements.
The story is set in the magical world of Lemuria, which is suffering under the rule of an evil Black Queen and her dark creatures which have overrun the land. The main protagonist is a young girl, Aurora. Aurora is the daughter of a duke from 1895 Austria who has found herself separated from her father and whisked away to Lemuria. Aurora must navigate the hazards of this beautiful, but dangerous world in order to return to Austria and reunite with her father.
Without spoiling the story, what I enjoyed the most about Child of Light's plot was that it managed to touch upon critical tropes integral to a fairytale story, while subverting ones which are no longer relevant in modern society. Aurora's adventure is a coming-of-age hero's journey, involving hidden destinies and familial strife. Despite her fear and uncertainty at being in an unfamiliar world, Aurora is no helpless damsel in distress; Aurora is a girl of strong morals and action who helps those in need, and who over the course of the story matures into a strong leader.
The art style evokes nostalgia for watercolored storybooks of childhoods past. Both the character sprites and the backgrounds are simple at first look, and extremely detailed upon closer inspection. The visuals themselves are beautiful and alone make this game a piece of art.
The soundtrack by Coeur de Pirate is a perfect accompaniment to the setting and story --  appropriately whimsical, triumphant, or haunting, as appropriate to the point in the story.
One element of the game that some may be put off by (though personally I enjoyed it) was the use of rhyming iambic verse in nearly all of the dialogue in the story.
All in all, I feel that Child of Light is a truly excellent adventure and well worth the full price of the game and deserving of the 2014 GOTY nomination it received from IGN.

I honestly don't get the hype and the praises for this game. If it was an original turn-based sqad tactics, it would be completely average. The only thing that makes it stand out is being a remake of the original X-com, and here it fails across the board. Yes, it look way better than the 20-something old original. Yes, it's 3d, better amimated and has actual voice acting. And that's it. For an actually enjoyable x-com game, get the original. Or Apocalyplse. Or one of the open-source clones. This is NOT X-com.
In case you;ve never heard about the original UFO defence, Earth is being attacked by BEMOS (Bug-Eyed Monsters from Outer Space) and national governments can't cope. So they created a global agency called X-com and put you in command. And since you're the first, last and only line of defence, they gave you one base, two fighter jets and a bunch of rookie soldiers (this point is equally weak in the old and new version, but let's let it slide, so the game mechanics can work). In the original game you scan for UFOs, send jets to shoot them down, then send in your soldiers to kill/capture survivors and salvage any goodies. Back at base, you can (and must) research alien corpses, weapons, UFO components and use their technology to build new equipment for your soldiers (including new aircraft). On a strategic level, which is real-time, you do the research and manufacturing, expand your base and build new ones and scan for and hunt down UFOs. LAter, you will find alien bases on Earth and take the fight to them, and they will probably do the same to you, so you will end up defending your own base. You will also learn to capture living specimen and "research" (=interrogate) them, find out where they're coming from and kick their butts completely.
The tactical missions (crash sites, bases) are turn-based, with your soldiers spending Time Units on actions. We're talking about, say 80 TUs per turn. A step takes 4, turning 90 degrees takes 2, an aimed shot takes 35. Your soldiers have names and RPG-style stats like strenght (carrying capacity), accuracy (no comment), speed (=more TUs), then later also psionic abilities. These stats improve over time and you really feel it when an experienced commando buys it in a mission. Your soldiers have a dozen equipment slots, starting with their hands, pockets, belt and backpack, so a strong guy can carry a bunch of grenades, magazines, a backup weapon and a medikit.
Now, 20+ years later, we have somthing dumbed down so much it hurts. The strategic part takes you by the hand (although this might be due to the tutorial - maybe with tut disabled, it would run better). Base locations are reduced to picking a continent. Equipment manufacturing is instant. Researching a corpse gives you a fighter jet upgrade, which you can't use on your fighter jets (maybe when you build your own in the future). You can customize your soldiers and waste hours and hours on the way they look, but they have exactly four equipment slots (armor, weapon, side-arm, backpack). The backpack carries one (as in ONE!) grenade and if you want to take a medikit, the granade needs to stay behind. After you've invented a stun gun, it will be called a side-arm, but occupies the backpack slot. No magazines in you soldiers' inventory, I guess you just reload with thin air. And no RPG-esque stats. Promotions. Your rookie gets promoted to a squaddie and assigned a specialist role (heavy, sniper, assault, support). His further promotions let you pick one of two special moves. That's it. I also don't know how the roles are assigned; it feels scripted, but again, that might be the tutorial acting up.
Then you load you squad into a plane and deliver them to the site of a mission. In the original X-com, mission were played in randomly generated locations with the apropriate environment (forrest, farmlands, city, desert, etc., depending on where you shot down the UFO). Here, they feel completely scripted. They even have names, ffs. The maps are way smaller, making the missions much shorter than before (this is not necessarily a bad thing). the lay of the land is such that you usually have only one direction to move - no exploration. Combat is based on moving from cover to cover, which will only help you slightly. The game calculates your odds of hitting an alien - these odds increase if you're standing higher than him and decrease if he's in cover and/or squatting down. Same for you - even if you're squatting behind a solid wall, there's still a chance that ET will hit you. Forget what you see: you see a solid wall between you and ET, but the game has decided that his shot hits you - you're dead. And if the shot misses, it will either destroy the cover, or do nothing. Gone are the old days when the game actually calculated the projectile's flight pass. Gone are the days when your missed shot hit another alien or one of you own soldiers. Hit probability is 68% - generate random Number - hit/miss. That's it.
My greatest fear about this game was when I read about canceling the TU game mechanic. And it's every bit as aweful as I have feared. You have two actions per turn. You can run twice, run and shoot, or shoot. Or perform special actions (reload, squat down, special shots or wait and shoot during aliens' turn). No, you can't shoot twice. You can't shoot then reload, since shooting end this soldier's turn. And some weapons, like the sniper rifle, need both actions to shoot, so you can't even move then shoot.
The scripting goes further in rescue missions: one of the first ones has you find and rescue a civilian who was captured by alines and managed to escape. You want to hear what she saw, obviously. So you move to the north to find her, then lead her back south to the plane. Cool. You have, of course, killed every ET so far, so just to give you a challenge, let's drop some aliens between you and the plane. Drop, as in literally drop from the sky. You're facing north, with a cover in front of you, guy drops south of you and waits (shooting during your turn). Your soldiers dont have a good angle for a shot, so you try to move the civi to cover. When she moves, she gets shot. Would it be so hard to spawn a big bunch of BEMs to the north of your position and have you make a fighting retreat? I guess it would. Oh, and if you were hoping for a nice chat with the lady you've rescued, sorry bro. It's just another completed mession.
Truth is, there is nothing in this game that makes me want to continue playing. No, I don't recommend.

You find yourself at a place known as the Inventory, a special speakeasy made during the prohibition for game enthusiasts who only wanted to have a drink, play a few games, and bet ridiculous amounts of money. Nowadays, the place still has it's fair share of strange patrons such as Max, Strong Bad, Heavy, and Tycho.
The guest stars aren't just around for show, they keep the games interesting and will sometimes offer to buy in using special items that are handed over to whoever knocks them out of the game. These prizes are:
Max: Lugermorph and License to Maim (custom pistol and police badge)
Strong Bad: Dangeresque, Too? (moonviewer glasses)
Heavy: Iron Curtain (custom minigun)
Tycho: Enthusiast's Timepiece (custom invisiwatch)
This game, while laughing and carefree in nature, will punish those who get too greedy when one of the coveted items comes into play. It make take a few tries, but the slow and cunning method will always triumph of rushing recklessly (except in Max's case, he doesn't even look at the cards).

Pros:
The most unique part of this game is the fact that you can change the outcome of the storyline and quests by what you say in conversations or by what you chose to say. Sometimes, this works wonders and you can make a shy person open up to you with important information or you can calm down an angry drunk to avoid a fight.
The dialogue is hilarious, each little joke, each innuendo just made it for me. I especially loved the animal to human dialogue.
You can do almost anything you want! You can murder people, you can steal from people, you can wander around aimlessly. You can even use your partner as a distraction and go into places you aren't allowed in.
The combat system is neat. I found it easy to understand (especially considering this was my first attempt at this genre) and I was actually pretty decent at it. I could combine attacks to create terrain that would cause effect damage to enemies when they entered it. This made it easier to defeat enemies higher levels than us.
The asthetics of the game are beautiful too, I felt genuinely immersed in every area I went into and I really appreciate the level of detail that went into it. In every field, you can see tones of the green/yellow grass depending on which way the sun is in the games sky. You can see shadows in the water which are fish or other objects.
Cons:
It was a lot of trial and error. I think we restarted the save a few dozen times as we'd managed to ruin it and promptly fail our quest.
I'm putting the combat system here too, because you do have to plan out your moves accordingly. I had to think about 3 steps ahead to ensure I could defeat the enemies, or I had to run.

To begin with I must say that I am a big fan of The Dark Eye Pen’n’Paper and really like  the world of Aventuria! I was really excited when the first Blackguards was released. It wasn’t the game I was expecting but still good with some interesting features and a thrilling combat system.
Therefore I knew what to expect from Blackguards 2 … and I was still surprised! In a positive way! The story is more interesting and the characters even more well-rounded than in the first one! As soon as you start you feel pity and a disgusted by Cassia!
The combat itself hasn’t changed a lot which is good in my eyes! I like the strategic approach and the possibility to use the environment for your advantage. It’s not always easy too keep track of the entire map but that doesn’t hurt. Spells always work and also you normally hit enemy when you attack. This is something I was skeptical about but as it turns out the battles feel more dynamic and faster which is big plus!
What has changed is the character development and again for the better! Even I, knowing and loving the complexity of the Dark Eye rule books was confused and overwhelmed! So the new approach is way more user friendly and even for beginners easy to get into as there are always information available what the e.g. talent improves. Also you can develop “your” Cassia more into the direction you want during the game and not thinking “shame, should’ve chosen blablabla right at the start..”
The game definitely has developed since the first part! Positively! For anyone with a hang towards strategic hex-field battles in fantasy settings this game is a must! Especially given the, just guessing now, 20+ hours of game for only 20-30€!!!

There's some contention when it comes to Telltale's Game of Thrones. I'll be honest I thoroughly enjoyed this, it had twists it had turns, I went in expecting Game of Thrones, and that's what I got. It's a dreary, almost hopeless story of betrayal with a tense atmosphere. All of which done in Telltale's signature style, except when it comes to most people's major problem; choices.
What many have noted is that your choices don't have significant impact on the overall story in the same way that other Telltale games' choices have. Whilst I do agree with this point, I didn't go in expecting such, I went in hoping for the same feeling of dread that I got from both the books and TV show, because I am not in control. What I do want to address is how Telltale themselves advertised this. It was thus assumed that our choices would have proper impact like previous TT games, had they openly stated that this would be more in line with their older games, Sam & Max for example, then it would be less of an insult for the game to be linear.
I'll quickly mention now, the graphics seem less impressive than previous Telltale games, however the soundtrack is solid. If you're getting this, maybe as a fan of the show or books, then I recommend not going in expecting choices to matter much, and also that you have watched up to at least Season 3 of the TV show. But if you're already a fan of GoT you've most likely already done so.
Oh, and I have never hated myself more.

After being nearly done with the game I can give a better review of the game:
Positive aspects:
- One of the best experiences for Turn based tactical combat. I really like this aspect of Blackguards since only a few games get turn based combat right.
- Witty and funny dialogue, this is one of the main reasons this game is charming
- Art and Sound are great just like in the first Blackguards.
- The Character building was streamlined and it is now harder to spec your character into a dead end. Removing some of the choices did not really dimminish the DSA rulesets.
-Most major bugs have been squashed after the lastest patch.
Negative aspects:
- Performance Issues related mostly to bad optimisation, the Engine is the same as Blackguards 1 and it feels like there are still the same issues present like the first one and there was no optimisation done.
- Some mission designs are very frustrating, the missions usually are challenging which is nice, but some missions are simply a test of will not to jump from a roof after you have to reload the mission for the 50th time because it either bugs out or the mission itself makes it near impossible to be beaten if you are not lucky.
- The Story and dialogue options dry up after half the towns are taken over. I have not had any new "banter" conversations after being done halfway from the game. The first Blackguards was far superior in Story and Character Design.
Overall the game is fun to play if you like tactical round based combat. The story and dialogue is good to a certain point however not troughout the whole game which saddens me.
Currently there are too many issues with the game so I recomment waiting a little bit till the worst bugs are fixed and hopefully the game a little bit revised.

I went into this game with no prior knowledge of the in-game mechanics or anything in this game aside from some positive reactions from friends on how it's "A sweet zombie apocalypse parkour game". I bought it with a friend during the sale, and at the time of writing I have 33 hours in the game, all with said friend. Loving it. Almost every single bit of it. The gameplay is amazing, with a limited backpack for weapons/ammo/battle tools (unlimited for resources and base items like medkits and lockpicks) and weapons with a durability that makes it so you won't be carrying your sweet overlevelled sword all game. There many amazing upgrades that make your weapons even cooler for the time you'll carry them. And a parkour system that beats assassin's creed by a longshot in terms of smoothness and player experience.
This isn't an entirely positive review though, as the base game does have a minor issue being the story. All characters in the main storyline of the Dying Light act like 10 year old kids. At no point did I feel any connection with any of the characters in the story. The player character is an idiot who makes many many many many many mistakes that no sane person would make in a lifetime and the final bossfight is a quicktime event in a forced solo-mission, while all other missions are co-op available. I'll admit that aside from the qte bossfight the story improves at the end, but altogether the main story is bad.
HOWEVER! The Dying Light now also comes with the Following DLC. A story after the main story which drastically improves on the problems the former story faced, and adds so much more fun to the game with upgradable buggies, sweet new weapons and a story that will stay interesting, rather than annoy you.
Altogether this game is amazing, best zombie apocalypse game I've played so far. And with the DLC now included when buying the game fixing the main problem the game faced, I can recommend this to anyone.

I understand that my point of view reflects almost a small minority; but I will state my opinion. I am a gamer since mid '80s, and almost explicitely play strategy and RPGs (not the action ones...).
This game is amazing fun. It's like fire emblem, but even better. It combiness strategy and RPG. It's neither dumbed down nor shallow on the contrary, it's deep and engaging. It throws you puzzles that you have to solve, so often you don't have to win by fighting, but by finding the right patterns. I played on hard and has been so far challenging and rewarding.
Speaking with nearly 40h playtime; I had encountered a few bugs during the first two days of release, but after the last patch all of them are fixed. I really don't get the complains about the broken and almost unplayable game (yup, I passed the druid and the adamant).
It runs very smoothly on my rig. I have no performance issues.
Frankly, why don't they make more games like this? It's one of the best turn based strategies, I have played - and believe me I have played a lot.
Overall, I loved this game and I would give it a 90/100. I recommend this to all players who are into strategy, puzzle solving and deep RPG rules.

I'm obviously not the intended audience for this game.  And that's fine, but it still didn't much impress me.
Starting out, the first thing I learned was that for a character designing engine that lets you screw up how a character looks so badly (see the many comedic YouTube videos that play with it) and claims to let you "Make the character YOU want to play," (direct quote from store page), I sure couldn't make a character look how I wanted.
Admittedly, I was trying to turn a giant into an orc, but I couldn't even get close. Big points off for that one. I eventually gave up on that and just settled for "vaugely neanderthal looking" before jumping into the game.
Next impressions did not really go to well.  I was treated to a movie with sub-par narration and a story that, well... I mean, I'm sure there was a story somewhere if I played long enough, but I see much and didn't feel too encouraged to dig for it.  Something about a stone and everything disappearing/dying?
Then, suddenly, some smoky shadowy thing with red eyes and a creepy voice teaches me how to walk?  I think it's supposed to be your Standard Anime Sidekick, and it felt like it was trying to be cute and creepy at the same time. It didn't quite work. It did succeed in one thing your Standard Anime Sidekick does in these games though: it annoyed me. I'd rather the blasted thing shut up and left me alone.
Meanwhile, I am visually overwhelmed by announcements in the middle of the screen, bars and data all along the edges, and no real clue what any of it means.  Nor is any of it explained to me during what I presume is supposed to be a tutorial.
Unfortunately, that tutorial largely consists of "Walk here. Walk there. Kill this group of things.  Now kill this slightly tougher group of things.  Then do it again."  Some video in the corner tried teaching me a combo at one point, but there was no real context for it, and it kept reappearing as though it was important.  I'm sure it would have been, eventually, if I'd kept at it.
To be fair, the combat did feel like it may have had some pretty neat potential, once I worked out comboing.  It seemed to utilize balancing resource management and skill execution.  I only really started to get the hang of it before I lost interest, but I will note it as one of the more positive experiences of my first-impressions phase.
Meanwhile, I'm hoping for some scrap of story, something that hints as to what I'm doing there, how I got there, what the creepy shadowy thingy is... I got as far as getting the shadowy thingy some teeth.  At that point, I just kinda gave up.  The voice acting not matching the words was rather jarring (I wonder if there was a way to switch audio language that may have remedied that?), but then I'm coming from Elder Scrolls Online where everything is fully voice acted.
I started to get the feel that the actual text and content of the story (or "story") was intended to just skip past like the quest systems of many MMOs, and that ended up turning me off.  The overall first impression, my 3+ hours of the game, left me feeling like there wouldn't be much to do except follow the "kill these things" quests.
I got a vague idea there may have been crafting or something, based on randomly picking up rubbish from bushes and critters, and being unable to skin animals because I didn't have a knife, but I was not introduced to it during my first-impression phase.
Those first impressions are important to a new player, to inform them if it's worth the investment of time and energy -- largely time.  The biggest turn-off was the fact that, on the days I logged in, I stumbled across some sort of current events listing.  One of the current events ongoing was an XP boost to celebrate grinding.  Yes: GRINDING.  CELEBRATE.
That pretty much did me in there.  I assessed the value of my time versus what I felt would be the entertainment value based on my first impressions, and the math did not favor this game.
Today, the game tried to update.  Steam choked on some kind of error.  It actually did this during the initial install too, as if trying to warn me away.  Well, hint taken.  I uninstalled it.  I also made sure to remove their xigncode3, as it seemed to have a questionable reputation.  The dev was kind enough to include instructions on how to do so... but not kind enough to actually remove it when you uninstall the game.
Again, I am obviously not the intended audience for this game.  But based on my experiences above, I wouldn't have expected to have a good time.  Using Bartle's Taxonomy, my priorities are: Explorer, Socializer, Achiever, Killer.  If you follow a similar set, you may have a similar experience.
Also, seriously, what kind of game doesn't let you be an orc?  Tsk tsk.

I was unfamiliar with the "roguelike"-genre when I first played FTL and I fell in love at once. Both with the genre and the game itself.
The combat is rewarding and surprisingly deep. You, as a player, have a lot of agency when choosing what to build and how to engage enemies.
There are, also, some random events when you're asked to make moral decitions. These don't inpact the game in any grand way; there are no "good vs evil"-morality bars that you fill up. They only leave you with less money and a sense that you did a good thing (if that's what you're into).
The gameplay is, like I described, very good but the real strength of the game is the world and atmosphere. The alien races are well defined, the random encounters are well written and the music is fantastic.
I cannot recommed this game enough.

Sometimes I wonder if the beatemup developers of today were actually around for the 90s. I keep thinking that they spent the decade hibernating, possibly in some cryogenic sleep-tank. I mean, how could they understand so little? Did they even play 90s beatemups? How is it possible to screw up so badly and not care at all? When I play games like Arson and Plunder: Unleashed, games that are so shockingly bad, that tears of blood stream down my broken and hollow soul, I just want to pluck out my beard and tear my monitor in half.
Through a twist of fate and a rip in the fabric of unreality, an Elf and an Orc become one. As Arson, you must burn 1000s of pitiful humans alive. As Plunder, you have to mercilessly crush the skulls of 1000s more. What should be the setup for a strategic as well as thrilling beatemup, is just another disappointing tale of boredom. All you can do is watch in horror as the very concept of fun is set alight and brutally torn asunder until nothing remains.
There are 5 levels with 5-6 zones each. The zones are your standard "move forward, kill all of the enemies, repeat" setup. It's pretty common for the beatemup genre, but the problems don't actually start until you play the game. The enemies tend to have a dash attack. This attack is a jumping shoulder-check. There's really not much you can do to counter this move, and you're likely not going to try because it does so little damage. Archers attack with arrows from practically anywhere. This is more damage you'll probably shrug off, because dodging arrows is too much work. It's worth pointing out that dodging in this game, just plain stinks. You're a rather large target, and even by dashing around, you're still liable to get clipped and surrounded.
Mainly you'll be relying on Arson to carry you through this game. She has a special move which causes fire to kill 5-6 enemies at a time. Special moves cost meter, but you replenish meter by killing enemies. As you can tell, this makes for a move that can be spammed at any and all opportunities. Is it cheating? Nope, not in the slightest. This game expects you to use and abuse that move, because the later zones pile on the enemies to an absurd degree. It's at this point where ignoring all of the minor damage bites you in the rear. Zones 5-2 and 5-4 are flat-out terrible, and that's because they're completely unbalanced. 5-2 throws more enemies at you than 90% of the rest of the game, and 5-4 expects you to deal with 5 waves of foes without any food items. There are a couple tantalizing watermelons placed in 5-4, but they're inexplicably background objects, because I haven't the faintest idea.
Oh yeah, I forgot to talk more about Plunder. I don't think anyone cares about him, including the people who developed the game. Well, he's an ugly green orc after all, not a sexy elf with all of the cleavage. Seriously though, the Orc suffers from poor special moves, and his melee attack is actually worse than Arson's. Yep, apparently a lot of muscles and a huge axe doesn't make you very tough. On the bright side, Plunder is better for dealing with the bosses. He can do a quick combo to knock the enemy down, take a few steps above or below them, then do another combo when they try to follow. This is an easy exploit to set up, but it's still the extent of the Orc's usefulness. If his dash-attack and special moves did more damage, switching between characters would actually make sense. Instead it's all about Arson spamming her "fire rain" over and over again.
Now if you haven't subjected your PC to a "fire rain" after several dozen attempts at 5-2 & 5-4, there is a Survival Mode. Before you ask, yes, Arson will be using
even more. There's also a co-op mode, in case you feel like making enemies of the people closest to you. Oh and most importantly, there are attempts at humor in-between some zones. Most of the jokes are made at the expense of the game, and beatemups in general. Sadly, the sense of humor displayed in this game is almost as bad as mine. You're more likely to laugh at the writer's tenuous grasp of the English language, until you consider the possibility that the engrish was done on purpose. Let's face it, there's no way this game will allow any entertainment to be gleaned from it.
Look, if you want a 90s beatemup, just play a 90s beatemup. It's obvious that the people who made Arson and Plunder: Unleashed don't understand the genre, and the more time you spend with this game, the more you'll hate yourself. Now if you'll excuse me, I have the sudden urge to buy some DLC, play Call of Duty, and enjoy a few QTEs.

I haven't got far in the game and classic is only version I went through before buying it on my own. Got to say it is something unique. I am not a big fan of turn based games, but this one makes up for me with other feautures like character customization, interactions with NPC's and humor.
Things that I liked:
-Character customisation is more deep than I thought. The fact that you can make your own class out of any default, just makes me create save files over and over to try out combinations of skills and experiment with "builds".
-Graphics are neat and world is beautiful, which I did not expect this from a turn based game.
-Combat mechanics are interesting. Field combinations can be really powerful sometimes and create an impression of imbalance or advantage from player's side. But enemies are getting really tough, which makes things tense and make a player to use tactics more than just brute force.
-Game is surprising and things that going on around as you explore and talk to NPC's will not keep you bored. Gameplay and exploration are not falling behind each other and both are interesting to do.
Things I disliked:
-As a new player to this kind of games I found it hard at the begining. Sure you destroy your enemies with a single skill or swing of a greatsword at the begining, but world exploration is not easy sometimes. Walk through wrong city gates and you will get in combat with enemies you can't fight yet. Party setup is something that need lots of thinking in my opinion too, since I got stuck on a boss fight for 2 days on my first playthrough. This made me realise that planing battles and party setup is more important than I thought, which new player may not find out from the begining. I ended up starting over which is not a big deal since it is exiting to try things out.
-Loading sometimes created issues for me. Things like some stats disapearing from characters, healthbar indicator doesnt match with number of hitpoints or textures on character just disapear (usually equipment and hair). Sometimes all tutorial notes I already viewed just start popping up.
-Party AI and most likely AI in whole game has tiny and anoying issues sometimes. After a battle characters stay away from fields that mean harm, but compleatly ignore ice fields. What ends up happening: trying to pick up loot from icefield make your characters to fall down, so cleaning those becomes a chore or makes you put points into telekinesis.
-Controlls are clumsy sometimes. If enemy will do suddenly an idle animation and your cursor is not over it's model, you end up clicking in wrong place, which happened fair amouths of times to me. Or how about healing an ally out of combat makes you almost unable to do any other actions (like using a skill with naother character or swaping them) until animation ends.
Overal the game is unique, beautiful and never keeps you bored. 10/10 would play again.

Blackguards 2 is a more combat-focus version of Blackguards 1.
While BG 1 was an RNG fest, BG2 removed so many of the annoying RNG and made strategical plays and puzzle stages a lot more common. Boss fights have you running around trying to abuse the stage hazard to the fullest to win. Certain stages will force you to complete objectives and leave or face infinite spawns unlike the old one where you can kill EVERYTHING except for one stage where you run away from the poison.
Outside of combat, you can now interact with characters more unlike the old one. You can capture prisoners, and interrogate them. Based on a choice, you can either make them spill the beans or spit at you. The informations required to make them answer can be obtained by paying for information from your beggar spies or by speaking around in your camp. After the interrogation, you can decide whether to hang them or let them go. Letting them go can be good but sometime, a certain person might come back to fight you again.
The customization has been greatly simplified. You no longer have the Strength, Charisma, etc from BG1. Instead, you just go with "+10 health" "+10 mana" "unlock tier 1 passive" in a straight line. Weapon level goes froml 1 - 100 and you unlock tier bonus at 50 80 100. While this means no weight limit from the removal of STR (Yes! No more weight issue!), it means much less customization. Even your mages will have as much hp as a fighter at the end making them unkillable.
And with that, let's move on to the balancing.
Endurance has been introduced. In BG1, all you had to do was buff someone and spam that 3x damage move like Hammer blow or Triple shot. You can't anymore. Endurance works like Astral point. When you use a combat skill, you use 10-20 points from you 40-80 endurance pool based on your stat. You regenerate a certain amount each turn based on passive (Endurance Regeneration) and gear bonus.
You can now have 100% hit rate. So much yes! If your offence (Hit rate) is high enough now to deal with their defense, you will always hit. Dodge and parry is one once per turn so sniping someone with a weak arrow first will move your hit rate on any further hit from 75% to 100% on the next one. Bow is a special case and its offense is reduced by range. You can easily check if you can hit people with bow now by simply holding X and moving around. It will show everything in range, the base hit rate and if the enemies are within the Line of Sight or not. Extremely useful and needed feature.
Damage is now consistent. Assuming no armor, if it says 6 damage, it will always deal 6 damage. Skills like "Hammer blow" was nerfed from *3 damage to +10 damage.
Most poison now lasts the entire fight and there are "Buff potions" around as well now.
And if you have nothing to do with your belt slot, they introduced the "Trinket" items that will boost your status while you are holding. Higher crit rate, damage or regeneration. All up to you!
You can place your characters starting location at the start of the battle now!
You can place traps in defensive stages when the enemies decide to attack your base (For every 3-4 conquers, they will attack once)
This should cover most of the new features. Now we will move on to the last part. The pro and con of this games.
Pro
-You now control an army. While everything was nerfed. this is because most combat now have you control 6-10 characters fighting against 6-15 characters as well. Before, you would just control one person with buff + Fast as lightning and tripleshot everything to death.
-Less RNG. More strategical plays and planning required to beat the game.
-Great dialogue just like BG1.
-Set bonus! Yes! no more "Just armor rating +1 and encumbrance reduction" now. You actually get stats from wearing a certain set!
-Your action now decide how good your characters will be and if they will be alive at the end or not. If you want, for the laugh of it, you can even order to execute your friends at the end before reloading a save after seeing their reactions.
Con
-Horribly unbalance. In BG1, all you do is abuse the same damaging weapon move like Triple shot or Hammer blow with buffs and fast as lightning to kill EVERYTHING. In BG2, with the damaging spell buffs and set items, mages are the most op beings ever in an army vs army fight. All you have to do is spam the same AoE spell to destroy everything in 3 - 4 turns assuming it's a "Kill everything" stage.
-Defensive battle doesn't give AP. The fight is already having you fight with gimped characters.
-Certain stage is horribly tedious, even more tedious than the last one. Infinite spawn happens every 2-3 stages and you have to do the "Rush in, Rush out" kind of gameplay. It's not fun because after you move all your 8 characters to the end of the stage, you also have to wait for the other 10 characters on the enemies side to move. BlackGuards 2 is the sequel to BlackGuards. When I first learned of another BlackGuards game I was a little worried because the first had just come out not even one year ago. Unfortunately I was correct to feel that way because BlackGuards 2 is filled with bugs and FPS drops.
I really like BlackGuards 2, but there always seems to be something that gets in the way of my enjoyment of the game. The first BlackGuards game was solid. I thought it could use some work, but it was a good game and I enjoyed playing through it with my created character.
BlackGuards 2 took more than one step backwards, but also took a step in the right direction too. I don’t know why Daedalic Entertainment decided to take away the character creator in BlackGuards. This is something that really bugged me throughout my entire playthrough of the game. Cassia is a nice character, but I would have preferred to create my own protagonist like I could back in BlackGuards 1.
You could have told the exact same story and had the exact same supporting characters. The game would literally be no different. Well… the beginning of the game would be drastically different, but I’m not going to spoil it for those of you that haven’t played the game yet.
Another big problem that I have with BlackGuards 2 is the fixed camera. The camera angle is never in a good spot on any map. The only thing you can do is scroll all the way out for an overhead view of the area and even then there’s no guarantee that you’ll see the whole battlefield.
The cast of characters range from mediocre to average at best. I never felt connected with anyone in this game. The only remotely interesting character in the entire game is Cassia. I love her insanity and will to rule despite having no real reason to want to rule the world. You can actually have full conversations with yourself and it’s up to you how they play out. Talking to myself was by far the most interesting dialogue in the game because you get to see just how far Cassia has fallen.
I mentioned that this game has it’s fair share of bugs. I can usually overlook some bugs and glitches, but I went through this entire game at 15-28 FPS. That is unacceptable; I can play Dragon Age Inquisition on Ultra at about 45-60 FPS. There is no reason why I shouldn’t be able to play this game at a solid 60 FPS. I even went as far as lowering the game to all the lowest settings and it didn’t make a difference and it really affected my playthrough.
I couldn’t go through a single map without some serious lag. You’re probably thinking that I really hate this game so far, but that couldn’t be further from the truth. I like BlackGuards 2 and I really wanted to come here and give a good review, but I can’t ignore the problems that it has right now. Hopefully there’s going to be a day one patch to straighten out some of these issues.
BlackGuards 2 isn’t all bad though. The one thing that BlackGuards always had going for it was gameplay and that’s no different here. BlackGuards 2 has really good gameplay. At the beginning of every battle you’ll have a chance to set your team up around the map. From there you’re placed on a grid and every character has a chance to perform an action. Some battles are pretty tricky while others might feel a little cheap because of the huge disadvantage that you’ll have.
Every fight is winnable with the right strategy, but there is a certain cheapness to it.  Another neat feature in BlackGuards 2 is the world map. The goal of the game is build a large enough army to take on the leader and rule the world.
There’s a problem with that though. I never actually felt like I was the leader of a massive army. Dragon Age Inquisition had this problem too, but it’s a much better game than BlackGuards 2. BlackGuards 2 is a solid sequel to a solid game, but it does have it’s fair share of problems right now. The truth is neither game would score very highly with me because of all the issues that they have and the developers have done nothing to really innovate the series.
If you’re considering BlackGuards 2 I would recommend you wait for it to go on sale because it’s not worth the asking price in it’s current state.
The Verdict: 6/10

First things first: buy this game? Oh hell, you should!
But before I jump to feed you with my opinion I would like to adress some of the most common concerns I stumbled upon while reading other reviews.
1. Le Bugs:
Even though I could play my somewhat above 10 hours without running into any of them - yes, they exist. But the developers are obviously working their asses off to fix them (with the first fix being released only one day after launch). Also you shouldn't forget that it's not the developer who choses a release date, it's the publisher. Never before have I experienced such intense and quick user support on a launch. If you can't live with a few bugs on release, don't buy a game on release. Also, don't just walk away from this title, maybe just wait a little until the issues are fixed.
2. The game being dumbed down:
First of all it's hilarious how people complain about how the game appears so easy yet they also complain about it being unbalanced. Here's what changed to Blackguards 1 and how:
- You have way less attributes, spells in tiers instead of slightly raising your skill until you hit a breakpoint, ect. As for the attributes, the system is still absolutely the same, it's just a different repesentation for you. So if you put a skill in "more Astral Energy", in the Background your intelligence gets higher. It's just easier to get what outcome your chosen skills have. For the Spells and their tiers...
- spells now have a 100% chance of hitting, makes the fights more predictable and fair. Not easier though, as this is countered with enemies resistances. You won't just run through missions fireballing everything and that's it
- new endurance-resource, that's to physical attacks what astral energy is to magical attacks.
3. Difficulty and tactics:
yes, this game is difficult as♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you want a game without losing, without restarting because you made one too many mistakes, go play Hello Kitty Online, because this game is going to make you flip tables. But in a good way. At no point have I felt the game to be unfair. Insanely difficult, yes, but never unfair. There are a lot of mean surprises like a sudden new wave of enemies rushing in, and yes it can be frustrating to have to restart a battle because you became too sloppy with victory just before you, but as you replay a fight you improve your tactics and get rewarded herefore. If you play it safe instead of rushing through battles mindlessly, you get rewarded for it. That's exactly how it's supposed to be.
There are tons of strategial possibilities, with some of them being:
- place your characters in a starting zone (least effect is that characters with high initiative won't get stuck in the behind - hehe)
- strategic world map where your choice of what stronghold you're going to attack next really has an impact (least of the impacts is which of your mercs improve in what way)
- various objectives and strategies for a lot (but not all) the battles
- next to unlimited possibilities to skill you characters, providing your very own winning strategy (the main character having astral points by default is just great, I completely messed that one up in Blackguards 1)
4 Graphics:
Yeah, so this is not Far Cry 4 or whatever game has the graphical high ground today, duh. If you care about the graphics, you will probably be disappointed. But if you care for atmosphere, impression and such, the graphics are just gold. It generally looks a lot like Blackguards 1, but far more polished, far more small details and impressive scenery. I just love it
5. My opinion:
Seing how big this review has become already, I'll try to make it short at this point:
Story is awesome, looks are awesome, gameplay is awesome, difficulty is hell but I love it. Can't say anything about bugs as I haven't encountered any, but if that's the reason you don't want to buy the game - do yourself a favour and come back in a few days, get it wenn the bugs are gone, is so worth it!

Mechanically, this is a pretty good game. Unfortunately everything besides the mechanics is terribly broken:
1) "Full controller support" is an outright lie.
2) Dumping text on the player is not an effective way of delivering narrative
3) Have you never heard of a tutorial? You know, that thing where it says "press X to attack"? The game just throws you in with no indication of how to do anything. That's fine in some 2D platformer where you only use one stick and two buttons but this game is complicated. If someone comes to this game having just spent 100+ hours playing Diablo 3 and can't figure out how to talk to an NPC, you're doing it wrong.
4) Coming back to the bogus controller support, it's obviously been jury-rigged after the fact with no real attempt to make sense. The game forces you to bind every action to a distinct button, so there aren't enough buttons. If they mapped similar actions, like "pick up" and "interact" to the same button, this wouldn't be an issue. You can't just map half the game actions to buttons and say the game has full controller support. If the first thing you have to do in the game is talk to someone, maybe "Down arrow" is not an intuitive binding for "interact".
5) A minor point: the developers missed a golden opportunity for couch co-op here.
I never would have bought this game if I knew how bad the controller support was.

FTL is one of those games that I don't know whether to love or hate. On the one hand, FTL is a magnificent game that provides tons of enjoyment and thus opportunity for many hours of enjoyment. On the other hand, once you pierce the surface you are not entirely sure what is left to keep you coming back: despite a plethora of options in terms of upgrades, weapons, drones, and crewmembers, after a while the selection seems less substantial than initial appearances. This appearance can change once you unlock more ships and ship layouts, but the task of unlocking these are overly complicated. In order to unlock ships and/or their layouts you need to complete tasks or beat "the game". The game is essentially the same concept: you must move through a series of sectors without being destroyed (either through crew death or ship explosion, although the latter certainly entails the former) until you reach the final sector and destroy the rebel "mothership": if there is more than that I could not tell you, for this task alone I have not been able to complete.
Why is the task so difficult? This can be seen partially out of skill: if you are not fighting properly or not upgrading your ship sufficientily you will be hard pressed to make it past the first 3 sectors. Yet even moreso it seems to be largely based on luck. You can find yourself really well off only to be completely annihilated on the next node for little more than what pops up and one selection you make. The harder the difficulty (even "easy" is not all that easy, at least not for many hours of practice and patience) the more likely your choices will provide negative results. For instance: you can come across a civilian crew in need help of this or that task. Sometimes you will have a unique solution to said task depending on your crew members (certain races have certain advantages/disadvantages), and in this case the outcome is almost always positive. Yet where such options are not present you can find yourself in a tough situation: you can help them and potentially gain a reward, or help them and lose a crew member or some other such unfortunate event. But if you never help civilians and never try your luck, you wind up with no resources to upgrade your ship and will be destroyed after a few sectors.
This creates a sort of "damned if you do, damned if you don't" feeling to the game. I have played this game practically non-stop since I have gotten it, I have gotten slightly better and learned more how to handle my ship and crew. Yet regardless of how well I have been improving, the "luck" aspect of the game seems to rule all: whether it be the consequences of your actions or even just a simple layout of a sector and the nodes within it you can quickly find yourself doomed regardless of how prepped your ship is. I have found myself armed to the teeth with nice weapons and shields only to be destroyed the next node do to some unforeseen environmental hazard or some unexpectedly powerful pirate ship.
So why do I still insist on recommending this game if I seem to have so many contentions with it? The answer is simple: because despite its challenges and infuriating random encounters that make or break your next move (and every move after), the game still manages to sucker you back in to keep playing it. You want to have that breakthrough, you want to have that moment of &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥yeah! I just wiped out an entire rebel fleet single-handedly!" Having said that, if you are not into diligently playing a game in order to master it, then this game certainly is not for you. But for those who admire a challenge and don't mind getting some life-force sucked out of them for many hours, there is perhaps no better game out there.
This game has the same infuriating charm as old platformers like Castlevania did (and still do): you want to learn the moves and master the castle. Yet unlike some of those old platformers, this game seems to create some new phenomenon in that there is no "move". Levels aren't one based on muscle-memory of when to press this or that button, but on an overall understanding of the situation and tried and true methods of dealing with said situation.
Is the game perfect? No. Is the game as customizable as it may seem? For me it wasn't, but that doesn't take away from its charm. Is the game worth playing? If you can deal with everything I have mentioned, then it is more than worth playing. Is there a reason why this review is so damn long? Probably, but I haven't talked with the proper professionals to figure that one out.

For those of you who have never played Relic Entertainment's Company of Heroes franchise, it's essentially a World War II real-time tactics series characterised by dynamic and destructable environments, a sophisticated cover system, quasi-realistic combat mechanics (such as range-dependent accuracy/fire-rate/penetration values, infantry suppression, facing-dependent vehicle armour values, etc), a variety of specialised infantry and vehicle types, and optional "commander trees" that grant the player a variety of specialised bonuses and off-map support.
As a huge fan of Relic and a dedicated modder of the original Company of Heroes, I awaited Company of Heroes 2 with a huge degree of anticipation. After playing the sequel (and allowing time for several post-release patches) my thoughts are as follows:
PROS
- New faction: the Red Army.
- Numerous engine optimisations (Essence 3.0).
- Numerous gameplay enhancements (truesight, vaulting, vehicle reversing, etc). Coldtech may or may not count, depending on personal preference.
- Fantastic graphics (although not as groundbreaking as the original CoH's).
- Even better audio. The weapon effects are amongst the best I've ever heard (having been recorded from real-life sources), and the blending of different sound levels on the battlefield is perfect.
- New additions, such as Theatre of War mode and a wealth of additional customisation options.
CONS
- Disappointingly little innovation despite seven years having passed. Gameplay, while slightly tweaked and not objectively worse, is simply too unambitious and safe.
- The Soviets are portrayed too stereotypically throughout the singleplayer campaign, with Relic attempting to fill a 'per mission atrocity quota'. That said, the consequent reaction from the game's Eastern European fanbase has been overdramatic at best.
- DLC. Jesus Christ, the DLC. I paid AU $90 for this game, and yet on release day alone, RELEASE DAY, there was already $60 worth of DLC (additional commanders and skins) avaiable on Steam and omitted from the base game. It's immediately apparent that the game has been designed around DLC (likely THQ's desperate doing), even extending to Relic's disablement of modding infrastructure in order to boost sales of their own content.
- The Soviet faction is limited to a few  viable competitive builds.
All in all, Company of Heroes 2 is still a very good game in its own right regardless of its flaws, and I'd definitely recommend it to others. It's a quality game. But if you're tired of the original CoH and are looking for an all-new experience, CoH2 will leave you unsatisfied.

This game is really fun, simple to learn but hard to master. It's like ping pong and marvelVcapcom had a baby. Characters have different skills, playstyles, and some cool and goofy personalities. Some hit the ball different angles, some characters jump higher, some lower, some double jump, some climb walls, some ride their skateboard across the roof. It's fun trying out all the characters and seeing which one fits your playstyle. The online match making works great 99% of the time. There are times where  it will take a few minutes to match you up with another player but that only happens to me if it's really late in my time zone. Any other time I can find a match within seconds. The soundtrack is awesome all around. I have my favorite stages but overall all of them have great music. Not to mention some of the stages are different in size so it affects your playstyle and forces you to adapt. There is a practice mode where you can improve on your timing and you can also play againt the computer and adjust the difficulty level. There is also an arcade challenge mode. This is a mode where you fight through all the other characters with a final boss battle. It's not very challenging but it's nice to do once. There are different modes (free for all, strikers, and teams) Strikers is trying to hit a target on the opponents side. Everyone online plays free for all but it's good to have the other game modes as options to play with your friends. What I love the most about this game is how intense games can get when the ball is going super fast. Very satisfying moments when you win those fast paced battles.

There is not much I dislike about this game. I would like to see a few more characters added. I would also want to be able to set the online games to different modes. Everyone online plays free for all which is the funnest game mode in my opinion, but it would be nice to do some 2 vs 2 online with random people. Once in a while there's lag but its rare and most likely due to one of the players internet connection being bad. Game has crashed a few times but I wouldn't call it a problem. It's happened just a few times in the many hours I've played.
Recommendation: Buy at full price. If you like ping pong, if you like fighting games, if you like intense fast paced gameplay then you'll have fun with this one.
Pros
- Different Characters with varying playstyles and skills
- Easy to learn hard to master
- Intense and fun gameplay
- Different game modes
- Up to 4 players free for all makes for some chaotic games
- GREAT Soundtrack that meshes very well with the game.

Cons
- Wish there were more characters
- Online matchmaking could use more customization

An instersting concept for an online FPS. You can think of it like "Minecraft meets (insert perfered online FPS here)".
You build traps, health/ammo stations, etc. as you play, the environment is entierlly distructable and how you approach the objective is largely up to you and your team. Matches can be crazy and chaotic or slow as both sides stick to their base, building defenses on top of defenses.
There is a selection of hereos, all with their own weapons, special abilites and unique blocks, but the game uses the same system as most MOBAs, in that you have to buy heroes and some are offered free to try on a rotation. It's a system I'm not a fan of, even in MOBAs. If you watch a video and play a match you get enough gold to buy one hero, but I find this type of system just leads players to grind and not enjoy the game as much.
As I said, it's an interesting concept that seem well put together, and leaving aside the whole MOBA-like aspects of how heroes work, the gameplay is solid and it handles like a decent shooter with a build mechanic attached. Whether or not this'll hold a lot of players interest for any length of time is the question.

Now keep in mind I'm playing on the hardest difficulty expert with no beast companion and only half way through with the map having only done one or two Izila missions. The combat now conists of me getting hit three or four times without dying (If I'm not paying attention) followed by me one shotting everything with the double bow but the big ogre guys, who are easy if you keep your distance anyways. Wtf? Why would the developers not see this major issue in the combat numbers system and make it so you had a somewhat consistent playing experience from start to finish? Clearly the upgraded weapons and upgrading to six health bars are WAYYYYY over powered as well as the frequency of rare resources! Now all the incentive to interact with the environment is gone, all the suspense and tension of capturing an outpost is gone, and thus the entire reason I played through the first half is gone as well.
Still though, the first 30 hours were definitely worth the purchase, it's a shame though that I can't say the same about the second half. If I could I'd give this game somewhere inbetween a thumb up and a thumb down...

After finishing this one I am definitely torn, as it was a real love hate relationship I had while playing this game. It felt a lot like the exact opposite of wolf among us where people respected and feared your character. If you dont get too into the story and just click pick the responses based on what you think is best you will probably find it much less annoying than I did, but I cant detatch myself from my characters in games like this.
The main problem I have is with the running theme of being in a position of weakness. You are constantly kissing someones a55  "for the good of your house", despite the fact that they killed your brother, mother, sister and father .
You experience the GOT world playing as a Squire, Handmaiden, little Kid around 13, Cripple and thank god at least one soldier. So basically 80% of your characters are doormats. You are always trying to be diplomatic and turn the other cheek, because it looks and feels as though you dont have a viable alternative. I play games to have fun and log off with a smile. Sadly, I mostly just logged off this one annoyed. Coupled with so many logic defying elements it became to hard to give this a thumbs up, but i did in the end all the same. I would say get it if you love GOT, maybe not so much if you dont.

I went into this game with no prior knowledge of the in-game mechanics or anything in this game aside from some positive reactions from friends on how it's "A sweet zombie apocalypse parkour game". I bought it with a friend during the sale, and at the time of writing I have 33 hours in the game, all with said friend. Loving it. Almost every single bit of it. The gameplay is amazing, with a limited backpack for weapons/ammo/battle tools (unlimited for resources and base items like medkits and lockpicks) and weapons with a durability that makes it so you won't be carrying your sweet overlevelled sword all game. There many amazing upgrades that make your weapons even cooler for the time you'll carry them. And a parkour system that beats assassin's creed by a longshot in terms of smoothness and player experience.
This isn't an entirely positive review though, as the base game does have a minor issue being the story. All characters in the main storyline of the Dying Light act like 10 year old kids. At no point did I feel any connection with any of the characters in the story. The player character is an idiot who makes many many many many many mistakes that no sane person would make in a lifetime and the final bossfight is a quicktime event in a forced solo-mission, while all other missions are co-op available. I'll admit that aside from the qte bossfight the story improves at the end, but altogether the main story is bad.
HOWEVER! The Dying Light now also comes with the Following DLC. A story after the main story which drastically improves on the problems the former story faced, and adds so much more fun to the game with upgradable buggies, sweet new weapons and a story that will stay interesting, rather than annoy you.
Altogether this game is amazing, best zombie apocalypse game I've played so far. And with the DLC now included when buying the game fixing the main problem the game faced, I can recommend this to anyone.

This game is really great and you should buy it.
First, the cons:
- There's a bit of a curve in figuring out exactly what the people think is reasonable (for example, protip: housing prices should be 1/3 of the person's salary, rounded down, and entertainment should be exactly their salary).
- The missions are very scripted and the gameplay very freeform, resulting in occasional basically-guaranteed losses or complete non-challenges after you complete an objective and the next impossible-to-predict-the-first-time-trying scripted event occurs.
- Being a tyrant is really underpowered vs. being totally nice and helpful.
Besides that, this game is packed with wit, charm, and fun. Tropico 3 was just a remake of Tropico 1, but this game really takes strides in perfecting the forumula. Any good sim-builder needs lots of knobs and buttons to fiddle with, and this game has a bunch of them - and best of all, they're generally not packed painfully into drab numerical menus. There are no up and down buttons for employment; you actually click a socket for a worker's face to close it off and limit how many people the building will employ. This and *actually helpful* tooltips (some devs get it wrong, somehow) make the game immediately accessible. You'll have your work cut out for you balancing the desires of the various factions, and who you decide to please and who you decide to push to the brink of rebellion will often depend entirely on the resources of the island and your mission objectives. A huge problem with most games of this genre is the tendency for a single strategy to win every time; while this is still present in Tropico 4 to some degree, the missions are crafted carefully enough, with enough special conditions to disrupt your winning strategies, that it's less of a problem here than in any other game I've ever played in this genre.
The writing in the game is top-notch and if you don't find yourself smirking from time to time at the bald-faced satire, then you need to get your sense of humor checked out. This game finds creative ways to poke fun at cold-war banana republics, stereotypes, popular video games, and more. At no point do you feel guilty for being a big, stupid tyrant, because all the international powers are bigger, stupider, and more tyrannical. This gives a fun sense of empathy to El Presidente despite his self-serving nature, and motivates you to shelter the helpless people of Tropico from the uncaring ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s on both sides of the iron curtain... and maybe launder some tax money as payment while you're doing them the service.
I can't recommend this game highly enough. I've bought all the DLC and earned every achievement because I can't get enough of El Presidente. If you're actually considering this game enough to be here reading reviews about it, do yourself a favor and go for it.

Tropico 3 with more features and some improvements.
You now have to elect Ministers in order to issue certain edicts. There's alos a randomized mission system to give you new objectives. A few new buildings, but nothign major. There's now two more factions, China and the Middle East, to deal with, but it's not that big of a game change. There are natural disasters and your island can now catch fire, so you now need firemen. Some tweaking under the hood as occurred, making traffic easier to contend with, although it can still be a PITA to deal with.
One of the biggest changes is the map editor. Your islands are stil randomly generated, like in Tropico 3, but you can now go in and edit resources, atrting buildings, change the terrain types, alter heightmaps, etc. It's a lot more robust and makes playing on your own custom island much easier and much more fun.
If you're a fan, it has enough improvements to be worth it. If you're new, this is the better version.

I finished Blackguards 2 after a bit more than 25 hours and I tried not to enter the final stage, before I had really done everything. I find the game very  entertaining, it has not-too-easy tactical combats, tells an interesting story of a once lovely lady, that is made into an insane and kind-of-evil conquerer. The Player can also decide, if he is more like a Robin Hood-Rogue or a true brutal and ruthless bandit, who seeks only his own fortune.
A big variety on weapons and spells, all based on the dark eye license (Das Schwarze Auge in german) and a lot of known places gives fans of DSA/The Dark Eye a great familiar feeling and everyone else a dense world, with its own logic, history and myths, that has grown for over 30 years.
Compared to the first Blackguards, the Combats are bigger, offer more variety and a few very important changes have been made, that adjust the Dark-Eye-Ruleset to fit better into a PC Game. For example there are now exakt percentage-forcasts on your chances to hit, additional to Lifepoints and mana, there is now Stamina.
You do not only control a group of heroes but also get a mercenary army under your command with differnt classes of fighters or special units. With those troops you try to conquer the part of the World where the game takes place and you must repell sudden counterattacks from your AI-Opponent. This feels a bit like the good old Jagged Alliance with its sectors.
Overall, Blackguards 2 is one of the game to really dive in for several hours/days.
Looking forward to part 3 ;)

Lets start by saying that this is a solid game, because it is. Would i recommend it? No.
Lets go over the whats and whys.
The inifial concept of the story struck me as something at least somewhat new and unique. Starting as a semi insane person is novelty in a way, if we forget Malkavians and the like. But it quickly slided down in terms of quality. The story is not entirely compelling and no matter what you do. You, ONCE AGAIN will never not in a million yeas get a good ending. Doesnt matter how good you are, doesnt matter how amazing was your decisionmaking or fighting. It just doesnt matter. The ending is set in stone,  you will die after 1 day of ruling, No matter what. Im ♥♥♥♥ing sick of every recent game in my memory doing that. It started with atrocious ending of ME3 and then it went on and on and on, - PC and NIiam dead in original Blackguards, tons of other games its like the new trademark: make endings spit you in the face. ♥♥♥♥ your efforts we want it to be remembered. And yes its understtandable from the story perspective and all but sersiously im sick of it.
Character creation and advancement.
Stats were removed. And the system refined a bit, now you see what you pay for immediately. Its more user friendly, but i found that to me game lost a bit of charm with that decision, but dont get me wrong, i think its for the better. A lot of rebalancing, like the Witches Bile being nerfed aswell as some others, like the poison removal. No more wound persisting. Overall its way more user friendly.
Story Discontinuity.
This is a small problem which will probably be adressed in the near future -> there are some minor bugs with how story progresses, namely in the beginning you are teleported from dwarf mansion into a conversation with a mage already without a mask. That is done on a few occasions buts its very minor.
Characters.
Well if you liked Naurim, his best buddy mage and Takashi or whats his face then i got great news for you! Unfortunately you will not have a designated ranged weapon specialist unless you will specialise into it. Oh! But let me tell you, you will want to  have a few spells up your sleeve! Thats right, you can progress anything any time! No more restrictions! On the other hand you WILL be forced to take Heal on your main guy for some fights. Otherwise you cant win them or will have to lower difficulty. Literally no other way. (unless you are willing to burn through consumables like crazy)
Fights.
Fights were great in the original game, they are even better here. Extremely challenging just by sheer ammount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t some of them entail. How would you like to have 2 of your characters berzerking hitting everything that moves including friendlies, one envelopped in sand and immobile and last one trying to fidget with levers watching in terror as his teammates are torn to bits. Over and over and over and over. Or the neverending 2-4 mobs spawning every turn. Some fights are stupidly hard, some are ridiculously easy with double mage setup. Regardless the combat is way better then it was in the 1st game.
Better camera controlls aswell, - all issues of the old game were adressed. Somehow though im not happy with this one. By all rational thought process this IS a better game in every aspect. Grey Goo is basically an older style macro-focused RTS. If you're used to playing APM-fests like starcraft 2, this will feel slow to you.
Grey Goo is pretty nice though. I have played and enjoyed many different types of RTS games, but I always wanted to see a newer game in the vein of Tiberian Sun, and this game reminds me a lot of Tiberian Sun. The graphics are really nice, in-game the 3 different faction units all are tied together thematically. Humans having a smooth plastic-like design with lasers and energy weapons, the Beta more industrial and metallic with cannons and machine guns. The goo is pretty much what you would expect, all their units resemble different shapes of shimmering metallic liquid.
The human and beta races play fairly similarly, the goo however plays entirely different as there are no goo buildings, everything the goo can make is a movable unit.
There are essentially no mico-abilities on units, so the micro in this game is limited to positioning and targeting.
I would say this game is very close to being a perfect successor to the westwood RTS games, if anything the game feels like a cross between tiberian sun and starcraft. Base building isn't as good as it was in tiberian sun, but it's far more interesting than in starcraft 2.
Grey Goo also happens to be on a short list of RTS games that have had a really cool single player story. The animated cutscenes in this game are top notch.
As much as I like Grey Goo, it really doesn't add anything new to the RTS genre other than a cool concept and story. In terms of gameplay it's less demanding than starcraft 2, but not as full of content as tiberian sun. As well made as it is, it will likely not blow you away, but it is certainly a fun game.

Grim Dawn is the game that i wanted, but didn't get from Diablo 3.
If you are a fan of Action RPGs, this is probably for you. It's the best attempt I've played in about a decade - since what i would call the glory days of the genre, when Diablo 2 and Titan Quest were among my top played games. Which is just what this game reminds me of - everything great about the Diablo and Titan Quest franchises mushed up into one new product with a new world and some small quality of life enhancements. This game was clearly designed for fans of those games - you don't have to take my word for it, you can still go to the developers forums and look - they actively asked for input from backers, and listened! And boy did it work!
I'm not trying to say that Torchlight, Path of Exile, or Diablo 3 are bad. I'm just saying Grim Dawn personally tickles a particular itch that those games did not. If you are looking for that late 90s / early 2000's style point-and-click action RPG loot fest, this is it. Heck, If you've ever liked any action RPG, this is worth checking out.
Pros:
+Plenty of Diversity in Character Builds - 6 Skill trees to put experience points into while leveling, of which two can be unlocked by one character, plus a web of "devotion" unlocks for more passive buffs and extra abilities as rewards for exploration.
+Tons of loot. Game includes a filter to hide / show only certain grades or above of loot, for when your character is already well equipped and you dont want to pick up and lug junk back to sell off.
+All items are augmentable, and there are tons of Augment Components to slot into weapons and armor, again adding to diversity.
+Gorgeous hand-crafted world. The game engine might not be the best, but it renders the world gloriously.
+Satisfying Combat. Just smacking baddies with a sword has the right visuals and sounds to make it feel great - spells and abilities make it even better, just killing things for hours on end is fun and feels great.
+LAN mode. You never know when you might want to take a few friends and some laptops to the woods to play a game, no internet connection is required, you can host local lobbies without doing any work arounds or sneaky things, even with the steam version of the game.
+Controller Support. I mean, i think you are insane if you want to use a controller to play this game, but, it's there!
+Moddable. There are already several great mods out there, expanding gameplay options, adding new skill trees, items, and more. One mod adds a Necromancer class, for example. Another adds all the classes from Titan Quest.
+Ongoing development. While the game has made it to its final release, there are still hotfix patches coming out, and an expected expansion pack - this game should have legs, and support will likely be around for a while.
Cons:
- Hand-Crafted World. There is some randomization in where obstructions and secret areas appear, but as of now there is virtualy no randomly generated content. (Rumor is a patch, DLC, or Expansion may add this.) For some people this may limit gameplay, as exploration wont have the same appeal since most of the world is exactly the same.
- Visibility Issues - Most games of the ARPG variety use an isometric, fixed camera angle. Grim Dawn allows more freedom, and sometimes this means unusual angles and obstructions may cause enemies to be hard to see, or the rotation of the camera to throw off your environmental awareness.
- No Character Cosmetic Options Other Than Gear - When you make a character, you pick male or female. Thats it. No customization of the appearance at all. While some items exist to paint an illusion on top of an item to make it look different, the system seems limited - certainly nowhere near as robust as Diablo 3's Transmogrify system.

Beat Hazard turns your favorite songs against you in an intense onslaught of music-fueled, seisure-inducing carnage. Using a fantastic engine that analizes your music, you'll find that certain sounds spawn different waves of enemies. This system is 100% consistent, so you can learn the ins and outs of a piece and truly master its unique gameplay. The unlocakble perks are fun, and can be maxed out to rediculous extents, allowing you to spew torrents of rockets and lasers at your alien opponents.
A hanger full of unlockable ships increases the replay value and changes up gameplay style, and the option to create and share custom ships via the Workshop is super fun (I found a ship that's literally a can of Dr. Pepper).
The replay value is pretty much infinite, so long as you have music to listen to. You can also sync Beat Hazard with online radio stations, and play along with their programming.
It also includes a 2-man multiplayer mode, although this can be a bit tricky to use. Both players will have to own identical copies of the same song before it can be played. You and your buddies just pick up the newest album by your favorite artist? You're ready to go. Want to play some obscure single you ripped from YouTube? You'll have a few issues.
All in all, Beat Hazard is well worth the $10, and is an excellent experience.

This is no doubt one of the best RPG games in recent years.  That says a lot when there are tough competition like The Witcher 3 and Fall Out 4.  The game has a lot of humour, just the right amount of dialog, and the gameplay is simply fantastic.  The environmental effects is perhaps the best feature.  It's not just a gimmick, but something you can use to your full advantage.  The skills for different classes are also distinct, and yet is balanced well enough that you can beat the game with a variety of group compositions.  I think there are enough people who talk about what's good, so I'm going to list the two things that really disappointed me.
1. Crafting system isn't that great.  I like the system itself, but most things you craft aren't that useful, and the only reason you would want to invest in crafting is to buff the weapons you find.  I'm not sure how much it's improved in the Enchanced Edition, but in Classic Divinity, it's pretty meh.
2. Many people compare this game to Ultima VII and Boulder's Gate, but that really set me up for disappointment.  Ultima VII is one of my all time favorites, but Divinity didn't have many of the features I loved about Ultima.  There's no day/night transition, NPCs don't have a daily schedule, the number of things you can move around are quite limited, there are only two towns in this game while Utlima had several, most NPCs don't have much of a back story, etc.  When I play Ultima, I can even make and sell bread to the bakers in town for some extra money.  If I want, I can even go and sit at a restaurant and watch the people come and go.  Divinity have none of this.
If you like gambling, poker, and getting Team Fortress 2 items, then.....this is it.
