This is my first review, and this game is so awesome I had to create one for it. And don't be fooled by my hours, I'm quite sure there are many more to come.
TL:DR? Then just buy it.
If you want to know though, Leath league is...
Super Smash... On PC... with Pixel Art... With a ball... Wait what?! Yea, you can't attack each other. And there's a ball, and you only have 2 attacks, one to hit the ball and one to throw it up.
So... why is this even good?
The Ball speeds up when you hit it, and even more if you throw it up then hit it. And the most important thing is... if you get hit by the ball and your opponent was the one to hit it last, you're out. No hp bar, just out.
Soon you realize you get into some intense Sudden death action, when the ball is flying around on the screen at 50 speed and you're a one shot out. But if you hit the ball and it goes fast enough that the enemy dosen't have enough time to stop it,  they're out. You start to go crazy waiting for the inevitable out of yourself or the other player, nobody ever has a sure chance of winning. You even start to scream and squel every time you die or kill the enemy.
All in all, epic game. Buy it if you like crazy intense action. If not, buy it anyway.

This is stuck between the two best star wars games ever made, the other being of course knights of the old republic. The gameplay is fluid and fun, the choice between third and first person makes the game easily adaptable to any shooter fan. Although it has aged since 2005 it surely is still a great game. Unfortuneatly as GameSpy shut down, the multiplayer has become unavailable but you can still play against bots in instant action, galactic conquest or the single player campaign. This brings me to my next point, the galactic conquest mode, it is very enjoyable as it brings a strategic style to the game and prevents you from getting bored of playing the same maps over and over again. The game is highly moddable, allowing for new maps, characters and game modes which allows the game to still have the same level of fun as when it was first released.
The single player campaign follows various soldiers of the 501st legion, also known as "vader's fist", as you fight to conquer the galaxy and closely follows the 3rd prequel to the star wars films. the story is relatively well written but what makes the campaign different to the other game modes is that you will be given specific objectives throughout the map, for example you will be told to attack or defend a certain station, or destroy a vehicle etc.
This game is a definite must play and I highly reccomend that you pay the US $10 for this game as it holds many good times and can be friendly to kids and adults of all ages. It is definitely a treasure among the star wars expanded universe media and one of the best games ever made in my opinion.
Also if you are a fan of the battlefield series this game would be very good for you as many game modes and such are remniscient of the series

Since the announcment of Battlefront 3, I decided to rebuy Battlefront 2 on Steam because I previously owned it on the Playstation 2. Since then I've been having a blast with this game.
The PC version if it is for sure the best version out there (like most games PC master race) I find the visuals to be extremely good for the time aswell. It's hard to review a game that's almost ten years old now, but I still feel like no matter what, every game has it's flaws.
I personally prefer playing games in first person rather than third person, luckily, this game has the option to switch between them during combat just by pressing the V key or by changing the setting in the options. The animation quality in third person is absolutly amazing and feels real, although the animation quality when playing in first person really lacks. It just seems boring to play in first person with this game. The game's AI system is also whack. I'm pointing this out because the multiplayer servers are down so you're basically limited just to single player.
That's basically it for the complaints. The stuff I really love about this game though involves the map layout, concept, and the gameplay. It lacks a good story but wins at the gameplay most of all. You get an amazing rush through your body while sprinting into a battle as a Clone trooper while lazers shoot at all angles while hearing screams, droid chatter, and explosions. Or not to mention flying through space while ships spin out around you, just for you to single handedly board a ship and destroy it. Not to mention playing as a Jedi or Sith, tearing through droids, rebels, and clones. Each time you play a map it always feels different, you can flank from different routes or play through it as a different type of class.
Overall, this game is worth the buy, and certainly is still not outdated.

I admit that this game is nostalgic for me. Whenever I was about 10 or 11, my dad would play this game and I would watch him, sometimes even I would play it. This became my favorite game ever. I decided to get it for myself so I could play the whole game on my own, and I went into it thinking it had no huge flaws, but was I right?
Yes and no.
I was right about its amazing story, level design, physics, gameplay, character design, and puzzles, and while it does those things well, there are some things that aren't as well done, and that's where I'm going to begin.
Flaws:
I thought this game had amazing graphics, because I had my nostalgia goggles on, but that changed the second I entered the train at the beginning of the game, and saw what the human models look like. (They don't look that good) I mean, the game is from 2004, so you shouldn't expect next-gen graphics, but seeing it made me think of how dated Half-Life 2 really looks, and that is one of the problems, just how dated the game is. This personally didn't bother me, but I can see why others would be turned away. Personally, this benefitted me because I'm running Half-Life 2 on a potato, but I'll talk more about that later.
Another issue with the game is that there are some levels which require you working with a group of AI allies, and those levels feel extremely cramped, and it wouldn't be like that if they'd just back up a little. I can not tell you how many times I'd be in a small space trying to find health, or trying to run away from an enemy to get some health, or even just trying to find a way to go, and the d**m AI get in the way. Luckily there are few of those levels.
What some may consider a flaw are the vehicle sections of the game. There are two of these in the game, a car section, and a boat section. They don't bother me much, but I can see why some people dislike these parts.
Positives:
This game has really good physics, and they really let you interact with the world.
The weapons are pretty standard, except for the Gravity Gun, which allows you to pick up heavy objects and throw them with a lot of force.
The puzzles are pretty easy, but they don't ever feel stupid.
This game can run on a lot of different computers, unless your computer is absolutely unusable, you can probably run Half-Life 2.
The levels are extremely well made, and they feel like a real environment rather than just a level with textures that resemble real environments, and translations to different places and environments feel smooth.
The enemy placement is also well done, and enemies are consistent with the types of places they spawn in. For example, zombies are usually in darker places, and there is almost always blood surrounding them, and maybe even some organs or a corpse.
Without spoilers, the main characters are pretty interesting, and I can't think of one I didn't like.
Conclusion:
Half-Life 2 is a great game. It has a demo anyway, so I suggest you download it. If you like the demo, you'll most likely like the full game. So in conclusion, the game is amazing, and I highly recommend it.

Child of Light is a beautiful RPG game developed and published by Ubisoft. From start to finish it shows a solid gameplay, a vibrant world, and a quite interesting story with more than a few twists.
Sound design is amazing, and graphically speaking, the game looks magnificent, and everytime you reach a new place, you find yourself looking at every place of the screen, mindblowing designs and drawings that are taken out of a fairy tale, beautiful. The magic of the game is greatly resembled too, and it's one of the strongest points in the game.
The amount of hours might look short for an RPG, but it's not really short clocking in at around 10-11 hours in total. The game doesn't drag on, some battles are indeed hard but can be overtaken by strategy, the story from start to finish feels good, like reading a book. It's all fun from start to finish, and at the end you feel realized and full because it doesn't leave you wanting for more like some other games
The gameplay is a turn-based fighting RPG, which is fast, there's no long animations and it's really fun thanks to constantly being in motion, you will be using characters in the fight that you can swap at any time, there are quite a few characters. They of course level up, and you'll have to see what's the best course of action regarding their skills. I want to mention that it's very fun to move as the protagonist too, specially with the amount of secrets that are everywhere! Nothing falls short in the gameplay portion of the game!
I love the fact that the story is told in rhyme which adds a lovely touch to the game. Overall, Child of Light is a game that offers a great time guaranteed for RPG players, you can't really go wrong with this game. Shame about the forced DRM of Uplay but it's Ubisoft, what do you expect?

This is the only game I ever bought in Early Access. I had played the previous game of most of the developers involved (Titan Quest) and I had really enjoyed that. Also, the reviews I had read painted a good enough picture of the state of the game. I believe it had the first three acts and most of the classes in the game at the time. I was impressed how stable and relative bug-free the game was.
Now that it is finished with all the content, is officially released and has been "in the wild" for a some months, I am confident to be able to have a go at reviewing this game.
For whom is this game? For anyone who has played Titan Quest, the old Diablo (2) and other Action-RPGs before.
It basically is a Hack&Slash game. It is full of loot in several quality tiers. The world is big (not randomly generated) and diverse. The story is nothing great but adequate. The story and the quests are numerous and will keep you busy for quite a while. I always try to do all side quests and the game kept me busy for about 30-40 hours on one play-through. And there are two more difficulty levels to try.
There are quite a few classes and as with Titan Quest at level 10 you can select a second class which you can level up as your primary class. This opens up quite a few possible class combinations to try and master. And on top of this is the new Devotion system where you get points for shrines that you cleanse and you can put these points in a completely different tree than the class tree. This adds another level of complexity to the game.
If you are a fan of Action-RPGs, I can only recommend this game. It may not be as poilished as some of the other games but this is a very small developer and with their comparatively limited ressources they have created something fun and expansive. It will keep you busy for quite a while.

One of the best video games I've played that's in the sci-fi genre: In my early years playing video games, I've not heard of Half-Life before, nor valve or even Steam. And now that I got my dosh, I seized my chance to buying the critically-acclaimed game that is Half-Life 2. So, after buying it and playing it from start to finish, what're my thoughts?
I can describe Half-Life 2 with a couple words: Ambitious and righteous.
Half-Life 2 does many things right being made in one of the Golden Ages of video games, HL immerses players into its world with its scientific but also realistic and urban look. The game introduces you to a variety of characters like Alyx and Eli Vance, Dr. Breen, Barney, Dr. Kleiner and a few more. The gameplay is as solid as a rock -- Natural and fast-paced. None of that "in-your-face and over-the-top" b*ll*cks that you'd experience in twitch-shooters like Call of Duty and #everyf2pshooters in the market.
The game also lets you explore the areas that you are in, even if they're tight and small. You'll get some cool sites of landmarks and a couple of sweet views of the Citadel. When there are no fighting with zombies and combine soldiers, the game gives you room to breath and lets you check out secrets that may be laid around. This is a video-game franchise that wants to tell you a story about The Freeman and his adventures with his companions, in addition giving you a rock-solid gameplay-design. It's a shame that VALVe stopped bothering with Half-Life, because the franchise is desperately asking for a continuation.
This may be an under-statement, but I hope that developers and modders alike who loves and are fans of Half-Life takes the helm. Until that news arrives, I'm going to bury myself in stupid memes and smelly pig-sh*t of controversy from bloody noras that hardly knows c*ck about... well, anything. Also 2017 sucks -- K thnx bye.

I've been a fan of the Eisenwald series since the original Discord Times way back in 2004. Most of my friends were obsessing over Oblivion back then, but I've gotten my hands on a demo copy of Discord Times and have imediately fallen in love with it.
And now comes the third game in the series. Blood of November is a follow up on Legend of Eisenwald with one big difference. Instead of a campaign, it has a sandbox mode - and only that, not counting a short tutorial. So how does it hold up? Well, I originaly thought that a sandbox mode would work out perfectly in Legend of Eisenwald. Capturing castles, amassing armies, chasing down bandits... you name it. However, after playing it around 10 hours, I'm not sure it lived up to my expectations.
I'm not going over all the mechanics, since most of them are identical to Legend of Eisenwald. I'll rather explain what's the difference.
You start with a castle and a small militia. You then have to make a choice on which of the two leaders to join, declering war on the other. Both of the leaders are based on the presidental candidates of this years American elections (I don't really care about this part as much because I'm not from America, if you want to know more about this, there are many reviews here that explain it in detail). The conquest (where your so called "allies" do a♥♥♥♥♥♥job of helping you) takes around 8-10 hours, which is quite good for the low price.
However...
The map is bland, without many points of interest. You can't speak to most of parties wandering around and visit some locations, which is odd. It gave me a feeling that the game is not quite finished yet and the developers had to rush it out for the time of the elections. There are also some bugs that were already present in Legend of Eisenwald, such as a white minimap and bugged textures, but they didn't really bother me that much. A simple load of the last save fixed the issue (the autosave mechanic is brilliant by the way).
Another thing to mention is the low FPS count in the world map, mostly because the game is very CPU intensive. I've tried it on two different processors, an i3 4150 (around 25-30FPS) and an i7 4790 (45-55FPS) and it really should have worked far better than that. Granted, the FPS is not that important in these type of games and it didn't really ruin the game for me but some might find it irritating.
Conclusion
To sum it all up, Blood of November is almost identical to Legend of Eisenwald and if you loved either of them, buy the other one. It has some flaws but it's very fun and equiping and growing your army has never been so fun. The political background might bother some, but if you aren't one of them, you're going to enjoy the sandbox experience. Just don't expect a great story and tens of hours of gameplay, because you're going to be disappointed.
Final Rating:
7.5/10

Let's get the obvious out of the way; this game is stunning to look at, from the idle combat animations to the vistas to the dialogue scenes. It's also well written and choices have real consequences - mostly.
The actual game part though? I'm not as impressed. Stoic are on record as saying their 'I go, You go' system was designed to mix it up a bit (instead of using an initiative-based system or proper turn order) but all it actually does is teaches you to maim, not kill most enemies before you then can start killing. Some people like it, lots don't. I wasn't a great fan. Likewise, there were a number of abilities that took a lot of meticulous planning (and a bit of luck) to set-up; whilst the payoff was sometimes worth it, many times it would be foiled by either the turn order changing (due to a kill) or movement.
It meant that I just didn't really find the combat that much fun. Add in the fact that promotions and gear felt very lightweight and it made it all a bit more of an effort than it needed to be to get through - it's taken me 2 and a half years to complete it, with 50% of my playing time being over the last couple of weeks.
So it came down to the writing and general premise to keep things interesting. I liked that stuff was drip-fed, that it didn't feel the need to explain everything (or, indeed, most things) but...those choices. Many were pretty arbitrary in their results (some which only played-out a long way down the line) but at least they made sense within the world these characters inhabited and let you role play if you so desired. The one massive caveat to this, though, was that whilst you were constantly urged to ensure people were safe and fed, there was absolutely no consequence to whether you reached the end with 1,000 clansmen left, 1 or none.
Indeed, the game doesn't actually care about those you are protecting because it never impacts (or leads to meaningful) choices, it basically never means anything to keep people alive - outside of your will to do so. Whether that plays out down the line I don't know (does it in the second game?) but nothing throughout the game gives any indication that it matters, so it means you can be a bit more cavalier in your choices involving the camp. I suspect you could probably have everybody except the main story cast die and it wouldn't make a difference.
In conclusion, I'd like to know what happens over the course of this trilogy - because the story is good - but I have no desire to play any more of the games so, for me, my Saga ends here.

As a bit of context, before playing this game I had only heard bad things about the Neptunia series. That its gameplay was bland, its plot was terrible, its characters walking fanservice otaku-bait, etc. I only bought the game because it went on sale and I wanted to see for myself whether these claims were unfounded.
After finishing the game, I had to admit that they were right. All those claims above are indeed true to a point.
Nevertheless, I enjoyed the hell out of this game, way more than any game I had played recently.
This is because, despite its shortcomings, Neptunia has managed to create the most compelling characters I have played in a while, and I say this with complete sincerity. Each character is a caricature of anime tropes but they meshed together so well that I didn't even care. It was fun to see them interact back and forth about inane random Japanese crap while breaking the fourth wall with abundant anime/manga/game references. The plot is very basic, but I found myself continuing to play onward just to see what the characters would do next. The experience is similar to being on an anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ing forum but without the virulent hatred, if you can relate to that. There isn't really any deep character development, but I still found the characters relatable and likeable, and this had nothing to do with the "plot." Hell, you could take out all the fanservice and It'd still be great (at least for me.)
The actual gameplay portion of the game is decidedly lackluster. You will be playing recycled maps with recycled enemies using the same damn move over and over again. Luckily, the game seems to be aware of this and gives you a good deal of tools to combat the grindy experience. There are in-game mods ("plans") that do things such as weaken the enemy and massively increase the rate your super moves ("ex drive") charges. Furthermore, there is a skip-all-combat-animations button, that is a godsend for grinding exp and drops. Once you start picking up the pace, and reliably killing large exp "dangerous" enemies, the game becomes almost laughably easy. It'll take a while to get there though, so keep in mind that the early chapters are still a fairly large grind. Overall, whether you're going for 100% completion or merely completing the story as fast as possible the game caters to you either way at the expense of combat difficulty.
The soundtrack is nothing special, and somewhat grates on the ears after a while, but it does fit with the upbeat tone of the game and has an acceptable variety of tracks. The voice acting however is excellent. I only played with Japanese voices, but the voice actors did a very good job of capturing the personalities of the CPUs. The game would not be as enjoyable as it is without the quality of the voice work.
Finally, there's a good deal of fanservice if you're into that.
If you're bothered by it, I will warn that it only gets increasingly prevalent in the sequels.
In conclusion, Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a real love-it or hate-it type of game in a real love-it or hate-it series. There are some glaring gameplay issues and the humor is not for everyone.
Nevertheless, against all my better judgement, I really love this game.

Fanservice. This game is a big helping of fanservice; but who said fanservice was always a bad thing? The dialogue that goes on between the Heavy, Tycho, Max, and Strong Bad has a "real" quality to it. It's as if you really just joined a poker game with them. Fanservice aside, it's just a Texas Hold 'Em game. Only two difficulties (normal and hard) are present. However, there are a wide array of tables and card decks that are unlocked as you win games to spice things up a bit.  There are also unlockables for Team Fortress 2.  They don't have any special stats, but they do look nice. If you're not into poker or gambling, I'd pass this up. That being said, I do recommend it to anyone half-decent at card games or if you want the tf2 stuff. On a related note, the fanservice feel wears off after a little bit of gameplay (like a new car smell...strange analogy, but it works). Conversations will be repeated and it will lose that magic that captivated you in the first place. Ultimately, it's a decent poker game that's well worth the money.

FTL is rad rouge-like-like which presents you with battle and narrative scenarios which one might liken to Star Trek. A Rebellion armada is conquering the galaxy and only the sensitive inforamtion you carry aboard your ship can turn the tide of battle in favor of The Federation. FTL is broken up into a couple of different systems that provide hours of fun and experimentation. Upgrade your ship by collecting scrap from battle or from different types of encounters. Then spend that scrap on your ship systems like shields, weapons, life support, or even better doors. The combat system fits incredibly well with the theme and makes a vairety of strategies vialble for success. For example, you can use missle type weapons that by pass shileds, laser weapons that have infinte ammunition, ion cannons that disrupt systems without doing damage, automated bots that chip at enemey shileds, teleporters for boarding ships, or any combination of the previoulsy mentioned.
On top of the great mechanics, FTL provides narrative choices that are so much more than basic black and white morality calls. Do you want your crew to investigate a mysterious derlict ship or should they blow it up and collect the valuable leftover scrap? Slavers with supeiror fire power have cornered you and are demanding you turn over one of your crew members in order for you to continue unharmed. It's up to you wether or not you send that crew member to his fate or stand up to the pirates, all while the balance of the galaxy rests on your shoulders.
Customize and command your ship throughout the cosmos, meet all sorts of new alien races, and experience all the cool nuances of this awesome world created by Subset Games - you won't regret it! Play FTL: Faster Than Light!

If you've never played a Tropico game before, this is the one to get. If you already have Tropico 3 though, you might want to wait until Tropico 4's price goes down to $10 or $15, since the game is largely an expansion of Tropico 3. Still, the new elements of Tropico 4 are considerably fun.
The most noticable difference is the 'trait levelling' system. As you play through the game, you'll gain experience in your chosen traits and start levelling them up, improving their beneficial effects. This adds a lot of replay value to the game, since it encourages you to pick different traits for your avatar and try playing with them in order to improve them, rather than simply picking a single set of traits you favor early on and never changing them.
Tropico 4 also adds deeper levels of political intrigue; along with Tropico's usual internal factions and Cold War sabre-rattling between the US and USSR, there's now the European Union, China, and the Middle East.

As a point of disclosure: I did not pay for this game, I received it as a gift and was asked to provide a review when I had a chance.
I wanted to like this game more than I actually do. At first, I thought the reviews that mention the US election must be off base, but it really is the basic premise of the game, albeit in an attempt at a humour. The game has you supporting a caricature of one of the candidates for the US election and going to war on their behalf along with some subquests that allude to various rumours that had been made during the election news cycle. The presentation is tongue in cheek, but how amusing you find this will depend on your sensibilities - I had a few laughs, but spent most of the time I've played so far groaning or rolling my eyes when confronted with the storyline and dialogs such as in tavern rumours. The "Blood in November" alludes to wiping out as much of the opposing side as you can before November 8th, which was the day of the US election this year.
The overall quality of the writing isn't bad, but there are times it's very apparent that this game wasn't written by native English speakers and could likely use an edit.
As far as gameplay goes, it's the same system as Legends of Eisenwald if you've played that. You have a choice of one of three characters to use while you build up an army to fight with. The characters are a ranged attacking baroness, a melee fighting knight or a support mystic.
Combat plays out in a turn based system, but the strategy involved tends to be more about whether or not to get involved in a fight in the first place, which characters to bring with you, or which character to give equipment to more than anything else. Once you're in combat, the system boils down to prioritizing targets out of those characters you're allowed to target. You cannot move your characters independently of attacking, so ranged characters tend to have the option of firing at anyone they can see (assuming there aren't buffs or other factors that prevent a characters from being targeted), while melee characters must attack the closest enemy character and only have options if there is more than one character at the same distance. I find that the system feels fairly simplistic and not strategic which really hurts a game that relies so heavily on combat to attract you if the subject matter has fallen flat for you. I know that some players aren't bothered by the movement being part of the attack though, so your mileage may vary.
Other than that, the graphics are fairly attractive - the screenshots on the product page are pretty indicative of what you'll be looking at. I also enjoyed the music in the game and on the title screen. Unfortunately, the whole package didn't really draw me in.
If you loved Legends of Eisenwald and wanted more whatever the storyline, you'll probably like this. If you love any type of turn based combat, you may like this. If you prefer more complicated strategy or RPG mechanics or want a more involved story, this game will probably leave you feeling similar to me.

Tropico is a SimCity-like game, but much easier to pick up. You are the leader of a bananna republic island, and it's your job to make your island a strong nation. There's plenty of ways to play the game, without it being overwhelming. Play as a brutal dictator or a freedom-loving tree-hugging hippie.
The game uses cartoonish characters as your advisors who dispense information while humorously lavishing praise on you, out of fear for their jobs (or their lives)! Crack down on dissidents by personally marking them for arrest or assassination, or enforce Sensitivity Training on your police force to make them more gentle... or do both at once, with the help of your Secret Police.
Tropico's developers have learned from the previous three games and turned out something that's fun for novices and detail-oriented experts alike. Play the game casually, or with an eye for micromanaging every aspect of the island. Regardless of your choice, Tropico 4 is a pleasure to play.

Eisenwald: Blood of November is sort of a stand alone expansion to the original Legends of Eisenwald, it's a pseudo turn based strategy game much in the same vein as Heroes of Might and Magic only with much more focus on character development (eg RPG elements). One of the most defining aspects of the game is it's "oldschool" difficulty, even on the easiest difficulty I found myself confronting unbeatable enemies frequently.
In addition to focusing more on the RPG side of the game (vs Heroes of Might and Magic) Blood of November also has a striped down economy, you only have one resource (gold) and everything do you has that goal in mind. Equipment costs gold, healing your army costs gold, hiring new recruits costs gold, capturing buildings and castles gives you gold, etc. You get the point, far fewer resources to consider when coming up with a strategy.
But that's mostly just Eisenwald in general, what's different about Blood of November? To be fair, not much, the original game has a much more engaging narrative, Blood of November banks heavily on it's theme to shift units, it's a laugh at the U.S. 2016 presidential election but that veneer is very thin. It's mostly an excuse to choose a side and fight, sure you'll find some comical references in Taverns to some of the inane stuff the presidential candidates said during the race but it barely touches the gameplay. If you are worried about being bombarded by political propaganda, don't worry, this game really doesn't.
So that kinda comes down to 'do I recommend it'? With reservations, yes. I think it's a competent product for the cost and you'll get at least a dozen or so hours out of it if you don't cheat and use console commands but the original game is still superior. Sure it costs more and is a year older, but you get a much better thought-out campaign. If you ever wanted to take U.S. political sides though in a strategy game this is probably one of the few games that natively allows you to do that.
To hear more of my thoughts on the game, please check out my First Impressions "Review" after 5 hours of gameplay.

This is a fun RPG which feels a lot like a modern version of Ultima 7 (even the story starts with investigating a murder).
You have your 2 main characters whom you create, and can add other party members. There's a lot of text dialogue with NPCs to get story and proceed in quests. A lot. I like that because I like to read & learn about the world & lore of my games; however without being fully voice acted, like say ESO is, it might bog down some players' flow.
UPDATE: They added voice over lines for most quest text and interactions!
I really enjoy the turn-based, action points-based combat system. It feels like the original 90s X-COM but more streamlined (but not so streamlined distilled down to "2 actions per turn" like the new XCOM is). There's a lot of strategy available, especially if you want to play with the synergies of your party. Fun!
The elemental effects and how they interact are the "killer app" feature of Divinity: Original Sin's combat IMHO. Make it rain with one spell to get everyone wet (wet is a status, a buff/debuff), then cast an icy spell on an enemy and they'll freeze. Say the enemy has fires around, giving everyone the "warm" status (and therefore easier to get lit on fire). Now the enemy shoots a fireball and lit your character on fire -- cast that rain spell to put yourself out, and all the fires in that area.
The music is great! Fitting and melodic. Just writing this review conjures up one of the tunes in my head.
Two negative comments I have:
1. Outside of combat in free movement mode, the movement of characters, the responsiveness to changing direction or from walk-to-run speed feels slow, sluggish. It makes the characters feel like they weigh 300+ pounds. I *think* it's because the walking animations are sync'd to something. I installed an add-on to increase movement speed by +100% and the sluggish responsiveness remains.
This is NOT a game-breaker; it's minor kinematics.
2. You're nearly locked into combat once combat is triggered. You do have the option for each character to try & run away, but turning your back on an enemy confers a large bonus to the enemies' attack, so in my experience you're more likely to die than escape. Time to reload the last save!
I only point it out as a con because you have little to no direction for where to go outside of town and can very easily trigger combat with multiple enemies of significantly higher level that you. To some that's a challenge, to others it's a learning experience (followed by a reload!), and to the "hold my hand every step of the way" babies it's a point to whine about.

Beautiful RPG game, from start to finish it shows a solid gameplay, a vibrant world, and a quite interesting story with more than a few twists.
Sound design is jaw-dropping, and I had to download the soundtrack after completing the game, it's epic a lá Final Fantasy. Regarding the sound FX of the world, everything fits, a monster yapping, a jump, the wind, it all connects and doesn't feel out of place nor breaks the immension, this game, like Ori, are excellent in this regard, probably the bests. Quality.
Graphically speaking, the game looks magnificent, and everytime you reach a new place, you find yourself looking at every place of the screen, mindblowing designs and drawings that are taken out of a fairy tale, beautiful. The magic of the game is greatly resembled too, and it's one of the strongest points in the game.
The amount of hours might look short for an RPG, but it's not really short. Let me explain: The game doesn't drag on and there's no needed grind to proceed, some battles are indeed hard but can be overtaken by strategy, the story from start to finish feels good, like reading a book, there's no stupid fillers, no "lets walk for 25 mins doing nothing". It's all fun from start to finish, and at the end you feel realized and full because it doesn't leave you wanting for more like some other games, it's a perfect time.
Now, regarding the gameplay, it's a turn-based fighting RPG, which is fast, there's no long animations that you can't wait for them to end (Final Fantasy X, anyone?), it's really fun thanks to constantly being in motion, you will be using characters in the fight that you can swap at any time, there are quite a few characters. They of course level up, and you'll have to see what's the best course of action regarding their skills. I want to mention that it's very fun to move as the protagonist too, specially with the amount of secrets that are everywhere! (And you will have to backtrack if you want some sweet secrets ;) ) nothing falls short in the gameplay, except maybe a bigger variety of movements/actions in the fights.
Story: Fairy tale. You will feel like you're playing a tale, it's a beautiful story and quite touching in my opinion, I won't spoil a single thing.
Overall, the game is a great time guaranteed for RPG players, you can't really go wrong with this game.

I recommend you try the game out for free for 7 days from Kakao Games's website before judging if you should play this yourself.
This game is heavily exploration based. Every unique NPC you talk to, every single monster, every new place you discover, they all contribute toward your overall energy, which you can spend to do the various skills around the game. There is no fast travel, and the various transportations around the game, like ships, take real time to get anywhere. I took a ship from Epheria to Altinova, because I was curious and saw the ship roll in - I was waiting for a good 30-40 minutes, although the novelty of adventure didn't wear off for me.
The game has one of the best character creators I've seen, best one in any MMO by far. The facemorphing can make your characters unique, if you do it yourself. Or you can simply see what others have done through the online photobook thing and apply what they did to yours, just to see. However the game has genderlocked classes, a few of which have similar counterparts with the other sex, for example Musa and Meahwa. And I don't think I've ever heard of any male Valkyries hah.
Each class does feel unique enough to not worry about it too much, in my opinion. The combat is combo focused, but kinda spammy. It's actually similar to a brawler, in fact, there is one class that is strictly hand to hand.
The game rewards you for making alts since there is no requirements on armor or weapons, and even energy and contribution points are shared between all of them, but energy recharges independently on each character, thankfully. One could also strategically place their alts and switch between them with a 10 second interval, if say, a world boss shows up and your character isnt anywhere near it but your alt is.
This game is also very VERY grindy, through the various lifeskills or your characters' fitness. Thankfully the game encourages afk play quite a bit. Can't afk combat though.
All in all, it is a very unique MMO. I typically don't enjoy them too much, but this one hooked me. Like I said before, I recommend trying before putting money towards it. But this gets my thumbs up.

This is one of those games I wish I hadn't left sitting on my wish list for so long.  The artwork is excellent, and parts of it are reminiscient of the Bayeux Tapestry. The music is top drawer and evocitive of the times past (though it is by no means historically accurate, as the game is fantasy, and is located "in a place far, far away and long, long ago"). I did think I heard some ancient instruments (such as a cornetto, aka a zink) but I saw no reference in the credits to anyone playing one). The writing isn't Dickens or Dostoyevsky, but as game story lines go it's top notch. It gives me hope that someday a game will be made where the art compares favorably to Rembrandt or Vangough, the music to Handel or Beethoven, and the writing to the afore mentioned authors. Such colaborative efforts are few and far between though, so I won't hold my breath waiting for it.
All that aside, this is an excellent game worth both the money, and the extra play-through or two that it takes to get all the achevements.

Basically an interactive visualizer for your music. It's actually pretty easy when you get the hang of it (compared to other shooters I mean) but that isn't a bad thing. It's more of a casual game despite its intense visuals, and sometimes that's exactly what you need.
The only major downside IMO is that you can't turn off the effects. I like explosions and stuff but some of the effects are unnecessary, such as debris having strobe lights too, making it somewhat confusing especially at higher difficulties when you blast a lot of things at a time. If only pieces of an asteroid or broken ship didn't blink, the effects would've been perfectly fine with me.
Notes:
- The more complicated your song, the harder it gets really. So if you have songs that shift around between low and high intensity sections (progressive rock/metal, trance, many orchestral pieces, etc.), it tends to get harder because the power if your guns and the enemies slow down but continuously spawn, which allows them to build up. After that low intensity part if it suddenly gets a high intensity part, you'll likely be facing a lot of explosions.
- It doesn't like non-English song/file/folder names, but it'll read the file properly. It just displays as gibberish (ASCII) in-game. Minor issue but it makes it harder to find certain songs (unless you rename them, which I don't want to do) especially if most of your music is non-English. I have to wait for the song to play in preview to figure out what it is.
All in all a good time waster and eye strainer. If you were just gonna chill and listen to your music anyway, do it with this game instead so you get to sharpen your reflexes, eye-to-hand coordination and whatnot while you're at it.

Despite an interesting narrative approach I would have liked to have seen pan out, I was unable to finish the cartel because of dissatisfying gameplay mechanics and meaningless sidequests. While I'll concede that Call of Juarez has been the closest PC port you'll get to Red Dead Redemption in terms of great level design, environments, and characters, this is the only installation in the franchise that fails to get it right. Watch the extra credits video and move on to Gunslinger.
From what I wiki'd, the redeeming factor and the reason for the mixed reviews was how elaborate the story seemed. The story surrounds three characters with unique backstories that tie into the natural enemies of the teamed-up trio of crimefighters – the cartel, and the FBI that hired them. No matter which character you pick, their roles in each level differ slightly. You begin to learn more about their ulterior motives, and it all come to a head towards the end of the game in what would seem to be an epic climax were it not for how non-epic the rest of the game is.
The game kills itself on not knowing their own settings, dull design, and just plain gameplay that shouldn't've passed by 2011 FPS standards. The inaccuracy of Mexicans stealing women from the US to send back to Mexico. The achievement for killing a bunch of black people. The countless black henchmen in the middle of a mexican desert. Maybe we can account this to overlooked minor details, since the devs publicly stated that the game was rushed, and largely incomplete due to strict deadlines.
While I know that it's true, there's not much polishing you could do. Incentives to do side quests and "rank up" only meant getting weapons you could easily get throughout the progression of a level. Even then, most weapons didn't have a distinctive feel to them, and felt largely the same. Actual levels had too many recycled assets and all too linear-feeling levels. Combat and combat scenarios were also stale (likely due to poor integration of environments), and they ditched their great cover system that they used in the previous entry.
It's just unfortunate – the sheer concept of having a game that covers a fascinating part of international crime is something that, if done moderately well, could turn heads and open wallets. And the story was there. So there that you should YouTube it. But the cat doodie in the cornflakes is the repetitiveness of the levels, redundancy of the incentives, and lacklustre combat. It surrounds the gem of a story like a fat of liquid horse tranquilizer, which sleeps anyone who makes it past character selection.

Campaign looks okay to me but the multiplayer sucks. Grey Goo resembles another RTS called Etherium but it's just not as interesting. Some of the ideas, like teleportation, are kind of badly executed in Grey Goo. You can find similar ideas in Starcraft 2 but better executed to suit how the user plays the game.
I completed the Beta and Human campaigns but the gameplay just wasn't engaging enough to make me want to play more. I uninstalled just before the Grey Goo campaign.
PROS
1. Campaign looks Good
I like the single player map, looks really good. Very well designed.
2. Marketing
I've heard of Grey Goo.
3. Tree Cover
Good to hide in. Like the way you can attack from cover, this is the part that resembles Etherium.
4. Graphics ***
Top notch. These are the best that I've seen out of most the RTS games that I have played. E.g. Lucy Tang, the commander of the Human faction just looks so real.
CONS
1. Multiplayer
Every single race is the same, they just have different skins. Units are basically divided into Light, Heavy, Air, Stealth and Ultimate.
2. Complex Building Puzzles
Every race has their own jigsaw puzzle to figure out.
a. Goo
You need Mother Goos to slime their way to the resource pool and grow fat. After growing fat, they split like an amoeba and form Small/Large Proteans, which have to be split into the actual units. This notion is really ridiculous.
b. Beta
Aliens in this game. Absolutely horrible, you have to attach attachments to Factories just to build the required units, wasting a ridiculous amount of time
c. Humans
Just like the Beta with even more complex building jigsaws as you have to lay power lines that cost resources. In this game, the humans resemble an alien race instead. Their buildings can teleport but it's rubbish since you have to connect them to a power conduit.
3. Multiple Annoying Steps
You have to do so many tiny steps to achieve your objective that it's no longer fun. Here are a few examples.
a. Building High Tier Units
For every factory, you have to add attachments. You have 4 to choose from, Air, Tank, Stealth and Artillery. In order to build certain units, you have to add combinations like Tank and Artillery REPEATEDLY FOR EVERY NEW FACTORY. You can share certain upgrades for the Humans by building an upgrade in between 2 factories but that's only possible if you build a conduit long enough to build them side by side.
b. Beta Defenses
Beta's have some sort of garrisoning procedure where their units climb onto walls/platforms to shoot from. Instead of building a defense turret, you have to first build a wall, then build a unit, then get him to jump on it. What's worse is that each factory only produces 1 unit and each wall tower only garrisons 1 unit.
c. Goo Spawning
You have to keep splitting up the Small/Large Goos or feed them to the Protean Purger. What the hell is this?
4. Short Campaign
Way to short
5. Repairing
It is so annoying to have to click and repair each individual item.
6. Air Units Reloading and Landing Deck
Ammunition reloading? You also need a landing deck to keep the air units in. This is reminiscent of Command and Conquer's flaws. Also, the air units in this game are horribly underpowered.
7. Extractors and Vision
In order to build an Extractor on a Catalyst Pool, you actually need vision of the pool. Somehow, the developers designed the Refinery's vision to be just out of reach of the pool. Thus, forcing one to send 1 unit just to scout.
8. Extractor Resource Rate
Depending on exact location of where you place your Extractor, you will get +8/+10/+13 resource rate and this is all a matter of placing your cursor 1 milimetre to the left or right. This is also linked to point 7.

A game that tells the tale of four ancient goddesses engaged in an eternal divine war for control of the world itself, and most importantly which video game console is the best, how piracy will destroy the world, and how close girls can get before it's no longer subtext.
The game is very competent, without anything that particularly lacks or stands out. The story really just boils down to "what if game companies and consoles were anime ladies", but the writing is amusing and the little jokes and nods towards the companies (the Wii girl has incredible defenses, the Xbox wears a red ring, etc.) are a nice touch. The battle system revolves around setting up combos, choosing from weak attacks that raise a meter for powerful attacks, attacks that reduce the enemy's guard, or high HP damage above all else.
The world, art, and locations look very pretty, and the music is enjoyable, but there could stand to be more variety and many dungeons are "The dungeon from before but with an extra path and area added". The enemies are standard RPG fare, with the occasional anime joke or game parody such as Mario's pipes or Pac-Man ghosts. The game also boasts crafting recipes that allow you to add items to the shops, access new dungeons, or change the items and enemies that can be found within a dungeon.
The only real concerns with the game are the grinding and fanservice. With the former, you'll often reach a boss and find yourself suddenly outgunned, and needing to go back until you've gained a few levels, with one early boss apparently enough to send people to forums, convinced that victory is impossible. Regarding fanservice, most early introductions include cutscenes where the only animation is jiggling, and certain outfits and attacks will mean upskirt city. That said, if you're looking at this game, it's probably a selling point for you.
If you play, keep in mind that the "camera reset" button lets you skip attack animations.

Tropico is a SimCity-like game, but much easier to pick up. You are the leader of a bananna republic island, and it's your job to make your island a strong nation. There's plenty of ways to play the game, without it being overwhelming. Play as a brutal dictator or a freedom-loving tree-hugging hippie.
The game uses cartoonish characters as your advisors who dispense information while humorously lavishing praise on you, out of fear for their jobs (or their lives)! Crack down on dissidents by personally marking them for arrest or assassination, or enforce Sensitivity Training on your police force to make them more gentle... or do both at once, with the help of your Secret Police.
Tropico's developers have learned from the previous three games and turned out something that's fun for novices and detail-oriented experts alike. Play the game casually, or with an eye for micromanaging every aspect of the island. Regardless of your choice, Tropico 4 is a pleasure to play.

Team Reptile's Lethal League is a shining example of one game designs most treasured principles. It's easy to play but difficult to master. The game isn't very complicated at first glance, just hit or ricochet the ball in the players direction to take a stock off their health bar. In this simple concept is a plethora of tactics and variables in player choice which propel this seemingly casual plinker into competitve territories.
What makes Lethal League easy to pick up might be it's familiarity. It borrows heavily from Super Smash Brothers (Melee's font makes an appearence :P), Street Fighter and Pong. It then takes a lot of these already familiar mechanics and visuals to blend an unique concoction of the "fighting-party-sport genre".
One aspect I personally love about this game is it's pick up and play nature. Anytime I'm bored or waiting for something, I jump onto Lethal League just for some viseral entertainment
Along with it's killer fun and rewarding gameplay, comes a stylish Japanese inspired graffiti artstyle that's highly remincent to SEGA's Jet Set Radio series. This isn't without mention of the awesome and memorable soundtrack ranging from hip-hop flavored techno tunes to EDM.
Can't emphasis how amazing this game is enough. Please consider getting it if you have the spare cash.

There are a set of characters, each with a unique move set, and their sole method of attack is manipulating a ball so that it hits their opponent. Every hit of the ball makes it faster and, thus, harder to avoid or hit back. Each player has a set of lives, one of which is lost each time they are knocked out by the ball. Once your life counter hits zero, you’re out, until only one player (or team) remains.

I first watched on YouTube, as a guy in Slovenia played through it.  I still love and play the original X-Com games from the 1990s, so I wanted to see the new version.  I was a little disappointed to find out that the largest ground force the game allows is 6 soldiers.  But I understand that to have the level of 3D graphics and framework, something had to give.  And I enjoyed watching the game so much that I bought it on sale, even before I had a computer that would run it.
I've since been able to run the game on a monster system with 16 GB of RAM, and on my laptop which has only an AMD Turion X2, and only the minimum 4GB of RAM.  On my laptop, the game loads slower, but otherwise isn't significantly slower, for me.  On my laptop, I have to run it windowed, with all graphics settings on Low, but it runs, and I'm still having fun.  I've been playing for months in real time.  In saved games, I'm past number 2200.  And I haven't tried any of the DlC, as far as I know, and have yet to try Enemy Within.  I'll get to it eventually.
If you like turn-based tactical games, with some research and building elements, I think you should at least check out some YouTube video of game play.  The old Time Unit system has been replaced with two actions that can be: move-then-shoot; for certain level-dependent options, shoot-then-move-or-shoot-again; or double-move.  I don't miss calculating TUs in my head.
I hope you all give it a look.
